title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
text: > **Source:** Response 1 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-01.txt`, lines 1–1213) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch01-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> Let's start from **zero at the conceptual level**, but I’ll move quickly where you already have CS knowledge. The goal of this response is to build the mental model for the entire field. By the end, you should understand **what Cloud and DevOps actually mean, why companies use them, and how all the technologies we'll learn fit together.** ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 1. First: What problem are Cloud & DevOps solving?
text: Imagine you've built a backend: ```text React/Next.js ↓ Node.js + TypeScript API ↓ PostgreSQL ``` It works perfectly on your laptop. But now you have 100,000 users. Your laptop obviously can't be the production server. You need: - computers to run your application - networking - storage - databases - security - backups - monitoring - scaling - deployment - reliability Traditionally, a company might buy physical servers: ```text Company │ ├── Physical servers ├── Network equipment ├── Storage ├── Firewalls ├── Database servers └── Data center ``` That's expensive and difficult to manage. **Cloud computing** changes this model. Instead of buying and maintaining all the infrastructure yourself, you can rent computing resources from cloud providers such as AWS. ```text Your Application ↓ AWS ↓ ┌─────┼─────────┐ EC2 S3 RDS ``` You can provision infrastructure when you need it and scale it as demand changes. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 2. What exactly is Cloud Computing?
text: A simple definition: > **Cloud computing means using computing resources over a network instead of owning and managing all the physical infrastructure yourself.** These resources can include: - Compute - Storage - Databases - Networking - Security - Messaging - AI/ML services - Monitoring - Serverless functions For example: Instead of buying a server: ```text Buy server ↓ Install OS ↓ Configure network ↓ Maintain hardware ↓ Replace failed hardware ``` You can use AWS: ```text AWS ↓ Create EC2 instance ↓ Deploy application ``` ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 3. Why Cloud?
text: Suppose your application normally gets: ```text 1,000 requests/minute ``` But during a sale: ```text 100,000 requests/minute ``` You don't want to permanently buy enough hardware for 100,000 requests if you only need it occasionally. Cloud allows you to dynamically provision resources. ```text Normal traffic ↓ 2 servers High traffic ↓ 10 servers Traffic decreases ↓ 2 servers ``` This leads to some fundamental cloud concepts. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 4. Scalability
text: **Scalability = ability of a system to handle increasing workload by adding resources.** There are two major ways.

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Vertical scaling
text: Make one machine more powerful. ```text Before: CPU: 2 cores RAM: 4 GB ↓ After: CPU: 16 cores RAM: 64 GB ``` This is called: > **Scale Up** ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Horizontal scaling
text: Add more machines. ```text Load Balancer / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ Server Server Server ``` This is: > **Scale Out** Horizontal scaling is extremely important in distributed systems. You'll see it repeatedly in: - AWS - Docker - Kubernetes - Load balancing - System design ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 5. Elasticity
text: Don't confuse **scalability** and **elasticity**.

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Scalability
text: Can the system handle growth?

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Elasticity
text: Can the system **automatically adjust resources according to demand**? For example: ```text Traffic ↓ 2 instances Traffic increases ↓ 4 instances Traffic increases ↓ 8 instances Traffic decreases ↓ 3 instances Traffic decreases ↓ 2 instances ``` That's elasticity. Cloud platforms are particularly useful because they make this kind of dynamic resource management possible. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 6. Availability
text: Suppose you have one server: ```text Users ↓ Server ``` If that server dies: ```text Users ↓ 💥 Server DEAD ``` Your application is unavailable. So we introduce redundancy: ```text Load Balancer / \ ↓ ↓ Server A Server B ``` If A dies: ```text Load Balancer ↓ Server B ``` Users can continue using the application. This is **High Availability (HA).** ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 7. Reliability vs Availability
text: These are related but not identical.

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Availability
text: > Is the system accessible when users need it?

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Reliability
text: > Does the system consistently perform correctly over time? A system can technically be available but still unreliable. Example: ```text API responds but 50% of requests return incorrect results ``` It's available, but not reliable. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 8. Fault Tolerance
text: A fault-tolerant system continues operating even when some components fail. Example: ```text Load Balancer / \ ↓ ↓ Server A Server B ❌ FAILED ↓ Users ``` The system tolerates the failure of Server A. Cloud architectures often use redundancy to achieve this. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 9. Disaster Recovery
text: Now imagine something much bigger happens. For example: ```text Entire AWS Region ↓ 💥 ``` You need a way to recover. That's **Disaster Recovery (DR).** You might maintain infrastructure in another region: ```text Users ↓ Region A │ Database │ Replication ↓ Region B ``` If Region A becomes unavailable, you can recover in Region B. Two important DR concepts:

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: RTO — Recovery Time Objective
text: > How quickly must the system be restored? Example: ```text RTO = 1 hour ``` Means the business targets restoring service within one hour.

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: RPO — Recovery Point Objective
text: > How much data loss can the business tolerate? Example: ```text RPO = 5 minutes ``` Means the business targets losing no more than about five minutes of data in a disaster. We'll revisit these when discussing AWS architecture. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 10. Cloud Service Models
text: You'll hear these constantly: ```text IaaS PaaS SaaS ``` Let's make them intuitive. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service
text: You rent infrastructure. Example: **AWS EC2** AWS gives you: ```text Physical hardware Virtualization Networking Data center ``` You manage: ```text OS Runtime Application Dependencies ``` Think: > **"Give me a computer."** ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: PaaS — Platform as a Service
text: The provider manages more of the infrastructure/platform. Think: > **"Give me a platform where I can run my application."** You focus more on your application instead of managing the server. Examples include various managed application platforms. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: SaaS — Software as a Service
text: You simply use the finished software. Examples: - Gmail - Google Docs - Slack Think: > **"I just want to use the software."** ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: The spectrum
text: ```text More control Less control IaaS ───────── PaaS ───────── SaaS │ │ │ EC2 App Platform Gmail ``` As you move toward SaaS, the provider manages more. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Public Cloud
text: Infrastructure provided by companies such as: - AWS - Microsoft Azure - Google Cloud Multiple customers use the provider's infrastructure, with isolation between them. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Private Cloud
text: Cloud infrastructure dedicated to one organization. Often used when organizations need specific control or regulatory arrangements. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Hybrid Cloud
text: Combination: ```text Private infrastructure + Public cloud ``` For example: ```text Company Data Center ↕ VPN ↕ AWS ``` ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 12. What is a Cloud Region?
text: A **Region** is a geographic area containing cloud infrastructure. For example, AWS has regions around the world. You might deploy your application to an Indian region for users primarily located in India. Conceptually: ```text AWS │ ├── Region A │ ├── AZ1 │ ├── AZ2 │ └── AZ3 │ ├── Region B │ ├── AZ1 │ ├── AZ2 │ └── AZ3 ``` ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 13. What is an Availability Zone?
text: An **Availability Zone (AZ)** is an isolated infrastructure location within a region. Suppose: ```text AWS Region │ ├── AZ-A │ ├── AZ-B │ └── AZ-C ``` Instead of putting your entire application in one AZ: ```text ALB │ AZ-A EC2 ``` you can distribute it: ```text ALB / \ ↓ ↓ AZ-A AZ-B EC2 EC2 ``` If one AZ has a failure, the other can continue serving traffic. This is a fundamental AWS architecture concept. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 14. Now: What is DevOps?
text: Cloud and DevOps are related, but they're **not the same thing**. Cloud is primarily about: > **Infrastructure and services.** DevOps is primarily about: > **How development and operations teams build, test, deploy, and operate software together efficiently and reliably.** Traditional workflow: ```text Developer ↓ Writes code ↓ "Throw it over the wall" ↓ Operations ↓ Deploy manually ``` This creates friction. DevOps tries to create a continuous process: ```text Code ↓ Build ↓ Test ↓ Package ↓ Deploy ↓ Monitor ↓ Improve ↖──────────┘ ``` ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 15. CI/CD
text: This is one of the most important DevOps concepts.

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: CI — Continuous Integration
text: Developers frequently integrate code into a shared repository. A CI pipeline can automatically: ```text Git Push ↓ Install dependencies ↓ Lint ↓ Build ↓ Run tests ↓ Generate artifact ``` For example: ```yaml name: CI on: [push] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npm ci - run: npm run lint - run: npm test - run: npm run build ``` Don't worry about understanding every line yet. **[Chapter 6](../03-cicd-gitops/ch06-cicd-github-actions.md) will go deep into this.** The important idea now is: > **Every code change can automatically be checked.** ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 16. Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
text: These terms are often confused.

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Continuous Delivery
text: Code is automatically built and prepared for deployment. But production deployment may require approval. ```text Code ↓ Build ↓ Test ↓ Ready for production ↓ Manual approval ↓ Production ```

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Continuous Deployment
text: Deployment to production happens automatically after the pipeline passes. ```text Code ↓ Build ↓ Test ↓ Production ``` ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 17. What is DevSecOps?
text: Security shouldn't be something you think about only at the end. Traditional: ```text Develop ↓ Test ↓ Deploy ↓ Security ``` DevSecOps: ```text Security ↓ Throughout the entire lifecycle ``` Examples: - dependency scanning - secret detection - container scanning - IAM - vulnerability scanning - security testing - infrastructure security We'll incorporate this into AWS/Docker/CI/CD rather than making it an enormous separate subject. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 18. What is Infrastructure as Code?
text: Imagine you manually create: - VPC - subnets - EC2 - security groups - load balancer - RDS through the AWS Console. That's difficult to reproduce. Instead, describe infrastructure using code. For example, Terraform: ```hcl resource "aws_instance" "app" { ami = "ami-example" instance_type = "t3.micro" } ``` Now infrastructure can be: ```text Code ↓ Review ↓ Version control ↓ Terraform ↓ AWS infrastructure ``` That's **Infrastructure as Code (IaC).** We'll learn Terraform properly later. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 19. What are Containers?
text: Suppose your Node.js application needs: ```text Node.js 22 npm dependencies environment variables system libraries application code ``` It works on your machine. But another machine may have: ```text Node.js 20 different libraries different OS configuration ``` and your application may behave differently. A container packages the application and its dependencies into a standardized environment. ```text ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ Container │ │ │ │ Node.js │ │ Dependencies │ │ Application │ └──────────────────────────┘ ``` Docker is the technology we'll use to learn this deeply. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 20. Containers vs Virtual Machines
text: A simplified picture:

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: VM
text: ```text Physical Machine ↓ Hypervisor / \ VM VM │ │ OS OS │ │ App App ``` Each VM includes its own guest operating system.

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Containers
text: ```text Physical Machine ↓ Container Runtime / | \ Container Container Container \ | / Host OS ``` Containers are generally more lightweight because they share the host kernel. We'll explore the actual mechanics in the Docker responses. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 21. What is Serverless?
text: Serverless doesn't mean: > "There are no servers." There **are** servers. It means: > **You don't manage the underlying servers directly.** For example, AWS Lambda: ```text HTTP Request ↓ API Gateway ↓ Lambda ↓ Your Function ``` You provide the function: ```javascript export const handler = async (event) => { return { statusCode: 200, body: "Hello World" }; }; ``` AWS handles much of the underlying infrastructure. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 22. What is SRE?
text: **Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)** is an engineering approach to operating reliable production systems. It focuses on things like: - reliability - availability - latency - monitoring - incident response - automation - capacity - error budgets You'll encounter:

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: SLA
text: A commitment/expectation around service availability or performance.

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: SLI
text: A measurement. Example: ```text Successful requests / Total requests ```

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: SLO
text: A target for that measurement. Example: ```text 99.9% successful requests ``` Don't worry about memorizing these yet—we'll revisit them in the observability response. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 23. Putting Cloud + DevOps Together
text: Now we can connect everything. Imagine your TypeScript backend.

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Development
text: ```text Developer ↓ GitHub ```

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: CI/CD
text: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Test ↓ Build ↓ Docker Image ```

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Infrastructure
text: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS ```

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Deployment
text: ```text Docker ↓ EC2 / Kubernetes ```

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Application infrastructure
text: ```text Internet │ Route53 │ CloudFront │ ALB / \ EC2 EC2 │ │ Docker Docker \ / Node API / | \ / | \ Redis RDS S3 ```

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Operations
text: ```text Application ↓ CloudWatch ↓ Metrics / Logs / Alerts ``` And the entire lifecycle becomes: ```text ┌───────────────┐ │ GitHub │ └───────┬───────┘ ↓ CI ↓ Build + Test ↓ Docker Image ↓ CD ↓ AWS / Kubernetes ↓ Application ↓ Logs + Metrics ↓ Monitoring ↓ Improvement │ └────→ Git ``` **That is the big picture of Cloud + DevOps.** ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: 24. Technologies We'll Learn
text: Now you should understand why these technologies exist: | Technology | Main purpose | |---|---| | **Linux** | Operating system/environment | | **Bash** | Automation/scripting | | **Git** | Version control | | **GitHub** | Code collaboration | | **Docker** | Containerization | | **AWS** | Cloud infrastructure/services | | **EC2** | Compute | | **S3** | Object storage | | **RDS** | Managed databases | | **VPC** | Cloud networking | | **ALB** | Load balancing | | **Lambda** | Serverless compute | | **SQS/SNS** | Messaging | | **Route 53** | DNS | | **CloudFront** | CDN | | **CloudWatch** | Monitoring | | **GitHub Actions** | CI/CD | | **Kubernetes** | Container orchestration | | **Terraform** | Infrastructure as Code | | **Prometheus/Grafana** | Monitoring/visualization | | **OpenTelemetry** | Observability | | **Helm** | Kubernetes package management | And: | Technology | Our depth | |---|---| | GitOps | Concept + architecture | | ArgoCD | Interview-level understanding | | Jenkins | Concept/comparison | | Ansible | Concept + basic usage | | Service Mesh | Awareness | ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: The Mental Model You Should Leave With
text: Don't memorize 20 definitions. Remember this: ```text CLOUD │ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Compute Storage Networking │ │ │ EC2 S3 VPC ECS EBS ALB Lambda RDS Route53 │ AWS │ ↓ DEVOPS │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Git CI/CD Docker │ ↓ Kubernetes │ ↓ Terraform │ ↓ Observability ``` And underneath all of it: ```text Linux + Networking + Security ``` Those are the foundations. ---

title: Chapter 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Quick Self-Test
text: Before moving to [Chapter 2](ch02-linux.md), try answering these **without looking back**: 1. What problem does cloud computing solve? 2. Scalability vs elasticity? 3. Horizontal vs vertical scaling? 4. High availability vs fault tolerance? 5. RTO vs RPO? 6. IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS? 7. Region vs Availability Zone? 8. Cloud vs DevOps? 9. CI vs CD? 10. Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment? 11. Why do we use containers? 12. Containers vs VMs? 13. What does Infrastructure as Code mean? 14. What is serverless? 15. What problem does DevOps ultimately try to improve? If you can explain these **in your own words**, you're ready. <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** [Chapter 2: Linux for Cloud & DevOps](ch02-linux.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch01-revision.md)

title: Revision 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Chapter 1 — Revision Sheet: Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/01-foundations/ch01-cloud-devops-fundamentals.md). Read the chapter first; use this sheet to revise.

title: Revision 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: The one-paragraph mental model
text: Cloud = renting compute, storage, networking and managed services over a network instead of owning hardware. DevOps = the practices (CI/CD, IaC, containers, monitoring) that let one team build, test, ship and operate software continuously. Cloud supplies the *infrastructure*; DevOps supplies the *process and automation*. Underneath both: **Linux + networking + security**.

title: Revision 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Terms that are easy to confuse
text: | Pair | Difference | |---|---| | Scalability vs Elasticity | Scalability = *can* it handle growth by adding resources. Elasticity = it *automatically* grows **and shrinks** with demand. | | Vertical vs Horizontal scaling | Vertical (scale **up**) = bigger machine. Horizontal (scale **out**) = more machines behind a load balancer. | | Availability vs Reliability | Availability = reachable when needed. Reliability = behaves *correctly* consistently. An API that answers fast with wrong data is available but not reliable. | | High availability vs Fault tolerance | HA = redundancy so the service stays up. Fault tolerance = the system keeps *operating correctly* through component failure (user sees nothing). | | RTO vs RPO | RTO = how fast must service be restored (time). RPO = how much data loss is tolerable (time-window of data). | | IaaS / PaaS / SaaS | IaaS = "give me a computer" (EC2). PaaS = "give me a platform to run my app". SaaS = "I just use the software" (Gmail). Control decreases left → right. | | Public / Private / Hybrid | Shared provider infra / dedicated to one org / both connected (e.g. VPN). | | Region vs AZ | Region = geographic area. AZ = isolated infrastructure location *inside* a region. Spread across AZs for HA, across regions for DR. | | Continuous Delivery vs Deployment | Delivery = always *ready* to release, a human approves. Deployment = auto-released to production if pipeline passes. | | Container vs VM | VM = own guest OS on a hypervisor. Container = shares the host kernel → lighter. | | SLI / SLO / SLA | SLI = measurement (successful / total requests). SLO = target (99.9%). SLA = external commitment. |

title: Revision 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Key flows to be able to draw
text: 1. Developer → GitHub → CI (lint, build, test) → Docker image → CD → AWS/Kubernetes → Logs + Metrics → Monitoring → Improvement → back to Git. 2. Internet → Route 53 → CloudFront → ALB → EC2 (Docker) in two AZs → Redis / RDS / S3. 3. Terraform code → review → version control → `terraform` → AWS infrastructure.

title: Revision 1 — Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals
heading: Interview questions (from the chapter's self-test, with short answers)
text: 1. *What problem does cloud solve?* Owning/maintaining/over-provisioning hardware; cloud lets you rent resources on demand. 2. *Scalability vs elasticity?* See table. 3. *Horizontal vs vertical?* See table. 4. *HA vs fault tolerance?* See table. 5. *RTO vs RPO?* See table. 6. *IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS?* See table. 7. *Region vs AZ?* See table. 8. *Cloud vs DevOps?* Cloud = infrastructure and services; DevOps = how teams build/test/deploy/operate together. 9. *CI vs CD?* CI = frequent integration with automated checks; CD = delivery/deployment automation. 10. *Delivery vs Deployment?* Manual approval gate vs fully automatic. 11. *Why containers?* Same packaged environment everywhere ("works on my machine" fix). 12. *Containers vs VMs?* Shared kernel vs separate guest OS. 13. *What is IaC?* Describing infrastructure in versioned, reviewable code (Terraform). 14. *What is serverless?* Servers exist, you don't manage them (AWS Lambda). 15. *What does DevOps improve?* The friction and delay between writing code and running it reliably in production. <!-- NAV --> --- [Full chapter 1](../docs/01-foundations/ch01-cloud-devops-fundamentals.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 2](ch02-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
text: > **Source:** Response 2 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-02.txt`, lines 7–1589) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch02-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> Linux is one of the most important foundations for Cloud and DevOps. Why? Because eventually you'll encounter things like: ```text AWS EC2 ↓ Linux Server ↓ Docker ↓ Node.js ↓ Your Application ``` If something breaks, you need to understand the Linux system underneath it. Our goal here is not to become a Linux kernel developer. It's to become someone who can **comfortably operate, understand, deploy, and troubleshoot applications on Linux servers.** ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 1. What is Linux?
text: Linux is an **operating-system kernel**. Strictly speaking: > Linux itself is the kernel; distributions such as Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, and Amazon Linux package the kernel with utilities and software to form a usable operating system. For practical purposes, you'll often hear people simply say "Linux OS." Examples: - Ubuntu - Debian - Fedora - Arch - Amazon Linux - RHEL For our Cloud/DevOps learning, **Ubuntu-style Linux commands** will be the primary examples because they're widely encountered and easy to transfer to other distributions. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 2. Why Linux is so important in Cloud
text: A cloud server is still a computer. For example, an AWS EC2 instance might look like: ```text AWS │ └── EC2 │ └── Ubuntu Linux │ ├── Node.js ├── Docker ├── Nginx └── Your application ``` When you SSH into that server: ```bash ssh ubuntu@<server-ip> ``` you're interacting with Linux. You'll need to know: ```text Files Processes Users Permissions Networking Services Logs Packages Environment variables Resources ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 3. Linux Architecture
text: A simplified view: ```text ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Applications │ │ Node.js | Docker | Nginx | ...│ ├───────────────────────────────┤ │ System Utilities │ │ bash | ls | ps | systemctl │ ├───────────────────────────────┤ │ Kernel │ │ Process | Memory | Network │ │ Filesystem | Drivers │ ├───────────────────────────────┤ │ Hardware │ │ CPU | RAM | Disk | Network │ └───────────────────────────────┘ ``` The **kernel** is the core component. It manages things such as: - CPU - memory - processes - filesystems - networking - hardware - system calls Applications don't normally directly control hardware. They interact with the kernel. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 4. Terminal and Shell
text: When you open something like: ```text Terminal ``` you interact with a **shell**. A common shell is: ```text bash ``` For example: ```bash ls ``` You type a command into Bash. Conceptually: ```text You ↓ Terminal ↓ Bash ↓ Linux system ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 5. Your First Commands
text: Let's start with navigation.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `pwd`
text: Print working directory: ```bash pwd ``` Example: ```text /home/rachit ``` Meaning: > "Where am I?" ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `ls`
text: List files: ```bash ls ``` More useful: ```bash ls -la ``` - `-l` → detailed listing - `-a` → include hidden files ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `cd`
text: Change directory: ```bash cd /home ``` Go up: ```bash cd .. ``` Go home: ```bash cd ~ ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 6. Linux Filesystem
text: Linux has a tree-like filesystem. ```text / ├── bin ├── boot ├── dev ├── etc ├── home │ └── rachit ├── opt ├── proc ├── root ├── tmp ├── usr └── var ``` `/` is the root of the filesystem. Don't confuse: ```text / ``` with: ```text /root ``` `/` = filesystem root. `/root` = home directory of the root user. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 7. Important Directories
text: You don't need to memorize every Linux directory, but these matter for DevOps.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `/home`
text: Regular users' home directories. ```text /home/rachit ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `/root`
text: Root user's home directory.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `/etc`
text: System configuration. For example: ```text /etc/ssh/ /etc/nginx/ /etc/hosts ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `/var`
text: Frequently changing data. Important: ```text /var/log ``` contains logs.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `/tmp`
text: Temporary files.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `/usr`
text: Many user-space programs and libraries.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `/opt`
text: Often used for optional/additional software.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `/dev`
text: Device files.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: `/proc`
text: Virtual filesystem exposing information about processes and the kernel. We'll use `/proc` later for troubleshooting. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 8. Creating Files and Directories
text: Create a directory: ```bash mkdir project ``` Enter it: ```bash cd project ``` Create a file: ```bash touch app.txt ``` Write: ```bash echo "Hello Linux" > app.txt ``` Read: ```bash cat app.txt ``` Output: ```text Hello Linux ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 9. `>` vs `>>`
text: This is a small thing that becomes very useful.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
text: Overwrite: ```bash echo "Hello" > file.txt ``` Then: ```bash echo "World" > file.txt ``` The file becomes: ```text World ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
text: Append: ```bash echo "Hello" > file.txt echo "World" >> file.txt ``` Now: ```text Hello World ``` This becomes useful when working with logs. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Copy
text: ```bash cp app.txt backup.txt ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Move/rename
text: ```bash mv app.txt application.txt ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Delete
text: ```bash rm application.txt ``` Delete directory recursively: ```bash rm -r project ``` Be careful with: ```bash rm -rf ``` On a Linux server, blindly running something like: ```bash rm -rf / ``` can be catastrophic. The important lesson is: > Linux gives you powerful control, so commands should be understood before being executed. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 11. Absolute vs Relative Paths
text: This is important.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Absolute path
text: Starts from `/`. ```bash /home/rachit/project/app.js ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Relative path
text: Relative to your current directory. If you're here: ```text /home/rachit ``` then: ```bash project/app.js ``` means: ```text /home/rachit/project/app.js ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 12. Hidden Files
text: Linux files beginning with `.` are hidden. Example: ```text .env .gitignore .ssh ``` Run: ```bash ls -la ``` to see them. This is especially important because `.env` files often contain configuration/secrets. **Never casually commit secrets to Git.** ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 13. Users
text: Linux is multi-user. For example: ```text root ubuntu deploy developer ``` Each user has an identity. Check your current user: ```bash whoami ``` Example: ```text ubuntu ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 14. Root User
text: `root` is the superuser. It has extremely broad privileges. For example: ```bash sudo apt update ``` `sudo` means: > Execute this command with elevated privileges, subject to the user's sudo permissions. You might see: ```bash sudo systemctl restart nginx ``` because ordinary users shouldn't necessarily be allowed to control system services. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 15. Why permissions exist
text: Imagine every application could modify every file. That would be dangerous. Linux uses permissions to control access. Example: ```text -rwxr-xr-- ``` This looks confusing initially, but let's break it down. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 16. Linux Permissions
text: Three categories: ```text User Group Others ``` And three basic permissions: ```text r = read w = write x = execute ``` For example: ```text -rwxr-xr-- ``` Break it down: ```text Owner Group Others rwx r-x r-- ``` Therefore: Owner: ```text read + write + execute ``` Group: ```text read + execute ``` Others: ```text read ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 17. Numeric Permissions
text: You may see: ```bash chmod 755 script.sh ``` Numbers correspond to: ```text r = 4 w = 2 x = 1 ``` Therefore: ```text 7 = 4 + 2 + 1 = rwx 5 = 4 + 1 = r-x 5 = 4 + 1 = r-x ``` So: ```text 755 ``` means: ```text Owner → rwx Group → r-x Others → r-x ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 18. `chmod`
text: Change permissions: ```bash chmod +x script.sh ``` Now the script can be executed. Or: ```bash chmod 755 script.sh ``` Then: ```bash ./script.sh ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 19. `chown`
text: Change ownership. ```bash sudo chown ubuntu:ubuntu app.log ``` Meaning: ```text Owner = ubuntu Group = ubuntu ``` This becomes important when deploying applications. A classic production problem: > "The application is running but can't write to this directory." Often, permissions or ownership are involved. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 20. Processes
text: A **process** is a running program. If you execute: ```bash node server.js ``` Linux creates a process for Node.js. You can see processes: ```bash ps ``` More commonly: ```bash ps aux ``` You'll see things such as: ```text USER PID %CPU %MEM COMMAND root 1 ... ... ... ubuntu 1234 ... ... node server.js ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 21. PID
text: Every process has a **Process ID (PID)**. Example: ```text node server.js PID = 1234 ``` You can terminate it: ```bash kill 1234 ``` Normally, `kill` sends a signal asking the process to terminate gracefully. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 22. Signals
text: Linux processes communicate/control behavior through signals. Common ones: ```text SIGTERM SIGKILL SIGINT ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: SIGTERM
text: Request termination. ```bash kill PID ``` Generally gives the application a chance to clean up.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: SIGKILL
text: Forcefully terminate. ```bash kill -9 PID ``` The process doesn't get the same opportunity to gracefully shut down.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: SIGINT
text: Interrupt, commonly generated by: ```text Ctrl + C ``` This distinction becomes important with **Docker and Kubernetes graceful shutdown**, which we'll revisit. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 23. `top`
text: See resource usage: ```bash top ``` You can monitor: ```text CPU Memory Processes Load ``` A more interactive alternative commonly found on systems is: ```bash htop ``` if installed. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 24. CPU and Memory
text: Important commands: ```bash free -h ``` Memory. ```bash df -h ``` Disk filesystem usage. ```bash du -sh * ``` Approximate size of items in the current directory. CPU information: ```bash lscpu ``` These are useful when diagnosing: > "Why is my server slow?" ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 25. Services
text: Servers run background services. Examples: ```text nginx ssh docker postgresql ``` Modern Linux systems commonly use **systemd** to manage services. Check service status: ```bash systemctl status nginx ``` Start: ```bash sudo systemctl start nginx ``` Stop: ```bash sudo systemctl stop nginx ``` Restart: ```bash sudo systemctl restart nginx ``` Enable at boot: ```bash sudo systemctl enable nginx ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 26. Logs
text: When something doesn't work: > **Check the logs.** This is one of the most important operational habits you'll develop. System logs often live under: ```text /var/log ``` For systemd services: ```bash journalctl ``` For a specific service: ```bash journalctl -u nginx ``` Follow logs live: ```bash journalctl -u nginx -f ``` `-f` means follow. This is similar to: ```bash tail -f application.log ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 27. Searching Through Files
text: Suppose you have a huge log: ```text application.log ``` Find lines containing `ERROR`: ```bash grep "ERROR" application.log ``` Case-insensitive: ```bash grep -i "error" application.log ``` Search recursively: ```bash grep -r "DATABASE_URL" . ``` This is incredibly useful when debugging. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 28. Finding Files
text: ```bash find /var/log -name "*.log" ``` This searches for files matching the pattern. Example: ```bash find . -name "Dockerfile" ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 29. Environment Variables
text: Applications frequently depend on environment variables. Example: ```bash export PORT=3000 ``` Check: ```bash echo $PORT ``` Output: ```text 3000 ``` Node.js can access it: ```typescript const port = process.env.PORT || 3000; console.log(`Server running on ${port}`); ``` This is extremely important because we'll use environment variables everywhere: ```text Node.js Docker AWS CI/CD Kubernetes ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 30. Why `.env` exists
text: Locally, you might have: ```text PORT=3000 DATABASE_URL=... REDIS_URL=... ``` in: ```text .env ``` Your application can load those values. But **production secrets should not simply be committed into Git or baked into Docker images**. Later we'll learn proper secret management with: - AWS Secrets Manager - Parameter Store - Kubernetes Secrets - CI/CD secrets ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 31. Package Management
text: On Ubuntu/Debian: ```bash sudo apt update ``` Update package metadata. Install: ```bash sudo apt install nginx ``` Remove: ```bash sudo apt remove nginx ``` Different distributions use different package managers. For example: ```text Ubuntu/Debian → apt RHEL/Fedora → dnf Arch → pacman ``` You don't need to memorize every package manager. Understand the concept. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 32. SSH — Extremely Important
text: Suppose AWS gives you an EC2 instance: ```text Public IP: 13.xxx.xxx.xxx ``` You need to access it. SSH: ```bash ssh -i my-key.pem ubuntu@13.xxx.xxx.xxx ``` Conceptually: ```text Your Laptop │ │ SSH ↓ Internet │ ↓ EC2 │ ↓ Linux Shell ``` Now you're operating the remote machine. We'll go much deeper into SSH and networking later. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 33. Linux Networking Commands
text: A few you'll start using:

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Check IP addresses
text: ```bash ip addr ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Check routes
text: ```bash ip route ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Test connectivity
text: ```bash ping google.com ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Make HTTP request
text: ```bash curl https://example.com ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Check listening ports
text: ```bash ss -tulpn ``` This one is extremely useful. Suppose your Node application is supposed to run on: ```text localhost:3000 ``` Run: ```bash ss -tulpn | grep 3000 ``` You can investigate whether something is listening on that port. We'll cover networking properly in **[Chapter 4](ch04-networking.md)**. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 34. A Real Debugging Example
text: Imagine you deployed your Node.js application. User says: > "The API is down." Don't immediately restart everything. Think systematically.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Step 1 — Is the process running?
text: ```bash ps aux | grep node ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Step 2 — Is the port listening?
text: ```bash ss -tulpn | grep 3000 ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Step 3 — Check logs
text: ```bash journalctl -u my-api ``` or: ```bash tail -f application.log ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Step 4 — Test locally
text: ```bash curl http://localhost:3000 ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Step 5 — Check firewall/security/networking
text: Later we'll investigate: ```text Security Group Firewall Load Balancer DNS ``` This is the kind of **reasoning** I want you to develop. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 35. Linux Command Cheat Sheet
text: Keep this mental map: ```text Navigation ────────── pwd ls cd Files ───── touch cat cp mv rm mkdir Search ────── grep find Permissions ─────────── chmod chown Processes ───────── ps top kill Resources ───────── free df du Services ──────── systemctl journalctl Networking ────────── ip ss ping curl Users ───── whoami id sudo Packages ──────── apt Remote ────── ssh Environment ─────────── env export echo ``` Don't try to memorize all of these today. **Use them repeatedly and they'll become natural.** ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: 36. Mini Practical Exercise
text: If you have a Linux machine, WSL, Ubuntu VM, or cloud instance, do this yourself.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Part A — Files
text: ```bash mkdir cloud-lab cd cloud-lab mkdir app logs config touch app/server.log echo "Server started" > app/server.log echo "Request received" >> app/server.log cat app/server.log ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Part B — Search
text: ```bash grep "Server" app/server.log ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Part C — Permissions
text: ```bash chmod 600 app/server.log ls -l app/server.log ``` Think: > Who can now read/write this file?

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Part D — Processes
text: Run: ```bash sleep 300 & ``` Find it: ```bash ps aux | grep sleep ``` Then terminate it: ```bash kill <PID> ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Part E — Resources
text: Run: ```bash free -h df -h ```

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Part F — Networking
text: Run: ```bash ip addr ip route ss -tulpn curl https://example.com ``` Don't worry if some output differs between systems. ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Interview Questions You Should Now Be Able to Approach
text: Don't memorize answers yet. Try reasoning about them.

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Beginner
text: **1. What is Linux?** **2. What is the difference between a process and a program?** **3. What is PID?** **4. What does `chmod 755` mean?** **5. What is `sudo`?** **6. What is the difference between `/` and `/root`?** **7. What is an environment variable?** ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Intermediate
text: **8. How would you find which process is using a port?** Hint: ```bash ss ``` **9. Your application is running but users can't connect. How would you debug it?** **10. Your server's disk is full. What would you investigate?** Possible starting points: ```bash df -h du -sh ``` **11. Your Node.js process keeps crashing. What would you check?** Think: ```text Process ↓ Logs ↓ Resources ↓ Configuration ↓ Dependencies ``` ---

title: Chapter 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Interview scenario
text: > **You SSH into an EC2 instance and users report that your API is down. What do you do?** A strong engineer shouldn't immediately say: > "Restart the server." Instead: ```text 1. Check process ↓ 2. Check logs ↓ 3. Check port ↓ 4. curl localhost ↓ 5. Check application configuration ↓ 6. Check CPU/memory/disk ↓ 7. Check firewall/security group ↓ 8. Check load balancer ↓ 9. Check DNS ``` We'll become much better at this systematic debugging approach as the course progresses. ---

title: Revision 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Chapter 2 — Revision Sheet: Linux for Cloud & DevOps
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/01-foundations/ch02-linux.md).

title: Revision 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Core ideas
text: - **Linux = kernel**; Ubuntu/Debian/Fedora/Amazon Linux/RHEL are *distributions* (kernel + utilities + packages). - **Layers:** Hardware → Kernel (process, memory, network, filesystem, drivers) → System utilities (bash, ls, ps, systemctl) → Applications (Node.js, Docker, Nginx). Applications talk to the kernel (system calls), never directly to hardware. - **You → Terminal → Bash (shell) → Linux.** - A cloud server is just a Linux computer: `AWS → EC2 → Ubuntu → Node/Docker/Nginx → your app`.

title: Revision 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Filesystem map (know these cold)
text: | Path | Purpose | |---|---| | `/` | Root of the whole filesystem tree | | `/root` | Home directory of the *root user* (not the same as `/`) | | `/home/<user>` | Normal users' home dirs | | `/etc` | System configuration (`/etc/ssh`, `/etc/nginx`, `/etc/hosts`) | | `/var` | Frequently changing data; `/var/log` = logs | | `/tmp` | Temporary files | | `/usr` | User-space programs and libraries | | `/opt` | Optional/additional software | | `/dev` | Device files | | `/proc` | Virtual FS exposing process + kernel info (used in troubleshooting) |

title: Revision 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Permissions
text: ```text -rwxr-xr-- → owner rwx | group r-x | others r-- r=4 w=2 x=1 755 = rwx r-x r-x 600 = rw- --- --- ``` - `chmod +x script.sh` makes it executable; `chmod 755 script.sh` then `./script.sh`. - `chown ubuntu:ubuntu app.log` sets owner:group. Classic prod bug: "app runs but can't write to directory" → ownership/permissions.

title: Revision 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Command groups (cheat sheet)
text: | Area | Commands | |---|---| | Navigation | `pwd`, `ls -la`, `cd`, `cd ..`, `cd ~` | | Files | `touch`, `cat`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `rm -r`, `mkdir`, `>` overwrite, `>>` append | | Search | `grep "ERROR" f`, `grep -i`, `grep -r "DATABASE_URL" .`, `find /var/log -name "*.log"` | | Permissions | `chmod`, `chown` | | Processes | `ps aux`, `top`/`htop`, `kill PID` (SIGTERM), `kill -9 PID` (SIGKILL) | | Resources | `free -h` (memory), `df -h` (disk), `du -sh *` (sizes), `lscpu` | | Services (systemd) | `systemctl status/start/stop/restart/enable`, `journalctl -u svc -f` | | Networking | `ip addr`, `ip route`, `ping`, `curl`, `ss -tulpn` | | Users | `whoami` (current user), `id` (uid, gid, groups — *added explanation*), `sudo` | | Packages | `apt update`, `apt install`, `apt remove` (Ubuntu/Debian); `dnf` (RHEL/Fedora); `pacman` (Arch) | | Remote | `ssh -i my-key.pem ubuntu@<ip>` | | Environment | `export PORT=3000`, `echo $PORT`, `env` (lists all environment variables — *added explanation*); Node: `process.env.PORT` |

title: Revision 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Signals (important for Docker/Kubernetes graceful shutdown)
text: | Signal | Meaning | How | |---|---|---| | SIGTERM | Polite request to terminate; app can clean up | `kill PID` | | SIGKILL | Force kill; no cleanup | `kill -9 PID` | | SIGINT | Interrupt | `Ctrl+C` |

title: Revision 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Traps
text: - `/` ≠ `/root`. - `>` **overwrites**, `>>` appends. - `rm -rf` — understand a command before running it on a server. - `.env` files are hidden (`ls -la`); never commit secrets to Git or bake them into Docker images. - Do **not** answer "API is down" with "restart it". Diagnose.

title: Revision 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: The systematic debugging order (memorise)
text: 1. Is the process running? `ps aux | grep node` 2. Is the port listening? `ss -tulpn | grep 3000` 3. Logs: `journalctl -u my-api` / `tail -f application.log` 4. Test locally: `curl http://localhost:3000` 5. App configuration 6. CPU / memory / disk (`top`, `free -h`, `df -h`) 7. Firewall / Security Group 8. Load balancer 9. DNS

title: Revision 2 — Linux for Cloud & DevOps
heading: Interview questions — with answers
text: > The chapter lists these without answers. Answers below are **added for revision** (not source text). 1. **What is Linux?** An operating-system *kernel*; distributions bundle it with utilities to make a usable OS. 2. **Process vs program?** A program is a file on disk (e.g. the `node` binary / `server.js`); a process is a running instance of it with a PID, memory, and state. Running `node server.js` twice creates two processes of one program. 3. **PID?** Unique process ID the kernel assigns; used to signal/kill it. PID 1 is the init process (systemd on modern systems). 4. **`chmod 755`?** Owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x. 5. **`sudo`?** Run a command with elevated privileges, subject to the user's sudo permissions. 6. **`/` vs `/root`?** Filesystem root vs home directory of the root user. 7. **Environment variable?** Named key/value in a process's environment, used for configuration (PORT, DATABASE_URL); inherited by child processes. 8. **Which process uses a port?** `sudo ss -tulpn | grep :3000` (shows PID/program; `sudo` needed to see other users' processes). 9. **App running but users can't connect?** Use the 9-step order above (listening address — `127.0.0.1` vs `0.0.0.0` — security group, LB, DNS). 10. **Disk full?** `df -h` to find the full filesystem, `du -sh *` down the tree to find big directories, check `/var/log`, then clean/rotate. 11. **Node process keeps crashing?** Process → logs → resources (OOM) → configuration (env vars) → dependencies. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 1](ch01-revision.md) · [Full chapter 2](../docs/01-foundations/ch02-linux.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 3](ch03-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
text: > **Source:** Response 3 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-03.txt`, lines 1–1862) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch03-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> In [Chapter 2](ch02-linux.md), we learned how to **operate Linux manually**. Now we learn how to **automate Linux**. This is where Bash becomes important. The central idea is simple: > If you find yourself repeatedly typing the same commands, you can probably turn them into a script. For DevOps, this matters because servers often need repetitive operations such as: ```text Install software ↓ Configure application ↓ Create directories ↓ Set permissions ↓ Start services ↓ Check health ↓ Collect logs ↓ Backup data ``` Instead of manually doing all of this, we automate it. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 1. What is Bash?
text: **Bash = Bourne Again SHell.** It's both: 1. A **shell** through which you interact with Linux. 2. A **scripting language** used to automate commands. For example, manually: ```bash mkdir app cd app touch server.log echo "Application started" > server.log ``` Bash lets us put this into a script: ```bash #!/bin/bash mkdir app cd app touch server.log echo "Application started" > server.log ``` Then execute the script. ```text One command ↓ Multiple operations ↓ Automation ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 2. Your First Bash Script
text: Create: ```bash nano hello.sh ``` Put: ```bash #!/bin/bash echo "Hello from Linux!" echo "Starting DevOps journey..." ``` Save it. Give execute permission: ```bash chmod +x hello.sh ``` Run: ```bash ./hello.sh ``` Output: ```text Hello from Linux! Starting DevOps journey... ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 3. What is `#!/bin/bash`?
text: This is called a **shebang**. ```bash #!/bin/bash ``` It tells the operating system which interpreter should execute the script. Conceptually: ```text hello.sh ↓ #!/bin/bash ↓ Bash ↓ Commands executed ``` You may also see: ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash ``` This finds Bash through the environment. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 4. Variables
text: Bash variables are simple. ```bash name="Rachit" age=21 ``` Important: ❌ Don't put spaces around `=`: ```bash name = "Rachit" ``` That's incorrect Bash syntax. Use: ```bash name="Rachit" ``` Access the variable: ```bash echo "$name" ``` Output: ```text Rachit ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 5. Why `$`?
text: When defining: ```bash name="Rachit" ``` `name` refers to the variable. When accessing: ```bash echo "$name" ``` `$name` means: > Give me the value stored in `name`. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 6. Environment Variables
text: This is particularly important for DevOps. You can define: ```bash export PORT=3000 ``` Then: ```bash echo "$PORT" ``` Output: ```text 3000 ``` A child process can inherit exported environment variables. For example: ```bash export NODE_ENV=production node server.js ``` Your Node.js application can access: ```typescript console.log(process.env.NODE_ENV); ``` Output: ```text production ``` This same idea appears in: - Docker - Kubernetes - AWS - CI/CD - production applications ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 7. Command Substitution
text: Sometimes you want the output of one command inside another command. Use: ```bash $(command) ``` Example: ```bash current_dir=$(pwd) echo "$current_dir" ``` Or: ```bash today=$(date) echo "Today is $today" ``` Conceptually: ```text date ↓ output ↓ store in variable ↓ use output ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 8. User Input
text: Use `read`. ```bash #!/bin/bash echo "Enter your name:" read name echo "Hello $name" ``` Run: ```bash ./hello.sh ``` Then: ```text Enter your name: Rachit Hello Rachit ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 9. Script Arguments
text: This is very useful for automation. Suppose: ```bash ./deploy.sh production ``` Inside the script: ```bash echo "$1" ``` Output: ```text production ``` `$1` = first argument. Similarly: ```text $1 → first argument $2 → second $3 → third ``` Example: ```bash ./deploy.sh production v2.4 ``` Script: ```bash echo "Environment: $1" echo "Version: $2" ``` Output: ```text Environment: production Version: v2.4 ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 10. Special Bash Variables
text: Some useful ones: ```text $0 Script name $1 First argument $2 Second argument $# Number of arguments $@ All arguments $? Exit status of previous command $$ Current process ID ``` Example: ```bash echo "Script: $0" echo "Arguments: $#" echo "All: $@" ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 11. Conditions
text: Bash supports `if`. ```bash if [ "$ENV" = "production" ]; then echo "Production environment" else echo "Non-production environment" fi ``` Notice: ```bash [ "$ENV" = "production" ] ``` The spaces matter. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 12. Numeric Comparisons
text: For numbers: ```bash if [ "$age" -ge 18 ]; then echo "Adult" else echo "Minor" fi ``` Common operators: ```text -eq equal -ne not equal -gt greater than -ge greater/equal -lt less than -le less/equal ``` Example: ```bash if [ "$count" -gt 10 ]; then echo "High count" fi ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 13. File Conditions
text: This is extremely useful in automation. Check whether a file exists: ```bash if [ -f "app.log" ]; then echo "Log exists" fi ``` Directory: ```bash if [ -d "logs" ]; then echo "Logs directory exists" fi ``` Common checks: ```text -f → regular file -d → directory -e → exists -r → readable -w → writable -x → executable ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 14. Loops
text: Automation often requires repetition.

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: `for`
text: ```bash for server in server1 server2 server3 do echo "Deploying to $server" done ``` Output: ```text Deploying to server1 Deploying to server2 Deploying to server3 ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 15. Loop Through Files
text: ```bash for file in *.log do echo "Processing $file" done ``` If the directory contains: ```text app.log error.log access.log ``` the loop processes each file. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 16. `while` Loop
text: ```bash count=1 while [ "$count" -le 5 ] do echo "Count: $count" count=$((count + 1)) done ``` Output: ```text Count: 1 Count: 2 Count: 3 Count: 4 Count: 5 ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 17. Arithmetic
text: Bash can perform basic arithmetic. ```bash a=10 b=20 sum=$((a + b)) echo "$sum" ``` Output: ```text 30 ``` You can use: ```bash + - * / % ``` For serious numerical/data processing, you'd normally use another language such as Python rather than Bash. Bash's strength is **system automation**, not complex computation. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 18. Functions
text: Instead of repeating commands, create functions. ```bash backup_logs() { echo "Backing up logs..." mkdir -p backup cp *.log backup/ } ``` Call it: ```bash backup_logs ``` A better script: ```bash #!/bin/bash backup_logs() { mkdir -p backup cp *.log backup/ echo "Backup complete" } backup_logs ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 19. Function Arguments
text: ```bash greet() { echo "Hello $1" } greet "Rachit" ``` Output: ```text Hello Rachit ``` Inside the function: ```text $1 ``` refers to the function's first argument. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 20. Pipes — One of the Most Important Bash Concepts
text: Consider: ```bash ps aux ``` It produces lots of output. Suppose you only want Node processes: ```bash ps aux | grep node ``` The `|` is a **pipe**. It takes the output of the command on the left and feeds it to the command on the right. ```text ps aux ↓ output ↓ pipe ↓ grep node ↓ filtered output ``` This is fundamental to Linux operations. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 21. More Pipe Examples
text: Count Node processes: ```bash ps aux | grep node | wc -l ``` Conceptually: ```text ps ↓ grep ↓ wc ``` Another: ```bash cat application.log | grep ERROR ``` Although for simple cases: ```bash grep ERROR application.log ``` is cleaner. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 22. Redirection
text: We've already seen: ```bash echo "Hello" > file.txt ``` This redirects output into a file.

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Standard output
text: ```text stdout ``` Normally goes to the terminal. You can redirect: ```bash command > output.txt ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Append
text: ```bash command >> output.txt ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Standard error
text: Errors are generally sent to: ```text stderr ``` Redirect stderr: ```bash command 2> error.log ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Both stdout and stderr
text: A common form: ```bash command > output.log 2>&1 ``` Meaning: ```text stdout → output.log stderr → same place ``` This becomes useful in scripts and CI/CD. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 23. Standard Streams
text: A process generally has: ```text stdin stdout stderr ``` Think: ```text Process / | \ stdin stdout stderr ```

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: stdin
text: Input.

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: stdout
text: Normal output.

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: stderr
text: Error output. Example: ```bash cat existing.txt ``` Normal result → stdout. ```bash cat does-not-exist.txt ``` Error → stderr. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 24. Exit Codes — VERY Important
text: Every Linux command returns an **exit status**. Generally: ```text 0 → success non-0 → failure ``` Check the previous command: ```bash echo $? ``` Example: ```bash true echo $? ``` Output: ```text 0 ``` And: ```bash false echo $? ``` Output: ```text 1 ``` This becomes extremely important in: - Bash scripts - CI/CD - Docker - Kubernetes - deployment automation because automation needs to know: > **Did the previous operation succeed?** ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 25. Using Exit Codes
text: Example: ```bash npm test if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "Tests passed" else echo "Tests failed" fi ``` A cleaner approach: ```bash if npm test; then echo "Tests passed" else echo "Tests failed" exit 1 fi ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 26. `exit`
text: You can terminate a script: ```bash exit 0 ``` Success. Or: ```bash exit 1 ``` Failure. Example: ```bash if [ ! -f "config.json" ]; then echo "Config missing" exit 1 fi ``` Now your CI/CD pipeline can detect the failure. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 27. `&&` and `||`
text: These are very useful.

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
text: Execute the second command only if the first succeeds. ```bash mkdir app && cd app ``` Conceptually: ```text mkdir succeeds? ↓ YES ↓ cd app ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
text: Execute the second command if the first fails. ```bash cd app || echo "Directory doesn't exist" ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Combining
text: ```bash npm test && npm run build ``` Meaning: > Only build if tests succeed. This is exactly the type of logic you'll encounter in CI/CD. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 28. `set -e`
text: A useful Bash scripting option: ```bash set -e ``` It tells Bash to generally exit when a command returns a non-zero status. Example: ```bash #!/bin/bash set -e npm ci npm test npm run build echo "Build successful" ``` If `npm test` fails, the script stops rather than blindly continuing. There are subtleties around `set -e`, so don't treat it as a universal replacement for explicit error handling. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 29. `set -u`
text: Another useful option: ```bash set -u ``` It makes Bash complain about unset variables. Often you'll see: ```bash set -euo pipefail ``` This is a common defensive pattern for Bash scripts. We'll break down `pipefail` next. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 30. `pipefail`
text: Suppose: ```bash command1 | command2 ``` A pipeline can hide failures depending on which command's exit status is considered. With: ```bash set -o pipefail ``` the pipeline can fail if an earlier command fails. Therefore: ```bash set -euo pipefail ``` is a common starting point for robust scripts. You don't need to blindly put it everywhere, but you should understand what it does. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 31. Practical Deployment Script
text: Now let's make something realistic. Imagine you want to deploy a Node.js application. ```bash #!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail echo "Starting deployment..." git pull origin main npm ci npm run build npm test sudo systemctl restart my-api echo "Deployment successful." ``` Conceptually: ```text Git ↓ Pull latest code ↓ Install dependencies ↓ Build ↓ Test ↓ Restart application ``` If a step fails: ```text Deployment stops ``` That's basic DevOps automation. **In production, you'd usually make this safer than the simplified example above**—for example, test before taking down the current version and have a rollback strategy. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 32. Health Check Script
text: Suppose your API should run on port `3000`. We can automate checking it: ```bash #!/bin/bash if curl -fs http://localhost:3000/health > /dev/null; then echo "API is healthy" exit 0 else echo "API is unhealthy" exit 1 fi ``` Now another system can execute this script and determine whether: ```text 0 → healthy 1 → unhealthy ``` This idea eventually connects to: - Docker health checks - Kubernetes probes - load balancers - monitoring ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 33. Cron — Scheduling Automation
text: What if you want something to run automatically? Linux has **cron**. For example: > Run a backup every day at 2 AM. Edit your cron jobs: ```bash crontab -e ``` A simplified entry: ```text 0 2 * * * /home/ubuntu/backup.sh ``` Meaning: ```text minute = 0 hour = 2 day = * month = * weekday= * ``` Therefore: > Every day at 02:00. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 34. Cron Format
text: The five fields: ```text ┌──── minute (0-59) │ ┌── hour (0-23) │ │ ┌── day of month (1-31) │ │ │ ┌── month (1-12) │ │ │ │ ┌── day of week (0-7) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` Examples: Every hour: ```text 0 * * * * ``` Every day at midnight: ```text 0 0 * * * ``` Every Sunday at 3 AM: ```text 0 3 * * 0 ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 35. Real Backup Script
text: Let's combine what we've learned. ```bash #!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail SOURCE="/var/log/myapp" BACKUP="/var/backups/myapp" mkdir -p "$BACKUP" TIMESTAMP=$(date +"%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S") tar -czf "$BACKUP/logs_$TIMESTAMP.tar.gz" "$SOURCE" echo "Backup created successfully" ``` What's happening? ```text SOURCE ↓ Application logs TIMESTAMP ↓ Current date/time tar ↓ Compress logs BACKUP ↓ Store archive ``` Now this script could be scheduled using cron. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 36. `tar`
text: You'll encounter `tar` often on Linux. Create archive: ```bash tar -cf archive.tar files/ ``` Compressed gzip archive: ```bash tar -czf archive.tar.gz files/ ``` Extract: ```bash tar -xzf archive.tar.gz ``` You don't need to memorize all flags right now. Understand: > `tar` packages files into an archive and can work with compression. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 37. Useful Text Processing Tools
text: Bash becomes powerful because Linux provides many small utilities. Important ones: ```text grep sed awk cut sort uniq wc head tail tr xargs ``` We don't need a giant separate lesson for each, but you should understand their purpose.

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: `head`
text: ```bash head application.log ``` First lines.

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: `tail`
text: ```bash tail application.log ``` Last lines. Live logs: ```bash tail -f application.log ```

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: `wc`
text: ```bash wc -l application.log ``` Count lines. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 38. `sort` and `uniq`
text: Example: ```bash sort users.txt | uniq ``` Sort and remove adjacent duplicates. Count unique values: ```bash sort users.txt | uniq | wc -l ``` This style of composing small commands is one of Bash's biggest strengths. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 39. `xargs`
text: Suppose you have: ```text server1 server2 server3 ``` and want to run a command against each. `xargs` can turn input into command arguments. Example: ```bash cat servers.txt | xargs -n1 echo ``` You'll encounter more advanced uses later. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 40. Bash vs Python
text: Since you know Python, this distinction is important.

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Bash is excellent for:
text: ```text Linux commands File operations Process management Deployment scripts System configuration Pipelines Simple automation ```

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Python is better for:
text: ```text Complex logic Data processing APIs Large automation systems Parsing complicated formats Machine learning ``` Don't try to build a 1,000-line automation system in Bash just because Bash can technically do it. Use the right tool. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 41. A More Realistic DevOps Script
text: Here's a simplified deployment automation: ```bash #!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail APP_DIR="/opt/my-api" echo "Deploying application..." cd "$APP_DIR" echo "Pulling latest code..." git pull origin main echo "Installing dependencies..." npm ci echo "Building..." npm run build echo "Running tests..." npm test echo "Restarting service..." sudo systemctl restart my-api echo "Checking application..." if curl -fs http://localhost:3000/health > /dev/null; then echo "Deployment successful" else echo "Deployment failed: health check unsuccessful" exit 1 fi ``` Notice how many concepts from this response come together: ```text Variables ↓ Commands ↓ Exit codes ↓ Conditions ↓ Environment ↓ Git ↓ Node.js ↓ systemd ↓ curl ↓ Automation ``` This is exactly why we're learning Bash. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 42. The DevOps Mental Model
text: You should now see Bash as: ```text Linux Commands ↓ Bash ↓ Automation ↓ Repeatable Operations ↓ DevOps ``` For example: ```text Manual: git pull npm install npm test npm build restart service check health ↓ Automated: ./deploy.sh ``` And later: ```text GitHub Push ↓ CI/CD ↓ Automated deployment ``` Bash is one of the building blocks underneath this. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 43. What You Should Actually Memorize
text: Don't memorize every command. Remember the **categories**: ```text Variables ↓ $NAME Input ↓ read Arguments ↓ $1, $2, $@ Conditions ↓ if Loops ↓ for / while Functions ↓ function_name() Output ↓ echo Pipes ↓ | Redirect ↓ > >> 2> Exit status ↓ $? Success/failure ↓ && || Scheduling ↓ cron Automation ↓ .sh scripts ``` Once you understand these, you can look up exact syntax when necessary. ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Practical Assignment
text: Don't just read this one. Create: ```text devops-lab/ ├── scripts/ ├── logs/ ├── backups/ └── config/ ``` Then create: ```text scripts/system-check.sh ``` It should:

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 1. Print the hostname
text: ```bash hostname ```

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 2. Print current date
text: ```bash date ```

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 3. Print memory usage
text: ```bash free -h ```

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 4. Print disk usage
text: ```bash df -h ```

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 5. Check whether Docker is running
text: Use: ```bash systemctl is-active docker ```

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 6. Write the result to a log
text: Something like: ```text 2026-09-18 11:30 Hostname: ... Docker: active Disk: ... ```

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: 7. Return an appropriate exit code
text: If Docker isn't running: ```bash exit 1 ``` Otherwise: ```bash exit 0 ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Interview Questions
text: Try answering these yourself.

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Basic
text: 1. What is Bash? 2. What is a shell? 3. What is the difference between Bash and Linux? 4. What is a shebang? 5. What is an environment variable? 6. What is `$1`? 7. What is `$@`? 8. What does `$?` represent?

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Intermediate
text: 9. What is a pipe? ```bash ps aux | grep node ``` Explain exactly what happens. 10. What's the difference between: ```bash > >> ``` 11. What are stdin, stdout, and stderr? 12. What does: ```bash 2>&1 ``` mean? 13. What does: ```bash chmod +x script.sh ``` do? 14. Why are exit codes important in CI/CD? 15. What does: ```bash set -euo pipefail ``` generally accomplish?

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Scenario
text: > You have a deployment script with 6 commands. Command #3 fails, but commands #4–6 continue executing and corrupt the deployment. How would you design the script to prevent that? You should now be thinking about: ```text exit codes ↓ error handling ↓ set -e ↓ explicit conditions ↓ rollback ``` ---

title: Chapter 3 — Bash & Linux Automation
heading: Chapter 2 vs Chapter 3
text: You've now covered:
