title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
text: > **Source:** Response 6 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-06.txt`, lines 1–1726) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch06-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> This response is where **Git + Bash + testing + Docker + deployment** start becoming one complete DevOps workflow. By the end, you should be able to look at a CI/CD pipeline and understand: ```text Developer ↓ Git push ↓ GitHub ↓ CI ↓ Build + Test + Security checks ↓ Artifact / Docker image ↓ CD ↓ Deployment ↓ Production ↓ Monitoring ``` And importantly, you'll understand **how to build this yourself**. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 1. What problem does CI/CD solve?
text: Imagine 20 developers working on a backend. Without automation: ```text Developer ↓ "Hey, I finished my code." ↓ Someone manually tests it ↓ Someone builds it ↓ Someone copies files to server ↓ Someone restarts application ``` This creates: - human error - slow deployments - inconsistent environments - forgotten tests - difficult rollbacks CI/CD automates much of this. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 2. CI — Continuous Integration
text: CI means developers integrate changes frequently and have automated checks run against those changes. Typical flow: ```text git push ↓ CI starts ↓ Install dependencies ↓ Lint ↓ Type check ↓ Test ↓ Build ``` For a TypeScript project: ```bash npm ci npm run lint npm run typecheck npm test npm run build ``` If something fails: ```text ❌ Pipeline failed ``` If everything succeeds: ```text ✅ Pipeline passed ``` ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 3. Why CI is Valuable
text: Suppose you modify authentication. You accidentally break payment functionality. Your code may compile. But automated tests might catch it: ```text Pull Request ↓ CI ↓ 500 tests ↓ 3 failed ❌ ``` Now the problem is detected **before production**. This is the fundamental value of CI: > **Find integration problems early and automatically.** ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 4. Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
text: Let's separate them clearly.

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Continuous Delivery
text: Every successful change is automatically prepared and made **ready to deploy**, but production may require approval. ```text Code ↓ CI ↓ Build ↓ Test ↓ Production-ready ↓ Manual approval ↓ Production ```

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Continuous Deployment
text: Successful changes automatically go to production. ```text Code ↓ CI ↓ Build ↓ Test ↓ Production ``` Both are legitimate approaches. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 5. CI/CD Pipeline
text: A pipeline is a sequence of automated steps. Example: ```text Git Push │ ↓ Checkout │ ↓ Install Dependencies │ ↓ Lint │ ↓ Type Check │ ↓ Tests │ ↓ Build │ ↓ Docker Build │ ↓ Push Image to Registry │ ↓ Deploy │ ↓ Health Check ``` This is the architecture we'll understand. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 6. GitHub Actions
text: We'll use **GitHub Actions** as our primary CI/CD tool. It allows workflows to execute automatically in response to GitHub events. For example: ```text git push ↓ GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ``` Workflow files are typically stored in: ```text .github/workflows/ ``` Example: ```text .github/ └── workflows/ └── ci.yml ``` ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 7. Your First GitHub Actions Workflow
text: Create: ```text .github/workflows/ci.yml ``` ```yaml name: CI on: push: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Setup Node uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 - name: Install dependencies run: npm ci - name: Run tests run: npm test - name: Build run: npm run build ``` Don't memorize this yet. Let's understand every part. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 8. `name`
text: ```yaml name: CI ``` Just gives the workflow a name. GitHub will show: ```text CI ``` in the Actions interface. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 9. `on`
text: ```yaml on: push: branches: [main] ``` This defines the **trigger**. Meaning: > Run this workflow when code is pushed to `main`. You could also trigger on: ```yaml on: pull_request: branches: [main] ``` Meaning: > Run when a Pull Request targeting `main` is created/updated. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 10. Jobs
text: ```yaml jobs: test: ``` A workflow contains one or more **jobs**. Think: ```text Workflow │ ├── Job A ├── Job B └── Job C ``` A job runs on a runner. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 11. Runner
text: ```yaml runs-on: ubuntu-latest ``` This tells GitHub which environment executes the job. Conceptually: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ Ubuntu machine ↓ Your commands ``` Other runner types can include Windows or macOS. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 12. Steps
text: Inside the job: ```yaml steps: ``` we define individual operations. Example: ```yaml - name: Install dependencies run: npm ci ``` `run` executes a shell command. So: ```yaml run: npm test ``` is essentially: ```bash npm test ``` on the runner. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 13. `uses`
text: This: ```yaml uses: actions/checkout@v4 ``` uses an existing GitHub Action. It checks your repository's code into the runner. Without checkout, the runner doesn't automatically have your repository files available for your build commands. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 14. Why `npm ci` Instead of `npm install`?
text: This is an excellent interview detail. For CI environments, `npm ci` is generally preferred because it performs a clean, lockfile-based installation. It uses: ```text package-lock.json ``` to reproduce the dependency tree. Conceptually: ```text package.json + package-lock.json ↓ npm ci ↓ Same dependency versions ``` This makes builds more reproducible. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 15. Pipeline Failure
text: Suppose: ```yaml - name: Run tests run: npm test ``` returns a non-zero exit code. Remember [Chapter 3](../01-foundations/ch03-bash-automation.md)? ```text 0 → success non-0 → failure ``` GitHub Actions detects the failed command. Then the job normally stops. ```text Install ↓ Lint ↓ Tests ❌ ↓ Build doesn't run ``` This is where **Linux exit codes → Bash → CI/CD** connect. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 16. Multiple Jobs
text: Suppose you want: ```text test security build ``` You can have: ```yaml jobs: test: ... security: ... build: ... ``` Conceptually: ```text Workflow / | \ Test Security Build ``` Independent jobs can run in parallel. That can make pipelines faster. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 17. Job Dependencies
text: Suppose build should happen only after tests pass. You can use: ```yaml jobs: test: ... build: needs: test ... ``` Now: ```text test ↓ build ``` instead of: ```text test ─────┐ ↓ build ``` This is useful when designing pipelines. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 18. A Better CI Pipeline
text: For your TypeScript backend: ```yaml name: CI on: pull_request: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 - run: npm ci - run: npm run lint - run: npm run typecheck - run: npm test - run: npm run build ``` Now every Pull Request can be automatically validated. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 19. Type Checking
text: Because you're using TypeScript: ```bash npm run typecheck ``` might run: ```bash tsc --noEmit ``` This checks TypeScript correctness without producing build output. Your pipeline can therefore catch: ```typescript const userId: number = "123"; ``` before merging. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 20. Linting
text: Linting catches code-quality problems. For example: ```bash npm run lint ``` might detect: - unused variables - suspicious patterns - formatting issues - style violations Linting isn't a replacement for tests. Think: ```text Lint ↓ Code quality Typecheck ↓ Type correctness Tests ↓ Behavior correctness Build ↓ Production artifact ``` ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 21. Unit Tests vs Integration Tests
text: CI can run different levels of tests.

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Unit tests
text: Test small pieces: ```text function service utility ```

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Integration tests
text: Test multiple components together: ```text API ↓ Database ```

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: End-to-end tests
text: Test the system from the user's perspective: ```text Browser ↓ API ↓ Database ``` A production pipeline might have: ```text Lint ↓ Unit Tests ↓ Integration Tests ↓ E2E ↓ Build ``` We won't build an entire testing course here, but you should understand where each fits. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 22. Artifacts
text: Suppose your TypeScript build produces: ```text dist/ ``` You may want to save that output from the workflow. That's a **build artifact**. Conceptually: ```text Source Code ↓ Build ↓ dist/ ↓ Artifact ``` Artifacts can be: - binaries - compiled JavaScript - packages - reports - test results They can be passed to later workflow stages or retained for inspection. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 23. Docker in CI/CD
text: Now we connect [Chapter 7](../02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md)/8 later with CI/CD. Instead of deploying raw source code, build a Docker image. ```text GitHub ↓ CI ↓ Tests ↓ Docker Build ↓ Docker Image ↓ Container Registry ↓ Deployment ``` Example: ```yaml - name: Build Docker image run: docker build -t my-api:${{ github.sha }} . ``` Notice: ```text ${{ github.sha }} ``` This gives the image a unique identifier corresponding to the commit. That is much better than blindly deploying: ```text latest ``` for production traceability. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 24. Container Registry
text: You need somewhere to store Docker images. Examples include: - GitHub Container Registry - Amazon ECR - Docker Hub For our AWS-focused roadmap, you'll learn **Amazon ECR** later. Conceptually: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ Docker build ↓ Image ↓ ECR ↓ AWS deployment ``` ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 25. Why Use Immutable Image Tags?
text: Imagine: ```text my-api:latest ``` today means: ```text version A ``` Tomorrow: ```text my-api:latest ``` means: ```text version B ``` Now it's difficult to know exactly what production is running. Instead: ```text my-api:a83f91c my-api:7b12e44 my-api:f82d911 ``` Each can correspond to a specific commit. This makes deployment and rollback much easier. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 26. Secrets
text: CI/CD often needs credentials. For example: ```text AWS credentials Database credentials API keys Signing keys ``` **Do not put them directly in YAML.** Bad: ```yaml env: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "super-secret" ``` Instead use GitHub Secrets/appropriate secret-management mechanisms. Conceptually: ```text GitHub Secret ↓ Workflow ↓ Environment variable ↓ Command ``` Later we'll discuss how production workloads should use services such as **AWS Secrets Manager** rather than embedding long-lived credentials. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 27. Environment Variables
text: You can define: ```yaml env: NODE_ENV: production ``` Then: ```bash echo "$NODE_ENV" ``` Your application: ```typescript const env = process.env.NODE_ENV; ``` This connects directly to the Bash concepts from [Chapter 3](../01-foundations/ch03-bash-automation.md). ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 28. GitHub Environments
text: You might have: ```text development staging production ``` Each can have different: - secrets - variables - protection rules - approvals Conceptually: ```text CI │ Build/Test │ ┌──────┴──────┐ ↓ ↓ Staging Production │ Approval ``` Production can require manual approval. This is useful for **Continuous Delivery**. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 29. Deployment Example
text: A simplified pipeline: ```text Pull Request ↓ Lint ↓ Test ↓ Build ↓ Merge ↓ Docker Build ↓ Push to ECR ↓ Deploy ↓ Health Check ``` That is a realistic high-level CI/CD architecture. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 30. Deployment Strategies
text: Suppose you're replacing: ```text v1 ``` with: ```text v2 ``` You don't necessarily want: ```text v1 → 💥 → v2 ``` There are different strategies. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Recreate
text: Stop old version. Start new version. ```text v1 ↓ STOP ↓ v2 ``` Simple, but may cause downtime. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Rolling Deployment
text: Gradually replace instances. ```text v1 v1 v1 v1 ↓ v2 v1 v1 v1 ↓ v2 v2 v1 v1 ↓ v2 v2 v2 v1 ↓ v2 v2 v2 v2 ``` Good for gradual replacement. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Blue-Green
text: Maintain two environments: ```text Blue → v1 Green → v2 ``` Initially: ```text Users ↓ Blue ``` Test Green: ```text Green → v2 ``` Then switch: ```text Users ↓ Green ``` If something goes wrong, traffic can potentially be switched back to Blue. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Canary
text: Send a small percentage of users to the new version: ```text Users │ ├── 95% → v1 │ └── 5% → v2 ``` Monitor: ```text errors latency performance ``` If healthy: ```text 5% ↓ 25% ↓ 50% ↓ 100% ``` These strategies become particularly important when we reach Kubernetes. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 31. Rollback
text: Suppose: ```text v1 → production ``` Then: ```text v2 → production ``` and errors spike. You need to return to v1. ```text v2 ↓ ❌ ↓ v1 ``` If your images are versioned: ```text my-api:v1 my-api:v2 ``` rollback becomes much easier. This is another reason **immutable/versioned artifacts** matter. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 32. CI/CD Security
text: A production pipeline should also consider: ```text Dependency vulnerabilities Secrets Docker image vulnerabilities Infrastructure configuration Permissions Supply-chain security ``` Possible checks: ```text Code ↓ Dependency scanning ↓ SAST ↓ Container scanning ↓ Build ↓ Deploy ``` You don't need to memorize every security tool. Understand the principle: > **The pipeline itself is part of the production security boundary.** ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 33. Caching
text: CI can become slow. Suppose dependencies take: ```text 2 minutes ``` every run. Caching can reduce repeated downloads. For example: ```text First run ↓ Download dependencies ↓ Cache Next run ↓ Restore cache ↓ Faster ``` GitHub Actions supports caching through actions and workflow configuration. But be careful: > Cache correctness matters. A stale or incorrectly keyed cache can produce confusing builds. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 34. Matrix Builds
text: Suppose you want to test your application on multiple Node versions: ```yaml strategy: matrix: node: [20, 22, 24] ``` Then: ```text Test / | \ Node 20 Node 22 Node 24 ``` This is called a **matrix strategy**. Useful when compatibility across environments matters. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 35. Reusable Workflows
text: Large organizations may have many repositories. Instead of duplicating: ```text 100 lines of CI YAML ``` everywhere, workflows can be reused. Conceptually: ```text Central CI workflow ↓ Repo A Repo B Repo C Repo D ``` This improves consistency. You don't need to master this immediately, but recognize it as a scaling pattern for CI/CD configuration. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 36. Complete TypeScript CI Pipeline
text: Here's a reasonable starting point: ```yaml name: CI on: pull_request: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Setup Node uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 cache: npm - name: Install run: npm ci - name: Lint run: npm run lint - name: Type check run: npm run typecheck - name: Test run: npm test - name: Build run: npm run build ``` This is something you should eventually be able to write **without copying it**. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 37. CI + Docker + AWS
text: Now imagine production. ```text Developer │ │ git push ↓ GitHub │ ↓ GitHub Actions │ ├── Lint ├── Typecheck ├── Test └── Build │ ↓ Docker Build │ ↓ ECR │ ↓ AWS Deploy │ ↓ EC2/ECS/EKS │ ↓ Health Check │ ↓ Production ``` This is the architecture you should keep in your head. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 38. CI vs CD — Interview Answer
text: If an interviewer asks: > **What's the difference between CI and CD?** A strong concise answer: > **CI continuously integrates code changes and automatically validates them through checks such as builds and tests. CD extends that process toward deployment: Continuous Delivery keeps changes production-ready with a deployment step that may require approval, while Continuous Deployment automatically releases successful changes to production.** That's substantially better than: > "CI is testing and CD is deployment." ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 39. What Happens If CI Fails?
text: Suppose: ```text Developer ↓ Pull Request ↓ CI ↓ Tests ❌ ``` The PR should generally not be merged until the failure is understood/resolved, depending on repository protection rules. This creates: ```text Developer ↓ Fast feedback ↓ Fix ↓ CI ↓ Pass ↓ Merge ``` This is the essence of continuous integration. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 40. A Production Pipeline
text: Eventually, your pipeline could look like: ```text Developer │ Git Push │ ↓ GitHub │ ┌───────┴───────┐ ↓ ↓ PR CI Security │ │ └───────┬───────┘ ↓ Merge │ ↓ Build │ ↓ Docker Image │ ↓ ECR │ ↓ Deployment │ ┌─────┴─────┐ ↓ ↓ Staging Production │ │ └─────┬─────┘ ↓ Health Check │ ↓ Monitoring ``` Now you can see how: **Git → Bash → Docker → AWS → Kubernetes → Monitoring** will eventually connect. ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: 41. Important CI/CD Concepts to Know
text: You should now recognize: ```text Workflow Job Step Runner Trigger Artifact Environment Secret Variable Cache Matrix Dependency Pipeline Build Test Deploy Rollback Approval ``` But don't just memorize these terms. Think of them as components of: ```text Code ↓ Validate ↓ Package ↓ Release ↓ Deploy ↓ Observe ↓ Rollback if necessary ``` ---

title: Chapter 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Practical Assignment
text: Create a small Node.js/TypeScript project. Your workflow should: ```text GitHub push ↓ Checkout ↓ Node setup ↓ npm ci ↓ Lint ↓ Typecheck ↓ Tests ↓ Build ``` Then deliberately break something. For example: ```typescript const port: number = "3000"; ``` Push it. You should see: ```text CI ❌ ``` Fix it. Push again: ```text CI ✅ ``` Then add: ```yaml - name: Build Docker image run: docker build -t my-api:${{ github.sha }} . ``` Now your pipeline is beginning to produce a deployable artifact. ---

text: > **You pushed a new version of your Node.js backend. CI passes, Docker image builds successfully, deployment succeeds, but users suddenly receive 500 errors. What would you investigate?** Don't simply answer "restart it." Think: ```text Deployment ↓ Correct image? ↓ Environment variables? ↓ Secrets? ↓ Database migrations? ↓ Application logs? ↓ Health checks? ↓ Dependency connectivity? ↓ Traffic/load balancer? ↓ Rollback if necessary ``` That is the type of production reasoning we're building. ---

title: Revision 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: What CI/CD solves
text: Manual flow ("I finished" → someone tests → builds → copies to server → restarts) causes human error, slow deploys, inconsistent environments, forgotten tests, painful rollbacks. CI/CD automates it. | Term | Meaning | |---|---| | **CI** | Integrate frequently; automated checks on every change → find integration problems early (e.g. 500 tests, 3 fail ❌ *before* production). | | **Continuous Delivery** | Every good change is automatically built/tested and **ready**; production release needs **manual approval**. | | **Continuous Deployment** | Passing changes go to production **automatically**. | **Strong interview answer:** *CI continuously integrates changes and validates them (builds, tests). CD extends that toward deployment: Continuous Delivery keeps changes production-ready with a deploy step that may need approval, while Continuous Deployment releases successful changes automatically.* (Not "CI is testing and CD is deployment".)

title: Revision 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Pipeline stages
text: Git push → Checkout → Install deps → Lint → Type check → Tests → Build → Docker build → Push image to registry → Deploy → Health check → Monitoring. | Check | Catches | |---|---| | Lint (`npm run lint`) | Code quality: unused vars, suspicious patterns, formatting/style | | Typecheck (`tsc --noEmit`) | Type correctness, e.g. `const userId: number = "123"` — no build output | | Tests | Behaviour correctness | | Build | Production artifact | Test levels: **unit** (function/service/utility) → **integration** (API ↔ DB) → **E2E** (browser ↔ API ↔ DB).

title: Revision 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: GitHub Actions anatomy
text: ```yaml name: CI # label in Actions UI on: # TRIGGER push: { branches: [main] } # or pull_request: { branches: [main] } jobs: # one or more jobs (parallel by default) test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest # RUNNER environment (also Windows/macOS) steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 # reuse an Action: put repo code on runner - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm } - run: npm ci # run a shell command - run: npm run lint - run: npm run typecheck - run: npm test - run: npm run build build: needs: test # job dependency → build only after test passes ``` - Workflow files live in `.github/workflows/*.yml`. - A command returning **non-zero** fails the step and normally stops the job (Linux exit codes → Bash → CI/CD, Ch.3). - **Why `npm ci`:** clean, lockfile-based install from `package-lock.json` → reproducible dependency tree. - **Matrix:** `strategy: matrix: node: [20, 22, 24]` → same job fanned out across versions. - **Cache:** reuse downloaded dependencies (`cache: npm`); beware stale/wrongly-keyed caches. - **Reusable workflows:** one central CI workflow used by many repos for consistency. - **Artifacts:** saved build output (`dist/`, binaries, packages, reports, test results) passed to later stages or kept for inspection. - **Env vars:** `env: NODE_ENV: production`. **Secrets:** use GitHub Secrets, never write keys in YAML. Flow: GitHub Secret → workflow → environment variable → command. - **GitHub Environments** (development / staging / production) have their own secrets, variables, protection rules and **approvals** → implements Continuous Delivery.

title: Revision 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Docker in CI
text: ```yaml - name: Build Docker image run: docker build -t my-api:${{ github.sha }} . ``` - `${{ github.sha }}` = unique tag per commit → traceability + easy rollback. **Avoid deploying `latest`** in production (mutable: today's `latest` ≠ tomorrow's). - Registries: GitHub Container Registry, **Amazon ECR**, Docker Hub. - Full picture: Dev → git push → GitHub → Actions (lint/typecheck/test/build) → Docker build → ECR → AWS deploy (EC2/ECS/EKS) → health check → production.

title: Revision 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: Deployment strategies
text: | Strategy | How | Trade-off | |---|---|---| | **Recreate** | Stop v1, start v2 | Simple; downtime | | **Rolling** | Replace instances gradually (v2 v1 v1 v1 → … → v2 v2 v2 v2) | Gradual; mixed versions during rollout | | **Blue-Green** | Two environments (Blue=v1, Green=v2); test Green; switch traffic; switch back if bad | Fast rollback; needs double capacity | | **Canary** | Send small % (95/5) to v2, watch errors/latency/performance; 5→25→50→100% | Safer; needs good monitoring | **Rollback** = return to previous version; easy only with versioned/immutable artifacts (`my-api:v1`, `my-api:v2`).

title: Revision 6 — CI/CD + GitHub Actions
heading: CI/CD security
text: Consider dependency vulnerabilities, secrets, Docker image vulnerabilities, infrastructure config, permissions, supply-chain. Stages: dependency scanning → SAST → container scanning → build → deploy. Principle: **the pipeline itself is part of the production security boundary.**

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
text: > **Source:** Response 7 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-07.txt`, lines 1–1716) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch07-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> Now we move into one of the **most important technologies in modern backend + DevOps interviews**. You should eventually be able to take your TypeScript/Node.js backend, containerize it, run it locally, connect it to a database, and understand how that same image can move through CI/CD into AWS/Kubernetes. This response focuses on the **fundamentals**. [Chapter 8](ch08-docker-production.md) will go deeper into production Docker. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 1. The Problem Docker Solves
text: Imagine your Node.js application works perfectly on your laptop. ```text Your Laptop Node 22 npm packages Environment variables OS configuration ``` You give it to another developer: ```text Other Laptop Node 20 Different OS Different npm version Missing dependency ``` Suddenly: ```text ❌ It works on my machine. ``` Docker addresses this by packaging the application and its environment requirements into a **container image**. Conceptually: ```text Application + Dependencies + Runtime configuration ↓ Docker Image ↓ Container ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 2. What Is Docker?
text: Docker is a platform/tooling ecosystem for building, distributing, and running applications in **containers**. A container provides an isolated execution environment for a process and its dependencies while sharing the host operating system's kernel. Think: > **A container is an isolated process environment, not a complete virtual machine.** ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 3. VM vs Container
text: This distinction is extremely important.

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Virtual Machine
text: ```text Physical Machine ↓ Hypervisor ↓ ┌──────────────┐ │ VM │ │ Guest OS │ │ Application │ └──────────────┘ ┌──────────────┐ │ VM │ │ Guest OS │ │ Application │ └──────────────┘ ``` Each VM normally has its own guest operating system. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Containers
text: ```text Physical/Cloud Machine ↓ Host OS Kernel ↓ Container Runtime ↓ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ App │ │ App │ │ App │ │ Libraries│ │ Libraries│ │ Libraries│ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ ``` Containers share the host kernel. Therefore containers are generally: - lighter - faster to start - more efficient in resource usage than full VMs. But they provide a different isolation model and are **not simply "tiny VMs."** ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 4. Docker's Core Concepts
text: You need to understand these five first: ```text Image Container Dockerfile Registry Volume ``` And later: ```text Network Compose ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 5. Docker Image
text: An image is a packaged, immutable template used to create containers. For example: ```text node:22 ``` is a Node.js image. You can build your own: ```text my-api:1.0 ``` Think: ```text Image = blueprint Container = running instance ``` Similar idea: ```text Class ↓ Object ``` Not exactly the same technically, but useful intuition. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 6. Container
text: A container is a running or created instance of an image. ```text Image ↓ docker run ↓ Container ``` For example: ```bash docker run node:22 ``` Docker creates a container from the Node image. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 7. Image vs Container
text: Very common interview question: > What's the difference between a Docker image and a container? Answer: > **An image is an immutable packaged template containing the application and its required filesystem/dependencies. A container is an isolated running or created instance of that image.** Example: ```text node:22 image │ ├── container A ├── container B └── container C ``` One image can create many containers. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 8. Docker Architecture
text: At a high level: ```text Docker CLI │ ↓ Docker Daemon │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Images Containers Networks │ Volumes ``` The Docker CLI is what you interact with: ```bash docker build docker run docker ps docker images ``` The Docker daemon manages Docker objects and operations. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 9. Docker CLI
text: Check Docker: ```bash docker --version ``` Check information: ```bash docker info ``` List available commands: ```bash docker help ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 10. Your First Container
text: Run: ```bash docker run hello-world ``` Docker will: ```text Find image ↓ Download image if needed ↓ Create container ↓ Start container ↓ Application executes ↓ Container exits ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 11. Pulling Images
text: You can explicitly download an image: ```bash docker pull node:22 ``` Then: ```bash docker images ``` You might see: ```text REPOSITORY TAG IMAGE ID node 22 ... ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 12. Running Node.js
text: Try: ```bash docker run node:22 node --version ``` Conceptually: ```text Node image ↓ Container ↓ node --version ↓ v22.x.x ↓ process exits ``` This demonstrates an important idea: > **A container normally exists to run a process.** ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 13. Container Lifecycle
text: A container can go through states such as: ```text Created ↓ Running ↓ Stopped ↓ Removed ``` Commands: ```bash docker ps ``` shows running containers. ```bash docker ps -a ``` shows running + stopped containers. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 14. Start an Interactive Container
text: Try: ```bash docker run -it ubuntu bash ``` Meaning: ```text -i → interactive -t → terminal ``` Now you're inside the container. Try: ```bash ls ``` or: ```bash cat /etc/os-release ``` Exit: ```bash exit ``` The container stops if its main process was the shell. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 15. Detached Mode
text: For a long-running application: ```bash docker run -d nginx ``` `-d` means detached mode. Your terminal returns immediately. Check: ```bash docker ps ``` You'll see the container running. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 16. Container Names
text: Docker can automatically generate names. You can provide one: ```bash docker run -d --name my-nginx nginx ``` Now: ```bash docker ps ``` shows: ```text my-nginx ``` instead of relying on an autogenerated name. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 17. Stop and Start
text: Stop: ```bash docker stop my-nginx ``` Start again: ```bash docker start my-nginx ``` Restart: ```bash docker restart my-nginx ``` Remove: ```bash docker rm my-nginx ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 18. Important Distinction: Stop vs Remove
text: This is frequently misunderstood. ```bash docker stop my-nginx ``` means: > Stop the container. The container still exists. ```bash docker rm my-nginx ``` means: > Remove the container. You can verify with: ```bash docker ps -a ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 19. Logs
text: Suppose your application is running: ```bash docker run -d --name my-nginx nginx ``` View logs: ```bash docker logs my-nginx ``` Follow logs: ```bash docker logs -f my-nginx ``` This connects directly to the Linux debugging concepts you learned earlier. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 20. Executing Commands Inside Containers
text: Suppose: ```text my-nginx ``` is running. You can execute: ```bash docker exec -it my-nginx bash ``` Now you're inside the running container. For images that don't contain Bash, you may need: ```bash docker exec -it my-nginx sh ``` This is an important production debugging technique. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 21. Port Mapping
text: This is one of the most important Docker concepts. Suppose your application listens inside the container on: ```text 3000 ``` That does **not automatically mean** your host's port 3000 reaches it. You can map: ```text Host:3000 ↓ Container:3000 ``` with: ```bash docker run -p 3000:3000 my-api ``` Format: ```text -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 22. Node.js Example
text: Suppose your application has: ```typescript import express from "express"; const app = express(); app.get("/", (_req, res) => { res.json({ message: "Hello Docker" }); }); app.listen(3000, "0.0.0.0", () => { console.log("Server running on port 3000"); }); ``` The important part: ```typescript app.listen(3000, "0.0.0.0"); ``` Inside a container, binding to `0.0.0.0` is usually necessary when you want the application reachable through the container's network interface. Then: ```bash docker run -p 3000:3000 my-api ``` Request: ```text Browser ↓ localhost:3000 ↓ Docker host port 3000 ↓ Container port 3000 ↓ Node.js ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 23. Why `localhost` Can Cause Problems
text: This is a classic Docker debugging issue. Inside the container: ```text localhost ``` means: > **this container itself** It does not mean: > your laptop or: > another container. This becomes extremely important when we discuss Docker networking. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 24. Dockerfile
text: Now we get to the most important practical concept. A **Dockerfile** contains instructions for building an image. Example TypeScript backend: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] ``` Let's understand it line by line. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 25. `FROM`
text: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 ``` This selects the base image. Your image starts from: ```text Node.js 22 environment ``` Docker images are often built from other images. ```text node:22 ↓ your Dockerfile ↓ my-api ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 26. `WORKDIR`
text: ```dockerfile WORKDIR /app ``` Sets the working directory. Commands afterward operate from: ```text /app ``` Instead of repeatedly doing: ```bash cd /app ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 27. `COPY`
text: ```dockerfile COPY package*.json ./ ``` Copies package files into the image. Then: ```dockerfile RUN npm ci ``` installs dependencies. Then: ```dockerfile COPY . . ``` copies the rest of the application. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 28. Why Copy `package.json` First?
text: This introduces an important Docker optimization. Suppose your Dockerfile was: ```dockerfile COPY . . RUN npm ci ``` Every source-code change could invalidate the dependency installation layer. Instead: ```dockerfile COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . ``` means Docker can potentially reuse the dependency layer when only application source code changes. This becomes even more important in [Chapter 8](ch08-docker-production.md). ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 29. `RUN`
text: ```dockerfile RUN npm ci ``` executes a command **while building the image**. Another: ```dockerfile RUN npm run build ``` compiles TypeScript. Remember: ```text Docker build ↓ RUN commands ↓ Image created ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 30. `CMD`
text: ```dockerfile CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] ``` defines the default command used when the container starts. So: ```bash docker run my-api ``` effectively starts: ```bash node dist/index.js ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 31. `CMD` vs `RUN`
text: Very important.

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: RUN
text: Happens during **image build**. ```dockerfile RUN npm ci ```

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: CMD
text: Defines the default process when a **container starts**. ```dockerfile CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] ``` Think: ```text docker build ↓ RUN ↓ IMAGE ↓ docker run ↓ CMD ↓ CONTAINER PROCESS ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 32. `EXPOSE`
text: ```dockerfile EXPOSE 3000 ``` This documents that the application intends to listen on port 3000. It does **not itself publish the port to your host**. You still need: ```bash docker run -p 3000:3000 my-api ``` Excellent interview trick. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 33. Build the Image
text: Suppose your project contains: ```text Dockerfile package.json package-lock.json src/ tsconfig.json ``` Build: ```bash docker build -t my-api:1.0 . ``` Meaning: ```text docker build │ ├── -t my-api:1.0 │ └── . ← build context ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 34. Build Context
text: The final: ```text . ``` means: > Use the current directory as the build context. Docker can access files within that context for instructions such as: ```dockerfile COPY ``` This is why you should be careful about what is in your build context. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 35. Run Your Image
text: After: ```bash docker build -t my-api:1.0 . ``` run: ```bash docker run -p 3000:3000 --name my-api my-api:1.0 ``` Then: ```text Browser ↓ localhost:3000 ↓ Docker ↓ my-api container ↓ Node.js ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 36. `.dockerignore`
text: You should usually have: ```text .dockerignore ``` Example: ```text node_modules .git .env dist npm-debug.log ``` Why? Because you don't want to send unnecessary files into the Docker build context. Especially: ```text .env ``` because it may contain secrets. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 37. Environment Variables
text: Don't hardcode configuration: ```typescript const dbPassword = "mypassword"; ``` Instead: ```typescript const dbPassword = process.env.DB_PASSWORD; ``` Then run: ```bash docker run \ -e DB_PASSWORD="..." \ my-api:1.0 ``` Now: ```text Container ↓ process.env.DB_PASSWORD ``` gets the value. For real production systems, secrets should generally come from proper secret-management mechanisms rather than being casually placed in command history or deployment files. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 38. Docker Images Have Layers
text: A Docker image is built from layers. For example: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build ``` Conceptually: ```text ┌────────────────────┐ │ Build output │ ├────────────────────┤ │ Source code │ ├────────────────────┤ │ npm dependencies │ ├────────────────────┤ │ Working filesystem │ ├────────────────────┤ │ Node base image │ └────────────────────┘ ``` Docker can reuse unchanged layers. This is one reason Docker builds can be fast after the initial build. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 39. Image Tags
text: You can have: ```text my-api:1.0 my-api:1.1 my-api:latest ``` Format: ```text repository:tag ``` For production, we'll later discuss why immutable/version-specific tags are preferable to relying on `latest`. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 40. Docker Registry
text: A registry stores and distributes images. Examples: ```text Docker Hub GitHub Container Registry Amazon ECR ``` Conceptually: ```text Developer ↓ docker build ↓ Image ↓ docker push ↓ Registry ``` Another machine can then: ```bash docker pull my-api:1.0 ``` and run it. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 41. The Real Power of Docker
text: Suppose: ```text Developer machine ↓ Docker image ↓ CI/CD ↓ Registry ↓ AWS ↓ Kubernetes ``` The same application artifact can move through environments. ```text SAME IMAGE │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Testing Staging Production ``` This greatly reduces "works on my machine" problems. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 42. Docker Networking — Basic Idea
text: Suppose you have: ```text Node API + PostgreSQL ``` You could run: ```text Container A Node.js Container B PostgreSQL ``` They need to communicate. Docker provides networking mechanisms that allow containers to communicate without exposing every internal service directly to the host. Later we'll go much deeper into this. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 43. Docker Volumes
text: Containers have writable filesystem layers, but container-local data is not a good default place for important persistent data. For example: ```text PostgreSQL container ↓ Database files ``` If the container is removed, you don't want your database to disappear. A **volume** provides persistent storage managed separately from the container lifecycle. Conceptually: ```text Container │ ↓ Volume │ ↓ Persistent data ``` Create: ```bash docker volume create postgres-data ``` Then: ```bash docker run \ -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \ postgres ``` Now the database data lives in the volume. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Bind mount
text: Maps a host path: ```bash -v ./src:/app/src ``` Useful during local development.

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Named volume
text: Managed by Docker: ```bash -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data ``` Often useful for persistent container data. Think: ```text Bind mount Host directory ↔ Container Volume Docker-managed storage ↔ Container ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 45. Why Containers Should Usually Be Stateless
text: Suppose you have: ```text API Container A API Container B API Container C ``` You don't want important user data stored only inside Container A. Why? Container A could disappear. Instead: ```text API ↓ Database ↓ Persistent storage ``` The application containers can be replaced freely. This principle becomes extremely important in Kubernetes and cloud architecture. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 46. One Main Process
text: A common container design principle is: > A container should generally have one primary responsibility/process. For example: ```text Container 1 → Node API Container 2 → Redis Container 3 → PostgreSQL ``` Rather than: ```text One container ├── Node ├── PostgreSQL ├── Redis └── Nginx ``` This makes scaling and lifecycle management easier. There are exceptions and specialized designs, but this is the standard mental model. ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 47. Docker Compose — Preview
text: If you have: ```text Node API PostgreSQL Redis ``` managing three separate `docker run` commands becomes annoying. Docker Compose lets you describe a multi-container application declaratively. Example: ```yaml services: api: build: . ports: - "3000:3000" postgres: image: postgres:17 redis: image: redis:7 ``` Then: ```bash docker compose up ``` creates the required services. We'll cover Compose properly in [Chapter 8](ch08-docker-production.md). ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 48. Docker vs Kubernetes
text: Don't confuse these.

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Docker
text: Primarily helps you: ```text Build Package Run Distribute ``` containers.

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Kubernetes
text: Helps you manage containers at scale: ```text Deploy Scale Network Self-heal Roll out Roll back ``` across a cluster. Conceptually: ```text Docker ↓ Containerization Kubernetes ↓ Container orchestration ``` We'll reach Kubernetes in Chapters [18](../05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md)–[20](../05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md). ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 49. Complete Docker Workflow
text: You should now visualize: ```text Source Code │ ↓ Dockerfile │ ↓ docker build │ ↓ Docker Image │ ┌───────┴───────┐ ↓ ↓ Registry Local │ ↓ docker pull │ ↓ Container │ ┌────┴────┐ ↓ ↓ Network Volume ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: 50. What You Should Be Able to Do Now
text: By the end of Chapter 7, you should be comfortable with:

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Commands
text: ```bash docker pull docker images docker build docker run docker ps docker ps -a docker stop docker start docker restart docker rm docker logs docker exec docker inspect docker volume ```

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Dockerfile
text: Understand: ```dockerfile FROM WORKDIR COPY RUN EXPOSE CMD ```

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Concepts
text: ```text Image Container Registry Layer Build context Port mapping Environment variables Volumes Networks Container lifecycle Container vs VM ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Practical Lab
text: Create a small TypeScript API.

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Step 1 — Build normally
text: ```bash npm install npm run build npm start ``` Verify: ```text localhost:3000 ```

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Step 2 — Create Dockerfile
text: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] ```

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Step 3 — Create `.dockerignore`
text: ```text node_modules .git .env dist ```

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Step 4 — Build
text: ```bash docker build -t my-api:1.0 . ```

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Step 5 — Run
text: ```bash docker run -p 3000:3000 --name my-api my-api:1.0 ```

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Step 6 — Check
text: ```bash docker ps docker logs my-api ```

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Step 7 — Debug
text: ```bash docker exec -it my-api sh ``` Explore: ```bash ls ``` Then: ```bash exit ``` ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Interview Questions
text: Make sure you can explain these in simple language: 1. What is Docker? 2. Docker container vs VM? 3. Image vs container? 4. What is a Dockerfile? 5. What does `FROM` do? 6. `RUN` vs `CMD`? 7. What does `EXPOSE` actually do? 8. What does `-p 3000:3000` mean? 9. Why use `0.0.0.0` in a containerized Node server? 10. What is a Docker layer? 11. Why is Docker caching useful? 12. What is a Docker registry? 13. What is a volume? 14. Volume vs bind mount? 15. Why shouldn't important application state live only inside a container? 16. What is `.dockerignore`? 17. Why shouldn't `.env` or secrets be copied into an image? 18. What happens when you run `docker run nginx`? 19. How do you inspect container logs? 20. How do you execute a command inside a running container? 21. What happens when a container's main process exits? 22. Why are stateless containers useful for scaling? ---

title: Chapter 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: One Scenario You Should Understand
text: Interviewer: > "Your Node.js application works locally but doesn't respond when running inside Docker. What would you check?" Think systematically: ```text 1. Is container running? ↓ docker ps 2. Did application crash? ↓ docker logs 3. Is Node listening on correct port? ↓ 3000 4. Is it bound to 0.0.0.0? ↓ not only localhost 5. Did you publish the port? ↓ -p 3000:3000 6. Is Dockerfile correct? ↓ COPY / RUN / CMD 7. Are environment variables present? ↓ docker exec / configuration 8. Is another service unreachable? ↓ Docker networking ``` That's **DevOps troubleshooting thinking**, rather than memorizing Docker commands. <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 6: CI/CD + GitHub Actions](../03-cicd-gitops/ch06-cicd-github-actions.md) · [Chapter 8: Docker Deep Dive + Production](ch08-docker-production.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch07-revision.md)

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Why Docker
text: "Works on my machine" (Node 22 vs Node 20, different OS, npm version, missing deps) → package **app + dependencies + runtime config** into an **image**, run it as a **container** anywhere. A container is an **isolated process environment sharing the host kernel — not a tiny VM**. | VM | Container | |---|---| | Hypervisor + full guest OS per VM | Shares host OS kernel via container runtime | | Heavier, slower to boot | Lighter, faster start, more efficient | | Different isolation model | Isolated *process* — not "a small VM" |

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Core objects
text: - **Image** = immutable blueprint (class). **Container** = running/created instance (object). One image → many containers. - **Dockerfile** (build recipe), **Registry** (Docker Hub / GHCR / ECR), **Volume** (persistent data), later **Network**, **Compose**. - **Architecture:** Docker CLI → Docker Daemon → images, containers, networks, volumes. - **Layers:** every instruction adds a cached layer; unchanged layers are reused → fast rebuilds. - **Tags:** `repository:tag` (`my-api:1.0`, `latest`). Prefer immutable/version-specific tags in production.

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Dockerfile (TypeScript backend)
text: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 # base image WORKDIR /app # working dir for later instructions COPY package*.json ./ # copy manifests first (cache!) RUN npm ci # build-time: install deps COPY . . # then the rest of the source RUN npm run build # build-time: compile TS EXPOSE 3000 # documentation only – does NOT publish CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] # default process at container START ``` | Instruction | Key point | |---|---| | `FROM` | Base image; images are built from other images | | `WORKDIR` | Like `cd /app` for the rest of the file | | `COPY` | Copy from build context into image | | `RUN` | Executes **during image build** | | `CMD` | Default process when the **container starts** | | `EXPOSE` | Documents the port; you still need `-p` | **Why copy `package*.json` first?** If you `COPY . .` before `npm ci`, any source change invalidates the dependency layer. Copying manifests first lets Docker reuse the cached `npm ci` layer when only source changes. **Build:** `docker build -t my-api:1.0 .` — `-t` names/tags, `.` = **build context** (files Docker may `COPY`). **`.dockerignore`:** `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env`, `dist`, `npm-debug.log` — keeps junk and especially secrets out of the context.

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Commands
text: | Task | Command | |---|---| | Check | `docker --version`, `docker info`, `docker help` | | Pull / list | `docker pull node:22`, `docker images` | | Run | `docker run hello-world`, `docker run node:22 node --version`, `docker run -it ubuntu bash` (`-i` interactive, `-t` terminal), `docker run -d nginx` (detached), `docker run -d --name my-nginx nginx` | | Lifecycle | `docker ps` (running), `docker ps -a` (all), `docker stop/start/restart/rm my-nginx` | | Debug | `docker logs my-nginx`, `docker logs -f my-nginx`, `docker exec -it my-nginx bash` (or `sh` if no bash), `docker inspect` | | Ports | `docker run -p 3000:3000 my-api` → `-p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT` | | Env | `docker run -e DB_PASSWORD="..." my-api:1.0` | | Volumes | `docker volume create postgres-data`; `docker run -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres` | | Registry | `docker push`, `docker pull my-api:1.0` | | Compose | `docker compose up` | **Stop ≠ remove:** `docker stop` leaves the container (visible in `docker ps -a`); `docker rm` deletes it. **Lifecycle:** Created → Running → Stopped → Removed. A container normally exists to run a process; when the **main process exits, the container stops** (e.g. `exit` from the shell).

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Networking & ports
text: - Inside a container **`localhost` = the container itself** — not your laptop, not another container. - Bind Node to **`0.0.0.0`** (`app.listen(3000, "0.0.0.0")`) so the server is reachable through the container's network interface. Then publish with `-p`. - Request path: Browser → `localhost:3000` → Docker host port 3000 → container port 3000 → Node.js. - Containers can talk to each other via Docker networks without exposing every service to the host (deep dive: [Chapter 8](../docs/02-containers/ch08-docker-production.md)).

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Persistence
text: - Container writable layers aren't a good home for important data; removing the container loses it. - **Volume** = Docker-managed persistent storage. **Bind mount** = host path ↔ container (good for local dev: `-v ./src:/app/src`; see note below). - **Stateless containers:** keep user data in DB/persistent storage so app containers can be replaced freely — key for scaling, Kubernetes and cloud. - **One main process per container** (Node, Redis, PostgreSQL in separate containers) → easier scaling and lifecycle management (exceptions exist).

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Compose preview
text: ```yaml services: api: build: . ports: ["3000:3000"] postgres: image: postgres:17 redis: image: redis:7 ```

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Docker vs Kubernetes
text: Docker = build, package, run, distribute containers. Kubernetes = orchestrate at scale: deploy, scale, network, self-heal, roll out, roll back.

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Same image everywhere
text: Developer machine → image → CI/CD → registry → AWS → Kubernetes. The **same image** moves Testing → Staging → Production.

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Secrets
text: Never hardcode (`const dbPassword = "mypassword"`); read `process.env.DB_PASSWORD`. Don't copy `.env`/secrets into images. In real production use secret-management systems rather than command history/deployment files.

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Scenario — "works locally, not in Docker"
text: 1. Container running? (`docker ps`) 2. Crashed? (`docker logs`) 3. Correct port? 4. Bound to `0.0.0.0`? 5. Port published (`-p 3000:3000`)? 6. Dockerfile correct (COPY/RUN/CMD)? 7. Env vars present (`docker exec`)? 8. Another service unreachable → Docker networking.

title: Revision 7 — Docker Fundamentals
heading: Verification notes (see [Corrections](../CORRECTIONS.md))
text: - Relative paths in `docker run -v ./src:/app/src` — use `-v "$(pwd)/src:/app/src"` to be safe. - Official `postgres` image layout changed in newer major versions; check the image README when mounting the data volume.

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
text: > **Source:** Response 8 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-08.txt`, lines 119–1661) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch08-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) · *includes an editorial supplement at the end* <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> [Chapter 7](ch07-docker-fundamentals.md) taught you: > **What Docker is and how to use it.** Now the goal is: > **Build Docker images that are efficient, secure, reproducible, debuggable, and suitable for production.** This is where Docker becomes an actual engineering skill rather than a collection of commands. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 1. Production Docker Architecture
text: Our basic application: ```text TypeScript Source ↓ Dockerfile ↓ docker build ↓ Docker Image ↓ Container ↓ Node.js API ``` Production adds: ```text Developer ↓ Git ↓ CI/CD ↓ Docker Build ↓ Image Registry ↓ Deployment Platform ↓ Containers ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Users ``` Later: ```text AWS │ Load Balancer │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Container Container Container │ │ │ └─────────┼─────────┘ ↓ Database ``` ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 2. Why Our First Dockerfile Isn't Production-Ready
text: We previously had: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] ``` It works. But there are problems. For example: - Development dependencies may remain in the final image. - The image may be unnecessarily large. - The application may run as root. - Build tools don't necessarily belong in production. - We could improve caching. - We haven't added a health check. - We haven't separated build and runtime environments. This leads us to **multi-stage builds**. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 3. Multi-Stage Builds
text: Suppose: ```text Build environment ``` needs: ```text TypeScript tsc dev dependencies build tools ``` But production only needs: ```text Node.js compiled JavaScript production dependencies ``` Why ship the build tools? We don't need them. So: ```text Build Stage ↓ Compile ↓ Production Stage ↓ Copy only required output ``` ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 4. Multi-Stage Dockerfile
text: Example: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY tsconfig.json ./ COPY src ./src RUN npm run build FROM node:22-slim AS production WORKDIR /app ENV NODE_ENV=production COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] ``` Now we have: ```text Stage 1 builder ├── dependencies ├── source ├── TypeScript └── build tools ↓ dist ↓ Stage 2 production ├── Node ├── production dependencies └── dist ``` The final image doesn't need the TypeScript compiler. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 5. Why Multi-Stage Builds Matter
text: Suppose your build environment is: ```text 800 MB ``` while the runtime requires: ```text 200 MB ``` Without multi-stage builds: ```text Production image ≈ 800 MB ``` With multi-stage: ```text Production image ≈ 200 MB ``` Smaller images can mean: - faster pulls - faster deployments - less storage - smaller attack surface ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 6. Build Dependencies vs Runtime Dependencies
text: This distinction is important.

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Build dependencies
text: Needed to create the application: ```text TypeScript tsc Webpack/Vite/etc. test tooling ```

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Runtime dependencies
text: Needed to execute it: ```text Express Fastify database drivers application libraries ``` Production image should ideally contain only what it needs. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 7. `npm ci --omit=dev`
text: In production: ```bash npm ci --omit=dev ``` means: > Install dependencies while excluding development dependencies. So things like test frameworks don't need to be shipped with the production application. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 8. Docker Layer Caching
text: Remember layers? Consider: ```dockerfile COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . ``` Suppose you change: ```text src/user.ts ``` but not: ```text package.json package-lock.json ``` Docker can potentially reuse: ```text RUN npm ci ``` instead of reinstalling everything. Therefore: ```text Dependencies unchanged ↓ Reuse dependency layer ↓ Build faster ``` This is why Dockerfile instruction ordering matters. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 9. Bad Layer Ordering
text: Avoid: ```dockerfile COPY . . RUN npm ci ``` when you can structure it as: ```dockerfile COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . ``` Because source-code changes happen frequently. Dependencies generally change less frequently. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 10. `.dockerignore`
text: A good Node project might have: ```text node_modules .git .github .env .env.* dist coverage npm-debug.log Dockerfile* docker-compose* README.md ``` But be careful. Don't blindly exclude files your build actually requires. The principle is: > **Send only the files required to build the image.** ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 11. Never Put Secrets in the Image
text: Bad: ```dockerfile ENV DATABASE_PASSWORD=myPassword ``` or: ```dockerfile COPY .env . ``` Why? Because secrets can end up inside image layers or otherwise become accessible through image history/artifacts. Instead: ```text Secret Manager ↓ Deployment environment ↓ Container ↓ process.env ``` For example: ```typescript const databaseUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL; ``` We'll later use AWS's secret-management capabilities. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 12. Run Containers as Non-Root
text: Containers shouldn't unnecessarily run the application as root. Example: ```dockerfile FROM node:22-slim WORKDIR /app RUN useradd --system --uid 1001 appuser COPY --chown=appuser:appuser package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev COPY --chown=appuser:appuser dist ./dist USER appuser CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] ``` Now the application runs as: ```text appuser ``` rather than root. This is a security hardening technique. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 13. Why Root Is Dangerous
text: Suppose an application vulnerability allows an attacker to execute commands. If the process runs as root: ```text Application vulnerability ↓ Command execution ↓ Root privileges ``` Potential impact can be greater. With a non-root process: ```text Application vulnerability ↓ Command execution ↓ Limited privileges ``` This is an example of: > **Principle of least privilege** Give processes only the permissions they need. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 14. Docker Health Checks
text: Your container being alive doesn't necessarily mean your application is healthy. For example: ```text Container = running Node process = running Database connection = broken API = unusable ``` So health checks can test application health. Example endpoint: ```typescript app.get("/health", (_req, res) => { res.status(200).json({ status: "ok" }); }); ``` Then Docker can perform a health check. Example: ```dockerfile HEALTHCHECK \ --interval=30s \ --timeout=5s \ --start-period=10s \ --retries=3 \ CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/health').then(r => { if (!r.ok) process.exit(1) }).catch(() => process.exit(1))" ``` The important distinction: ```text Running ≠ Healthy ``` ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 15. Liveness vs Readiness
text: You'll encounter these more heavily in Kubernetes.

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Liveness
text: > Is the application still alive?

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Readiness
text: > Is the application ready to receive traffic? Imagine: ```text Container started ↓ Node starting ↓ Database connection initializing ↓ Application ready ``` During startup: ```text Alive = yes Ready = no ``` That's why production orchestration systems distinguish these concepts. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 16. Docker Networking
text: Now let's understand containers communicating with each other. Suppose: ```text API PostgreSQL Redis ``` You could have: ```text API container │ ├──── PostgreSQL container │ └──── Redis container ``` Docker networks allow containers to communicate over a virtual network. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 17. Create a Network
text: ```bash docker network create app-network ``` Then: ```bash docker run -d \ --name postgres \ --network app-network \ postgres ``` And: ```bash docker run -d \ --name api \ --network app-network \ my-api ``` Containers on the same Docker network can communicate using service/container names in appropriate configurations. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 18. Don't Use Container IPs
text: Avoid hardcoding: ```text 172.x.x.x ``` for another container. Container IPs can change. Instead use a stable service/container name where supported. For example: ```text postgres ``` Conceptually: ```text API ↓ postgres ↓ PostgreSQL container ``` This is similar to service discovery. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 19. Host Port vs Container Port
text: This distinction is crucial. Suppose: ```bash docker run -p 8080:3000 my-api ``` means: ```text Host 8080 ↓ Container 3000 ``` So users access: ```text localhost:8080 ``` while Node listens on: ```text 3000 ``` inside the container. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 20. Container-to-Container Ports
text: Suppose API connects to PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL listens on: ```text 5432 ``` The API doesn't need PostgreSQL's host-published port if both containers are on the same Docker network. It can connect to: ```text postgres:5432 ``` rather than: ```text localhost:5432 ``` This is one of the most common Docker networking mistakes. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 21. Docker Compose
text: Managing: ```text API PostgreSQL Redis ``` manually is annoying. Compose lets you describe the application in YAML. Example: ```yaml services: api: build: . ports: - "3000:3000" environment: DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:password@postgres:5432/app REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379 depends_on: - postgres - redis postgres: image: postgres:17 environment: POSTGRES_USER: postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password POSTGRES_DB: app volumes: - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data redis: image: redis:7 volumes: postgres-data: ``` Then: ```bash docker compose up ``` You get: ```text Docker Network │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ API PostgreSQL Redis │ ↓ Volume ``` ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 22. `depends_on`
text: We used: ```yaml depends_on: - postgres - redis ``` This expresses startup dependency ordering. But here's an important production concept: > **Starting a dependency does not necessarily mean the dependency is ready.** PostgreSQL container may be running while PostgreSQL itself is still initializing. Therefore robust systems need proper health/readiness handling and application-level retry behavior. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 23. Application Retry Logic
text: Imagine: ```text API starts ↓ Database unavailable ↓ API crashes ``` A more resilient application might: ```text API starts ↓ Database unavailable ↓ Wait ↓ Retry ↓ Retry ↓ Database available ↓ Start serving ``` This is especially important in distributed systems because startup ordering isn't a guarantee of service readiness. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 24. Resource Limits
text: A container can consume significant resources if unrestricted. You can impose limits in appropriate container runtimes/configurations. Conceptually: ```text Container ├── CPU limit └── Memory limit ``` Why? Imagine: ```text Container A → memory leak ↓ Consumes all host memory ↓ Other applications affected ``` Resource limits help prevent one workload from consuming everything. Kubernetes provides much richer resource management later. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 25. Container Logs
text: Applications should generally write logs to: ```text stdout stderr ``` For example: ```typescript console.log("Server started"); console.error("Database connection failed"); ``` Then: ```bash docker logs api ``` can retrieve them. This is preferable to relying on arbitrary log files inside ephemeral containers. Later, cloud logging systems can collect these streams. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 26. Don't Treat Containers Like Traditional Servers
text: Traditional mindset: ```text SSH into server Edit files Restart process ``` Container mindset: ```text Build new image ↓ Deploy new container ↓ Replace old container ``` Instead of manually modifying production containers. Why? Because containers are intended to be **reproducible and replaceable**. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 27. Immutable Infrastructure
text: This leads to an important DevOps concept: > **Don't manually patch production instances whenever possible; build a new version and replace the old one.** Instead of: ```text Production container ↓ SSH ↓ apt install something ↓ manual changes ``` prefer: ```text Dockerfile ↓ New image ↓ Test ↓ Deploy ``` Now the infrastructure/application artifact is reproducible. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 28. Docker Image Security
text: Important security practices: ```text Use trusted base images ↓ Keep images updated ↓ Run as non-root ↓ Don't embed secrets ↓ Minimize packages ↓ Scan images ↓ Use least privilege ``` For example, instead of: ```dockerfile FROM ubuntu ``` and installing everything manually, a purpose-built runtime image may be smaller. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 29. Alpine vs Slim
text: You'll often see: ```text node:22 node:22-slim node:22-alpine ``` The general idea: ```text Full image ↓ More packages Slim ↓ Fewer packages Alpine ↓ Very small base ``` But: > **Smaller does not automatically mean better.** Some packages/native dependencies can behave differently on Alpine because Alpine commonly uses musl libc rather than glibc. So don't blindly choose Alpine just because it has a small image size. For many Node applications, a Debian-based slim image is a straightforward production choice. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 30. Image Scanning
text: Before deploying: ```text Docker Image ↓ Vulnerability Scanner ↓ Potential CVEs ``` You want to identify: - vulnerable OS packages - vulnerable application dependencies - outdated base images This can be integrated into CI/CD. Conceptually: ```text Git Push ↓ Tests ↓ Docker Build ↓ Image Scan ↓ Push ↓ Deploy ``` ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 31. Docker Image Tagging
text: Avoid relying entirely on: ```text latest ``` Instead: ```text my-api:1.4.2 my-api:git-a82f9c1 ``` or another immutable identifier. Then: ```text Production ↓ my-api:git-a82f9c1 ``` You know exactly which build is running. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 32. Registry Workflow
text: The production workflow becomes: ```text Dockerfile ↓ docker build ↓ Image ↓ docker tag ↓ docker push ↓ Registry ``` Another machine: ```text Registry ↓ docker pull ↓ docker run ``` In AWS: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ Docker build ↓ Amazon ECR ↓ ECS / EKS / EC2 ``` We'll learn ECR and AWS compute later. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 33. Docker + CI/CD
text: Now connect Chapters 6–8. ```text Developer ↓ Git push ↓ GitHub ↓ CI ├── Lint ├── Typecheck ├── Tests └── Build ↓ Docker Build ↓ Image Scan ↓ Push Image ↓ Registry ↓ Deploy ``` This is a very important architecture to understand for interviews. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 34. Production Dockerfile
text: A more realistic TypeScript example: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY tsconfig.json ./ COPY src ./src RUN npm run build FROM node:22-slim AS production WORKDIR /app ENV NODE_ENV=production COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist RUN useradd --system --uid 1001 appuser \ && chown -R appuser:appuser /app USER appuser EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] ``` Notice the principles: ```text Multi-stage + Dependency caching + Production dependencies only + Smaller runtime image + Non-root user + No secrets + Immutable artifact ``` ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 35. What Happens When You Deploy This?
text: Imagine: ```text git push ``` Then: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ npm ci ↓ tests ↓ npm run build ↓ docker build ↓ my-api:commit-sha ↓ image scan ↓ ECR ↓ deployment platform ↓ new container ↓ health check ↓ traffic ``` That's a genuine production-style workflow. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 36. Docker Troubleshooting Framework
text: If a container isn't working, don't randomly restart things. Use:

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 1. Is it running?
text: ```bash docker ps ```

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 2. Did it exit?
text: ```bash docker ps -a ```

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 3. Why did it exit?
text: ```bash docker logs <container> ```

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 4. Inspect configuration
text: ```bash docker inspect <container> ```

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 5. Enter container
text: ```bash docker exec -it <container> sh ```

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 6. Check networking
text: ```bash docker network ls docker network inspect <network> ```

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: 7. Check ports
text: ```bash docker port <container> ``` This is a repeatable debugging methodology. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Problem 1
text: ```text Container immediately exits ``` Check: ```bash docker logs ``` Likely application/process failure. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Problem 2
text: ```text Cannot access localhost:3000 ``` Check: ```text Application binding Port mapping Container status Firewall/networking ``` ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Problem 3
text: ```text API cannot connect to PostgreSQL ``` Check: ```text Same Docker network? Correct hostname? Correct port? Credentials? Database ready? ``` Remember: ```text localhost ``` inside API means the API container itself. ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Problem 4
text: ```text Image is huge ``` Investigate: ```text Base image Dependencies Layers Build artifacts Multi-stage build .dockerignore ``` ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Problem 5
text: ```text Secret appears in image ``` Bad: ```text COPY .env . ``` Fix: ```text Remove secret from image Rotate exposed secret Use runtime secret injection ``` ---

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: The Most Important Mental Model
text: Don't memorize Docker commands independently. Think: ```text DOCKER │ ┌────────┼────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Build Run Distribute │ │ │ Dockerfile Container Registry │ │ │ ↓ ↓ ↓ Image Network Push/Pull Volume │ ↓ Production ``` And production: ```text Git ↓ CI/CD ↓ Docker Build ↓ Security Scan ↓ Image Registry ↓ Deployment Platform ↓ Containers ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Users ``` That architecture will keep appearing throughout the rest of this roadmap. <!-- SOURCE-END --> ---
