text: > **Added by the knowledge-base editor — not part of the original source.** It fills gaps the source leaves open (for example concepts named in the interview list but never explained, or configuration the chapter only describes in words). Treat the text above as the original material and this section as clearly separated additions.

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: `CMD` vs `ENTRYPOINT` (asked in the interview list, not explained in the chapter body)
text: Both define what runs when a container starts. | | `ENTRYPOINT` | `CMD` | |---|---|---| | Role | The executable that **always** runs | The **default** command/arguments | | Overriding at `docker run` | Hard: needs `--entrypoint` | Easy: anything after the image name replaces it | | Typical use | Make the image behave like one program | Provide default arguments or a default command | ```dockerfile # CMD only – `docker run my-api sh` replaces the whole command CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] # ENTRYPOINT + CMD – CMD becomes the default *arguments* to ENTRYPOINT ENTRYPOINT ["node"] CMD ["dist/index.js"] # `docker run my-api dist/other.js` runs node dist/other.js ``` **Exec form vs shell form.** `CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]` (JSON array, *exec form*) starts Node directly as **PID 1**, so it receives signals such as `SIGTERM` from `docker stop` (see the signal discussion in [Chapter 2](../01-foundations/ch02-linux.md)). `CMD node dist/index.js` (*shell form*) runs under `/bin/sh -c`, and the shell may not forward signals, which breaks graceful shutdown. A process running as PID 1 also has no default signal handlers on Linux, so a Node server should handle `SIGTERM` itself, or you can run the container with `docker run --init` (a tiny init process).

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Node images already contain a non-root user
text: The chapter creates `appuser` with `useradd`. The official `node` images also ship a non-root user called `node` (UID 1000), so `USER node` is a common alternative that needs no `useradd`.

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Resource limits in practice
text: The chapter describes limits conceptually. With plain Docker: ```bash docker run -d --memory=512m --cpus=1.0 my-api:1.0 ``` A container that exceeds its memory limit can be killed by the kernel's out-of-memory (OOM) killer. Kubernetes expresses the same idea as resource *requests* and *limits* (see [Chapter 20](../05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md)).

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: `depends_on` with real readiness
text: To wait until PostgreSQL is actually ready (not just started), give it a healthcheck and use a health condition: ```yaml services: postgres: image: postgres:17 environment: POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"] interval: 5s timeout: 3s retries: 10 api: build: . depends_on: postgres: condition: service_healthy ``` Application-level retry logic (section 23) is still recommended: a database can become unavailable after startup too.

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Container name resolution works only on user-defined networks
text: On the default `bridge` network, containers can reach each other by IP but **not by name**. Containers on a **user-defined** bridge network (such as `app-network`, or the network Compose creates automatically) get automatic DNS resolution of container/service names. That is why the chapter's `docker network create app-network` step matters.

title: Chapter 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Why the health check uses Node instead of `curl`
text: `node:22-slim` does not ship `curl`. The `HEALTHCHECK` in section 14 therefore uses the Node runtime that is already in the image (`fetch` is built into modern Node), avoiding an extra package in the final image. --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 7: Docker Fundamentals](ch07-docker-fundamentals.md) · [Chapter 9: AWS Fundamentals + IAM](../04-aws/ch09-aws-fundamentals-iam.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch08-revision.md)

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Chapter 8 — Revision Sheet: Docker Deep Dive + Production
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/02-containers/ch08-docker-production.md). Goal: images that are **efficient, secure, reproducible, debuggable, production-ready**.

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Why the first Dockerfile isn't production-ready
text: Dev dependencies remain in the final image · image unnecessarily large · runs as root · build tools shipped to production · caching could be better · no health check · build and runtime not separated.

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Multi-stage build
text: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY tsconfig.json ./ COPY src ./src RUN npm run build FROM node:22-slim AS production WORKDIR /app ENV NODE_ENV=production COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist RUN useradd --system --uid 1001 appuser && chown -R appuser:appuser /app USER appuser EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] ``` - Build stage has TypeScript, `tsc`, dev deps, source; final stage has only Node, **production deps**, and `dist`. - Example sizing: ~800 MB build env vs ~200 MB runtime → **faster pulls/deploys, less storage, smaller attack surface**. - **Build deps** (TypeScript, `tsc`, Webpack/Vite, test tooling) vs **runtime deps** (Express, Fastify, DB drivers). - `npm ci --omit=dev` = install without devDependencies.

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Layer caching
text: Order instructions from least → most frequently changing: `COPY package*.json` → `RUN npm ci` → `COPY . .`. Change `src/user.ts` only → `npm ci` layer is reused. **Bad ordering:** `COPY . .` before `npm ci`.

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: `.dockerignore` (extended)
text: `node_modules`, `.git`, `.github`, `.env`, `.env.*`, `dist`, `coverage`, `npm-debug.log`, `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `README.md`. Principle: **send only what the build needs** — but don't exclude files the build actually requires.

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Security
text: | Practice | Why | |---|---| | Never `ENV DATABASE_PASSWORD=…` or `COPY .env .` | Secrets persist in image layers/history | | Inject secrets at runtime (Secret Manager → deployment env → container → `process.env`) | Keeps images clean | | `USER appuser` (non-root) | **Least privilege**: exploit yields limited privileges not root | | Trusted, updated, minimal base images; minimise packages | Smaller attack surface | | **Scan images** (OS packages, app deps, outdated bases → CVEs) in CI before push | Catch vulnerabilities early | | Immutable infrastructure | Don't SSH into prod containers and patch; rebuild image → test → deploy → replace | **Alpine vs slim:** `node:22` (full), `node:22-slim` (fewer packages), `node:22-alpine` (very small). Smaller ≠ automatically better — Alpine uses **musl libc** (not glibc), so some native modules behave differently. For many Node apps a Debian **slim** image is a safe production choice.

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Health, liveness, readiness
text: - **Running ≠ Healthy** (container up + Node up + DB connection broken = unusable API). - `/health` endpoint + Dockerfile `HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=10s --retries=3 CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/health')…"`. - **Liveness** = is it alive? **Readiness** = can it receive traffic? During startup: alive yes, ready no. Heavily used in Kubernetes.

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Networking
text: ```bash docker network create app-network docker run -d --name postgres --network app-network postgres docker run -d --name api --network app-network my-api ``` - Use service/container **names** (`postgres:5432`), not container IPs (`172.x.x.x`, which change). - `-p 8080:3000` → host 8080 → container 3000; users hit `localhost:8080`. - Container-to-container on the same network needs **no host-published port**: use `postgres:5432` not `localhost:5432`. (Most common Docker networking mistake: `localhost` inside API = the API container.)

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Compose (full example)
text: ```yaml services: api: build: . ports: ["3000:3000"] environment: DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:password@postgres:5432/app REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379 depends_on: [postgres, redis] postgres: image: postgres:17 environment: { POSTGRES_USER: postgres, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password, POSTGRES_DB: app } volumes: [postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data] redis: image: redis:7 volumes: postgres-data: ``` - `docker compose up` → one Docker network, three services, one volume. - **`depends_on` = start order, not readiness.** The Postgres container can be running while Postgres initialises → need health/readiness + **application retry logic** (API starts → DB unavailable → wait → retry → serve).

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Resource limits, logs, immutability
text: - Limit CPU/memory so a leaking container can't starve the host (Kubernetes does this far better, later). - **Log to stdout/stderr** (`console.log`, `console.error`) → `docker logs api` → cloud log collectors. Don't rely on files inside ephemeral containers. - Container mindset: **build new image → deploy new container → replace old**; don't SSH, edit, restart.

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Tagging & registry
text: Tags: `my-api:1.4.2`, `my-api:git-a82f9c1` — avoid relying on `latest`. Workflow: `docker build` → `docker tag` → `docker push` → registry; elsewhere `docker pull` → `docker run`. In AWS: GitHub Actions → build → **Amazon ECR** → ECS/EKS/EC2. Full CI/CD: push → lint → typecheck → tests → build → docker build (`my-api:commit-sha`) → image scan → push (ECR) → deploy → new container → health check → traffic.

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Troubleshooting framework
text: 1. `docker ps` (running?) 2. `docker ps -a` (exited?) 3. `docker logs <c>` (why?) 4. `docker inspect <c>` 5. `docker exec -it <c> sh` 6. `docker network ls` / `docker network inspect <n>` 7. `docker port <c>`. | Problem | Check | |---|---| | Container exits immediately | `docker logs` – app/process failure | | Can't reach `localhost:3000` | App binding (`0.0.0.0`), port mapping, container status, firewall | | API can't connect to PostgreSQL | Same network? hostname? port? credentials? DB ready? (`localhost` = API itself) | | Image is huge | Base image, deps, layers, build artifacts, multi-stage, `.dockerignore` | | Secret in image | Remove from image, **rotate the secret**, use runtime injection |

title: Revision 8 — Docker Deep Dive + Production
heading: Added (see supplement in the chapter)
text: `CMD` vs `ENTRYPOINT`; exec vs shell form & PID 1 signals; `USER node`; `--memory/--cpus`; Compose healthcheck + `service_healthy`; name resolution only on user-defined networks.

heading: Interview questions (29) — pointers

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
text: > **Source:** Response 9 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-09.txt`, lines 1–1484) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch09-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> Now we enter the **AWS section**, which is one of the highest-value parts of this roadmap for your SWE/backend placement preparation. The goal isn't to memorize hundreds of AWS services. The goal is to understand: > **How a real application is deployed, secured, connected, scaled, and operated on AWS.** We'll build that understanding service-by-service. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 1. What Is AWS?
text: **Amazon Web Services (AWS)** is a cloud platform that provides infrastructure and managed services over the internet. Instead of buying: ```text Servers Storage Networking equipment Databases Load balancers Firewalls ``` you can provision them through AWS. For example: ```text Your TypeScript API ↓ AWS ├── EC2 ├── RDS ├── S3 ├── VPC ├── IAM └── CloudWatch ``` You pay for the resources/services you use according to their pricing models. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 2. Why AWS Matters for You
text: As a backend/SWE engineer, you don't necessarily need to become an AWS administrator. But you should understand how your backend operates in the cloud. For example: ```text User ↓ DNS ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Node.js containers ↓ PostgreSQL ↓ S3 ``` And: ```text AWS │ ┌──────┴──────┐ ↓ ↓ Application Data │ │ EC2/ECS/EKS RDS/S3 ``` You should know **what each component does and why you'd use it**. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 3. AWS Global Infrastructure
text: Three concepts are fundamental: ```text Region Availability Zone Edge Location ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 4. Region
text: A **Region** is a geographic AWS location containing multiple Availability Zones. Examples: ```text ap-south-1 us-east-1 eu-west-1 ``` For example: ```text Mumbai Region │ ├── Availability Zone A ├── Availability Zone B └── Availability Zone C ``` You choose a region when deploying many AWS resources. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 5. Why Multiple Regions?
text: Suppose your application operates primarily in India. You might deploy in: ```text ap-south-1 ``` because geographical proximity can influence latency and regulatory/data requirements. For global systems, you might have: ```text Users ├── India → Mumbai ├── Europe → Europe region └── US → US region ``` Multi-region architecture can improve resilience and latency, but introduces substantial complexity. Don't assume: > "Multi-region is always better." It depends on the requirements. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 6. Availability Zone
text: An Availability Zone, or **AZ**, is an isolated location within an AWS Region designed to reduce the impact of failures. Conceptually: ```text AWS Region │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ AZ-A AZ-B AZ-C ``` You don't want your entire production system depending on one AZ. For example: ```text Bad: API → AZ-A only ``` If AZ-A has a major failure: ```text API ❌ ``` Better: ```text Load Balancer / \ AZ-A AZ-B │ │ API API ``` We'll use this heavily when we discuss load balancing and scaling. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 7. Region vs Availability Zone
text: Interview question: > What's the difference between an AWS Region and an Availability Zone? Answer: > **A Region is a geographic AWS infrastructure area containing multiple isolated Availability Zones. An Availability Zone is an isolated location within a Region used to improve availability and fault isolation.** Remember: ```text Region ├── AZ ├── AZ └── AZ ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 8. Edge Locations
text: AWS also operates edge locations closer to end users. These are important for services such as: ```text CloudFront ``` which we'll study later. Conceptually: ```text Origin │ ↓ CloudFront │ ├── Edge location → India ├── Edge location → Europe └── Edge location → US ``` Users can retrieve cached content from locations closer to them. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 9. AWS Account
text: An AWS account is an important security and billing boundary. Inside your account you can have: ```text IAM VPCs EC2 S3 RDS Lambda etc. ``` Organizations may use multiple AWS accounts: ```text AWS Organization │ ├── Production account ├── Development account ├── Security account └── Logging account ``` For your interview preparation, understand the concept rather than memorizing enterprise account structures. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 10. IAM — The Most Important AWS Security Concept
text: IAM = **Identity and Access Management**. It answers: > **Who are you, and what are you allowed to do?** For example: ```text Developer ↓ Can access EC2 Cannot delete production database ``` or: ```text Node.js application ↓ Can read S3 bucket Cannot modify IAM ``` This is authorization. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 11. Authentication vs Authorization
text: Very important.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Authentication
text: > Who are you? Example: ```text Username + password MFA Access credentials ```

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Authorization
text: > What are you allowed to do? Example: ```text Read S3 Write S3 Delete S3 Launch EC2 ``` Think: ```text Authentication ↓ WHO? ↓ Authorization ↓ WHAT? ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 12. IAM Components
text: The main things you should understand are: ```text IAM User IAM Group IAM Role IAM Policy ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 13. IAM User
text: An IAM user represents an identity within an AWS account. Example: ```text Alice ↓ IAM User ``` A user can have permissions attached directly or through groups/policies. Historically, developers sometimes used IAM users with long-lived access keys for CLI/programmatic access. For production workloads, however, AWS generally recommends using **IAM roles and temporary credentials** instead of embedding long-lived credentials. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 14. IAM Group
text: A group allows permissions to be managed for multiple users. Example: ```text Developers │ ├── Alice ├── Bob └── Charlie ``` You can attach policies to the group. Then the users inherit those permissions. This avoids manually attaching identical permissions to every user. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 15. IAM Role
text: **Roles are extremely important.** A role is an identity that can be assumed by a trusted entity. For example: ```text EC2 ↓ Assume IAM Role ↓ Temporary credentials ↓ Access S3 ``` Your application doesn't need: ```text AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=... ``` hardcoded inside the application. Instead: ```text EC2 ↓ IAM Role ↓ Temporary credentials ↓ AWS API ``` This is a much better security model. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 16. Example
text: Suppose your Node.js backend needs to upload files to S3. Bad architecture: ```text Node.js ↓ Hardcoded AWS credentials ↓ S3 ``` Better: ```text Node.js ↓ EC2/ECS/EKS ↓ IAM Role ↓ Temporary AWS credentials ↓ S3 ``` This is an extremely useful interview answer. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 17. IAM Policy
text: A policy defines permissions. A policy is generally represented as JSON. Example: ```json { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*" } ] } ``` This essentially says: ```text Allow ↓ s3:GetObject ↓ objects inside my-bucket ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 18. Understanding the Policy
text: Break it down: ```json "Effect": "Allow" ``` means permission is allowed. ```json "Action": "s3:GetObject" ``` defines what operation is allowed. ```json "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*" ``` defines what resource the permission applies to. Conceptually: ```text WHO ↓ CAN DO WHAT ↓ TO WHICH RESOURCE ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 19. Least Privilege
text: This is one of the most important security principles. Suppose your API only needs: ```text Read S3 objects ``` Don't give it: ```text AdministratorAccess ``` Instead: ```text s3:GetObject ``` for the required bucket/path. Think: ```text Required permission ↓ Give exactly that ↓ Nothing unnecessary ``` This is **least privilege**. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 20. Bad vs Good IAM
text: Bad: ```text Application ↓ AdministratorAccess ``` If the application is compromised: ```text Attacker ↓ Application ↓ Administrator permissions ↓ Potentially huge blast radius ``` Better: ```text Application ↓ Limited IAM role ↓ s3:GetObject ↓ Specific bucket ``` Now the potential blast radius is smaller. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 21. IAM Role vs IAM User
text: Very common interview question.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: User
text: Typically represents a person or persistent identity. ```text Developer ↓ IAM User ```

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Role
text: Designed to be assumed by trusted entities. ```text EC2 ↓ IAM Role ``` or: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ IAM Role ``` or: ```text Lambda ↓ IAM Role ``` Roles are particularly important for workloads because they can provide temporary credentials. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 22. IAM and CI/CD
text: Remember [Chapter 6](../03-cicd-gitops/ch06-cicd-github-actions.md)? We discussed GitHub Actions. Suppose: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ Deploy to AWS ``` A naive approach is storing: ```text AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY ``` as long-lived GitHub secrets. A better modern architecture is: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ OIDC ↓ AWS IAM Role ↓ Temporary credentials ↓ AWS ``` The key idea is: > **Use short-lived credentials and federated identity instead of long-lived static credentials where possible.** We'll use this when connecting CI/CD to AWS. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 23. AWS CLI
text: AWS provides a command-line interface. Install/configure it and then commands look like: ```bash aws sts get-caller-identity ``` This is an excellent command to understand. It tells you which AWS identity your CLI is currently using. Conceptually: ```text Your terminal ↓ AWS CLI ↓ AWS STS ↓ Current identity ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 24. Why `get-caller-identity` Is Useful
text: Suppose your deployment says: ```text AccessDenied ``` Before changing random permissions, check: ```bash aws sts get-caller-identity ``` You might discover: ```text Wrong account Wrong role Wrong identity ``` This is a very practical troubleshooting technique. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 25. AWS Credentials
text: AWS CLI/application SDKs need credentials to make authenticated API calls. Common sources include: ```text Environment variables AWS credential/config files IAM role credentials Federated identity ``` For cloud workloads, prefer role-based temporary credentials where applicable. Don't put credentials in: ```text Git repository Docker image Source code ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 26. AWS SDK with Node.js
text: Your TypeScript application can use AWS SDK packages. For example, S3. Conceptually: ```typescript import { S3Client } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3"; const s3 = new S3Client({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION }); ``` Notice something important: We didn't write: ```typescript const accessKey = "..."; const secretKey = "..."; ``` The AWS SDK can obtain credentials through the standard AWS credential provider mechanisms. This is the architecture you want. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 27. AWS Resource Naming
text: AWS resources often have identifiers such as: ```text ARN ``` ARN = **Amazon Resource Name**. Example: ```text arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket ``` An ARN uniquely identifies many AWS resources. IAM policies frequently use ARNs to specify resources. You don't need to memorize every ARN format. Understand: ```text ARN ↓ Specific AWS resource identifier ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 28. AWS Shared Responsibility Model
text: Very important for interviews. AWS secures: ```text Cloud infrastructure Physical facilities Hardware Underlying infrastructure ``` You are responsible for things such as: ```text Your application IAM configuration Data Operating system configuration on certain services Network configuration Security settings ``` The exact responsibility varies depending on the service. Think: ```text AWS ↓ Security OF the cloud Customer ↓ Security IN the cloud ``` This is a simplification, but a useful mental model. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 29. Example: EC2
text: With EC2, you're responsible for more of the operating environment. Conceptually: ```text AWS ↓ Physical infrastructure ↓ Hypervisor ↓ EC2 instance ↓ Your responsibility ├── OS ├── Packages ├── Application └── Configuration ``` This is different from a more managed service where AWS handles more of the underlying infrastructure. We'll explore this in [Chapter 10](ch10-ec2-compute.md). ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 30. AWS VPC — Preview
text: You'll hear VPC constantly. VPC = **Virtual Private Cloud**. It gives you a logically isolated network in AWS. Conceptually: ```text AWS Region │ ↓ VPC │ ┌──┴───────────┐ ↓ ↓ Public subnet Private subnet ``` Inside it you'll eventually learn: ```text CIDR Subnets Route tables Internet Gateway NAT Gateway Security Groups NACLs ``` We already learned the networking fundamentals in [Chapter 4](../01-foundations/ch04-networking.md). Now we're going to map those concepts onto AWS. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 31. AWS Service Categories
text: You don't need to memorize every AWS service. Think in categories.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Compute
text: ```text EC2 Lambda ECS EKS ```

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Storage
text: ```text S3 EBS EFS ```

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Database
text: ```text RDS DynamoDB ElastiCache ```

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Networking
text: ```text VPC Route 53 CloudFront ELB ```

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Security
text: ```text IAM KMS WAF Secrets Manager ```

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Monitoring
text: ```text CloudWatch CloudTrail ``` We'll cover the important ones throughout the roadmap. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 32. AWS CLI Practical Flow
text: Suppose you have AWS CLI configured. Check identity: ```bash aws sts get-caller-identity ``` List S3 buckets: ```bash aws s3 ls ``` Get region configuration: ```bash aws configure get region ``` You can also specify a region: ```bash aws s3 ls --region ap-south-1 ``` The goal isn't to memorize every command. You should understand that: ```text AWS CLI ↓ AWS API ↓ AWS service ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 33. IAM Policy Evaluation — Basic Mental Model
text: When AWS receives a request: ```text Application ↓ AWS API request ↓ Identity ↓ Policies ↓ Allowed? ``` Conceptually: ```text Explicit Deny ↓ Overrides Allow ``` Otherwise, an explicit applicable Allow is needed. If no permission grants the action, the request is generally denied. This is why IAM debugging often involves examining: ```text Who? ↓ What action? ↓ Which resource? ↓ Which policies? ↓ Any explicit deny? ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 34. Common IAM Mistake
text: Suppose you have: ```text Role A ``` with: ```text s3:GetObject ``` but your application tries: ```text s3:PutObject ``` Result: ```text AccessDenied ``` The solution isn't: ```text Give AdministratorAccess ``` Instead ask: ```text Does the application actually need PutObject? ``` If yes: ```text Add narrowly scoped PutObject permission. ``` This demonstrates least-privilege thinking. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Rule 1
text: Don't commit credentials.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Rule 2
text: Don't put credentials in Docker images.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Rule 3
text: Prefer IAM roles for AWS workloads.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Rule 4
text: Use temporary credentials where possible.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Rule 5
text: Use least privilege.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Rule 6
text: Use MFA for appropriate human identities.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Rule 7
text: Don't give applications unnecessary administrative permissions. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 36. AWS Architecture We Are Building
text: You should now visualize the future architecture: ```text AWS │ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ Region │ │ │ │ VPC │ │ │ │ ┌─────┐ │ │ │ ALB │ │ │ └──┬──┘ │ │ │ │ │ ┌──┴───┐ │ │ │ EC2 │ │ │ │ API │ │ │ └──┬───┘ │ │ │ │ │ RDS │ │ │ └───────────┘ ``` And IAM controls who/what can access these resources. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 37. Connect This to Docker
text: Previously: ```text Docker ↓ Container ↓ Node.js API ``` Now: ```text AWS ↓ EC2 ↓ Docker ↓ Node.js container ``` Later: ```text AWS ↓ ECS / EKS ↓ Docker containers ``` So we're building the stack progressively. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 38. Connect This to CI/CD
text: Previously: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Docker ``` Now: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Docker Build ↓ AWS ``` Security: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ OIDC ↓ IAM Role ↓ Temporary credentials ↓ AWS ``` That's the production-grade direction we'll build toward. ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 39. Interview Questions
text: You should be able to answer these:

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: AWS fundamentals
text: 1. What is AWS? 2. What is a Region? 3. What is an Availability Zone? 4. Region vs AZ? 5. Why deploy across multiple AZs? 6. What is an edge location? 7. What is a VPC?

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: IAM
text: 8. What is IAM? 9. Authentication vs authorization? 10. IAM user vs role? 11. What is an IAM policy? 12. What is least privilege? 13. What is an ARN? 14. Why should applications use IAM roles? 15. Why are long-lived access keys dangerous? 16. What happens if an application gets `AdministratorAccess`?

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Practical
text: 17. How would a Node.js application upload to S3 securely? 18. How would GitHub Actions deploy to AWS securely? 19. How would you debug an `AccessDenied` error? 20. How do you find which AWS identity your CLI is using? 21. What is the AWS shared responsibility model? ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Practical Lab
text: If you have an AWS account, do these carefully.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 1. Install/configure AWS CLI
text: Then: ```bash aws sts get-caller-identity ``` Understand the returned identity.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 2. Explore IAM
text: Create/inspect: ```text User Group Role Policy ``` Do **not** create overly broad production permissions just for experimentation.

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 3. Understand a policy
text: Take a policy like: ```json { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/*" } ] } ``` Answer: ```text Who? → Identity receiving policy What? → s3:GetObject Where? → example-bucket objects Effect? → Allow ```

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: 4. Connect the concepts
text: Draw: ```text Node API ↓ IAM Role ↓ S3 ``` Then explain why this is better than: ```text Node API ↓ Hardcoded AWS keys ↓ S3 ``` ---

title: Chapter 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: The AWS Mental Model
text: Don't try to memorize AWS as: ```text EC2 = X S3 = Y RDS = Z ... ``` Instead think: ```text AWS │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Compute Storage Database │ │ │ EC2 S3 RDS │ ↓ Network │ VPC │ ↓ Security │ IAM │ ↓ Monitoring │ CloudWatch ``` And your backend: ```text User ↓ AWS ↓ Networking ↓ Compute ↓ TypeScript API / \ ↓ ↓ RDS S3 \ / \ / IAM Roles ``` That is the foundation for the next AWS responses. <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 8: Docker Deep Dive + Production](../02-containers/ch08-docker-production.md) · [Chapter 10: EC2 + AWS Compute](ch10-ec2-compute.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch09-revision.md)

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Chapter 9 — Revision Sheet: AWS Fundamentals + IAM
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/04-aws/ch09-aws-fundamentals-iam.md). Goal: understand **how a real application is deployed, secured, connected, scaled and operated on AWS** — not memorise hundreds of services.

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: AWS basics
text: - **AWS** = cloud platform of infrastructure + managed services over the Internet; pay per use. - **Region** (e.g. `ap-south-1` Mumbai, `us-east-1`, `eu-west-1`) = geographic location with multiple AZs. **AZ** = isolated location in a Region to reduce failure impact. **Edge location** = closer-to-user points used by CloudFront for caching. - *Region vs AZ answer:* A Region is a geographic area containing multiple isolated AZs; an AZ is an isolated location within a Region used for availability and fault isolation. - Don't put everything in one AZ (bad: API → AZ-A only). Better: Load Balancer → API in AZ-A and AZ-B. Multi-region improves resilience/latency but adds substantial complexity — not always better. - **AWS account** = security + billing boundary. Organizations use multiple accounts (production, development, security, logging) under an AWS Organization. - **VPC** (preview) = logically isolated network: CIDR, subnets, route tables, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, Security Groups, NACLs (Ch.12).

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Service categories
text: | Category | Services | |---|---| | Compute | EC2, Lambda, ECS, EKS | | Storage | S3, EBS, EFS | | Database | RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache | | Networking | VPC, Route 53, CloudFront, ELB | | Security | IAM, KMS, WAF, Secrets Manager | | Monitoring | CloudWatch, CloudTrail |

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: IAM — "Who are you, and what are you allowed to do?"
text: - **Authentication** = *who?* (username+password, MFA, access credentials). **Authorization** = *what?* (read/write/delete S3, launch EC2). - **User** = a person/persistent identity (historically with long-lived access keys). **Group** = manage permissions for many users. **Role** = identity *assumed by trusted entities* (EC2, Lambda, GitHub Actions) giving **temporary credentials**. **Policy** = JSON permission document. ```json { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*" }] } ``` WHO → CAN DO WHAT (`Action`) → TO WHICH RESOURCE (`Resource`, an **ARN**). Example ARN: `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket`. - **Least privilege:** give exactly the permission needed (e.g. `s3:GetObject` on one bucket/path, not `AdministratorAccess`). A compromised admin app = huge **blast radius**. - `AccessDenied` for `PutObject` with only `GetObject` → don't grant admin; ask whether PutObject is truly needed, then add a narrowly scoped permission. - **Policy evaluation:** explicit **Deny overrides Allow**; otherwise an applicable explicit Allow is needed; no grant = denied. Debug: who? action? resource? which policies? any explicit deny?

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Secure patterns
text: | Need | Insecure | Better | |---|---|---| | Node.js uploads to S3 | Hard-coded keys | EC2/ECS/EKS → **IAM Role** → temporary credentials → S3 (the SDK finds credentials via the default provider chain: `new S3Client({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION })`) | | GitHub Actions → AWS | Long-lived `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET` in GitHub secrets | **OIDC** federation → IAM Role → short-lived credentials | Credential sources: environment variables, credential/config files, IAM role credentials, federated identity. **Never** in Git, Docker images or source code.

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: IAM rules (memorise)
text: 1. Don't commit credentials. 2. Don't put credentials in Docker images. 3. Prefer IAM roles for workloads. 4. Use temporary credentials. 5. Least privilege. 6. MFA for human identities. 7. No unnecessary admin for apps.

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: AWS CLI
text: `aws sts get-caller-identity` (which identity am I? — first step when debugging `AccessDenied`: wrong account/role/identity?), `aws s3 ls`, `aws configure get region`, `aws s3 ls --region ap-south-1`. CLI → AWS API → service.

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Shared responsibility model
text: AWS = security **OF** the cloud (facilities, hardware, underlying infrastructure). Customer = security **IN** the cloud (application, IAM config, data, OS config on certain services, network config, security settings). Varies by service — on EC2 you own OS, packages, application, configuration.

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Architecture preview
text: Region → VPC → ALB → EC2 (API) → RDS; IAM controls who/what can access resources. Progression: Docker container → EC2+Docker → ECS/EKS. CI/CD: GitHub Actions → Docker build → AWS via OIDC role.

title: Revision 9 — AWS Fundamentals + IAM
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - An IAM **role has two policy types**: a **trust policy** (who may assume the role — e.g. `ec2.amazonaws.com` or GitHub's OIDC provider) and **permission policies** (what the role can do). - For S3, `s3:ListBucket` applies to the **bucket ARN** (`arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket`), whereas `s3:GetObject` applies to **object ARNs** (`arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*`). - Protect the account **root user** with MFA and avoid using it for daily work. - Policy types beyond identity policies (resource-based policies, permission boundaries, Organizations SCPs) are not covered in this chapter.

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
text: > **Source:** Response 10 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-10.txt`, lines 1–1746) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch10-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We're continuing the roadmap exactly as planned. You now know: ```text Linux → Networking → Git → CI/CD → Docker → AWS/IAM ``` Now we're going to put your **Dockerized TypeScript backend onto an actual cloud server** using **Amazon EC2**. The goal isn't merely to know what EC2 stands for. By the end, you should understand: > **How a request travels from a user → AWS networking → EC2 → Docker → Node.js application, and how to deploy, secure, troubleshoot, and scale that server.** ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 1. What Is EC2?
text: **Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud)** provides virtual servers that you can run in AWS. Think of it as: ```text Your laptop ↓ Virtual computer in AWS ↓ EC2 ``` An EC2 instance is essentially a virtual machine with: - CPU - RAM - storage - network interface - operating system You control much more of the machine than you would with highly managed services. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 2. Why Do We Need EC2?
text: Suppose you've built: ```text TypeScript ↓ Node.js ↓ Express API ``` Locally: ```text localhost:3000 ``` But users on the internet need to access it. EC2 gives you a server in AWS: ```text Internet ↓ AWS ↓ EC2 ↓ Docker ↓ Node.js ↓ Your API ``` ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 3. EC2 vs Your Laptop
text: Your laptop: ```text CPU RAM Disk Network OS Applications ``` EC2: ```text Virtual CPU Virtual RAM EBS storage Virtual network Linux/Windows Applications ``` The major difference is that EC2 is provisioned in AWS infrastructure and can be managed remotely and integrated with AWS services. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 4. EC2 Architecture
text: At a high level: ```text AWS Region │ VPC │ Subnet │ EC2 Instance │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ EBS Network Storage Interface │ │ ↓ ↓ OS + App IP address ``` You learned VPCs and networking earlier. Now we're connecting those concepts to an actual compute resource. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 5. What Is an EC2 Instance?
text: An **instance** is a virtual machine created from an image/AMI and configured with a particular hardware profile. For example: ```text Instance ├── CPU ├── Memory ├── Network ├── Storage └── OS ``` You choose the instance type based on workload requirements. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 6. AMI
text: AMI = **Amazon Machine Image**. It provides the software configuration used to launch an EC2 instance. Conceptually: ```text AMI ↓ Launch ↓ EC2 Instance ``` An AMI can contain things such as: - operating system - preinstalled software - configuration For example: ```text Ubuntu-based AMI ↓ EC2 instance ↓ Ubuntu server ``` ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 7. AMI vs Instance
text: Very important: ```text AMI ↓ Blueprint/template EC2 instance ↓ Running virtual machine ``` Similar mental model: ```text Docker image ↓ Docker container ``` The analogy isn't exact, but it's useful. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 8. Instance Types
text: EC2 offers different hardware configurations. For example, you may see families designed around: ```text General purpose Compute optimized Memory optimized Storage optimized Accelerated computing ``` Think: ```text Workload ↓ Required CPU/RAM/network ↓ Instance type ``` You don't need to memorize every instance type. For interviews, understand **why** you would choose one family over another. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 9. General Purpose
text: General-purpose instances are designed for balanced workloads. For example: ```text Node.js API Moderate traffic Normal CPU + RAM requirements ``` You generally don't need an extremely CPU-heavy machine. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 10. Compute Optimized
text: Suppose: ```text CPU-heavy workload ``` Examples could include: - computation-heavy services - batch processing - CPU-intensive APIs A compute-optimized family may be appropriate. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 11. Memory Optimized
text: Suppose your workload needs lots of RAM: ```text Large in-memory dataset Caching Memory-heavy processing ``` Then memory-optimized instances can make sense. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 12. Storage Optimized
text: For workloads requiring high local storage performance/capacity, storage-optimized instance families exist. The key interview concept: > **Choose compute resources based on workload characteristics rather than simply choosing the biggest instance.** ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 13. EC2 Pricing Models — Basic Understanding
text: You should know the major models: ```text On-Demand Reserved / Savings-oriented commitments Spot ```

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: On-Demand
text: Pay for usage without a long-term commitment. Useful when: ```text Workload is unpredictable Need flexibility ```

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Commitment-based pricing
text: You commit to usage for a period in exchange for discounted pricing. Useful for predictable workloads.

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Spot
text: Uses spare AWS capacity at potentially large discounts, but instances can be interrupted. Good for workloads that can tolerate interruption: ```text Batch jobs Distributed processing Flexible workloads ``` Don't use Spot blindly for a workload that cannot tolerate interruption. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 14. Launching an EC2 Instance
text: At a high level, launching involves choosing: ```text AMI ↓ Instance type ↓ Network/subnet ↓ Security group ↓ Storage ↓ IAM role ↓ Launch ``` This is what you'll encounter in the AWS console. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 15. Key Pair
text: When using SSH to access a Linux EC2 instance, you commonly use a key pair. Conceptually: ```text Private key ↓ Your computer Public key ↓ EC2 ``` You use the private key to authenticate. Example: ```bash ssh -i my-key.pem ubuntu@<server-ip> ``` Never commit: ```text my-key.pem ``` to Git. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 16. Why SSH Keys Instead of Passwords?
text: SSH public-key authentication allows the server to verify possession of the private key without transmitting the private key. Conceptually: ```text Your machine │ Private key │ ↓ SSH authentication │ ↓ EC2 │ Public key ``` Keep the private key secure. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 17. Linux Connection
text: Once you're inside: ```bash ssh -i my-key.pem ubuntu@<server-ip> ``` you're basically operating a Linux server. Everything from [Chapter 2](../01-foundations/ch02-linux.md) becomes useful: ```bash ls cd ps top free df systemctl journalctl curl ss grep ``` This is why learning Linux first was important. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 18. Security Groups
text: An EC2 instance usually has one or more **Security Groups** controlling inbound/outbound traffic. Think of a security group as a virtual firewall associated with network interfaces/resources. Example: ```text Internet │ ├── SSH :22 ├── HTTP :80 └── HTTPS :443 ``` You might configure: ```text Port 22 → SSH Port 80 → HTTP Port 443 → HTTPS ``` But don't automatically open everything to the internet. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 19. Security Group Example
text: Suppose your Node API listens on: ```text 3000 ``` You could technically allow: ```text TCP 3000 Source: 0.0.0.0/0 ``` But in a production architecture, exposing application ports directly to the internet is often unnecessary. A better architecture can be: ```text Internet ↓ Load Balancer :443 ↓ EC2 :3000 ``` Then the EC2 security group can allow port 3000 **only from the load balancer/security-group path**, rather than from the whole internet. We'll build this architecture in [Chapter 14](ch14-load-balancing-scaling.md). ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 20. Security Group Is Stateful
text: This is an important networking detail. Security groups are **stateful**. If an allowed inbound connection is established, the corresponding response traffic is automatically allowed. You don't generally need to create a separate inbound rule just for the return packets. Compare this later with NACLs, which are stateless. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 21. Public vs Private EC2
text: An EC2 instance can be placed in a public or private subnet depending on the architecture.

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Public application server
text: ```text Internet ↓ Public IP ↓ EC2 ```

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Private application server
text: ```text Internet ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Private EC2 ``` The second is often preferred for application tiers because the EC2 instances aren't directly exposed to the public internet. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 22. Public IP
text: A public IP allows internet-based communication when the surrounding networking configuration permits it. Example: ```text EC2 ↓ Public IPv4 ↓ Internet ``` But don't confuse: ```text Public IP ``` with: ```text Security permission ``` Having an IP doesn't automatically mean traffic is allowed. Networking requires multiple pieces to align: ```text Route + Security Group + Network configuration + Application listening ``` ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 23. Private IP
text: Inside a VPC, EC2 has a private IP. For example: ```text 10.0.1.25 ``` This can be used for communication inside the VPC. Example: ```text EC2 │ └──→ RDS private IP ``` This is usually preferable to exposing databases publicly. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 24. Elastic IP — Basic Concept
text: An EC2 public IPv4 address can change under certain stop/start scenarios. If you need a persistent public IPv4 address, AWS provides **Elastic IP** addresses. Conceptually: ```text Elastic IP ↓ EC2 ``` However, in modern architectures you often don't want users connecting directly to an EC2 IP at all. Instead: ```text Users ↓ DNS ↓ Load Balancer ↓ EC2 ``` We'll get there later. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 25. EBS
text: EBS = **Elastic Block Store**. Think of it as persistent block storage attached to EC2. ```text EC2 │ └── EBS volume ↓ Disk data ``` It can store: ```text OS files Application files Logs Other persistent data ``` depending on your architecture. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 26. EC2 Local Disk vs EBS
text: An important concept: ```text EC2 compute + EBS storage ``` The instance is compute. EBS is block storage. This separation lets storage persist independently of the compute lifecycle in many common scenarios. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 27. Don't Put Your Database on EC2 by Default
text: You technically can: ```text EC2 ↓ PostgreSQL ``` but then **you** have to handle much more: ```text Backups Updates Replication Failover Monitoring Storage management ``` That's why managed databases such as RDS exist. We'll cover RDS in [Chapter 13](ch13-rds-databases.md). ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 28. User Data
text: When launching an EC2 instance, you can provide **user data**. It's commonly used for startup/bootstrap commands. Example: ```bash #!/bin/bash apt update -y apt install -y docker.io systemctl enable docker systemctl start docker ``` Conceptually: ```text EC2 starts ↓ User data executes ↓ Install/configure software ↓ Server becomes ready ``` This is a simple form of instance bootstrapping. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 29. EC2 Instance Metadata
text: EC2 exposes instance metadata to the instance itself. Applications can use it to obtain information about the instance/environment. Modern AWS security guidance emphasizes using the **Instance Metadata Service v2 (IMDSv2)** rather than older approaches. You don't need to memorize the endpoint details yet. Understand: ```text EC2 ↓ Instance metadata ↓ Instance information / temporary role credentials ``` This becomes important when discussing IAM roles on EC2. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 30. EC2 IAM Role
text: Remember [Chapter 9](ch09-aws-fundamentals-iam.md)? Instead of: ```text EC2 ↓ AWS access key hardcoded in application ``` use: ```text EC2 ↓ IAM role ↓ Temporary credentials ↓ AWS services ``` For example: ```text Node API ↓ EC2 IAM Role ↓ S3:GetObject ``` The AWS SDK can obtain temporary credentials through the instance role mechanism. This is a **very important interview concept**. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 31. Deploying Docker on EC2
text: Now we're finally connecting our Docker knowledge to AWS. Suppose you've already built: ```text my-api:1.0 ``` You could: ```text EC2 ↓ Install Docker ↓ Pull image ↓ Run container ``` For example: ```bash docker pull <registry>/my-api:1.0 ``` Then: ```bash docker run -d \ --name api \ -p 3000:3000 \ my-api:1.0 ``` Now: ```text EC2:3000 ↓ Docker ↓ Node.js ``` ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 32. Complete Request Flow
text: This is one of the most important diagrams in the entire roadmap. Suppose you have a public EC2 server. ```text Internet │ ↓ Public IP │ ↓ Security Group │ ↓ EC2 │ ↓ Docker :3000 │ ↓ Node.js API │ ↓ Express ``` A request: ```text GET /users ``` travels through that stack. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 33. More Production-Like Architecture
text: Instead of exposing EC2 directly: ```text User ↓ Internet ↓ Load Balancer ↓ EC2 ↓ Docker ↓ Node.js ``` We'll eventually add: ```text Internet ↓ DNS ↓ Load Balancer / \ EC2 EC2 ↓ ↓ Docker Docker \ / \ / RDS ``` This is where high availability starts becoming meaningful. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 34. Installing Docker on EC2
text: On a Linux EC2 instance, you can install Docker using the appropriate distribution packages/repository. The exact commands depend on whether you're using: ```text Ubuntu Amazon Linux ``` For example, conceptually: ```bash sudo apt update sudo apt install docker.io ``` Then: ```bash sudo systemctl enable docker sudo systemctl start docker ``` Verify: ```bash docker --version ``` Then: ```bash sudo docker ps ``` The exact package-management commands aren't the important part. The architecture is. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 35. Deployment Manually
text: A basic manual deployment: ```text Developer ↓ Build Docker image ↓ Push to registry ↓ SSH into EC2 ↓ docker pull ↓ Stop old container ↓ Start new container ``` For example: ```bash docker pull registry/my-api:abc123 ``` Then: ```bash docker stop api docker rm api ``` Then: ```bash docker run -d \ --name api \ -p 3000:3000 \ registry/my-api:abc123 ``` This works, but it's not a sophisticated production deployment. That's why CI/CD and orchestration exist. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 36. Connect to Chapter 6
text: We previously had: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Test ↓ Build ↓ Docker Image ``` Now: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Docker Image ↓ Container Registry ↓ EC2 ↓ Docker ↓ Node.js ``` Eventually we'll automate the entire process. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 37. EC2 Monitoring
text: Once your application is running, you need to know: ```text CPU Memory Disk Network Application health ``` Linux commands can help: ```bash top free -h df -h ss -tulpn ``` AWS also provides monitoring capabilities through **CloudWatch**, which we'll study later. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 38. CPU Problem
text: Suppose your API suddenly becomes slow. You SSH into EC2: ```bash top ``` and see: ```text CPU = 100% ``` Possible causes: ```text Infinite loop CPU-heavy operation Traffic spike Memory pressure causing other effects Poorly optimized code ``` Don't immediately upgrade the instance. First investigate the cause. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 39. Memory Problem
text: Check: ```bash free -h ``` Suppose: ```text RAM nearly exhausted ``` Possible causes: ```text Memory leak Too many processes Large workload Insufficient instance size ``` Again: > Diagnose first, resize second. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 40. Disk Problem
text: Check: ```bash df -h ``` Suppose: ```text Disk = 100% ``` Your application may fail to: - write logs - create temporary files - write application data Possible causes: ```text Logs Docker images Temporary files Application data ``` This is a classic production troubleshooting problem. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 41. Network Problem
text: Check: ```bash ss -tulpn ``` You might discover: ```text Node listening on 127.0.0.1:3000 ``` instead of: ```text 0.0.0.0:3000 ``` Then external connections may fail. Remember [Chapter 7](../02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md): ```typescript app.listen(3000, "0.0.0.0"); ``` ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 42. EC2 Instance States
text: You should understand: ```text Pending Running Stopping Stopped Shutting-down Terminated ``` The important distinction:

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Stop
text: Instance is shut down but can generally be started again.

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Terminate
text: Instance is deleted/terminated and cannot simply be started again. Be careful with terminology. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 43. Auto Scaling
text: What if one EC2 instance isn't enough? ```text Users ↓ EC2 ↓ CPU 100% ``` Instead: ```text Users ↓ Load Balancer ↓ ┌──────┬──────┬──────┐ EC2 EC2 EC2 ``` And when traffic increases: ```text 3 instances ↓ 5 instances ↓ 10 instances ``` When traffic decreases: ```text 10 ↓ 5 ↓ 3 ``` This is the foundation of **Auto Scaling**. We'll study load balancing and scaling in [Chapter 14](ch14-load-balancing-scaling.md). ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 44. Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
text: You already learned this in [Chapter 1](../01-foundations/ch01-cloud-devops-fundamentals.md).

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Vertical
text: Make instance bigger: ```text 2 CPU / 4 GB ↓ 8 CPU / 16 GB ```

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Horizontal
text: Add instances: ```text 1 EC2 ↓ 3 EC2 ↓ 10 EC2 ``` For highly available stateless APIs, horizontal scaling is often a key architectural pattern. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 45. Stateless API
text: Suppose: ```text EC2 A EC2 B EC2 C ``` A user's request can go to any instance. That works best when the API doesn't store critical session state locally. Instead: ```text API instances ↓ Shared database + Shared cache/session store ``` This is why stateless backend design is important. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 46. What Should NOT Live Only on EC2?
text: Avoid treating one EC2 machine as the permanent home of everything. For example: ```text ❌ User uploads only on EC2 disk ❌ Database only on EC2 ❌ Important state only inside Docker container ``` Prefer appropriate managed/shared services: ```text Files → S3 Database → RDS Cache → ElastiCache/Redis Compute → EC2/ECS/EKS/Lambda ``` We'll learn these services in later responses. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 47. EC2 Security Checklist
text: For an internet-facing application: ```text ✓ Least-privilege IAM role ✓ Restrictive security groups ✓ Keep OS/packages updated ✓ Don't expose unnecessary ports ✓ Use HTTPS ✓ Don't store secrets in source code ✓ Don't expose database publicly unnecessarily ✓ Monitor logs/metrics ✓ Use backups where appropriate ✓ Use SSH carefully ``` And ideally: ```text Internet ↓ Load Balancer :443 ↓ Private EC2 ``` rather than: ```text Internet ↓ EC2 :22, :3000, :5432... ``` ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 48. SSH Security
text: SSH commonly uses: ```text Port 22 ``` Don't blindly open: ```text 0.0.0.0/0 → port 22 ``` if you can avoid it. Depending on your architecture, you can restrict administrative access through: - specific trusted IPs - VPN/private connectivity - AWS Systems Manager mechanisms For modern AWS environments, **Systems Manager Session Manager** can often reduce the need for direct public SSH access. You don't need to master Session Manager yet; know why it exists. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 49. EC2 + IAM + Docker
text: Put everything we've learned together: ```text AWS │ VPC │ Private Subnet │ EC2 │ IAM Role / \ / \ S3 access Other AWS APIs │ Docker │ Node.js │ Express ``` The EC2 instance gets permissions through its role, while Docker runs your application. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 50. Real Deployment Architecture
text: Here's the architecture we're building toward: ```text Users │ ↓ DNS │ ↓ Load Balancer / \ / \ AZ-A AZ-B │ │ EC2 EC2 │ │ Docker Docker │ │ Node API Node API \ / \ / ↓ ↓ RDS │ S3 ``` And: ```text IAM ↓ controls access ``` while: ```text CloudWatch ↓ monitors everything ``` That architecture will emerge naturally over the next few responses. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: 51. EC2 Interview Questions
text: You should be able to answer these.

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Question
text: > Your Node.js application is running successfully on EC2, but users can't access it from the internet. How do you debug it? Don't jump to one answer. Walk through the layers: ```text 1. Is EC2 running? ↓ 2. Does Node process exist? ↓ 3. docker ps ↓ 4. docker logs ↓ 5. Is Node listening on 0.0.0.0:3000? ↓ 6. Is Docker port mapping correct? ↓ 7. Security Group allows required traffic? ↓ 8. Subnet route is correct? ↓ 9. Public IP / load balancer configuration? ↓ 10. Application itself returning errors? ``` This is exactly why we learned: ```text Linux + Networking + Docker + AWS ``` in that order. ---

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute

title: Chapter 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: The Most Important Mental Model
text: EC2 isn't just: > "AWS's virtual machine service." Think: ```text AWS │ VPC │ Subnet │ EC2 ┌───────┼────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Linux Docker IAM Role │ ↓ Node.js API │ ↓ Port ``` And an actual request: ```text User ↓ Internet ↓ DNS ↓ Load Balancer ↓ EC2 ↓ Security Group ↓ Docker ↓ Node.js ↓ Express ↓ Database / S3 ``` Once you understand this flow, AWS becomes much less intimidating. <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 9: AWS Fundamentals + IAM](ch09-aws-fundamentals-iam.md) · [Chapter 11: S3 + AWS Storage](ch11-s3-storage.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch10-revision.md)

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Chapter 10 — Revision Sheet: EC2 + AWS Compute
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/04-aws/ch10-ec2-compute.md).

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: What EC2 is
text: **Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud)** = virtual servers in AWS. An instance = virtual machine with vCPU, RAM, storage (EBS), network interface, OS (Linux/Windows). You control much more than with managed services. Placement: Region → VPC → Subnet → Instance (+ EBS + network interface/IP). - **AMI** (Amazon Machine Image) = blueprint (OS + preinstalled software + configuration). **Instance** = running VM launched from it. Analogy: Docker image → container (not exact). - **Launch checklist:** AMI → instance type → network/subnet → security group → storage → IAM role → launch.

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Instance types & pricing
text: | Family | Use | |---|---| | General purpose | Balanced; Node.js API with moderate traffic | | Compute optimized | CPU-heavy: batch, computation-heavy services | | Memory optimized | Large in-memory datasets, caching | | Storage optimized | High local storage performance/capacity | | Accelerated computing | GPUs/accelerators | Principle: **choose by workload characteristics, not the biggest instance.** | Pricing | Notes | |---|---| | **On-Demand** | Pay per use, no commitment; unpredictable workloads/flexibility | | **Commitment-based (Reserved / Savings)** | Commit for a period → discount; predictable workloads | | **Spot** | Spare capacity, big discounts, **can be interrupted**; for batch/distributed/flexible work — never for interruption-intolerant workloads |

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Access & security
text: - **Key pair:** private key on your computer, public key on EC2. `ssh -i my-key.pem ubuntu@<server-ip>`. Never commit `.pem`. SSH keys let the server verify possession of the private key without transmitting it. - **Security Group:** virtual firewall on the instance's network interface; **stateful** (return traffic of allowed connections is automatically allowed; NACLs are stateless). Open only what's needed (22/80/443). Better: Internet → LB :443 → EC2 :3000 with the EC2 SG allowing 3000 **only from the load balancer's security group**. - **Public vs private EC2:** public (Internet → public IP → EC2) vs private (Internet → LB → private EC2, preferred for application tier). - **Public IP ≠ permission:** reachability needs *Route + Security Group + network config + app listening*. - **Private IP** (e.g. `10.0.1.25`) for in-VPC traffic, e.g. EC2 → RDS private IP (don't expose DBs publicly). - **Elastic IP:** persistent public IPv4 (a normal public IPv4 can change after stop/start). In modern designs users hit DNS → LB, not an EC2 IP. - **SSH hardening:** don't open `0.0.0.0/0 → 22` if avoidable; restrict to trusted IPs, VPN/private connectivity, or **AWS Systems Manager Session Manager** (reduces need for public SSH). - **Security checklist:** least-privilege IAM role · restrictive SGs · updated OS/packages · no unnecessary ports · HTTPS · no secrets in source · DB not public · logs/metrics monitored · backups · careful SSH.

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Storage
text: - **EBS (Elastic Block Store)** = persistent block storage attached to EC2 (OS files, app files, logs, data). Compute and storage are separate, so storage can persist independently of compute in many scenarios. - Don't run the DB on EC2 by default — you'd handle backups, updates, replication, failover, monitoring, storage → use **RDS** (Ch.13). - What should NOT live only on EC2: ❌ uploads on EC2 disk, ❌ DB only on EC2, ❌ state only in a container → Files → **S3**, DB → **RDS**, Cache → **ElastiCache/Redis**, Compute → EC2/ECS/EKS/Lambda.

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Bootstrapping & identity
text: - **User data** = startup script at launch, e.g. `apt update -y; apt install -y docker.io; systemctl enable docker; systemctl start docker`. - **Instance metadata** = info (and temporary role credentials) exposed to the instance; use **IMDSv2**. - **EC2 IAM role** → temporary credentials → AWS APIs (Node API → EC2 role → `s3:GetObject`); SDK obtains credentials through the instance-role mechanism. **Very important interview concept.**

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Docker on EC2
text: Install Docker (Ubuntu: `sudo apt install docker.io`; `systemctl enable/start docker`; `docker --version`; `sudo docker ps`), then `docker pull <registry>/my-api:1.0` → `docker run -d --name api -p 3000:3000 my-api:1.0`. Manual deploy: build image → push to registry → SSH → `docker pull` → `docker stop api; docker rm api` → `docker run …` (works, but not sophisticated → CI/CD + orchestration). Request path: Internet → Public IP → Security Group → EC2 → Docker :3000 → Node.js → Express. Production: Users → DNS → Load Balancer → EC2 (AZ-A/AZ-B) → Docker → Node API → RDS / S3, with IAM controlling access and CloudWatch monitoring.

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Troubleshooting on a live instance
text: | Symptom | Check | Notes | |---|---|---| | Slow API / CPU 100% | `top` | Infinite loop, CPU-heavy op, traffic spike, memory pressure, poor code — **diagnose before resizing** | | Memory | `free -h` | Leak, too many processes, big workload, undersized | | Disk 100% | `df -h` | Can't write logs/temp/data; causes: logs, Docker images, temp files, app data | | Unreachable externally | `ss -tulpn` | Listening on `127.0.0.1:3000` vs `0.0.0.0:3000` | **Scenario (running app, no Internet access):** EC2 running? → Node process? → `docker ps` → `docker logs` → listening on `0.0.0.0:3000`? → Docker port mapping? → Security Group? → subnet route? → public IP / LB config? → app errors?

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Instance states
text: Pending → Running → Stopping → Stopped → Shutting-down → Terminated. **Stop** = shut down, can be started again. **Terminate** = deleted, cannot simply be started again.

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Scaling
text: Single EC2 at 100% CPU → Load Balancer + multiple EC2 → **Auto Scaling** (3 → 5 → 10 → back down). Vertical (2 CPU/4 GB → 8 CPU/16 GB) vs horizontal (1 → 3 → 10 EC2). Horizontal scaling works best with **stateless APIs**: shared DB + shared cache/session store (any instance can serve any request).

title: Revision 10 — EC2 + AWS Compute
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **Instance store vs EBS:** some instance types have *instance store* (ephemeral local disk lost when the instance stops/terminates); EBS volumes persist. The chapter heading "EC2 Local Disk vs EBS" only discusses EBS. - EBS volumes live in **one AZ**; back them up with snapshots. - **User data** by default runs once, at first boot, as root. - **IMDSv2** is session-oriented (a token is requested with a PUT, then sent as a header) to mitigate SSRF-style credential theft. - AWS charges for **public IPv4 addresses** (including those attached to running instances) since 2024 — relevant when choosing Elastic IPs vs a load balancer. *(Verify current pricing before relying on it.)* - To run `docker` without `sudo`, users are added to the `docker` group — this is effectively root-equivalent access; be careful. - Amazon Linux uses `dnf`/`yum` rather than `apt`.
