title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
text: > **Source:** Response 13 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-13.txt`, lines 1–1643) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch13-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We're continuing the **locked 24-response roadmap**. At this point, you've learned how to build the network around your backend. Now we're going inside the **database layer**. You already know DBMS and SQL, so I won't re-teach SQL. Instead, we'll focus on: > **How databases actually run in AWS, how to secure them, scale them, back them up, and connect your Node.js backend to them.** ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 1. What is Amazon RDS?
text: **RDS = Relational Database Service.** It is AWS's managed service for relational databases. Instead of doing: ```text EC2 ├── Linux ├── PostgreSQL ├── Configure PostgreSQL ├── Configure backups ├── Configure updates ├── Monitor database └── Maintain database ``` you can use: ```text AWS │ └── RDS └── PostgreSQL ``` AWS handles much of the underlying database infrastructure. You focus primarily on: - schema - queries - users - connections - configuration - application behavior - performance ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 2. Which Databases Can RDS Run?
text: RDS supports several relational engines, including: - PostgreSQL - MySQL - MariaDB - Oracle - SQL Server For your backend career, the most important ones are: ```text PostgreSQL MySQL ``` Your mental model should therefore be: ```text Node.js / NestJS ↓ PostgreSQL ↓ RDS ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 3. RDS vs Database on EC2
text: This is a classic interview question.

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Database on EC2
text: You manage: ```text EC2 ├── OS ├── PostgreSQL ├── Updates ├── Backups ├── Monitoring ├── Replication └── Recovery ```

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: RDS
text: AWS manages much of: ```text Infrastructure Maintenance Backups Patching mechanisms Monitoring integrations High availability features ``` while you manage the database itself and its configuration/data. The fundamental tradeoff: > **RDS reduces operational burden in exchange for less infrastructure-level control than running the database yourself.** ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 4. Where Should RDS Live?
text: Remember [Chapter 12](ch12-vpc-networking.md). You generally don't want: ```text Internet ↓ RDS ``` Instead: ```text Internet ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ↓ RDS ``` And the database should generally be in private subnets. Example: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ ALB │ ↓ Private App Subnet ┌───┴───┐ ↓ ↓ EC2 EC2 │ │ └───┬───┘ ↓ Private DB Subnet │ RDS ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 5. RDS and Security Groups
text: Suppose PostgreSQL uses: ```text 5432 ``` Create: ```text ALB-SG API-SG DB-SG ``` Then: ```text Internet ↓ ALB-SG :443 ↓ API-SG :3000 ↓ DB-SG :5432 ``` RDS's security group should allow: ```text TCP 5432 Source = API-SG ``` Not: ```text TCP 5432 Source = 0.0.0.0/0 ``` That's a fundamental production security principle. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 6. How Does Node.js Connect to RDS?
text: Suppose RDS provides a database endpoint such as: ```text mydb.xxxxx.region.rds.amazonaws.com ``` Your Node.js application connects using: ```text Host Port Username Password Database name ``` Example: ```typescript import { Pool } from "pg"; const pool = new Pool({ host: process.env.DB_HOST, port: 5432, user: process.env.DB_USER, password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD, database: process.env.DB_NAME, }); ``` Your application should **not** hardcode these values. Use environment/configuration management. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 7. Never Put Database Credentials in Git
text: Bad: ```typescript const password = "mySuperSecretPassword"; ``` And especially: ```text GitHub ↓ database password ❌ ``` Instead: ```text Secrets/configuration ↓ Application ↓ RDS ``` We'll go deeper into AWS secrets/security later. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 8. Connection Pooling
text: This is extremely important for backend interviews. Imagine 1,000 API requests. If every request creates a brand-new database connection: ```text Request ↓ Create DB connection ↓ Query ↓ Close connection ``` you can waste resources and overwhelm the database. Instead: ```text Node.js │ ↓ Connection Pool ┌─┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ C1 C2 ... Cn │ ↓ PostgreSQL ``` The pool maintains reusable connections. Example: ```typescript const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL, max: 20, }); ``` Then: ```typescript const result = await pool.query( "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", [userId] ); ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 9. Why Connection Pooling Becomes Important in Cloud
text: Suppose: ```text 10 EC2 instances ``` and each creates: ```text 100 DB connections ``` Potentially: ```text 10 × 100 = 1000 connections ``` Your database may not be able to handle that. Therefore: > **Application scaling can cause database connection pressure.** This is a very common system-design problem. We'll revisit it in later responses. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 10. RDS Storage
text: RDS needs storage for: ```text Database data Indexes Logs Temporary data ``` You configure storage depending on the database and workload. Important concepts include: - storage capacity - storage type - IOPS - throughput - autoscaling options Don't memorize every storage configuration. Understand: ```text More workload ↓ More I/O ↓ Storage performance becomes important ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 11. IOPS
text: IOPS = **Input/Output Operations Per Second**. Imagine a database performing many random reads/writes. ```text Application ↓ Database ↓ Storage ↓ IO operations ``` If storage cannot handle the workload: ```text Database latency ↑ ``` So database performance isn't just: ```text CPU ``` It can also be: ```text CPU Memory Storage throughput IOPS Connections Locks Queries Indexes ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 12. RDS Multi-AZ
text: One of the most important RDS concepts. Suppose: ```text AZ-A └── Primary DB AZ-B └── Standby ``` Conceptually: ```text RDS │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ AZ-A AZ-B Primary Standby ``` The standby is intended for **high availability/failover**, not as your normal read-scaling mechanism. If the primary fails: ```text Primary ❌ ↓ Failover ↓ Standby becomes primary ``` Your application continues using the RDS endpoint rather than manually changing the database IP. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 13. Multi-AZ ≠ Read Scaling
text: This distinction is frequently tested.

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Multi-AZ
text: Primary + standby for: ```text High availability Failover ```

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Read Replica
text: Copies data for: ```text Read scaling ``` Conceptually: ```text Primary / \ ↓ ↓ Replica 1 Replica 2 ↓ ↓ Reads Reads ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 14. Read Replicas
text: Suppose your application has: ```text 90% reads 10% writes ``` A single database may become read-heavy. You can use read replicas: ```text Primary / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ R1 R2 R3 ``` Application: ```text Writes ↓ Primary Reads ↓ Replicas ``` This is a common scaling strategy. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 15. But Replicas Introduce a Problem
text: Replication can have **lag**. Suppose: ```text t=1 User updates profile Primary name = Rachit ``` Replica may temporarily still have: ```text name = OldValue ``` So: ```text Write → Primary Read immediately → Replica ``` could potentially return stale data. This is called: > **Replication lag / eventual consistency behavior** depending on the architecture. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 16. Read-After-Write Problem
text: Example: ```text POST /profile ``` updates: ```text name = Rachit ``` Then immediately: ```text GET /profile ``` If the GET goes to a lagging replica: ```text Old profile ❌ ``` Solutions can include: - route critical immediate reads to primary - use consistency-aware routing - tolerate small delays where acceptable - design the application around consistency requirements This is an excellent system-design discussion. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 17. Automated Backups
text: RDS supports automated backup capabilities. Conceptually: ```text Database ↓ Automated backups ↓ Recovery ``` These help with: - accidental deletion - corruption - operational recovery You should understand the distinction between: ```text Backup ``` and: ```text Snapshot ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 18. RDS Snapshot
text: A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of an RDS database's storage/data state. Conceptually: ```text RDS ↓ Snapshot ↓ Create new database ``` Useful for: - migrations - cloning environments - backups - testing - recovery workflows ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 19. Backup vs Snapshot
text: Think: ```text Automated backups → ongoing recovery capability Snapshot → explicitly created point-in-time copy ``` The exact operational behavior depends on the RDS engine/configuration, but that mental distinction is enough for SWE interviews. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 20. Point-in-Time Recovery
text: Suppose: ```text Monday Database normal Tuesday 10:00 Database normal Tuesday 14:37 Bad deployment deletes data ❌ ``` With appropriate backup configuration, you can restore to a suitable point before the incident. Conceptually: ```text Backups ↓ Choose recovery point ↓ Restore database ``` This is part of disaster recovery. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 21. RDS Maintenance
text: Databases need: ```text Patching Updates Maintenance Configuration changes ``` RDS provides mechanisms to manage these without requiring you to manually manage the underlying server OS like you would with EC2. But: > Managed service does **not** mean zero operational responsibility. You still need to think about: - maintenance windows - application compatibility - migrations - backups - performance - connections - security - recovery ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 22. Parameter Groups
text: RDS database engines have configuration parameters. For example, database behavior can depend on: ```text memory settings connection limits logging query behavior ``` RDS provides **parameter groups** for managing engine configuration. Mental model: ```text RDS │ └── Parameter Group ↓ DB configuration ``` Don't memorize individual parameters yet. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 23. Option Groups
text: Some RDS engines/features use **option groups** to configure supported additional functionality. For SWE interviews: > Know that RDS has engine-specific configuration mechanisms; parameter groups are especially important for database parameters. No need to spend significant study time memorizing option-group details. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 24. RDS Encryption
text: Database data can be encrypted at rest. Conceptually: ```text Application ↓ Encrypted storage ↓ RDS ``` AWS Key Management Service (**KMS**) can be involved in encryption key management. Also: ```text Application ↓ HTTPS/TLS Database ``` can protect data in transit where supported/configured. Think: ```text At rest → encryption In transit → TLS ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 25. Secrets Management
text: Instead of: ```text DB_PASSWORD=abc123 ``` sitting everywhere, use a secrets-management approach. Architecture: ```text Application ↓ Secrets Manager / secure configuration ↓ DB credentials ↓ RDS ``` The application retrieves credentials securely according to its permissions. This is significantly better than hardcoding credentials. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 26. RDS Monitoring
text: You need to monitor: ```text CPU Memory-related metrics Database connections Storage IOPS Latency Throughput ``` and application-level metrics such as: ```text request latency error rate query latency timeouts ``` This gives you: ```text Application ↓ Database ↓ Metrics ↓ Monitoring ``` We'll go much deeper into CloudWatch and observability in Chapters [17](ch17-monitoring-security.md) and [22](../07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md). ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 27. Database Doesn't Scale Like EC2
text: This is important. For EC2: ```text Need more capacity? → Add instances ``` For databases: ```text Need more capacity? ``` You need to consider: ```text Vertical scaling Read replicas Caching Query optimization Indexes Partitioning Sharding Connection pooling Database architecture ``` The database is often one of the hardest components to scale. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 28. Vertical Scaling
text: Suppose: ```text RDS 4 vCPU 16 GB RAM ``` and workload grows. You may increase instance capacity: ```text 8 vCPU 32 GB RAM ``` This is vertical scaling. Advantage: ```text Simple ``` Limitation: ```text There is a ceiling. ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 29. Read Scaling
text: Instead of making one database increasingly powerful: ```text Primary ↑ Writes ``` add replicas: ```text Primary / \ ↓ ↓ Replica Replica ↑ ↑ Reads Reads ``` This scales read workloads. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 30. Caching
text: Suppose the application repeatedly asks: ```sql SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = 10; ``` Instead of hitting PostgreSQL every time: ```text Request ↓ Redis ↓ cache hit Response ``` If cache miss: ```text Request ↓ Redis ↓ miss PostgreSQL ↓ Redis ↓ Response ``` You've already seen Redis in Docker. Later, we'll connect this to AWS and production architecture. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 31. RDS vs DynamoDB
text: Another common interview question.

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: RDS
text: Relational: ```text Tables Rows Columns SQL Relationships Transactions ``` Good when: - relationships matter - complex SQL queries matter - relational consistency matters - schema is relational

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: DynamoDB
text: NoSQL/key-value/document-oriented database service. Good for workloads designed around: ```text key-value access very high scale predictable access patterns low-latency requests ``` Don't think: > DynamoDB is simply "faster RDS." They're designed around different data models and access patterns. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 32. RDS vs EC2 vs DynamoDB
text: | | RDS | DB on EC2 | DynamoDB | |---|---|---|---| | Type | Managed relational | Self-managed relational | Managed NoSQL | | SQL | Yes | Yes | No traditional relational SQL | | OS management | AWS handles much of it | You manage | AWS handles infrastructure | | Relationships | Strong fit | Strong fit | Different modeling approach | | Scaling model | Managed DB scaling + replicas/etc. | You manage | Designed for high-scale NoSQL workloads | | Operational burden | Lower | Higher | Lower infrastructure burden | ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 33. RDS in Your Node.js Architecture
text: Let's combine everything we've learned. ```text INTERNET │ ↓ Route 53 │ ↓ ALB │ ┌──────────┴──────────┐ ↓ ↓ EC2-A EC2-B │ │ └──────────┬──────────┘ ↓ RDS PostgreSQL ``` Networking: ```text ALB SG ↓ API SG :3000 ↓ DB SG :5432 ``` Application: ```text Node.js ↓ Connection Pool ↓ PostgreSQL ``` Security: ```text Secrets ↓ DB credentials Encryption ↓ Data at rest / transit ``` Availability: ```text Multi-AZ ``` Scaling: ```text EC2 → horizontal scaling RDS → vertical scaling / replicas / optimization ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 34. What Happens When a User Makes a Request?
text: Suppose: ```text GET /users/123 ``` Flow: ```text User ↓ DNS ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ↓ Node.js ↓ Connection Pool ↓ RDS PostgreSQL ↓ Query ↓ Node.js ↓ ALB ↓ User ``` That's the full backend path. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 35. What If RDS Is Down?
text: Your application might show: ```text 500 ``` But don't immediately blame Node.js. Debug systematically: ```text 1. Is RDS available? 2. Is the endpoint correct? 3. Is the DB port correct? 4. Can EC2 reach RDS? 5. Is DB SG allowing EC2 SG? 6. Is the database accepting connections? 7. Is connection pool exhausted? 8. Are credentials correct? 9. Are queries timing out? 10. Is the database overloaded? ``` This is how production debugging works. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 36. Connection Pool Exhaustion
text: Suppose: ```text API instances = 20 pool.max = 50 ``` Potential theoretical maximum: ```text 20 × 50 = 1000 connections ``` If RDS can only handle a smaller number: ```text Database ↑ Too many connections ↓ Failures / timeouts ``` Therefore: > **Scaling application servers without considering database connection limits can make the system less stable.** Very important interview concept. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 37. Database Migration
text: Your application schema changes over time. For example: ```text users ``` becomes: ```text users ├── id ├── name ├── email └── created_at ``` You might add: ```text last_login ``` You should manage this using database migrations rather than manually editing production databases. Common tools in Node ecosystems include: ```text Prisma Migrate Drizzle migrations TypeORM migrations Knex migrations ``` For your stack, Prisma is particularly relevant. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 38. Example Prisma Flow
text: Your code: ```text schema.prisma ↓ Migration ↓ PostgreSQL ↓ RDS ``` Example conceptual command: ```bash npx prisma migrate deploy ``` This would typically be part of a controlled deployment process. Later, your CI/CD response will connect these pieces. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 39. Important Production Rule
text: Don't blindly run destructive database migrations during deployment. Bad deployment: ```text Deploy ↓ DROP COLUMN ↓ Old application still running ↓ 💥 ``` Production deployments need compatibility thinking. For example: ```text Expand ↓ Deploy compatible application ↓ Migrate data ↓ Switch usage ↓ Contract/remove old structure later ``` This is commonly called an **expand-and-contract** migration strategy. Very useful system-design knowledge. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 40. RDS Architecture Checklist
text: When designing production PostgreSQL on AWS, think: ```text RDS PostgreSQL │ ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Networking Security Reliability │ │ │ Private subnet SG :5432 Multi-AZ │ Encryption Backups │ Secrets Recovery ↓ Application │ Connection Pool │ ↓ PostgreSQL ``` Then scaling: ```text Vertical scaling + Read replicas + Caching + Query optimization + Indexes + Connection pooling ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: 41. What You Need to Know Deeply
text: For your SWE interviews, **master these**:

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Must know deeply
text: - RDS concept - RDS vs EC2 database - private database architecture - security groups - PostgreSQL connectivity - connection pooling - Multi-AZ - read replicas - replication lag - backups - snapshots - point-in-time recovery concept - encryption - Secrets Manager concept - database scaling - database connection exhaustion - migrations - RDS vs DynamoDB

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Medium depth
text: - storage/IOPS - parameter groups - monitoring - maintenance windows - RDS Proxy concept

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Awareness
text: - every supported RDS engine - obscure engine-specific features - advanced database administration You **do not** need to become a PostgreSQL DBA for this roadmap. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Practical Lab
text: Take your Node.js API from the Docker sections. Current: ```text Node.js ↓ Docker ↓ PostgreSQL container ``` Now imagine production: ```text Node.js ↓ EC2 ↓ RDS PostgreSQL ``` Configure your application around: ```env DB_HOST= DB_PORT=5432 DB_NAME= DB_USER= DB_PASSWORD= ``` Then verify that your mental architecture is: ```text Internet ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 private subnet ↓ RDS private subnet ``` and: ```text EC2 SG → RDS SG :5432 ``` not: ```text Internet → RDS :5432 ❌ ``` ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Question:
text: > Your Node.js backend has been scaled from 2 EC2 instances to 20. Suddenly PostgreSQL starts rejecting connections. What could have happened? Your reasoning should be: ```text 2 instances × connection pool size = manageable connections ``` Then: ```text 20 instances × connection pool size = much larger connection count ``` Potential result: ```text RDS connection limit reached ↓ Connection failures ↓ API errors ``` Possible solutions: ```text Tune pool sizes + Control application concurrency + Use RDS Proxy where appropriate + Optimize queries + Caching + Scale database appropriately ``` That's the kind of reasoning interviewers want. ---

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Final Mental Model
text: Remember this: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ ALB │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ EC2 EC2 │ │ └────────┬────────┘ ↓ Connection Pool ↓ RDS PostgreSQL │ │ │ └── Read Replicas │ └── Multi-AZ ``` And around it: ```text Security Groups Encryption Secrets Backups Monitoring Private Subnets ```

title: Chapter 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: The key distinction to remember:
text: ```text Multi-AZ → availability / failover Read Replica → read scaling Connection Pool → efficient DB connections Cache → reduce DB traffic Vertical Scaling → more DB resources Backups → recovery Private Subnet → network isolation ``` <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 12: VPC + AWS Networking](ch12-vpc-networking.md) · [Chapter 14: Load Balancing + Scaling](ch14-load-balancing-scaling.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch13-revision.md)

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Chapter 13 — Revision Sheet: RDS + Databases on AWS
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/04-aws/ch13-rds-databases.md). Focus: how databases run on AWS, how to secure, scale and back them up, and how Node.js connects.

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: RDS basics
text: - **RDS = Relational Database Service**, AWS-managed relational databases. Engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server (PostgreSQL and MySQL matter most for this career path). - You manage: schema, queries, users, connections, configuration, app behaviour, performance. AWS manages much of: infrastructure, maintenance, backups, patching mechanisms, monitoring integrations, HA features. - **RDS vs DB on EC2:** RDS reduces operational burden in exchange for less infrastructure-level control. On EC2 you own OS, updates, backups, monitoring, replication, recovery. - **Managed ≠ zero responsibility:** still think about maintenance windows, app compatibility, migrations, backups, performance, connections, security, recovery.

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Placement & networking
text: Internet → ALB → EC2 (private app subnets) → RDS (private DB subnets). `ALB-SG :443 → API-SG :3000 → DB-SG :5432`; DB SG allows `TCP 5432` from **Source = API-SG**, never `0.0.0.0/0`.

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Connecting from Node.js
text: ```typescript import { Pool } from "pg"; const pool = new Pool({ host: process.env.DB_HOST, port: 5432, user: process.env.DB_USER, password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD, database: process.env.DB_NAME, }); // or: new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL, max: 20 }); const result = await pool.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", [userId]); ``` Endpoint looks like `mydb.xxxxx.region.rds.amazonaws.com`. Never hard-code credentials or commit them; use configuration + **Secrets Manager** (app retrieves DB credentials according to its IAM permissions).

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Connection pooling & exhaustion (very important)
text: - Without a pool every request opens/closes a DB connection → wasted resources, overwhelmed DB. A **pool** keeps reusable connections. - **Total connections = instances × pool size.** 10 EC2 × 100 = 1000; 20 API instances × `max: 50` = 1000 → DB may hit its connection limit → failures/timeouts. - **Key lesson:** scaling application servers without considering DB connection limits can make the system *less* stable. - **Scenario (2 → 20 EC2, PostgreSQL rejects connections):** connection count multiplied by instances. Fixes: tune pool sizes, control app concurrency, use **RDS Proxy**, optimise queries, caching, scale the DB.

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: High availability vs scaling
text: | Mechanism | Purpose | |---|---| | **Multi-AZ** | Primary (AZ-A) + standby (AZ-B) for **HA/failover**, not read scaling. On failure the standby becomes primary; the app keeps using the same RDS **endpoint** | | **Read replica** | Copies data for **read scaling**: writes → primary, reads → replicas (good for ~90% read workloads) | | **Connection pool** | Efficient DB connections | | **Cache (Redis)** | Reduce DB traffic: request → Redis hit → response; miss → PostgreSQL → populate Redis | | **Vertical scaling** | More vCPU/RAM (e.g. 4 vCPU/16 GB → 8 vCPU/32 GB): simple but has a ceiling | | **Backups** | Recovery | | **Private subnet** | Network isolation | **Databases don't scale like EC2** (can't just add instances): consider vertical scaling, read replicas, caching, query optimisation, indexes, partitioning, sharding, connection pooling, architecture. **Replication lag / read-after-write problem:** `POST /profile` (write to primary) then immediate `GET /profile` served by a lagging replica returns stale data (eventual consistency behaviour). Mitigations: route critical immediate reads to primary, consistency-aware routing, tolerate small delays where acceptable, design around consistency requirements.

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Backup & recovery
text: - **Automated backups** = ongoing recovery capability (accidental deletion, corruption, operational recovery). **Snapshot** = explicit point-in-time copy of the database storage/state (migrations, cloning environments, backups, testing, recovery). - **Point-in-time recovery:** e.g. bad deployment deletes data Tuesday 14:37 → restore to a point before the incident (part of disaster recovery).

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Configuration, storage, security, monitoring
text: - **Parameter groups** manage engine configuration (memory, connection limits, logging, query behaviour). **Option groups** configure additional engine-specific features (low priority). - **Storage/IOPS:** capacity, type, IOPS, throughput, autoscaling options. **IOPS** = I/O operations per second; low storage performance → higher latency. DB performance = CPU, memory, storage throughput, IOPS, connections, locks, queries, indexes. - **Encryption:** at rest (storage encryption, **KMS**-managed keys) and in transit (TLS). - **Monitor:** CPU, memory-related metrics, connections, storage, IOPS, latency, throughput + app-level request latency, error rate, query latency, timeouts (CloudWatch, Ch.17/22).

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: RDS vs DynamoDB vs DB on EC2
text: | | RDS | DB on EC2 | DynamoDB | |---|---|---|---| | Type | Managed relational | Self-managed relational | Managed NoSQL (key-value/document) | | SQL | Yes | Yes | No traditional relational SQL | | OS mgmt | AWS handles much | You | AWS handles infrastructure | | Fit | Relationships, complex SQL, relational consistency | Same | Key-value access, very high scale, predictable access patterns, low latency | | Ops burden | Lower | Higher | Lower | DynamoDB is not "faster RDS" — different data model and access patterns.

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Migrations
text: Manage schema changes with migration tools (Prisma Migrate, Drizzle, TypeORM, Knex) — never hand-edit production. Flow: `schema.prisma` → migration → PostgreSQL → RDS; `npx prisma migrate deploy` in a controlled deployment. **Don't blindly run destructive migrations:** deploy `DROP COLUMN` while the old app version is running → 💥. **Expand-and-contract:** expand → deploy compatible app → migrate data → switch usage → remove old structure later.

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Request path
text: User → DNS → ALB → EC2 → Node.js → connection pool → RDS PostgreSQL → query → Node.js → ALB → User. **If RDS "is down" (500s):** RDS available? endpoint? port? EC2 can reach RDS? DB SG allows EC2 SG? DB accepting connections? pool exhausted? credentials? queries timing out? DB overloaded?

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Depth guide (from the chapter)
text: Know deeply: RDS concept, RDS vs EC2 DB, private DB architecture, SGs, PostgreSQL connectivity, pooling, Multi-AZ, read replicas, replication lag, backups, snapshots, PITR, encryption, Secrets Manager, scaling, connection exhaustion, migrations, RDS vs DynamoDB. Medium: storage/IOPS, parameter groups, monitoring, maintenance windows, RDS Proxy. Awareness: every engine, obscure features, advanced DBA.

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **RDS Proxy** (mentioned but not explained): a managed proxy that pools/multiplexes connections between apps (e.g. many Lambda/EC2 clients) and the DB, reduces connection storms, and speeds up failover handling. - Multi-AZ comes in two shapes: a *Multi-AZ DB instance* (standby is **not** readable) and a *Multi-AZ DB cluster* (readable standbys). **Aurora** is a separate AWS-built engine family not covered in this chapter. - Failover works by switching the endpoint's DNS to the standby, so apps should **reconnect with retries** and avoid caching DNS too long. - Read replicas replicate **asynchronously** (hence lag); a replica can be promoted to a standalone DB. - PITR needs automated backups enabled (retention period configurable) and restores into a **new** DB instance. Automated backups are tied to the instance's retention window; manual snapshots persist until you delete them. - A PostgreSQL instance's `max_connections` scales with instance size/memory and is set via parameter group. - `prisma migrate deploy` applies existing migrations (CI/production); `prisma migrate dev` is for development.

title: Revision 13 — RDS + Databases on AWS
heading: Interview scenario answer skeleton
text: *Design prod PostgreSQL on AWS:* private subnets + SG from API-SG only + encryption + Secrets Manager + Multi-AZ + automated backups/snapshots/PITR + pooling + monitoring; scale reads with replicas/cache, writes with vertical scaling/optimisation; control connections (pool size × instances, RDS Proxy). <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 12](ch12-revision.md) · [Full chapter 13](../docs/04-aws/ch13-rds-databases.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 14](ch14-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
text: > **Source:** Response 14 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-14.txt`, lines 1–1849) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch14-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We're following the roadmap exactly. You've now learned: - EC2 - VPC - subnets - route tables - security groups - RDS - connection pooling - Multi-AZ - read replicas Now we're going to solve the next problem: > **What happens when one EC2 server isn't enough?** This response is extremely important for **backend + system design + AWS interviews**. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 1. The Problem With One Server
text: Imagine your Node.js application: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ EC2 │ Node.js ``` Initially: ```text 100 users ``` No problem. Then: ```text 10,000 users ``` Then: ```text 100,000 users ``` Eventually: ```text CPU ↑ Memory ↑ Requests ↑ Latency ↑ ``` Your single EC2 instance becomes a bottleneck. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 2. Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
text: There are two fundamental ways to scale.

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Vertical Scaling
text: Make the machine bigger. ```text Before: EC2 4 CPU 16 GB RAM ↓ After: EC2 16 CPU 64 GB RAM ``` Also called: > **Scale up** ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Horizontal Scaling
text: Add more machines. ```text EC2 ↓ EC2 EC2 ↓ EC2 EC2 EC2 ``` Also called: > **Scale out** For web applications, horizontal scaling is extremely important. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 3. Why Horizontal Scaling?
text: Suppose: ```text 1 EC2 → 1,000 requests/sec ``` You need: ```text 3,000 requests/sec ``` You could potentially use: ```text 3 EC2 instances ``` and distribute traffic. ```text INTERNET │ ↓ Load Balancer / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ EC2-A EC2-B EC2-C ``` Now your workload is distributed. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 4. But Who Decides Which EC2 Gets the Request?
text: That's the job of a: > **Load Balancer** A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers. Conceptually: ```text Client │ ↓ Load Balancer │ ├──→ EC2 A ├──→ EC2 B └──→ EC2 C ``` AWS provides **Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)**. The most relevant load balancer for your backend work is: > **Application Load Balancer (ALB)** ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 5. ALB
text: ALB = **Application Load Balancer**. It's designed for application-layer traffic such as HTTP/HTTPS. Example: ```text https://api.example.com/users ``` Flow: ```text User ↓ ALB ↓ Node.js ``` Instead of: ```text User ↓ EC2 directly ``` ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 6. Why Put ALB in Front of EC2?
text: Without ALB: ```text Internet ├── EC2-A ├── EC2-B └── EC2-C ``` How does the client know which EC2 to use? With ALB: ```text Internet ↓ ALB ↓ ┌────┼────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ EC2 EC2 EC2 ``` The client only needs to know the ALB's endpoint/domain. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 7. Target Groups
text: ALB doesn't simply have a random list of EC2 instances. It uses a **Target Group**. Conceptually: ```text ALB │ ↓ Target Group │ ├── EC2-A ├── EC2-B └── EC2-C ``` The target group represents the backend destinations receiving traffic. Targets can include supported resources such as: - EC2 instances - IP addresses - containers, depending on architecture ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 8. Health Checks
text: This is one of the most important ALB concepts. Imagine: ```text EC2-A → healthy EC2-B → healthy EC2-C → crashed ``` You don't want: ```text ALB ├── EC2-A ✅ ├── EC2-B ✅ └── EC2-C ❌ ``` to keep sending requests to C. So ALB performs health checks. Example: ```text GET /health ``` Expected: ```text 200 OK ``` Then: ```text EC2-C ❌ ``` is removed from normal traffic distribution. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 9. Health Endpoint in Node.js
text: You can implement: ```typescript app.get("/health", (req, res) => { res.status(200).json({ status: "ok", }); }); ``` Then the load balancer checks: ```text GET /health ``` If the application responds correctly: ```text 200 ``` the instance can remain healthy. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 10. Health Check vs Application Monitoring
text: Don't confuse these. A basic load balancer health check asks: > **Can I successfully reach this backend and get an acceptable response?** Observability can answer much more: ```text CPU memory latency errors database failures request rate ``` We'll study that more in Chapters [17](ch17-monitoring-security.md) and [22](../07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md). ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 11. Load Balancing Algorithms
text: Conceptually, a load balancer can distribute requests using strategies such as:

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Round Robin
text: ```text Request 1 → A Request 2 → B Request 3 → C Request 4 → A ```

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Least Outstanding Requests
text: Send traffic toward a target with fewer active requests, depending on the configured balancing behavior. You don't need to memorize every algorithm. Understand: > **The load balancer decides which healthy target should receive each request.** ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 12. ALB Listener
text: A listener waits for incoming traffic. Example: ```text ALB │ ├── Listener :80 └── Listener :443 ``` For production: ```text HTTPS :443 ``` is generally what users connect to. The listener can then route traffic to a target group. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 13. ALB Routing Rules
text: One powerful ALB feature is application-level routing. Suppose: ```text api.example.com/users api.example.com/orders ``` You could conceptually route: ```text /users/* ↓ Users Target Group /orders/* ↓ Orders Target Group ``` You can also route based on hostnames. For example: ```text api.example.com ↓ API targets admin.example.com ↓ Admin targets ``` This is why ALB is called an **Application** Load Balancer. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 14. Security Group Architecture
text: Remember [Chapter 12](ch12-vpc-networking.md). Don't do: ```text Internet ↓ EC2 :3000 ``` Instead: ```text Internet ↓ ALB :443 ↓ EC2 :3000 ``` Security groups: ```text Internet ↓ ALB-SG ↓ API-SG ↓ EC2 ``` ALB SG: ```text Allow HTTPS 443 from internet ``` EC2 SG: ```text Allow 3000 from ALB-SG ``` This is a very common interview architecture. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 15. The Bigger Architecture
text: Now combine everything: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ ALB :443 │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ EC2-A EC2-B EC2-C │ │ │ └────────────┼────────────┘ ↓ RDS ``` Now we've solved: ```text Multiple application servers + Traffic distribution + Health checking + Database connectivity ``` But there's another problem. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 16. What If Traffic Changes?
text: Suppose: ```text 2 AM 100 users ``` You need: ```text 2 EC2 instances ``` At: ```text 8 PM 100,000 users ``` you might need: ```text 10 EC2 instances ``` Then at: ```text 3 AM ``` you don't need 10 machines. You want infrastructure to adjust automatically. That's where: > **Auto Scaling Groups** come in. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 17. Auto Scaling Group
text: An **Auto Scaling Group (ASG)** manages a group of EC2 instances and can adjust the number of instances according to configured rules. Conceptually: ```text Auto Scaling Group / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ EC2-A EC2-B EC2-C ``` It can: ```text Scale out ``` or: ```text Scale in ``` ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 18. Scale Out
text: Traffic increases: ```text CPU ↑ Requests ↑ Latency ↑ ``` ASG might increase: ```text 2 EC2 ↓ 3 EC2 ↓ 4 EC2 ``` Architecture: ```text ALB / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ EC2 EC2 EC2 ``` ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 19. Scale In
text: Traffic decreases: ```text 100,000 users ↓ 5,000 users ``` ASG might reduce: ```text 6 EC2 ↓ 4 EC2 ↓ 2 EC2 ``` This reduces infrastructure usage and potentially cost. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 20. Desired / Minimum / Maximum Capacity
text: An ASG can conceptually have: ```text Minimum = 2 Desired = 3 Maximum = 10 ``` Meaning: ```text Normal: 3 instances Never intentionally below: 2 Can scale up to: 10 ``` This gives you controlled scaling boundaries. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 21. Launch Template
text: How does ASG know what kind of EC2 instance to create? A **Launch Template** defines important instance configuration. Conceptually: ```text Launch Template │ ├── AMI ├── Instance type ├── Security Group ├── IAM role ├── User data └── Other configuration ``` Then: ```text ASG ↓ Launch Template ↓ New EC2 instances ``` ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 22. Why This Is Powerful
text: Suppose EC2-A dies. ASG can replace it. ```text Before: EC2-A ✅ EC2-B ✅ EC2-C ❌ ↓ ASG ↓ EC2-A ✅ EC2-B ✅ EC2-D ✅ ``` This is a core reliability concept: > **Replace failed instances rather than depending on manually repairing them.** ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 23. Immutable Infrastructure
text: This connects directly to Docker. Instead of: ```text Server broken ↓ SSH into server ↓ Manually fix ``` you can use: ```text Broken instance ↓ Terminate ↓ Create fresh instance ↓ Deploy known image/application ``` This is much more repeatable. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 24. Scaling Policies
text: ASG can use metrics to decide when to scale. For example: ```text CPU > threshold ↓ Scale out ``` or: ```text CPU < threshold ↓ Scale in ``` You can also use other workload signals depending on architecture. Important idea: > **Scaling should respond to actual workload, not just arbitrary server count.** ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 25. Target Tracking
text: A common scaling approach is: ```text Target CPU = 50% ``` The system tries to adjust capacity so the metric stays around the target. Conceptually: ```text CPU = 80% ↓ Need more capacity ↓ Scale out CPU = 20% ↓ Potentially too much capacity ↓ Scale in ``` ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 26. Step Scaling
text: Another strategy: ```text CPU > 70% → add 1 CPU > 85% → add 2 CPU > 95% → add 4 ``` The exact configuration depends on the workload. For interviews, know: ```text Target tracking Step scaling Scheduled scaling ``` at a conceptual level. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 27. Scheduled Scaling
text: Some workloads are predictable. Example: ```text Every day: 8 AM → traffic starts rising 8 PM → traffic drops ``` You could proactively increase capacity before traffic arrives. ```text 7:30 PM ↓ Scale in 7:30 AM ↓ Scale out ``` This is **scheduled scaling**. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 28. Auto Scaling Doesn't Mean Infinite Scaling
text: This is important. Suppose: ```text ASG max = 10 ``` and traffic requires: ```text 20 instances ``` Your ASG won't magically create 20. It stops at: ```text 10 ``` Then you'll have to address the bottleneck through: - larger instances - higher max capacity - better application performance - caching - database scaling - architectural changes ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 29. The Database Problem Again
text: Suppose: ```text EC2 = 2 ``` and: ```text RDS = handles workload ``` Now ASG scales: ```text 2 → 20 EC2 ``` But all 20 connect to: ```text RDS ``` Now: ```text DB connections ↑ Queries ↑ CPU ↑ IO ↑ ``` The application tier scales, but the database may become the bottleneck. This is why: > **Scaling one layer doesn't automatically scale the entire system.** Excellent system-design concept. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 30. Stateless Architecture
text: Horizontal scaling works best when your application servers are **stateless**. Suppose: ```text EC2-A ``` stores user session in its local memory: ```text Session: user123 → logged in ``` Then the next request goes to: ```text EC2-B ``` EC2-B doesn't know about the session. Problem. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 31. Bad Stateful Design
text: ```text ALB / \ ↓ ↓ EC2-A EC2-B │ Session in RAM ``` Request 1: ```text User → EC2-A ``` Request 2: ```text User → EC2-B ``` EC2-B: ```text "Who is this user?" ❌ ``` ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 32. Stateless Design
text: Instead: ```text ALB / \ ↓ ↓ EC2-A EC2-B \ / \ / Redis ``` Or use other appropriate centralized/state-management mechanisms. Then: ```text EC2-A ↓ Redis ``` and: ```text EC2-B ↓ Redis ``` Both instances can access shared state. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 33. JWT and Stateless Authentication
text: Another common approach is JWT-based authentication. Conceptually: ```text Client ↓ JWT ↓ EC2-A ``` Later: ```text Client ↓ Same JWT ↓ EC2-B ``` EC2-B can validate the token without needing the login session stored in EC2-A's memory, assuming the architecture is designed appropriately. But JWT itself introduces other concerns: - token expiry - revocation - refresh tokens - key management - token size - compromised tokens So don't treat "JWT = automatically perfect scaling." ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 34. Sticky Sessions
text: Load balancers can also support session stickiness in appropriate configurations. Conceptually: ```text User A ↓ ALB ↓ EC2-A ``` and future requests from that user tend to go to: ```text EC2-A ``` This can help legacy/stateful applications. But it has drawbacks: ```text EC2-A ↓ Many users ``` while: ```text EC2-B ↓ Few users ``` You can get uneven load. Therefore: > **Stateless architecture is generally preferable for horizontally scaled web applications when practical.** ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 35. Session State vs Application State
text: Don't confuse: ```text Application code ``` with: ```text User/session state ``` Your Node.js application code should ideally be identical across instances: ```text EC2-A → same application EC2-B → same application EC2-C → same application ``` Shared state should live in appropriate external systems: ```text Redis Database Object storage Dedicated state services ``` depending on what the data is. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 36. Scaling Requests vs Scaling Resources
text: There are several levels of scaling. ```text System │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Compute Database Cache │ │ │ EC2/ASG RDS Redis ``` If compute is overloaded: ```text Scale EC2 ``` If DB is overloaded: ```text Optimize DB + Scale DB + Replicas + Cache ``` If cache is overloaded: ```text Scale/configure cache appropriately ``` You need to identify the **actual bottleneck**. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 37. Load Balancer Failure
text: What if you have: ```text Internet ↓ ALB ``` and the ALB itself fails? AWS load-balancing services are designed as managed, highly available infrastructure across Availability Zones. Conceptually: ```text ALB / \ AZ-A AZ-B ``` You don't normally manage a single physical load-balancer server yourself. That's another benefit of using managed cloud infrastructure. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 38. Multi-AZ Application Architecture
text: A better architecture is: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ ALB ┌──────┴──────┐ ↓ ↓ AZ-A AZ-B │ │ Private Private subnet subnet │ │ EC2 EC2 │ │ └──────┬──────┘ ↓ RDS ``` Now losing one AZ doesn't necessarily mean your whole application disappears. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 39. Auto Scaling + ALB
text: These two services solve different problems.

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: ALB
text: Answers: > **Where should this request go?**

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: ASG
text: Answers: > **How many EC2 instances should exist?** Together: ```text ALB / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ EC2 EC2 EC2 ↑ ↑ ↑ └────┴────┘ ASG ``` That's a key distinction. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 40. Health Checks + ASG
text: There can be multiple layers of health checking. ```text ALB health check ↓ Is application target healthy? ``` ASG can also use health information to determine whether instances should be replaced. Conceptually: ```text EC2 unhealthy ↓ ASG detects unhealthy instance ↓ Terminate/replace ↓ New EC2 ↓ ALB health check ↓ Healthy? ↓ Receive traffic ``` This is an excellent production lifecycle. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 41. Complete Production Flow
text: Let's put everything together. ```text INTERNET │ ↓ Route 53 / DNS │ ↓ ALB ┌──────┴──────┐ ↓ ↓ AZ-A AZ-B │ │ EC2 EC2 │ │ └──────┬──────┘ ↓ RDS ``` Scaling: ```text Traffic ↑ ↓ ASG ↓ More EC2 ↓ ALB distributes traffic ``` Failure: ```text EC2 fails ↓ ALB stops sending traffic ↓ ASG replaces instance ↓ New instance becomes healthy ↓ ALB sends traffic ``` Database: ```text EC2 ↓ Connection Pool ↓ RDS ``` Caching: ```text EC2 ↓ Redis ↓ RDS when needed ``` ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 42. What About Deployments?
text: Suppose: ```text EC2-A → version 1 EC2-B → version 1 EC2-C → version 1 ``` You deploy version 2. You don't necessarily want: ```text v1 ❌ v2 ❌ ``` all at once. This leads to deployment strategies such as:

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Rolling deployment
text: ```text v1 v1 v1 ↓ v2 v1 v1 ↓ v2 v2 v1 ↓ v2 v2 v2 ```

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Blue-Green
text: ```text Blue → v1 Green → v2 ``` Switch traffic: ```text Blue ↓ Green ```

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Canary
text: ```text 99% → v1 1% → v2 ``` Then gradually increase: ```text 90/10 70/30 50/50 0/100 ``` These concepts connect directly to CI/CD from [Chapter 6](../03-cicd-gitops/ch06-cicd-github-actions.md). ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 43. Load Balancing vs Reverse Proxy
text: You learned reverse proxies in [Chapter 4](../01-foundations/ch04-networking.md). They overlap conceptually. A reverse proxy: ```text Client ↓ Reverse Proxy ↓ Backend ``` A load balancer: ```text Client ↓ Load Balancer ├── Backend A ├── Backend B └── Backend C ``` An ALB performs load balancing and application-level routing functions. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 44. When Should You Scale?
text: Don't blindly use: ```text CPU > 70% ``` as the only answer. A better engineering approach is: ```text Identify bottleneck ↓ Measure it ↓ Understand workload ↓ Choose scaling strategy ↓ Test ↓ Monitor ``` Possible bottlenecks: ```text CPU Memory Network Database Disk Connections External APIs Locks Application code ``` ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 45. Scaling Doesn't Fix Bad Code
text: Suppose your API performs: ```text O(n²) ``` work unnecessarily. You add: ```text 10 EC2 instances ``` You may temporarily increase capacity, but you've not fixed the fundamental inefficiency. Always ask: ```text Can I optimize? ``` before blindly scaling. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: 46. Scaling and Cost
text: More instances: ```text Performance ↑ Cost ↑ ``` Too few: ```text Cost ↓ Latency ↑ Reliability ↓ ``` So production engineering involves balancing: ```text Performance Availability Reliability Cost Complexity ``` This becomes especially important in system design. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: "Your Node.js API is receiving 10× normal traffic. What would you do?"
text: Strong reasoning: ```text 1. Check metrics 2. Identify bottleneck 3. Ensure ALB is distributing traffic 4. Scale EC2 horizontally if compute is bottleneck 5. Verify database isn't bottleneck 6. Check connection pool 7. Use caching where appropriate 8. Verify external dependencies 9. Monitor latency/error rate 10. Scale back when traffic decreases ``` Don't simply say: > "Add more EC2." ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: "One EC2 instance is unhealthy. What happens?"
text: Potential flow: ```text EC2 unhealthy ↓ ALB health check fails ↓ ALB stops routing requests there ↓ ASG detects unhealthy instance ↓ Instance replaced ↓ New instance starts ↓ Application starts ↓ ALB health check passes ↓ Traffic resumes ``` That's a very strong interview explanation. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: "Why is your application stateless?"
text: Answer: > Because any request should be able to reach any healthy application instance without depending on state stored locally on a particular server. Shared state can be moved to systems such as a database or Redis, which makes horizontal scaling and instance replacement easier. Excellent backend answer. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Practical Exercise
text: Take your Node.js backend and design: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ ALB ┌─────┴─────┐ ↓ ↓ EC2-A EC2-B │ │ └─────┬─────┘ ↓ RDS ``` Then answer:

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: If traffic increases 5×:
text: ```text What scales? ``` Expected reasoning: ```text ALB ↓ ASG ↓ EC2 instances ↑ ``` Then ask: ```text What could become the next bottleneck? ``` Possible: ```text RDS Redis External API Network Connection pool ``` Then ask: > What happens if EC2-A crashes? You should be able to explain the complete health-check + replacement flow without looking at notes. ---

title: Chapter 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: The Most Important Mental Model
text: Remember these four lines: ```text ALB → distributes traffic Target Group → defines backend targets Health Check → determines whether targets should receive traffic ASG → determines how many EC2 instances should exist ``` And: ```text Horizontal scaling → more instances Vertical scaling → bigger instance Stateless application → easier horizontal scaling Multi-AZ → better availability ``` --- <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 13: RDS + Databases on AWS](ch13-rds-databases.md) · [Chapter 15: Lambda + Serverless + Messaging](ch15-lambda-serverless-messaging.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch14-revision.md)

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Chapter 14 — Revision Sheet: Load Balancing + Scaling
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/04-aws/ch14-load-balancing-scaling.md). Core question: **what happens when one EC2 server isn't enough?**

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: The pieces
text: | Piece | Answers | |---|---| | **Load balancer / ELB / ALB** | *Where should this request go?* ALB = Application Load Balancer (HTTP/HTTPS, application-layer) | | **Target group** | Defines the backend destinations (EC2 instances, IP addresses, containers) | | **Health check** | Should this target receive traffic? (e.g. `GET /health` → `200 OK`; failing targets are removed from rotation) | | **Listener** | Waits for traffic on a port/protocol (`:80`, `:443`); forwards to a target group. Production = HTTPS `:443` | | **ASG (Auto Scaling Group)** | *How many EC2 instances should exist?* — scale out / scale in, replace failed instances | | **Launch template** | What ASG launches: AMI, instance type, security group, IAM role, user data, other config | ```text ALB → distributes traffic Target Group → backend targets Health check → who receives traffic ASG → how many instances exist ``` - Client only needs the ALB endpoint/domain, not individual EC2s. - **ALB routing rules:** path-based (`/users/*` → Users TG, `/orders/*` → Orders TG) and host-based (`api.example.com` → API targets, `admin.example.com` → Admin targets) — why it's *Application* LB. - **Algorithms:** round robin; least outstanding requests (fewer active requests). Principle: the LB decides which *healthy* target gets each request. - **Health check vs monitoring:** health check = "can I reach this backend and get an acceptable response?"; observability = CPU, memory, latency, errors, DB failures, request rate (Ch.17/22). - **Security groups:** `Internet → ALB-SG (443 from Internet) → API-SG (3000 from ALB-SG) → EC2`. - **LB availability:** ELB is managed, highly available across AZs; you don't run a single LB server. - **LB vs reverse proxy:** overlapping concepts; ALB does load balancing + application-level routing.

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Scaling concepts
text: - **Vertical (scale up)** vs **Horizontal (scale out)**. For web apps, horizontal scaling matters most; it needs **stateless** app servers. - **ASG capacity:** Minimum / Desired / Maximum (e.g. 2 / 3 / 10) — normal 3, never intentionally below 2, can scale to 10. **Auto Scaling ≠ infinite scaling**: stops at max; then larger instances, higher max, better code, caching, DB scaling, architectural change. - **Scale out** when CPU/requests/latency rise; **scale in** when traffic drops (cost saving). - **Policies:** **Target tracking** (e.g. keep CPU ≈ 50%) · **Step scaling** (CPU>70% add 1, >85% add 2, >95% add 4) · **Scheduled scaling** (predictable load, e.g. scale before 8 AM / after 8 PM). Scaling should respond to workload, not arbitrary server count. - **Self-healing:** failed instance replaced by ASG (replace instead of repairing). Immutable infrastructure: broken instance → terminate → fresh instance from known image. **Full failure flow:** EC2 unhealthy → ALB health check fails → ALB stops routing there → ASG detects unhealthy instance → replaces it → new instance starts → app starts → ALB health check passes → traffic resumes.

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Stateless architecture
text: - **Bad:** session in EC2-A's RAM; request 2 hits EC2-B → "Who is this user?" ❌. - **Good:** shared state in Redis / database / object storage / dedicated state services; application code identical on all instances. - **JWT:** any instance can validate the token without local session — but adds expiry, revocation, refresh tokens, key management, token size, compromised-token concerns ("JWT ≠ automatically perfect scaling"). - **Sticky sessions:** requests from a user tend to go to the same instance — helps legacy stateful apps but can cause uneven load. Stateless is generally preferable. - *Why is your app stateless? Any request can reach any healthy instance without relying on local state; shared state lives in a DB/Redis, making horizontal scaling and instance replacement easier.*

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Bottlenecks, cost, and code
text: - **Scaling one layer doesn't scale the system**: ASG 2 → 20 EC2 multiplies DB connections/queries/CPU/IO → RDS becomes the bottleneck (see Ch.13). - Identify the **actual bottleneck** (CPU, memory, network, database, disk, connections, external APIs, locks, application code): identify → measure → understand workload → choose strategy → test → monitor. - **Scaling doesn't fix bad code** (O(n²) unnecessarily + 10 EC2 only hides it): optimise first. - Cost trade-off: more instances = performance↑ cost↑; too few = latency↑ reliability↓. Balance performance, availability, reliability, cost, complexity.

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Multi-AZ application architecture
text: Internet → ALB → AZ-A/AZ-B private subnets → EC2 → RDS. Losing one AZ doesn't necessarily lose the app. Full flow: Route 53/DNS → ALB → EC2 (ASG) → connection pool → RDS; Redis for caching.

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Deployments (interaction)
text: Rolling (v1 v1 v1 → v2 v1 v1 → … → v2 v2 v2); Blue-Green (switch traffic Blue → Green); Canary (99/1 → 90/10 → 70/30 → 50/50 → 0/100). See [Chapter 6](../docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch06-cicd-github-actions.md).

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Scenarios
text: 1. **10× traffic:** check metrics → identify bottleneck → ensure ALB distributes → scale EC2 horizontally if compute-bound → verify DB isn't the bottleneck → check connection pool → cache → verify external dependencies → monitor latency/errors → scale back later. (Not just "add more EC2".) 2. **One EC2 unhealthy:** see failure flow above. 3. **Practical exercise:** ALB → EC2-A/EC2-B → RDS; if traffic ×5 "what scales?" ALB → ASG → more EC2; next bottleneck: RDS, Redis, external API, network, connection pool.

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Depth guide
text: Master: LB concept, ALB, target groups, listeners, health checks, SGs, horizontal vs vertical, ASG, launch templates, min/desired/max, scaling policies, multi-AZ, stateless design, sessions, DB bottleneck, pooling, failure replacement, rolling/blue-green/canary. Medium: target tracking, step, scheduled, sticky sessions, routing rules, deployment interaction. Awareness: Network Load Balancer, Gateway Load Balancer, advanced ELB.

title: Revision 14 — Load Balancing + Scaling
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **ELB types:** ALB (Layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS), NLB (Layer 4 TCP/UDP, very high throughput, static IPs), GWLB (inline virtual appliances). - **ASG health check type:** by default an ASG uses **EC2 status checks**; to have it replace instances that the **ALB** marks unhealthy, enable **ELB health checks** on the ASG (the source's "ASG can also use health information" glosses over this). - Health check settings to know: path, interval, timeout, healthy/unhealthy threshold counts, success codes. - **Deregistration delay / connection draining** lets in-flight requests finish before a target is removed during scale-in or deployments. - ASG **cooldown / instance warm-up** prevents flapping while new instances boot. - ALB terminates TLS (certificate from **AWS Certificate Manager**), can redirect `:80` → `:443`, adds `X-Forwarded-For` so the app can see the client IP. - Target types for target groups: `instance`, `ip`, `lambda`.
