title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
text: > **Source:** Response 15 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-15.txt`, lines 9–1807) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch15-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> This response has two major goals: 1. Understand **serverless + Lambda** 2. Understand **messaging/event-driven systems** and actually use them ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: PART 1 — What Problem Does Lambda Solve?
text: Until now, we've mostly used: ```text GitHub ↓ CI/CD ↓ Docker ↓ EC2 ↓ Node.js ``` You have to maintain: ```text EC2 OS Docker Application Scaling Health Deployment ``` But what if you have a small function that only needs to run occasionally? For example: ```text User uploads image ↓ Resize image ``` Why keep an EC2 server running 24/7 just for that? Lambda gives you: ```text Event ↓ Lambda ↓ Function executes ↓ Done ``` You don't manage the underlying server. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 2. Lambda Mental Model
text: Traditional backend: ```text EC2 │ ┌──────┴──────┐ │ Node.js API │ └─────────────┘ │ Running 24/7 ``` Lambda: ```text Event ↓ Lambda ↓ Function ↓ Execution finishes ``` Think: > **Lambda = run code without managing servers.** ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 3. Lambda Function
text: A Lambda function is basically: ```typescript export const handler = async (event) => { return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ message: "Hello from Lambda", }), }; }; ``` AWS invokes: ```text handler(event) ``` You don't manually run: ```bash node server.js ``` AWS invokes your function when an event occurs. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Traditional Express
text: ```typescript app.get("/hello", (req, res) => { res.json({ message: "Hello" }); }); app.listen(3000); ``` You need: ```text Server Port Process Infrastructure ```

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Lambda
text: ```typescript export const handler = async (event) => { return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ message: "Hello", }), }; }; ``` AWS manages the execution environment. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 5. Important Lambda Terms
text: You should know: ```text Function Runtime Handler Event Invocation Execution environment Timeout Memory Environment variables Concurrency Cold start Layers ``` We'll understand each through practice. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 6. Runtime
text: Lambda needs to know what environment to execute your code in. For you: ```text Node.js ``` is particularly relevant. Conceptually: ```text Lambda └── Node.js runtime └── your function ``` ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 7. Handler
text: Suppose your file is: ```text index.ts ``` and exports: ```typescript export const handler = async () => { return "Hello"; }; ``` The handler tells Lambda which function to invoke. Conceptually: ```text index.handler ``` means: ```text index.js ↓ handler() ``` ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 8. Lambda Event
text: Lambda doesn't have to be triggered by HTTP. An event could come from: ```text API Gateway S3 SQS SNS EventBridge CloudWatch Events ``` For example: ```text S3 upload ↓ Lambda ↓ Process file ``` or: ```text SQS message ↓ Lambda ↓ Process job ``` This is where Lambda becomes extremely powerful. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: PART 2 — Actually Creating a Lambda
text: There are several ways to deploy Lambda. For learning, know all three: ```text AWS Console AWS CLI Infrastructure as Code ``` We'll start conceptually with the CLI/IaC mindset because that's closer to DevOps. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 9. AWS CLI
text: You already learned: ```bash aws sts get-caller-identity ``` First verify: ```bash aws sts get-caller-identity ``` You should see your AWS identity. Then: ```bash aws configure ``` can configure credentials for local development, although for production CI/CD we'll prefer temporary credentials through IAM roles/OIDC rather than long-lived access keys. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 10. Create a Simple Lambda Project
text: Create: ```text lambda-demo/ ├── package.json ├── src/ │ └── index.ts └── tsconfig.json ``` Install TypeScript: ```bash npm init -y npm install npm install -D typescript @types/aws-lambda ``` Example: ```typescript import type { APIGatewayProxyHandlerV2, } from "aws-lambda"; export const handler: APIGatewayProxyHandlerV2 = async () => { return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ message: "Hello from Lambda!", }), }; }; ``` Compile: ```bash npx tsc ``` Now you have JavaScript for Lambda. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 11. Lambda Deployment Package
text: Lambda can be deployed as a package containing: ```text index.js node_modules/ other files ``` Conceptually: ```text TypeScript ↓ Compile ↓ JavaScript ↓ Package ↓ Lambda ``` This is exactly where your CI/CD knowledge becomes relevant. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 12. Manual Deployment vs DevOps
text: You *could* manually upload: ```text ZIP ↓ AWS Console ↓ Lambda ``` But that's not a good production workflow. Instead: ```text Developer ↓ git push ↓ GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ npm ci ↓ npm test ↓ npm run build ↓ package ↓ AWS Lambda ``` **That's DevOps in practice.** ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 13. Environment Variables
text: Don't hardcode: ```typescript const dbPassword = "secret"; ``` Use: ```typescript const dbHost = process.env.DB_HOST; ``` Lambda supports environment variables. Conceptually: ```text Lambda ├── Code ├── Environment variables └── IAM permissions ``` For sensitive values, use proper secrets-management mechanisms rather than treating ordinary environment variables as a secret vault. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 14. Lambda IAM Role
text: Lambda often needs permission to access other AWS services. For example: ```text Lambda ↓ S3 ``` Lambda should have an IAM execution role allowing only what it needs. Example: ```text Lambda Execution Role Allow: s3:GetObject Resource: specific bucket/path ``` Not: ```text Allow: * ``` This is the same **least privilege** principle you learned in [Chapter 9](ch09-aws-fundamentals-iam.md). ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 15. Lambda + S3
text: Now we have a practical architecture. Suppose a user uploads: ```text photo.jpg ``` to: ```text S3 ``` S3 can generate an event: ```text S3 ↓ Lambda ↓ Process image ``` For example: ```text User uploads image ↓ S3 ↓ Lambda ↓ Resize / validate / analyze ↓ S3 ``` This is event-driven architecture. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: PART 3 — Messaging
text: Now we reach a very important backend concept. Suppose your API receives: ```text POST /send-email ``` Should your API wait for the email provider? Bad architecture: ```text Client ↓ Node API ↓ Email provider ↓ Wait ↓ Response ``` If the email service is slow: ```text API latency ↑ ``` Instead: ```text Client ↓ Node API ↓ Queue ↓ Immediate response Queue ↓ Worker ↓ Email provider ``` This is **asynchronous processing**. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 16. What Is a Queue?
text: A queue is basically: > **A buffer of work waiting to be processed.** Example: ```text Producer ↓ Queue ↓ Consumer ``` Producer: ```text Node.js API ``` Queue: ```text SQS ``` Consumer: ```text Lambda ``` Architecture: ```text Node.js ↓ SQS ↓ Lambda ↓ Email service ``` ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 17. Why Use a Queue?
text: Without queue: ```text API ↓ Heavy job ↓ Wait 10 seconds ↓ Response ``` With queue: ```text API ↓ Queue ↓ Response quickly ``` Then: ```text Queue ↓ Worker ↓ Heavy job ``` Benefits: - decoupling - buffering - retrying - asynchronous processing - traffic smoothing - failure isolation ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 18. SQS
text: SQS = **Simple Queue Service**. Mental model: ```text Producer ↓ ┌──────────────┐ │ SQS │ │ │ │ Job 1 │ │ Job 2 │ │ Job 3 │ └──────────────┘ ↓ Consumer ``` ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 19. Standard Queue
text: SQS Standard is designed for highly scalable asynchronous messaging. But don't assume: ```text exactly once ``` processing. Your application should generally be designed to tolerate duplicate processing. This leads to an extremely important concept: > **Idempotency** ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 20. Idempotency
text: Suppose your queue contains: ```json { "orderId": "123", "action": "charge" } ``` What if the worker processes it twice? Bad: ```text ₹100 charged ₹100 charged again ``` You need an idempotent design. For example: ```text orderId = 123 payment already processed? ↓ Yes → don't charge again No → process ``` This is one of the most important concepts in distributed systems. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 21. SQS Visibility Timeout
text: Imagine: ```text Queue ↓ Message ``` Worker receives the message. You don't want another worker immediately processing the same message while the first worker is working. So the message becomes temporarily invisible. Conceptually: ```text Queue ↓ Worker A receives message ↓ Message temporarily invisible ``` If Worker A successfully finishes: ```text Delete message ``` If Worker A crashes: ```text Message becomes visible again ``` This enables retry behavior. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 22. Retry
text: Suppose: ```text Lambda ↓ External API ``` External API returns: ```text 500 ``` You don't necessarily want to permanently lose the job. Instead: ```text Attempt 1 ❌ ↓ Retry ↓ Attempt 2 ❌ ↓ Retry ↓ Attempt 3 ❌ ``` Eventually: ```text Success ``` or: ```text Dead Letter Queue ``` ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 23. Dead Letter Queue
text: DLQ = **Dead Letter Queue**. If a message repeatedly fails: ```text SQS ↓ Worker ↓ ❌ ↓ Retry ↓ ❌ ↓ Retry ↓ ❌ ↓ DLQ ``` Now you can inspect failed jobs instead of silently losing them. This is a very important production pattern. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 24. Lambda + SQS
text: AWS can connect Lambda to SQS. Architecture: ```text Node.js API ↓ SQS ↓ Lambda ↓ Process message ``` Lambda can poll/process messages from the queue through an event source integration. You don't have to maintain: ```text Worker EC2 ``` yourself. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 25. Practical Example — Order Processing
text: Suppose: ```text POST /orders ``` Node.js: ```typescript await sqs.send( new SendMessageCommand({ QueueUrl: process.env.ORDER_QUEUE_URL, MessageBody: JSON.stringify({ orderId, userId, }), }) ); ``` Then return: ```json { "message": "Order accepted" } ``` The API doesn't need to perform every downstream task synchronously. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 26. Lambda Consumer
text: Conceptually: ```typescript export const handler = async (event) => { for (const record of event.Records) { const message = JSON.parse(record.body); await processOrder(message.orderId); } }; ``` Architecture: ```text POST /orders ↓ Node.js ↓ SQS ↓ Lambda ↓ processOrder() ``` This is a **real backend production pattern**. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 27. SNS
text: SNS = **Simple Notification Service**. Think: > **Publish a message and let multiple subscribers receive it.** Architecture: ```text SNS Topic / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ SQS Lambda Email ``` This is different from a simple queue. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Queue
text: ```text Producer ↓ Queue ↓ Consumer ``` Usually the work is distributed among consumers.

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Pub/Sub
text: ```text Publisher ↓ Topic / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ A B C ``` Multiple subscribers can independently receive the event. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 29. Example SNS Architecture
text: Suppose an order is created. ```text Order Service ↓ SNS Topic / \ ↓ ↓ Email Analytics Lambda Lambda ``` Now the order service doesn't need to know the internal implementation of each consumer. That's **decoupling**. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 30. SQS vs SNS
text: | | SQS | SNS | |---|---|---| | Main idea | Queue | Pub/Sub | | Consumer model | Work queue | Multiple subscribers | | Buffer messages | Yes | Not primarily | | Decoupling | Yes | Yes | | Common use | Background jobs | Event fan-out | A common architecture combines them: ```text SNS / \ ↓ ↓ SQS-A SQS-B ↓ ↓ Worker Worker ``` ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 31. Why Not Directly Connect Everything?
text: Bad: ```text Order Service ├── Email Service ├── Analytics ├── Inventory ├── Notification └── Shipping ``` Now Order Service knows about everything. Better: ```text Order Service ↓ SNS ┌────────┼────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ SQS SQS Lambda ↓ ↓ Inventory Shipping ``` Now services are more loosely coupled. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 32. Event-Driven Architecture
text: This leads to: > **Event-driven architecture** Instead of: ```text Service A ↓ directly call ↓ Service B ``` you can have: ```text Service A ↓ Event ↓ Message infrastructure ↓ Service B ``` For example: ```text OrderCreated ``` could trigger: ```text Inventory Notification Analytics Email ``` independently. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 33. Lambda Cold Starts
text: Lambda execution environments can be reused, but sometimes AWS needs to initialize a new execution environment. This can introduce: ```text Cold start ``` Conceptually: ```text Request ↓ Create environment ↓ Load runtime ↓ Load application ↓ Execute ``` versus a warm execution environment: ```text Request ↓ Existing environment ↓ Execute ``` Cold starts can matter for latency-sensitive workloads. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 34. Lambda Concurrency
text: Suppose: ```text 1 request ↓ 1 Lambda execution ``` Now: ```text 100 requests ``` Lambda can execute multiple instances of the function concurrently, subject to account/function limits and configuration. Conceptually: ```text Lambda / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ Exec 1 Exec 2 Exec 3 ``` This is another form of automatic horizontal execution scaling. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 35. The Danger of Uncontrolled Scaling
text: Suppose: ```text SQS ↓ Lambda ``` Suddenly: ```text 1,000,000 messages ``` Lambda may process a large number concurrently. But downstream: ```text Lambda ↓ RDS ``` could overwhelm your database. Again: > **Scaling one component can overload another component.** This is the same lesson we learned with EC2 + RDS. You need: - concurrency controls - batching - queue design - connection management - backpressure - database capacity planning ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 36. Lambda + RDS
text: This architecture deserves attention: ```text Lambda ↓ RDS ``` It can work, but high Lambda concurrency can create database connection pressure. For relational databases, AWS provides **RDS Proxy** as one option for managing database connections between applications such as Lambda and RDS. Mental model: ```text Lambda Lambda Lambda Lambda \ | | / ↓ RDS Proxy ↓ RDS ``` You don't need deep RDS Proxy administration for this roadmap, but understand **why it exists**. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 37. Lambda vs EC2
text: | | EC2 | Lambda | |---|---|---| | Server management | You manage more | AWS manages execution infrastructure | | Runtime | Long-running | Event/function execution | | Scaling | ASG etc. | Managed concurrency model | | Billing model | Instance/resource usage | Invocation/execution based | | Best fit | Long-running APIs/workloads | Event-driven/short-lived workloads | | Control | High | Lower | Don't interpret this as: > Lambda is always better. It's a different execution model. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 38. Lambda vs Containers
text: You now have three important choices: ```text Compute │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ EC2 Containers Lambda │ ECS/EKS ```

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: EC2
text: Maximum infrastructure control.

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Containers
text: Package application + dependencies consistently.

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Lambda
text: Run event-driven functions without managing servers. We'll later connect these choices to Kubernetes. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: PART 4 — Actually Using DevOps With Lambda
text: Here's where your earlier criticism matters. A proper workflow looks like: ```text Developer ↓ Git ↓ GitHub ↓ Pull Request ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Install ↓ Lint ↓ Typecheck ↓ Test ↓ Build ↓ Package ↓ Deploy Lambda ↓ AWS ``` That is **DevOps**, not just knowing what Lambda is. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 39. Example GitHub Actions Pipeline
text: Conceptually: ```yaml name: Deploy Lambda on: push: branches: - main jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: id-token: write contents: read steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 - run: npm ci - run: npm test - run: npm run build - run: | zip -r lambda.zip dist node_modules - name: Configure AWS credentials uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE }} aws-region: ap-south-1 - run: | aws lambda update-function-code \ --function-name my-function \ --zip-file fileb://lambda.zip ``` The exact production pipeline can be improved later, but understand the workflow. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 40. What Happened Here?
text: You should be able to explain every stage: ```text checkout ↓ Get code setup-node ↓ Install Node npm ci ↓ Reproducible dependencies npm test ↓ Quality gate npm run build ↓ TypeScript → JavaScript zip ↓ Deployment artifact AWS credentials ↓ OIDC → IAM role aws lambda update-function-code ↓ Deploy ``` **That is the practical DevOps skill we're going to emphasize from here onward.** ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 41. Better Production Approach
text: As we progress, you'll learn Infrastructure as Code. Eventually: ```text Terraform ↓ Create: ├── Lambda ├── IAM role ├── SQS ├── SNS ├── API Gateway ├── VPC └── other infrastructure ``` Then: ```text Git ↓ Terraform plan ↓ Review ↓ Terraform apply ``` That's much more reproducible than manually clicking around AWS Console. Terraform is [Chapter 21](../06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md), so we're intentionally building toward it. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 42. Complete Example Architecture
text: Here's a realistic serverless order system: ```text USER │ ↓ API Gateway │ ↓ Lambda API │ ↓ SQS │ ↓ Lambda Worker / \ ↓ ↓ RDS SNS / \ ↓ ↓ Email Analytics ``` Now imagine DevOps around it: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Test ↓ Build ↓ Deploy ↓ Lambda + SQS + SNS + infrastructure ``` ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 43. Where Docker Fits
text: Important question: > If Lambda exists, why did we spend so much time learning Docker? Because Lambda doesn't replace containers. Your production architecture could be: ```text ALB ↓ ECS/EKS/EC2 ↓ Main Node API │ ↓ SQS ↓ Lambda ``` Use: ```text Containers → main long-running backend Lambda → event-driven/background functions ``` depending on workload. ---

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: 44. Production Decision Framework
text: When choosing:

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: EC2
text: Ask: > Do I need maximum server-level control?

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Containers
text: Ask: > Do I have a long-running application that I want packaged consistently?

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Lambda
text: Ask: > Is this naturally event-driven and suitable for function-based execution?

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: SQS
text: Ask: > Do I need asynchronous work buffering?

title: Chapter 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: SNS
text: Ask: > Do multiple consumers need to receive an event? That's much more useful than memorizing definitions. ---

heading: Your Practical Assignment
text: Build this locally first: ```text Node.js API ↓ Queue ↓ Worker ``` The API should expose: ```text POST /jobs ``` Request: ```json { "type": "send-email", "userId": "123" } ``` Instead of processing the email immediately: ```text POST /jobs ↓ Queue ↓ 202 Accepted ``` Worker: ```text Queue ↓ Worker ↓ processJob() ``` Then add: ```text retry idempotency failure handling ``` Once you understand that locally, move the architecture toward: ```text Node.js ↓ AWS SQS ↓ AWS Lambda ``` And eventually: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ AWS ``` That progression will teach you **DevOps by actually doing it**, rather than simply memorizing AWS services. ---

title: Revision 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Chapter 15 — Revision Sheet: Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/04-aws/ch15-lambda-serverless-messaging.md). Two goals: understand **serverless/Lambda**, and understand **messaging/event-driven systems** and actually use them.

title: Revision 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Lambda in one page
text: - **Lambda = run code without managing servers.** Event → Lambda → function executes → done (vs EC2 running 24/7 for an occasional job such as image resize). - **Terms:** Function · Runtime (e.g. Node.js) · Handler (`index.handler` = `handler()` exported from `index.js`) · Event · Invocation · Execution environment · Timeout · Memory · Environment variables · Concurrency · Cold start · Layers. - **Handler:** ```typescript import type { APIGatewayProxyHandlerV2 } from "aws-lambda"; export const handler: APIGatewayProxyHandlerV2 = async () => ({ statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ message: "Hello from Lambda!" }), }); ``` - **Express vs Lambda:** Express needs server, port, process, infrastructure; Lambda: AWS manages the execution environment and calls `handler(event)`. - **Event sources:** API Gateway, S3, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, CloudWatch Events. Examples: S3 upload → Lambda → process file; SQS message → Lambda → process job. - **Project:** `lambda-demo/ {package.json, src/index.ts, tsconfig.json}`; `npm init -y`, `npm install -D typescript @types/aws-lambda`, `npx tsc` → JavaScript → package (zip) → deploy. Deploy ways: Console, CLI, Infrastructure as Code (CLI/IaC mindset preferred). - **Environment variables** (`process.env.DB_HOST`); don't treat plain env vars as a secret vault — use proper secrets management. - **Execution role (IAM):** least privilege (e.g. `s3:GetObject` on a specific bucket/path, never `*`). - **Cold start:** new execution environment must be created → load runtime → load app → execute (a warm environment skips this); matters for latency-sensitive paths. - **Concurrency:** many concurrent executions automatically (subject to account/function limits). - **Danger of uncontrolled scaling:** 1,000,000 SQS messages → massive Lambda concurrency → downstream RDS overwhelmed. Needs concurrency controls, batching, queue design, connection management, **backpressure**, DB capacity planning. **Lambda + RDS** → connection pressure → **RDS Proxy** (Lambda × N → RDS Proxy → RDS).

title: Revision 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: EC2 vs containers vs Lambda
text: | | EC2 | Lambda | |---|---|---| | Server management | You manage more | AWS manages execution infrastructure | | Runtime | Long-running | Event/function execution | | Scaling | ASG etc. | Managed concurrency | | Billing | Instance/resource usage | Invocation/execution based | | Best for | Long-running APIs/workloads | Event-driven, short-lived workloads | | Control | High | Lower | Decision: EC2 = max server control · Containers = long-running app packaged consistently · Lambda = naturally event-driven functions · SQS = async buffering · SNS = multiple consumers need the event. Containers (ECS/EKS/EC2) run the main backend; Lambda handles event-driven/background functions — **Lambda doesn't replace Docker**.

title: Revision 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Messaging
text: **Async processing:** `POST /send-email` → API puts job in queue → responds immediately → worker calls email provider. Prevents API latency growth when the provider is slow. Benefits: decoupling, buffering, retrying, async processing, traffic smoothing, failure isolation. | | **SQS** | **SNS** | |---|---|---| | Idea | Queue (buffer of work): producer → queue → consumer | Pub/Sub: publisher → topic → many subscribers | | Consumers | Work distributed among consumers | Multiple subscribers independently receive the event | | Buffering | Yes | Not primarily | | Use | Background jobs | Event fan-out | Combined pattern: SNS → SQS-A, SQS-B → workers. Order Service publishes to SNS; Inventory/Shipping via SQS, email/analytics via Lambda; the producer needn't know the consumers (**decoupling**; event-driven architecture, e.g. `OrderCreated`).

title: Revision 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Reliability concepts (high-yield)
text: - **SQS Standard** is highly scalable but don't assume exactly-once → design for duplicates → **idempotency**: e.g. `orderId=123`, "payment already processed?" yes → skip, no → process (don't charge twice). - **Visibility timeout:** a received message becomes temporarily invisible; success → delete; worker crash → visible again → retry. - **Retry:** failed attempts retried; persistent failures go to a **Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)** so failed jobs can be inspected instead of silently lost. - **Lambda + SQS:** Lambda consumes through an event-source integration (no worker EC2 to run). ```typescript // Producer (Node API) await sqs.send(new SendMessageCommand({ QueueUrl: process.env.ORDER_QUEUE_URL, MessageBody: JSON.stringify({ orderId, userId }), })); // → respond { "message": "Order accepted" } (e.g. 202) // Consumer (Lambda) export const handler = async (event) => { for (const record of event.Records) { const message = JSON.parse(record.body); await processOrder(message.orderId); } }; ```

title: Revision 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Lambda CI/CD pipeline (concept)
text: ```yaml name: Deploy Lambda on: { push: { branches: [main] } } jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read } # needed for OIDC steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: { node-version: 22 } - run: npm ci - run: npm test - run: npm run build - run: zip -r lambda.zip dist node_modules - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE }} aws-region: ap-south-1 - run: aws lambda update-function-code --function-name my-function --zip-file fileb://lambda.zip ``` checkout (get code) · setup-node · `npm ci` (reproducible) · `npm test` (quality gate) · build (TS→JS) · zip (artifact) · OIDC → IAM role (no static keys) · `update-function-code` (deploy). Better: Terraform creates Lambda, IAM role, SQS, SNS, API Gateway, VPC → `plan` → review → `apply` (Ch.21).

heading: Serverless order system
text: User → API Gateway → Lambda API → SQS → Lambda Worker → RDS + SNS → (Email, Analytics).

title: Revision 15 — Lambda + Serverless + Messaging
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **Limits to remember (verify current docs):** Lambda timeout up to 15 min; memory 128 MB–10 GB with CPU proportional to memory; synchronous payload ≈ 6 MB; default regional concurrency ≈ 1,000 (use *reserved concurrency* or the SQS event-source *maximum concurrency* to cap load on a database). - **SQS Standard** = at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering; **FIFO** queues give ordering and deduplication. Set the queue's **visibility timeout ≥ the Lambda function timeout** (AWS recommends a multiple); configure the DLQ with `maxReceiveCount`. - The consumer loop above fails the **whole batch** if one record throws, so successful records are retried (duplicates) — use *partial batch responses* (`ReportBatchItemFailures`) and idempotent processing. - Idempotency techniques: idempotency key stored with a unique constraint, conditional writes, upsert, state checks. - `aws lambda update-function-code` returns before the update is complete; use `aws lambda wait function-updated` before publishing/invoking in pipelines. - `zip -r lambda.zip dist node_modules` ships dev dependencies too; prune with `npm ci --omit=dev` (or bundle with esbuild) to reduce package size and cold starts. - `${{ secrets.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE }}` holds a role ARN — not secret by nature, but kept in a secret/variable for convenience. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 14](ch14-revision.md) · [Full chapter 15](../docs/04-aws/ch15-lambda-serverless-messaging.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 16](ch16-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
text: > **Source:** Response 16 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-16.txt`, lines 1–1951) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch16-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> Yes — and we're now making the course **hands-on**, as you requested. This response will teach you not only **what Route 53, CloudFront, CDN, and WAF are**, but also **how they fit into the AWS architecture, how you'd configure them, what traffic actually does, and how you'd deploy/use them.** ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 0. Where We Are
text: Our production architecture is becoming: ```text USER │ ↓ Route 53 DNS │ ↓ CloudFront CDN │ ↓ ALB │ ┌──────────┴──────────┐ ↓ ↓ EC2 EC2 │ │ └──────────┬──────────┘ ↓ RDS ``` And we also have: ```text S3 Lambda SQS IAM VPC Security Groups GitHub Actions Docker ``` Today's job is to understand the **front door of your application**. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 1. What Problem Does DNS Solve?
text: Suppose your EC2 server has: ```text 13.234.56.78 ``` You don't want users to remember: ```text http://13.234.56.78 ``` Instead: ```text api.myapp.com ``` DNS translates: ```text api.myapp.com ↓ 13.234.56.78 ``` But in production, the destination may not even be a fixed IP. For example: ```text api.myapp.com ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 2. Route 53
text: **Route 53** is AWS's DNS and domain-routing service. Think: ```text Domain ↓ Route 53 ↓ AWS resource ``` For example: ```text api.example.com ↓ Application Load Balancer ``` or: ```text www.example.com ↓ CloudFront ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 3. Domain Structure
text: Suppose you own: ```text example.com ``` You can create: ```text www.example.com api.example.com admin.example.com cdn.example.com ``` These are DNS records. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 4. Important DNS Records
text: You should know: | Record | Purpose | |---|---| | A | hostname → IPv4 | | AAAA | hostname → IPv6 | | CNAME | hostname → another hostname | | MX | mail servers | | TXT | arbitrary verification/text information | | NS | name servers | For SWE interviews, focus especially on: ```text A AAAA CNAME TXT NS ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 5. A Record
text: Example: ```text api.example.com ↓ A record ↓ 13.234.56.78 ``` Meaning: > Resolve this hostname to this IPv4 address. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 6. CNAME
text: Example: ```text www.example.com ↓ CNAME ↓ some-target.example.com ``` It maps one hostname to another hostname. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 7. DNS Lookup
text: From Linux: ```bash dig example.com ``` or: ```bash nslookup example.com ``` You can inspect: ```text DNS response records TTL addresses ``` This becomes useful when debugging domains. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 8. TTL
text: TTL = **Time To Live**. Suppose: ```text api.example.com TTL = 300 ``` DNS resolvers can cache the result for roughly: ```text 300 seconds ``` This means DNS changes aren't necessarily visible everywhere instantly. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 9. Why TTL Matters
text: Suppose: ```text api.example.com ↓ Old ALB ``` You change it to: ```text api.example.com ↓ New ALB ``` If clients/resolvers still have the old DNS result cached: ```text Old destination ``` may continue being used until the cache expires. Therefore: > **DNS changes have propagation/caching considerations.** ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 10. Route 53 Hosted Zone
text: A hosted zone contains DNS information for a domain. Conceptually: ```text Route 53 │ └── Hosted Zone │ ├── example.com ├── www.example.com ├── api.example.com └── admin.example.com ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Public Hosted Zone
text: Used for: ```text Internet users ``` Example: ```text api.example.com ```

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Private Hosted Zone
text: Used for DNS names inside your VPC/private environment. Example: ```text db.internal api.internal ``` Conceptually: ```text VPC └── Private DNS ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 12. Our Application
text: Suppose: ```text example.com ``` We have: ```text Internet ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ``` We want: ```text api.example.com ``` to reach the ALB. Architecture: ```text User ↓ api.example.com ↓ Route 53 ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 13. How You Configure It
text: In AWS: ```text Route 53 ↓ Hosted Zones ↓ example.com ↓ Create Record ``` Then: ```text Name: api Record: A Alias: ALB ``` AWS supports alias records for supported AWS resources. So you don't need to hardcode the ALB's changing infrastructure details. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 14. Why This Is Better Than EC2 IP
text: Bad: ```text api.example.com ↓ EC2 public IP ``` If EC2 changes: ```text Old EC2 ❌ New EC2 ``` your DNS target becomes problematic. Better: ```text api.example.com ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 fleet ``` The ALB becomes the stable application entry point. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 15. What Is a CDN?
text: CDN = **Content Delivery Network**. Suppose your server is in: ```text Mumbai ``` and a user is in: ```text New York ``` Without CDN: ```text New York ↓ Mumbai ↓ Your server ``` Every request travels to your origin. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 16. CDN Idea
text: Instead: ```text Origin │ ┌──────┼──────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Edge Edge Edge ↑ ↑ ↑ Users Users Users ``` The CDN caches content closer to users. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 17. CloudFront
text: **Amazon CloudFront** is AWS's CDN. Think: ```text User ↓ CloudFront Edge Location ↓ Origin ``` The origin could be: - S3 - ALB - EC2 - other supported origins ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 18. Why Use CloudFront?
text: Benefits can include:

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Lower latency
text: Content can be served closer to users.

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Caching
text: Repeated requests may be served from the edge.

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Reduced origin load
text: Instead of: ```text 100,000 requests ↓ Origin ``` some requests can be served: ```text 100,000 requests ↓ CloudFront ↓ Origin receives fewer requests ```

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Security
text: CloudFront integrates with other AWS security features and TLS. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 19. What Should You Cache?
text: Good candidates: ```text Images CSS JavaScript Fonts Videos Static files Public assets ``` Potentially: ```text API GET responses ``` but only when your caching/consistency requirements make that safe. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 20. What Shouldn't You Blindly Cache?
text: Be careful with: ```text POST PUT DELETE ``` and personalized/private responses. For example: ```text GET /profile ``` might return: ```text Rachit's profile ``` You don't want another user receiving that cached response. So caching requires understanding: ```text Who can see the response? How long is it valid? Can it become stale? ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 21. CloudFront Architecture
text: For your application: ```text USER │ ↓ CloudFront │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ S3 ALB │ │ Static Dynamic Assets API ``` This is a very common architecture. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 22. Frontend + Backend Architecture
text: Suppose you have: ```text React / Next.js frontend Node.js backend ``` A possible architecture: ```text USER │ ↓ CloudFront / \ ↓ ↓ S3 ALB Frontend API │ ┌──────┴──────┐ ↓ ↓ EC2 EC2 │ │ └──────┬──────┘ ↓ RDS ``` Now: ```text Static content → S3 + CloudFront API → ALB + EC2 Database → RDS ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 23. Cache Hit
text: Suppose: ```text GET /logo.png ``` First user: ```text User ↓ CloudFront ↓ Cache MISS ↓ S3 ↓ CloudFront ↓ User ``` CloudFront caches it. Next user: ```text User ↓ CloudFront ↓ CACHE HIT ↓ User ``` No request to S3 is needed for that hit. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 24. Cache Miss
text: If the requested content isn't cached: ```text User ↓ CloudFront ↓ MISS ↓ Origin ↓ Response ↓ CloudFront ↓ User ``` Depending on cache behavior, CloudFront may cache the response. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 25. Cache-Control
text: Your application/origin can provide HTTP caching headers such as: ```http Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 ``` Meaning the response can be cached according to that policy. For immutable frontend assets: ```text app.a8f3c1.js ``` you can often use long cache lifetimes because the filename changes when the content changes. This is a powerful production pattern. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 26. Cache Invalidation
text: Suppose CloudFront has: ```text logo.png ``` cached. You upload a new: ```text logo.png ``` The edge may still have the old version. You can invalidate cached objects when necessary. Conceptually: ```text CloudFront ↓ Invalidate ↓ /logo.png ``` But frequent invalidations aren't always the best cache strategy. A better frontend pattern is often: ```text app.v1.js app.v2.js app.v3.js ``` using content-hashed filenames. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 27. Why HTTPS?
text: Without TLS: ```text HTTP ``` data can potentially be intercepted/modified in transit. With: ```text HTTPS ``` TLS protects communication between client and endpoint. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 28. AWS Certificate Manager
text: AWS provides **Certificate Manager (ACM)** for managing TLS certificates for supported AWS services. Conceptually: ```text example.com ↓ TLS Certificate ↓ CloudFront / ALB ``` For your architecture: ```text User ↓ HTTPS CloudFront ↓ HTTPS ALB ↓ EC2 ``` depending on your chosen configuration. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 29. Redirect HTTP → HTTPS
text: You generally want: ```text http://example.com ``` to redirect to: ```text https://example.com ``` For example: ```text HTTP :80 ↓ Redirect ↓ HTTPS :443 ``` This should be part of your production configuration. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 30. What Is WAF?
text: WAF = **Web Application Firewall**. Think: > A firewall designed specifically to inspect web/application requests. Architecture: ```text User ↓ WAF ↓ CloudFront / ALB ↓ Application ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 31. Why WAF?
text: Suppose attackers send: ```text malicious requests ``` WAF can inspect requests and apply rules. For example: ```text Request ↓ WAF ├── allowed → application └── blocked → rejected ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 32. Common Threat Categories
text: WAF can help mitigate certain classes of web attacks, including patterns associated with: - SQL injection - cross-site scripting - malicious bots - abusive request patterns - unwanted IP addresses - excessive request rates It is not a replacement for secure application code. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 33. Rate Limiting
text: Suppose someone sends: ```text 1,000 requests/sec ``` to: ```text /login ``` You may want to limit suspicious/request-heavy traffic. Conceptually: ```text Client ↓ WAF ↓ Rate-based rule ↓ Too many? ↓ BLOCK ``` This can help mitigate some abusive traffic patterns. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 34. AWS Managed Rules
text: AWS WAF supports managed rule groups. Instead of writing every security rule yourself: ```text WAF ↓ Managed Rules ↓ Common attack patterns ``` For example, managed rules can help detect common web attack patterns. For your interviews: > **Managed rules reduce the burden of writing and maintaining every rule manually.** ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 35. WAF Placement
text: Common patterns include: ```text User ↓ CloudFront ↓ WAF ↓ Origin ``` or: ```text User ↓ ALB ↓ WAF ↓ EC2 ``` AWS WAF can associate with supported AWS resources such as CloudFront and ALB. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 36. CloudFront + WAF
text: A very common architecture: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ CloudFront │ WAF │ ↓ ALB │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ EC2 EC2 └────────┬────────┘ ↓ RDS ``` This gives you: ```text CDN + Caching + Edge delivery + Web security filtering + Load balancing + Horizontal scaling + Database ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: PART 6 — ACTUALLY SETTING THIS UP
text: Now let's move from concepts to **doing it**. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 37. Step 1 — Buy/Use a Domain
text: You need a domain such as: ```text example.com ``` You can register one through Route 53 or another registrar. If your registrar is external, you can configure its DNS delegation to Route 53. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 38. Step 2 — Create Hosted Zone
text: In AWS: ```text Route 53 ↓ Hosted Zones ↓ Create Hosted Zone ``` Enter: ```text example.com ``` Choose: ```text Public Hosted Zone ``` Route 53 gives you name servers. Your registrar needs to delegate the domain to those Route 53 name servers. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 39. Step 3 — Create ALB
text: From previous responses, you should have: ```text VPC ├── Public Subnet A └── Public Subnet B ``` Create: ```text EC2 instances ``` and: ```text Target Group ``` Then: ```text ALB ↓ Target Group ↓ EC2 ``` Listener: ```text HTTPS :443 ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 40. Step 4 — Configure DNS
text: Route 53: ```text example.com ↓ Create record ``` For: ```text api.example.com ``` use an alias to the ALB. Final: ```text api.example.com ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ``` Test: ```bash curl https://api.example.com/health ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 41. Step 5 — Add CloudFront
text: Suppose your frontend is stored in S3: ```text S3 └── index.html ``` Create: ```text CloudFront Distribution ``` Origin: ```text S3 bucket ``` Then: ```text User ↓ CloudFront ↓ S3 ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 42. Step 6 — Configure Custom Domain
text: Instead of: ```text d123abc.cloudfront.net ``` you want: ```text www.example.com ``` CloudFront supports alternate domain names and TLS certificates. Architecture: ```text www.example.com ↓ Route 53 ↓ CloudFront ↓ S3 ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 43. Step 7 — Add WAF
text: Create: ```text AWS WAF Web ACL ``` Then associate it with the relevant supported resource. Example: ```text CloudFront ↑ WAF ``` or: ```text ALB ↑ WAF ``` Then configure rules. Start conceptually with: ```text Managed rules + Rate-based protection ``` rather than trying to write hundreds of custom rules. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 44. What the Final System Looks Like
text: You now have: ```text USER │ ↓ Route 53 DNS │ ┌────────────┴────────────┐ ↓ ↓ CloudFront ALB │ │ WAF WAF │ │ ↓ ↓ S3 EC2 / EC2 Frontend Backend │ ↓ RDS ``` There are different valid ways to place WAF and structure the domains; the diagram is showing the concept rather than requiring this exact topology. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 45. Frontend Domain + API Domain
text: A clean architecture could be: ```text www.example.com ↓ CloudFront ↓ S3 ``` and: ```text api.example.com ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ``` So: ```text Browser ├── www.example.com │ ↓ │ CloudFront → S3 │ └── api.example.com ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ↓ RDS ``` This is a very realistic architecture for a web application. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: PART 7 — DEVOPS AUTOMATION
text: Now let's connect this to your earlier concern. You don't want: ```text Developer ↓ AWS Console ↓ Click 50 things ``` Instead: ```text Developer ↓ Git ↓ GitHub ↓ CI/CD ↓ Infrastructure as Code ↓ AWS ``` Terraform comes later in [Chapter 21](../06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md). ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 46. What Should CI/CD Deploy?
text: Your GitHub Actions pipeline might handle: ```text Code ↓ Test ↓ Build ↓ Docker image ↓ Push registry ↓ Deploy backend ``` For frontend: ```text React ↓ npm run build ↓ dist/ ↓ S3 ↓ CloudFront ``` For example: ```yaml - name: Build frontend run: | npm ci npm run build - name: Upload to S3 run: | aws s3 sync dist/ s3://my-frontend-bucket ``` Then CloudFront serves the updated files. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 47. Frontend Deployment Pipeline
text: The actual DevOps flow: ```text Developer ↓ git push ↓ GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ npm ci ↓ npm test ↓ npm run build ↓ S3 ↓ CloudFront ``` That's a real deployment pipeline. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 48. Backend Deployment Pipeline
text: Your backend: ```text Developer ↓ GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Test ↓ Build ↓ Docker image ↓ Registry ↓ EC2 / ECS / EKS ↓ ALB ``` DNS doesn't change during each deployment. That's another reason to put stable infrastructure such as ALB/CloudFront in front of replaceable application instances. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 49. What Happens During a User Request?
text: Let's trace the complete system. User opens: ```text https://www.example.com ``` Flow: ```text Browser ↓ DNS ↓ Route 53 ↓ CloudFront ↓ WAF ↓ S3 ↓ Frontend ``` Then React calls: ```text https://api.example.com/users ``` Flow: ```text Browser ↓ Route 53 ↓ ALB ↓ WAF ↓ EC2 ↓ Node.js ↓ RDS ``` That's the architecture you should be able to draw in an interview. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 50. Debugging DNS
text: Suppose: ```text api.example.com ``` doesn't work. Start with: ```bash dig api.example.com ``` Check: ```text Does DNS resolve? ``` If no: ```text Route 53 record Hosted zone Name servers Registrar delegation ``` If yes: ```text DNS works ``` Continue: ```bash curl -v https://api.example.com/health ``` Then investigate: ```text TLS ALB WAF Security Groups Target Group EC2 Application ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 51. Debugging CloudFront
text: Suppose: ```text www.example.com ``` returns old content. Check: ```text 1. Is DNS pointing to CloudFront? 2. Is CloudFront distribution deployed? 3. Is origin correct? 4. Is object cached? 5. Cache-Control headers? 6. Does origin have new file? 7. Is invalidation needed? ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: 52. Debugging WAF
text: Suppose legitimate requests get: ```text 403 Forbidden ``` Potential causes: ```text WAF rule IP restriction rate-based rule managed rule false positive ``` Check: ```text WAF logs/metrics ``` and determine which rule blocked the request. Don't simply disable WAF. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Route 53 vs CloudFront?
text: Simple answer: ```text Route 53 → DNS / domain routing CloudFront → CDN / edge caching / content delivery ``` They solve different problems. ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: CloudFront
text: ```text Global edge delivery Caching CDN ```

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: ALB
text: ```text Application load balancing Target routing Health checks ``` Typical architecture: ```text CloudFront ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ``` ---

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Security Group
text: Controls network-level access such as: ```text TCP 443 TCP 3000 TCP 5432 ```

title: Chapter 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: WAF
text: Understands web/application requests and can inspect HTTP behavior/rules. Think: ```text Security Group → Network access WAF → Web/application request filtering ``` They complement each other. ---

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Chapter 16 — Revision Sheet: Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/04-aws/ch16-route53-cloudfront-waf.md). Theme: the **front door** of your application.

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: DNS & Route 53
text: - DNS lets users use `api.myapp.com` instead of `13.234.56.78`; in production the target is often an **ALB**, not a fixed IP. **Route 53** = AWS DNS/domain-routing service (`api.example.com → ALB`, `www.example.com → CloudFront`). - Records: **A** (→ IPv4), **AAAA** (→ IPv6), **CNAME** (→ another hostname), **MX** (mail), **TXT** (verification/arbitrary text), **NS** (name servers). Focus: A, AAAA, CNAME, TXT, NS. - Debug with `dig example.com` / `nslookup` (response, records, TTL, addresses). - **TTL** (e.g. 300 s): resolvers may cache for ~that long → DNS changes (old ALB → new ALB) aren't instantly visible everywhere. - **Hosted zone** = container of DNS records for a domain. **Public** (Internet users, `api.example.com`) vs **Private** (names inside a VPC, `db.internal`, `api.internal`). - **Route 53 → ALB:** Route 53 → Hosted Zones → `example.com` → Create Record → Name `api`, Type `A`, **Alias → ALB**. Alias records for supported AWS resources mean you don't hard-code the ALB's changing infrastructure details. Pointing at an EC2 IP is fragile; the ALB is the **stable entry point** in front of a replaceable fleet.

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: CDN & CloudFront
text: - **CDN** caches content at edge locations near users (New York user → nearby edge instead of Mumbai origin). **CloudFront** = AWS CDN; origins: S3, ALB, EC2, other supported origins. - Benefits: lower latency, caching, **reduced origin load**, security/TLS integration. - **What to cache:** images, CSS, JS, fonts, videos, static files, public assets; maybe API GET responses when safe. **Careful:** POST/PUT/DELETE and personalized/private responses (e.g. `GET /profile` must not leak one user's page to another). Ask: who can see it? how long valid? can it be stale? - **Cache hit** (served at the edge, no origin request) vs **miss** (CloudFront → origin → cache per behaviour → user). - **Cache-Control:** `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600`. Immutable frontend assets with **content-hashed filenames** (`app.a8f3c1.js`) can use long TTLs because the name changes when content changes. - **Invalidation:** CloudFront can invalidate (`/logo.png`) but frequent invalidation isn't the best strategy; prefer versioned/hashed filenames (`app.v1.js`, `app.v2.js`). - **Typical architecture:** `USER → CloudFront → {S3: static assets / frontend, ALB: dynamic API → EC2 → RDS}`. Custom domain: `www.example.com → Route 53 → CloudFront → S3` (CloudFront supports alternate domain names + TLS certs).

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: HTTPS
text: - TLS protects client ↔ endpoint. **ACM (AWS Certificate Manager)** manages certificates for supported services (CloudFront/ALB). User →HTTPS→ CloudFront →HTTPS→ ALB → EC2 (depending on configuration). - Redirect **HTTP :80 → HTTPS :443** as part of production configuration.

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: WAF
text: - **WAF = Web Application Firewall**: inspects HTTP/web requests, applies rules (allow → app, block → rejected). Mitigates classes such as SQL injection, XSS, malicious bots, abusive patterns, unwanted IPs, excessive request rates — **not a replacement for secure application code**. - **Rate-based rule** (e.g. 1,000 req/s to `/login` → block). **AWS Managed Rules** = prebuilt rule groups for common attack patterns (reduce burden of writing/maintaining rules). Start with managed rules + rate-based protection, not hundreds of custom rules. - **Placement:** WAF is associated with supported resources — **CloudFront** and **ALB** (diagrams show the concept; several valid topologies). - **WAF vs Security Group:** SG = network-level access (TCP 443/3000/5432); WAF = understands HTTP requests and rules. They complement each other.

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Full architecture to draw
text: ```text www.example.com → Route 53 → CloudFront (+WAF) → S3 (frontend) api.example.com → Route 53 → ALB (+WAF) → EC2 (Node.js) → RDS ``` Browser loads the frontend through CloudFront, then the React app calls `https://api.example.com/users`. DNS does not change during deployments — stable infrastructure (ALB/CloudFront) fronts replaceable instances.

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Hands-on setup (7 steps)
text: 1. Domain (Route 53 or external registrar → delegate to Route 53 name servers). 2. Public hosted zone `example.com` (note NS records). 3. ALB + target group + EC2 across public subnets A/B; HTTPS :443 listener. 4. Route 53 `api` alias → ALB; test `curl https://api.example.com/health`. 5. CloudFront distribution with S3 origin. 6. Custom domain (`www.example.com`) + certificate. 7. WAF Web ACL associated with CloudFront/ALB (managed rules + rate-based).

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Deployment pipelines
text: ```yaml - name: Build frontend run: | npm ci npm run build - name: Upload to S3 run: aws s3 sync dist/ s3://my-frontend-bucket ``` Frontend: push → Actions → `npm ci` → `npm test` → `npm run build` → S3 → CloudFront. Backend: Actions → test → build → Docker image → registry → EC2/ECS/EKS → ALB. Prefer Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, Ch.21) over clicking in the console.

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Troubleshooting
text: - **DNS:** `dig api.example.com` — resolves? If not: Route 53 record, hosted zone, name servers, registrar delegation. If yes: `curl -v https://api.example.com/health` → TLS → ALB → WAF → SGs → target group → EC2 → app. - **CloudFront serves old content:** DNS pointing to CloudFront? distribution deployed? origin correct? object cached? Cache-Control headers? origin has the new file? invalidation needed? - **WAF 403 for legitimate requests:** WAF rule, IP restriction, rate-based rule, managed-rule false positive → check WAF logs/metrics to find the rule. Don't just disable WAF.

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Comparisons
text: | | Route 53 | CloudFront | ALB | WAF | Security Group | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Role | DNS/domain routing | CDN/edge caching | Load balancing, target routing, health checks | HTTP request filtering | Network access |

heading: Depth guide
text: Deep: DNS, Route 53, hosted zones, A/AAAA/CNAME/TXT/NS, TTL, Route 53 → ALB/CloudFront, CDN caching, hit/miss, cache-control, invalidation, custom domains, HTTPS/ACM, WAF + vs SG, rate-based, managed rules, S3+CloudFront, ALB API, troubleshooting. Medium: CloudFront behaviours, origin groups, signed URLs/cookies, advanced routing policies. Awareness: latency-based, weighted, failover, geolocation/geoproximity routing, Route 53 health checks.

title: Revision 16 — Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **Alias vs CNAME:** a CNAME cannot exist at the **zone apex** (`example.com`); Route 53 **alias** records can point the apex at an ALB/CloudFront/S3 website and are free for AWS targets (no TTL to set). - For CloudFront, the **ACM certificate must be in `us-east-1`**, and WAF web ACLs for CloudFront are in the **global/us-east-1** scope; for an ALB, ACM and WAF live in the ALB's Region. - Keep the S3 origin **private** and use **Origin Access Control (OAC)** so only CloudFront can read the bucket. - After `aws s3 sync dist/ s3://bucket --delete`, run `aws cloudfront create-invalidation --paths "/index.html"` (or version assets); `index.html` itself is the file that usually must not be cached long. - Redirect HTTP→HTTPS at the ALB listener (80 → 443 redirect action) or via CloudFront's *viewer protocol policy*. - Frontend (`www`) and API (`api`) are different origins → configure **CORS** on the API. - Route 53 routing policies beyond simple: weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity, multivalue. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 15](ch15-revision.md) · [Full chapter 16](../docs/04-aws/ch16-route53-cloudfront-waf.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 17](ch17-revision.md) →
