And as you pointed out earlier, we're going to make this practical: **Understand → Set up → Use → Test → Break → Debug → Automate.** ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 0. Our System So Far
text: We have: ```text USERS │ ↓ Route 53 / \ ↓ ↓ CloudFront ALB │ │ WAF WAF │ │ ↓ ↓ S3 EC2 / EC2 │ ↓ RDS ``` And: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Docker ↓ AWS ``` Now we're adding: ```text ┌──────────────┐ │ Monitoring │ │ CloudWatch │ └──────┬───────┘ │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Logs Metrics Alarms ``` and: ```text Security ├── IAM ├── Secrets Manager ├── KMS ├── CloudTrail ├── Security Groups ├── WAF └── Encryption ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 1. Why Do We Need Monitoring?
text: Imagine users report: > "The API is very slow." Without monitoring: ```text 🤷 ``` With monitoring: ```text CPU 92% Memory 80% Latency 4.2 sec Errors 12% DB CPU 88% ``` Now you have evidence. Monitoring answers: > **What is happening?** Observability goes further and helps answer: > **Why is it happening?** We'll cover observability more deeply in [Chapter 22](../07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md). ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 2. CloudWatch
text: **Amazon CloudWatch** is AWS's primary monitoring/observability platform. Think: ```text AWS resources │ ├── EC2 ├── ALB ├── RDS ├── Lambda └── other services │ ↓ CloudWatch / | \ Logs Metrics Alarms ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 3. Three Things You Must Understand
text: The most important CloudWatch concepts are: ```text Metrics Logs Alarms ``` Think: ```text Metrics → numbers Logs → events/details Alarms → decisions/actions based on metrics ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 4. Metrics
text: A metric is a numerical measurement over time. Examples: ```text EC2 CPU utilization RDS CPU utilization ALB request count ALB latency Lambda invocations Lambda errors ``` Example: ```text CPU: 10% 15% 23% 45% 91% 95% ``` You can visualize it: ```text CPU % 100 | ███ 80 | █████ 60 | █████ 40 | ████ 20 | ███████ +-------------------- Time → ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 5. Why Metrics Matter
text: Suppose API latency increased. You can compare: ```text API latency CPU DB CPU request count network traffic ``` and determine whether the issue correlates with: ```text traffic spike CPU saturation database overload ``` This is the beginning of production debugging. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 6. CloudWatch Logs
text: Logs contain detailed events/messages. Your Node.js application might produce: ```text Server started on port 3000 Request GET /users Database connected Request completed ``` CloudWatch Logs lets you centralize logs from supported AWS resources/applications. Instead of: ```text EC2-A → local logs EC2-B → local logs EC2-C → local logs ``` you want centralized visibility: ```text CloudWatch Logs / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ EC2-A EC2-B EC2-C ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 7. Node.js Logging
text: Don't rely on: ```typescript console.log("something"); ``` alone as your entire production logging strategy. At minimum, make logs structured and useful. For example: ```typescript console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: "info", event: "user_created", userId, timestamp: new Date().toISOString(), })); ``` Now logs are machine-readable. A production logging library can take this further. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 8. Log Levels
text: Common levels: ```text DEBUG INFO WARN ERROR ``` Example: ```typescript logger.info("User created"); logger.warn("Slow database query"); logger.error("Database connection failed"); ``` Think: ```text DEBUG → detailed development information INFO → normal important events WARN → unusual but not necessarily failure ERROR → failure/problem ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 9. What Should You Log?
text: Useful: ```text request ID user/request context where appropriate endpoint status code latency error information service name timestamp ``` Avoid logging: ```text passwords access tokens API keys credit card information sensitive personal data ``` This is both a security and compliance concern. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 10. Centralized Logs
text: Imagine three EC2 instances: ```text EC2-A EC2-B EC2-C ``` A request fails. If logs are only on local disk: ```text Which server handled it? ``` could become annoying. Centralized logs let you search across instances. ```text EC2-A ─┐ EC2-B ─┼──→ CloudWatch Logs EC2-C ─┘ ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 11. Log Groups and Streams
text: CloudWatch Logs organizes logs into **log groups** and **log streams**. Conceptually: ```text Log Group │ ├── Stream: EC2-A ├── Stream: EC2-B └── Stream: EC2-C ``` Think: > Log group = collection/category of logs > Log stream = sequence of logs from a particular source/context ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 12. CloudWatch Agent
text: Your EC2 instance can use the CloudWatch agent to send additional system/application information to CloudWatch. Conceptually: ```text EC2 │ └── CloudWatch Agent ↓ CloudWatch ``` This can provide additional logs and system-level metrics depending on configuration. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 13. Installing an Agent — The DevOps Perspective
text: You could manually SSH: ```bash ssh ec2-user@server ``` and install/configure the agent. But that's not ideal for many servers. Instead: ```text Launch Template ↓ User Data ↓ Install/configure agent ↓ Every new EC2 gets monitoring automatically ``` This is an important DevOps principle: > **Automate machine configuration so replacement servers are reproducible.** ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 14. CloudWatch Alarms
text: Suppose: ```text CPU > 80% ``` for a sustained period. You can create: ```text CloudWatch Alarm ``` Conceptually: ```text Metric ↓ CPU > threshold ↓ Alarm ↓ Action ``` Possible actions can include notifying or triggering supported automation/scaling mechanisms. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 15. Example Alarm
text: ```text Metric: EC2 CPU utilization Condition: > 80% Period: 5 minutes Action: Notify ``` Then: ```text CPU = 90% ↓ Alarm ↓ Notification ``` Now you don't need a human continuously watching dashboards. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 16. Alarms + Auto Scaling
text: You already learned Auto Scaling. Now connect them: ```text EC2 ↓ CloudWatch Metric ↓ CPU > threshold ↓ Auto Scaling policy ↓ Add EC2 ``` This is where monitoring becomes operational automation. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 17. ALB Monitoring
text: Your ALB can expose metrics such as: ```text Request count HTTP errors Target health Latency-related metrics ``` So: ```text User ↓ ALB ↓ CloudWatch ``` You can investigate: ```text Are requests increasing? Are targets unhealthy? Are errors increasing? Is latency increasing? ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 18. RDS Monitoring
text: For RDS, monitor things such as: ```text CPU Database connections Storage IOPS Latency-related metrics ``` Example: ```text RDS CPU = 95% Connections = near limit ``` Possible diagnosis: ```text Database is becoming overloaded ``` You now have evidence instead of guessing. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 19. Lambda Monitoring
text: Lambda provides useful metrics such as: ```text Invocations Errors Duration Concurrency Throttles ``` Example: ```text Lambda │ ├── Invocations ↑ ├── Duration ↑ ├── Errors ↑ └── Throttles ↑ ``` This can reveal: ```text Traffic spike Slow function Concurrency limit Downstream bottleneck ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 20. Dashboards
text: A CloudWatch dashboard can bring metrics together. For example: ```text ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Production Dashboard │ ├───────────────┬─────────────────────┤ │ CPU │ Request Rate │ │ 62% │ 12k/min │ ├───────────────┼─────────────────────┤ │ Error Rate │ Latency │ │ 0.4% │ 180ms │ ├───────────────┼─────────────────────┤ │ DB CPU │ DB Connections │ │ 71% │ 120 │ └───────────────┴─────────────────────┘ ``` This gives you a quick production overview. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: PART 2 — SECURITY
text: Now let's switch to security. A good production system needs: ```text Authentication Authorization Encryption Secrets management Network security Auditing Monitoring ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 21. IAM Recap
text: You already learned: ```text IAM ├── Users ├── Groups ├── Roles └── Policies ``` The most important production principle: > **Use roles and temporary credentials wherever practical instead of long-lived access keys.** ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 22. IAM Policy
text: Example: ```json { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/uploads/*" } ``` This means the identity can read objects under the specified path. Not: ```json { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" } ``` unless there's an exceptional, justified reason. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 23. Least Privilege
text: Suppose Lambda only needs: ```text S3 GetObject ``` Give it: ```text s3:GetObject ``` not: ```text s3:* ``` And preferably restrict: ```text specific bucket specific path ``` Mental model: ```text Need: READ files Give: READ files Don't give: CONTROL entire AWS account ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 24. IAM Roles in Our Architecture
text: Example: ```text EC2 ↓ IAM Role ↓ S3 permissions ``` and: ```text Lambda ↓ IAM Execution Role ↓ SQS permissions ``` The application doesn't need to contain AWS credentials. This is one of the most important security improvements we've made. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 25. GitHub Actions Security
text: Recall our CI/CD architecture: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ OIDC ↓ AWS IAM Role ↓ Temporary AWS credentials ``` This is preferable to putting a permanent AWS access key into GitHub secrets when OIDC federation is available. The important idea: > **CI gets temporary permissions to perform the deployment.** ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 26. Secrets Management
text: What are secrets? Examples: ```text Database passwords API keys OAuth client secrets Private tokens ``` Bad: ```text GitHub ↓ DB_PASSWORD=secret ``` or: ```text Docker image ↓ embedded password ``` or: ```text source code ↓ API key ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 27. AWS Secrets Manager
text: AWS provides **Secrets Manager** for storing and retrieving secrets. Conceptually: ```text Secrets Manager │ ↓ DB password │ ↓ Application ``` The application needs IAM permission to retrieve the secret. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 28. Secret Rotation
text: Secrets should ideally not live forever. For example: ```text Password A ↓ rotation ↓ Password B ``` Secrets Manager supports rotation workflows for supported scenarios. The key concept: > **Secret management should be centralized and controlled rather than scattered across source code and servers.** ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 29. KMS
text: KMS = **Key Management Service**. Think: > A managed service for creating and controlling cryptographic keys used by AWS services and applications. Conceptually: ```text KMS ↓ Encryption key ↓ Data encryption ``` KMS integrates with many AWS services. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 30. Encryption at Rest
text: We've already seen this with S3 and RDS. Examples: ```text S3 ↓ Encrypted objects RDS ↓ Encrypted storage ``` KMS can be involved in managing encryption keys. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 31. Encryption in Transit
text: Example: ```text Browser ↓ HTTPS/TLS CloudFront / ALB ↓ Application ``` And database connections can use TLS where configured/supported. Remember: ```text At rest → stored data In transit → network communication ``` You generally want both. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 32. CloudTrail
text: This is different from CloudWatch.

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: CloudWatch
text: > What is happening to my infrastructure/application?

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: CloudTrail
text: > What AWS API/account activity happened? For example: ```text Someone changed: Security Group IAM policy S3 bucket EC2 configuration ``` CloudTrail can provide an audit trail of AWS API activity. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 33. CloudTrail Example
text: Suppose suddenly: ```text S3 bucket became public ``` You ask: > Who changed it? CloudTrail can help identify relevant API activity such as: ```text Identity Time API action Resource Source information ``` This is extremely important for security investigations. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 34. CloudWatch vs CloudTrail
text: Memorize this: ```text CloudWatch → Monitoring CloudTrail → Auditing AWS API activity ``` Example: ```text CPU reached 95% → CloudWatch Someone changed IAM policy → CloudTrail ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 35. Security Groups
text: From [Chapter 12](ch12-vpc-networking.md): ```text ALB SG ↓ API SG ↓ DB SG ``` Rules should be as narrow as practical. Example: ```text Internet ↓ ALB SG 443 ALB SG ↓ API SG 3000 API SG ↓ DB SG 5432 ``` This is **network segmentation**. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 36. Network Security Layers
text: Your application now has multiple security layers: ```text Internet ↓ CloudFront ↓ WAF ↓ ALB ↓ Security Group ↓ EC2 ↓ Security Group ↓ RDS ``` And IAM: ```text EC2 ↓ IAM Role ↓ AWS services ``` And encryption: ```text TLS + KMS/encryption at rest ``` And auditing: ```text CloudTrail ``` This is defense in depth. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: PART 3 — ACTUALLY SETTING UP MONITORING
text: Now let's make this practical. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 37. AWS CLI — View CloudWatch Metrics
text: The AWS CLI can interact with CloudWatch. For example: ```bash aws cloudwatch list-metrics ``` You can filter metrics by namespace/resource. You can also query metric statistics with: ```bash aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics ... ``` You don't need to memorize every CLI option. The important DevOps skill is: > **Know that AWS CLI/API can automate monitoring configuration and inspection.** ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 38. Create an Alarm
text: Conceptually: ```bash aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \ --alarm-name high-cpu \ --metric-name CPUUtilization \ --namespace AWS/EC2 \ --statistic Average \ --period 300 \ --threshold 80 \ --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \ --evaluation-periods 2 ``` The exact command also needs appropriate dimensions/actions depending on your setup. The important idea is: ```text Metric ↓ Threshold ↓ Alarm ↓ Action ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 39. Application-Level Metrics
text: CloudWatch isn't only about AWS infrastructure. Your application should expose useful metrics such as: ```text request_count request_latency error_count active_requests database_latency ``` Conceptually: ```text Node.js ↓ Application metrics ↓ Monitoring system ``` Later in [Chapter 22](../07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md) we'll build the broader observability model around: ```text Metrics Logs Traces ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 40. Health Endpoint
text: Remember our ALB health check: ```text GET /health ``` We can improve it. Basic: ```typescript app.get("/health", (req, res) => { res.status(200).json({ status: "ok", }); }); ``` But you can also have a deeper readiness check. For example: ```text GET /ready ↓ Check DB connectivity ↓ Check dependencies ↓ Return status ``` Be careful not to make health endpoints so expensive that the health check itself becomes a problem. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Liveness
text: > Is the application process alive? ```text Process running? ```

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Readiness
text: > Can the application currently serve traffic? ```text Can connect to required dependencies? ``` This distinction becomes **very important in Kubernetes**. You'll use it heavily in Chapters [18](../05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md)–[20](../05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md). ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 42. Production Incident Example
text: Imagine: ```text Users: "The API is down!" ``` You investigate.

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Step 1
text: CloudWatch: ```text ALB 5xx ↑ ```

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Step 2
text: Target health: ```text EC2-A ❌ EC2-B ❌ ```

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Step 3
text: EC2 metrics: ```text CPU = 98% ```

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Step 4
text: Application logs: ```text Database timeout ```

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Step 5
text: RDS: ```text Connections = max ``` Now you've discovered: ```text EC2 ↓ Too many DB connections ↓ RDS connection exhaustion ↓ API failures ``` This connects directly to [Chapter 13](ch13-rds-databases.md). ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 43. Security Incident Example
text: Suppose: ```text Someone changed an IAM policy. ``` Your investigation: ```text CloudTrail ↓ Find API event ↓ Identity ↓ Timestamp ↓ Action ``` Then: ```text IAM ↓ Review permissions ``` And: ```text CloudWatch / application logs ↓ Look for resulting behavior ``` This is how monitoring and security work together. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 44. AWS Security Checklist
text: For your interviews and projects: ```text ☑ Least privilege IAM ☑ IAM roles instead of hardcoded AWS credentials ☑ GitHub OIDC for CI/CD ☑ Private databases ☑ Restrictive Security Groups ☑ WAF for web-facing applications where appropriate ☑ HTTPS/TLS ☑ Encryption at rest ☑ Secrets Manager for secrets ☑ KMS where appropriate ☑ CloudTrail enabled/retained appropriately ☑ CloudWatch monitoring ☑ Backups ☑ No secrets in Git ☑ No secrets in Docker images ☑ No unnecessary public resources ☑ MFA for human identities where applicable ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 45. Practical DevOps Setup
text: For the application we've been building, your target setup should eventually resemble: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ CloudFront │ WAF │ ↓ ALB │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ EC2 EC2 │ │ └────────┬────────┘ ↓ RDS ``` Monitoring: ```text EC2 ───────────┐ ALB ───────────┤ RDS ───────────┼──→ CloudWatch Lambda ────────┤ Application ───┘ ``` Security: ```text IAM │ ├── EC2 Role ├── Lambda Role └── CI/CD Role Secrets Manager │ └── DB/API secrets KMS │ └── encryption keys CloudTrail │ └── AWS API audit ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 46. DevOps Automation — The Direction We're Going
text: Here's the important evolution.

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Beginner
text: ```text AWS Console ↓ Create EC2 ↓ Install things manually ```

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Better
text: ```text AWS CLI ↓ Scripts ```

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Professional
text: ```text Terraform ↓ Infrastructure as Code ```

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Complete DevOps
text: ```text Git ↓ GitHub ↓ CI/CD ↓ Terraform ↓ AWS infrastructure ↓ Deploy application ↓ Monitoring ↓ Alerts ↓ Troubleshooting ``` **[Chapter 21](../06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md) will make Terraform the missing piece here.** ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Master
text: - CloudWatch - metrics - logs - alarms - dashboards - application logging - centralized logging - EC2 monitoring - ALB monitoring - RDS monitoring - Lambda monitoring - IAM least privilege - IAM roles - Secrets Manager - KMS fundamentals - CloudTrail - security groups - WAF - encryption - HTTPS/TLS - monitoring + incident debugging

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Medium
text: - CloudWatch Agent - custom metrics - log insights/querying - alarm actions - advanced CloudWatch configuration

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Awareness
text: - AWS Config - GuardDuty - Security Hub - Inspector - Macie Know **what these services are for**, but don't spend our limited roadmap responses becoming an AWS security specialist. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: 48. Interview Questions
text: You should now be able to answer:

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Monitoring
text: **1. CloudWatch vs CloudTrail?** ```text CloudWatch → monitoring/metrics/logs/alarms CloudTrail → AWS API auditing ``` **2. How would you monitor an EC2 server?** ```text CloudWatch + system/application logs + CPU/memory/disk/network + alarms ``` **3. How would you detect database overload?** ```text RDS metrics + connections + latency + application logs ``` **4. How would you investigate a 500 error spike?** ```text ALB metrics ↓ application logs ↓ dependency metrics ↓ RDS/Redis/external services ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Security
text: **5. Why use IAM roles?** > To provide permissions to AWS resources without embedding long-lived credentials in the application. **6. What is least privilege?** > Give an identity only the permissions it actually needs. **7. Where should database passwords be stored?** > A proper secrets-management system such as Secrets Manager, not source code or Git. **8. What does KMS do?** > Provides managed cryptographic key management used for encryption and related cryptographic operations. **9. What does CloudTrail do?** > Records AWS API/account activity for auditing and investigation. **10. Security Group vs WAF?** ```text Security Group → network-level access WAF → web/application request filtering ``` ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Final Practical Assignment
text: Take your Node.js API and create this mental/actual production setup: ```text Node.js │ ├── /health ├── /ready └── structured logs ``` Then configure: ```text ALB ↓ Health checks ``` ```text EC2 ↓ CloudWatch monitoring ``` ```text RDS ↓ CloudWatch monitoring ``` ```text IAM Role ↓ AWS access ``` ```text Secrets Manager ↓ Database credentials ``` ```text CloudTrail ↓ AWS API auditing ``` Then deliberately simulate: ```text High CPU ``` and reason: ```text Metric ↓ Alarm ↓ Investigation ↓ Root cause ↓ Fix ``` And simulate: ```text Application can't connect to RDS ``` and debug: ```text Application ↓ DNS ↓ Route ↓ Security Group ↓ RDS ↓ Credentials ↓ Connections ``` That's the kind of practical thinking we want you to develop. ---

title: Chapter 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: The Core Mental Model
text: You should now think of production AWS as: ```text ┌────────── SECURITY ──────────┐ │ IAM │ WAF │ KMS │ Secrets │ │ │ SG │ TLS │ CloudTrail │ └──────────────┬───────────────┘ │ USER → Route53 → CloudFront → ALB │ EC2 / Lambda │ SQS / Redis │ RDS │ ↓ CloudWatch ┌────────┼────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Logs Metrics Alarms ``` And the DevOps loop is: ```text CODE ↓ BUILD ↓ TEST ↓ DEPLOY ↓ MONITOR ↓ DETECT ISSUE ↓ TROUBLESHOOT ↓ FIX ↓ DEPLOY ``` **That loop is DevOps.** <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 16: Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF](ch16-route53-cloudfront-waf.md) · [Chapter 18: Kubernetes Fundamentals](../05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch17-revision.md)

title: Revision 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Chapter 17 — Revision Sheet: AWS Monitoring + Security
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/04-aws/ch17-monitoring-security.md). Questions this chapter answers: *Is it healthy? Is it secure? What broke? Why? Who changed it?* Method: **Understand → Set up → Use → Test → Break → Debug → Automate.**

title: Revision 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Monitoring with CloudWatch
text: - **Monitoring** = what is happening (CPU 92%, latency 4.2 s, errors 12%, DB CPU 88%). **Observability** = why (Ch.22). - **CloudWatch** = AWS monitoring/observability platform: **Metrics → numbers · Logs → events/details · Alarms → decisions/actions on metrics** (+ dashboards). - **Metrics:** numeric time series — EC2/RDS CPU utilization, ALB request count & latency, Lambda invocations/errors. Compare latency vs CPU vs DB CPU vs request count vs network traffic to see whether it correlates with a traffic spike, CPU saturation or DB overload. - **Logs:** centralise logs from EC2-A/B/C into **CloudWatch Logs** (instead of local files). Organised in **log groups** (collection/category) and **log streams** (sequence from one source, e.g. per instance). - **CloudWatch agent:** on EC2, sends extra logs and system-level metrics; install/configure it via **Launch Template → User Data** so every new EC2 is monitored automatically (*automate machine configuration so replacement servers are reproducible*). - **Alarms:** Metric → threshold → Alarm → Action (notify, or trigger supported automation like Auto Scaling policies). Example: EC2 CPU > 80%, period 5 min, notify. **Alarms + Auto Scaling:** metric → CPU > threshold → scaling policy → add EC2. - **Per-service metrics:** ALB (request count, HTTP errors, target health, latency) · RDS (CPU, connections, storage, IOPS, latency) · Lambda (Invocations, Errors, Duration, Concurrency, Throttles). - **Dashboards:** one-screen production overview (CPU, request rate, error rate, latency, DB CPU, DB connections). ```bash aws cloudwatch list-metrics aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics ... aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \ --alarm-name high-cpu --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 \ --statistic Average --period 300 --threshold 80 \ --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --evaluation-periods 2 # (real use also needs dimensions and alarm actions) ```

title: Revision 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Application logging & metrics
text: - Don't rely on bare `console.log("something")`; emit **structured JSON**: ```typescript console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: "info", event: "user_created", userId, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() })); ``` - Log levels: DEBUG (detailed dev info) · INFO (normal important events) · WARN (unusual, not necessarily failure) · ERROR (failure). Example: `logger.info("User created")`, `logger.warn("Slow database query")`, `logger.error("Database connection failed")`. - **Log:** request ID, user/request context where appropriate, endpoint, status code, latency, error info, service name, timestamp. **Never log:** passwords, access tokens, API keys, credit-card data, sensitive personal data (security + compliance). - **App-level metrics:** `request_count`, `request_latency`, `error_count`, `active_requests`, `database_latency`. (Observability = metrics + logs + traces, Ch.22.) - **Health vs readiness:** `/health` (process alive) vs `/ready` (can connect to DB/dependencies). Don't make the check so expensive that it becomes a problem. Liveness/readiness matter heavily in Kubernetes (Ch.18–20).

title: Revision 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Security building blocks
text: | Topic | Key points | |---|---| | **IAM** | Use roles + temporary credentials instead of long-lived keys. Policy example: `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/uploads/*` — never `Action:"*"`, `Resource:"*"` without justification. **Least privilege**: Lambda needing S3 read gets `s3:GetObject` on a specific bucket/path, not `s3:*`. | | **Roles in the architecture** | EC2 → IAM Role → S3 permissions; Lambda → Execution Role → SQS permissions; CI/CD → role via OIDC. App holds no AWS credentials. | | **GitHub Actions** | GitHub Actions → OIDC → IAM Role → temporary credentials (rather than permanent access key in GitHub secrets). | | **Secrets Manager** | Stores/retrieves DB passwords, API keys, OAuth secrets, tokens; app needs IAM permission to read; supports **rotation** (Password A → B) for supported scenarios. Centralised, not scattered in code/servers/images. | | **KMS** | Managed service for creating/controlling cryptographic keys used by AWS services and apps (S3, RDS encryption, …). | | **Encryption** | At rest (S3 objects, RDS storage; KMS keys) + in transit (HTTPS/TLS, DB TLS). Want both. | | **CloudTrail** | Audit trail of AWS API/account activity: who/when/what/resource/source. E.g. who made the S3 bucket public, changed an IAM policy or SG. | | **Security Groups** | Narrow rules: Internet → ALB SG 443; ALB SG → API SG 3000; API SG → DB SG 5432 = **network segmentation**. | | **Defense in depth** | CloudFront → WAF → ALB → SG → EC2 → SG → RDS; IAM roles; TLS + at-rest encryption; CloudTrail auditing. | **CloudWatch vs CloudTrail:** CloudWatch = monitoring ("CPU reached 95%"); CloudTrail = auditing AWS API activity ("someone changed an IAM policy").

title: Revision 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Incident walkthroughs (memorise the pattern)
text: - **Performance incident:** CloudWatch ALB 5xx ↑ → target health EC2-A/B ❌ → EC2 CPU 98% → app logs "Database timeout" → RDS connections = max ⇒ EC2 → too many DB connections → RDS connection exhaustion → API failures (ties to Ch.13). - **Security incident:** CloudTrail → find API event → identity, timestamp, action → review IAM → check CloudWatch/app logs for resulting behaviour. - **Simulations to practise:** high CPU (metric → alarm → investigation → root cause → fix); app can't connect to RDS (app → DNS → route → SG → RDS → credentials → connections).

Detect DB overload — RDS metrics + connections + latency + app logs. 4. 500-error spike — ALB metrics → app logs → dependency metrics → RDS/Redis/external. 5. IAM roles — permissions without embedding long-lived credentials. 6. Least privilege — only the permissions needed. 7. DB passwords — Secrets Manager, not source/Git. 8. KMS — managed cryptographic key management. 9. CloudTrail — records AWS API/account activity. 10. SG vs WAF — network access vs web request filtering.

title: Revision 17 — AWS Monitoring + Security
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **EC2 memory and disk-usage metrics are not collected by default** — default EC2 metrics are hypervisor-level (CPU, network, disk I/O, status checks); memory and filesystem usage need the **CloudWatch agent**. Basic monitoring is 5-minute resolution; *detailed monitoring* is 1-minute. - Alarm states: `OK`, `ALARM`, `INSUFFICIENT_DATA`. The `--period 300 --evaluation-periods 2` example means two consecutive 5-minute periods breaching; `--alarm-actions` (e.g. an SNS topic ARN) is what sends the notification. - CloudWatch log groups **never expire by default** — set a retention period to control cost. - CloudTrail: management events are recorded by default and visible in *Event history* for 90 days; create a **trail delivering to S3** for long-term retention (data events such as S3 object reads are opt-in). - Secrets Manager vs **SSM Parameter Store**: Parameter Store is cheaper/simple configuration + secure strings; Secrets Manager adds built-in rotation and cross-account/resource-policy features. - KMS keys are **AWS managed** (automatic) or **customer managed** (you control the key policy, rotation, grants); services use *envelope encryption* (a data key encrypts data, KMS protects the data key). <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 16](ch16-revision.md) · [Full chapter 17](../docs/04-aws/ch17-monitoring-security.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 18](ch18-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
text: > **Source:** Response 18 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-18.txt`, lines 11–2172) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch18-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN -->

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: What Kubernetes Actually Solves
text: You've already learned Docker. You can run: ```text Docker ↓ Node.js container ``` For one application: ```text EC2 └── Docker └── Node.js ``` Fine. But imagine: ```text 100 containers 10 servers multiple applications multiple environments frequent deployments failed containers scaling requirements ``` Manually managing them becomes painful. That's the problem Kubernetes solves. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 1. What Is Kubernetes?
text: Kubernetes is a **container orchestration platform**. Simple definition: > **Kubernetes manages containers across a cluster of machines.** Instead of manually doing: ```bash docker run ... docker stop ... docker restart ... docker scale ... ``` you tell Kubernetes what you want: ```text "I want 5 copies of my API running." ``` Kubernetes works toward maintaining that desired state. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 2. Docker vs Kubernetes
text: This distinction is extremely important.

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Docker
text: Runs containers. ```text Docker ↓ Container ↓ Node.js ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Kubernetes
text: Manages containers at scale. ```text Kubernetes ├── Node │ ├── Container │ └── Container │ ├── Node │ ├── Container │ └── Container │ └── Node └── Container ``` Think: ```text Docker → container technology Kubernetes → container orchestration ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 3. Why Not Just Docker?
text: Suppose you have: ```text EC2-A ├── API ├── Worker └── Payments EC2-B ├── API ├── Worker └── Payments ``` Now: ```text EC2-A crashes ``` What happens? You need automation to: - detect failure - restart workloads - place them somewhere else - maintain desired replicas - route traffic - manage configuration - perform deployments Kubernetes is designed to solve these orchestration problems. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 4. Kubernetes Cluster
text: A Kubernetes environment is called a **cluster**. Conceptually: ```text Kubernetes Cluster │ ├── Control Plane │ └── Worker Nodes ├── Node ├── Node └── Node ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 5. Control Plane
text: The control plane is responsible for managing the cluster. Conceptually: ```text Control Plane │ ├── API Server ├── Scheduler ├── Controller Manager └── etcd ``` You don't need to memorize implementation details yet. Understand their responsibilities. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 6. API Server
text: The API Server is essentially the main interface to Kubernetes. When you run: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` you're interacting with the Kubernetes API. Conceptually: ```text kubectl ↓ API Server ↓ Kubernetes ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 7. etcd
text: `etcd` is the distributed key-value store used by Kubernetes for cluster state. Conceptually: ```text Kubernetes ↓ etcd ↓ Cluster state ``` For example, Kubernetes needs to know things such as: ```text What deployments exist? How many replicas are desired? What configuration is stored? What cluster objects exist? ``` You generally don't manually manipulate etcd. For your interview level: > **etcd stores Kubernetes cluster state.** That's enough. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 8. Scheduler
text: Suppose you request: ```text 5 Pods ``` Kubernetes needs to determine: > Which worker node should run each Pod? That's the scheduler's responsibility. ```text Pod ↓ Scheduler ↓ Node A ``` or: ```text Pod ↓ Scheduler ↓ Node B ``` It considers resource availability and scheduling constraints. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 9. Controller Manager
text: Controllers continuously compare: ```text Desired state ``` with: ```text Actual state ``` Example: You specify: ```text replicas: 3 ``` but currently: ```text 2 Pods ``` Controller logic notices: ```text Desired = 3 Actual = 2 ``` and Kubernetes works toward: ```text 3 Pods ``` This is the heart of Kubernetes. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 10. Desired State
text: This concept is **extremely important**. You don't normally tell Kubernetes: ```text "Start container A. Then wait. Then start container B." ``` Instead: ```yaml replicas: 3 ``` You're saying: > **I want 3 replicas to exist.** Kubernetes continuously tries to make reality match your declaration. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 11. Worker Node
text: A worker node is a machine that runs workloads. Conceptually: ```text Worker Node │ ├── kubelet ├── container runtime └── Pods ``` The container runtime actually runs the containers. Modern Kubernetes environments commonly use **containerd** or another CRI-compatible runtime rather than Docker Engine itself. This is an important clarification: > **Kubernetes does not require Docker Engine to run containers.** Your Docker knowledge is still extremely valuable because you're learning container images, Dockerfiles, registries, networking, volumes, etc. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 12. kubelet
text: `kubelet` runs on each worker node. It communicates with the Kubernetes control plane and makes sure the workloads assigned to that node are running. Conceptually: ```text Control Plane ↓ kubelet ↓ Node ↓ Pods ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 13. Pod
text: Now the most important Kubernetes object: > **Pod** A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. Most commonly: ```text Pod └── Container └── Node.js ``` But a Pod can contain multiple tightly coupled containers: ```text Pod ├── Container A └── Container B ``` For your normal backend: ```text Pod └── Node.js container ``` is the common mental model. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 14. Docker Container vs Kubernetes Pod
text: Don't say: > Pod = container. That's not technically correct. Think: ```text Pod └── Container ``` A Pod provides a shared execution/network context for its containers. Multiple containers in one Pod can share: - network namespace - localhost - volumes where configured Example: ```text Pod ├── API container └── Sidecar container ``` The API could reach the sidecar through localhost. But don't put unrelated applications into one Pod just because you can. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 15. Pod IP
text: Pods receive IP addresses within the Kubernetes networking model. Example: ```text Pod A 10.x.x.x Pod B 10.x.x.x ``` But here's an important point: > **Pod IPs are generally ephemeral.** A Pod can die and be replaced. The replacement may receive a different IP. Therefore: ```text Client ↓ Pod IP ❌ ``` is generally not how you expose an application. That's why Kubernetes has **Services**. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 16. Creating Your First Pod
text: Here's a basic Pod manifest. ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: api-pod spec: containers: - name: api image: node:22 ports: - containerPort: 3000 ``` This says: ```text Create a Pod ↓ Run node:22 container ↓ Container port = 3000 ``` But this isn't yet a useful production deployment. We'll improve it. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 17. kubectl
text: `kubectl` is the primary command-line tool for interacting with Kubernetes. Think: ```text kubectl ↓ Kubernetes API ``` Common commands: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` ```bash kubectl describe pod api-pod ``` ```bash kubectl logs api-pod ``` ```bash kubectl exec -it api-pod -- sh ``` ```bash kubectl delete pod api-pod ``` These commands are extremely important. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 18. Create the Pod
text: Save: ```text pod.yaml ``` Then: ```bash kubectl apply -f pod.yaml ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You might see: ```text NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS api-pod 1/1 Running 0 ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 19. Describe a Pod
text: If something is wrong: ```bash kubectl describe pod api-pod ``` This can show: - events - scheduling information - container state - image - volumes - networking information - errors Very useful for troubleshooting. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 20. Pod Logs
text: Application logs: ```bash kubectl logs api-pod ``` Follow them: ```bash kubectl logs -f api-pod ``` This connects directly to your Linux/Docker knowledge. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 21. Exec Into a Container
text: You can inspect a running container: ```bash kubectl exec -it api-pod -- sh ``` Then: ```bash ls ``` or: ```bash env ``` or: ```bash curl localhost:3000/health ``` This is one of the most useful debugging skills. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 22. Why Pods Alone Aren't Enough
text: Suppose: ```text Pod ↓ Node.js ``` and the Pod crashes. Kubernetes won't necessarily recreate it in the way you want just because you manually created a standalone Pod. For application deployments, we generally use a: > **Deployment** ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 23. What Is a Deployment?
text: A Deployment manages a set of Pods. Conceptually: ```text Deployment │ ├── Pod ├── Pod └── Pod ``` You specify: ```yaml replicas: 3 ``` and Kubernetes maintains the desired number of Pods. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 24. Our Node.js Deployment
text: Suppose you have already built: ```text my-api:1.0 ``` Docker image. Deployment: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: api spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: api template: metadata: labels: app: api spec: containers: - name: api image: my-api:1.0 ports: - containerPort: 3000 ``` This says: ```text Deployment ↓ 3 Pods ↓ my-api:1.0 ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 25. Apply It
text: ```bash kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get deployments ``` and: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You should see multiple Pods. For example: ```text api-7c9d8f7c5d-a1b2c api-7c9d8f7c5d-b3c4d api-7c9d8f7c5d-d5e6f ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 26. Kubernetes Replica Self-Healing
text: Suppose: ```text 3 Pods ``` Then: ```text Pod B crashes ``` Now: ```text Actual = 2 Desired = 3 ``` Kubernetes creates another Pod. ```text Pod A ✅ Pod B ❌ Pod C ✅ Pod D 🆕 ``` Eventually: ```text 3 healthy Pods ``` This is one of Kubernetes' core benefits. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 27. Labels
text: You saw: ```yaml labels: app: api ``` Labels are key-value metadata attached to Kubernetes objects. For example: ```text app=api environment=production version=v1 ``` They're heavily used to identify/select resources. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 28. Selectors
text: Suppose: ```yaml selector: matchLabels: app: api ``` This means: > Select objects with `app=api`. This becomes extremely important with Services. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 29. Why Do We Need a Service?
text: Remember: ```text Pod IPs change. ``` Suppose: ```text Pod A → 10.0.1.5 Pod B → 10.0.1.6 Pod C → 10.0.1.7 ``` Pod A dies. New Pod: ```text Pod D → 10.0.2.8 ``` Now clients can't rely on individual Pod IPs. Enter: > **Service** ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 30. Kubernetes Service
text: A Service provides a stable network endpoint for a set of Pods. Conceptually: ```text Service / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod A Pod B Pod C ``` Clients talk to: ```text Service ``` not: ```text Pod IP ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 31. Service Manifest
text: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: api-service spec: selector: app: api ports: - port: 80 targetPort: 3000 type: ClusterIP ``` Meaning: ```text Service port = 80 ↓ Pod port = 3000 ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 32. ClusterIP
text: `ClusterIP` exposes the service inside the Kubernetes cluster. Architecture: ```text Internal Service ↓ ┌─────┼─────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod Pod Pod ``` Useful for: ```text API → internal service API → worker API → internal backend ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 33. NodePort
text: Another Service type: ```text NodePort ``` Conceptually: ```text External ↓ Node IP:port ↓ Service ↓ Pods ``` Useful to understand, but you generally won't expose production internet traffic this way in modern cloud architectures. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 34. LoadBalancer
text: Kubernetes also has: ```yaml type: LoadBalancer ``` In a cloud environment, the Kubernetes integration can provision or configure an external load-balancing mechanism depending on the platform/controller. Conceptually: ```text Internet ↓ Cloud Load Balancer ↓ Kubernetes Service ↓ Pods ``` This connects directly to the AWS ALB knowledge you already learned. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 35. Deployment + Service
text: Now combine: ```text Deployment │ ├── Pod ├── Pod └── Pod ↑ │ Service ``` Client: ```text Client ↓ Service ↓ healthy Pod ``` If a Pod dies: ```text Service ↓ other healthy Pod ``` This gives you stable access despite ephemeral Pods. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 36. Your First Real Kubernetes Architecture
text: ```text Client │ ↓ Load Balancer │ ↓ K8s Service │ ┌──────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod A Pod B Pod C │ │ │ └──────────┼──────────┘ ↓ Node.js API ``` Now we have: ```text Docker + Kubernetes + Load balancing + Self-healing + Scaling ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 37. What Is a Namespace?
text: Namespaces logically separate Kubernetes resources. Example: ```text Cluster │ ├── development │ ├── API │ └── Redis │ ├── staging │ ├── API │ └── Redis │ └── production ├── API └── Redis ``` You can have: ```text kubectl get pods -n production ``` This is useful for organizing environments and teams. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 38. Why Not Separate Clusters?
text: Sometimes you might use: ```text Dev → Cluster A Prod → Cluster B ``` Other architectures use: ```text One cluster ├── dev namespace ├── staging namespace └── production namespace ``` The correct choice depends on isolation, security, scale, and operational requirements. For interviews, understand both concepts. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: PART 5 — KUBERNETES CONFIGURATION
text: We'll go deeper in [Chapter 19](ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md), but you should already understand the basics. Applications need configuration: ```text PORT=3000 NODE_ENV=production DATABASE_HOST=... ``` Don't bake environment-specific configuration directly into your image. We can use: ```text ConfigMap Secret ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 39. ConfigMap
text: Used for non-sensitive configuration. Example: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: api-config data: NODE_ENV: production PORT: "3000" ``` Then inject it into the container. Conceptually: ```text ConfigMap ↓ Pod ↓ Environment variables ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 40. Secret
text: For sensitive configuration: ```text Database credentials API tokens ``` Kubernetes provides: ```text Secret ``` Conceptually: ```text Secret ↓ Pod ↓ Environment ``` But an important security point: > Kubernetes Secrets are not automatically equivalent to a fully fledged external secrets-management system. Their storage/protection depends on cluster configuration. In production on AWS, you may integrate Kubernetes with services such as AWS Secrets Manager. We'll cover this more deeply later. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: PART 6 — ACTUALLY RUNNING KUBERNETES LOCALLY
text: Now let's make this practical. You have several options: ```text Docker Desktop Kubernetes Minikube kind ``` For learning, **kind** is excellent because it runs Kubernetes nodes using containers. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 41. Install kubectl
text: On Windows, you can install `kubectl` through the Kubernetes documentation/package manager appropriate to your environment. Then verify: ```bash kubectl version --client ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 42. Install kind
text: Verify: ```bash kind version ``` Create a cluster: ```bash kind create cluster --name devops-learning ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get nodes ``` You should see something like: ```text NAME devops-learning-control-plane ``` Congratulations — you have a Kubernetes cluster. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 43. Deploy Your Node.js App
text: Build your Docker image: ```bash docker build -t my-api:1.0 . ``` If you're using kind, load the image into the cluster: ```bash kind load docker-image my-api:1.0 \ --name devops-learning ``` Now Kubernetes can use: ```text my-api:1.0 ``` without needing to pull it from Docker Hub. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 44. Deploy
text: Create: ```text deployment.yaml service.yaml ``` Apply: ```bash kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml kubectl apply -f service.yaml ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` ```bash kubectl get svc ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 45. Inspect Everything
text: ```bash kubectl get all ``` Then: ```bash kubectl describe deployment api ``` ```bash kubectl describe service api-service ``` ```bash kubectl logs <pod-name> ``` This is where your DevOps skills start becoming practical. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 46. Test the API
text: If you're using a local ClusterIP service, one simple learning approach is: ```bash kubectl port-forward service/api-service 3000:80 ``` Then: ```bash curl http://localhost:3000/health ``` Flow: ```text localhost:3000 ↓ port-forward ↓ Kubernetes Service ↓ Pod ↓ Node.js ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: PART 7 — BREAK IT
text: This is **very important**. Don't just deploy something and declare Kubernetes learned. Break it. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 47. Delete a Pod
text: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` Then: ```bash kubectl delete pod <pod-name> ``` Immediately: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You should see Kubernetes create a replacement because the Deployment wants the desired replica count. That's self-healing. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 48. Scale the Application
text: Currently: ```yaml replicas: 3 ``` Change to: ```yaml replicas: 5 ``` Apply: ```bash kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You should now have five Pods. Or scale directly: ```bash kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=5 ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 49. Scale Back
text: ```bash kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=2 ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` Kubernetes removes excess replicas. Again: ```text Desired = 2 Actual = 5 ``` Kubernetes works toward: ```text Actual = 2 ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 50. Break the Container
text: You can intentionally configure an invalid image: ```yaml image: my-api:does-not-exist ``` Apply it. Then: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You may see states such as: ```text ImagePullBackOff ErrImagePull ``` Now: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` Look at the Events section. This is exactly how you learn Kubernetes troubleshooting. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 51. Common Pod States
text: Know these: ```text Pending Running Succeeded Failed Unknown ``` And common problems: ```text CrashLoopBackOff ImagePullBackOff ErrImagePull ``` Don't memorize only the names. Understand the debugging workflow: ```text kubectl get pods ↓ kubectl describe pod ↓ kubectl logs ↓ kubectl exec ↓ Check image/config/network/resources ``` ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: PART 8 — KUBERNETES + YOUR AWS KNOWLEDGE
text: Now everything starts connecting. Previously: ```text AWS ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ↓ Docker ``` With Kubernetes: ```text AWS ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Kubernetes ↓ Service ↓ Pods ↓ Containers ``` And: ```text Pod ↓ Application ↓ RDS ``` So your architecture becomes: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ Route 53 │ ↓ CloudFront/WAF │ ↓ ALB │ ↓ Kubernetes Service │ ┌──────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod Pod Pod │ │ │ └──────────┼──────────┘ ↓ RDS ``` This is the architecture we're going to develop further. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 52. EKS
text: On AWS, Kubernetes can be provided as: > **Amazon EKS — Elastic Kubernetes Service** Instead of manually building the Kubernetes control plane: ```text You ↓ EKS ↓ Kubernetes cluster ``` AWS manages significant portions of the control-plane infrastructure. Worker capacity can be provided through mechanisms such as managed node groups or other compute options. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 53. EKS Mental Model
text: Eventually: ```text AWS │ └── EKS │ ├── Control Plane │ └── Worker Nodes ├── Pods ├── Pods └── Pods ``` We'll cover EKS more practically in the later Kubernetes responses. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 54. Docker → Kubernetes Deployment Pipeline
text: Now your DevOps pipeline becomes: ```text Developer ↓ Git push ↓ GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Tests ↓ Docker build ↓ Push image to registry ↓ Kubernetes deployment ↓ Rolling update ↓ Pods ``` This is the workflow you should eventually be able to implement yourself. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 55. Image Registry
text: Kubernetes needs access to your container image. Production example: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ Docker build ↓ Amazon ECR ↓ Kubernetes/EKS ↓ Pull image ↓ Pod ``` ECR = **Elastic Container Registry**. We'll use this when we build the full deployment workflow. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 56. Rolling Update
text: Suppose you're running: ```text api:v1 api:v1 api:v1 ``` Deploy: ```text api:v2 ``` Kubernetes can perform a rolling update: ```text v1 v1 v1 ↓ v2 v1 v1 ↓ v2 v2 v1 ↓ v2 v2 v2 ``` This connects directly to the deployment strategies you learned earlier. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 57. Kubernetes vs Docker Compose
text: You've seen Docker Compose.

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Compose
text: Great for: ```text Local development ``` Example: ```text Node.js PostgreSQL Redis ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Kubernetes
text: Designed for: ```text Container orchestration Scaling Self-healing Service discovery Production workloads Rolling deployments ``` They aren't direct substitutes in every situation. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: 58. Kubernetes vs EC2
text: Remember: ```text EC2 → virtual machine ``` Kubernetes: ```text → orchestration platform ``` They operate at different levels. A Kubernetes cluster can itself run on EC2-based worker nodes. So: ```text AWS ↓ EC2 ↓ Kubernetes ↓ Pod ↓ Container ``` is perfectly possible. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Deep
text: - Why Kubernetes exists - Docker vs Kubernetes - cluster - control plane - worker nodes - API server - scheduler - controllers - etcd concept - kubelet - Pods - Deployments - replicas - desired state - labels/selectors - Services - ClusterIP - LoadBalancer - namespaces - kubectl - YAML manifests - Pod lifecycle - self-healing - scaling - basic rolling deployments - container images in Kubernetes - local Kubernetes setup - basic Kubernetes debugging

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Medium
text: - EKS - NodePort - ReplicaSets - readiness/liveness - resource requests/limits - ConfigMaps - Secrets We'll go deeper into many of these in Chapters [19](ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md)–[20](ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md).

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Awareness
text: - StatefulSets - DaemonSets - Jobs/CronJobs - Operators - CRDs - service mesh Don't worry about mastering those yet. ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Your Kubernetes Lab
text: This is the lab I want you to actually perform.

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 1
text: Create cluster: ```bash kind create cluster --name devops-learning ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 2
text: Build your Node.js Docker image: ```bash docker build -t my-api:1.0 . ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 3
text: Load it: ```bash kind load docker-image my-api:1.0 \ --name devops-learning ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 4
text: Create: ```text deployment.yaml service.yaml ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 5
text: Deploy: ```bash kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml kubectl apply -f service.yaml ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 6
text: Verify: ```bash kubectl get pods kubectl get deployments kubectl get services ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 7
text: Access it: ```bash kubectl port-forward service/api-service 3000:80 ``` Then: ```bash curl http://localhost:3000/health ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 8 — Break it
text: Delete a Pod: ```bash kubectl delete pod <pod-name> ``` Watch: ```bash kubectl get pods -w ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 9 — Scale it
text: ```bash kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=5 ```

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Step 10 — Debug a broken image
text: Change: ```yaml image: my-api:does-not-exist ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get pods kubectl describe pod <pod-name> ``` Find the problem. **If you can perform this lab and explain every step, you've genuinely started learning Kubernetes rather than memorizing Kubernetes terminology.** ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: The Kubernetes Mental Model
text: Remember this: ```text CLUSTER │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ ↓ ↓ CONTROL PLANE WORKER NODES │ ┌────┴────┐ ↓ ↓ Pod Pod │ │ Container Container ``` Then: ```text Deployment ↓ maintains Pods ↓ Pods ↓ Service ↓ stable networking ``` And: ```text kubectl ↓ API Server ↓ Kubernetes ``` The central idea: > **You declare the desired state; Kubernetes continuously works to make the actual state match it.** ---

title: Chapter 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: And Yes — Containers Are Fully Part of This Roadmap
text: Your concern from the beginning is valid, so let's make the scope explicit. We've covered: ```text CONTAINERS │ ├── Docker │ ├── Images │ ├── Containers │ ├── Dockerfiles │ ├── Layers │ ├── Volumes │ ├── Networks │ ├── Compose │ ├── Multi-stage builds │ ├── Production images │ ├── Security │ ├── Registries │ └── CI/CD integration │ └── Kubernetes ├── Pods ├── Deployments ├── Services ├── Scaling ├── Self-healing ├── Configuration ├── Networking └── Production deployment ``` And later: ```text Docker ↓ ECR ↓ EKS ↓ Kubernetes ↓ Terraform ↓ AWS ``` So **yes, containers are a major part of the DevOps curriculum, not an afterthought.** <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 17: AWS Monitoring + Security](../04-aws/ch17-monitoring-security.md) · [Chapter 19: Kubernetes Configuration + Storage](ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch18-revision.md)

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Chapter 18 — Revision Sheet: Kubernetes Fundamentals
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md). Core idea: **you declare the desired state; Kubernetes continuously works to make the actual state match it.**

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Why Kubernetes
text: 100 containers / 10 servers / many apps and environments / frequent deploys / failures / scaling → manual management is painful. If EC2-A (API + Worker + Payments) crashes you need to **detect failure, restart workloads, place them elsewhere, maintain desired replicas, route traffic, manage configuration, perform deployments**. Kubernetes = **container orchestration platform**: manages containers across a cluster. You say "I want 5 copies of my API", not `docker run/stop/restart/scale`. | Docker | Kubernetes | |---|---| | Runs containers (container technology) | Manages containers at scale (orchestration) — deploy, scale, network, self-heal, roll out/back | | Compose: local dev | Production orchestration, scaling, self-healing, service discovery, rolling deployments | | EC2 = virtual machine | A cluster can itself run on EC2 worker nodes: AWS → EC2 → Kubernetes → Pod → container |

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Architecture
text: ```text Cluster ├── Control Plane: API Server · Scheduler · Controller Manager · etcd └── Worker Nodes: kubelet · container runtime · Pods ``` | Component | Role | |---|---| | **API Server** | Main interface to Kubernetes; `kubectl` talks to it | | **etcd** | Distributed key-value store holding cluster state (what deployments exist, desired replicas, configuration, objects). Interview level: *etcd stores Kubernetes cluster state* | | **Scheduler** | Decides which worker node runs each Pod (resource availability + constraints) | | **Controller Manager** | Controllers continuously compare **desired vs actual** state (replicas: 3 but 2 Pods → create one) — "the heart of Kubernetes" | | **kubelet** | Agent on each worker node; talks to control plane and ensures assigned workloads run | | **Container runtime** | Actually runs containers; modern clusters use **containerd** (or another CRI-compatible runtime) — **Kubernetes does not require Docker Engine** (your image/Dockerfile/registry knowledge still applies) | **Desired state:** write `replicas: 3` (declarative), not step-by-step imperative commands.

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Pod
text: - Smallest deployable unit. Usually Pod → one container (Node.js). A Pod can hold tightly coupled containers (API + sidecar) sharing **network namespace/localhost and volumes**. **Pod ≠ container.** Don't put unrelated apps in one Pod. - **Pod IPs are ephemeral** (replacement Pod gets a new IP) → never use Pod IPs for clients → Services. - Basic Pod manifest: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: api-pod spec: containers: - name: api image: node:22 ports: - containerPort: 3000 ``` (not a useful production deployment; standalone Pods aren't recreated the way you want → Deployments) - **kubectl:** `get pods`, `describe pod api-pod` (events, scheduling, container state, image, volumes, networking, errors), `logs api-pod` / `logs -f`, `exec -it api-pod -- sh` (then `ls`, `env`, `curl localhost:3000/health`), `delete pod api-pod`, `apply -f pod.yaml`.

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Deployment, labels, selectors
text: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: { name: api } spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: { app: api } template: metadata: labels: { app: api } spec: containers: - name: api image: my-api:1.0 ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }] ``` - Deployment manages a set of Pods and keeps `replicas` alive; Pod names look like `api-7c9d8f7c5d-a1b2c`. - **Self-healing:** Pod B crashes → actual 2 / desired 3 → new Pod D created → 3 healthy. - **Labels** = key-value metadata (`app=api`, `environment=production`, `version=v1`); **selectors** (`matchLabels`) pick objects by label — crucial for Services.

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Services
text: | Type | What it does | |---|---| | **ClusterIP** | Stable endpoint **inside** the cluster (API → internal service/worker) | | **NodePort** | Exposes on each node's IP:port → Service → Pods; understand it, but not for production Internet traffic | | **LoadBalancer** | In the cloud provisions/configures an external load balancer (Internet → cloud LB → Service → Pods) | ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: { name: api-service } spec: selector: { app: api } ports: - port: 80 # Service port targetPort: 3000 # Pod port type: ClusterIP ``` Client → Service → healthy Pod; if a Pod dies, traffic goes to other healthy Pods.

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Namespaces and configuration
text: - **Namespace** = logical separation (development / staging / production), `kubectl get pods -n production`. Alternative: separate clusters (Dev → Cluster A, Prod → Cluster B); choice depends on isolation, security, scale, operations. - **ConfigMap** (non-sensitive: `NODE_ENV: production`, `PORT: "3000"`) and **Secret** (credentials/tokens) injected as env vars. Don't bake environment-specific config into images. **Kubernetes Secrets aren't automatically equal to a full secrets-management system**; on AWS integrate with Secrets Manager (Ch.19/33).

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Local lab with kind
text: ```bash kubectl version --client kind version kind create cluster --name devops-learning kubectl get nodes # devops-learning-control-plane docker build -t my-api:1.0 . kind load docker-image my-api:1.0 --name devops-learning # no registry needed kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml kubectl apply -f service.yaml kubectl get pods ; kubectl get deployments ; kubectl get svc ; kubectl get all kubectl describe deployment api ; kubectl describe service api-service ; kubectl logs <pod> kubectl port-forward service/api-service 3000:80 ; curl http://localhost:3000/health ``` Options: Docker Desktop Kubernetes, Minikube, **kind** (runs nodes as containers).

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: "Break it" exercises
text: | Action | Command | Expect | |---|---|---| | Delete a Pod | `kubectl delete pod <pod>` / `kubectl get pods -w` | Replacement created (self-healing) | | Scale up | edit `replicas: 5` + apply, or `kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=5` | 5 Pods | | Scale down | `kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=2` | Excess removed (desired 2 / actual 5 → 2) | | Bad image | `image: my-api:does-not-exist` | `ImagePullBackOff` / `ErrImagePull`; read **Events** in `describe pod` | **Pod phases:** Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown. **Common problems:** `CrashLoopBackOff`, `ImagePullBackOff`, `ErrImagePull`. **Debug workflow:** `get pods` → `describe pod` → `logs` → `exec` → check image/config/network/resources.

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Kubernetes + AWS
text: Route 53 → CloudFront/WAF → ALB → Kubernetes Service → Pods → RDS. **EKS** = Elastic Kubernetes Service: AWS manages significant parts of the control plane; workers via managed node groups or other compute. **ECR** (Elastic Container Registry) holds images pulled by EKS. Pipeline: git push → GitHub Actions → tests → Docker build → push to registry → Kubernetes deployment → **rolling update** (v1 v1 v1 → v2 v1 v1 → v2 v2 v1 → v2 v2 v2) → Pods.

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Depth guide
text: Deep: why Kubernetes, Docker vs K8s, cluster, control plane, worker nodes, API server, scheduler, controllers, etcd, kubelet, Pods, Deployments, replicas, desired state, labels/selectors, Services, ClusterIP, LoadBalancer, namespaces, kubectl, YAML, Pod lifecycle, self-healing, scaling, rolling deployments, images, local setup, debugging. Medium: EKS, NodePort, ReplicaSets, readiness/liveness, requests/limits, ConfigMaps, Secrets. Awareness: StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs/CronJobs, Operators, CRDs, service mesh.

title: Revision 18 — Kubernetes Fundamentals
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - A Deployment actually manages **ReplicaSets**, which manage Pods; each rollout creates a new ReplicaSet (this is what enables rollback). Useful commands: `kubectl rollout status deployment/api`, `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api`. - The worker node also runs **kube-proxy** (implements Service routing); a cloud cluster also has a **cloud-controller-manager**. - Services get cluster **DNS** names: `api-service.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` (just `api-service` inside the same namespace). - Kubernetes **Secrets are only base64-encoded** by default (not encrypted); enable encryption at rest for etcd and restrict RBAC. - **Namespaces don't isolate network traffic** by themselves — use NetworkPolicies. - Docker Engine support via "dockershim" was removed from Kubernetes in v1.24; clusters use CRI runtimes such as containerd. - `CrashLoopBackOff`/`ImagePullBackOff` are status reasons shown by `kubectl get pods`, not Pod phases. - A Pod running only `node:22` with no `command` exits immediately (no app started); the chapter notes this manifest is a learning stepping stone. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 17](ch17-revision.md) · [Full chapter 18](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 19](ch19-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
text: > **Source:** Response 19 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-19.txt`, lines 1–1677) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch19-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We're continuing exactly from [Chapter 18](ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md). The key problem now is: > **How do we give our containers configuration, secrets, resources, and persistent data without hardcoding everything inside the Docker image?** We'll go from **concept → YAML → actual commands → Node.js usage → debugging → interview level**. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 1. The Problem We're Solving
text: Our application currently looks like: ```text Deployment ↓ Pods ↓ Node.js Container ``` But a real application needs: ```text PORT=3000 NODE_ENV=production DATABASE_URL=... REDIS_URL=... JWT_SECRET=... ``` And potentially: ```text uploaded files database data logs application state ``` We don't want to: ```text ❌ hardcode secrets into code ❌ bake environment configuration into Docker images ❌ lose important data when a Pod dies ``` Kubernetes gives us several mechanisms. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 2. Configuration Mental Model
text: Think of Kubernetes configuration as: ```text Configuration │ ┌──────────┴──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ConfigMap Secret │ │ non-sensitive sensitive │ │ └──────────┬──────────┘ ↓ Pod ↓ Container ``` Storage is separate: ```text Pod │ └── Volume ↓ Persistent storage ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 3. What Is a ConfigMap?
text: A **ConfigMap** stores non-sensitive configuration. Examples: ```text NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 LOG_LEVEL=info API_TIMEOUT=5000 ``` Create: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: api-config data: NODE_ENV: production PORT: "3000" LOG_LEVEL: info ``` Apply: ```bash kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get configmap ``` Inspect: ```bash kubectl describe configmap api-config ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 4. Using ConfigMap as Environment Variables
text: Deployment: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: api spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: api template: metadata: labels: app: api spec: containers: - name: api image: my-api:1.0 envFrom: - configMapRef: name: api-config ports: - containerPort: 3000 ``` Now the container receives: ```text NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 LOG_LEVEL=info ``` Check: ```bash kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- env ``` You'll see the variables. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 5. ConfigMap vs `.env`
text: In local development you might have: ```text .env ``` For example: ```env PORT=3000 NODE_ENV=development ``` That's fine for local development. Kubernetes provides a way to inject configuration into Pods. So: ```text Local: .env Kubernetes: ConfigMap / Secret ``` But don't assume Kubernetes ConfigMaps automatically replace every configuration-management system in production. Larger environments may use external secret/configuration systems. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 6. Why Secrets?
text: Suppose we have: ```text DATABASE_PASSWORD JWT_SECRET AWS credentials API keys ``` These shouldn't go into: ```yaml ConfigMap ``` Use: ```text Secret ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 7. Creating a Secret
text: For learning: ```bash kubectl create secret generic api-secret \ --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD='supersecret' ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get secrets ``` Describe: ```bash kubectl describe secret api-secret ``` Notice that `describe` doesn't simply print the secret value. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 8. Using a Secret
text: Deployment: ```yaml env: - name: DB_PASSWORD valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: api-secret key: DB_PASSWORD ``` Now inside the container: ```text DB_PASSWORD=supersecret ``` Your Node.js application can read it: ```ts const password = process.env.DB_PASSWORD; ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 9. Important Kubernetes Secret Security Point
text: You will often hear: > "Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted." That's an oversimplification. Historically, Secret manifests commonly contain **base64-encoded** values. Base64 is **not encryption**. For example: ```text hello ↓ aGVsbG8= ``` Anyone can decode that. So: ```text Base64 ≠ encryption ``` Production clusters should use appropriate encryption-at-rest and access controls, and production AWS applications can integrate with systems such as: ```text AWS Secrets Manager ``` We'll connect this with the AWS security knowledge from [Chapter 17](../04-aws/ch17-monitoring-security.md). ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 10. ConfigMap vs Secret
text: | Feature | ConfigMap | Secret | |---|---|---| | Normal configuration | ✅ | | | Passwords | | ✅ | | API keys | | ✅ | | Environment settings | ✅ | | | Sensitive values | | ✅ | | Port numbers | ✅ | | | JWT secret | | ✅ | Mental shortcut: > **ConfigMap = configuration. Secret = sensitive configuration.** ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 11. Why Do Containers Need Volumes?
text: Remember Docker. Containers are generally treated as ephemeral. Suppose: ```text Pod ↓ Container ↓ /app/data/file.txt ``` Container gets destroyed. That data may disappear with it. Kubernetes therefore provides **Volumes**. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 12. Basic Kubernetes Volume
text: Example: ```yaml volumes: - name: app-data emptyDir: {} ``` Mount it: ```yaml containers: - name: api image: my-api:1.0 volumeMounts: - name: app-data mountPath: /app/data ``` Now: ```text Pod │ └── /app/data ↓ Volume ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 13. What Is `emptyDir`?
text: `emptyDir` creates temporary storage associated with the Pod. Example: ```text Pod └── emptyDir ``` Useful for: - temporary files - scratch space - intermediate processing - cache-like temporary data But: > **Do not use `emptyDir` for data that must survive Pod replacement.** When the Pod is removed, the `emptyDir` contents disappear. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 14. Example
text: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: storage-demo spec: containers: - name: app image: nginx volumeMounts: - name: data mountPath: /data volumes: - name: data emptyDir: {} ``` Apply: ```bash kubectl apply -f storage.yaml ``` Enter: ```bash kubectl exec -it storage-demo -- sh ``` Create: ```bash echo "hello" > /data/test.txt ``` Check: ```bash cat /data/test.txt ``` The file exists. But if the Pod itself is removed: ```bash kubectl delete pod storage-demo ``` and a completely new Pod is created, the `emptyDir` data won't persist. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: PART 4 — PERSISTENT STORAGE
text: Now consider: ```text PostgreSQL ``` You absolutely don't want: ```text Pod dies ↓ Database data disappears ``` We need persistent storage. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 15. PersistentVolume
text: A **PersistentVolume (PV)** represents persistent storage available to Kubernetes. Conceptually: ```text Persistent Storage ↓ PV ↓ Pod ``` The actual storage may come from cloud/block/file storage depending on the Kubernetes environment. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 16. PersistentVolumeClaim
text: Applications generally shouldn't have to care about the exact physical disk. Instead, the application requests storage through a: > **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** Think: ```text Application ↓ PVC ↓ PV ↓ Actual Storage ``` The PVC says: > "I need 20 GiB of persistent storage." ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 17. PVC Example
text: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: api-storage spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce resources: requests: storage: 5Gi ``` Apply: ```bash kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get pvc ``` You'll see something like: ```text NAME STATUS api-storage Bound ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 18. Mount PVC Into Pod
text: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: storage-app spec: containers: - name: app image: nginx volumeMounts: - name: persistent-data mountPath: /data volumes: - name: persistent-data persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: api-storage ``` Now: ```text Pod ↓ /data ↓ PVC ↓ PV ↓ Persistent storage ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 19. Why This Matters
text: Suppose: ```text Pod A ↓ /data ↓ PVC ``` Pod A dies. Deployment creates: ```text Pod B ``` Pod B can mount the same claim according to the storage/access-mode constraints. Therefore: ```text Pod A ❌ ↓ PVC ↓ Pod B ✅ ``` The storage isn't tied to the lifecycle of one ephemeral Pod. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 20. What Is StorageClass?
text: In cloud environments, you don't normally manually create every PV. A `StorageClass` describes how storage can be dynamically provisioned. Conceptually: ```text PVC ↓ StorageClass ↓ Cloud storage provisioned ↓ PV ``` This is called: > **Dynamic provisioning** For example, on AWS, Kubernetes can work with cloud storage through the relevant CSI drivers. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 21. Kubernetes Storage on AWS
text: This connects directly to your AWS knowledge. Common concepts include: ```text EBS EFS ```

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: EBS
text: Block storage. Useful for workloads requiring block storage semantics.

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: EFS
