text: Managed network file storage. Useful when multiple workloads need shared file storage under appropriate access patterns. Mental model: ```text Kubernetes ↓ CSI driver ↓ AWS storage ``` You don't need to memorize every CSI implementation detail for SWE interviews. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: PART 6 — REQUESTS & LIMITS
text: This is another important production concept. Suppose a Node.js container consumes CPU. Kubernetes needs to know: > How much resource should this workload request? ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 22. Requests
text: Example: ```yaml resources: requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" ``` This means: > Kubernetes should reserve/schedule the workload based on approximately these requested resources. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 23. Limits
text: ```yaml resources: limits: cpu: "500m" memory: "512Mi" ``` This specifies a maximum resource boundary for the container under Kubernetes resource management. Example: ```yaml resources: requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" limits: cpu: "500m" memory: "512Mi" ``` Mental model: ```text Request → what the workload asks/reserves for scheduling Limit → maximum resource boundary ``` These become very important when we get to autoscaling. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 24. Why Resources Matter
text: Imagine: ```text Pod A → memory hungry Pod B → memory hungry Pod C → memory hungry ``` Without resource management, workloads can interfere with each other. With requests/limits: ```text Kubernetes ↓ Scheduling decisions + Resource constraints ``` This becomes especially important in production clusters. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: PART 7 — HEALTH PROBES
text: We touched on this earlier. Your application needs to tell Kubernetes: > "Am I alive?" and: > "Am I ready to receive traffic?" These are different questions. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 25. Liveness Probe
text: Liveness asks: > Is the application alive? Example: ```yaml livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /health port: 3000 initialDelaySeconds: 10 periodSeconds: 15 ``` If the container gets into a broken state and repeatedly fails its liveness probe, Kubernetes can restart the container according to the configured behavior. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 26. Readiness Probe
text: Readiness asks: > Can this instance receive traffic right now? Example: ```yaml readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /ready port: 3000 initialDelaySeconds: 5 periodSeconds: 10 ``` This is extremely important for backend applications. Imagine: ```text New Pod starts ↓ Node.js starts ↓ Database connection isn't ready ``` You don't want traffic immediately hitting it. Readiness can prevent the Pod from being considered ready for traffic until it passes the readiness condition. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 27. Liveness vs Readiness
text: Remember: ```text Liveness → Should Kubernetes restart this container? Readiness → Should this Pod receive traffic? ``` Example: ```text Pod running ↓ Database temporarily unavailable ↓ Readiness ❌ ↓ Don't send traffic ``` The container may still be alive. That's why readiness and liveness are **not interchangeable**. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: PART 8 — COMPLETE NODE.JS DEPLOYMENT
text: Now let's combine what we've learned. Imagine your Node API has: ```text /health /ready ``` and needs: ```text PORT NODE_ENV DATABASE_URL JWT_SECRET ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: ConfigMap
text: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: api-config data: NODE_ENV: production PORT: "3000" ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Secret
text: ```bash kubectl create secret generic api-secret \ --from-literal=DATABASE_URL='postgresql://user:password@db:5432/app' \ --from-literal=JWT_SECRET='change-me' ``` For a real production environment, don't casually commit this command containing credentials into Git. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Deployment
text: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: api spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: api template: metadata: labels: app: api spec: containers: - name: api image: my-api:1.0 ports: - containerPort: 3000 envFrom: - configMapRef: name: api-config env: - name: DATABASE_URL valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: api-secret key: DATABASE_URL - name: JWT_SECRET valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: api-secret key: JWT_SECRET resources: requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" limits: cpu: "500m" memory: "512Mi" readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /ready port: 3000 initialDelaySeconds: 5 periodSeconds: 10 livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /health port: 3000 initialDelaySeconds: 10 periodSeconds: 15 ``` Now we're getting much closer to a real backend deployment. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 29. Node.js Side
text: Your Node.js application can simply read: ```ts const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000); const databaseUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL; const jwtSecret = process.env.JWT_SECRET; ``` Your application doesn't need to know whether the values came from: ```text ConfigMap Secret Docker AWS ``` It simply receives environment variables. This is a very useful separation of concerns. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: PART 9 — STATEFUL VS STATELESS
text: This is an important architecture concept. Your API: ```text Node.js API ``` should ideally be: > **stateless** Meaning one Pod doesn't have irreplaceable application state. Example: ```text Request 1 → Pod A Request 2 → Pod B Request 3 → Pod C ``` All should work. State belongs in external systems: ```text PostgreSQL Redis S3 ``` rather than only inside a Pod's filesystem. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 30. Why Stateless Matters
text: Imagine: ```text Pod A └── user session ``` Pod A dies. Session disappears. Bad architecture. Instead: ```text Pod A ──┐ Pod B ──┼──→ Redis Pod C ──┘ ``` Now all Pods can access shared state. Similarly: ```text Pods ↓ RDS ``` for persistent relational data. And: ```text Pods ↓ S3 ``` for object/file storage. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 31. Should You Run PostgreSQL Inside Kubernetes?
text: You **can**. But for your SWE/cloud architecture, don't automatically do it. You already learned: ```text AWS RDS ``` A common architecture is: ```text EKS ↓ Node.js Pods ↓ RDS PostgreSQL ``` rather than: ```text EKS ↓ PostgreSQL Pod ``` Why? Managed databases provide things like: - backups - failover capabilities - maintenance - monitoring - managed storage - operational tooling Running databases in Kubernetes introduces additional operational complexity. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: PART 10 — STATEFULSET
text: You should still know: > **StatefulSet** StatefulSet is designed for workloads requiring stable identity and/or persistent storage semantics. Conceptually: ```text StatefulSet ├── postgres-0 ├── postgres-1 └── postgres-2 ``` Pods have predictable identities. This is useful for certain stateful distributed systems. For your backend: ```text Node.js API → Deployment PostgreSQL → preferably managed RDS in AWS ``` is a much more important architecture to understand. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: PART 11 — PRACTICAL LAB
text: Now let's turn this response into an actual exercise.

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Lab architecture
text: ```text Deployment │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod A Pod B Pod C │ │ │ └────┬────┴────┬────┘ ↓ ↓ ConfigMap Secret │ │ └────┬────┘ ↓ Node.js API ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Step 1 — Create ConfigMap
text: ```bash kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get configmap ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Step 2 — Create Secret
text: ```bash kubectl create secret generic api-secret \ --from-literal=API_KEY='test-key' ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get secrets ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Step 3 — Deploy
text: ```bash kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Step 4 — Inspect Environment
text: ```bash kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- env ``` Verify: ```text NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 API_KEY=test-key ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Step 5 — Test Readiness
text: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod-name> ``` Look for: ```text Readiness probe ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Step 6 — Break the Health Endpoint
text: Temporarily make `/health` fail. Then: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` Watch: ```bash kubectl get pods -w ``` Inspect: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod-name> ``` You should understand why Kubernetes considers the container unhealthy. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 32. Storage Lab
text: Create: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: volume-demo spec: containers: - name: app image: nginx volumeMounts: - name: data mountPath: /data volumes: - name: data emptyDir: {} ``` Apply: ```bash kubectl apply -f volume.yaml ``` Enter: ```bash kubectl exec -it volume-demo -- sh ``` Create: ```bash echo "hello kubernetes" > /data/message.txt ``` Check: ```bash cat /data/message.txt ``` Then delete the Pod. Understand what happens to the data. That's the difference between: ```text ephemeral storage ``` and: ```text persistent storage ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 33. Debugging Checklist
text: When configuration doesn't work: ```text kubectl get pods ↓ kubectl describe pod <pod> ↓ kubectl logs <pod> ↓ kubectl exec -it <pod> -- env ``` Check: - ConfigMap exists? - Secret exists? - Correct key? - Correct namespace? - Environment variable name correct? - Image contains expected application? - Application actually reads `process.env`? - Probe endpoint exists? - Probe port correct? ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Pod can't start
text: Check: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Secret not found
text: Possible issue: ```text Secret exists in namespace A Pod is in namespace B ``` Remember: > Kubernetes resources such as Secrets and ConfigMaps are generally namespace-scoped. ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: ConfigMap changed but application still uses old value
text: Environment variables injected into an already-running container don't magically update the running process. You may need to restart/redeploy Pods. Example: ```bash kubectl rollout restart deployment api ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: PVC stuck Pending
text: Check: ```bash kubectl get pvc kubectl describe pvc <name> ``` Possible causes: - no suitable storage provisioner - wrong StorageClass - insufficient capacity - access-mode mismatch ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 35. The Big Picture
text: You now have: ```text Kubernetes │ ┌─────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Deployment ConfigMap Secret │ ↓ Pods │ ┌────┴────┐ ↓ ↓ Container Volume │ ┌───────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ ephemeral persistent emptyDir PVC ↓ PV ↓ Cloud Storage ``` And your application architecture: ```text Internet │ ↓ ALB / LB │ ↓ K8s Service │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod A Pod B Pod C │ │ │ └────────────┼────────────┘ ↓ Node.js API / \ ↓ ↓ Redis RDS │ Persistent DB ``` Configuration: ```text ConfigMap ───────→ Pod Secret ──────────→ Pod ``` Files: ```text Pod → PVC → Persistent Storage ``` ---

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: 36. What You Should Be Able to Explain Now
text: If an interviewer asks:

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: "What happens when a Pod dies?"
text: You should explain: ```text Deployment ↓ desired replica count ↓ controller notices missing Pod ↓ replacement Pod created ↓ scheduler places it ↓ container starts ↓ readiness probe passes ↓ Service can send traffic ```

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: "Where do your database passwords live?"
text: ```text Secret / external secret manager ``` not: ```text Dockerfile ❌ GitHub repository ❌ source code ❌ ```

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: "Where should application files be stored?"
text: Depends on their nature: ```text temporary → emptyDir persistent filesystem data → PVC/cloud storage objects/uploads → S3 relational data → RDS cache/session → Redis ```

title: Chapter 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: "Why are APIs generally stateless?"
text: Because: ```text Any healthy Pod can process any request ``` making: ```text horizontal scaling load balancing Pod replacement rolling deployments ``` much easier. <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 18: Kubernetes Fundamentals](ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md) · [Chapter 20: Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production](ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch19-revision.md)

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Chapter 19 — Revision Sheet: Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md). Problem: give containers **configuration, secrets, resources and persistent data** without hard-coding them into the image or losing data when a Pod dies.

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Configuration
text: | | ConfigMap | Secret | |---|---|---| | Holds | Non-sensitive config: `NODE_ENV`, `PORT`, `LOG_LEVEL`, `API_TIMEOUT` | Sensitive: DB password, JWT secret, API keys, AWS credentials | | Create | YAML (`data:` map) / `kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml` | `kubectl create secret generic api-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD='supersecret'` | | Inspect | `kubectl get configmap`, `kubectl describe configmap api-config` | `kubectl get secrets`, `kubectl describe secret api-secret` (doesn't print values) | | Inject all keys | `envFrom: - configMapRef: { name: api-config }` | — | | Inject one key | — | `env: - name: DB_PASSWORD valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: api-secret, key: DB_PASSWORD } }` | | Verify | `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- env` | same | - Mnemonic: **ConfigMap = configuration, Secret = sensitive configuration.** Local dev uses `.env`; Kubernetes uses ConfigMap/Secret (larger environments may use external secret/config systems). - **"Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted" is an oversimplification:** manifests typically hold **base64-encoded** values — **base64 ≠ encryption** (`hello` → `aGVsbG8=`). Use encryption at rest + access controls; on AWS integrate with **Secrets Manager** (Ch.17). - Node.js just reads env vars (`Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000)`, `process.env.DATABASE_URL`, `process.env.JWT_SECRET`) and doesn't care whether they came from ConfigMap/Secret/Docker/AWS. - Never casually commit `kubectl create secret ... --from-literal=...password...` commands to Git.

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Volumes and persistence
text: - Containers are ephemeral — data in the container filesystem disappears with it. - **`emptyDir`** = temporary storage tied to the Pod (temp files, scratch space, intermediate processing, cache-like data). **Data is lost when the Pod is removed** — never for data that must survive Pod replacement. ```yaml volumes: - name: app-data emptyDir: {} containers: - name: api image: my-api:1.0 volumeMounts: - name: app-data mountPath: /app/data ``` - **PersistentVolume (PV)** = persistent storage available to the cluster. **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** = application's request ("I need 5 GiB"): `App → PVC → PV → actual storage`. ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: { name: api-storage } spec: accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce] resources: { requests: { storage: 5Gi } } ``` `kubectl get pvc` → `Bound`. Mount: `volumes: - name: persistent-data persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: api-storage }`. Pod A dies → Deployment creates Pod B → can mount the same claim (subject to storage/access-mode constraints). - **StorageClass** = how storage is **dynamically provisioned** (PVC → StorageClass → cloud storage provisioned → PV). On AWS via CSI drivers: **EBS** (block storage) and **EFS** (managed network file storage, shared across workloads). Kubernetes → CSI driver → AWS storage.

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Requests & limits
text: ```yaml resources: requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" } limits: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" } ``` **Request** = what the workload asks/reserves for scheduling. **Limit** = maximum boundary. Without them workloads interfere with each other; important for autoscaling later (Ch.20).

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Probes
text: | | Liveness | Readiness | |---|---|---| | Question | Is it alive? → should Kubernetes **restart** the container? | Can this Pod receive traffic **now**? | | Example | `httpGet: /health :3000`, `initialDelaySeconds: 10`, `periodSeconds: 15` | `httpGet: /ready :3000`, `initialDelaySeconds: 5`, `periodSeconds: 10` | | Case | Broken state repeatedly failing → restart | DB temporarily unavailable → readiness ❌ → don't send traffic, container still alive | Not interchangeable. New Pod starts → Node starts → DB not ready: readiness prevents early traffic.

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Complete Node.js Deployment (shape)
text: ConfigMap (`NODE_ENV`, `PORT`) + Secret (`DATABASE_URL`, `JWT_SECRET`) + Deployment (replicas 3, `envFrom` ConfigMap, `env` from `secretKeyRef`, resources requests/limits, readinessProbe `/ready`, livenessProbe `/health`).

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Stateless vs stateful
text: - API should be **stateless** (any Pod can serve any request); state lives in PostgreSQL / Redis / S3 — not the Pod filesystem. Session only in Pod A is lost when A dies → use shared Redis. - **Should PostgreSQL run in Kubernetes?** You can, but prefer **RDS** (backups, failover, maintenance, monitoring, managed storage) → `EKS → Node.js Pods → RDS`. - **StatefulSet:** stable identities (`postgres-0`, `postgres-1`, `postgres-2`) and persistent storage semantics for certain stateful distributed systems. For a backend: Node API → Deployment; PostgreSQL → preferably RDS. - **Where to put data:** temporary → emptyDir; persistent filesystem data → PVC/cloud storage; objects/uploads → S3; relational data → RDS; cache/session → Redis.

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Interview: "What happens when a Pod dies?"
text: Deployment desired replica count → controller notices missing Pod → replacement Pod created → scheduler places it → container starts → readiness probe passes → Service can send traffic.

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Debugging checklist
text: `kubectl get pods` → `describe pod` → `logs` → `exec -- env`. Check: ConfigMap/Secret exist? correct key? correct **namespace** (Secrets/ConfigMaps are namespace-scoped; "Secret exists in namespace A, Pod in B")? env name correct? image contains expected app? app reads `process.env`? probe endpoint and port exist? - **ConfigMap changed but app still uses old value:** env vars injected into a running container don't update → `kubectl rollout restart deployment api`. - **PVC stuck Pending:** `kubectl get pvc`, `kubectl describe pvc <name>` — no suitable provisioner, wrong StorageClass, insufficient capacity, access-mode mismatch.

title: Revision 19 — Kubernetes Configuration + Storage
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **Access modes:** `ReadWriteOnce` (mounted read-write by a single node — typical for EBS, which is also **AZ-bound**), `ReadOnlyMany`, `ReadWriteMany` (e.g. EFS), `ReadWriteOncePod`. A multi-replica Deployment sharing one RWO PVC often fails; StatefulSets use `volumeClaimTemplates` for one PVC per Pod. - PV **reclaim policy**: `Delete` or `Retain`. StorageClass `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` delays provisioning until a Pod is scheduled (so the volume lands in the right AZ). - ConfigMaps/Secrets can also be **mounted as files**; mounted volumes are updated eventually when the ConfigMap changes, **env vars are not**. - `emptyDir` survives *container* restarts within the same Pod but not Pod deletion; `medium: Memory` backs it by RAM. - **Units:** `250m` = 0.25 CPU core; `256Mi` = mebibytes. Exceeding a **CPU limit** throttles; exceeding a **memory limit** gets the container **OOMKilled**. The scheduler uses **requests**; QoS classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort. - **`startupProbe`** protects slow-starting apps. Keep liveness checks lightweight and independent of external dependencies (a DB outage shouldn't make Kubernetes restart every Pod); readiness failing removes the Pod from the Service's endpoints and gates rolling updates. - The chapter's lab creates a Secret with `API_KEY` while the Deployment reads `DATABASE_URL`/`JWT_SECRET` — adapt one of them to match (see [Corrections](../CORRECTIONS.md)). <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 18](ch18-revision.md) · [Full chapter 19](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 20](ch20-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
text: > **Source:** Response 20 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-20.txt`, lines 1–1852) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch20-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> This is the **last major Kubernetes response** in our roadmap. By the end of this response, you should be able to look at a production Kubernetes architecture and understand **how traffic enters the cluster, how it reaches Pods, how Pods communicate, how they scale, and how Kubernetes handles failures and deployments.** We'll keep this practical. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 1. Where We Are
text: You've already learned: ```text Docker ↓ Container ↓ Kubernetes ↓ Pod ↓ Deployment ↓ Service ↓ ConfigMap / Secret ↓ Volumes / PVC ``` Now we need to solve: ```text How does traffic reach my application? How do Pods communicate? How does the application scale? How do I expose it to the Internet? How do I secure it? How do I run this in AWS? How do I troubleshoot it? ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 2. Kubernetes Networking Mental Model
text: A simplified architecture: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ Load Balancer │ ↓ Ingress │ ↓ Service │ ┌──────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod Pod Pod │ │ │ └──────────┼──────────┘ ↓ RDS/Redis ``` There are several networking layers here. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 3. Pod-to-Pod Communication
text: Suppose: ```text Pod A Node.js API ``` needs to communicate with: ```text Pod B Worker ``` Kubernetes networking is designed so Pods can communicate with one another using their cluster networking. Conceptually: ```text Pod A 10.x.x.1 │ │ ↓ Pod B 10.x.x.2 ``` But remember: > **Pod IPs are ephemeral.** So don't hardcode: ```text 10.x.x.2 ``` in your application. Instead, use a Service. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 4. Service Discovery
text: Suppose you have: ```text API Worker Redis ``` Create a Redis Service: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: redis spec: selector: app: redis ports: - port: 6379 targetPort: 6379 ``` Now your API can connect to: ```text redis:6379 ``` instead of: ```text 10.0.4.17:6379 ``` This is called **service discovery**. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 5. Kubernetes DNS
text: Kubernetes provides DNS-based service discovery. Conceptually: ```text redis ↓ Kubernetes DNS ↓ Redis Service IP ↓ Redis Pods ``` Your Node.js code could use: ```ts const redisHost = process.env.REDIS_HOST ?? "redis"; ``` and: ```text redis:6379 ``` becomes the network destination. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 6. Namespaces and DNS
text: Suppose: ```text namespace: production service: redis ``` Within the same namespace: ```text redis ``` can usually resolve the Service. Across namespaces, you can use the namespace-qualified service name: ```text redis.production ``` and Kubernetes DNS supports a fuller service DNS structure. You don't need to memorize the complete FQDN yet, but understand: > **Service names provide stable discovery even when Pods change.** ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 2 — SERVICE TYPES
text: We've already seen: ```text ClusterIP NodePort LoadBalancer ``` Let's understand when to use each. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 7. ClusterIP
text: Default Service type. ```text Cluster │ └── Service ↓ Pods ``` Accessible inside the cluster. Perfect for: ```text API → Redis API → internal worker API → internal service ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 8. NodePort
text: Exposes a port on each node. ```text Internet ↓ NodeIP:NodePort ↓ Service ↓ Pods ``` Example: ```yaml type: NodePort ``` Useful for learning and certain scenarios, but generally not your preferred production internet-facing architecture. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 9. LoadBalancer
text: Cloud integrations can provision an external load-balancing mechanism. Conceptually: ```text Internet ↓ Cloud Load Balancer ↓ Kubernetes Service ↓ Pods ``` This is common in cloud environments. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 3 — INGRESS
text: Now we get to a very important production concept. Imagine you have: ```text api.example.com app.example.com admin.example.com ``` You don't necessarily want a separate public load-balancing endpoint for every internal service. You can use an **Ingress** abstraction. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 10. What Is Ingress?
text: Ingress defines HTTP/HTTPS routing rules into your cluster. Example: ```text api.example.com ↓ Ingress ↓ API Service ``` And: ```text admin.example.com ↓ Ingress ↓ Admin Service ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 11. Host-Based Routing
text: Example: ```yaml rules: - host: api.example.com ... - host: admin.example.com ... ``` Traffic: ```text api.example.com ↓ API Service admin.example.com ↓ Admin Service ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 12. Path-Based Routing
text: You can also route: ```text example.com/api example.com/admin ``` to different Services. Conceptually: ```text Ingress │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ /api /admin ↓ ↓ API Service Admin Service ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 13. Important Ingress Clarification
text: Ingress is **not itself necessarily the complete load-balancing implementation**. You need an **Ingress Controller** to actually implement the routing behavior. Examples include controllers based on: ```text NGINX AWS Load Balancer Controller Traefik ``` For AWS/EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller is particularly relevant. The mental model is: ```text Ingress → routing configuration Ingress Controller → implements that routing ``` This distinction is frequently asked in interviews. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 4 — AWS + EKS NETWORKING
text: Now connect this with everything you've already learned about AWS. Your previous architecture: ```text Route 53 ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 ↓ RDS ``` Kubernetes version: ```text Route 53 ↓ AWS Load Balancer ↓ EKS ↓ Kubernetes routing ↓ Pods ↓ RDS ``` Depending on the exact EKS architecture and controller, AWS load-balancing resources can integrate with Kubernetes Services/Ingress. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 14. Production EKS Architecture
text: A simplified design: ```text Internet │ ↓ Route 53 │ ↓ CloudFront │ ↓ WAF │ ↓ AWS Load Balancer │ ↓ EKS Cluster │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Node/Pod Node/Pod Node/Pod │ │ │ └─────────────┼─────────────┘ ↓ RDS PostgreSQL │ Redis ``` Not every application needs every component, but you should understand how they fit together. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 5 — NETWORK POLICIES
text: Security Groups protect AWS network interfaces. Kubernetes can additionally implement **NetworkPolicy** controls for Pod traffic when the cluster networking implementation supports them. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 15. Why Network Policies?
text: Suppose: ```text Frontend API Database Worker ``` You don't want: ```text Frontend → Database ``` directly. You want: ```text Frontend → API → Database ``` A NetworkPolicy can express restrictions around which Pods/namespaces/network sources can communicate. Conceptually: ```text Frontend │ ↓ allowed API │ ↓ allowed Database Frontend │ ✕ Database ``` This is **defense in depth**. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 16. Basic NetworkPolicy
text: Conceptual example: ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: allow-api-to-db spec: podSelector: matchLabels: app: database policyTypes: - Ingress ingress: - from: - podSelector: matchLabels: app: api ``` This says roughly: > Only traffic from Pods labeled `app=api` should be allowed into the selected database Pods, assuming the cluster's networking implementation enforces the policy. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 6 — READINESS + LOAD BALANCING
text: This is an important production interaction. Suppose: ```text Pod A → healthy Pod B → starting Pod C → healthy ``` Pod B shouldn't receive production traffic yet. That's why: ```text readinessProbe ``` matters. Flow: ```text Pod starts ↓ Readiness check ↓ Fails ❌ ↓ Not considered ready ↓ Service doesn't route normal traffic to it ``` Then: ```text Application ready ↓ Readiness passes ✅ ↓ Pod becomes eligible for traffic ``` This is extremely important during deployments. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 7 — HORIZONTAL POD AUTOSCALING
text: Now let's scale Kubernetes. Suppose: ```text 3 Pods ``` are handling traffic. Traffic increases: ```text CPU ↑ Requests ↑ ``` We might want: ```text 3 Pods ↓ 5 Pods ↓ 10 Pods ``` Kubernetes provides: > **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)** ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 17. What HPA Does
text: Conceptually: ```text Metrics ↓ HPA ↓ Desired replica count ↓ Deployment ↓ More/fewer Pods ``` For example: ```text CPU target = 60% ``` If average CPU goes significantly above the target: ```text 3 Pods ↓ HPA ↓ 5 Pods ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 18. HPA Example
text: A simplified example: ```yaml apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: name: api-hpa spec: scaleTargetRef: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment name: api minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 10 metrics: - type: Resource resource: name: cpu target: type: Utilization averageUtilization: 60 ``` This says: ```text Minimum → 2 Maximum → 10 Target → 60% CPU utilization ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 19. Important HPA Dependency
text: HPA needs metrics. A common Kubernetes setup uses: ```text Metrics Server ``` for resource metrics. If metrics aren't available: ```text HPA ↓ No useful metrics ↓ Autoscaling won't work as expected ``` This is a common troubleshooting point. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 20. HPA Doesn't Magically Create More Machines
text: This distinction is very important. Suppose: ```text Worker Node └── Pods ``` HPA wants: ```text 10 Pods ``` but there isn't enough node capacity. Then you have a second scaling layer. ```text HPA ↓ Pod demand ↑ ↓ Not enough node capacity ↓ Cluster/node autoscaling ↓ More nodes ↓ Pods scheduled ``` So: ```text Pod scaling ≠ Node scaling ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 8 — CLUSTER AUTOSCALING
text: At the infrastructure level, Kubernetes environments can use node autoscaling mechanisms to add/remove worker capacity. Conceptually: ```text Pod demand ↑ ↓ No node capacity ↓ Node autoscaler ↓ New worker node ↓ Pod scheduled ``` AWS EKS environments can use mechanisms such as: ```text Managed Node Groups Karpenter ``` You should know these names and their purpose. You don't need deep Karpenter internals for a normal SWE interview. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 21. Two Levels of Scaling
text: Remember: ```text SCALING │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ ↓ ↓ Pod scaling Node scaling ↓ ↓ HPA Node autoscaling ``` Example: ```text Traffic ↑ ↓ HPA ↓ More Pods ↓ No capacity ↓ More Nodes ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 9 — RESOURCE REQUESTS + HPA
text: This connects [Chapter 19](ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md). We had: ```yaml resources: requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" limits: cpu: "500m" memory: "512Mi" ``` HPA can use CPU/memory utilization relative to configured resource requests. So resource requests aren't just about scheduling. They can also affect how resource-based autoscaling behaves. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 10 — ROLLING DEPLOYMENTS
text: Suppose you're running: ```text v1 v1 v1 ``` Deploy: ```text v2 ``` Kubernetes can gradually replace Pods. ```text v1 v1 v1 ↓ v2 v1 v1 ↓ v2 v2 v1 ↓ v2 v2 v2 ``` During this process: ```text readiness probes + Service + Deployment strategy ``` work together. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 22. Rollout Commands
text: Check: ```bash kubectl rollout status deployment/api ``` View history: ```bash kubectl rollout history deployment/api ``` Undo: ```bash kubectl rollout undo deployment/api ``` Restart: ```bash kubectl rollout restart deployment/api ``` These commands are worth knowing. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 23. Why Readiness Is Critical During Rollouts
text: Without readiness: ```text New Pod starts ↓ Traffic immediately arrives ↓ Application isn't ready ↓ Requests fail ``` With readiness: ```text New Pod ↓ Not ready ↓ No normal traffic ↓ Application initializes ↓ Ready ✅ ↓ Traffic ``` This is one of the simplest ways to understand production Kubernetes. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 11 — POD DISRUPTION
text: Suppose you have: ```text 3 Pods ``` and someone needs to perform maintenance on a node. You don't necessarily want: ```text 3 → 0 ``` at once. Kubernetes provides concepts such as: > **PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)** A PDB can help limit voluntary disruptions so that a specified level of availability is maintained. You should know the concept, not memorize every YAML option. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 12 — JOBS AND CRONJOBS
text: Not everything is a long-running API. Suppose you need: ```text Generate monthly report ``` You might use a Kubernetes: > Job For scheduled work: > CronJob Conceptually: ```text CronJob ↓ Job ↓ Pod ↓ Task ``` Examples: ```text database cleanup report generation batch processing scheduled synchronization ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 13 — DAEMONSETS
text: Another useful awareness-level object: > **DaemonSet** A DaemonSet ensures a Pod runs on appropriate nodes according to its scheduling rules. Conceptually: ```text Node A → monitoring agent Node B → monitoring agent Node C → monitoring agent ``` Common use cases include: ```text log collection node monitoring network agents ``` Don't spend huge amounts of time here. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 14 — KUBERNETES PRODUCTION SECURITY
text: You already learned AWS IAM and Kubernetes Secrets. Now combine them. A production application should avoid: ```text AWS access key ↓ hardcoded in source code ❌ ``` or: ```text AWS access key ↓ Docker image ❌ ``` Instead use appropriate workload identity mechanisms. On EKS, one important approach is: ```text Pod ↓ AWS workload identity ↓ IAM permissions ↓ AWS service ``` This allows workloads to obtain AWS permissions without embedding long-lived credentials in the container. The exact mechanism depends on the EKS setup, but **the principle is what you need to understand**: > **Give workloads identities and least-privilege permissions instead of putting permanent AWS keys inside Pods.** ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 24. Example
text: Suppose your Node.js API needs S3 access. Bad: ```text AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=... ``` baked into Docker. Better: ```text Pod ↓ IAM-based workload identity ↓ S3 ``` This connects directly to your IAM [Chapter 9](../04-aws/ch09-aws-fundamentals-iam.md). ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 15 — KUBERNETES LOGGING
text: Your application: ```ts console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: "info", event: "order_created", orderId })); ``` Kubernetes captures container stdout/stderr through the container runtime/logging architecture. You can inspect: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> ``` Production environments generally centralize logs into an observability system rather than relying only on `kubectl logs`. For example: ```text Pod ↓ stdout ↓ logging agent ↓ central logging ``` We'll go much deeper into observability in [Chapter 22](../07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md). ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 16 — KUBERNETES TROUBLESHOOTING
text: This is one of the **most valuable interview skills**. Don't just memorize commands. Learn the debugging flow. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Scenario 1 — Pod is Pending
text: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You see: ```text api-xxx Pending ``` Run: ```bash kubectl describe pod api-xxx ``` Look at Events. Possible causes: ```text insufficient CPU insufficient memory node selector mismatch taints/tolerations PVC issue scheduling constraints ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 25. Scenario 2 — CrashLoopBackOff
text: ```text CrashLoopBackOff ``` Means the container repeatedly crashes/restarts and Kubernetes is backing off between attempts. Check: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> ``` If the previous container instance crashed: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> --previous ``` Then: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` Common causes: ```text application crash missing environment variable bad configuration database connection failure wrong command failed startup ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 26. Scenario 3 — ImagePullBackOff
text: Check: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` Possible causes: ```text wrong image name wrong tag private registry authentication problem image doesn't exist registry unavailable ``` Remember your pipeline: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ Docker build ↓ ECR ↓ Kubernetes ↓ Pod ``` A failure anywhere can cause deployment problems. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 27. Scenario 4 — Service Has No Traffic
text: Suppose: ```text Service ↓ ??? ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get svc ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get endpoints ``` or, on modern Kubernetes: ```bash kubectl get endpointslices ``` Then inspect: ```bash kubectl describe service api-service ``` Very common problem: ```text Service selector: app: api Pod label: app: backend ``` They don't match. Therefore: ```text Service ↓ No matching Pods ``` No traffic. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 28. Scenario 5 — Port Mismatch
text: Suppose: ```text Service: targetPort: 3000 ``` but Node.js actually listens on: ```text 8080 ``` Then: ```text Service ↓ 3000 ↓ Pod ↓ nothing listening there ``` Result: ```text connection failure ``` Check: ```bash kubectl describe service api-service kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` and inspect the application. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 29. Scenario 6 — Readiness Probe Failing
text: Check: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` You might see: ```text Readiness probe failed ``` Possible reasons: ```text wrong path wrong port application isn't ready database dependency unavailable startup takes longer than expected ``` Don't blindly increase timeout values. Understand **why** the application isn't ready. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 30. Scenario 7 — HPA Doesn't Scale
text: Check: ```bash kubectl get hpa ``` Then: ```bash kubectl describe hpa api-hpa ``` Possible issues: ```text Metrics Server unavailable resource requests missing metrics unavailable wrong target no traffic/load maxReplicas already reached ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 17 — PRACTICAL PRODUCTION LAB
text: Now let's combine everything. Your application: ```text Node.js API ``` Container: ```text my-api:1.0 ``` Kubernetes: ```text Deployment 3 replicas ``` Service: ```text ClusterIP ``` Configuration: ```text ConfigMap Secret ``` Health: ```text /health /ready ``` Scaling: ```text HPA 2–10 replicas ``` Architecture: ```text Internet │ ↓ Route 53 │ ↓ CloudFront │ ↓ WAF │ ↓ AWS Load Balancer │ ↓ Ingress │ ↓ API Service │ ┌──────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod A Pod B Pod C │ │ │ └──────────┼──────────┘ ↓ RDS │ Redis ``` ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 31. Your Deployment Pipeline
text: Now combine **everything you've learned across 20 responses**: ```text Developer │ ↓ Git │ ↓ GitHub │ ↓ GitHub Actions │ ├── lint ├── typecheck ├── tests ├── build │ ↓ Docker Build │ ↓ Container Image │ ↓ ECR │ ↓ Kubernetes / EKS │ ↓ Deployment │ ↓ Pods │ ↓ Service │ ↓ Load Balancer │ ↓ Internet ``` Infrastructure: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS ├── VPC ├── Subnets ├── EKS ├── RDS ├── S3 ├── IAM └── Load Balancer ``` Monitoring: ```text Pods ↓ Logs + Metrics + Traces ↓ Observability ``` We'll make that connection much deeper in Chapters [21](../06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md)–[23](../08-production/ch23-production-architecture-troubleshooting.md). ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: PART 18 — WHAT YOU SHOULD KNOW FOR SWE INTERVIEWS
text: At this point, you should be able to explain:

text: ```text What is Kubernetes? Why do we need it? Docker vs Kubernetes? What is a cluster? What is a Pod? What is a Deployment? What is a ReplicaSet? What is a Service? ```

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Networking
text: ```text How does a request reach a Pod? Why can't we use Pod IPs directly? What is ClusterIP? What is NodePort? What is LoadBalancer? What is Ingress? What is an Ingress Controller? How does service discovery work? ```

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Scaling
text: ```text How do you scale Pods? What is HPA? What is node autoscaling? Pod scaling vs node scaling? Why do resource requests matter? ```

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Production
text: ```text How do you deploy without downtime? Why is readiness important? How do you handle a crashed Pod? How do you store secrets? How do you persist data? How do you secure Pod-to-Pod traffic? How do Pods access AWS services securely? ```

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Troubleshooting
text: ```text Pending? CrashLoopBackOff? ImagePullBackOff? Service has no endpoints? Readiness failing? HPA not scaling? ``` These are much more valuable than memorizing 100 Kubernetes commands. ---

title: Chapter 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: 32. The Kubernetes Mental Model — FINAL
text: If you remember only one architecture: ```text KUBERNETES CLUSTER │ ┌───────────┴───────────┐ │ │ Control Plane Worker Nodes │ ┌─────┼─────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod Pod Pod │ │ │ └─────┼─────┘ ↑ Service ↑ Ingress ↑ Load Balancer ↑ Internet ``` And: ```text Deployment ↓ maintains replicas ↓ Pods ↓ Service ↓ stable networking ``` And: ```text HPA ↓ more/fewer Pods Node autoscaling ↓ more/fewer worker nodes ``` And: ```text ConfigMap → configuration Secret → sensitive configuration PVC → persistent storage NetworkPolicy → Pod traffic control Probe → health/readiness ``` ---

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Chapter 20 — Revision Sheet: Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md). Goal: understand **how traffic enters the cluster, reaches Pods, how Pods communicate, scale, and how failures/deployments are handled.**

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Request path and discovery
text: `Internet → Load Balancer → Ingress → Service → Pods → RDS/Redis`. - **Pod-to-Pod** traffic works via cluster networking, but Pod IPs are ephemeral → don't hard-code (`10.x.x.2`); use a **Service**. - **Service discovery:** create a Service (`name: redis`, selector `app: redis`, port 6379/targetPort 6379) and the API connects to `redis:6379`. `const redisHost = process.env.REDIS_HOST ?? "redis";` - **Kubernetes DNS:** `redis` → cluster DNS → Redis Service IP → Redis Pods. Same namespace: `redis`. Cross-namespace: `redis.production` (a fuller service DNS structure exists). Service names give stable discovery as Pods change.

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Service types
text: | Type | Use | |---|---| | **ClusterIP** (default) | Inside the cluster: API → Redis, internal worker/service | | **NodePort** | `NodeIP:NodePort → Service → Pods`; learning/certain scenarios, not preferred for production Internet-facing | | **LoadBalancer** | Cloud integration provisions an external LB → Service → Pods |

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Ingress
text: - **Ingress** = HTTP/HTTPS routing rules into the cluster, so you don't need one public LB per service. **Host-based:** `api.example.com → API Service`, `admin.example.com → Admin Service`. **Path-based:** `example.com/api → API Service`, `example.com/admin → Admin Service`. - **Ingress ≠ the implementation.** You need an **Ingress Controller** (NGINX, AWS Load Balancer Controller, Traefik). *Ingress = routing configuration; Ingress Controller = implements it.* (Frequently asked.) On EKS the AWS Load Balancer Controller integrates AWS load balancers with Services/Ingress. - EKS production flow: Route 53 → CloudFront → WAF → AWS Load Balancer → EKS cluster (Node/Pod ×3) → RDS PostgreSQL → Redis.

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: NetworkPolicy
text: Security Groups protect AWS network interfaces; **NetworkPolicy** controls Pod traffic (when the cluster networking implementation enforces it). Example: Frontend → API → Database allowed; Frontend → Database blocked. Defense in depth. ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: { name: allow-api-to-db } spec: podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: database } } policyTypes: [Ingress] ingress: - from: - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } } ```

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Readiness + load balancing
text: Pod B starting (A, C healthy) → readiness fails → not ready → Service doesn't route normal traffic; passes → eligible. Critical in deployments: without readiness, new Pod gets traffic before the app is ready → failed requests.

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Scaling
text: **HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler):** metrics → HPA → desired replicas → Deployment → more/fewer Pods. ```yaml apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: { name: api-hpa } spec: scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api } minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 10 metrics: - type: Resource resource: name: cpu target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } ``` - Needs **Metrics Server** for resource metrics; otherwise HPA has no useful metrics. - HPA uses CPU/memory **relative to the configured resource requests** (so requests matter beyond scheduling — Ch.19). - **HPA creates Pods, not machines.** Not enough node capacity → **node/cluster autoscaling** adds worker nodes (EKS: Managed Node Groups, **Karpenter**). *Pod scaling ≠ node scaling.* Traffic ↑ → HPA → more Pods → no capacity → more Nodes.

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Rolling deployments & rollout commands
text: v1 v1 v1 → v2 v1 v1 → v2 v2 v1 → v2 v2 v2 (readiness probes + Service + Deployment strategy cooperate). ```bash kubectl rollout status deployment/api kubectl rollout history deployment/api kubectl rollout undo deployment/api kubectl rollout restart deployment/api ```

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Other workload objects (awareness)
text: - **PodDisruptionBudget (PDB):** limit voluntary disruptions (e.g. node maintenance) so a level of availability is maintained (don't go 3 → 0). - **Job / CronJob:** one-off or scheduled tasks (database cleanup, report generation, batch processing, scheduled sync): CronJob → Job → Pod → task. - **DaemonSet:** a Pod on each (matching) node — log collection, node monitoring, network agents.

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Security & logging
text: - No AWS access keys in code/images. On EKS use **workload identity**: Pod → AWS workload identity → IAM permissions → AWS service (e.g. API needs S3 → IAM-based identity, not `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` baked into Docker). *Give workloads identities and least-privilege permissions instead of permanent AWS keys inside Pods.* - **Logging:** write JSON to stdout; `kubectl logs <pod>`; production centralises: Pod → stdout → logging agent → central logging (Ch.22).

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Troubleshooting scenarios (high-yield)
text: | Symptom | Investigate | |---|---| | **Pending** | `kubectl describe pod` → Events: insufficient CPU/memory, node selector mismatch, taints/tolerations, PVC issue, scheduling constraints | | **CrashLoopBackOff** | `kubectl logs <pod>`, `kubectl logs <pod> --previous`, `describe`; app crash, missing env var, bad config, DB connection failure, wrong command, failed startup | | **ImagePullBackOff** | wrong image name/tag, private-registry auth, image doesn't exist, registry unavailable (pipeline: Actions → Docker build → ECR → K8s → Pod) | | **Service has no traffic** | `kubectl get svc`, `kubectl get endpoints` (or `endpointslices`), `describe service` — **selector/label mismatch** (`app: api` vs Pod `app: backend`) | | **Port mismatch** | Service `targetPort: 3000` but Node listens on 8080 → connection failure | | **Readiness failing** | wrong path/port, app not ready, DB dependency down, slow startup — understand *why*, don't just raise timeouts | | **HPA doesn't scale** | `kubectl get hpa`, `describe hpa api-hpa`; Metrics Server unavailable, resource requests missing, wrong target, no load, `maxReplicas` reached |

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Final mental models
text: - Cluster: Control Plane + Worker Nodes (Pods) ← Service ← Ingress ← Load Balancer ← Internet. - Deployment maintains replicas → Pods → Service gives stable networking. HPA = more/fewer Pods; node autoscaling = more/fewer nodes. ConfigMap = config; Secret = sensitive config; PVC = persistent storage; NetworkPolicy = Pod traffic control; Probe = health/readiness.

title: Revision 20 — Kubernetes Networking + Scaling + Production
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **HPA scaling formula:** `desiredReplicas = ceil( currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / targetMetricValue )` — e.g. 3 Pods at 90% CPU with target 60% → ceil(3 × 90/60) = 5. HPA also has stabilization windows and conflicts with a hard-coded `replicas` in a re-applied Deployment manifest. `kubectl top pods` needs Metrics Server. - **A complete Ingress** (the chapter only shows the `rules` fragment): ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: { name: api-ingress } spec: ingressClassName: alb # or nginx rules: - host: api.example.com http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: { name: api-service, port: { number: 80 } } ``` - **Gateway API** is the newer, more expressive successor to Ingress; Ingress remains widely used. - **Rolling update tuning:** `strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge` / `maxUnavailable` (default 25% each). - **NetworkPolicy:** by default all Pod traffic is allowed; once a policy selects a Pod, traffic of that type not explicitly allowed is denied; enforcement requires a CNI that supports it (Calico, Cilium, or AWS VPC CNI network policy support). - On EKS the workload-identity mechanisms are **IRSA** (IAM Roles for Service Accounts via OIDC) and **EKS Pod Identity** — see Ch.31. - AWS Load Balancer Controller: Ingress → **ALB**, Service type `LoadBalancer` → **NLB**; target type `ip` routes straight to Pod IPs. - Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter: both add nodes for unschedulable Pods; Karpenter provisions right-sized nodes directly. - Example CronJob: `schedule: "0 2 * * *"` (same cron syntax as Ch.3). - PDB example: `minAvailable: 2` (or `maxUnavailable: 1`) with a `selector` for the Pods. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 19](ch19-revision.md) · [Full chapter 20](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 21](ch21-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
text: > **Source:** Response 21 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-21.txt`, lines 1–2076) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch21-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> This is an important transition in the roadmap. Until now, we've mostly learned: ```text AWS Console / CLI ↓ Create infrastructure ↓ EC2 / VPC / S3 / RDS / EKS ``` But imagine you need to recreate your entire infrastructure tomorrow. You don't want to manually click: ```text Create VPC → Create subnet → Create route table → Create EC2 → Create security group → Create RDS → ... ``` Instead: ```text Terraform code ↓ terraform plan ↓ terraform apply ↓ Infrastructure ``` That's **Infrastructure as Code (IaC)**. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 1. What Is Terraform?
text: Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code tool. You describe the infrastructure you want: ```text "I want a VPC." "I want 2 subnets." "I want an S3 bucket." "I want an EC2 instance." ``` using configuration files. Terraform then creates and manages those resources. The core idea: > **Infrastructure becomes code that can be version-controlled, reviewed, reproduced, and automated.** ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 2. Why Terraform Exists
text: Without IaC: ```text Developer ↓ AWS Console ↓ click click click ↓ Infrastructure ``` Problems: - difficult to reproduce - easy to make manual mistakes - difficult to review changes - difficult to document - difficult to recreate environments - configuration can drift With Terraform: ```text Git ↓ Terraform ↓ AWS ``` You can review infrastructure changes just like application code. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 3. Terraform vs Docker vs Kubernetes
text: This distinction is extremely important.

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Docker
text: Packages/runs applications: ```text Dockerfile ↓ Image ↓ Container ```

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Kubernetes
text: Orchestrates containers: ```text Kubernetes ↓ Pods ↓ Containers ```

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Terraform
text: Creates/manages infrastructure: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS infrastructure ├── VPC ├── EC2 ├── S3 ├── RDS └── EKS ``` So: ```text Terraform → infrastructure Docker → application packaging Kubernetes → container orchestration ``` They complement each other. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 4. Terraform Architecture
text: The basic flow: ```text Terraform Configuration ↓ Terraform CLI ↓ Provider ↓ Cloud API ↓ Infrastructure ``` For AWS: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS Provider ↓ AWS APIs ↓ AWS Resources ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 5. Terraform Configuration
text: Terraform normally uses: ```text .tf ``` files. Example: ```text main.tf variables.tf outputs.tf ``` Terraform uses **HCL** — HashiCorp Configuration Language. It's declarative. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 6. Your First Terraform Program
text: Create: ```text main.tf ``` Example: ```hcl terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "~> 6.0" } } } provider "aws" { region = "ap-south-1" } ``` This says: ```text Use AWS provider Region = Mumbai ``` The exact provider version should be chosen intentionally for your project rather than blindly copying an old tutorial. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 7. Install Terraform
text: After installing Terraform: ```bash terraform version ``` You should get something like: ```text Terraform vX.Y.Z ``` Then create: ```text terraform/ └── main.tf ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 8. Terraform Init
text: Run: ```bash terraform init ``` What happens? Terraform: - initializes the project - downloads required providers - prepares the working directory You should see something similar to: ```text Terraform has been successfully initialized! ``` This is usually the **first Terraform command** you run in a new project. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 9. Terraform Validate
text: Run: ```bash terraform validate ``` This checks whether your Terraform configuration is syntactically and structurally valid. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 10. Terraform Plan
text: Run: ```bash terraform plan ``` This is extremely important. Terraform asks: > What changes would happen if I applied this configuration? Conceptually: ```text Current infrastructure + Terraform configuration ↓ Terraform plan ↓ Proposed changes ``` Example: ```text + create aws_s3_bucket.app ``` `+` generally means create. You may also encounter: ```text ~ update - destroy -/+ replace ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 11. Terraform Apply
text: Then: ```bash terraform apply ``` Terraform shows the proposed changes and normally asks for confirmation. You can approve: ```text yes ``` Terraform then calls the provider APIs. For AWS: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS Provider ↓ AWS API ↓ S3/VPC/EC2/etc. ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 12. Terraform Destroy
text: You can remove resources managed by Terraform: ```bash terraform destroy ``` This is powerful. **Be extremely careful with it in real environments.** For learning infrastructure: ```text terraform apply ↓ build ↓ test ↓ terraform destroy ``` is a great workflow. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 13. Terraform Resource
text: A resource represents something Terraform manages. Example S3 bucket: ```hcl resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app" { bucket = "my-unique-learning-bucket" } ``` Structure: ```text resource ↓ provider resource type ↓ local name ↓ configuration ``` Here: ```text aws_s3_bucket ``` is the resource type. ```text app ``` is Terraform's local name. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 14. Resource Reference
text: Suppose: ```hcl resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app" { bucket = "my-unique-learning-bucket" } ``` Terraform refers to it as: ```text aws_s3_bucket.app ``` Other resources can reference it. Example: ```hcl some_resource { bucket = aws_s3_bucket.app.id } ``` This creates a dependency. Terraform can determine the order in which resources need to be created. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 15. Create an S3 Bucket
text: A minimal learning example: ```hcl resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app" { bucket = "rachit-terraform-learning-example" } ``` Then: ```bash terraform init terraform validate terraform plan terraform apply ``` Check AWS. The bucket should exist. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 16. Terraform State
text: Now we reach one of the **most important Terraform concepts**. After: ```bash terraform apply ``` Terraform creates: ```text terraform.tfstate ``` This is the Terraform **state**. Conceptually: ```text Terraform code ↓ State ↓ Real infrastructure ``` State helps Terraform understand: > "What infrastructure do I currently manage?" ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 17. Why State Exists
text: Suppose Terraform knows: ```text S3 bucket ID = X ``` Your configuration says: ```text S3 bucket should exist ``` Terraform can compare: ```text Desired state vs Known state / real infrastructure ``` and determine what needs to change. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 18. Never Treat State as Disposable Metadata
text: This is important. `terraform.tfstate` may contain sensitive information depending on the resources/configuration. Therefore: ```text ❌ Don't casually commit terraform.tfstate to Git. ``` Add: ```gitignore .terraform/ *.tfstate *.tfstate.* ``` to `.gitignore`. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 19. `.terraform.lock.hcl`
text: Terraform also creates: ```text .terraform.lock.hcl ``` Unlike state, this file is generally useful to commit. It helps lock provider selections/checksums so different environments use consistent provider packages. So: ```text .terraform/ → don't commit terraform.tfstate → don't commit .terraform.lock.hcl → generally commit ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 20. Hardcoding Is Bad
text: Instead of: ```hcl provider "aws" { region = "ap-south-1" } ``` you might want configurable values. Create: ```text variables.tf ``` ```hcl variable "aws_region" { type = string default = "ap-south-1" } ``` Then: ```hcl provider "aws" { region = var.aws_region } ``` Now: ```text var.aws_region ``` references the variable. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 21. Variable Values
text: You can override variables using: ```text terraform.tfvars ``` Example: ```hcl aws_region = "ap-south-1" ``` Or: ```bash terraform apply -var="aws_region=ap-south-1" ``` Don't put sensitive secrets into files that you'll commit. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 22. Variable Types
text: Terraform supports types such as: ```hcl string number bool list set map object ``` Example: ```hcl variable "instance_count" { type = number default = 2 } ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 23. Outputs
text: Suppose Terraform creates an EC2 instance. You may want: ```text Public IP DNS name Resource ID ``` Use outputs. ```hcl output "bucket_name" { value = aws_s3_bucket.app.bucket } ``` Then: ```bash terraform apply ``` Terraform can show: ```text bucket_name = "rachit-terraform-learning-example" ``` You can also retrieve it: ```bash terraform output ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 24. Input vs Output
text: Simple mental model: ```text Variables ↓ Terraform ↓ Infrastructure ↓ Outputs ``` Example: ```text Input: region Output: EC2 public IP ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 5 — DATA SOURCES
text: Terraform can also read information that already exists. For example: ```text Existing AWS VPC Existing AMI Existing subnet ``` Terraform can use **data sources** to query provider information without necessarily creating the object. Conceptually: ```text data ↓ read existing information ``` versus: ```text resource ↓ manage/create infrastructure ``` This distinction is useful in larger Terraform projects. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 6 — DEPENDENCIES
text: Suppose: ```text EC2 ↓ needs ↓ Security Group ``` Terraform can understand explicit/implicit dependencies. Example: ```hcl resource "aws_instance" "app" { ami = "..." instance_type = "t3.micro" security_groups = [ aws_security_group.app.name ] } ``` Terraform sees: ```text Security Group ↓ EC2 ``` and creates them in the appropriate order. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 25. `depends_on`
text: Sometimes Terraform can't infer a dependency. Then: ```hcl depends_on = [ aws_some_resource.example ] ``` can explicitly express it. Don't use `depends_on` everywhere. Prefer natural references when Terraform can infer dependencies. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 7 — FORMATTING
text: Terraform provides: ```bash terraform fmt ``` This formats your Terraform files. Typical workflow: ```bash terraform fmt terraform validate terraform plan ``` Very similar to normal software development tooling. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 8 — LOCALS
text: Terraform supports local values: ```hcl locals { environment = "dev" project = "my-api" } ``` Then: ```hcl tags = { Project = local.project Environment = local.environment } ``` Useful for avoiding repetition. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 9 — MODULES
text: Now imagine your Terraform project grows: ```text VPC EC2 RDS EKS S3 IAM CloudFront ``` Putting everything into one giant `main.tf` becomes messy. Terraform provides: > **Modules** Think: ```text root module │ ├── vpc module ├── ec2 module ├── rds module └── eks module ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 26. Example Module Structure
text: ```text terraform/ │ ├── main.tf ├── variables.tf ├── outputs.tf │ └── modules/ ├── network/ │ ├── main.tf │ ├── variables.tf │ └── outputs.tf │ └── app/ ├── main.tf ├── variables.tf └── outputs.tf ``` This is similar to modular programming. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 27. Module Usage
text: Root: ```hcl module "network" { source = "./modules/network" environment = "dev" } ``` Now: ```text Root Terraform ↓ Network module ↓ VPC/Subnets/etc. ``` Modules become extremely important when infrastructure gets larger. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 10 — ENVIRONMENTS
text: You might have: ```text development staging production ``` You don't want: ```text dev → production infrastructure accidentally ``` A common approach is to maintain separate state/configuration for environments. Possible structures include: ```text environments/ ├── dev/ ├── staging/ └── prod/ ``` or reusable modules with separate environment configurations. The exact structure depends on team conventions. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 28. Terraform Workspaces
text: Terraform also has: ```text terraform workspace ``` which can maintain separate state instances. You should know it exists. But don't think: > "Workspaces are automatically the best way to manage every production environment." Large teams often use separate root configurations/state backends for stronger isolation. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 11 — STATE DRIFT
text: Imagine Terraform says: ```text EC2 type = t3.micro ``` But someone manually changes AWS: ```text EC2 type = t3.medium ``` Now: ```text Terraform configuration ≠ Real infrastructure ``` That's **drift**. Running: ```bash terraform plan ``` can reveal changes Terraform believes are needed to reconcile infrastructure with the configuration. This is one of the biggest reasons IaC is useful. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 29. The Terraform Principle
text: ```text Git ↓ Terraform code ↓ Plan ↓ Review ↓ Apply ↓ Infrastructure ``` Instead of: ```text Someone manually changed production at 2 AM ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 12 — REMOTE STATE
text: Local state: ```text Developer laptop └── terraform.tfstate ``` works for learning. But a team needs shared state. You don't want: ```text Developer A → state on laptop A Developer B → state on laptop B ``` Instead: ```text Terraform State │ ↓ Remote Backend │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ ↓ ↓ Developer A Developer B ``` On AWS, a common pattern uses an S3-backed Terraform state backend. Current Terraform/AWS capabilities also support native S3 state locking; older tutorials often show a separate DynamoDB locking table, so don't blindly copy that older pattern. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 30. Why State Locking?
text: Imagine: ```text Developer A terraform apply ``` at the same time as: ```text Developer B terraform apply ``` Both modifying state simultaneously can cause problems. State locking helps prevent conflicting operations. Mental model: ```text Terraform Apply ↓ Acquire lock ↓ Modify state ↓ Release lock ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 13 — AWS CREDENTIALS
text: This connects directly to [Chapter 9](../04-aws/ch09-aws-fundamentals-iam.md). Don't put: ```text AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY ``` inside: ```text main.tf ❌ Git ❌ Dockerfile ❌ terraform.tfvars committed to Git ❌ ``` Terraform's AWS provider can use standard AWS credential mechanisms. For local development you can use: ```bash aws configure ``` or appropriate AWS credential/environment mechanisms. For CI/CD, prefer: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ OIDC ↓ AWS IAM Role ↓ Temporary credentials ↓ Terraform ``` This is exactly the security model we learned earlier. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 14 — TERRAFORM + GITHUB ACTIONS
text: Now we're getting into **real DevOps**. Your infrastructure can be managed through CI/CD. Example pipeline: ```text Git push ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ terraform fmt ↓ terraform validate ↓ terraform plan ↓ Review/approval ↓ terraform apply ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 31. Basic GitHub Actions Workflow
text: Example: ```yaml name: Terraform on: pull_request: push: branches: - main jobs: terraform: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: id-token: write contents: read steps: - name: Checkout uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Setup Terraform uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3 - name: Terraform Init run: terraform init - name: Terraform Format run: terraform fmt -check - name: Terraform Validate run: terraform validate - name: Terraform Plan run: terraform plan ``` The important thing isn't memorizing this YAML. Understand the workflow: ```text Code ↓ CI ↓ Validate ↓ Plan ↓ Review ↓ Apply ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 32. Should Every PR Automatically Run `terraform apply`?
text: Not necessarily. A safer common pattern is: ```text Pull Request ↓ fmt validate plan ↓ review ↓ merge ↓ controlled apply ``` For production, teams often add: ```text approval permissions environment protection ``` before applying changes. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 15 — REAL TERRAFORM PROJECT
text: Now let's build something closer to your actual stack. Goal: ```text AWS │ ├── VPC │ ├── Public Subnet │ └── Private Subnet │ ├── Security Groups │ ├── EC2 │ ├── S3 │ └── RDS ``` Later this can become: ```text VPC ↓ EKS ↓ Pods ↓ RDS ↓ S3 ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 33. Project Structure
text: Start: ```text infra/ │ ├── main.tf ├── variables.tf ├── outputs.tf ├── terraform.tfvars ├── .gitignore │ └── modules/ ├── network/ ├── compute/ └── database/ ``` Don't try to create the entire production architecture on your first Terraform run. Start small. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Phase 1
text: Create: ```text S3 ``` Learn: ```text provider resource init plan apply destroy state ```

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Phase 2
text: Create: ```text VPC Subnet Route Table Internet Gateway Security Group ``` Learn AWS networking through Terraform.

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Phase 3
text: Create: ```text EC2 ``` Learn: ```text dependencies outputs variables ```

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Phase 4
text: Add: ```text RDS ``` Learn: ```text network dependencies security groups private infrastructure ```

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Phase 5
text: Convert into: ```text modules ```

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Phase 6
text: Add: ```text remote state CI/CD OIDC ``` That's a much better learning progression than copying a 500-line Terraform project. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 16 — TERRAFORM COMMANDS YOU SHOULD KNOW
text: These are worth memorizing: ```bash terraform init ``` Initialize project. ```bash terraform fmt ``` Format code. ```bash terraform validate ``` Validate configuration. ```bash terraform plan ``` Preview changes. ```bash terraform apply ``` Apply changes. ```bash terraform destroy ``` Destroy managed infrastructure. ```bash terraform show ``` Inspect state/current configuration details. ```bash terraform output ``` Show outputs. ```bash terraform state list ``` List resources tracked in state. ```bash terraform state show <resource> ``` Inspect a particular state entry. ```bash terraform import ``` Bring an existing resource under Terraform management. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 35. Terraform Import
text: Suppose someone manually created: ```text S3 bucket ``` and you want Terraform to manage it. You can use: ```bash terraform import ... ``` Conceptually: ```text Existing AWS resource ↓ terraform import ↓ Terraform state ``` But import alone doesn't magically create a perfect configuration file for every resource. You still need to ensure the Terraform configuration correctly represents the desired resource. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Mistake 1 — Hardcoding secrets
text: ```hcl password = "mypassword" ``` ❌ Use appropriate secret-management mechanisms. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Mistake 2 — Committing state
text: ```text terraform.tfstate ``` ❌ It may contain sensitive information. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Mistake 3 — Running apply blindly
text: Always understand: ```bash terraform plan ``` before applying important changes. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Mistake 4 — Manual AWS changes
text: If Terraform owns a resource and someone constantly changes it manually: ```text Terraform ↕ AWS ``` you create drift. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Mistake 5 — Giant Terraform file
text: Avoid: ```text main.tf 5000 lines ``` Use: ```text modules variables outputs environment structure ``` where appropriate. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 18 — TERRAFORM + YOUR ENTIRE DEVOPS STACK
text: Now look at what you've learned. ```text GitHub │ ↓ GitHub Actions / \ / \ ↓ ↓ Application CI Terraform CI │ │ ↓ ↓ Docker AWS APIs │ │ ↓ ↓ ECR Infrastructure │ ┌────┴─────┐ │ ↓ ↓ │ VPC EKS │ │ │ Pods │ │ └─────────────────────┘ ↓ RDS + S3 + Redis ``` This is the **real DevOps picture**. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 19 — WHAT TERRAFORM DOES NOT DO
text: This distinction is very important. Terraform is not: ```text ❌ Docker ❌ Kubernetes ❌ CI/CD ❌ application runtime ❌ monitoring system ``` Instead: ```text Terraform → creates/manages infrastructure ``` For example: ```text Terraform → creates EKS Kubernetes → manages Pods in EKS Docker → builds container images GitHub Actions → runs CI/CD CloudWatch/Prometheus → monitors ``` ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: 36. Terraform vs Ansible
text: You may hear: > "Why Terraform when we have Ansible?" Simplified distinction:

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Terraform
text: Infrastructure provisioning: ```text VPC EC2 RDS EKS S3 ```

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Ansible
text: Configuration/automation on machines: ```text install package configure service copy configuration run commands ``` There can be overlap, and modern immutable/containerized environments reduce the need for traditional server configuration management. For your roadmap: ```text Terraform → deep Ansible → awareness/basic ``` That's intentional. ---

title: Chapter 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: PART 20 — TERRAFORM VS CLOUDFORMATION
text: AWS also has: > CloudFormation Both are Infrastructure as Code approaches. Terraform: ```text multi-cloud / broad provider ecosystem ``` CloudFormation: ```text AWS-native ``` For your SWE interviews, understand the distinction. You don't need to deeply learn both. ---

text: I want you to actually do this.

text: If an interviewer asks: > "How does Terraform work?" You can explain: ```text Terraform Configuration ↓ terraform init ↓ Provider ↓ terraform plan ↓ Compare desired state with tracked/real infrastructure ↓ terraform apply ↓ Cloud APIs ↓ Infrastructure ↓ State updated ``` ---
