title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Chapter 21 — Revision Sheet: Terraform — Infrastructure as Code
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md). Shift: from "I know how to configure AWS/Kubernetes" to "I can **create and manage** the infrastructure using code."

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Why IaC / Terraform
text: Without IaC: Console clicking → hard to reproduce, manual mistakes, hard to review/document/recreate environments, configuration **drift**. With Terraform: **Git → Terraform → AWS**; infra becomes code that is **version-controlled, reviewed, reproduced, automated**. | Tool | Role | |---|---| | **Terraform** | Creates/manages infrastructure (VPC, EC2, S3, RDS, EKS) | | **Docker** | Packages applications (Dockerfile → image → container) | | **Kubernetes** | Orchestrates containers (Pods) | | GitHub Actions | CI/CD | | CloudWatch/Prometheus | Monitoring | | **Ansible** | Configuration/automation on machines (install package, configure service, copy config) — awareness/basic; immutable/containerised environments reduce its need | | **CloudFormation** | AWS-native IaC; Terraform = multi-cloud/broad provider ecosystem | Architecture: **Terraform configuration → Terraform CLI → Provider → Cloud API → Infrastructure** (AWS: Terraform → AWS Provider → AWS APIs → AWS resources). Files: `.tf` (`main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`) in **HCL** (HashiCorp Configuration Language), **declarative**.

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: First program and core commands
text: ```hcl terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 6.0" } } } provider "aws" { region = "ap-south-1" } resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app" { bucket = "my-unique-learning-bucket" } ``` (Choose the provider version intentionally, not from an old tutorial.) | Command | Purpose | |---|---| | `terraform version` | Check install | | `terraform init` | First command in a project: initialise, download providers, prepare directory | | `terraform fmt` | Format code | | `terraform validate` | Syntax/structure check | | `terraform plan` | Preview: current infra + config → proposed changes. `+` create, `~` update in place, `-` destroy, `-/+` replace | | `terraform apply` | Show changes, ask `yes`, call provider APIs | | `terraform destroy` | Remove managed resources — **extreme care in real environments** (great for learning: apply → build → test → destroy) | | `terraform show` | Inspect state/current config | | `terraform output` | Show outputs | | `terraform state list` / `state show <resource>` | List/inspect tracked resources | | `terraform import` | Bring an existing resource under Terraform management (config still must be written correctly) | Typical dev loop: `terraform fmt` → `terraform validate` → `terraform plan`.

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Resources, references, dependencies
text: - `resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app" {…}`: `aws_s3_bucket` = resource type, `app` = local name; referenced as `aws_s3_bucket.app` (e.g. `aws_s3_bucket.app.id`). References create **implicit dependencies** — Terraform orders creation (Security Group → EC2). `depends_on = [...]` is an **explicit** dependency for cases Terraform can't infer — don't overuse. - **Data sources** (`data`) read existing info (existing VPC/AMI/subnet) without creating it; `resource` manages/creates. - **Locals** (`locals { environment = "dev"; project = "my-api" }` → `local.project`) avoid repetition (tags).

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Variables and outputs
text: ```hcl variable "aws_region" { type = string default = "ap-south-1" } provider "aws" { region = var.aws_region } output "bucket_name" { value = aws_s3_bucket.app.bucket } ``` - Override via `terraform.tfvars`, or `terraform apply -var="aws_region=ap-south-1"`. Types: `string`, `number`, `bool`, `list`, `set`, `map`, `object`. Don't commit secrets in tfvars. - Mental model: variables (input) → Terraform → infrastructure → outputs (`terraform output`).

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: State (most important concept)
text: - After `apply`, Terraform writes `terraform.tfstate`: *Terraform code → State → Real infrastructure*; answers "what do I currently manage?" so it can compare desired vs known/real state. - State may contain sensitive data → **don't commit** it. `.gitignore`: `.terraform/`, `*.tfstate`, `*.tfstate.*`. `.terraform.lock.hcl` (provider selections/checksums) **is generally committed**. - **Drift:** someone manually changes AWS (t3.micro → t3.medium) → config ≠ real; `terraform plan` reveals what Terraform would change. A major reason IaC matters. - **Remote state:** teams need shared state (not on laptops) → remote backend, commonly **S3**. **State locking** prevents two simultaneous `apply`s (acquire lock → modify state → release). Current Terraform/AWS also supports **native S3 locking**; older tutorials show a separate DynamoDB lock table — don't blindly copy that.

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Modules and environments
text: - **Modules** (root module + child modules): `module "network" { source = "./modules/network" environment = "dev" }`; layout `modules/network/{main,variables,outputs}.tf`, `modules/app/…`. Avoid a 5,000-line `main.tf`. - **Environments:** `environments/{dev,staging,prod}/` or reusable modules with separate configs. **Workspaces** (`terraform workspace`) keep separate state instances but aren't automatically best for production; large teams often use separate root configs/state backends for stronger isolation.

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Credentials and CI/CD
text: - Never put `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET` in `main.tf`, Git, Dockerfile, committed tfvars. Local: `aws configure`/credential mechanisms. CI: GitHub Actions → **OIDC** → IAM Role → temporary credentials → Terraform. - Pipeline: PR → `fmt`, `validate`, `plan` → review → merge → **controlled apply** (approval, permissions, environment protection). Don't auto-apply every PR. ```yaml name: Terraform on: pull_request: push: { branches: [main] } jobs: terraform: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read } steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3 - run: terraform init - run: terraform fmt -check - run: terraform validate - run: terraform plan ```

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Learning plan and lab
text: Phases: (1) S3 — provider/resource/init/plan/apply/destroy/state → (2) VPC, Subnet, Route Table, IGW, SG → (3) EC2 (dependencies, outputs, variables) → (4) RDS (network dependencies, SGs, private infra) → (5) modules → (6) remote state, CI/CD, OIDC. Project layout `infra/{main,variables,outputs}.tf, terraform.tfvars, .gitignore, modules/{network,compute,database}`. Lab (12 steps): create dir + provider + learning bucket → `init` → `fmt`/`validate` → `plan` (read it!) → `apply` → check AWS → `state list` → `output` → change tags and `plan` → `destroy`.

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Common mistakes
text: 1. Hard-coded secrets (`password = "mypassword"`). 2. Committing state. 3. Running `apply` blindly (read `plan`). 4. Manual AWS changes → drift. 5. Giant Terraform file.

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Explain Terraform in an interview
text: Configuration → `init` (providers) → `plan` (compare desired config with tracked/real infrastructure) → `apply` (cloud APIs create/modify) → state updated.

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Depth guide
text: Deep: IaC, HCL, provider, resource, variables, outputs, dependencies, init/fmt/validate/plan/apply/destroy, state, drift, modules, remote state, locking, secrets, CI/CD. Medium: data sources, locals, workspaces, import, lifecycle rules, dynamic blocks, `for_each`, `count`. Awareness: Terraform Cloud, Terragrunt, Ansible, CloudFormation, Pulumi.

title: Revision 21 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **Code correction:** in the chapter's EC2 example, `security_groups = [aws_security_group.app.name]` is the form for EC2-Classic/default VPC; for an instance in a VPC use `vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.app.id]`. See [Corrections](../CORRECTIONS.md). - The CI workflow above sets `id-token: write` but never configures AWS credentials; add `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` (role-to-assume) before `plan`, and configure a remote backend, otherwise `plan` can't reach AWS/state. - `terraform plan -out=tfplan` + `terraform apply tfplan` guarantees you apply exactly what was reviewed; `apply -auto-approve` skips the prompt (CI only, after an approval gate). - Terraform 1.5+ supports declarative **`import` blocks**; Terraform ≥1.10 supports S3-native locking (`use_lockfile = true` in the `s3` backend) — verify against current docs. - Variable values can also come from `TF_VAR_name` environment variables or `*.auto.tfvars`; mark secrets `sensitive = true` (still stored in state). - `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` protects critical resources; `create_before_destroy`, `ignore_changes` also exist. `count` and `for_each` create multiple instances of a resource (see [Chapter 32](../docs/06-iac-config/ch32-advanced-terraform.md)). - Terraform's licence changed to BSL in 2023; **OpenTofu** is the open-source fork — worth knowing for interviews. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 20](ch20-revision.md) · [Full chapter 21](../docs/06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 22](ch22-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
text: > **Source:** Response 22 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-22.txt`, lines 1–1872) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch22-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We're now at the part of DevOps that answers: > **"My system is running in production. How do I know whether it's healthy, why it's slow, and what do I do when something fails?"** This response ties together almost everything you've learned: ```text Node.js ↓ Docker ↓ Kubernetes ↓ AWS ↓ Database ↓ Monitoring ↓ Alerts ↓ Incident response ``` And again, we're doing this **hands-on**, not just definitions. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 1. What Is Observability?
text: Suppose your production API suddenly becomes slow. Users report: ```text "API is taking 8 seconds." ``` You need to answer: ```text Why? ``` Maybe: ```text CPU is high Memory is exhausted Database is slow Redis is unavailable Network is failing One endpoint is slow External API is slow Too many requests Pod is restarting ``` Observability gives you the information needed to understand what's happening inside the system from its external behavior. The classic three pillars are: ```text OBSERVABILITY │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Logs Metrics Traces ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 2. Logs
text: Logs answer: > **What happened?** Example: ```json { "level": "error", "event": "database_connection_failed", "requestId": "abc123", "timestamp": "2026-09-19T10:30:00Z" } ``` You can inspect them with: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> ``` or: ```bash docker logs <container> ``` or through AWS CloudWatch / a centralized logging platform. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 3. Metrics
text: Metrics answer: > **How much / how often / how long?** Examples: ```text CPU usage Memory usage Request count Request latency Error rate Database connections Queue depth ``` For example: ```text Requests/sec = 850 p95 latency = 240 ms Error rate = 1.8% CPU = 72% ``` Metrics are generally numerical time-series data. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 4. Traces
text: Traces answer: > **Where did this particular request spend its time?** Suppose: ```text POST /orders ``` takes 2 seconds. A trace might show: ```text API │ ├── Authentication 20ms │ ├── Order Service 100ms │ ├── PostgreSQL 1700ms │ └── Response 80ms ``` Now you immediately know: ```text Database = bottleneck ``` rather than randomly optimizing the Node.js code. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 5. Logs vs Metrics vs Traces
text: Remember: | Tool | Main question | |---|---| | Logs | What happened? | | Metrics | How much/how often? | | Traces | Where did the request spend time? | Example: ```text Metrics: p95 latency = 2 seconds Trace: DB query = 1.7 seconds Logs: DB timeout occurred ``` Together they're far more useful than any one alone. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 6. Don't Do This Everywhere
text: Avoid production logging like: ```ts console.log("something happened"); ``` It lacks useful context. Prefer structured logs. For example: ```ts console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: "info", event: "server_started", port, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() })); ``` Now log aggregation systems can parse fields. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 7. Request Logging
text: Conceptually: ```ts console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: "info", event: "request_completed", method: req.method, path: req.path, statusCode: res.statusCode, durationMs, requestId })); ``` Now you can search: ```text requestId = abc123 ``` and follow a request through the system. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 8. Request IDs
text: Suppose: ```text Client ↓ ALB ↓ API Pod ↓ Database ``` A request fails. You want to correlate all relevant logs. Generate/propagate a: ```text requestId ``` Example: ```text abc123 ``` Then: ```text API log → abc123 DB-related log → abc123 worker log → abc123 ``` This is extremely useful when debugging distributed systems. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 9. What NOT to Log
text: Never casually log: ```text ❌ passwords ❌ JWT secrets ❌ API keys ❌ access tokens ❌ database credentials ❌ sensitive personal information ``` Bad: ```ts console.log(process.env.DATABASE_URL); ``` Don't do this. Observability itself must be secure. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 2 — CLOUDWATCH
text: You've already learned CloudWatch in [Chapter 17](../04-aws/ch17-monitoring-security.md). Now understand how it fits into observability. ```text AWS Resources ↓ CloudWatch ├── Metrics ├── Logs ├── Alarms └── Dashboards ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 10. CloudWatch Metrics
text: Examples: ```text EC2 CPUUtilization ALB RequestCount ALB TargetResponseTime RDS CPUUtilization RDS DatabaseConnections Lambda Invocations Lambda Errors ``` You can inspect metrics through AWS tooling. The idea is: ```text System ↓ metric ↓ time series ↓ dashboard / alarm ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 11. CloudWatch Logs
text: Your Node application can produce: ```text stdout/stderr ``` which can be collected into centralized logging. Conceptually: ```text Node.js ↓ Container stdout ↓ Kubernetes logging ↓ Log collector ↓ CloudWatch / log platform ``` Don't rely on one exact collection architecture; it depends on your Kubernetes/AWS setup. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 12. CloudWatch Alarm
text: Suppose: ```text CPU > 80% ``` for a sustained period. Create an alarm: ```text Metric ↓ Threshold ↓ Alarm ↓ Notification / action ``` Example concept: ```text Average CPU > 80% for 5 minutes ``` Then trigger: ```text SNS notification ``` or another appropriate response mechanism. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 3 — PROMETHEUS
text: Now we move into cloud-native observability. > **Prometheus is a monitoring and metrics system widely used in Kubernetes environments.** Mental model: ```text Application ↓ Metrics ↓ Prometheus ↓ Queries ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 13. Prometheus Pull Model
text: A key thing to know: Prometheus commonly **scrapes** metrics from targets. For example: ```text Prometheus │ ├── scrape API ├── scrape Kubernetes ├── scrape node └── scrape services ``` Your application can expose a metrics endpoint such as: ```text /metrics ``` Prometheus periodically retrieves it. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 14. Node.js Metrics
text: Conceptually: ```text GET /metrics ``` might expose: ```text http_requests_total http_request_duration_seconds process_cpu_seconds_total ``` Prometheus then stores those metrics as time series. In a Node.js project, libraries such as `prom-client` are commonly used to expose Prometheus metrics. Example: ```ts import client from "prom-client"; client.collectDefaultMetrics(); const httpRequests = new client.Counter({ name: "http_requests_total", help: "Total HTTP requests" }); ``` Then increment: ```ts httpRequests.inc(); ``` You expose: ```text /metrics ``` and Prometheus scrapes it. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 15. Why Metrics Matter
text: Suppose you see: ```text http_requests_total ``` increasing rapidly. That tells you traffic is increasing. But more useful is something like: ```text request rate error rate latency ``` which leads us to an important framework. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 4 — RED METHOD
text: For request-driven services, remember: > **RED** ```text R → Rate E → Errors D → Duration ```

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Rate
text: How many requests? ```text 1000 requests/sec ```

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Errors
text: How many fail? ```text 2% 5xx ```

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Duration
text: How long do requests take? ```text p95 = 250ms ``` For a backend API, this is an extremely useful monitoring framework. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 16. Percentiles
text: Don't only look at average latency. Suppose: ```text Requests: 10ms 20ms 20ms 30ms 3000ms ``` Average might hide the bad experience. Use percentiles: ```text p50 p90 p95 p99 ``` For example: ```text p50 = 40ms p95 = 250ms p99 = 900ms ``` Meaning approximately: ```text 95% of requests are at or below 250ms 99% are at or below 900ms ``` Percentiles are very important in production systems. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 5 — GRAFANA
text: Prometheus is primarily the metrics collection/query system. Grafana is commonly used for visualization and dashboards. ```text Prometheus ↓ Grafana ↓ Dashboard ``` Example dashboard: ```text ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │ API Requests/sec 850 │ ├─────────────────────────────────┤ │ Error Rate 0.8% │ ├─────────────────────────────────┤ │ P95 Latency 210ms │ ├─────────────────────────────────┤ │ CPU 65% │ ├─────────────────────────────────┤ │ Memory 72% │ └─────────────────────────────────┘ ``` You can visually detect incidents quickly. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 17. Grafana Is Not Prometheus
text: Common interview question. ```text Prometheus → collects/stores/queries metrics Grafana → visualizes data and creates dashboards ``` Grafana can also connect to other data sources, so it isn't limited to Prometheus. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 6 — OPENTELEMETRY
text: Now traces become more practical. > **OpenTelemetry (OTel)** is a vendor-neutral framework/ecosystem for generating and collecting telemetry such as traces, metrics, and logs. Mental model: ```text Node.js ↓ OpenTelemetry ↓ Telemetry backend ``` Instead of tightly coupling your application to one observability vendor. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 18. Distributed Tracing
text: Imagine: ```text User ↓ API ↓ Order Service ↓ Payment Service ↓ PostgreSQL ``` One request: ```text traceId = abc ``` contains spans: ```text Trace abc │ ├── API 20ms ├── Order Service 80ms ├── Payment Service 400ms └── PostgreSQL 50ms ``` Now you can identify: ```text Payment Service ``` as the slow component. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 19. Trace vs Log
text: Logs: ```text "Payment request failed" ``` Trace: ```text Request ↓ API 20ms ↓ Order 80ms ↓ Payment 400ms ❌ ``` Traces give you **request-level causal context**. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 7 — SLI / SLO / SLA
text: This is important for interviews.

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 20. SLI
text: **Service Level Indicator** A measurement. Example: ```text API availability = 99.95% ``` or: ```text p95 latency = 180ms ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 21. SLO
text: **Service Level Objective** A target. Example: ```text 99.9% successful requests ``` or: ```text p95 latency < 300ms ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 22. SLA
text: **Service Level Agreement** A formal agreement/commitment, typically between a service provider and customer, potentially including consequences if commitments aren't met. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 23. Easy Mental Model
text: ```text SLI → What did we measure? SLO → What target do we want? SLA → What commitment/agreement exists with customers? ``` Example: ```text SLI: 99.95% availability SLO: ≥99.9% SLA: Formal customer commitment ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 8 — ERROR BUDGET
text: If your SLO is: ```text 99.9% availability ``` then you're allowing: ```text 0.1% ``` of unavailability/error budget over the relevant period. Conceptually: ```text SLO ↓ Allowed failure ↓ Error budget ``` If your service is consuming the error budget too quickly, engineering teams may prioritize reliability work over risky releases. This is a major SRE concept. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 9 — ALERTING
text: A common beginner mistake: ```text CPU > 50% ↓ ALERT! ``` This can create noisy alerts. Better alerts are tied to meaningful user impact or sustained risk. For example: ```text 5xx error rate > 5% for 5 minutes ``` or: ```text p95 latency > 1 second for 10 minutes ``` depending on the service's actual SLOs. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 24. Alert Quality
text: A good alert should ideally answer: ```text What is wrong? How serious is it? Who needs to act? What should they check? ``` Bad: ```text CPU high ``` Better: ```text API 5xx rate > 5% for 5 minutes. Check ALB → Pods → RDS. ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 10 — RELIABILITY
text: Observability tells you: > Something is wrong. Reliability engineering asks: > How do we design the system so failures are handled safely? This is where resilience patterns matter. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 25. Timeouts
text: Imagine: ```text API ↓ Payment Service ``` Payment service never responds. Without timeout: ```text API request ↓ waiting... ↓ waiting... ↓ waiting... ``` Eventually resources get exhausted. With timeout: ```text Request ↓ wait 2 seconds ↓ timeout ↓ fail gracefully ``` Every network call should have a sensible timeout. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 26. Retries
text: Suppose: ```text API → external service ``` fails due to a transient network problem. Retry: ```text Attempt 1 ❌ Attempt 2 ❌ Attempt 3 ✅ ``` But retries can make things worse. Imagine: ```text 1000 requests ↓ each retries 3 times ↓ 3000 requests ``` Now the already-overloaded service gets even more traffic. This is called a **retry storm**. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 27. Exponential Backoff
text: Instead of: ```text retry immediately retry immediately retry immediately ``` use increasing delays. Example: ```text 100ms 200ms 400ms 800ms ``` Often with **jitter** to avoid many clients retrying simultaneously. Conceptually: ```text failure ↓ wait ↓ retry ↓ wait longer ↓ retry ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 28. Idempotency
text: This connects to your earlier SQS/Lambda learning. Suppose: ```text POST /payment ``` is sent. Network timeout happens. Client doesn't know whether payment succeeded. It retries. Now you could accidentally charge twice. Use an: ```text Idempotency-Key ``` Example: ```text payment request Idempotency-Key: abc123 ``` Server records: ```text abc123 → payment result ``` If the same request arrives again: ```text abc123 ``` return the previous result instead of creating another payment. This is extremely important in production backend systems. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 11 — CIRCUIT BREAKER
text: Suppose: ```text API ↓ Payment Service ``` Payment Service is completely down. Without protection: ```text 1000 API requests ↓ 1000 calls to broken service ↓ timeouts ↓ retries ↓ more load ``` A circuit breaker can stop repeatedly calling a failing dependency. Conceptually: ```text Healthy ↓ Failures increase ↓ OPEN ↓ Stop calls ↓ Wait ↓ Half-open ↓ Test request ↓ Healthy → CLOSED ``` States: ```text CLOSED OPEN HALF-OPEN ``` Know these three. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 29. Circuit Breaker
text: ```text Payment Service ↑ │ API → Circuit Breaker │ ├── healthy → call │ └── open → fail fast ``` This protects both systems. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 12 — BULKHEAD
text: Imagine one service has several dependency pools. If one dependency consumes all available resources: ```text Payment calls ████████████████ ``` it shouldn't necessarily starve: ```text User calls ``` Bulkhead isolation separates resource pools so one failure doesn't consume everything. Think: > **Contain the blast radius.** ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 30. Rate Limiting
text: Suppose: ```text Normal traffic: 100 requests/sec ``` Suddenly: ```text 10,000 requests/sec ``` Your service might collapse. Rate limiting can enforce: ```text 100 requests/sec per client ``` or another appropriate policy. Possible locations: ```text CloudFront WAF API Gateway Load balancer layer Application Redis-based distributed limiter ``` depending on architecture. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 13 — GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN
text: This is particularly relevant to Node.js + Kubernetes. Suppose Kubernetes wants to terminate a Pod. Don't immediately kill the process while requests are running. Your application should handle signals such as: ```text SIGTERM ``` Conceptually: ```ts process.on("SIGTERM", async () => { console.log("Shutting down"); server.close(); await databasePool.end(); process.exit(0); }); ``` The exact implementation depends on your HTTP framework and infrastructure. The goal: ```text Stop accepting new work ↓ Finish/close existing work ↓ Close resources ↓ Exit ``` This is important during: - rolling deployments - node maintenance - scaling - Pod termination ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 14 — KUBERNETES + RELIABILITY
text: Now combine [Chapter 20](../05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md) and this response. ```text Deployment ↓ multiple Pods ↓ Readiness Probe ↓ only ready Pods receive traffic ``` If one Pod dies: ```text Deployment ↓ replacement Pod ``` If traffic increases: ```text HPA ↓ more Pods ``` If a node fails: ```text scheduler ↓ Pods can be recreated/rescheduled ``` If application is overloaded: ```text HPA + resource limits + rate limiting ``` If dependency fails: ```text timeout + retry/backoff + circuit breaker ``` This is reliability engineering. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 15 — PRACTICAL NODE.JS OBSERVABILITY
text: Let's build a simplified production-style setup. Your API: ```text Node.js ``` should expose: ```text /health /ready /metrics ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: `/health`
text: Answers: > Is the application process alive? Example: ```ts app.get("/health", (_req, res) => { res.status(200).json({ status: "ok" }); }); ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: `/ready`
text: Answers: > Can I serve traffic? Example concept: ```ts app.get("/ready", async (_req, res) => { try { await pool.query("SELECT 1"); res.status(200).json({ status: "ready" }); } catch { res.status(503).json({ status: "not_ready" }); } }); ``` Don't make readiness checks excessively expensive. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 31. `/metrics`
text: Using a Prometheus client library: ```ts import client from "prom-client"; client.collectDefaultMetrics(); app.get("/metrics", async (_req, res) => { res.set("Content-Type", client.register.contentType); res.end(await client.register.metrics()); }); ``` Now: ```text GET /metrics ``` returns metrics that Prometheus can scrape. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 32. Local Observability Architecture
text: Conceptually: ```text Node.js API / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ Logs Metrics Traces │ │ │ ↓ ↓ ↓ Logger Prometheus OTel │ ↓ Grafana ``` A production setup can be significantly more sophisticated, but this is the correct mental model. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 16 — INCIDENT RESPONSE
text: Observability is useless if you don't know how to respond. Suppose: ```text ALERT: API 5xx rate = 8% ``` Don't immediately restart everything. Use a structured process. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 33. Incident Debugging Flow
text: ```text ALERT ↓ Confirm impact ↓ Check metrics ↓ Check recent deployments ↓ Check logs ↓ Trace failing requests ↓ Identify dependency ↓ Mitigate ↓ Verify recovery ↓ Root-cause analysis ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 34. Example Incident
text: Suppose: ```text 5xx ↑ ``` First: ```text ALB 5xx? ``` Then: ```text Pod errors? ``` Then: ```text RDS connections? ``` Maybe you discover: ```text RDS connections = 1000/1000 ``` Then: ```text API Pods increased ↓ each Pod created too many DB connections ↓ RDS connection exhaustion ↓ requests fail ``` This connects directly to the RDS scaling scenario from [Chapter 13](../04-aws/ch13-rds-databases.md). ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: 35. Another Incident
text: ```text p95 latency ↑ ``` Metrics: ```text CPU normal Memory normal ``` Trace: ```text API 20ms Redis 1500ms DB 30ms ``` Conclusion: ```text Redis dependency is slow. ``` Now investigate Redis rather than randomly scaling API Pods. That's the value of observability. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 17 — RELIABILITY CHECKLIST
text: For your Node.js production service: ```text Application ├── structured logs ├── request IDs ├── metrics ├── tracing ├── /health ├── /ready └── graceful shutdown Networking ├── timeouts ├── rate limiting └── retries with backoff Dependencies ├── connection pooling ├── circuit breakers where appropriate └── idempotency for retry-sensitive operations Kubernetes ├── readiness probes ├── liveness probes ├── resource requests ├── resource limits ├── HPA └── rolling deployments AWS ├── CloudWatch ├── alarms ├── CloudTrail └── load balancer metrics ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: PART 18 — IMPORTANT TRADEOFF
text: Reliability isn't: > "Add every resilience mechanism." For example: ```text Retry + Circuit breaker + Timeout + Queue + Cache + Rate limiter + Proxy + Service mesh ``` can create a massively complicated system. Instead: > **Use the simplest mechanism that solves the actual failure mode.** Example: ```text External API ↓ 5 second timeout + bounded retry + exponential backoff ``` may be enough. You don't automatically need a service mesh. ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Observability
text: You should comfortably explain: ```text Logs vs metrics vs traces Prometheus Grafana OpenTelemetry CloudWatch structured logging request IDs percentiles RED method ```

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Reliability
text: Know: ```text timeouts retries exponential backoff jitter idempotency circuit breaker bulkhead rate limiting graceful shutdown health checks ```

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: SRE concepts
text: Know: ```text SLI SLO SLA error budget incident response ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: The Complete Mental Model
text: You now have: ```text PRODUCTION SYSTEM │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Logs Metrics Traces │ │ │ └─────────────┼─────────────┘ ↓ Observability │ ↓ Detection │ ↓ Investigation │ ↓ Mitigation │ ↓ Recovery │ ↓ Root Cause Analysis ``` And reliability: ```text FAILURE │ ┌─────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Timeout Retry Circuit Breaker │ │ │ └─────────┼──────────┘ ↓ Graceful failure ↓ System survives ``` ---

title: Chapter 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Your Full DevOps Stack Is Now Almost Complete
text: Look at what you can now connect: ```text Developer │ ↓ Git │ ↓ GitHub │ ↓ GitHub Actions │ ├── Test ├── Build ├── Docker └── Terraform │ ↓ AWS │ ┌──────┼────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ VPC EKS RDS │ Kubernetes │ ┌──┴───┐ ↓ ↓ Pods Services │ ↓ App │ ┌────┼─────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Redis RDS S3 ↓ Observability ┌─────┼─────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Logs Metrics Traces │ │ │ └─────┼─────┘ ↓ Dashboards ↓ Alerts ↓ Incident Response ``` That's a **very solid SWE-level Cloud + DevOps foundation**. <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 21: Terraform: Infrastructure as Code](../06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md) · [Chapter 23: Production Architecture + Troubleshooting](../08-production/ch23-production-architecture-troubleshooting.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch22-revision.md)

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Chapter 22 — Revision Sheet: Observability + Reliability
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md). Question: *"My system is in production. How do I know it's healthy, why it's slow, and what do I do when it fails?"*

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Three pillars
text: | Pillar | Answers | Example | |---|---|---| | **Logs** | What happened? | `{"level":"error","event":"database_connection_failed","requestId":"abc123","timestamp":…}` (via `kubectl logs`, `docker logs`, CloudWatch/central logging) | | **Metrics** | How much / how often / how long? (numeric time series) | CPU, memory, request count/latency, error rate, DB connections, queue depth: "850 req/s, p95 240 ms, error rate 1.8%, CPU 72%" | | **Traces** | Where did *this request* spend its time? | `POST /orders` 2 s: Auth 20 ms, Order Service 100 ms, **PostgreSQL 1700 ms**, Response 80 ms → DB is the bottleneck | Together: metrics say p95 = 2 s → trace says DB query = 1.7 s → logs say DB timeout occurred.

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Logging in Node.js
text: - Avoid bare `console.log("something happened")`. Use structured JSON (`level`, `event`, `port`, `timestamp`). - **Request logging:** `level, event:"request_completed", method, path, statusCode, durationMs, requestId`. - **Request ID:** generate/propagate `requestId` (Client → ALB → API Pod → DB/worker logs) to correlate a failing request across services. - **Never log:** passwords, JWT secrets, API keys, access tokens, DB credentials, sensitive personal data (e.g. never `console.log(process.env.DATABASE_URL)`). Observability itself must be secure.

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: CloudWatch (recap, Ch.17)
text: Metrics (EC2 `CPUUtilization`, ALB `RequestCount`/`TargetResponseTime`, RDS `CPUUtilization`/`DatabaseConnections`, Lambda `Invocations`/`Errors`), Logs (container stdout → logging collector → CloudWatch; architecture depends on K8s/AWS setup), Alarms (Average CPU > 80% for 5 min → SNS notification or other action), Dashboards.

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry
text: - **Prometheus:** metrics collection/storage/query system common in Kubernetes. **Pull model:** it **scrapes** targets (API, Kubernetes, nodes, services) — your app exposes `/metrics`. ```ts import client from "prom-client"; client.collectDefaultMetrics(); const httpRequests = new client.Counter({ name: "http_requests_total", help: "Total HTTP requests" }); httpRequests.inc(); app.get("/metrics", async (_req, res) => { res.set("Content-Type", client.register.contentType); res.end(await client.register.metrics()); }); ``` Typical metrics: `http_requests_total`, `http_request_duration_seconds`, `process_cpu_seconds_total`. - **Grafana:** visualisation/dashboards (can use many data sources, not only Prometheus). **Prometheus = collects/stores/queries; Grafana = visualises.** - **OpenTelemetry (OTel):** vendor-neutral framework for generating/collecting traces, metrics, logs (Node.js → OTel → telemetry backend; avoids vendor lock-in). - **Distributed tracing:** one request has a `traceId` and multiple **spans** (API 20 ms, Order Service 80 ms, Payment Service 400 ms ❌, PostgreSQL 50 ms) → find the slow component. Traces give request-level causal context (logs say "Payment request failed"). - Local architecture: Node API → Logs (logger) / Metrics (Prometheus → Grafana) / Traces (OTel).

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: RED method and percentiles
text: - **RED** (request-driven services): **R**ate (1000 req/s) · **E**rrors (2% 5xx) · **D**uration (p95 = 250 ms). - **Percentiles, not just averages:** requests 10, 20, 20, 30, **3000 ms** — the average hides the bad experience. p50/p90/p95/p99: e.g. p50 40 ms, p95 250 ms (95% of requests ≤ 250 ms), p99 900 ms.

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: SLI / SLO / SLA and error budget
text: | | Meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **SLI** | What did we measure? | availability 99.95%; p95 latency 180 ms | | **SLO** | Target | ≥ 99.9% successful requests; p95 < 300 ms | | **SLA** | Formal customer commitment, possibly with consequences if missed | | **Error budget:** SLO 99.9% allows **0.1%** unavailability over the period → SLO → allowed failure → error budget. If it's consumed too quickly, teams prioritise reliability work over risky releases (major SRE concept; deep dive in Ch.34).

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Alerting
text: - Bad: `CPU > 50%` → ALERT (noisy). Better: tied to user impact/sustained risk, e.g. `5xx error rate > 5% for 5 minutes`, `p95 latency > 1 second for 10 minutes` (depending on SLOs). - A good alert says: what's wrong, how serious, who acts, what to check. Bad: "CPU high". Better: "API 5xx rate > 5% for 5 minutes. Check ALB → Pods → RDS."

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Reliability patterns
text: | Pattern | Idea | |---|---| | **Timeouts** | Every network call needs one (without: requests wait forever and exhaust resources); e.g. wait 2 s then fail gracefully | | **Retries** | Recover transient failures, but **retry storm** risk: 1000 requests × 3 retries = 3000 requests onto an already-overloaded service | | **Exponential backoff + jitter** | 100 → 200 → 400 → 800 ms, with randomness so clients don't retry simultaneously | | **Idempotency** | `Idempotency-Key: abc123` → server records `abc123 → result`; same request again returns the stored result (no double charge on `POST /payment`) | | **Circuit breaker** | Healthy (**CLOSED**) → failures increase → **OPEN** (stop calls, fail fast) → wait → **HALF-OPEN** (test request) → healthy → CLOSED. Protects both systems | | **Bulkhead** | Separate resource pools so a failing dependency (payment calls) can't starve others (user calls) — contain the blast radius | | **Rate limiting** | e.g. 100 req/s per client; at CloudFront, WAF, API Gateway, load balancer, application, Redis-based distributed limiter | | **Graceful shutdown** | On SIGTERM: stop accepting new work → finish/close existing work → close resources → exit | ```ts process.on("SIGTERM", async () => { console.log("Shutting down"); server.close(); await databasePool.end(); process.exit(0); }); ``` Matters during rolling deployments, node maintenance, scaling, Pod termination. **Kubernetes + reliability:** multiple Pods + readiness probe (only ready Pods get traffic); Pod dies → replacement; traffic ↑ → HPA; node fails → scheduler recreates Pods; overload → HPA + limits + rate limiting; dependency failure → timeout + retry/backoff + circuit breaker. **Trade-off:** don't add every mechanism (retry + breaker + timeout + queue + cache + limiter + proxy + service mesh) — use the simplest mechanism that solves the failure mode (e.g. 5 s timeout + bounded retry + exponential backoff may be enough; you don't automatically need a service mesh).

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Endpoints to implement
text: `/health` (process alive → `{status:"ok"}`), `/ready` (e.g. `await pool.query("SELECT 1")` → 200 `ready`, else 503 `not_ready`; keep it cheap), `/metrics` (Prometheus).

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Incident response flow
text: ALERT → confirm impact → check metrics → check recent deployments → check logs → trace failing requests → identify dependency → mitigate → verify recovery → root-cause analysis. (Don't immediately restart everything.) - *5xx rate 8%:* ALB 5xx? → Pod errors? → RDS connections = 1000/1000 ⇒ API Pods increased, each created too many DB connections ⇒ RDS connection exhaustion (Ch.13). - *p95 latency ↑, CPU/memory normal:* trace API 20 ms, **Redis 1500 ms**, DB 30 ms ⇒ investigate Redis instead of randomly scaling API Pods.

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Reliability checklist
text: Application: structured logs, request IDs, metrics, tracing, `/health`, `/ready`, graceful shutdown · Networking: timeouts, rate limiting, retries with backoff · Dependencies: pooling, circuit breakers where appropriate, idempotency · Kubernetes: readiness, liveness, requests, limits, HPA, rolling deployments · AWS: CloudWatch, alarms, CloudTrail, LB metrics.

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Interview checklist
text: Observability: logs vs metrics vs traces, Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, CloudWatch, structured logging, request IDs, percentiles, RED. Reliability: timeouts, retries, backoff, jitter, idempotency, circuit breaker, bulkhead, rate limiting, graceful shutdown, health checks. SRE: SLI, SLO, SLA, error budget, incident response.

title: Revision 22 — Observability + Reliability
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - **Error-budget arithmetic:** `budget = (1 − SLO) × period`. For a 30-day month (43,200 min): 99% → 432 min (7.2 h); 99.9% → **43.2 min**; 99.99% → 4.32 min. - **Backoff formula:** `delay = min(cap, base × 2^attempt)`, then add jitter (e.g. "full jitter": random between 0 and that delay). - Prometheus extras: query language **PromQL**, **Alertmanager** routes alerts, **exporters** expose metrics for systems you can't instrument; latency is best recorded as a **histogram** (`http_request_duration_seconds`) so percentiles can be computed — averaging per-instance percentiles is incorrect. - Trace context is propagated between services via headers (W3C `traceparent`); OTel spans share a `traceId`. - Google SRE's **four golden signals**: latency, traffic, errors, saturation (RED + saturation); the **USE** method (utilization, saturation, errors) targets resources (see [Chapter 34](../docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md)). - Graceful shutdown in Kubernetes also depends on `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` and often a `preStop` delay so the Pod is removed from Service endpoints before the process stops; `server.close()` stops new connections but in-flight keep-alive connections may linger. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 21](ch21-revision.md) · [Full chapter 22](../docs/07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 23](ch23-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
text: > **Source:** Response 23 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-23.txt`, lines 1–1924) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch23-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> This is the **integration response**. You've learned the individual pieces. Now we're going to think like a backend/SWE engineer who is responsible for getting an application from: ```text Code ↓ GitHub ↓ CI/CD ↓ Docker ↓ AWS ↓ Production ``` and keeping it alive when things go wrong. The goal is **not** to memorize one architecture. The goal is to understand **why each component exists and what you would change when requirements change.** ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 1. Our Production Application
text: Let's use a realistic application: > **TypeScript + Node.js backend API** Suppose it provides: ```text POST /users POST /orders GET /orders/:id POST /payments POST /files ``` Technologies: ```text TypeScript Node.js PostgreSQL Redis Docker AWS Kubernetes Terraform GitHub Actions ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 2. Complete Production Architecture
text: Here's the architecture we'll reason through: ```text INTERNET │ ↓ Route 53 │ ↓ CloudFront │ ↓ WAF │ ↓ Load Balancer │ ↓ EKS / Kubernetes │ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod A Pod B Pod C │ │ │ └───────────┼───────────┘ │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Redis RDS S3 PostgreSQL ``` Supporting infrastructure: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Docker Build ↓ ECR ↓ EKS ``` Infrastructure: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS ├── VPC ├── Subnets ├── IAM ├── EKS ├── RDS ├── S3 └── Load Balancer ``` Observability: ```text Application ├── Logs ├── Metrics └── Traces ↓ Observability platform ↓ Dashboards ↓ Alerts ``` Now let's understand why. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 3. VPC
text: Our AWS environment starts with: ```text VPC ``` Example: ```text 10.0.0.0/16 ``` Inside: ```text VPC │ ├── Public Subnets │ └── Private Subnets ``` Across multiple Availability Zones: ```text VPC ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ AZ-A AZ-B │ │ Public subnet Public subnet Private subnet Private subnet ``` Multiple AZs improve availability. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 4. What Goes Where?
text: A simplified production arrangement: ```text Public ├── Load Balancer └── NAT Gateway Private ├── EKS worker capacity ├── RDS └── internal services ``` You don't want your database directly exposed to the public Internet. So: ```text Internet ❌ ↓ RDS ``` Instead: ```text Internet ↓ Load Balancer ↓ EKS ↓ RDS ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 5. Security Group Architecture
text: Think in terms of allowed flows. ```text Internet │ │ HTTPS :443 ↓ ALB Security Group │ │ application traffic ↓ EKS/API Security Group │ │ PostgreSQL :5432 ↓ RDS Security Group ``` Conceptually: ```text Internet → ALB ALB → API API → RDS API → Redis ``` But: ```text Internet → RDS ❌ ``` This is **least privilege at the network level**. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 6. Route 53
text: User enters: ```text https://api.example.com ``` DNS needs to determine where the request goes. Conceptually: ```text api.example.com ↓ Route 53 ↓ CloudFront / Load Balancer ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 7. TLS
text: The user should communicate over: ```text HTTPS ``` not: ```text HTTP ``` TLS protects the connection in transit. AWS services such as ACM can manage certificates for appropriate AWS-integrated endpoints. So: ```text Client ↓ HTTPS Edge/load-balancing layer ↓ Application ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 8. CloudFront
text: For cacheable content: ```text User ↓ CloudFront Edge ↓ Origin ``` Good candidates include: ```text images JavaScript CSS static files ``` Don't blindly cache: ```text POST /payment GET /account private user-specific responses ``` Caching strategy depends on the application's semantics. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 9. WAF
text: WAF can inspect HTTP requests and apply rules. For example: ```text Internet ↓ WAF ↓ Application ``` Possible protections include: ```text rate limiting managed attack rules IP-based rules request filtering ``` WAF is one layer of defense. It's not a replacement for: ```text IAM Security Groups application authorization input validation ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 10. Load Balancer
text: Suppose: ```text 3 Pods ``` We don't want the user to know their individual IP addresses. Traffic goes through a stable entry point: ```text Client ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Kubernetes networking ↓ Pods ``` The load-balancing layer distributes requests across eligible healthy backends. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 11. Health Checks
text: Suppose: ```text Pod A → healthy Pod B → unhealthy Pod C → healthy ``` The routing layer should avoid sending normal traffic to unhealthy backends. This is why we learned: ```text /health /ready ``` Earlier. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 12. EKS
text: AWS manages the Kubernetes control-plane service through: ```text EKS ``` Your workloads run as Kubernetes workloads. Conceptually: ```text EKS │ ├── Node │ ├── Pod │ └── Pod │ ├── Node │ ├── Pod │ └── Pod │ └── Node └── Pod ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 13. Deployment
text: Our API might use: ```yaml replicas: 3 ``` So: ```text Deployment ↓ 3 Pods ``` If one dies: ```text 3 desired 2 actual ↓ replacement ↓ 3 actual ``` That's self-healing. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 14. Kubernetes Service
text: Our API Pods are behind a Service: ```text Load Balancer ↓ Service ↓ ┌────┼────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod Pod Pod ``` The Service provides stable discovery while Pods remain replaceable. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 15. Configuration
text: We don't bake production configuration into our Docker image. Instead: ```text ConfigMap ↓ Pod Secret / external secret system ↓ Pod ``` Application: ```ts const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000); const databaseUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL; ``` Same application image can run in: ```text development staging production ``` with different configuration. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 16. RDS PostgreSQL
text: Our API needs relational data. Use: ```text RDS PostgreSQL ``` rather than making your API container responsible for database persistence. Architecture: ```text API Pods │ ↓ RDS PostgreSQL ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 17. Connection Pooling
text: Suppose: ```text 10 API Pods ``` and each creates: ```text 100 DB connections ``` Potentially: ```text 10 × 100 = 1000 connections ``` Your database may not support that workload. So connection pooling and appropriate pool sizing matter. This is a classic production scaling problem. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 18. Redis
text: Redis can be used for things such as: ```text caching sessions rate limiting short-lived state queues ``` Example: ```text Request ↓ API ↓ Redis ↓ cache hit ``` instead of: ```text Request ↓ API ↓ RDS ``` every time. But don't cache everything. Caching introduces: ```text invalidation consistency memory TTL failure ``` tradeoffs. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 7 — S3
text: Suppose users upload: ```text profile.jpg invoice.pdf video.mp4 ``` Don't put large objects directly inside PostgreSQL. Use: ```text S3 ``` Architecture: ```text User ↓ API ↓ S3 ``` Often the backend can generate a presigned URL: ```text Backend ↓ Presigned URL ↓ Client ↓ S3 ``` This can reduce unnecessary application-server bandwidth. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 19. Application Image
text: Our Node application gets packaged: ```text Dockerfile ↓ Docker image ``` Example production structure: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 AS build WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build FROM node:22-slim WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist USER node EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] ``` Important production principles: ```text multi-stage build small runtime image production dependencies non-root user no secrets in image ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 20. Image Registry
text: We don't expect every Kubernetes node to have the image already. Push it to: ```text ECR ``` Flow: ```text Docker build ↓ ECR ↓ EKS ↓ Pod ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 21. GitHub Actions
text: Developer: ```bash git push ``` Pipeline: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ├── checkout ├── npm ci ├── lint ├── typecheck ├── tests ├── build ├── Docker build ├── Docker scan └── push image ``` Then deployment proceeds through the chosen deployment mechanism. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 22. Image Tagging
text: Don't rely only on: ```text latest ``` Prefer immutable/versioned identifiers. For example: ```text my-api:8f31a7c ``` where the identifier corresponds to a Git commit. Then: ```text Git commit ↓ Docker image ↓ ECR ↓ Kubernetes ``` You can determine exactly what code is running. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 23. Deployment
text: Conceptually: ```text ECR ↓ Kubernetes Deployment ↓ new Pods ↓ readiness checks ↓ traffic ``` If the deployment is bad: ```bash kubectl rollout undo deployment/api ``` Rollback becomes much easier when images are immutable. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 24. Infrastructure as Code
text: Instead of manually creating: ```text VPC EKS RDS S3 IAM ``` Terraform manages them. ```text Terraform ↓ AWS APIs ↓ Infrastructure ``` The repository might look like: ```text infra/ ├── main.tf ├── variables.tf ├── outputs.tf └── modules/ ├── network/ ├── eks/ └── database/ ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 25. Infrastructure Pipeline
text: ```text Pull Request ↓ Terraform fmt ↓ Terraform validate ↓ Terraform plan ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ Controlled apply ``` This prevents random manual infrastructure changes. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 26. Application Monitoring
text: Every request should generate useful telemetry. Example: ```json { "level": "info", "event": "request_completed", "requestId": "abc123", "method": "GET", "path": "/orders/123", "statusCode": 200, "durationMs": 84 } ``` Now you have: ```text Logs Metrics Traces ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 27. Metrics
text: Monitor: ```text request rate error rate p50 latency p95 latency p99 latency CPU memory Pod restarts database connections Redis latency queue depth ``` For APIs: ```text RED │ ├── Rate ├── Errors └── Duration ``` is an excellent starting framework. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: 28. Alerts
text: Don't alert on everything. Meaningful examples: ```text 5xx rate > threshold p95 latency > threshold RDS connections near limit disk/storage pressure Pods repeatedly restarting queue backlog growing ``` Alerts should correspond to something actionable. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 12 — NOW LET'S BREAK THE SYSTEM
text: This is arguably the most important part of Chapter 23. A production engineer isn't judged only by whether they can build the happy path. They need to diagnose failures. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Incident 1 — API Returns 503
text: User reports: ```text "API is down." ``` Don't randomly restart Pods. Start: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` Suppose: ```text api-a Running api-b Running api-c CrashLoopBackOff ``` Then: ```bash kubectl logs api-c ``` You discover: ```text DATABASE_URL is undefined ``` Now inspect: ```bash kubectl describe pod api-c ``` Maybe the Secret wasn't correctly mounted/injected. Root cause: ```text Secret/configuration problem ``` Not Kubernetes itself. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Incident 2 — All Pods Running, API Still Returns 503
text: Now: ```text Pods = Running ``` But requests fail. Check: ```bash kubectl get svc ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get endpointslices ``` Suppose: ```text API Service Endpoints = none ``` Check the Service selector: ```yaml selector: app: api ``` Pods: ```yaml labels: app: backend ``` Mismatch. Therefore: ```text Service ↓ selector doesn't match Pods ↓ no endpoints ``` Fix the labels/selectors. This is a classic Kubernetes issue. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Incident 3 — Pods Are Healthy but Requests Are Slow
text: Metrics: ```text CPU = 30% Memory = 40% ``` So you don't immediately scale. Check traces: ```text API 20ms Redis 15ms RDS 1800ms ``` Database is taking: ```text 1.8 seconds ``` Investigate: ```text slow queries missing indexes connection pool locks database load ``` The problem isn't Kubernetes. It's the database path. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Incident 4 — RDS Connection Exhaustion
text: Metrics: ```text RDS connections = 100% ``` API Pods: ```text 3 → 10 ``` Potential explanation: ```text Pods increased ↓ each Pod created a connection pool ↓ total connections increased ↓ RDS exhausted ``` Possible remedies depend on the architecture: ```text reduce pool size use connection pooling/proxying optimize DB usage scale DB appropriately limit application concurrency ``` This is why: > **Scaling the API does not automatically mean the whole system scales.** Always look for the bottleneck. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Incident 5 — ImagePullBackOff
text: Deployment: ```text ImagePullBackOff ``` Debug: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` Check: ```text image name tag registry permissions image existence ``` Pipeline: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ Docker build ↓ ECR push ↓ Kubernetes ``` Maybe CI pushed: ```text my-api:abc123 ``` but Kubernetes requests: ```text my-api:abc124 ``` Simple tag mismatch. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Incident 6 — Deployment Works but New Pods Receive No Traffic
text: Check: ```text readiness probe ``` Maybe: ```text /ready ``` returns: ```text 503 ``` because the database connection isn't ready. Therefore: ```text Pod = Running Pod = not Ready ``` This distinction is extremely important: ```text Running ≠ Ready ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Incident 7 — HPA Isn't Scaling
text: You observe: ```text CPU = 90% ``` but: ```text replicas = 2 ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get hpa ``` Then: ```bash kubectl describe hpa api-hpa ``` Potential issue: ```text metrics unavailable ``` or: ```text resource requests aren't configured correctly ``` or: ```text maxReplicas already reached ``` Never assume HPA is broken before checking its metrics and events. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Incident 8 — Database Is Fine, API Is Fine, Users Still Can't Connect
text: Check DNS. ```bash dig api.example.com ``` Then: ```bash curl -v https://api.example.com/health ``` Potential problem: ```text DNS record ↓ wrong target ``` or: ```text TLS certificate ↓ configuration issue ``` or: ```text WAF ↓ request blocked ``` This demonstrates why troubleshooting must happen **layer by layer**. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 13 — THE TROUBLESHOOTING MODEL
text: When something breaks, think: ```text INCIDENT │ ↓ DNS / TLS │ ↓ WAF / Edge │ ↓ Load Balancer │ ↓ Kubernetes │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod Service Ingress │ ↓ Container │ ↓ Node.js app │ ┌─────┼─────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Redis RDS S3 ``` At every layer ask: > **Is this layer healthy?** ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: DNS
text: ```bash dig api.example.com ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: HTTP/TLS
text: ```bash curl -v https://api.example.com/health ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Kubernetes
text: ```bash kubectl get pods kubectl get svc kubectl get ingress ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Pod details
text: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Logs
text: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Previous crashed container
text: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> --previous ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Service endpoints
text: ```bash kubectl get endpointslices ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Resource usage
text: ```bash kubectl top pods kubectl top nodes ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Deployment
text: ```bash kubectl rollout status deployment/api ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Rollback
text: ```bash kubectl rollout undo deployment/api ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: AWS
text: Use the relevant AWS console/CLI/CloudWatch metrics to inspect: ```text ALB EKS RDS Lambda S3 CloudWatch ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 14 — A REAL DEPLOYMENT FAILURE
text: Let's simulate an entire incident. Suppose you deploy: ```text v2 ``` Immediately: ```text 5xx ↑ ``` What do you do?

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Step 1
text: Check deployment: ```bash kubectl rollout status deployment/api ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Step 2
text: Check Pods: ```bash kubectl get pods ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Step 3
text: Logs: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> ``` Suppose: ```text Redis connection refused ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Step 4
text: Check Redis. ```text Redis unavailable ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Step 5
text: Could v2 be responsible? Maybe the new application version changed: ```text REDIS_URL ``` or authentication.

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Step 6
text: If production impact is severe: ```bash kubectl rollout undo deployment/api ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Step 7
text: Verify: ```text 5xx ↓ latency ↓ requests successful ```

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Step 8
text: Investigate the root cause. This is: ```text Detect ↓ Diagnose ↓ Mitigate ↓ Recover ↓ Root Cause Analysis ``` ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 15 — ROLLBACK VS ROLLFORWARD
text: An important engineering decision. Sometimes: ```text Rollback ``` is fastest. Other times: ```text Fix forward ``` is safer. For example: ```text Security vulnerability in v1 ``` Rolling back to v1 might be dangerous. So: > **Rollback isn't automatically the right answer.** You need to understand what changed and the risk of each option. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 16 — AVAILABILITY
text: Suppose: ```text one EC2 one AZ one database ``` Failure: ```text EC2 dies ``` Application: ```text DOWN ``` More resilient: ```text Load Balancer / \ ↓ ↓ AZ-A AZ-B Pod Pod \ / RDS ``` Now one application instance can fail without necessarily taking down the entire service. But availability isn't free. You introduce: ```text more infrastructure more complexity more cost ``` This is why architecture is about **tradeoffs**. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 17 — COST THINKING
text: Suppose someone says: > "Let's use EKS for our tiny internal CRUD application." You should ask: ```text Why? ``` Kubernetes can be powerful, but it introduces: ```text cluster complexity networking complexity monitoring upgrades security operational overhead ``` For a simple service: ```text ECS/Fargate EC2 + Docker Lambda ``` may sometimes be simpler depending on requirements. You shouldn't use Kubernetes simply because it appears on your resume. For interviews, explain **why you chose it**. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 18 — WHEN TO USE WHAT?
text: A useful decision framework: | Requirement | Possible choice | |---|---| | Simple long-running API | EC2/ECS | | Containerized workload | Docker | | Many containers + orchestration | Kubernetes | | AWS-managed Kubernetes | EKS | | Event-driven short task | Lambda | | Object storage | S3 | | Relational database | RDS | | Cache | Redis | | Async jobs | SQS | | Pub/sub notifications | SNS | | CDN | CloudFront | | DNS | Route 53 | | HTTP filtering | WAF | | Infrastructure as Code | Terraform | | Metrics | Prometheus/CloudWatch | | Dashboards | Grafana | | Distributed traces | OpenTelemetry-compatible stack | The answer is always dependent on requirements. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 19 — COMPLETE DEVOPS LIFECYCLE
text: You can now describe the complete lifecycle: ```text CODE │ ↓ Git │ ↓ GitHub │ ↓ GitHub Actions │ ┌──────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Tests Build Security │ ↓ Docker │ ↓ ECR │ ↓ Kubernetes │ ↓ Deploy │ ↓ Production │ ┌──────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Logs Metrics Traces │ │ │ └──────────┼──────────┘ ↓ Monitoring │ ↓ Alert │ ↓ Investigation │ ↓ Fix / Rollback │ ↓ Recovery ``` Infrastructure: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS ``` That's the complete picture. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: PART 20 — THE INTERVIEW QUESTION YOU SHOULD NOW BE ABLE TO ANSWER
text: > **"How would you deploy a production Node.js application?"** A strong answer would sound roughly like: ```text I would containerize the Node.js application using a multi-stage Docker build and push immutable images to a container registry such as ECR. I would run the application using a managed container platform such as EKS if Kubernetes is justified by the requirements. The application would run as multiple stateless Pods behind a Kubernetes Service and an external load balancer. The infrastructure would be provisioned with Terraform. I'd keep PostgreSQL in RDS, object files in S3, and use Redis where caching or shared ephemeral state is appropriate. I'd keep the database private and restrict network access using security groups and Kubernetes networking controls. CI/CD would run tests, build the application, build and scan the container image, push it to ECR, and deploy the selected image version. I'd use readiness and liveness probes, resource requests and limits, HPA where appropriate, and rolling deployments. For observability, I'd collect structured logs, metrics, and distributed traces, with alerts based on meaningful service health indicators. If something failed, I'd troubleshoot from the outside in: DNS/TLS → WAF/load balancer → Kubernetes Service/Ingress → Pods → application → Redis/RDS/S3. ``` That's the level of answer we're aiming for. ---

title: Chapter 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: THE MOST IMPORTANT LESSON OF RESPONSE 23
text: Don't think: ```text "I know AWS." "I know Kubernetes." "I know Docker." "I know Terraform." ``` Think: ```text SYSTEM │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Application Infrastructure Operations │ │ │ Node.js AWS/K8s Monitoring Docker Terraform Reliability Database Network Debugging ``` The valuable skill is knowing: > **How these technologies interact.** That's what turns a list of technologies on a resume into actual engineering knowledge. <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 22: Observability + Reliability](../07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md) · [Chapter 24: Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery](../09-interview/ch24-interview-oa-mastery.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch23-revision.md)
