title: Revision 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Reference architecture
text: ```text Internet → Route 53 → CloudFront → WAF → Load Balancer → EKS (Pods A/B/C) → Redis · RDS PostgreSQL · S3 GitHub → GitHub Actions → Docker build (+scan) → ECR → EKS Terraform → VPC, subnets, IAM, EKS, RDS, S3, LB App → logs + metrics + traces → observability platform → dashboards → alerts ``` | Layer | Decisions | |---|---| | **Network** | VPC (e.g. `10.0.0.0/16`) across AZ-A/AZ-B with public + private subnets. Public: Load Balancer, NAT Gateway. Private: EKS worker capacity, RDS, internal services. DB never directly Internet-exposed. | | **Security groups** | Internet →(HTTPS 443) ALB SG → API/EKS SG → RDS SG (5432); API → Redis; **Internet → RDS ❌** (least privilege at network level) | | **DNS/TLS** | Route 53 `api.example.com` → CloudFront/LB; HTTPS everywhere; ACM manages certificates | | **CloudFront/WAF** | Cache images, JS, CSS, static files; **don't** blindly cache `POST /payment`, `GET /account`, private responses. WAF: rate limiting, managed rules, IP rules, request filtering — one layer, not a replacement for IAM, SGs, authorization, input validation | | **Load balancing** | Stable entry point (users never see Pod IPs); distributes to healthy backends; `/health`, `/ready` | | **Kubernetes** | EKS control plane managed by AWS; Deployment `replicas: 3` self-heals; Service gives stable discovery; ConfigMap + Secret/external secrets (same image for dev/staging/prod) | | **Data** | RDS PostgreSQL (not in the API container); connection pooling + pool sizing (10 Pods × 100 = 1000 connections!); Redis for caching, sessions, rate limiting, short-lived state, queues (caching brings invalidation, consistency, memory, TTL, failure trade-offs); S3 for large objects, with presigned URLs | | **Docker** | Multi-stage build, `node:22-slim`, `npm ci --omit=dev`, `USER node`, no secrets in image, `EXPOSE 3000`, `CMD ["node","dist/server.js"]` | | **CI/CD** | `git push` → checkout, `npm ci`, lint, typecheck, tests, build, Docker build, Docker scan, push image → deploy. Immutable tags (`my-api:8f31a7c` = Git commit) → Git commit → Docker image → ECR → Kubernetes tells you exactly what runs. Deploy: ECR → Deployment → new Pods → readiness → traffic; bad deploy → `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api` | | **Terraform** | `infra/{main,variables,outputs}.tf + modules/{network,eks,database}`; PR → fmt → validate → plan → review → merge → controlled apply | | **Observability** | JSON request logs (`requestId`, method, path, statusCode, durationMs); metrics: request rate, error rate, p50/p95/p99, CPU, memory, Pod restarts, DB connections, Redis latency, queue depth (RED); alerts only when actionable: 5xx > threshold, p95 > threshold, RDS connections near limit, storage pressure, Pods restarting, queue backlog growing |

title: Revision 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Incident playbooks (memorise the reasoning)
text: | # | Symptom | Diagnosis path | Root cause example | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | API returns 503 | `kubectl get pods` → one `CrashLoopBackOff` → `kubectl logs api-c` → "DATABASE_URL is undefined" → `describe pod` | Secret/config not injected — not Kubernetes itself | | 2 | All Pods Running, still 503 | `kubectl get svc` → `kubectl get endpointslices` → Endpoints = none → Service selector `app: api` vs Pod label `app: backend` | Selector mismatch → no endpoints | | 3 | Pods healthy but slow (CPU 30%, mem 40%) | Don't scale; traces: API 20 ms, Redis 15 ms, **RDS 1800 ms** | Slow queries, missing indexes, connection pool, locks, DB load | | 4 | RDS connections 100% after Pods 3 → 10 | Each Pod has its own pool → total connections ↑ | Reduce pool size, use pooling/proxy, optimise DB usage, scale DB, limit concurrency. *Scaling the API doesn't scale the whole system* | | 5 | `ImagePullBackOff` | `kubectl describe pod`; image name/tag/registry/permissions/existence | CI pushed `my-api:abc123`, Kubernetes requests `abc124` | | 6 | New Pods get no traffic | Readiness probe `/ready` returns 503 because DB not ready | **Running ≠ Ready** | | 7 | CPU 90% but replicas = 2 | `kubectl get hpa`, `describe hpa api-hpa`: metrics unavailable, requests not configured, `maxReplicas` reached | Never assume HPA is broken before checking metrics/events | | 8 | DB and API fine, users can't connect | `dig api.example.com`, `curl -v https://api.example.com/health` | Wrong DNS target, TLS certificate issue, WAF blocking | **Troubleshooting model (outside-in):** DNS/TLS → WAF/Edge → Load Balancer → Kubernetes (Pod / Service / Ingress) → Container → Node.js app → Redis / RDS / S3. At every layer ask *"Is this layer healthy?"* **Layer commands:** `dig`, `curl -v`, `kubectl get pods|svc|ingress`, `kubectl describe pod`, `kubectl logs <pod>`, `kubectl logs <pod> --previous`, `kubectl get endpointslices`, `kubectl top pods|nodes`, `kubectl rollout status|undo deployment/api`; AWS console/CLI/CloudWatch for ALB, EKS, RDS, Lambda, S3.

title: Revision 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Deployment failure walkthrough
text: Deploy v2 → 5xx ↑: (1) `rollout status` (2) `get pods` (3) logs → "Redis connection refused" (4) check Redis (5) did v2 change `REDIS_URL`/authentication? (6) severe impact → `kubectl rollout undo` (7) verify 5xx ↓, latency ↓ (8) investigate root cause. **Detect → Diagnose → Mitigate → Recover → Root Cause Analysis.** **Rollback vs fix-forward:** rollback is often fastest, but not automatically right — e.g. a security vulnerability in v1 makes rolling back dangerous. Understand what changed and the risk of each option.

title: Revision 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Trade-offs
text: - **Availability isn't free:** single EC2/AZ/DB = outage on failure; multi-AZ (LB → Pods in AZ-A/B → RDS) adds infrastructure, complexity, cost. - **Cost/complexity:** EKS for a tiny internal CRUD app? Ask *why*. Kubernetes adds cluster/network complexity, monitoring, upgrades, security, operational overhead; ECS/Fargate, EC2 + Docker, or Lambda may be simpler. Don't use Kubernetes just for the resume — explain why you chose it.

title: Revision 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: "When to use what"
text: | Requirement | Choice | |---|---| | Simple long-running API | EC2/ECS | | Containerised workload | Docker | | Many containers + orchestration | Kubernetes (AWS-managed: EKS) | | Event-driven short task | Lambda | | Object storage / relational DB / cache | S3 / RDS / Redis | | Async jobs / pub-sub | SQS / SNS | | CDN / DNS / HTTP filtering | CloudFront / Route 53 / WAF | | IaC | Terraform | | Metrics / dashboards / traces | Prometheus or CloudWatch / Grafana / OpenTelemetry-compatible stack | The answer always depends on requirements.

title: Revision 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: The interview answer — "How would you deploy a production Node.js application?"
text: Containerise with a multi-stage Docker build, push **immutable images** to ECR; run on EKS only if Kubernetes is justified; multiple **stateless Pods** behind a Service and external load balancer; infrastructure via **Terraform**; PostgreSQL in **RDS**, files in **S3**, **Redis** where caching/shared ephemeral state fits; keep the DB private (security groups + Kubernetes networking controls); CI/CD: tests, build, build + scan image, push to ECR, deploy the selected version; readiness/liveness probes, resource requests/limits, HPA, rolling deployments; structured logs, metrics, distributed traces with alerts on meaningful health indicators; troubleshoot outside-in: DNS/TLS → WAF/LB → Service/Ingress → Pods → app → Redis/RDS/S3.

title: Revision 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Key lesson
text: Don't think "I know AWS / Kubernetes / Docker / Terraform." Think **Application (Node.js, Docker, database) + Infrastructure (AWS/K8s, Terraform, network) + Operations (monitoring, reliability, debugging)** — the valuable skill is how they **interact**.

title: Revision 23 — Production Architecture + Troubleshooting
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - `kubectl rollout undo` reverts the Deployment's Pod template only; it does **not** revert database migrations, ConfigMaps/Secrets, or infrastructure — a reason to use backward-compatible (expand-and-contract) migrations (Ch.13). - The Dockerfile shown runs `npm ci` as root and then drops to `USER node`; that is acceptable because the app only needs read access to `node_modules`. - Layer ordering for a debugging session: confirm the *symptom* from outside (`curl -v`) before touching the cluster; many incidents are DNS/TLS/WAF, not Kubernetes. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 22](ch22-revision.md) · [Full chapter 23](../docs/08-production/ch23-production-architecture-troubleshooting.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 24](ch24-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: > **Source:** Response 24 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-24.txt`, lines 1–2173) · **Part I — Core curriculum (Responses 1–24)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch24-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> This is the **final response of the 24-response roadmap**. The objective now is not to learn another giant technology. It's to make sure you can take everything we've covered and **actually use it, explain it, troubleshoot it, and answer interview/OA questions from it.** ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 1. Your Complete Cloud + DevOps Map
text: You should now see DevOps as one connected system: ```text DEVELOPER │ ↓ Git │ ↓ GitHub │ ↓ GitHub Actions / \ ↓ ↓ Application Terraform CI/CD │ │ ↓ ↓ AWS Docker ┌────┼─────┐ │ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ VPC EKS RDS ECR │ │ │ │ ↓ └───────────┘ Pods │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Redis RDS S3 ↓ Observability ┌────────┼────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Logs Metrics Traces │ │ │ └────────┼────────┘ ↓ Dashboards ↓ Alerts ↓ Incident Response ``` That is the big picture. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 2. What "DevOps" Means for You
text: For your SWE/backend career, don't define DevOps as: > "Knowing Docker and Kubernetes." Your practical definition should be: > **The practices and tooling used to reliably build, test, package, deploy, operate, monitor, and troubleshoot software and infrastructure.** That includes: ```text Code ↓ Version control ↓ CI ↓ Testing ↓ Build ↓ Containerization ↓ Infrastructure ↓ Deployment ↓ Monitoring ↓ Reliability ↓ Troubleshooting ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 1 — LINUX MASTER CHECKLIST
text: You should be comfortable with:

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Filesystem
text: ```bash pwd ls cd mkdir touch cp mv rm cat less ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Permissions
text: ```bash chmod chown ``` Understand: ```text r = read w = write x = execute ``` and: ```text 755 644 ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Processes
text: ```bash ps top kill ``` Understand: ```text PID SIGTERM SIGKILL SIGINT ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Disk/memory
text: ```bash df du free ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Networking
text: ```bash ip ss ping curl ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Logs
text: ```bash journalctl tail grep ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Remote access
text: ```bash ssh ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Services
text: ```bash systemctl ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Question:
text: > A server is responding very slowly. What do you check? A reasonable investigation: ```text CPU ↓ Memory ↓ Disk ↓ Processes ↓ Network ↓ Application logs ↓ Dependencies ``` Commands: ```bash top free -h df -h ps aux ss -tulpn tail -f app.log ``` Don't blindly restart the server. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 2 — BASH
text: You should be able to write scripts involving: ```bash #!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail if curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/health; then echo "API healthy" else echo "API unhealthy" exit 1 fi ``` Understand: ```text variables arguments conditions loops functions exit codes pipes redirection cron ``` Especially: ```bash $? $1 $@ ``` and: ```bash set -euo pipefail ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 4. Bash Interview Question
text: > Why use `set -euo pipefail`? Simplified: ```text -e → stop on many command failures -u → catch unset variables -o pipefail → pipeline fails if an earlier command fails ``` It helps make scripts fail more predictably. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 3 — NETWORKING
text: This is one of the highest-value DevOps topics for SWE interviews. You should understand: ```text IP Subnet CIDR Port Socket TCP UDP DNS HTTP HTTPS TLS NAT Routing Firewall Proxy Load Balancer ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: TCP
text: ```text connection-oriented reliable ordered ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: UDP
text: ```text connectionless no built-in delivery guarantee lower overhead ``` Don't simply say: > TCP is faster than UDP. That's an oversimplification. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 6. DNS Flow
text: When you request: ```text https://api.example.com ``` conceptually: ```text Browser ↓ DNS resolver ↓ DNS hierarchy ↓ IP address ↓ TCP/TLS ↓ HTTP request ``` Know: ```text A AAAA CNAME MX TXT NS ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 7. HTTP
text: Know: ```text GET POST PUT PATCH DELETE ``` and status families: ```text 2xx → success 3xx → redirection 4xx → client/request problem 5xx → server-side failure ``` Especially: ```text 200 201 204 400 401 403 404 409 429 500 502 503 504 ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 8. Debugging Network Connectivity
text: If: ```text curl http://server:3000 ``` fails: Think: ```text DNS? ↓ IP? ↓ Route? ↓ Firewall / SG? ↓ Port? ↓ Process listening? ↓ Application? ``` Useful commands: ```bash dig example.com curl -v https://example.com ss -lntp ip route ping ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 4 — GIT
text: You should confidently understand: ```text working directory ↓ staging ↓ commit ↓ branch ↓ remote ``` Commands: ```bash git status git add git commit git log git diff git fetch git pull git push git branch git switch git merge git rebase git stash git cherry-pick git reset git revert git reflog ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 9. Reset vs Revert
text: Very common interview question.

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Reset
text: Moves branch/history references. Potentially rewrites local history. ```text git reset ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Revert
text: Creates a new commit that reverses an earlier commit. ```text git revert ``` For shared public history: ```text revert ``` is often safer than rewriting history. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 10. Rebase
text: Rebase changes the base of commits to produce a different history. Useful for: ```text cleaning local feature history updating a branch ``` Be careful with rebasing commits that other people already depend on. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 5 — CI/CD
text: Know the distinction: ```text Continuous Integration → frequently integrate and test code Continuous Delivery → keep software ready for release Continuous Deployment → automatically deploy qualifying changes ``` Pipeline: ```text Git push ↓ CI ↓ Install dependencies ↓ Lint ↓ Typecheck ↓ Tests ↓ Build ↓ Docker ↓ Registry ↓ Deployment ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 11. GitHub Actions
text: Know: ```text workflow event job runner step action artifact secret environment ``` Basic workflow: ```yaml name: CI on: push: pull_request: jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 - run: npm ci - run: npm run lint - run: npm run typecheck - run: npm test - run: npm run build ``` You don't need to memorize the exact YAML. You need to understand what each part does. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 6 — DOCKER
text: This should now be one of your strongest DevOps areas. Remember: ```text Dockerfile ↓ Image ↓ Container ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 12. Dockerfile Essentials
text: Know: ```dockerfile FROM WORKDIR COPY RUN ENV EXPOSE CMD ENTRYPOINT USER ``` Especially:

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: `RUN`
text: Executed while building the image.

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: `CMD`
text: Default command when the container starts. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 13. Production Dockerfile
text: Know why we use: ```text multi-stage builds small runtime image non-root user .dockerignore production dependencies layer caching immutable tags ``` Example: ```dockerfile FROM node:22 AS build WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build FROM node:22-slim WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist USER node EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 14. Docker Debugging
text: Container isn't working: ```bash docker ps docker logs <container> docker inspect <container> docker exec -it <container> sh ``` Check: ```text container running? port mapping? application listening on 0.0.0.0? environment variables? image? logs? network? ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 7 — AWS
text: You don't need to memorize every AWS service. You need to understand the **core backend architecture**. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 15. AWS Core Services
text: ```text IAM EC2 S3 VPC RDS ALB Auto Scaling Lambda SQS SNS Route 53 CloudFront WAF CloudWatch CloudTrail ECR EKS Secrets Manager KMS ``` You should be able to explain what each is for. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 16. IAM
text: Understand: ```text User Group Role Policy Permission ARN Least privilege Temporary credentials ``` Critical concept: ```text Authentication ≠ Authorization ``` And: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ OIDC ↓ IAM Role ↓ Temporary credentials ``` is preferable to putting long-lived AWS keys in GitHub secrets when the workflow can use OIDC. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 17. EC2
text: Know: ```text AMI Instance Instance type EBS Security Group Public/private IP IAM Role User Data IMDS ``` Architecture: ```text VPC ↓ Subnet ↓ Security Group ↓ EC2 ↓ Docker ↓ Node.js ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 18. S3
text: Know: ```text bucket object key storage class versioning lifecycle encryption presigned URL multipart upload ``` Remember: > **S3 is object storage, not a normal block filesystem.** ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 19. VPC
text: This is extremely important. Mental model: ```text VPC │ ├── Subnet ├── Route Table ├── Internet Gateway ├── NAT Gateway ├── Security Group ├── NACL └── VPC Endpoint ``` Production: ```text Internet ↓ ALB ↓ Private application ↓ Private RDS ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 20. RDS
text: Know: ```text Multi-AZ Read Replica Backup Snapshot PITR Connection Pool Encryption Monitoring ``` Critical: ```text Multi-AZ → availability/failover Read Replica → read scaling ``` They solve different problems. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 21. Scaling
text: Know: ```text vertical scaling horizontal scaling load balancing Auto Scaling stateless architecture ``` And: > **Scaling application servers doesn't necessarily scale the database.** ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 22. Lambda + Messaging
text: Understand: ```text Lambda SQS SNS ``` Architecture: ```text API ↓ SQS ↓ Lambda worker ↓ Database ``` Know: ```text visibility timeout retry DLQ idempotency cold start concurrency ``` Especially: > Never assume a message is processed exactly once simply because your application uses a queue. Design consumers to tolerate duplicate delivery where the system semantics require it. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 8 — KUBERNETES
text: This is another major interview area. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 23. Kubernetes Mental Model
text: ```text Cluster │ ├── Control Plane │ └── Worker Nodes │ └── Pods ``` Then: ```text Deployment ↓ ReplicaSet ↓ Pods ``` and: ```text Service ↓ Pods ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 24. Kubernetes Objects
text: Know: ```text Pod Deployment ReplicaSet Service Namespace ConfigMap Secret PV PVC StorageClass Ingress HPA Job CronJob DaemonSet StatefulSet ``` You don't need equal depth on all of them. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 25. Kubernetes Networking
text: Understand: ```text Pod ↓ Service ↓ Ingress ↓ Load Balancer ``` and: ```text Service discovery DNS ClusterIP NodePort LoadBalancer NetworkPolicy ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 26. Kubernetes Scaling
text: Know: ```text HPA ↓ more/fewer Pods ``` versus: ```text Node autoscaling ↓ more/fewer worker nodes ``` Important: ```text Pod scaling ≠ Node scaling ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 27. Kubernetes Troubleshooting
text: This sequence should become automatic: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` then: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` then: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> ``` then: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> --previous ``` then: ```bash kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh ``` For services: ```bash kubectl get svc kubectl get endpointslices ``` For deployments: ```bash kubectl rollout status deployment/api kubectl rollout history deployment/api kubectl rollout undo deployment/api ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 28. Kubernetes Failure Table
text: | Symptom | First things to investigate | |---|---| | `Pending` | Scheduling/resources/PVC | | `CrashLoopBackOff` | Application logs/config | | `ImagePullBackOff` | Image/tag/registry/auth | | Running but not Ready | Readiness probe | | Service has no traffic | Selector/endpoints | | HPA not scaling | Metrics/resources/config | | Pod OOMKilled | Memory usage/limits | | 503 | LB/Service/readiness/backend | | 502 | Proxy/LB → backend communication | | DNS failure | DNS/service configuration | Don't memorize this mechanically. Learn the reasoning. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 9 — TERRAFORM
text: Know the lifecycle: ```bash terraform init terraform fmt terraform validate terraform plan terraform apply terraform destroy ``` And: ```text Provider Resource Variable Output Data source Module State Remote state State locking Drift Import ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 29. Terraform Mental Model
text: ```text Terraform code ↓ Provider ↓ Plan ↓ Apply ↓ Cloud API ↓ Infrastructure ↓ State ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 30. Terraform Interview Question
text: > What happens if someone manually changes infrastructure created by Terraform? Answer: ```text Manual change ↓ Infrastructure differs from desired configuration ↓ Terraform detects drift during planning ↓ Plan proposes reconciliation ``` Then decide whether Terraform should restore the declared configuration or whether the code should be intentionally changed. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 10 — OBSERVABILITY
text: Know: ```text Logs Metrics Traces ``` And: ```text Prometheus Grafana OpenTelemetry CloudWatch ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 31. RED
text: For APIs: ```text Rate Errors Duration ``` Example: ```text Rate = 1000 req/s Errors = 2% p95 = 300ms ``` This gives a quick view of service health. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 32. SLI / SLO / SLA
text: Remember: ```text SLI → measurement SLO → target SLA → formal customer commitment ``` And: ```text SLO ↓ Error Budget ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 11 — RELIABILITY
text: Know these patterns: ```text Timeout Retry Exponential Backoff Jitter Circuit Breaker Bulkhead Rate Limiting Idempotency Graceful Shutdown ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: 33. The Golden Rule of Retries
text: Don't blindly retry. Think: ```text Is failure transient? ↓ Is operation safe to retry? ↓ How many retries? ↓ Backoff? ↓ Jitter? ↓ What happens if dependency stays down? ``` For payment-like operations: ```text idempotency ``` is especially important. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 12 — INTERVIEW SCENARIOS
text: These are probably more valuable than memorizing definitions. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Scenario 1
text: > Your API suddenly starts returning 500 errors. What do you do? Answer structure: ```text 1. Confirm impact 2. Check metrics 3. Check recent deployment 4. Check application logs 5. Check traces 6. Check dependencies 7. Mitigate 8. Verify recovery 9. Find root cause ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Scenario 2
text: > All Pods are Running, but users get 503. Think: ```text Running ≠ Ready ``` Check: ```text readiness Service endpoints Ingress/LB application ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Scenario 3
text: > API Pods are healthy but response time is 5 seconds. Don't immediately add Pods. Check: ```text metrics ↓ traces ↓ database ↓ Redis ↓ external APIs ``` Maybe: ```text RDS query = 4.5 seconds ``` Scaling API Pods won't fix the underlying database query. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Scenario 4
text: > Database connections suddenly reach 100%. Think: ```text Pods increased? Connection pool too large? Connection leak? Traffic spike? Slow queries? ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Scenario 5
text: > New deployment causes 5xx errors. Possible response: ```text check rollout ↓ logs ↓ compare v1/v2 ↓ rollback if appropriate ↓ investigate ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Scenario 6
text: > EC2 cannot access the Internet. Check: ```text subnet ↓ route table ↓ Internet Gateway/NAT ↓ Security Group ↓ NACL ↓ DNS ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Scenario 7
text: > Private EC2 can't download updates. Think: ```text Private subnet ↓ route to NAT Gateway? ↓ NAT route correct? ↓ NAT in public subnet? ↓ Internet Gateway? ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Scenario 8
text: > Kubernetes Pod can't pull an image. Think: ```text image name ↓ tag ↓ registry ↓ credentials ↓ network ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: PART 13 — OA / MCQ TRAPS
text: These are the kinds of distinctions you should be able to answer instantly.

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Docker
text: ```text Image ≠ Container ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Kubernetes
text: ```text Pod ≠ Container ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: AWS
text: ```text Multi-AZ ≠ Read Replica ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Networking
text: ```text Private subnet ≠ no Internet access ``` A private subnet can have outbound Internet access through NAT.

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Security
text: ```text Authentication ≠ Authorization ```

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery

text: Before considering this roadmap truly complete, make sure you can answer these without notes.

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **What happens from `git push` until a new Dockerized Node.js version reaches Kubernetes?** ```text Git ↓ GitHub ↓ Actions ↓ Tests ↓ Docker ↓ ECR ↓ Kubernetes ↓ Rolling deployment ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **Why can't you just use Pod IPs?** Because Pods are ephemeral. Use: ```text Service ``` for stable discovery. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **Why does Kubernetes need readiness probes?** Because: ```text Running ≠ Ready ``` A running application may not yet be capable of safely receiving traffic. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **Why doesn't adding API Pods automatically solve database scaling?** Because: ```text API ↓ DB ``` can make the DB the bottleneck. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **Why use Terraform?** To manage infrastructure declaratively and reproducibly as code. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **Why use Docker?** To package the application and its runtime dependencies consistently. ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **Why use Kubernetes?** To orchestrate containerized workloads: ```text scheduling scaling self-healing service discovery rolling deployments ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **How do you troubleshoot a production 503?** Layer by layer: ```text DNS ↓ WAF/edge ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Ingress/Service ↓ Pod readiness ↓ Container ↓ Application ↓ Dependencies ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **How do you know whether the system is healthy?** ```text Metrics Logs Traces Health checks Alerts ``` ---

title: Chapter 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
text: **What happens when a production deployment breaks?** ```text Detect ↓ Investigate ↓ Mitigate ↓ Rollback/fix-forward where appropriate ↓ Verify ↓ Root-cause analysis ↓ Prevent recurrence ``` If you can reason through all ten, you're thinking about DevOps rather than merely memorizing tools.

title: Revision 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: DevOps — your practical definition
text: *The practices and tooling used to reliably build, test, package, deploy, operate, monitor, and troubleshoot software and infrastructure* (not just "knowing Docker and Kubernetes"). Code → version control → CI → testing → build → containerisation → infrastructure → deployment → monitoring → reliability → troubleshooting.

title: Revision 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: High-value "X ≠ Y" distinctions (OA / MCQ traps)
text: | | | |---|---| | Image ≠ Container | Docker | | Pod ≠ Container | Kubernetes | | Multi-AZ ≠ Read Replica | RDS (availability/failover vs read scaling) | | Private subnet ≠ no Internet access | outbound possible through NAT | | Authentication ≠ Authorization | who vs what | | S3 ≠ EBS | object vs block | | Horizontal ≠ Vertical | scale out vs up | | Continuous Delivery ≠ Continuous Deployment | approval gate vs automatic | | Logs ≠ Metrics ≠ Traces | what happened / how much / where time went | | State ≠ configuration | Terraform | | Running ≠ Ready | Kubernetes readiness | | HPA ≠ node autoscaling | Pods vs nodes | | TCP is not simply "faster" than UDP | oversimplification; TCP = reliable/ordered/connection-oriented; UDP = connectionless, lower overhead |

title: Revision 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Checklists by domain (what to be able to do)
text: - **Linux:** `pwd ls cd mkdir touch cp mv rm cat less`; `chmod chown` (r/w/x, 755, 644); `ps top kill` (PID, SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGINT); `df du free`; `ip ss ping curl`; `journalctl tail grep`; `ssh`; `systemctl`. *Slow server:* CPU → memory → disk → processes → network → app logs → dependencies (`top`, `free -h`, `df -h`, `ps aux`, `ss -tulpn`, `tail -f app.log`); don't blindly restart. - **Bash:** `set -euo pipefail`; health script `if curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/health; then … else exit 1; fi`; variables, args (`$1 $@ $?`), conditions, loops, functions, exit codes, pipes, redirection, cron. `-e` stop on many failures, `-u` unset variables, `-o pipefail` pipeline fails if an earlier command fails. - **Networking:** IP, subnet, CIDR, port, socket, TCP/UDP, DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, TLS, NAT, routing, firewall, proxy, load balancer. DNS flow: browser → resolver → DNS hierarchy → IP → TCP/TLS → HTTP. Record types A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS. Methods GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE; status 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, **409**, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504. *Connectivity debug:* DNS → IP → route → firewall/SG → port → process listening → application (`dig`, `curl -v`, `ss -lntp`, `ip route`, `ping`). - **Git:** working dir → staging → commit → branch → remote; `status add commit log diff fetch pull push branch switch merge rebase stash cherry-pick reset revert reflog`. Reset moves history refs (may rewrite local history); revert adds a reversing commit (safer on shared history). Rebase changes the base of commits — useful for cleaning local feature history; careful with shared commits. - **CI/CD:** CI/Delivery/Deployment; pipeline: push → CI → deps → lint → typecheck → tests → build → Docker → registry → deployment. GitHub Actions vocabulary: workflow, event, job, runner, step, action, artifact, secret, environment. - **Docker:** Dockerfile → image → container; know `FROM WORKDIR COPY RUN ENV EXPOSE CMD ENTRYPOINT USER`; `RUN` = build time, `CMD` = default start command. Production: multi-stage, small runtime image, non-root, `.dockerignore`, production deps, layer caching, immutable tags. Debug: `docker ps`, `logs`, `inspect`, `exec -it … sh`; check running? port mapping? listening on `0.0.0.0`? env vars? image? logs? network? - **AWS core services:** IAM, EC2, S3, VPC, RDS, ALB, Auto Scaling, Lambda, SQS, SNS, Route 53, CloudFront, WAF, CloudWatch, CloudTrail, ECR, EKS, Secrets Manager, KMS. IAM: user/group/role/policy/permission/ARN/least privilege/temporary credentials; GitHub Actions → OIDC → IAM Role → temp credentials beats long-lived keys. EC2: AMI, instance, type, EBS, SG, public/private IP, IAM role, user data, IMDS. S3: bucket, object, key, storage class, versioning, lifecycle, encryption, presigned URL, multipart. VPC: subnet, route table, IGW, NAT GW, SG, NACL, VPC endpoint. RDS: Multi-AZ, read replica, backup, snapshot, PITR, pool, encryption, monitoring. Scaling: vertical/horizontal/LB/ASG/stateless — **scaling app servers doesn't scale the database**. Lambda/SQS/SNS: visibility timeout, retry, DLQ, idempotency, cold start, concurrency — **never assume exactly-once**. - **Kubernetes:** Cluster = Control Plane + Worker Nodes → Pods; Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods; Service → Pods. Objects: Pod, Deployment, ReplicaSet, Service, Namespace, ConfigMap, Secret, PV, PVC, StorageClass, Ingress, HPA, Job, CronJob, DaemonSet, StatefulSet. Networking: Pod → Service → Ingress → LB; DNS, ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, NetworkPolicy. Troubleshooting order: `get pods` → `describe pod` → `logs` → `logs --previous` → `exec -it … sh`; services: `get svc`, `get endpointslices`; deployments: `rollout status|history|undo`. - **Terraform:** `init fmt validate plan apply destroy`; provider, resource, variable, output, data source, module, state, remote state, locking, drift, import. - **Observability/Reliability/SRE:** logs/metrics/traces; Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, CloudWatch; RED (e.g. 1000 req/s, 2%, p95 300 ms); SLI/SLO/SLA/error budget; timeout, retry, exponential backoff, jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead, rate limiting, idempotency, graceful shutdown.

title: Revision 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Kubernetes failure table
text: | Symptom | Investigate first | |---|---| | `Pending` | Scheduling / resources / PVC | | `CrashLoopBackOff` | Application logs / config | | `ImagePullBackOff` | Image / tag / registry / auth | | Running but not Ready | Readiness probe | | Service has no traffic | Selector / endpoints | | HPA not scaling | Metrics / resources / config | | Pod `OOMKilled` | Memory usage / limits | | 503 | LB / Service / readiness / backend | | 502 | Proxy/LB → backend communication | | DNS failure | DNS / service configuration | (Learn the reasoning; don't memorise mechanically.)

title: Revision 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Golden rule of retries
text: Transient failure? safe to retry? how many retries? backoff? jitter? what if the dependency stays down? For payment-like operations → **idempotency**.

title: Revision 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: Interview scenarios (answer skeletons)
text: 1. **500 errors:** confirm impact → metrics → recent deployment → app logs → traces → dependencies → mitigate → verify recovery → root cause. 2. **Pods Running, users get 503:** Running ≠ Ready → readiness, Service, endpoints, Ingress/LB, application. 3. **Healthy Pods but 5 s responses:** don't add Pods → metrics → traces → database → Redis → external APIs (e.g. RDS query 4.5 s; scaling Pods won't fix it). 4. **DB connections 100%:** Pods increased? pool too large? connection leak? traffic spike? slow queries? 5. **New deployment → 5xx:** check rollout → logs → compare v1/v2 → rollback if appropriate → investigate. 6. **EC2 can't reach Internet:** subnet → route table → IGW/NAT → SG → NACL → DNS. 7. **Private EC2 can't download updates:** route to NAT GW? NAT route correct? NAT in a public subnet? IGW? 8. **Pod can't pull image:** image name → tag → registry → credentials → network.

text: - 🔥 **Master:** Linux, networking, Git, Docker, CI/CD, AWS fundamentals, VPC, IAM, EC2, S3, RDS, load balancing, Kubernetes fundamentals, Terraform, monitoring, troubleshooting — explain, configure, write, deploy, debug. - 🟡 **Strong working knowledge:** EKS, Lambda, SQS/SNS, CloudFront, WAF, Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, HPA, advanced Terraform modules. - 🟢 **Awareness** (what / why / when): ArgoCD, GitOps, Jenkins, Ansible, Service Mesh, Istio, Operators, CRDs, advanced Kubernetes administration, advanced networking internals, advanced SRE. *(These awareness topics are expanded in Part II, chapters 25–35.)* - Positioning: "Backend/SWE engineer with strong Cloud + DevOps capabilities" — don't claim "expert DevOps engineer".

title: Revision 24 — Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview & OA Mastery
heading: The final 10 questions
text: 1. `git push` → … → Kubernetes: Git → GitHub → Actions → tests → Docker → ECR → Kubernetes → rolling deployment. 2. Why not Pod IPs? Ephemeral → Service. 3. Why readiness probes? Running ≠ Ready. 4. Why doesn't adding API Pods solve DB scaling? DB becomes the bottleneck. 5. Why Terraform? Declarative, reproducible infrastructure as code. 6. Why Docker? Consistent packaging of app + runtime dependencies. 7. Why Kubernetes? Scheduling, scaling, self-healing, service discovery, rolling deployments. 8. Production 503? Layer by layer: DNS → WAF/edge → LB → Ingress/Service → Pod readiness → container → application → dependencies. 9. Is the system healthy? Metrics, logs, traces, health checks, alerts. 10. Deployment breaks? Detect → investigate → mitigate → rollback/fix-forward → verify → root-cause analysis → prevent recurrence.

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
text: > **Source:** Response 25 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-25.txt`, lines 1–1672) · **Part II — Advanced extension (Responses 25–36)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch25-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We're now entering the **advanced/remaining DevOps section**. You've already learned Kubernetes manifests, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, HPA, Ingress, etc. Helm builds directly on that knowledge. The goal here is **not just to know that Helm exists**. By the end, you should understand how to create, configure, install, upgrade, rollback, and troubleshoot a Helm-based Kubernetes application. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 1. First: Why Do We Need Helm?
text: Suppose your application has: ```text deployment.yaml service.yaml configmap.yaml secret.yaml ingress.yaml hpa.yaml ``` Without Helm, you might have: ```bash kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml kubectl apply -f service.yaml kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml kubectl apply -f hpa.yaml ``` That's okay for one application. But imagine you deploy: ```text dev staging production ``` and each environment has different: ```text image replicas CPU memory hostname database configuration ``` You don't want to copy-paste five versions of every YAML file. That's where **Helm** comes in. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 2. What Is Helm?
text: Think of Helm as: > **A package manager and templating system for Kubernetes applications.** Similar idea: ```text npm ↓ packages for Node.js apt ↓ packages for Linux Helm ↓ packages/releases for Kubernetes ``` Helm packages Kubernetes resources into something called a:

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Chart
text: A Helm Chart contains: ```text templates configuration metadata ``` that can generate Kubernetes manifests. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 3. The Problem Helm Solves
text: Without Helm: ```text deployment-dev.yaml deployment-staging.yaml deployment-prod.yaml ``` With Helm: ```text templates/deployment.yaml values.yaml values-dev.yaml values-prod.yaml ``` Then: ```bash helm install my-api ./my-chart -f values-dev.yaml ``` or: ```bash helm install my-api ./my-chart -f values-prod.yaml ``` Same chart. Different configuration. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 4. Helm Architecture
text: The important pieces are: ```text Helm CLI │ ↓ Chart │ ├── Templates ├── Values ├── Chart metadata └── Optional dependencies │ ↓ Kubernetes manifests │ ↓ Kubernetes API ``` You interact with Helm using: ```bash helm ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 5. Installing Helm
text: On Linux/macOS, one common installation method is: ```bash curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash ``` Verify: ```bash helm version ``` You should see the Helm version. For your learning environment, you can use the Kubernetes cluster you already created with `kind`. Check: ```bash kubectl get nodes ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 6. Create Your First Chart
text: Run: ```bash helm create my-api ``` You'll get something like: ```text my-api/ ├── Chart.yaml ├── values.yaml ├── charts/ ├── templates/ │ ├── deployment.yaml │ ├── service.yaml │ ├── ingress.yaml │ ├── hpa.yaml │ ├── serviceaccount.yaml │ ├── _helpers.tpl │ └── tests/ └── .helmignore ``` This is your first Helm Chart. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 7. Chart.yaml
text: Open: ```text Chart.yaml ``` Example: ```yaml apiVersion: v2 name: my-api description: A Helm chart for my Node.js API type: application version: 0.1.0 appVersion: "1.0.0" ``` Understand the difference:

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: `version`
text: Version of the **Chart**. ```text 0.1.0 ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: `appVersion`
text: Version of the **application**. ```text 1.0.0 ``` They aren't necessarily the same. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 8. values.yaml
text: This is one of the most important Helm concepts. Example: ```yaml replicaCount: 2 image: repository: my-api tag: "1.0.0" service: type: ClusterIP port: 80 containerPort: 3000 resources: requests: cpu: "100m" memory: "128Mi" limits: cpu: "500m" memory: "512Mi" ``` These are configurable values. Instead of hardcoding them inside your Kubernetes manifests, your templates reference them. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 9. Helm Templates
text: Suppose normal Kubernetes YAML says: ```yaml spec: replicas: 3 ``` Helm can turn it into: ```yaml spec: replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} ``` Now: ```yaml replicaCount: 3 ``` produces: ```yaml replicas: 3 ``` If you change: ```yaml replicaCount: 5 ``` Helm produces: ```yaml replicas: 5 ``` That's the basic idea. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 10. What Is `.Values`?
text: This: ```text .Values ``` represents values supplied to the Helm chart. For example: ```yaml image: repository: my-api tag: "1.0.0" ``` Then: ```yaml {{ .Values.image.repository }} ``` becomes: ```text my-api ``` and: ```yaml {{ .Values.image.tag }} ``` becomes: ```text 1.0.0 ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 11. Example Deployment Template
text: A simplified Helm template: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api spec: replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} selector: matchLabels: app: {{ .Release.Name }}-api template: metadata: labels: app: {{ .Release.Name }}-api spec: containers: - name: api image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}" ports: - containerPort: {{ .Values.containerPort }} resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }} ``` Notice: ```text {{ ... }} ``` Helm replaces these expressions with actual values. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 12. What Is `.Release.Name`?
text: When you install: ```bash helm install my-api ./my-api ``` the release name is: ```text my-api ``` Then: ```yaml {{ .Release.Name }} ``` becomes: ```text my-api ``` You can use it to generate resource names. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 13. Render Without Installing
text: This is extremely useful. Run: ```bash helm template my-api ./my-api ``` Helm generates the Kubernetes YAML locally. You can inspect exactly what Kubernetes would receive. This is one of the first debugging commands you should remember. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 14. Helm Lint
text: Run: ```bash helm lint ./my-api ``` This checks the chart for common problems. Typical workflow: ```text edit chart ↓ helm lint ↓ helm template ↓ helm install/upgrade ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 15. Installing a Chart
text: Run: ```bash helm install my-api ./my-api ``` Check: ```bash helm list ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` and: ```bash kubectl get svc ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 16. Helm Release
text: This is an important word. A **Chart** is the package/template. A **Release** is an installed instance of that chart. Think: ```text Chart │ ├── Release: dev ├── Release: staging └── Release: production ``` For example: ```bash helm install dev-api ./my-api helm install prod-api ./my-api ``` Same chart. Two releases. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 17. Different Environments
text: This is where Helm becomes really useful. Create: ```text values.yaml values-dev.yaml values-prod.yaml ``` Base: ```yaml replicaCount: 2 image: repository: my-api tag: "latest" ``` Development: ```yaml replicaCount: 1 image: tag: "dev" ``` Production: ```yaml replicaCount: 5 image: tag: "1.4.2" ``` Then:

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Development
text: ```bash helm install dev-api ./my-api \ -f values-dev.yaml ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Production
text: ```bash helm install prod-api ./my-api \ -f values-prod.yaml ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 18. Helm Upgrade
text: Suppose production currently has: ```text image: my-api:1.4.2 ``` You build: ```text my-api:1.5.0 ``` Change: ```yaml image: tag: "1.5.0" ``` Then: ```bash helm upgrade prod-api ./my-api \ -f values-prod.yaml ``` Helm updates the release. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 19. Helm History
text: You can inspect previous releases: ```bash helm history prod-api ``` You may see: ```text REVISION STATUS 1 deployed 2 deployed 3 deployed ``` This is extremely useful for deployments. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 20. Helm Rollback
text: Suppose revision 3 introduced a bug. You can rollback: ```bash helm rollback prod-api 2 ``` Then: ```bash helm history prod-api ``` Verify Kubernetes: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` This gives you a clean deployment-management workflow. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 21. Helm vs kubectl
text: This distinction is important.

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: kubectl
text: Directly manages Kubernetes resources. ```bash kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Helm
text: Manages applications/releases composed of Kubernetes resources. ```bash helm upgrade prod-api ./my-api ``` Think: ```text kubectl → Kubernetes resource management Helm → Kubernetes application packaging + release management ``` Helm still ultimately works with Kubernetes resources. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 22. Helm vs Docker
text: Another common interview question.

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Docker
text: Packages: ```text application + dependencies ``` into: ```text container image ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Helm
text: Packages: ```text Kubernetes manifests + configuration ``` into: ```text Helm Chart ``` So: ```text Source code ↓ Docker ↓ Container Image ↓ Helm ↓ Kubernetes deployment ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 23. Helm vs Terraform
text: Another important distinction.

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Terraform
text: Primarily manages **infrastructure**. For example: ```text VPC EKS RDS S3 IAM ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Helm
text: Primarily manages **Kubernetes applications/resources**. For example: ```text Deployment Service Ingress ConfigMap HPA ``` A realistic architecture can use both: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS infrastructure ↓ EKS ↓ Helm ↓ Applications ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 24. Helm Dependencies
text: A chart can depend on other charts. For example, your application might need: ```text Redis PostgreSQL ``` A chart can declare dependencies. But in production, you often won't install a production database directly inside your application chart if you're using managed services. For your AWS architecture: ```text Terraform ↓ RDS ↓ PostgreSQL ``` and: ```text Helm ↓ Node.js API ``` This separation is cleaner. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 25. Helm Repositories
text: Helm charts can be distributed through chart repositories. Conceptually: ```text Chart Repository ↓ helm repo ↓ Chart ↓ Install ``` Common commands: ```bash helm repo add <name> <url> helm repo update helm search repo <name> ``` Then: ```bash helm install ... ``` You don't need to memorize specific public repositories for interviews. Understand the mechanism. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 26. Helm Packaging
text: You can package a chart: ```bash helm package ./my-api ``` You might get: ```text my-api-0.1.0.tgz ``` This is a distributable chart package. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 27. Helm Values Precedence
text: Suppose: `values.yaml` contains: ```yaml replicaCount: 2 ``` and: `values-prod.yaml` contains: ```yaml replicaCount: 5 ``` and command line: ```bash helm upgrade prod-api ./my-api \ -f values-prod.yaml \ --set replicaCount=10 ``` The more specific override wins. Conceptually: ```text Default values ↓ values file ↓ --set ``` So: ```text replicaCount = 10 ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 28. Helm Secrets — Important Security Point
text: Don't assume Helm makes secrets secure. For example: ```yaml databasePassword: mypassword ``` inside: ```text values.yaml ``` is a bad idea. Better architecture: ```text AWS Secrets Manager ↓ External Secrets / secret integration ↓ Kubernetes Secret ↓ Pod ``` or another proper secret-management system. Helm is primarily a packaging/deployment tool, **not a secret-management solution**. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 29. Helm + Your Node.js API
text: Let's imagine your backend: ```text Node.js + TypeScript ``` Docker image: ```text 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/my-api:1.2.0 ``` Your `values-prod.yaml`: ```yaml replicaCount: 4 image: repository: 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/my-api tag: "1.2.0" service: type: ClusterIP port: 80 containerPort: 3000 ``` Helm generates: ```text Deployment Service Ingress ConfigMap HPA ``` Kubernetes then runs: ```text ECR Image ↓ Deployment ↓ 4 Pods ↓ Service ↓ Ingress ↓ Load Balancer ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 30. Helm + CI/CD
text: Now we connect this to everything you've learned. Your pipeline can become: ```text Developer ↓ Git push ↓ GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Tests ↓ Build ↓ Docker image ↓ Push to ECR ↓ Helm upgrade ↓ Kubernetes ``` For example: ```bash helm upgrade --install my-api ./helm/my-api \ --namespace production \ --create-namespace \ -f ./helm/my-api/values-prod.yaml \ --set image.tag=$GITHUB_SHA ``` This is a very realistic deployment pattern. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 31. Why Use Image Tags Like Git SHA?
text: Instead of: ```text my-api:latest ``` use: ```text my-api:8f42c91 ``` where: ```text 8f42c91 ``` identifies a Git commit. Then you can know: ```text production ↓ image 8f42c91 ↓ Git commit 8f42c91 ``` This makes deployments traceable and rollback easier. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 32. `helm upgrade --install`
text: You'll see this frequently: ```bash helm upgrade --install my-api ./my-api ``` Meaning roughly: ```text If release doesn't exist: install it If it exists: upgrade it ``` Very useful in CI/CD. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 33. Helm Dry Run
text: Before applying: ```bash helm upgrade my-api ./my-api \ --dry-run ``` This can help detect rendering/configuration issues before making the change. Combine with: ```bash helm template ``` for debugging. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 34. Helm Debugging Workflow
text: Suppose your deployment is broken. Don't immediately blame Kubernetes. Start: ```bash helm status my-api ``` Then: ```bash helm get values my-api ``` Then: ```bash helm get manifest my-api ``` This lets you inspect what Helm actually deployed. Then move into Kubernetes: ```bash kubectl get pods kubectl describe pod <pod> kubectl logs <pod> ``` Mental model: ```text Helm configuration ↓ Rendered YAML ↓ Kubernetes resources ↓ Pods ↓ Application ``` Find where the failure occurred. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Problem 1 — Template syntax error
text: Example: ```text unexpected EOF ``` Check: ```bash helm lint ./my-api ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Problem 2 — Wrong value
text: You expected: ```text replicas = 5 ``` but got: ```text replicas = 2 ``` Check: ```bash helm get values my-api ``` and: ```bash helm template ... ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Problem 3 — Correct Helm deployment, broken Pod
text: Helm can successfully deploy malformed application configuration. Then Kubernetes may show: ```text CrashLoopBackOff ``` Now use: ```bash kubectl logs kubectl describe ``` Helm isn't the problem anymore. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q1. What is Helm?
text: > Helm is a package manager and templating/release-management tool for Kubernetes applications. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q2. What is a Helm Chart?
text: > A package containing Kubernetes templates, configuration values, metadata, and optionally dependencies. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q3. Chart vs Release?
text: ```text Chart → package/template Release → installed instance of that chart ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q4. Why use Helm?
text: Main reasons: ```text templating configuration management reusable deployments versioning upgrades rollbacks ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q5. Helm vs kubectl?
text: ```text kubectl → directly interacts with Kubernetes resources Helm → packages/configures/manages Kubernetes applications ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q6. Helm vs Terraform?
text: ```text Terraform → infrastructure Helm → Kubernetes applications ``` Although their boundaries can overlap in real setups. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q7. How do you rollback?
text: ```bash helm history my-api helm rollback my-api 2 ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q8. How do you see what Helm rendered?
text: ```bash helm template my-api ./my-api ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q9. How do you inspect an installed release?
text: ```bash helm status my-api helm get values my-api helm get manifest my-api ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Q10. Should you store plaintext passwords in `values.yaml`?
text: **No.** Use a proper secret-management mechanism. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 37. Your Hands-On Helm Lab
text: Now actually do this.

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Step 1 — Create chart
text: ```bash helm create my-api ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Step 2 — Inspect
text: ```bash cd my-api ls ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Step 3 — Validate
text: ```bash helm lint . ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Step 4 — Render
text: ```bash helm template my-api . ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Step 5 — Install
text: ```bash helm install my-api . ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Step 6 — Check
text: ```bash helm list kubectl get pods kubectl get svc ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Step 7 — Change replicas
text: Edit: ```yaml replicaCount: 3 ``` Then: ```bash helm upgrade my-api . ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 38. Then Break It
text: This is where actual learning happens. Change: ```yaml image: repository: nonexistent-image ``` Run: ```bash helm upgrade my-api . ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You'll probably see something like: ```text ImagePullBackOff ``` Now troubleshoot: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` Fix the image. Then upgrade again. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 39. Practice Environment Configuration
text: Create: ```text values-dev.yaml values-prod.yaml ``` Dev: ```yaml replicaCount: 1 image: tag: "dev" ``` Prod: ```yaml replicaCount: 3 image: tag: "1.0.0" ``` Deploy: ```bash helm install dev-api . -f values-dev.yaml ``` and: ```bash helm install prod-api . -f values-prod.yaml ``` Now you've demonstrated one of Helm's most important real-world use cases. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 40. What You Actually Need to Remember
text: Don't memorize hundreds of Helm template functions. For your SWE/backend role, remember this: ```text Helm ↓ Chart ↓ values.yaml ↓ Templates ↓ Rendered Kubernetes YAML ↓ Release ``` And these commands: ```bash helm create helm lint helm template helm install helm upgrade helm upgrade --install helm list helm status helm history helm rollback helm get values helm get manifest helm uninstall ``` If you know those and understand what happens underneath, you're in good shape. ---

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: 41. Helm in Your Final Production Architecture
text: Eventually your stack becomes: ```text GitHub │ ↓ GitHub Actions │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ Docker Terraform │ │ ↓ ↓ ECR AWS │ │ └────────┬────────┘ ↓ EKS │ Helm │ ┌────────┼────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Deployment Service HPA │ Pods │ ┌──────┼───────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Redis RDS S3 ``` This is exactly where Helm fits into the larger DevOps system you've been learning. ---

heading: Chapter 25 Takeaway
text: You should now understand: ```text ✅ Why Helm exists ✅ What a Chart is ✅ What a Release is ✅ Chart.yaml ✅ values.yaml ✅ Templates ✅ .Values ✅ .Release ✅ Environment-specific values ✅ helm install ✅ helm upgrade ✅ helm rollback ✅ Helm history ✅ Helm repositories ✅ Chart dependencies ✅ Helm vs kubectl ✅ Helm vs Docker ✅ Helm vs Terraform ✅ Helm + ECR ✅ Helm + Kubernetes ✅ Helm + GitHub Actions ✅ Helm debugging ✅ Helm security considerations ```

title: Chapter 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Chapter 25 — Revision Sheet: Helm — Kubernetes Package Management
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md). Goal: create, configure, install, upgrade, roll back and troubleshoot a Helm-based Kubernetes application.

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Why Helm
text: Without Helm: `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml / service.yaml / configmap.yaml / ingress.yaml / hpa.yaml`, and per-environment copies (`deployment-dev/staging/prod.yaml`) that differ in image, replicas, CPU, memory, hostname, DB config. **Helm = package manager + templating system (+ release management) for Kubernetes applications** — like npm for Node.js and apt for Linux. | Term | Meaning | |---|---| | **Chart** | Package: templates + configuration (values) + metadata (+ optional dependencies) that generate Kubernetes manifests | | **Release** | An **installed instance** of a chart (`dev-api`, `prod-api` from the same chart) | | **values.yaml** | Configurable defaults (replicaCount, image.repository/tag, service, containerPort, resources) | | **Templates** | Kubernetes YAML with `{{ ... }}` expressions | Flow: Helm CLI → Chart (Templates + Values + metadata + dependencies) → rendered Kubernetes manifests → Kubernetes API. Same chart, different values per environment.

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Chart layout (`helm create my-api`)
text: ```text my-api/ ├── Chart.yaml # metadata ├── values.yaml # default configuration ├── charts/ # dependencies ├── templates/ # deployment.yaml service.yaml ingress.yaml hpa.yaml serviceaccount.yaml _helpers.tpl tests/ └── .helmignore ``` ```yaml # Chart.yaml apiVersion: v2 name: my-api description: A Helm chart for my Node.js API type: application version: 0.1.0 # version of the CHART appVersion: "1.0.0" # version of the APPLICATION (not necessarily equal) ``` ```yaml # values.yaml replicaCount: 2 image: { repository: my-api, tag: "1.0.0" } service: { type: ClusterIP, port: 80 } containerPort: 3000 resources: requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi" } limits: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" } ```

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Templating
text: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api spec: replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} selector: matchLabels: app: {{ .Release.Name }}-api template: metadata: labels: app: {{ .Release.Name }}-api spec: containers: - name: api image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}" ports: - containerPort: {{ .Values.containerPort }} resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }} ``` - `.Values` = values supplied to the chart (`.Values.image.repository` → `my-api`, `.Values.image.tag` → `1.0.0`). `.Release.Name` = release name given at install (`helm install my-api ./my-api` → `my-api`) — used to build resource names. `replicaCount: 5` ⇒ `replicas: 5`.

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Environments and precedence
text: `values.yaml` (base: replicaCount 2, tag latest) · `values-dev.yaml` (1 replica, tag `dev`) · `values-prod.yaml` (5 replicas, tag `1.4.2`): ```bash helm install dev-api ./my-api -f values-dev.yaml helm install prod-api ./my-api -f values-prod.yaml ``` **Precedence:** default values → values file(s) → `--set` (the more specific override wins; `--set replicaCount=10` beats `values-prod.yaml`'s 5 beats default 2).

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Commands (memorise)
text: | Command | Purpose | |---|---| | `helm version` | Verify install (common: `curl .../get-helm-3 \| bash`) | | `helm create my-api` | Scaffold chart | | `helm lint ./my-api` | Check chart for common problems (template syntax errors, e.g. "unexpected EOF") | | `helm template my-api ./my-api` | **Render YAML locally without installing** — first debugging command | | `helm install my-api ./my-api` | Install (creates a release) | | `helm list` | List releases | | `helm upgrade prod-api ./my-api -f values-prod.yaml` | Update a release | | `helm upgrade --install my-api ./my-api` | Install if absent, upgrade if present — **CI/CD staple** | | `helm upgrade my-api ./my-api --dry-run` | Detect rendering/config issues before changing the cluster | | `helm history prod-api` | Revisions (1 deployed, 2 deployed, 3 deployed) | | `helm rollback prod-api 2` | Roll back to revision 2 | | `helm status my-api` / `helm get values my-api` / `helm get manifest my-api` | Inspect what Helm actually deployed | | `helm uninstall my-api` | Remove release | | `helm repo add <name> <url>` / `helm repo update` / `helm search repo <name>` | Chart repositories | | `helm package ./my-api` | Produces `my-api-0.1.0.tgz` | Workflow: edit chart → `helm lint` → `helm template` → `helm install/upgrade`.

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: CI/CD
text: ```bash helm upgrade --install my-api ./helm/my-api \ --namespace production --create-namespace \ -f ./helm/my-api/values-prod.yaml \ --set image.tag=$GITHUB_SHA ``` Pipeline: git push → GitHub Actions → tests → build → Docker image → push to ECR → `helm upgrade` → Kubernetes. Tag images with the **Git SHA** (`my-api:8f42c91`) not `latest` → production ↔ image ↔ commit traceability and easier rollback. ECR example: `123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/my-api:1.2.0` with `values-prod.yaml` (replicaCount 4, ClusterIP, port 80, containerPort 3000).

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Debugging workflow
text: Helm configuration → rendered YAML → Kubernetes resources → Pods → application. `helm status` → `helm get values` → `helm get manifest` → then `kubectl get pods / describe pod / logs`. - *Template syntax error:* `helm lint`. *Wrong value (expected 5 replicas got 2):* `helm get values`, `helm template`. *Helm succeeded but Pod broken* (`CrashLoopBackOff`): Helm isn't the problem anymore → `kubectl logs/describe`.

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Comparisons
text: | | | |---|---| | **Helm vs kubectl** | kubectl: directly manages Kubernetes resources (`kubectl apply -f`); Helm: packages/configures/manages Kubernetes *applications/releases* (still ends up as Kubernetes resources) | | **Helm vs Docker** | Docker packages app + dependencies → container image; Helm packages Kubernetes manifests + configuration → chart. Source → Docker → image → Helm → Kubernetes deployment | | **Helm vs Terraform** | Terraform = infrastructure (VPC, EKS, RDS, S3, IAM); Helm = Kubernetes applications (Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, HPA). Often both: Terraform → AWS infra → EKS → Helm → applications (boundaries can overlap) | **Dependencies:** a chart can depend on others (Redis, PostgreSQL), but with managed services keep DB in Terraform/RDS and the Node.js API in Helm — cleaner separation. **Security:** don't put `databasePassword: mypassword` in `values.yaml`; **Helm is not a secret-management solution**. Better: AWS Secrets Manager → External Secrets/secret integration → Kubernetes Secret → Pod.

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Lab and practice
text: Create chart → inspect → `helm lint .` → `helm template my-api .` → `helm install my-api .` → `helm list`, `kubectl get pods/svc` → set `replicaCount: 3` → `helm upgrade my-api .`. **Break it:** set `image.repository: nonexistent-image` → `helm upgrade` → `ImagePullBackOff` → `kubectl describe pod` → fix → upgrade. **Environments:** `values-dev.yaml` (1 replica, tag dev) and `values-prod.yaml` (3 replicas, tag 1.0.0), install `dev-api` and `prod-api`.

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: One-line interview answer
text: *Helm lets us package and template Kubernetes applications so the same deployment definitions can be reused across environments with different configuration, while providing release versioning, upgrades and rollbacks.*

title: Revision 25 — Helm: Kubernetes Package Management
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - `toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12` converts the values map to YAML and indents it 12 spaces on a new line; `{{-` trims preceding whitespace. Other common template pieces: `_helpers.tpl` with `define`/`include`, `default`, `quote`, `required`, `if`, `range`, `with`. - Exact precedence (low → high): chart `values.yaml` < parent chart values < `-f` files (later files override earlier) < `--set`/`--set-string`/`--set-file` (later flags win). - `helm rollback` creates a **new revision** that re-applies an old one (history is preserved). Helm 3 has no Tiller; release state is stored as **Secrets** in the release namespace (`sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<rev>`). - CI hardening flags: `--atomic` (roll back automatically on failure), `--wait`, `--timeout`. The `helm diff` plugin previews changes; `helm test` runs chart tests; chart **hooks** run Jobs before/after install/upgrade (e.g. DB migrations). `helm dependency update` writes `Chart.lock`. - Secret handling options: External Secrets Operator, SOPS/helm-secrets, sealed-secrets. - Piping a script to `bash` (the install one-liner) trusts the download; prefer your package manager or verify the checksum.
