title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
text: > **Source:** Response 26 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-26.txt`, lines 1–1625) · **Part II — Advanced extension (Responses 25–36)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch26-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We now move from **Helm → GitOps → ArgoCD**. You already know Git, GitHub Actions, Docker, Kubernetes, Helm, and Terraform, so this response will connect them into a modern deployment model. The most important thing to understand is: > **GitOps means Git becomes the source of truth for the desired state of your infrastructure/application deployment, and an automated system continuously makes the actual environment match that state.** ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 1. Traditional Deployment vs GitOps
text: You've already learned a traditional CI/CD pipeline: ```text Developer ↓ GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Test ↓ Build ↓ Docker Image ↓ ECR ↓ kubectl / Helm ↓ Kubernetes ``` GitHub Actions performs the deployment. That's perfectly valid. With GitOps: ```text Developer ↓ GitHub ↓ CI ↓ Build Docker Image ↓ ECR ↓ Update deployment configuration ↓ GitOps Repository ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes ``` The important difference:

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Traditional CD
text: ```text CI/CD system ↓ "Deploy this" ↓ Kubernetes ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: GitOps
text: ```text Git ↓ "This is what production SHOULD look like" ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 2. Desired State vs Actual State
text: This is the core concept. Suppose Git says: ```yaml replicas: 5 ``` But Kubernetes currently has: ```text 3 Pods ``` Then: ```text Desired state = 5 Actual state = 3 ``` ArgoCD detects the difference. It attempts to reconcile: ```text Git ↓ 5 replicas ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes ↓ 5 replicas ``` This is called: > **Reconciliation** You already encountered this idea in Kubernetes itself. Kubernetes controllers continuously try to make: ```text actual state → desired state ``` ArgoCD applies the same general philosophy at the application deployment level. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 3. What Is GitOps?
text: A useful interview definition: > **GitOps is an operational model where Git stores the declarative desired state of applications/infrastructure, and automated controllers continuously reconcile the running environment with that state.** The important words are: ```text Git Declarative Desired state Automation Reconciliation ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 4. Why Git?
text: Suppose someone manually runs: ```bash kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=10 ``` Now Kubernetes has: ```text 10 replicas ``` But Git says: ```text 5 replicas ``` What should production be? With GitOps: ```text Git = source of truth ``` So the configuration should be changed in Git if the desired state really is 10. This gives you: ```text version history auditability review rollback reproducibility ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 5. GitOps Repository
text: A common structure: ```text gitops-repo/ │ ├── apps/ │ └── api/ │ ├── Chart.yaml │ ├── values.yaml │ ├── values-prod.yaml │ └── templates/ │ └── environments/ ├── dev/ ├── staging/ └── production/ ``` Another common approach: ```text my-app/ ├── src/ ├── Dockerfile └── package.json my-app-gitops/ ├── dev/ ├── staging/ └── production/ ``` The exact repository structure varies. The principle matters more: ```text Application source ≠ Deployment configuration ``` They can be separated. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 6. Application Repository vs GitOps Repository
text: You might have:

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Application repo
text: ```text backend/ ├── src/ ├── package.json ├── Dockerfile └── tests/ ``` This contains: ```text application code tests Dockerfile ``` Then:

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: GitOps repo
text: ```text backend-deployment/ ├── helm/ │ └── backend/ └── environments/ ├── dev/ ├── staging/ └── production/ ``` This contains: ```text Kubernetes configuration Helm values deployment configuration environment configuration ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 7. Where Does GitHub Actions Fit?
text: This is a very important interview question. GitHub Actions can handle: ```text CI ``` and potentially: ```text build artifacts/images ``` ArgoCD handles: ```text deployment synchronization ``` For example: ```text Developer ↓ Git push ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Tests ↓ Docker build ↓ Push image to ECR ↓ Update GitOps repo ↓ ArgoCD notices change ↓ Kubernetes ``` This creates a clean separation: ```text CI → GitHub Actions CD → ArgoCD ``` Not the only possible architecture, but a very common one. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 8. Why Not Just Let GitHub Actions Run `kubectl apply`?
text: You can. It's not inherently wrong. But consider: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ kubectl apply ↓ Kubernetes ``` What happens if someone manually changes Kubernetes? Or if the CI system isn't running? Or if the cluster drifts away from the configuration? GitOps gives you continuous reconciliation. ```text Git ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes ``` ArgoCD continuously checks whether: ```text desired state == actual state ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 9. ArgoCD
text: Argo CD is a declarative GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. Its job is essentially: ```text Git ↓ Read desired configuration ↓ Compare with Kubernetes ↓ Detect differences ↓ Synchronize ↓ Kubernetes ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 10. ArgoCD Architecture
text: Simplified: ```text Git Repository │ ↓ ArgoCD Server │ ↓ ArgoCD Controllers │ ↓ Kubernetes API │ ↓ Application ``` ArgoCD has multiple components internally, but for interviews you primarily need to understand: ```text ArgoCD API/UI Repository access Application controller Kubernetes API ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 11. Install ArgoCD Locally
text: Since you've already learned Kubernetes with `kind`, we can use that. Check: ```bash kubectl get nodes ``` Install ArgoCD: ```bash kubectl create namespace argocd ``` Then: ```bash kubectl apply -n argocd \ -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get pods -n argocd ``` You should eventually see ArgoCD components running. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 12. Access ArgoCD
text: One simple local-development approach is: ```bash kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server \ -n argocd 8080:443 ``` Then access the ArgoCD server through: ```text https://localhost:8080 ``` For local learning, this is enough. Production access would normally involve proper ingress/load balancing, TLS, authentication, networking, and security. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 13. ArgoCD CLI
text: Install the ArgoCD CLI appropriate for your OS. Then: ```bash argocd version ``` The CLI lets you interact with the ArgoCD server. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 14. ArgoCD Application
text: The central ArgoCD object is: ```text Application ``` An ArgoCD Application essentially says: > "Take this configuration from this Git repository/path and synchronize it to this Kubernetes cluster/namespace." Example: ```yaml apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: Application metadata: name: my-api spec: project: default source: repoURL: https://github.com/example/my-gitops-repo.git targetRevision: main path: apps/my-api destination: server: https://kubernetes.default.svc namespace: production syncPolicy: automated: {} ``` This is a **Custom Resource**. Remember [Chapter 20](../05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md)? We learned that Kubernetes can be extended using CRDs. ArgoCD uses Kubernetes APIs and custom resources such as: ```text Application ``` So this also connects directly to [Chapter 29](../05-kubernetes/ch29-crds-operators.md) later. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Source
text: ```yaml source: repoURL: ... targetRevision: main path: apps/my-api ``` Means: ```text Git repository ↓ branch/revision ↓ directory ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Destination
text: ```yaml destination: server: https://kubernetes.default.svc namespace: production ``` Means: ```text which Kubernetes cluster? which namespace? ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Sync Policy
text: ```yaml syncPolicy: automated: {} ``` means ArgoCD can automatically synchronize changes. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Manual
text: Git changes: ```text Git ↓ ArgoCD detects change ↓ OutOfSync ``` You then explicitly synchronize.

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Automatic
text: ```text Git ↓ change detected ↓ ArgoCD ↓ sync ↓ Kubernetes ``` Automatic synchronization is useful for environments where that operating model is appropriate. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 17. Sync Status
text: One important ArgoCD concept: ```text Synced ``` means: ```text Git desired state ≈ Kubernetes state ``` Whereas: ```text OutOfSync ``` means: ```text Git desired state ≠ Kubernetes state ``` This is extremely important. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 18. Health Status
text: ArgoCD also provides application health information. Conceptually: ```text Healthy Progressing Degraded Missing Unknown ``` This isn't exactly the same thing as sync status. For example: ```text Synced + Degraded ``` could mean: > Kubernetes has the desired manifests, but the deployed application isn't healthy. That's an important distinction. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 19. GitOps Flow With Helm
text: Now combine [Chapter 25](../05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md) and Chapter 26. Your GitOps repo might contain: ```text api-chart/ ├── Chart.yaml ├── values.yaml └── templates/ ``` ArgoCD can use the Helm chart. Flow: ```text Git ↓ Helm Chart ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Helm rendering ↓ Kubernetes manifests ↓ Kubernetes ``` You don't necessarily need to manually run: ```bash helm upgrade ``` ArgoCD can manage the application. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 20. Production Example
text: Suppose your Docker image is: ```text ECR: my-api:abc123 ``` GitOps repository has: ```yaml image: repository: 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/my-api tag: "abc123" ``` CI builds: ```text abc123 ``` pushes it to ECR, then updates the GitOps configuration: ```yaml tag: "abc123" ``` Commit: ```text Deploy my-api abc123 ``` ArgoCD sees: ```text Git changed ``` Then: ```text Git ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Helm ↓ Kubernetes ↓ New Pods ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 21. Complete GitOps Pipeline
text: This is the architecture I want you to understand: ```text Developer │ ↓ Git │ ↓ GitHub Actions │ ┌───────┴───────┐ ↓ ↓ Tests Docker Build │ ↓ ECR │ ↓ Update GitOps Repo │ ↓ Git Repository │ ↓ ArgoCD │ ↓ EKS │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Pod Pod Pod ``` This is a very strong interview architecture. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 22. GitOps vs CI/CD
text: Don't say: > "GitOps replaces CI/CD." Better: > **GitOps is an approach to continuous delivery/deployment where Git serves as the source of truth and a controller reconciles the cluster with that state.** You can still have: ```text CI → GitHub Actions CD → ArgoCD ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 23. GitOps vs Infrastructure as Code
text: Another common question.

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Terraform
text: Usually manages infrastructure: ```text VPC EKS RDS IAM S3 ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: GitOps/ArgoCD
text: Usually manages Kubernetes application state: ```text Deployment Service Ingress ConfigMap HPA ``` You might have: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS infrastructure ↓ EKS cluster ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes applications ↓ EKS ``` This is a very clean separation. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 24. What About Terraform + ArgoCD?
text: A common architecture: ```text Terraform ↓ VPC EKS IAM RDS S3 ↓ Cluster exists ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Applications deployed ``` Terraform creates the platform. ArgoCD manages workloads. This isn't an absolute rule, but it's a useful mental model. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 25. Drift Detection
text: This is one of GitOps' biggest advantages. Git says: ```yaml replicas: 3 ``` Someone manually runs: ```bash kubectl scale deployment my-api --replicas=10 ``` Now: ```text Desired = 3 Actual = 10 ``` ArgoCD detects: ```text OutOfSync ``` Depending on the sync policy, it can reconcile the cluster back toward Git's declared state. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 26. The Important GitOps Principle
text: This is worth remembering: > **Don't treat the Kubernetes cluster as the place where you permanently edit configuration. Treat Git as the place where desired configuration is changed and reviewed.** Instead of: ```bash kubectl edit deployment api ``` prefer: ```text change Git ↓ Pull Request ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes ``` This gives you an audit trail. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 27. Rollbacks
text: Suppose: ```text Production ↓ version 1.5 ``` You deploy: ```text version 1.6 ``` and it breaks. With GitOps, you can revert the Git commit: ```text Git history: A → B → C → D ↑ broken ``` Revert: ```text A → B → C → D → E ↑ rollback change ``` ArgoCD detects the desired state change and synchronizes it. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 28. Why GitOps Is Powerful
text: You gain:

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Auditability
text: Who changed production? ```text Git commit ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Review
text: Who approved the change? ```text Pull Request ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Reproducibility
text: What should production look like? ```text Git ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Rollback
text: What was the previous configuration? ```text Git history ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Drift detection
text: Does Kubernetes match Git? ```text ArgoCD ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 29. GitOps Security
text: GitOps doesn't magically make deployments secure. You still need: ```text RBAC Secrets management Least privilege Image scanning Signed/verified images where appropriate Protected branches PR reviews CI security ArgoCD access controls Kubernetes security Network security ``` Especially: **Don't put plaintext production passwords into Git just because it's a GitOps repository.** Use: ```text Secrets Manager External Secrets Sealed Secrets Vault ``` or another appropriate secret-management mechanism. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 30. What GitOps Does NOT Mean
text: GitOps does **not** mean: > "Everything must be stored directly in Git." Secrets may need special handling. It also doesn't mean: > "Never use kubectl." You will still use: ```bash kubectl get kubectl logs kubectl describe ``` for debugging and operations. The important distinction is: ```text kubectl → inspect/debug/operate GitOps → manage desired configuration ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 31. ArgoCD Troubleshooting
text: Suppose ArgoCD says: ```text OutOfSync ``` Check: ```text Git commit ↓ Repository ↓ Path ↓ Branch/revision ↓ Rendered Helm/manifests ↓ Kubernetes ``` Possible problems: ```text wrong repository wrong branch wrong path invalid YAML wrong values permission problem cluster access problem resource conflict ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 32. ArgoCD vs Helm
text: Very common interview question. They are not direct competitors.

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Helm
text: ```text Template/package Kubernetes applications ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: ArgoCD
text: ```text Continuously synchronize desired application state from Git to Kubernetes ``` They can work together: ```text Git ↓ Helm Chart ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Jenkins
text: General-purpose automation/CI/CD server. Can do: ```text build test package deploy ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: ArgoCD
text: Kubernetes-focused GitOps CD controller. ```text Git ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes ``` A company could use: ```text Jenkins → CI ArgoCD → CD ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: GitHub Actions
text: Excellent for: ```text CI tests builds Docker images security scans artifact creation ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: ArgoCD
text: Excellent for: ```text Kubernetes deployment reconciliation drift detection GitOps ``` A modern pipeline can therefore be: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ Build + Test + Docker ↓ ECR ↓ GitOps repo ↓ ArgoCD ↓ EKS ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 35. Hands-On Mini Project
text: Now let's make the concepts real. You already have: ```text kind cluster Helm chart Node.js API ``` Create: ```text my-gitops-repo/ └── apps/ └── my-api/ ├── Chart.yaml ├── values.yaml └── templates/ ``` Put your Helm chart there. Commit: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Add my-api GitOps deployment" git push ``` Then create an ArgoCD Application pointing to: ```text your Git repository + apps/my-api ``` ArgoCD will read the chart. Then: ```text Git ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Helm ↓ Kubernetes ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 36. Test GitOps Yourself
text: Change: ```yaml replicaCount: 2 ``` to: ```yaml replicaCount: 4 ``` Commit: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Scale API to four replicas" git push ``` ArgoCD detects the change. Then: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You should eventually see: ```text 4 Pods ``` You have now experienced GitOps. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 37. Test Drift Detection
text: Now manually do: ```bash kubectl scale deployment my-api --replicas=1 ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get deployment ``` Your cluster now differs from Git. ArgoCD should identify the application as out of sync. If automated synchronization is enabled, ArgoCD can reconcile it back toward the Git state. This experiment is **extremely valuable** because it makes the entire GitOps idea click. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Interviewer:
text: > A developer manually changed a Kubernetes deployment in production. How would you handle it in a GitOps environment? Good answer: > "I'd first determine whether the manual change was intentional. The desired state should normally be changed in the Git repository through the normal review process. I'd check ArgoCD's sync status and Git history, then either revert the manual drift or create the corresponding Git change. If automated sync is enabled, ArgoCD can reconcile the cluster back to the Git-defined state." That's much stronger than simply saying: > "Use ArgoCD." ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 39. Important Mental Model
text: Memorize this: ```text GIT │ Desired State │ ↓ ArgoCD │ Reconciliation │ ↓ Kubernetes │ Actual State ``` If: ```text Desired = Actual ``` everything is synchronized. If: ```text Desired ≠ Actual ``` you have drift/out-of-sync state. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Must know deeply
text: ```text GitOps Desired state Declarative configuration Reconciliation Drift ArgoCD Application Sync Auto-sync Git as source of truth Helm + ArgoCD CI + CD separation Rollback ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Must be able to do
text: ```text Install ArgoCD Create Application Connect Git repository Deploy Helm chart Sync application Check status Detect drift Rollback Git change Troubleshoot sync problems ```

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Awareness
text: ```text App-of-Apps ApplicationSet Multi-cluster ArgoCD Progressive delivery Argo Rollouts ``` We'll encounter some of these concepts later if useful, but they're not prerequisites for your SWE interviews. ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: 41. Final Comparison
text: | Tool | Primary purpose | |---|---| | Git | Version control | | GitHub Actions | CI/automation | | Docker | Containerization | | ECR | Container registry | | Kubernetes | Container orchestration | | Helm | Kubernetes packaging/templates | | ArgoCD | GitOps continuous delivery | | Terraform | Infrastructure as Code | | Ansible | Configuration management | Put them together: ```text Git ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Docker ↓ ECR ↓ GitOps Repository ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Helm ↓ Kubernetes/EKS ↓ AWS Infrastructure ``` And Terraform sits underneath managing much of the infrastructure: ```text Terraform ↓ VPC EKS RDS IAM S3 ... ``` ---

title: Chapter 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Chapter 26 Summary
text: You've now added another important layer: ```text GIT │ Source of Truth │ ↓ GitOps │ ↓ ArgoCD │ Reconcile │ ↓ Kubernetes │ Helm │ Application ``` You should now be able to explain **why GitOps exists, how ArgoCD works, how Helm fits into it, how GitHub Actions and ArgoCD complement each other, what drift is, and how a production GitOps deployment works.** <!-- SOURCE-END --> --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 25: Helm: Kubernetes Package Management](../05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md) · [Chapter 27: Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD](ch27-jenkins-advanced-cicd.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch26-revision.md)

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Chapter 26 — Revision Sheet: GitOps + ArgoCD
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch26-gitops-argocd.md). Core statement: **GitOps = Git is the source of truth for the desired state of infrastructure/application deployment, and an automated system continuously makes the actual environment match it.**

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Traditional CD vs GitOps
text: | Traditional | GitOps | |---|---| | GitHub → CI/CD → Test → Build → Docker → ECR → `kubectl`/Helm → Kubernetes (the pipeline *pushes* the deployment) | GitHub → CI → Build image → ECR → **update deployment config in GitOps repo** → **ArgoCD** → Kubernetes (Git says "this is what production SHOULD look like"; a controller applies it) | - **Interview definition:** *GitOps is an operational model where Git stores the declarative desired state of applications/infrastructure, and automated controllers continuously reconcile the running environment with that state.* Keywords: Git, declarative, desired state, automation, reconciliation. - **Desired vs actual:** Git `replicas: 5`, cluster 3 Pods → ArgoCD detects the difference and reconciles → **reconciliation** (same philosophy as Kubernetes controllers: actual → desired). - **Why Git:** version history, auditability, review (PRs), rollback, reproducibility. If someone runs `kubectl scale ... --replicas=10` while Git says 5, Git is the truth — change Git if 10 is truly desired.

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Repositories
text: ```text gitops-repo/ ├── apps/api/{Chart.yaml, values.yaml, values-prod.yaml, templates/} └── environments/{dev, staging, production} # or separate repos: my-app/ (src, Dockerfile, package.json) my-app-gitops/ (dev, staging, production) ``` **Application source ≠ deployment configuration** — they can be separated: application repo (code, tests, Dockerfile) vs GitOps repo (Kubernetes config, Helm values, environment config).

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Roles: CI vs CD
text: GitHub Actions = **CI** (tests, Docker build, push image to ECR, update GitOps repo, security scans, artifact creation). ArgoCD = **CD** (deployment sync, reconciliation, drift detection). Not the only architecture, but very common. *Don't say "GitOps replaces CI/CD"* — GitOps is an approach to CD where Git is the source of truth and a controller reconciles the cluster. Why not just `kubectl apply` from GitHub Actions? You can, but then manual cluster changes or a non-running CI leave the cluster drifting; GitOps gives **continuous reconciliation** (`desired == actual`).

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: ArgoCD
text: **Argo CD** = declarative GitOps CD tool for Kubernetes: Git → read desired configuration → compare with Kubernetes → detect differences → synchronise. Components to know: API/UI server, repository access, **application controller**, Kubernetes API. ```bash kubectl get nodes kubectl create namespace argocd kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml kubectl get pods -n argocd kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443 # https://localhost:8080 (local learning only) argocd version # CLI ``` Production access normally needs ingress/load balancing, TLS, authentication, networking, security.

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: The Application custom resource
text: ```yaml apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: Application metadata: name: my-api spec: project: default source: repoURL: https://github.com/example/my-gitops-repo.git targetRevision: main # branch/revision path: apps/my-api # directory destination: server: https://kubernetes.default.svc # which cluster namespace: production # which namespace syncPolicy: automated: {} ``` It says: *"Take this configuration from this Git repo/path and synchronise it to this cluster/namespace."* It is a **Custom Resource** (Kubernetes extended with CRDs — covered in [Chapter 29](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch29-crds-operators.md)). - **Sync:** manual (Git changes → ArgoCD detects → `OutOfSync` → you sync) vs automatic (detect → sync → Kubernetes). - **Sync status:** `Synced` (Git ≈ cluster) vs `OutOfSync` (Git ≠ cluster). - **Health status:** Healthy, Progressing, Degraded, Missing, Unknown — **not the same as sync status**; `Synced + Degraded` = the desired manifests are applied but the app isn't healthy. - **With Helm:** repo contains the chart (`api-chart/{Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/}`); ArgoCD renders Helm → manifests → Kubernetes; no manual `helm upgrade`.

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Production example flow
text: CI builds image `abc123` → push to ECR → update GitOps values (`image.repository: 1234….dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/my-api`, `tag: "abc123"`) → commit "Deploy my-api abc123" → ArgoCD sees Git changed → Helm → Kubernetes → new Pods. Full pipeline: Developer → Git → GitHub Actions (Tests ∥ Docker build) → ECR → update GitOps repo → ArgoCD → EKS → Pods.

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Drift, rollback, principles
text: - **Drift:** Git `replicas: 3`, someone runs `kubectl scale ... --replicas=10` → desired 3 / actual 10 → ArgoCD `OutOfSync`; depending on sync policy it can reconcile back. - **Principle:** don't treat the cluster as the place where you permanently edit config — change Git → PR → review → merge → ArgoCD → Kubernetes (audit trail). Instead of `kubectl edit deployment api`. - **Rollback:** revert the Git commit (A→B→C→D(broken)→E(revert)); ArgoCD synchronises the new desired state. - **Benefits:** auditability (who changed production = Git commit), review (who approved = PR), reproducibility (what should production look like = Git), rollback (Git history), drift detection (does Kubernetes match Git = ArgoCD). - **GitOps security:** RBAC, secrets management, least privilege, image scanning, signed/verified images, protected branches, PR reviews, CI security, ArgoCD access controls, Kubernetes + network security. **Don't put plaintext production passwords in Git** — use Secrets Manager, External Secrets, Sealed Secrets, Vault. - **What GitOps does NOT mean:** everything stored directly in Git (secrets need special handling), or "never use kubectl" — `kubectl` = inspect/debug/operate; GitOps = manage desired configuration.

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Troubleshooting `OutOfSync`
text: Git commit → repository → path → branch/revision → rendered Helm/manifests → Kubernetes. Causes: wrong repository, branch or path; invalid YAML; wrong values; permission problem; cluster-access problem; resource conflict.

title: Revision 26 — GitOps + ArgoCD
heading: Added notes / precision (not in source)
text: - **Self-heal precision:** `syncPolicy.automated: {}` only syncs when **Git changes**. To have ArgoCD **revert manual cluster edits** (the drift experiment) you need `automated: { selfHeal: true }`; to delete resources removed from Git you need `prune: true`. Without `selfHeal` the app just shows `OutOfSync`. - The Application object normally lives in the `argocd` namespace (`metadata.namespace: argocd`); the source YAML omits it. `destination.server: https://kubernetes.default.svc` means the cluster ArgoCD itself runs in. - Initial login: user `admin`, password from `kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d`. Large CRDs in `install.yaml` may require `kubectl apply --server-side`. - Health statuses also include `Suspended`. - **Pull model:** ArgoCD runs *inside* the cluster and pulls from Git, so CI does not need cluster credentials — a security advantage over push-style `kubectl apply` from CI. - How CI "updates the GitOps repo": a commit by the pipeline (e.g. `yq`/`kustomize edit set image`) or Argo CD Image Updater. - Argo CD also supports Kustomize and plain YAML; sync features include waves, hooks and retry policies. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 25](ch25-revision.md) · [Full chapter 26](../docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch26-gitops-argocd.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 27](ch27-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
text: > **Source:** Response 27 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-27.txt`, lines 1–1728) · **Part II — Advanced extension (Responses 25–36)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch27-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) · *includes an editorial supplement at the end* <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> You've already learned GitHub Actions in depth. So the goal of this response is **not to relearn CI/CD**. Instead, we're going to understand: - Why Jenkins exists - Jenkins architecture - Controllers and agents - Jenkinsfiles - Declarative pipelines - Credentials - Artifacts - Webhooks - Docker builds - Deployment pipelines - Jenkins vs GitHub Actions - Jenkins + Docker + Kubernetes - Jenkins + GitOps/ArgoCD - Security - Practical setup - Troubleshooting - Interview questions The key idea: > **Jenkins is a general-purpose automation server that can implement CI/CD pipelines through code.** ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 1. Why Jenkins Exists
text: Imagine a company has: ```text Git repositories ↓ Build servers ↓ Testing ↓ Docker ↓ Artifact repositories ↓ Kubernetes ↓ AWS ``` They need automation. Jenkins can coordinate: ```text Code ↓ Build ↓ Test ↓ Package ↓ Deploy ``` Jenkins became extremely popular before newer cloud-native CI systems such as GitHub Actions became widespread. You'll still encounter Jenkins heavily in: - large enterprises - legacy systems - organizations with custom CI/CD infrastructure - environments requiring highly customized pipelines ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 2. Jenkins vs GitHub Actions
text: You already know GitHub Actions. Think:

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: GitHub Actions
text: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Runner ↓ Pipeline ```

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Jenkins
text: ```text Git repository ↓ Jenkins ↓ Controller ↓ Agents ↓ Pipeline ``` Jenkins is more infrastructure-oriented. You generally manage the Jenkins installation, agents, plugins, credentials, etc. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 3. Jenkins Architecture
text: Basic architecture: ```text Jenkins │ Controller │ ┌──────────┼──────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Agent Agent Agent │ │ │ Linux Docker Windows ``` The important pieces:

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Controller
text: Coordinates Jenkins. It manages things like: ```text jobs pipelines configuration scheduling credentials agents ```

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Agent
text: Actually executes work. For example: ```text Agent ↓ npm ci ↓ npm test ↓ docker build ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 4. Why Use Agents?
text: Suppose you have: ```text Node.js builds Java builds Android builds Docker builds ``` You might use different agents. ```text Controller │ ├── Node Agent ├── Java Agent └── Android Agent ``` This keeps workloads isolated. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 5. Jenkins Pipeline
text: A Jenkins pipeline defines: ```text what should happen and in what order ``` Example: ```text Checkout ↓ Install ↓ Lint ↓ Test ↓ Build ↓ Docker ↓ Push ↓ Deploy ``` Modern Jenkins pipelines are generally written as code. That leads to:

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 6. Jenkinsfile
text: A `Jenkinsfile` lives in your repository. Example: ```groovy pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Checkout') { steps { checkout scm } } stage('Install') { steps { sh 'npm ci' } } stage('Test') { steps { sh 'npm test' } } stage('Build') { steps { sh 'npm run build' } } } } ``` This is called a: > **Declarative Pipeline** ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 7. Declarative Pipeline Structure
text: The basic structure: ```groovy pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Build') { steps { sh 'npm run build' } } } } ``` Understand: ```text pipeline ↓ agent ↓ stages ↓ stage ↓ steps ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 8. `agent`
text: Example: ```groovy agent any ``` means Jenkins can execute the pipeline on an available agent. You can also target specific agents/labels. Conceptually: ```groovy agent { label 'docker' } ``` Meaning: > Run this pipeline on an agent labeled `docker`. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 9. Environment Variables
text: You can define: ```groovy environment { NODE_ENV = 'test' } ``` Then: ```groovy sh 'echo $NODE_ENV' ``` Environment variables are useful for configuration. But: > **Don't put secrets directly into Jenkinsfiles.** ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 10. Jenkins Credentials
text: Jenkins has a credentials store. You can store: ```text AWS credentials SSH keys tokens passwords API keys ``` and inject them into jobs. For example, conceptually: ```groovy withCredentials([ string( credentialsId: 'api-token', variable: 'API_TOKEN' ) ]) { sh 'some-command' } ``` The important security principle: ```text Secret ↓ Jenkins credential store ↓ Pipeline ``` rather than: ```text Secret ↓ Git repository ❌ ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 11. Jenkins + Git
text: Jenkins can connect to: ```text GitHub GitLab Bitbucket self-hosted Git ``` A common flow: ```text Developer ↓ git push ↓ GitHub ↓ Webhook ↓ Jenkins ↓ Pipeline ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 12. Webhooks
text: Suppose you push: ```bash git push origin main ``` GitHub can send an HTTP request to Jenkins: ```text GitHub │ │ webhook ↓ Jenkins │ ↓ Pipeline starts ``` This is better than constantly polling Git. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 13. Jenkins Pipeline With Node.js
text: A more realistic example: ```groovy pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Checkout') { steps { checkout scm } } stage('Install') { steps { sh 'npm ci' } } stage('Lint') { steps { sh 'npm run lint' } } stage('Typecheck') { steps { sh 'npm run typecheck' } } stage('Test') { steps { sh 'npm test' } } stage('Build') { steps { sh 'npm run build' } } } } ``` This should look familiar because you already learned the same CI concepts through GitHub Actions. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 14. Post Actions
text: You can define behavior after pipeline execution. Example: ```groovy post { always { echo 'Pipeline finished' } success { echo 'Build succeeded' } failure { echo 'Build failed' } } ``` This is useful for: ```text notifications cleanup artifact handling reporting ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 15. Artifacts
text: Suppose your build generates: ```text dist/ ``` You may want Jenkins to preserve it. Example: ```groovy post { success { archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'dist/**', fingerprint: true } } ``` Now the build artifact can be associated with that Jenkins build. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 16. Why Artifacts Matter
text: Imagine: ```text Build #100 Build #101 Build #102 ``` You want to know: ```text Which binary/image came from which build? ``` Artifacts and immutable versioning help establish traceability. This is the same principle we've discussed with: ```text Git SHA Docker image tags ECR ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 17. Jenkins + Docker
text: Now let's connect Jenkins with Docker. Pipeline: ```text Git ↓ Jenkins ↓ Tests ↓ Docker build ↓ Docker image ↓ Registry ``` Example: ```groovy stage('Docker Build') { steps { sh 'docker build -t my-api:${BUILD_NUMBER} .' } } ``` Then: ```groovy stage('Docker Push') { steps { sh 'docker push my-api:${BUILD_NUMBER}' } } ``` In production you'd normally authenticate securely to your registry and use a proper immutable tag such as a Git commit SHA. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 18. Jenkins + ECR
text: For AWS: ```text Jenkins ↓ AWS credentials/role ↓ ECR authentication ↓ docker build ↓ docker push ↓ ECR ``` Conceptually: ```bash aws ecr get-login-password \ --region ap-south-1 | docker login \ --username AWS \ --password-stdin \ <account>.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com ``` Then: ```bash docker build \ -t <repository>:<git-sha> . docker push \ <repository>:<git-sha> ``` The exact credentials strategy depends on your Jenkins environment. Prefer short-lived identity/role-based credentials where practical instead of permanent access keys. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 19. Jenkins + Kubernetes
text: Jenkins can deploy to Kubernetes. Traditional model: ```text Jenkins ↓ kubectl ↓ Kubernetes ``` For example: ```groovy stage('Deploy') { steps { sh ''' kubectl set image deployment/my-api \ my-api=my-api:${GIT_COMMIT} ''' } } ``` This works. But remember what we learned in [Chapter 26](ch26-gitops-argocd.md): > In a GitOps environment, Jenkins doesn't necessarily need to directly modify Kubernetes. Instead: ```text Jenkins ↓ Build image ↓ Update GitOps repository ↓ ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes ``` That's often a cleaner separation. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 20. Jenkins + ArgoCD
text: This is an excellent interview architecture. ```text Git │ ↓ Jenkins │ ┌──────┴──────┐ ↓ ↓ Test Docker │ ↓ ECR │ ↓ GitOps Repository │ ↓ ArgoCD │ ↓ Kubernetes ``` Jenkins handles: ```text CI build test package image ``` ArgoCD handles: ```text CD synchronization reconciliation deployment ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 21. Jenkins vs GitHub Actions vs ArgoCD
text: This distinction is important. | Tool | Primary role | |---|---| | GitHub Actions | CI/CD automation integrated with GitHub | | Jenkins | General-purpose CI/CD automation server | | ArgoCD | Kubernetes GitOps CD | | Helm | Kubernetes packaging/templates | | Terraform | Infrastructure as Code | They can coexist. Example enterprise architecture: ```text GitHub │ ↓ Jenkins │ ├── Test ├── Build └── Docker │ ↓ ECR │ ↓ GitOps Repository │ ↓ ArgoCD │ ↓ EKS ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 22. Jenkins Plugins
text: Jenkins has a huge plugin ecosystem. Plugins can integrate with: ```text Git Docker Kubernetes AWS Slack JUnit SonarQube security scanners ``` This is one reason Jenkins is powerful. But it's also one reason Jenkins can become complicated. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 23. Jenkins Controller Shouldn't Do Everything
text: A common architectural mistake: ```text Controller ↓ Build everything ``` Better: ```text Controller ↓ Schedule/orchestrate ↓ Agents ↓ Execute workloads ``` Why? Because builds can consume: ```text CPU Memory Disk Network ``` and you don't want to overload the Jenkins controller. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 24. Jenkins Agents in Kubernetes
text: A more modern setup: ```text Jenkins ↓ Kubernetes ↓ Ephemeral build Pods ``` A build agent Pod is created when needed. Then: ```text Build ↓ Pod ↓ Build finishes ↓ Pod removed ``` Advantages: ```text isolation elasticity clean environments scaling ``` This connects directly to your Kubernetes knowledge. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 25. Pipeline Parallelism
text: You can run independent stages in parallel. For example: ```text Build │ ┌──────┼──────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Unit Lint Security │ │ │ └──────┼──────┘ ↓ Deploy ``` Jenkins supports parallel stages. This reduces pipeline time when tasks are independent. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 26. Sequential vs Parallel
text: Suppose: ```text Tests = 5 min Lint = 2 min Security scan = 4 min ``` Sequential: ```text 5 + 2 + 4 = 11 min ``` Parallel: ```text max(5,2,4) ≈ 5 min ``` assuming enough agents/resources. This is a common CI/CD optimization. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 27. Pipeline Parameters
text: You can make pipelines configurable. For example: ```text ENVIRONMENT: dev staging production ``` Then: ```text Deploy ↓ Choose environment ↓ Use appropriate configuration ``` But production deployment should normally have stronger controls than arbitrary user input. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 28. Production Approvals
text: A mature pipeline might be: ```text Commit ↓ CI ↓ Tests ↓ Build ↓ Staging ↓ Integration tests ↓ Approval ↓ Production ``` This is where deployment governance comes into play. GitHub Actions has environments/approvals; Jenkins can implement approval steps as well. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 29. Jenkins Security
text: This is important.

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Don't:
text: ```text hardcode AWS keys hardcode passwords run everything as root allow unrestricted Jenkins access install random plugins ```

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Do:
text: ```text RBAC least privilege credential store HTTPS authentication authorization plugin updates agent isolation audit logs network restrictions secret rotation ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 30. Jenkins Supply Chain Security
text: Your CI server has enormous privileges. Imagine Jenkins can: ```text push Docker images deploy to Kubernetes access AWS ``` If Jenkins is compromised: ```text attacker ↓ Jenkins ↓ AWS ↓ Kubernetes ``` Potentially catastrophic. Therefore: ```text least privilege short-lived credentials isolated agents protected branches dependency scanning image scanning signed artifacts where appropriate ``` are important. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 31. Jenkins Credentials vs GitHub OIDC
text: You've learned AWS OIDC already. Traditional Jenkins might use: ```text Jenkins ↓ AWS access key ↓ AWS ``` Better where supported: ```text Jenkins workload identity ↓ AWS IAM role ↓ temporary credentials ``` The exact implementation depends on where Jenkins runs. The principle remains: > Avoid unnecessary long-lived credentials. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 32. Jenkins Pipeline With Docker + ECR + Kubernetes
text: A simplified conceptual pipeline: ```groovy pipeline { agent any environment { IMAGE = "my-api:${GIT_COMMIT}" } stages { stage('Test') { steps { sh 'npm ci' sh 'npm test' } } stage('Build') { steps { sh 'npm run build' } } stage('Docker') { steps { sh "docker build -t ${IMAGE} ." } } stage('Push') { steps { sh "docker push ${IMAGE}" } } stage('Deploy') { steps { sh 'kubectl apply -f k8s/' } } } } ``` This is intentionally simplified. A production pipeline needs: ```text authentication security scanning immutable image naming environment controls deployment strategy rollback observability ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 33. Better Production Architecture With GitOps
text: Rather than: ```text Jenkins → kubectl ``` you can use: ```text Jenkins ↓ Build ↓ Test ↓ Docker ↓ ECR ↓ Update GitOps repo ↓ ArgoCD ↓ EKS ``` This connects our last two responses. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Pipeline suddenly fails.
text: Don't immediately rerun it repeatedly. Check: ```text What stage failed? ↓ Build? Test? Docker? Registry? Credentials? Deployment? ``` For example: ```text Docker push failed ``` Investigate: ```text ECR reachable? credentials valid? repository exists? image tag valid? permissions? ``` ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 35. Jenkins Agent Offline
text: Suppose: ```text Jenkins ↓ Agent offline ``` Check: ```text network agent process resource exhaustion disk credentials Jenkins-agent connection container/node status ``` If Kubernetes is providing agents: ```text kubectl get pods kubectl describe pod kubectl logs ``` Now your Kubernetes troubleshooting knowledge becomes useful. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 36. Jenkins Disk Full
text: CI systems can accumulate: ```text workspace Docker images build artifacts logs cache ``` Check: ```bash df -h du -sh * ``` Potential solutions: ```text cleanup old builds remove unused Docker images artifact retention workspace cleanup log rotation larger disk ``` This is a real-world DevOps problem. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 37. Jenkins Pipeline Best Practices
text: Remember:

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 1. Pipeline as code
text: ```text Jenkinsfile ```

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 2. Small stages
text: ```text test build scan package deploy ```

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 3. Immutable artifacts
text: Don't overwrite: ```text latest ``` blindly. Prefer: ```text Git SHA build number version ```

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 4. Fail fast
text: Tests should stop bad builds early.

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 5. Least privilege
text: Pipeline shouldn't have unlimited production access.

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 6. Reproducible builds
text: Same source should produce predictable artifacts. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 38. Jenkins vs GitHub Actions — Interview Answer
text: If asked: > "Why would a company use Jenkins when GitHub Actions exists?" Don't say one is universally better. Say: > "GitHub Actions provides tightly integrated CI/CD for GitHub repositories and is convenient because runners, workflows, permissions and repository events are integrated into GitHub. Jenkins is a mature, highly extensible automation server with a large plugin ecosystem and can integrate with many source-control systems and internal infrastructure. Organizations with existing Jenkins infrastructure or highly customized pipelines may continue using it." That's the right level of answer. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 39. When Would YOU Use Jenkins?
text: For your projects:

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD

text: I'd generally prefer: ```text GitHub Actions ``` because it's simpler.

heading: 40. Jenkins Hands-On Exercise
text: If you want to practice locally:

text: ```bash docker volume create jenkins_home ``` Then: ```bash docker run -d \ --name jenkins \ -p 8080:8080 \ -p 50000:50000 \ -v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home \ jenkins/jenkins:lts ``` Check: ```bash docker ps ``` Logs: ```bash docker logs jenkins ``` Then access the Jenkins UI locally. **Important:** this is a learning setup, not a production deployment. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 41. Create a Pipeline
text: Create a repository containing: ```text my-api/ ├── package.json ├── src/ └── Jenkinsfile ``` Jenkins pipeline: ```groovy pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Install') { steps { sh 'npm ci' } } stage('Test') { steps { sh 'npm test' } } stage('Build') { steps { sh 'npm run build' } } } } ``` Connect Jenkins to your repository. Push: ```bash git push ``` Then: ```text GitHub ↓ Webhook ↓ Jenkins ↓ Pipeline ↓ Install ↓ Test ↓ Build ``` You've now actually used Jenkins. ---

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: 42. Add Docker

title: Chapter 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Jenkinsfile syntax the chapter describes but does not show
text: The chapter explains parallel stages, parameters, approvals and conditional stages in words and diagrams. Here is the corresponding declarative syntax. ```groovy pipeline { agent none // choose an agent per stage options { timeout(time: 30, unit: 'MINUTES') // fail runaway builds disableConcurrentBuilds() } parameters { choice(name: 'ENVIRONMENT', choices: ['dev', 'staging', 'production'], description: 'Target environment') } triggers { githubPush() } // build when the GitHub webhook fires stages { stage('Checks') { parallel { // independent stages run at the same time stage('Unit tests') { agent any; steps { sh 'npm ci && npm test' } } stage('Lint') { agent any; steps { sh 'npm ci && npm run lint' } } stage('Dependency audit') { agent any; steps { sh 'npm audit --omit=dev' } } } } stage('Deploy to production') { when { branch 'main' } // conditional stage (multibranch pipelines) steps { input message: 'Deploy to production?', ok: 'Deploy' // manual approval gate sh './deploy.sh' } } } post { failure { echo 'Build failed' } } } ``` Notes: - **Declarative vs scripted pipelines.** The chapter's `pipeline { ... }` form is *declarative* (structured, validated, preferred). *Scripted* pipelines use `node { ... }` blocks with free-form Groovy and are more flexible but easier to get wrong. - **Docker inside the pipeline.** A plain Jenkins container does not ship the Docker CLI, so the `docker build` stages in the chapter need an agent that has Docker available. Two common options: an agent image/VM with Docker installed, or the Docker Pipeline plugin (`agent { docker { image 'node:22' } }`) to run the build steps inside a container. Mounting the host's `/var/run/docker.sock` into a build container gives that container root-equivalent control of the host, which is why it is a recognised security risk. - **Webhook endpoint.** With the GitHub plugin the webhook target is typically `http(s)://<jenkins-host>/github-webhook/`; Jenkins must be reachable from GitHub (or use polling as a fallback). - **First login to the local learning container.** Read the initial admin password with `docker exec jenkins cat /var/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword` (it is also printed in `docker logs jenkins`). - **Multibranch pipelines** discover branches and pull requests that contain a `Jenkinsfile` and create a job for each; this is also what makes `when { branch 'main' }` meaningful. - **Shared Libraries** (listed as awareness in the chapter) let many repositories reuse common pipeline code — the Jenkins equivalent of the reusable workflows described in [Chapter 6](../03-cicd-gitops/ch06-cicd-github-actions.md). --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 26: GitOps + ArgoCD](ch26-gitops-argocd.md) · [Chapter 28: Ansible: Configuration Management & Automation](../06-iac-config/ch28-ansible.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch27-revision.md)

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Why Jenkins
text: Coordinates Git repositories → build servers → testing → Docker → artifact repositories → Kubernetes → AWS. Extremely popular before cloud-native CI such as GitHub Actions; still common in **large enterprises, legacy systems, organisations with custom CI/CD infrastructure, highly customised pipelines**. | GitHub Actions | Jenkins | |---|---| | GitHub → Actions → Runner → Pipeline (integrated, hosted runners) | Git repo → Jenkins → Controller → Agents → Pipeline; **infrastructure-oriented** — you manage the installation, agents, plugins, credentials |

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Architecture
text: - **Controller**: coordinates Jenkins — jobs, pipelines, configuration, scheduling, credentials, agents. **Agent**: actually executes work (`npm ci`, `npm test`, `docker build`). Agents may be Linux, Docker, Windows; separate Node/Java/Android agents isolate workloads. - **Don't build everything on the controller** — builds consume CPU/memory/disk/network; the controller should schedule/orchestrate and agents execute. - **Agents in Kubernetes:** Jenkins → Kubernetes → **ephemeral build Pods** created when needed and removed afterwards → isolation, elasticity, clean environments, scaling (your Kubernetes troubleshooting applies: `kubectl get pods / describe / logs`).

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Jenkinsfile (Declarative Pipeline)
text: ```groovy pipeline { agent any // or: agent { label 'docker' } environment { NODE_ENV = 'test' } stages { stage('Checkout') { steps { checkout scm } } stage('Install') { steps { sh 'npm ci' } } stage('Lint') { steps { sh 'npm run lint' } } stage('Typecheck') { steps { sh 'npm run typecheck' } } stage('Test') { steps { sh 'npm test' } } stage('Build') { steps { sh 'npm run build' } } } post { always { echo 'Pipeline finished' } success { archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'dist/**', fingerprint: true } failure { echo 'Build failed' } } } ``` Structure: `pipeline → agent → stages → stage → steps`. `Jenkinsfile` lives in the repo (**pipeline as code**). `post` blocks (`always`/`success`/`failure`) handle notifications, cleanup, artifact handling, reporting. **Artifacts** (`archiveArtifacts`) preserve build output (`dist/`) and tie it to a build — traceability: build #100/#101/#102 ↔ which binary/image (same principle as Git SHA / image tags / ECR).

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Credentials, Git, webhooks
text: - **Credentials store** holds AWS credentials, SSH keys, tokens, passwords, API keys; inject with `withCredentials([string(credentialsId: 'api-token', variable: 'API_TOKEN')]) { sh 'some-command' }`. Secret → Jenkins credential store → pipeline; **never** secret → Git, and don't put secrets directly in Jenkinsfiles/env blocks. - Git integrations: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, self-hosted Git. Flow: `git push` → GitHub → **webhook** (HTTP request to Jenkins) → pipeline starts (better than constantly polling Git).

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Docker, ECR, Kubernetes
text: ```groovy stage('Docker Build') { steps { sh 'docker build -t my-api:${BUILD_NUMBER} .' } } stage('Docker Push') { steps { sh 'docker push my-api:${BUILD_NUMBER}' } } ``` Production: authenticate securely to the registry and use an immutable tag (Git SHA). ```bash aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | \ docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <account>.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com docker build -t <repository>:<git-sha> . docker push <repository>:<git-sha> ``` Prefer short-lived identity/role-based credentials over permanent access keys. Deploy (traditional): `kubectl set image deployment/my-api my-api=my-api:${GIT_COMMIT}` — or `kubectl apply -f k8s/`. **GitOps alternative (cleaner separation):** Jenkins → build → test → Docker → ECR → **update GitOps repo** → ArgoCD → EKS. Jenkins = CI (build, test, package, image); ArgoCD = CD (synchronisation, reconciliation, deployment). | Tool | Primary role | |---|---| | GitHub Actions | CI/CD automation integrated with GitHub | | Jenkins | General-purpose CI/CD automation server | | ArgoCD | Kubernetes GitOps CD | | Helm | Kubernetes packaging/templates | | Terraform | Infrastructure as Code | They coexist: GitHub → Jenkins (test, build, Docker) → ECR → GitOps repo → ArgoCD → EKS.

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Pipeline features
text: - **Plugins:** huge ecosystem (Git, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Slack, JUnit, SonarQube, security scanners) — powerful but can become complicated. - **Parallelism:** independent stages (Unit ∥ Lint ∥ Security) → sequential 5 + 2 + 4 = **11 min**, parallel `max(5,2,4)` ≈ **5 min** (given enough agents/resources). - **Parameters:** e.g. `ENVIRONMENT` (dev/staging/production) — but production deployment should have stronger controls than arbitrary user input. - **Approvals / governance:** Commit → CI → Tests → Build → Staging → Integration tests → **Approval** → Production (GitHub Actions has environments/approvals; Jenkins can implement approval steps).

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Security (very testable)
text: - **Don't:** hard-code AWS keys/passwords, run everything as root, allow unrestricted Jenkins access, install random plugins. - **Do:** RBAC, least privilege, credential store, HTTPS, authentication + authorization, plugin updates, agent isolation, audit logs, network restrictions, secret rotation. - **Supply-chain:** the CI server has enormous privileges (push images, deploy to Kubernetes, access AWS) → if compromised: attacker → Jenkins → AWS → Kubernetes. Use least privilege, short-lived credentials, isolated agents, protected branches, dependency scanning, image scanning, signed artifacts where appropriate. - **Jenkins credentials vs GitHub OIDC:** Jenkins + long-lived AWS key vs Jenkins workload identity → IAM role → temporary credentials (depends on where Jenkins runs). Principle: avoid unnecessary long-lived credentials.

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Troubleshooting
text: - **Pipeline suddenly fails:** don't rerun repeatedly; which stage? (Build / Test / Docker / Registry / Credentials / Deployment). *Docker push failed:* ECR reachable? credentials valid? repository exists? image tag valid? permissions? - **Agent offline:** network, agent process, resource exhaustion, disk, credentials, Jenkins-agent connection, container/node status. - **Disk full:** workspace, Docker images, build artifacts, logs, cache → `df -h`, `du -sh *`; clean old builds, remove unused Docker images, artifact retention, workspace cleanup, log rotation, bigger disk.

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Best practices
text: Pipeline as code (`Jenkinsfile`) · small stages (test, build, scan, package, deploy) · immutable artifacts (Git SHA / build number / version, not blind `latest`) · fail fast · least privilege · reproducible builds.

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Interview answer — "Why Jenkins when GitHub Actions exists?"
text: Don't say one is universally better. *GitHub Actions is tightly integrated CI/CD for GitHub repositories (runners, workflows, permissions and events integrated). Jenkins is a mature, highly extensible automation server with a large plugin ecosystem that integrates with many source-control systems and internal infrastructure; organisations with existing Jenkins or highly customised pipelines may continue using it.* Personal new project → GitHub Actions (simpler); enterprise → likely Jenkins, so be able to maintain its pipelines; Kubernetes GitOps → Jenkins/Actions (CI) → ArgoCD → EKS.

title: Revision 27 — Jenkins + Advanced CI/CD
heading: Hands-on
text: ```bash docker volume create jenkins_home docker run -d --name jenkins -p 8080:8080 -p 50000:50000 -v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home jenkins/jenkins:lts docker ps ; docker logs jenkins # learning setup, not production ``` Repo `my-api/{package.json, src/, Jenkinsfile}` (Install → Test → Build); connect Jenkins to the repo; push → webhook → pipeline. Add `Docker Build` (`docker build -t my-api:${BUILD_NUMBER} .`), later ECR.

Awareness: Blue Ocean, Shared Libraries, Kubernetes plugin internals, plugin development, distributed architecture internals. **Three CI/CD styles:** basic automation (Git → Jenkins → build/test/deploy), cloud-native CI (GitHub → Actions → Docker → ECR → Kubernetes), modern GitOps (Git → Actions/Jenkins → build/test → Docker → ECR → GitOps repo → ArgoCD → Kubernetes/EKS).
