title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: Chapter 29 — Revision Sheet: Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch29-crds-operators.md). Level up: from *using* Kubernetes to understanding **how Kubernetes itself can be extended**.

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: Core vocabulary (the "one thing to remember")
text: | Term | Meaning | |---|---| | **CRD** (Custom Resource Definition) | Extends the Kubernetes API with a **new resource type** (e.g. `PostgresCluster`) — the class/schema/type | | **Custom Resource (CR)** | An **instance** of that type (`PostgresCluster` named `production-db`) | | **Controller** | Watches resources and makes **desired state** match **actual state** — a reconciliation/control loop (Deployment controller: desired 3 Pods, actual 2 → create one) | | **Operator** | A controller that encodes **application/domain-specific operational knowledge** (replication, backups, failover, upgrades, scaling, configuration) | | **Reconciliation** | Compare desired vs actual and act so actual converges to desired; continuous | Analogy: `class User { name: string }` = CRD; `new User()` = Custom Resource. Before a CRD, Kubernetes knows Pod/Deployment/Service/ConfigMap; after, it also recognises `PostgresCluster`. **Why:** developers write ```yaml apiVersion: databases.example.com/v1 kind: PostgresCluster metadata: { name: production-db } spec: { replicas: 3, version: "16" } ``` instead of hand-crafting StatefulSets, Services, PVCs, Secrets, ConfigMaps, backup jobs and monitoring — the platform hides the complexity.

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: CRD alone isn't enough (critical)
text: A CRD tells Kubernetes the type exists, not **how to implement it**. Creating a CR stores an object; **nothing happens** until a controller/operator watches it. Flow: CRD defines type → CR created → Operator (controller) notices → creates StatefulSet/Service/PVC/config/backup resources → Kubernetes' own controllers create Pods. **Operators work with Kubernetes, not instead of it** (layered controllers: Operator → Kubernetes resources → Kubernetes controllers → Pods).

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: Creating a CRD and CR
text: ```yaml apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 kind: CustomResourceDefinition metadata: name: applications.platform.example.com # <plural>.<group> spec: group: platform.example.com names: kind: Application plural: applications singular: application shortNames: [app] scope: Namespaced versions: - name: v1 served: true storage: true schema: openAPIV3Schema: type: object properties: spec: type: object properties: image: { type: string } replicas: { type: integer } ``` ```yaml apiVersion: platform.example.com/v1 kind: Application metadata: { name: my-api } spec: { image: nginx:latest, replicas: 3 } ``` ```bash kubectl apply -f app-crd.yaml ; kubectl get crd kubectl apply -f application.yaml ; kubectl get applications # lists my-api, but creates NO Pods kubectl api-resources # shows the new type ``` Group `platform.example.com`, version `v1`, kind `Application`, plural `applications`. After installing a CRD: `kubectl get postgresclusters` just like `kubectl get deployments`. **Validation:** schema constraints such as `replicas: { type: integer, minimum: 1, maximum: 10 }` (so `replicas: 100` is rejected) and `required: [image, replicas]`.

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: spec vs status, conditions, finalizers
text: - **`spec` = what I want; `status` = what currently exists** (`spec.replicas: 3`, `status.readyReplicas: 2`). The controller keeps reconciling: spec → desired → controller → actual → status. - **Conditions** let controllers communicate state: `status.conditions: [{type: Ready, status: "True"}]` — understand the pattern. - **Finalizer:** *allows a controller to perform cleanup before Kubernetes completes deletion of a resource* (e.g. backup + delete the external cloud database before the object disappears).

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: Operator lifecycle / pattern
text: Create CR → Operator notices → reconcile → create/update resources → monitor state → reconcile again → update status — for the resource's whole lifetime. Generic: **Custom Resource → Controller → Observe → Compare desired vs actual → Take action → Observe again** (a control loop). **Why "Operator":** it encodes human operational knowledge ("if a replica fails recreate it", "if the primary fails promote a replica", "before upgrading perform these checks"). **Real operators:** PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis, Prometheus, Elasticsearch, MongoDB (e.g. `kind: Kafka`, `spec.replicas: 3`). **Writing operators:** Kubebuilder, Operator SDK, controller-runtime; usually in **Go** (the Kubernetes ecosystem language; good for concurrent controllers, network services, Kubernetes APIs). Understanding the pattern matters more than building one.

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: How it combines with your stack
text: - **Helm** can package CRD + Operator + Custom Resources (Helm → PostgreSQL Operator → CRD installed → `PostgreSQLCluster` → operator manages the DB). - **ArgoCD/GitOps** can manage CRDs and CRs (Git → ArgoCD → CRD → CR → Operator → Application). - **Terraform → EKS → Helm (operator) → Custom Resource**; GitOps manages the custom resources. Terraform provisions AWS; Helm installs the operator; GitOps manages the custom database resources. - **Platform engineering:** with 200 teams, expose `kind: PostgresCluster` and hide networking/storage/replication/backups/failover → Developer → simple Custom Resource → Platform Operator → complex infrastructure.

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: Comparisons
text: | | | |---|---| | **Operator vs Helm** | Helm = template, package, install, upgrade ("install this configuration"). Operator = observe, reconcile, recover, scale, back up, upgrade ("continuously manage this application") | | **Operator vs controller** | Controller = general reconciliation component; Operator = controller for a specific application/domain. Every Operator involves controller behaviour; not every controller is called an Operator | | **CRD vs Operator** | CRD defines the new API type; Operator watches resources and implements application-specific reconciliation |

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: Troubleshooting
text: 1. `kubectl get applications` fails → `kubectl get crd` (CRD not installed?). 2. CRD exists but CR fails → `kubectl describe application my-api` (validation errors, events, spec problems). 3. CR exists but nothing happens → operator not running: `kubectl get pods -n <operator-namespace>`, `kubectl logs <operator-pod>`. 4. Operator `CrashLoopBackOff` → `get pods`, `describe pod`, `logs`, `logs --previous`. 5. **RBAC:** operators run inside Kubernetes under a ServiceAccount; missing permissions (create Deployments/Services/Secrets/PVCs) → API DENIED; check `kubectl auth can-i ...`.

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: Interview answers (verbatim-style)
text: - *What happens if I create a Custom Resource?* The CRD defines the type and Kubernetes stores the CR; creating it alone doesn't implement behaviour — a controller/Operator must watch it and reconcile by creating/updating underlying resources. - *CRD vs Operator?* see table. *Why Operator instead of Helm?* Helm packages/templates; an Operator continuously observes and manages lifecycle. *What is reconciliation?* Comparing desired with actual state and acting so actual converges to desired. *Why are Operators useful?* They encode domain-specific operational knowledge so Kubernetes can automate provisioning, backups, failover, upgrades and recovery.

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: Depth guide
text: Know well: CRD, CR, controller, Operator, reconciliation, spec vs status, desired vs actual, finalizers, CRD validation, RBAC, CRDs + Helm/ArgoCD, operator troubleshooting. Awareness: Kubebuilder, Operator SDK, controller-runtime, admission webhooks, conversion webhooks, multi-version CRDs, advanced controller internals.

title: Revision 29 — Kubernetes CRDs + Operators
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - ⚠ **Name collision:** the chapter's example CRD uses `shortNames: [app]`; Argo CD's own `Application` CRD (Chapter 26) also uses `app`, so having both in one cluster makes `kubectl get app` ambiguous. Choose distinct kinds/short names (or fully qualify `applications.platform.example.com`). - To make `status` writable separately from `spec`, enable the **status subresource** in the CRD (`subresources: { status: {} }`); `kubectl explain applications.spec` shows the schema; v1 CRDs require a *structural* schema; newer clusters also support CEL validation rules. - Controllers are **level-triggered**: they reconcile toward the current desired state rather than reacting to individual events, so reconciliation must be idempotent. - Operators set **ownerReferences** on child resources so deleting the CR garbage-collects them (finalizers cover external cleanup). - **Danger:** `kubectl delete crd <name>` deletes **all** custom resources of that type. - Webhooks: *admission* webhooks validate/mutate objects on create/update; *conversion* webhooks translate between CRD versions. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 28](ch28-revision.md) · [Full chapter 29](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch29-crds-operators.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 30](ch30-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
text: > **Source:** Response 30 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-30.txt`, lines 1–1839) · **Part II — Advanced extension (Responses 25–36)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch30-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) · *includes an editorial supplement at the end* <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We're staying exactly on the roadmap. You've already learned Kubernetes networking, Services, Ingress, NetworkPolicies, HPA, Helm, ArgoCD, CRDs, and Operators. Now we're learning **Service Mesh** — an advanced Kubernetes/backend concept that becomes useful when you have many microservices. The goal for you is **strong SWE interview + practical understanding**, not becoming an Istio administrator. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 1. The Problem Service Mesh Solves
text: Imagine your application has: ```text Frontend ↓ API Gateway ↓ User Service ↓ Order Service ↓ Payment Service ↓ Notification Service ``` Now every service needs to handle: - HTTPS/mTLS - retries - timeouts - circuit breaking - service discovery - traffic routing - observability - authentication - authorization - metrics - tracing Without a service mesh, every application may implement these independently. For example, Node.js services might each implement: ```typescript fetchWithRetry() fetchWithTimeout() circuitBreaker() metrics() tracing() ``` That creates duplicated infrastructure logic. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 2. What Is a Service Mesh?
text: A **service mesh** is an infrastructure layer that manages communication between services. Instead of putting all networking logic inside the application: ```text Application ↓ Networking logic ``` you move much of it into infrastructure: ```text Application ↓ Service Mesh ↓ Network ``` This allows application developers to focus more on business logic. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 3. The Key Idea: Sidecar Proxy
text: This is the most important concept. Suppose you have: ```text Pod ├── Node.js container └── Envoy proxy ``` The Envoy proxy runs alongside your application. This is called a: > **Sidecar proxy** So instead of: ```text Pod └── Node.js ``` you have: ```text Pod ├── Node.js └── Envoy ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 4. How Traffic Flows
text: Suppose: ```text Order Service ``` calls: ```text Payment Service ``` Without mesh: ```text Order │ │ HTTP ▼ Payment ``` With a service mesh: ```text Order Pod ├── Order application └── Envoy │ │ ▼ Payment Pod ├── Envoy └── Payment application ``` Traffic essentially becomes: ```text Order App ↓ Order Envoy ↓ Payment Envoy ↓ Payment App ``` The proxies handle much of the networking behavior. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 5. Why Envoy?
text: Istio commonly uses **Envoy** as its data-plane proxy. Envoy is a high-performance proxy designed for service-to-service communication. For your interviews, remember: ```text Istio ↓ uses Envoy proxies ↓ to handle service traffic ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 6. Data Plane vs Control Plane
text: Another extremely important concept. A service mesh has two conceptual parts: ```text Service Mesh │ ├── Data Plane │ └── Control Plane ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 7. Data Plane
text: The data plane handles **actual traffic**. For Istio: ```text Envoy proxies ``` are the important data-plane components. Example: ```text Service A ↓ Envoy ↓ Envoy ↓ Service B ``` The Envoys actually process the network traffic. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 8. Control Plane
text: The control plane manages/configures the proxies. Conceptually: ```text Istio Control Plane ↓ configuration ↓ Envoy proxies ``` Modern Istio primarily uses: ```text istiod ``` as the control-plane component. It provides configuration and service information to proxies. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 9. Easy Mental Model
text: Remember: ```text Control Plane = "Tell proxies what to do" Data Plane = "Actually handle traffic" ``` This distinction appears throughout distributed systems. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 10. Sidecar Injection
text: How does Envoy get inside your Pods? Istio can automatically inject the sidecar. For example, you label a namespace: ```bash kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled ``` Then newly created Pods can receive the Envoy sidecar automatically. Instead of: ```text Pod └── Node.js ``` you get: ```text Pod ├── Node.js └── Envoy ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 11. Check the Sidecar
text: Run: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You might see: ```text NAME READY order-api 2/2 payment-api 2/2 ``` Why `2/2`? Because: ```text 1 application container + 1 Envoy container = 2 containers ``` This is a useful troubleshooting clue. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 12. What Does the Service Mesh Actually Give Us?
text: A mesh can provide: ```text Traffic management Security Observability Reliability ``` Let's examine each. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 13. Traffic Management
text: Suppose you have: ```text Payment v1 Payment v2 ``` You want: ```text 90% → v1 10% → v2 ``` A service mesh can implement traffic routing. Conceptually: ```text ┌── 90% → v1 Request ─────┤ └── 10% → v2 ``` This is useful for: - canary deployments - A/B testing - gradual releases ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 14. Canary Deployment
text: Suppose the current version is: ```text payment:v1 ``` New version: ```text payment:v2 ``` Instead of immediately switching everything: ```text 100% → v2 ``` you can gradually move: ```text 95% → v1 5% → v2 ↓ 90% → v1 10% → v2 ↓ 50% → v1 50% → v2 ↓ 0% → v1 100% → v2 ``` If errors increase: ```text rollback traffic ``` This is much safer than immediately replacing all traffic. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 15. VirtualService
text: Istio uses resources such as: ```text VirtualService DestinationRule ``` for traffic management. Example: ```yaml apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1 kind: VirtualService metadata: name: payment spec: hosts: - payment http: - route: - destination: host: payment subset: v1 weight: 90 - destination: host: payment subset: v2 weight: 10 ``` Conceptually: ```text 90% → v1 10% → v2 ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 16. DestinationRule
text: A `VirtualService` decides: > How should traffic be routed? A `DestinationRule` can define: > What subsets/policies exist for that destination? For example: ```yaml spec: subsets: - name: v1 labels: version: v1 - name: v2 labels: version: v2 ``` So: ```text VirtualService → routing rules DestinationRule → destination/subset policies ``` This distinction is important in interviews. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 17. Retries
text: Suppose: ```text Order → Payment ``` Payment temporarily fails. A mesh can retry certain requests. Conceptually: ```text Order ↓ Payment ↓ temporary failure ↓ retry ↓ Payment ``` Example: ```yaml retries: attempts: 3 perTryTimeout: 2s ``` But retries are **not automatically good**. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 18. Why Retries Can Be Dangerous
text: Suppose one request causes: ```text 3 retries ``` and 1,000 requests arrive. You could suddenly generate: ```text 1,000 × 3 = 3,000 additional requests ``` This can overload an already failing service. This is called a **retry storm**. Therefore: > Retries must be used carefully. Usually combine them with: ```text timeouts backoff limits idempotency ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 19. Timeouts
text: Suppose: ```text Order → Payment ``` and Payment never responds. Without a timeout: ```text Request ↓ waiting... ↓ waiting... ↓ waiting... ``` Resources remain occupied. With a timeout: ```text Request ↓ 2 seconds ↓ timeout ``` This prevents indefinitely hanging calls. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 20. Timeout + Retry
text: A common pattern: ```text Request ↓ timeout ↓ retry ↓ timeout ↓ fail ``` But you must make sure the **total request budget** is respected. For example: ```text API timeout = 5 seconds ``` You don't want internal retries accidentally taking: ```text 20 seconds ``` because downstream services each retry independently. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 21. Circuit Breaking
text: Imagine: ```text Order ↓ Payment ``` Payment is completely broken. Without circuit breaking: ```text Order ↓ request ↓ failure ↓ request ↓ failure ↓ request ↓ failure ... ``` This wastes resources. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 22. Circuit Breaker
text: A circuit breaker can move through states: ```text CLOSED ↓ failures increase ↓ OPEN ↓ requests rejected quickly ↓ after cooldown ↓ HALF-OPEN ↓ test request ↓ success → CLOSED failure → OPEN ``` This protects the system from cascading failures. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 23. Cascading Failure
text: This is an important interview concept. Suppose: ```text Payment ↓ slow Order ↓ waiting for Payment API Gateway ↓ waiting for Order Users ↓ waiting for Gateway ``` Eventually: ```text threads/connections memory CPU queues ``` can become exhausted. One service's failure can spread through the system. This is a: > **Cascading failure** Timeouts, circuit breakers, load shedding, and bulkheads help prevent this. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 24. mTLS
text: Now security. Normal HTTP: ```text Service A ───── HTTP ─────> Service B ``` HTTPS: ```text Service A ─── TLS ───> Service B ``` A service mesh can provide **mutual TLS**, or mTLS. Both sides authenticate each other. ```text Service A ↕ mTLS ↕ Service B ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 25. Why mTLS?
text: Without mutual authentication: ```text Service A ↓ "Who are you?" ↓ Service B ``` With mTLS: ```text A proves identity to B B proves identity to A ``` It provides: - encryption - service identity - mutual authentication ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 26. Application Code Doesn't Need to Implement mTLS
text: This is one of the biggest advantages. Without mesh, your Node.js application may need to handle: ```text certificates TLS configuration rotation verification ``` With a service mesh: ```text Node.js ↓ Envoy ↓ mTLS ↓ Envoy ↓ Node.js ``` The application can remain largely unaware of the transport-level security. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 27. Zero Trust
text: Service mesh can support a zero-trust architecture. Instead of: > "Anything inside the VPC is trusted." you can use: ```text service identity + authentication + authorization + encryption ``` So internal communication is also protected. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 28. Authorization
text: Authentication asks: > Who are you? Authorization asks: > What are you allowed to do? For example: ```text Order Service ↓ Payment Service ``` You might allow: ```text POST /payments ``` but deny: ```text DELETE /payments ``` Service mesh authorization policies can enforce such communication rules. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 29. Observability
text: Service meshes can provide networking-level telemetry. You can collect: ```text requests latency errors traffic connections ``` For example: ```text Order → Payment Requests: 20,000/min Success: 99.8% p95 latency: 120 ms 5xx: 0.2% ``` This is valuable because the proxy sees traffic even when application instrumentation is limited. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 30. Distributed Tracing
text: Consider: ```text Client ↓ API Gateway ↓ Order ↓ Payment ↓ Database ``` A request may have a trace: ```text Trace ID: abc123 ``` and spans: ```text Gateway 20ms Order 80ms Payment 150ms Database 100ms ``` You can identify: > Payment is consuming most of the latency. Service mesh can participate in this telemetry. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 31. Service Mesh + OpenTelemetry
text: You've already learned OpenTelemetry. Now connect the concepts: ```text Application + Service Mesh ↓ Metrics Logs Traces ↓ Observability platform ``` The mesh gives infrastructure-level visibility while application instrumentation gives business/application-level visibility. They complement each other. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 32. Istio Architecture
text: Simplified: ```text Istio Control Plane │ │ configuration ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ Envoy Proxy Envoy Proxy │ │ ▼ ▼ Order Service Payment Service ``` Data plane: ```text Envoy ↔ Envoy ``` Control plane: ```text istiod → Envoy ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 33. Installing Istio
text: For learning, Istio provides `istioctl`. After installing Istio: ```bash istioctl version ``` You can install a demo profile: ```bash istioctl install --set profile=demo -y ``` Then check: ```bash kubectl get pods -n istio-system ``` You should see Istio control-plane components. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 34. Enable Injection
text: For a namespace: ```bash kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled ``` Then deploy your application. For example: ```bash kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml ``` Check: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` You may see: ```text READY 2/2 ``` instead of: ```text 1/1 ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 35. Important Gotcha
text: Labeling a namespace doesn't necessarily inject a sidecar into **already existing Pods**. You may need to recreate/restart workloads. For example: ```bash kubectl rollout restart deployment order-api ``` Then: ```bash kubectl get pods ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 36. Istio Gateway
text: You've already learned Kubernetes Ingress. Istio also has its own traffic-management concepts. You may encounter: ```text Gateway VirtualService DestinationRule ``` Conceptually: ```text Internet ↓ Istio Gateway ↓ VirtualService ↓ Service ↓ Pods ``` Don't confuse an Istio Gateway with a Kubernetes Service. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 37. Service Mesh vs Kubernetes Service
text: Very important.

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Kubernetes Service
text: Provides: ```text stable network endpoint service discovery load balancing ``` Example: ```text payment.default.svc.cluster.local ```

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Service Mesh
text: Adds: ```text traffic policies mTLS retries timeouts circuit breaking telemetry authorization advanced routing ``` So: ```text Kubernetes Service = basic service networking Service Mesh = advanced service-to-service networking ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 38. Service Mesh vs API Gateway
text: Another common interview question.

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: API Gateway
text: Usually handles: ```text external → internal ``` Examples: ```text authentication rate limiting routing API policies ```

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Service Mesh
text: Primarily handles: ```text service → service ``` communication. Architecture: ```text Internet ↓ API Gateway ↓ Service Mesh ↓ Microservices ``` They can coexist. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 39. Service Mesh vs Ingress
text: Ingress typically handles: ```text external traffic ↓ cluster services ``` Service mesh primarily handles: ```text service ↕ service ``` Modern architectures can use mesh gateways for ingress/egress too, but the conceptual distinction remains useful. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 40. Service Mesh vs Application-Level Libraries
text: Without mesh: ```text Node.js ├── retry library ├── timeout library ├── tracing library ├── circuit breaker └── TLS configuration ``` With mesh: ```text Node.js ↓ Envoy ├── retries ├── timeout ├── mTLS ├── routing └── telemetry ``` However, application-level logic is still required for **business semantics**. A mesh cannot understand: ```text "Don't charge the customer twice." ``` That requires application-level idempotency. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 41. When NOT to Use a Service Mesh
text: This is extremely important. A service mesh isn't automatically necessary. For: ```text small application 3 services low traffic simple deployment ``` adding Istio can introduce unnecessary: ```text complexity CPU/memory overhead debugging difficulty operational burden ``` If your architecture is: ```text Frontend ↓ Node API ↓ PostgreSQL ``` you almost certainly don't need Istio just because Kubernetes is being used. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 42. When It Becomes Useful
text: A service mesh becomes more compelling when you have: ```text many microservices + complex traffic patterns + strong security requirements + mTLS requirements + advanced deployment strategies + need for uniform networking policies ``` For example: ```text 50+ services multiple teams multiple environments canary deployments strict service identity ``` Now centralized networking policies can become valuable. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 43. Cost of a Service Mesh
text: Every sidecar consumes resources. Suppose: ```text 100 Pods ``` and every Pod gets: ```text 1 Envoy ``` You now have: ```text 100 additional proxies ``` That means additional: ```text CPU memory network traffic configuration monitoring ``` This is why you should understand the tradeoff. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 44. Sidecar vs Ambient Mesh
text: Modern service-mesh architectures can also use an **ambient** approach, where mesh functionality doesn't necessarily require a sidecar proxy in every application Pod. For your placement preparation: ```text Sidecar model → know well Ambient mesh → know conceptually ``` You don't need deep implementation details unless a job specifically asks for them. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 45. Istio Traffic Flow
text: Let's put everything together. Suppose: ```text Order Service ``` calls: ```text Payment Service ``` The flow can be: ```text Order App ↓ Order Envoy │ ├── mTLS ├── timeout ├── retry ├── routing └── telemetry ↓ Payment Envoy │ ├── authentication ├── authorization └── telemetry ↓ Payment App ``` That's the central idea of a service mesh. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 46. A Practical Canary Architecture
text: Suppose: ```text payment-v1 payment-v2 ``` Pods: ```text payment-v1 ├── app └── envoy payment-v2 ├── app └── envoy ``` Istio: ```text Request ↓ Envoy ↓ VirtualService ├── 90% → v1 └── 10% → v2 ``` Monitor: ```text error rate latency CPU business metrics ``` If v2 behaves badly: ```text 100% → v1 ``` This combines: ```text Kubernetes + Helm + GitOps + Service Mesh + Observability ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 47. Important Reliability Trap
text: Suppose: ```text Service A ``` has: ```text timeout = 10 sec ``` and: ```text Service B ``` has: ```text timeout = 10 sec ``` and: ```text Service C ``` also: ```text timeout = 10 sec ``` Your total request path could become extremely slow. Good distributed-system design needs: ```text timeout budgets ``` and carefully chosen: ```text retries backoff circuit breaking ``` This is more important than memorizing Istio YAML. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q1. What is a service mesh?
text: > A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that manages service-to-service communication, providing capabilities such as traffic management, security, reliability, and observability. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q2. What is a sidecar?
text: > A sidecar is a secondary container deployed alongside the application container, typically used to handle cross-cutting infrastructure functionality. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q3. What is Envoy?
text: > Envoy is a high-performance proxy commonly used as the data-plane proxy in service meshes such as Istio. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q4. Control plane vs data plane?
text: > The data plane handles actual service traffic, while the control plane configures and manages the proxies. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q5. Why use mTLS?
text: > To encrypt service-to-service traffic and mutually authenticate the communicating services. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q6. What is a circuit breaker?
text: > A mechanism that stops repeatedly sending requests to a failing dependency, allowing the system to fail fast and recover instead of amplifying the failure. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q7. Why are retries dangerous?
text: > Excessive retries can amplify traffic to an already failing service and cause retry storms or cascading failures. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q8. Service mesh vs API Gateway?
text: ```text API Gateway → external/client → services Service Mesh → service → service ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q9. Service mesh vs Kubernetes Service?
text: ```text Kubernetes Service → discovery + stable endpoint + basic load balancing Service Mesh → advanced traffic/security/observability ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Q10. Do you always need Istio?
text: > No. It introduces operational and resource overhead and is most useful when service-to-service complexity justifies it. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 49. Your Mental Model
text: Remember this: ```text ISTIO │ ┌────────┴────────┐ │ │ CONTROL PLANE DATA PLANE │ │ istiod Envoy │ Actual traffic ``` And: ```text Envoy can provide: Traffic ├── routing ├── retries ├── timeouts └── circuit breaking Security ├── mTLS └── authorization Observability ├── metrics ├── traces └── telemetry ``` ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: 50. How This Fits Your Roadmap
text: You've now connected: ```text Kubernetes ↓ Service ↓ Ingress ↓ Helm ↓ ArgoCD ↓ CRDs / Operators ↓ Service Mesh ``` And the broader production architecture: ```text Internet │ Route53 │ CloudFront │ WAF │ Load Balancer │ EKS │ Istio / Mesh │ ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Order Service Payment Service User Service │ │ │ Envoy Envoy Envoy └────────────────┼────────────────┘ │ RDS/Redis ``` Terraform provisions the infrastructure. GitHub Actions builds and tests. Docker packages. ECR stores images. ArgoCD deploys through GitOps. Helm packages Kubernetes applications. Istio manages advanced service-to-service communication. Observability tells you what's happening. That's the complete picture. ---

title: Chapter 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: The Istio resources behind mTLS, authorization, timeouts and circuit breaking
text: The chapter explains these capabilities conceptually. In Istio they are configured with the following resources. (API versions change between releases — check the documentation for your Istio version; `networking.istio.io/v1` and `security.istio.io/v1` are the current stable versions.) **Mutual TLS — `PeerAuthentication`.** `PERMISSIVE` accepts both plaintext and mTLS (useful while migrating); `STRICT` requires mTLS. ```yaml apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: PeerAuthentication metadata: name: default namespace: production spec: mtls: mode: STRICT ``` **Authorization — `AuthorizationPolicy`.** Allow only the Order service to call `POST /payments` on the Payment service (anything not allowed by an `ALLOW` policy is denied for the selected workload): ```yaml apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: AuthorizationPolicy metadata: name: payment-allow-order namespace: production spec: selector: matchLabels: app: payment action: ALLOW rules: - from: - source: principals: ["cluster.local/ns/production/sa/order"] to: - operation: methods: ["POST"] paths: ["/payments"] ``` **Timeouts and retries — in the `VirtualService`.** Together they form the "timeout budget" discussed in the chapter: ```yaml spec: hosts: [payment] http: - route: - destination: { host: payment, subset: v1 } timeout: 5s # total budget for the request retries: attempts: 3 perTryTimeout: 2s retryOn: 5xx,reset,connect-failure ``` **Circuit breaking — in the `DestinationRule`.** Istio implements it with connection-pool limits plus *outlier detection* (ejecting unhealthy endpoints), not with a literal CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN state machine in the YAML: ```yaml apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1 kind: DestinationRule metadata: name: payment spec: host: payment trafficPolicy: connectionPool: tcp: { maxConnections: 100 } http: { http1MaxPendingRequests: 50, maxRequestsPerConnection: 10 } outlierDetection: consecutive5xxErrors: 5 interval: 10s baseEjectionTime: 30s subsets: - name: v1 labels: { version: v1 } - name: v2 labels: { version: v2 } ``` Further points worth knowing: - **Default retries.** Istio applies a default retry policy (about two retries for certain connection failures) even if you configure none, so retry amplification can happen without you writing a `retries:` block. Set explicit limits for non-idempotent calls. - **How traffic reaches the sidecar.** An init container (or the Istio CNI plugin) installs iptables rules that redirect the Pod's inbound and outbound traffic through Envoy; the application doesn't change its code or addresses. - **Installation profiles.** `profile=demo` (used in the chapter) enables extra features and is for learning only; `default` is the production-oriented profile, `minimal` installs the control plane only, and `ambient` enables the sidecar-less data plane. - **Injection mechanisms.** The `istio-injection=enabled` namespace label is the classic method; revision labels (`istio.io/rev=<revision>`) support canary control-plane upgrades; ambient mode uses the `istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient` label. - **Other Istio resources:** `Gateway` (ingress/egress proxies), `ServiceEntry` (add external services to the mesh), `Sidecar` (limit what a proxy knows about). - **Alternatives (awareness):** Linkerd (lightweight Rust proxy), Consul service mesh, Cilium (eBPF-based). *Verify:* AWS announced end of support for AWS App Mesh (Envoy-based) — check the current AWS status before recommending it. --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 29: Kubernetes CRDs + Operators](ch29-crds-operators.md) · [Chapter 31: Advanced Amazon EKS](ch31-advanced-eks.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch30-revision.md)

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Chapter 30 — Revision Sheet: Service Mesh + Istio
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch30-service-mesh-istio.md). Goal: strong interview + practical understanding of **service mesh**, not Istio administration.

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: The problem and the definition
text: Frontend → API Gateway → User → Order → Payment → Notification services. Each service needs HTTPS/mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, service discovery, traffic routing, observability, authentication, authorization, metrics, tracing. Without a mesh every Node.js service re-implements `fetchWithRetry()`, `fetchWithTimeout()`, `circuitBreaker()`, `metrics()`, `tracing()` → duplicated infrastructure logic. **Service mesh = an infrastructure layer that manages service-to-service communication** (traffic management, security, reliability, observability), freeing developers to focus on business logic.

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Core architecture
text: - **Sidecar proxy:** Pod = Node.js container + **Envoy** proxy. Order App → Order Envoy → Payment Envoy → Payment App; the proxies handle networking. - **Envoy:** high-performance proxy for service-to-service communication; Istio's data-plane proxy. - **Data plane vs control plane:** *data plane* = actual traffic (Envoy ↔ Envoy); *control plane* = "tell proxies what to do" — **`istiod`** provides configuration and service information to the proxies. - **Sidecar injection:** `kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled` → new Pods get Envoy; `kubectl get pods` shows **`2/2`** (app + Envoy) instead of `1/1` — a troubleshooting clue. - **Gotcha:** labeling a namespace doesn't inject into **already running Pods** → `kubectl rollout restart deployment order-api`. ```bash istioctl version istioctl install --set profile=demo -y # learning profile kubectl get pods -n istio-system # control-plane components kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml ; kubectl get pods # READY 2/2 ```

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: What a mesh gives you
text: | Area | Capabilities | |---|---| | **Traffic management** | Weighted routing (90% v1 / 10% v2), canary, A/B testing, gradual releases | | **Security** | mTLS, service identity, authorization policies, zero trust | | **Reliability** | Retries, timeouts, circuit breaking | | **Observability** | Request rate, latency, errors, traffic, connections; distributed tracing |

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Traffic management resources
text: ```yaml apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1 kind: VirtualService metadata: { name: payment } spec: hosts: [payment] http: - route: - destination: { host: payment, subset: v1 } weight: 90 - destination: { host: payment, subset: v2 } weight: 10 ``` `DestinationRule` defines subsets: `v1` → label `version: v1`, `v2` → label `version: v2`. **VirtualService = routing rules; DestinationRule = destination/subset policies.** Canary progression: 95/5 → 90/10 → 50/50 → 0/100; on errors roll back traffic (100% → v1). Istio `Gateway` + `VirtualService` + `DestinationRule`: Internet → Istio Gateway → VirtualService → Service → Pods (an Istio Gateway ≠ a Kubernetes Service).

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Reliability
text: - **Retries:** `retries: { attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s }` — not automatically good: 1,000 requests × 3 retries = 3,000 extra requests → **retry storm**. Combine with timeouts, backoff, limits, idempotency. - **Timeouts:** without them, requests hang and resources stay occupied; with a 2 s timeout the call fails quickly. **Timeout + retry:** respect the **total request budget** (API timeout 5 s must not become 20 s because each downstream retries independently). **Reliability trap:** Service A/B/C each with 10 s timeouts → path becomes extremely slow → need **timeout budgets** plus carefully chosen retries, backoff, circuit breaking. - **Circuit breaking:** CLOSED → failures increase → OPEN (reject quickly) → cooldown → HALF-OPEN (test request) → success → CLOSED / failure → OPEN. Protects against **cascading failures** (Payment slow → Order waits → Gateway waits → users wait → threads/connections/memory/CPU/queues exhausted). Defences: timeouts, circuit breakers, load shedding, bulkheads.

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Security
text: - **mTLS:** both sides authenticate; gives encryption, service identity, mutual authentication. Application code doesn't implement certificates/TLS config/rotation/verification — Node.js → Envoy → mTLS → Envoy → Node.js. - **Zero trust:** don't trust "anything inside the VPC"; use service identity + authentication + authorization + encryption. - **Authorization:** authentication = who; authorization = what (allow `POST /payments`, deny `DELETE /payments`) — enforced by mesh authorization policies.

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Observability
text: Proxy-level telemetry even when app instrumentation is limited, e.g. "Order → Payment: 20,000 req/min, success 99.8%, p95 120 ms, 5xx 0.2%". Distributed tracing: trace `abc123` with spans Gateway 20 ms, Order 80 ms, Payment 150 ms, Database 100 ms → Payment is the slowest. Mesh = infrastructure-level visibility; OpenTelemetry/application instrumentation = business/application-level; they complement each other.

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Comparisons
text: | | | |---|---| | **Mesh vs Kubernetes Service** | Service = stable endpoint, discovery, basic load balancing (`payment.default.svc.cluster.local`); Mesh adds traffic policies, mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, telemetry, authorization, advanced routing | | **Mesh vs API Gateway** | Gateway: external → internal (authentication, rate limiting, routing, API policies); Mesh: service → service. Internet → API Gateway → Service Mesh → Microservices (coexist) | | **Mesh vs Ingress** | Ingress: external traffic → cluster services; Mesh: service ↔ service (mesh gateways can also do ingress/egress) | | **Mesh vs app libraries** | Libraries (retry, timeout, tracing, circuit breaker, TLS) vs Envoy doing them — but **business semantics still need application code** ("don't charge the customer twice" = idempotency) |

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: When (not) to use
text: - **Don't:** small app, 3 services, low traffic, simple deployment (Frontend → Node API → PostgreSQL) — unnecessary complexity, CPU/memory overhead, debugging difficulty, operational burden. - **Use when:** many microservices (50+), multiple teams/environments, complex traffic, strict security/mTLS/service identity, canary deployments, need for uniform networking policies. - **Cost:** every sidecar uses resources — 100 Pods = 100 extra proxies (CPU, memory, network traffic, configuration, monitoring). - **Sidecar vs ambient:** ambient mesh doesn't require a sidecar proxy in each Pod — know sidecar well, ambient conceptually.

title: Revision 30 — Service Mesh + Istio
heading: Interview answers
text: Service mesh (infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication) · sidecar (secondary container alongside the app for cross-cutting infrastructure) · Envoy (high-performance data-plane proxy) · control vs data plane · mTLS (encrypt + mutually authenticate) · circuit breaker (stop sending requests to a failing dependency; fail fast) · why retries are dangerous (amplify load → retry storms/cascading failure) · mesh vs API Gateway · mesh vs Kubernetes Service · "Do you always need Istio?" No — overhead; use when complexity justifies it. Full request path: Order App → Order Envoy (mTLS, timeout, retry, routing, telemetry) → Payment Envoy (authentication, authorization, telemetry) → Payment App. Production: Route 53 → CloudFront → WAF → Load Balancer → EKS → Istio/mesh → Order/Payment/User services with Envoy sidecars → RDS/Redis. **Depth:** 🔥 service-mesh concepts, Envoy, sidecar, traffic management, mTLS, retries/timeouts, circuit breaking, API Gateway vs mesh · 🟡 Istio resources/configuration · ⚪ Istio internals, ambient internals, custom Envoy extensions.
