title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
text: > **Source:** Response 31 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-31.txt`, lines 1–3410) · **Part II — Advanced extension (Responses 25–36)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch31-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) · *includes an editorial supplement at the end* <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> Absolutely. This response will be **deep and complete**, because EKS sits at the intersection of almost everything you've learned: **AWS + VPC + IAM + Kubernetes + Docker + ECR + Load Balancing + Storage + Autoscaling + Security + Observability.** We will not just memorize EKS terms. We'll understand **what happens when you deploy a real backend to EKS**, why each AWS component exists, how traffic flows, how pods get AWS permissions, how networking works, how nodes scale, and how to troubleshoot failures. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 1. What Exactly Is EKS?
text: EKS = **Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service**. It is AWS's managed Kubernetes service. Instead of running Kubernetes yourself: ```text You manage: Kubernetes control plane etcd API server scheduler controller manager control-plane upgrades control-plane availability ``` AWS manages much of the Kubernetes control-plane infrastructure for you. You primarily manage: ```text Your applications Pods Deployments Services Ingress ConfigMaps Secrets Node infrastructure/configuration Networking configuration IAM integration Observability ``` Simplified: ```text AWS │ ┌──────┴──────┐ │ │ EKS Control Your Workloads Plane │ │ │ └───────┬───────┘ │ Kubernetes ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 2. Kubernetes vs EKS
text: You already know Kubernetes. Think: ```text Kubernetes = container orchestration platform ``` while: ```text EKS = AWS-managed Kubernetes + AWS infrastructure integration ``` EKS doesn't replace Kubernetes concepts. You still use: ```bash kubectl ``` and Kubernetes manifests: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment ``` The difference is that EKS integrates Kubernetes deeply with AWS. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 3. Why Would We Use EKS?
text: Suppose your backend has: ```text 20 microservices ``` You want: - automatic recovery - horizontal scaling - rolling deployments - private networking - load balancing - IAM - persistent storage - AWS integrations - observability - high availability EKS provides Kubernetes orchestration while AWS provides the surrounding infrastructure. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 4. EKS Architecture
text: A simplified production EKS architecture: ```text AWS Region │ ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐ │ │ EKS Control Plane Your VPC │ │ Kubernetes API ┌───────┴────────┐ │ │ │ Scheduler AZ-a AZ-b │ │ │ Controllers Worker Nodes Worker Nodes │ │ Pods Pods ``` The control plane and worker infrastructure should be thought of separately. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 5. EKS Control Plane
text: The control plane contains the Kubernetes components responsible for managing the cluster. Conceptually: ```text EKS Control Plane │ ├── Kubernetes API Server ├── Scheduler ├── Controllers └── etcd ``` You interact primarily through: ```text kubectl ``` which talks to the Kubernetes API. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 6. Kubernetes API Server
text: This is the main entry point. When you execute: ```bash kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml ``` the flow is roughly: ```text kubectl ↓ EKS Kubernetes API ↓ Authentication ↓ Authorization ↓ Validate request ↓ Store desired state ↓ Controllers reconcile ``` The API server is therefore central to the cluster. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 7. etcd
text: Kubernetes uses **etcd** as its distributed key-value store for cluster state. It stores information representing things such as: ```text Deployments Pods Services ConfigMaps Secrets CRDs Cluster configuration ``` Conceptually: ```text Kubernetes API ↓ etcd ↓ cluster state ``` With EKS, AWS manages the EKS control-plane infrastructure, including the managed control-plane components. You generally don't SSH into an EKS control-plane machine and manage etcd yourself. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 8. Worker Nodes
text: Your workloads ultimately run on worker nodes. A node could be: ```text EC2 instance ``` or, depending on the architecture: ```text AWS Fargate ``` or newer EKS compute approaches. For the core EKS mental model: ```text EKS ↓ Nodes ↓ Pods ↓ Containers ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 9. EKS Compute Options
text: You should know the major options.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: EC2 Managed Node Groups
text: AWS manages much of the node-group lifecycle. You still get: ```text EC2 instances ``` but EKS helps manage them as a Kubernetes node group. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Self-managed nodes
text: You manage more of the EC2 lifecycle yourself. Useful for specialized requirements, but more operational work. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Fargate
text: Pods run on serverless compute without you managing EC2 worker nodes. Conceptually: ```text Pod ↓ Fargate ``` rather than: ```text Pod ↓ EC2 Node ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Karpenter
text: Karpenter is an advanced Kubernetes node provisioning/autoscaling solution commonly used with EKS. It can dynamically provision appropriate EC2 capacity based on pending workload requirements. We'll discuss this later. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 10. Managed Node Groups
text: For most backend applications, Managed Node Groups are an important EKS concept. Example: ```text EKS Cluster │ ├── Node Group │ ├── EC2 │ ├── EC2 │ └── EC2 │ └── Node Group ├── EC2 └── EC2 ``` Pods are scheduled onto these nodes. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 11. Why Multiple Availability Zones?
text: Suppose all nodes are in: ```text AZ-a ``` and AZ-a fails. Potentially: ```text everything unavailable ``` Instead: ```text Region │ ├── AZ-a │ ├── Node │ └── Node │ ├── AZ-b │ ├── Node │ └── Node │ └── AZ-c ├── Node └── Node ``` Now workloads can survive an AZ-level failure better, assuming the application and supporting dependencies are also designed for that level of availability. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 12. EKS + VPC
text: This is one of the most important sections. EKS runs within your AWS networking environment. Think: ```text VPC │ ├── Public Subnets │ └── Private Subnets │ └── EKS nodes │ └── Pods ``` A common architecture is: ```text Internet ↓ Internet Gateway ↓ Public Load Balancer ↓ Private EKS Nodes ↓ Pods ↓ Private RDS ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 13. Why Put Nodes in Private Subnets?
text: Your worker nodes usually don't need to accept arbitrary inbound Internet traffic. Instead: ```text Internet ↓ Load Balancer ↓ Private nodes ``` This reduces the direct exposure of the compute layer. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 14. Private Nodes Need Outbound Access
text: A private node may still need to download: ```text container images OS packages AWS resources external APIs ``` So it may need outbound connectivity. Common architecture: ```text Private Subnet │ ↓ NAT Gateway │ ↓ Internet Gateway │ ↓ Internet ``` But AWS service traffic can also be routed through VPC endpoints where appropriate. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 15. EKS Networking
text: This is where EKS becomes more interesting. AWS commonly uses the **Amazon VPC CNI** for pod networking. The CNI is responsible for connecting Kubernetes Pods to the VPC networking environment. A simplified model: ```text Pod ↓ VPC networking ↓ ENI/IP allocation ↓ AWS network ``` This differs from the simple mental model of: > "Every Pod is just behind one node IP." With VPC-native networking, Pods can receive VPC-routable IP addresses depending on the configured networking mode. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 16. What Is a CNI?
text: CNI = **Container Network Interface**. It's a standard interface for configuring container networking. Kubernetes itself doesn't implement all networking mechanics. A CNI plugin handles networking. For EKS, one major component is: ```text Amazon VPC CNI ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 17. VPC CNI Architecture
text: Conceptually: ```text Kubernetes │ ↓ VPC CNI │ ↓ AWS VPC │ ↓ ENIs / IP addresses ``` This allows Pods to communicate using AWS networking. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 18. Why Pod IP Capacity Matters
text: This is a major EKS troubleshooting concept. Suppose your node can only obtain a limited number of usable Pod IPs. You attempt: ```text kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=100 ``` but eventually: ```text Pods Pending ``` because there aren't enough available IP addresses. Therefore: > **Subnet IP capacity and node networking limits can constrain Pod scaling.** This is why VPC CIDR planning matters. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 19. EKS Networking Limits
text: Different EC2 instance types have different networking capabilities. They can differ in: ```text network interfaces IP addresses network bandwidth ``` Therefore: ```text bigger node ≠ only more CPU/RAM ``` It may also provide more networking capacity. This matters when running many Pods. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 20. Secondary CIDR / Larger Pod Address Space
text: If your cluster's networking design needs more addresses, you need sufficient IP address space. You may encounter: ```text VPC CIDR Subnet CIDR Pod IP allocation ``` You should understand: ```text IP exhaustion ``` as a real production failure mode. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 21. How a Pod Gets an IP
text: Simplified: ```text Pod scheduled ↓ VPC CNI ↓ allocate IP ↓ attach/configure networking ↓ Pod receives network identity ``` The exact implementation has additional details, but this is the correct mental model. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 22. EKS + Security Groups
text: You already learned Security Groups. Now combine them with EKS. A simplified flow: ```text Internet ↓ Load Balancer SG ↓ Node/Pod networking ↓ Application ``` You must ensure traffic is allowed appropriately. Example: ```text Internet ↓ ALB :443 ↓ EKS application ↓ RDS :5432 ``` The security model needs to allow only the necessary traffic. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 23. Pod-Level Security Groups
text: EKS can also support associating security groups more directly with Pods through AWS networking capabilities. This is useful when different workloads require different network access policies. For example: ```text Payment Pod ↓ Payment-specific SG ↓ specific AWS resources ``` rather than giving every workload identical network access. For interviews, know the concept: > EKS can provide finer-grained AWS network security for workloads beyond simply securing the entire node. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 24. NetworkPolicy vs Security Group
text: Don't confuse them.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy
text: Controls Kubernetes/network traffic at the cluster/workload level depending on the networking implementation. Conceptually: ```text Pod A → Pod B allowed? ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: AWS Security Group
text: Controls network traffic at the AWS networking layer. Conceptually: ```text network interface/workload → AWS security rules ``` They can complement each other. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 25. EKS IAM
text: Now one of the most important EKS concepts: > **How does a Kubernetes Pod get permission to call AWS APIs?** For example, your Node.js application wants to: ```text upload to S3 read from SQS access Secrets Manager ``` You should **not** put: ```text AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY ``` inside the container. Instead, use workload identity mechanisms. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 26. Old Pattern vs Modern Pattern
text: Historically, EKS commonly used: ```text IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) ``` The broader modern AWS direction also includes: ```text EKS Pod Identity ``` For your interviews: ```text IRSA → know well EKS Pod Identity → know well as the newer EKS-native approach ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 27. The Basic Idea
text: You want: ```text Payment Pod ↓ Kubernetes ServiceAccount ↓ AWS IAM Role ↓ S3 permissions ``` So: ```text Pod identity ≠ AWS root credentials ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 28. Why This Is Better
text: Suppose your application only needs: ```text s3:GetObject ``` Give it only: ```text s3:GetObject ``` Don't give: ```text AdministratorAccess ``` This follows: > **Principle of least privilege.** ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 29. EKS Pod Identity Concept
text: The conceptual flow is: ```text Pod ↓ Kubernetes ServiceAccount ↓ EKS Pod Identity association ↓ IAM Role ↓ temporary AWS credentials ↓ AWS API ``` The application can use the AWS SDK without embedding long-lived AWS keys. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 30. Example IAM Policy
text: Suppose the application only needs to read: ```text my-company-assets ``` A policy might conceptually grant: ```json { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-company-assets/*" } ``` The exact resource/policy design should be carefully scoped. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 31. Kubernetes ServiceAccount
text: Example: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: backend-sa namespace: production ``` Deployment: ```yaml spec: template: spec: serviceAccountName: backend-sa ``` Now your Pods run under: ```text backend-sa ``` and AWS identity integration can associate that workload identity with an IAM role. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 32. Node IAM vs Pod IAM
text: This distinction is critical.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Node IAM role
text: Permissions belong broadly to the EC2 node. Potentially dangerous if every Pod can inherit broad permissions.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Pod identity
text: Permissions are associated with the specific workload. ```text Node ├── Pod A → S3 read ├── Pod B → SQS send └── Pod C → Secrets Manager read ``` This provides better isolation. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 33. Example
text: Imagine: ```text User Service → DynamoDB Image Service → S3 Payment Service → Secrets Manager ``` Don't give all three: ```text AdministratorAccess ``` Instead: ```text User Service → DynamoDB permissions Image Service → S3 permissions Payment Service → Secrets Manager permissions ``` This is exactly the kind of security reasoning interviewers like. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 34. ECR + EKS
text: You've already learned ECR. ECR = Elastic Container Registry. Your deployment pipeline becomes: ```text Developer ↓ Git ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Docker build ↓ ECR ↓ EKS ↓ Pod ``` The Kubernetes Deployment references an image: ```yaml containers: - name: backend image: <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/backend:<tag> ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 35. Why Immutable Image Tags?
text: Avoid: ```text backend:latest ``` Prefer: ```text backend:a82f31c ``` where: ```text a82f31c ``` could be a Git commit SHA. Then: ```text Git commit ↓ Docker image ↓ ECR ↓ EKS ``` You know exactly what version is running. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 36. ECR Authentication
text: Your EKS workloads/nodes need permission to pull images from ECR. The relevant AWS/Kubernetes integration ensures nodes or workloads can authenticate to ECR appropriately. If image pulling fails, you may see: ```text ImagePullBackOff ``` Troubleshoot: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` Look at Events. Potential causes: ```text wrong image wrong tag ECR permissions network connectivity registry issue ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 37. EKS Load Balancers
text: You already know: ```text Service Ingress Load Balancer ``` In AWS, Kubernetes can integrate with AWS load-balancing infrastructure. A common architecture: ```text Internet ↓ AWS Application Load Balancer ↓ Kubernetes Service ↓ Pods ``` This integration is commonly provided through AWS's load-balancing controller. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 38. AWS Load Balancer Controller
text: The **AWS Load Balancer Controller** allows Kubernetes resources to provision/configure AWS load-balancing resources. It can work with: ```text Ingress ``` to provision: ```text Application Load Balancer ``` and with certain Service configurations for: ```text Network Load Balancer ``` The exact behavior depends on the resource and configuration. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 39. Why Is This Useful?
text: Instead of manually creating: ```text ALB target groups listeners routing rules ``` you can declare Kubernetes resources. For example: ```yaml kind: Ingress ``` and the controller reconciles the AWS infrastructure. This is another example of: ```text desired state ↓ controller ↓ actual infrastructure ``` Notice how this connects directly to **[Chapter 29](ch29-crds-operators.md) — Operators and Controllers**. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 40. ALB vs NLB
text: You should know the basic distinction.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: ALB
text: Application Load Balancer. Layer 7. Understands things like: ```text HTTP HTTPS host path headers ``` Good for: ```text web applications REST APIs HTTP routing ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: NLB
text: Network Load Balancer. Layer 4-oriented. Good for: ```text TCP TLS high-performance network traffic ``` Don't memorize every edge case; understand the layer distinction. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 41. Target Type: Instance vs IP
text: This is an important EKS concept. AWS load balancers can route to: ```text EC2 instances ``` or directly to: ```text Pod IPs ``` depending on configuration. Conceptually:

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Instance target
text: ```text ALB ↓ Node ↓ Service ↓ Pod ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: IP target
text: ```text ALB ↓ Pod IP ``` Direct Pod targeting can reduce an extra networking hop and is common in modern EKS configurations. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 42. EBS + EKS
text: Now storage. You've learned: ```text EBS ``` is block storage. EKS can use EBS through the: ```text Amazon EBS CSI Driver ``` This allows Kubernetes PersistentVolumes to use EBS-backed storage. Architecture: ```text Pod ↓ PVC ↓ PV ↓ EBS volume ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 43. Important EBS Limitation
text: EBS volumes are generally associated with a specific Availability Zone. Suppose: ```text EBS AZ-a ``` and the Pod gets rescheduled to: ```text AZ-b ``` You can encounter volume attachment/scheduling constraints. This is one reason stateful workload design needs careful thought. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 44. EFS + EKS
text: EFS = Elastic File System. Unlike EBS, EFS is a managed network file system designed for shared file access across Availability Zones. Conceptually: ```text Pod A ─┐ ├── EFS Pod B ─┤ │ Pod C ─┘ ``` This can be useful when multiple Pods need shared filesystem access. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 45. EBS vs EFS
text: Remember: ```text EBS → block storage → commonly attached to workloads requiring block semantics → AZ-oriented EFS → shared network filesystem → can be accessed across AZs ``` For databases, however, don't blindly put a database on EFS just because it is shared. Managed database services like RDS are often a better architectural choice. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 46. StorageClass
text: You've already learned Kubernetes StorageClasses. EKS might have: ```text StorageClass ↓ EBS CSI driver ↓ EBS volume ``` Example conceptual flow: ```text PVC ↓ StorageClass ↓ CSI Driver ↓ AWS EBS ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 47. CSI
text: CSI = **Container Storage Interface**. It standardizes how Kubernetes interacts with storage systems. Examples: ```text EBS CSI EFS CSI ``` Mental model: ```text Kubernetes ↓ CSI driver ↓ AWS storage ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 48. EKS Autoscaling
text: Now one of the most important production topics. There are two different scaling levels.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Pod scaling
text: ```text HPA ``` changes: ```text number of Pods ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Node scaling
text: Cluster/node autoscaling mechanisms change: ```text number/type of nodes ``` So: ```text HPA → workload scaling Node autoscaling → compute capacity scaling ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 49. Example
text: Suppose: ```text 3 nodes 10 Pods ``` Traffic increases. HPA says: ```text 10 Pods → 30 Pods ``` But there isn't enough node capacity. Some Pods become: ```text Pending ``` Then node autoscaling needs to provide additional compute. ```text HPA ↓ more Pods ↓ insufficient capacity ↓ node autoscaler ↓ more nodes ↓ Pods scheduled ``` This relationship is extremely important. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 50. Cluster Autoscaler
text: Cluster Autoscaler traditionally scales node groups based on unschedulable Pods and node utilization/other configured conditions. Conceptually: ```text Pending Pods ↓ Cluster Autoscaler ↓ increase node group ↓ new EC2 node ↓ Pods scheduled ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 51. Karpenter
text: Karpenter takes a more flexible approach to node provisioning. Instead of simply thinking: ```text Node Group → add another identical node ``` Karpenter can consider workload requirements and provision appropriate compute capacity. For example: ```text Pod requires: 8 CPU 32 GB RAM ``` Karpenter can choose suitable capacity based on your configuration and constraints. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 52. Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter
text: Simplified interview-level distinction: ```text Cluster Autoscaler → primarily scales existing node groups Karpenter → dynamically provisions appropriate node capacity ``` Karpenter can provide more flexible capacity management. You don't need to memorize every Karpenter scheduling detail for SWE interviews. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 53. HPA + Karpenter
text: Production flow: ```text Traffic increases ↓ CPU increases ↓ HPA increases replicas ↓ Pods become Pending ↓ Karpenter provisions nodes ↓ Pods schedule ↓ Traffic handled ``` This is a very good interview scenario. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 54. Resource Requests
text: Remember: ```yaml resources: requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" limits: cpu: "500m" memory: "512Mi" ``` Requests tell Kubernetes: > "I need at least this much capacity for scheduling." Limits tell Kubernetes: > "Don't let this container exceed this configured resource ceiling." ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 55. Why Requests Matter for Autoscaling
text: Suppose a Pod says: ```text request = 1 CPU ``` The scheduler needs a node with sufficient allocatable capacity. So: ```text Node capacity + Pod requests ``` directly affect scheduling. Bad resource requests can lead to: ```text overprovisioning underprovisioning Pending Pods poor autoscaling behavior ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 56. EKS Security Layers
text: Production EKS security is defense in depth. Think: ```text Security │ ┌──────────────┼───────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ IAM Network Kubernetes │ │ │ Pod identity SG/NACL RBAC NetworkPolicy ServiceAccount │ ↓ AWS permissions ``` And: ```text Secrets Encryption Image security Pod security Audit logs ``` all contribute. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 57. Kubernetes RBAC
text: You've already learned RBAC. Example: ```text User ↓ Role / ClusterRole ↓ RoleBinding ↓ Kubernetes API ``` For workloads: ```text ServiceAccount ↓ RBAC permissions ``` Don't confuse: ```text Kubernetes RBAC ``` with: ```text AWS IAM ``` They control different authorization domains. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 58. IAM vs Kubernetes RBAC
text: This is an excellent interview question.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: IAM
text: Controls: ```text AWS resources ``` Examples: ```text S3 SQS DynamoDB Secrets Manager ECR ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Kubernetes RBAC
text: Controls: ```text Kubernetes API resources ``` Examples: ```text Pods Deployments Services Secrets ConfigMaps ``` So: ```text IAM → "Can this workload access AWS?" Kubernetes RBAC → "Can this identity perform this Kubernetes API action?" ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 59. Secrets in EKS
text: Don't put real secrets directly into Git. Avoid: ```yaml stringData: DATABASE_PASSWORD: "myrealpassword" ``` in a Git repository. Better architecture: ```text AWS Secrets Manager ↓ External Secrets / workload integration ↓ Kubernetes Secret ↓ Pod ``` or use an appropriate secret-management integration. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 60. EKS Encryption
text: You can encrypt sensitive Kubernetes data using AWS/KMS-backed mechanisms where supported. The important conceptual distinction: ```text TLS → protects data in transit Encryption at rest → protects stored data ``` You should know both. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 61. EKS Pod Security
text: Applications should follow least privilege. Important practices include: ```text non-root containers read-only filesystem where possible drop unnecessary Linux capabilities resource limits seccomp security contexts restricted permissions ``` Example: ```yaml securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true ``` Don't run everything as: ```text root ``` unless there is a legitimate reason. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 62. Image Security
text: Your container supply chain: ```text Git ↓ CI ↓ Docker ↓ ECR ↓ EKS ``` can be attacked. Therefore: ```text dependency scanning image scanning minimal images non-root signed/verified artifacts where appropriate immutable tags least privilege ``` matter. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 63. EKS Observability
text: You've already learned CloudWatch, Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry. Now combine them. You need visibility into: ```text Cluster Nodes Pods Containers Applications AWS resources ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Cluster level
text: ```text node availability API server health cluster capacity ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Node level
text: ```text CPU memory disk network ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Pod level
text: ```text restarts CPU memory readiness liveness ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Application level
text: ```text request rate error rate latency ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: AWS level
text: ```text ALB RDS EBS NAT Gateway S3 ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 65. Logs
text: Your application should produce structured logs. Example: ```json { "level": "info", "requestId": "abc123", "service": "order-api", "message": "Order created" } ``` Then centralized log collection can aggregate them. Avoid: ```text console.log("password =", password) ``` Obviously. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 66. Metrics
text: For Kubernetes workloads: ```text CPU Memory Pod count Restarts Request rate Error rate Latency ``` For backend services: ```text HTTP requests 5xx p95 p99 DB latency queue depth ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 67. Tracing
text: Suppose: ```text ALB ↓ Order ↓ Payment ↓ RDS ``` A distributed trace can show: ```text Request ├── Order: 50ms ├── Payment: 400ms └── DB: 350ms ``` Now you know where latency comes from. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 68. EKS Control Plane Logs
text: EKS can expose control-plane-related logging to CloudWatch Logs depending on enabled logging categories. These logs can help troubleshoot things involving: ```text API requests authentication authorization audit activity scheduler/controller behavior ``` Exact categories and current AWS behavior should be checked against current AWS documentation when implementing production logging. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 69. EKS Upgrade Strategy
text: Kubernetes versions evolve. You can't just think: ```text upgrade → done ``` A production upgrade requires planning. Typical process: ```text Check compatibility ↓ Check deprecated APIs ↓ Upgrade test environment ↓ Upgrade control plane ↓ Upgrade add-ons ↓ Upgrade nodes ↓ Validate workloads ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 70. Deprecated Kubernetes APIs
text: Suppose your application uses: ```yaml apiVersion: old/version ``` and that API disappears in a future Kubernetes version. Your deployment can break during an upgrade. Therefore: > Kubernetes upgrades require API compatibility checks. This is particularly important with: ```text Ingress CRDs operators admission controllers ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 71. EKS Add-ons
text: EKS clusters commonly depend on components such as: ```text VPC CNI CoreDNS kube-proxy EBS CSI driver ``` Some can be managed as EKS add-ons. When upgrading the cluster, compatibility of these components matters. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 72. CoreDNS
text: CoreDNS provides Kubernetes DNS. For example: ```text payment.default.svc.cluster.local ``` resolves to the appropriate Kubernetes Service. If DNS breaks: ```text Pod ↓ DNS lookup ↓ failure ``` services may appear unreachable even though Pods are healthy. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 73. EKS Troubleshooting Workflow
text: Let's build a real debugging process. Suppose: ```text Users receive 503. ``` Don't randomly restart Pods. Work from outside inward. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 74. Step 1 — Check Load Balancer
text: Check: ```text ALB/NLB ``` Questions: ```text Is it healthy? Are listeners correct? Are target groups healthy? Are security groups correct? ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 75. Step 2 — Check Ingress
text: ```bash kubectl get ingress kubectl describe ingress <name> ``` Check: ```text host path backend events ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 76. Step 3 — Check Service
text: ```bash kubectl get svc ``` Then: ```bash kubectl describe svc <service> ``` Check: ```text ports targetPort selector ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 77. Step 4 — Check Endpoints
text: ```bash kubectl get endpoints ``` or EndpointSlices: ```bash kubectl get endpointslices ``` If there are no endpoints: ```text Service ↓ no matching Pods ``` Check labels/selectors. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 78. Step 5 — Check Pods
text: ```bash kubectl get pods -o wide ``` Look for: ```text Pending CrashLoopBackOff ImagePullBackOff Running but not Ready ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 79. Step 6 — Describe the Pod
text: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` Look at: ```text Events ``` Events often tell you exactly what went wrong. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 80. Step 7 — Check Logs
text: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> ``` For previous crashed container: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> --previous ``` If multiple containers: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 81. Step 8 — Check Node
text: ```bash kubectl get nodes ``` Then: ```bash kubectl describe node <node> ``` Look for: ```text CPU pressure memory pressure disk pressure taints capacity allocatable resources ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 82. Step 9 — Check Networking
text: If the application cannot reach RDS: ```text Pod ↓ VPC networking ↓ Security Group ↓ RDS ``` Check: ```text DNS route security groups network policy port RDS availability ``` For PostgreSQL: ```text 5432 ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 83. Step 10 — Check IAM
text: If the application says: ```text AccessDenied ``` check: ```text ServiceAccount ↓ Pod identity/IRSA ↓ IAM role ↓ IAM policy ``` Don't immediately modify the node's IAM role. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Symptom:
text: ```text Pods stuck Pending ``` Possible causes: ```text insufficient CPU insufficient memory node selector mismatch taints/tolerations affinity constraints no available nodes IP exhaustion PVC problems ``` Use: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` The scheduler events are often the key. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Symptom:
text: ```text ImagePullBackOff ``` Check: ```text image name tag ECR permissions network registry ``` Command: ```bash kubectl describe pod <pod> ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Symptom:
text: ```text CrashLoopBackOff ``` Check: ```bash kubectl logs <pod> kubectl logs <pod> --previous ``` Potential causes: ```text bad environment variable application crash wrong command database unavailable missing Secret bad configuration ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Symptom:
text: ```text Application can't access S3 ``` Check: ```text ServiceAccount ↓ Pod Identity ↓ IAM role ↓ S3 policy ↓ bucket policy ``` Potentially also: ```text network/VPC endpoint/NAT ``` depending on the architecture. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Symptom:
text: ```text Pods cannot communicate ``` Check: ```text Service Endpoints DNS NetworkPolicy Security Groups CNI ports ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Symptom:
text: ```text Pods cannot obtain IPs ``` Think: ```text VPC CNI ↓ subnet IP capacity ↓ ENI/IP limits ``` This is an advanced EKS-specific troubleshooting skill. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 90. Production EKS Architecture
text: Now let's build the architecture you should be able to explain in an interview. ```text Internet │ ▼ Route 53 │ ▼ CloudFront │ ▼ WAF │ ▼ AWS Load Balancer │ ┌───────┴───────┐ │ │ AZ-a AZ-b │ │ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ EKS Node │ │ EKS Node │ │ │ │ │ │ Pod │ │ Pod │ │ Pod │ │ Pod │ └────────────┘ └────────────┘ │ │ └───────┬───────┘ │ Private Services │ │ RDS Redis │ S3/SQS ``` And: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS infrastructure GitHub Actions ↓ Docker ↓ ECR ArgoCD ↓ EKS Helm ↓ Kubernetes applications ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 91. Complete Request Flow
text: Let's follow a request. User: ```text GET /orders/123 ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Step 1
text: DNS: ```text orders.example.com ``` resolves through Route 53.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Step 2
text: Request reaches: ```text CloudFront/WAF ``` depending on architecture.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Step 3
text: Load balancer receives it.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Step 4
text: AWS load-balancing integration routes to EKS workload.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Step 5
text: Kubernetes Service routes to the appropriate Pod.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Step 6
text: Application executes.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Step 7
text: Application may access: ```text RDS Redis S3 SQS ``` using private networking and appropriate IAM.

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Step 8
text: Metrics/logs/traces are emitted. That's the production flow you should be able to draw. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 92. Complete Deployment Flow
text: Now the other direction. Developer: ```text git push ``` ↓ GitHub Actions: ```text lint typecheck test build security checks ``` ↓ Docker: ```text build image ``` ↓ ECR: ```text push image ``` ↓ GitOps repository: ```text update image tag ``` ↓ ArgoCD: ```text detect change ``` ↓ EKS: ```text Deployment update ``` ↓ Kubernetes: ```text rolling update ``` ↓ Pods: ```text new version ``` This is your complete CI/CD → EKS workflow. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 93. EKS + Terraform
text: Terraform can provision: ```text VPC Subnets IAM EKS Node Groups Security Groups RDS S3 Redis Load Balancing infrastructure ``` Then Kubernetes/Helm/ArgoCD manages workloads. This separation is useful: ```text Terraform → infrastructure Kubernetes → workload orchestration Helm → packaging ArgoCD → deployment/reconciliation ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 94. EKS + Operators
text: From [Chapter 29](ch29-crds-operators.md): ```text CRD + Operator ``` can run inside EKS. For example: ```text EKS ↓ PostgreSQL Operator ↓ Postgres Custom Resource ↓ database resources ``` So all of your previous topics are connecting together. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 95. EKS + Istio
text: From [Chapter 30](ch30-service-mesh-istio.md): ```text EKS ↓ Istio ↓ Envoy ↓ service-to-service traffic ``` Now you have: ```text AWS + Kubernetes + Operators + Service Mesh ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 96. EKS Cost Awareness
text: EKS isn't just a technical problem. There are costs from: ```text EKS control-plane/service charges EC2 EBS Load Balancers NAT Gateway Data transfer CloudWatch ECR RDS ElastiCache ``` A badly designed architecture can become expensive. For example: ```text many NAT Gateways + excessive cross-AZ traffic + oversized EC2 instances + unused load balancers + unbounded logging ``` can increase costs. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 97. Availability vs Cost
text: Suppose: ```text 1 node ``` is cheaper. But: ```text 3 AZs multiple nodes ``` provides better fault tolerance. So architecture involves tradeoffs: ```text cost vs availability vs performance vs operational complexity ``` You should be able to explain these tradeoffs rather than saying: > "Always use three AZs." ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 98. EKS Security Checklist
text: For a production EKS environment: ```text ☑ Private nodes where appropriate ☑ Least-privilege IAM ☑ Pod identity ☑ Kubernetes RBAC ☑ NetworkPolicies ☑ Security Groups ☑ Secrets Manager ☑ Encryption ☑ Non-root containers ☑ Image scanning ☑ Resource limits ☑ Audit/control-plane logging ☑ Regular upgrades ☑ Restricted API access ☑ Minimal permissions ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: 99. EKS Production Checklist
text: You should think about:

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Networking
text: ```text ☑ Multi-AZ ☑ private subnets ☑ CIDR planning ☑ VPC CNI ☑ IP capacity ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Compute
text: ```text ☑ Managed Node Groups ☑ autoscaling ☑ resource requests ☑ instance sizing ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Security
text: ```text ☑ IAM ☑ Pod Identity ☑ RBAC ☑ Secrets ☑ NetworkPolicy ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Deployment
text: ```text ☑ ECR ☑ immutable image tags ☑ Helm ☑ ArgoCD ☑ rolling deployment ```

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Observability
text: ```text ☑ logs ☑ metrics ☑ traces ☑ alerts ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q1. What is EKS?
text: > Amazon EKS is AWS's managed Kubernetes service that integrates Kubernetes with AWS infrastructure and services. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q2. Why use EKS instead of running Kubernetes yourself?
text: > EKS reduces the operational burden of managing the Kubernetes control plane and provides deep integration with AWS networking, IAM, load balancing, storage, and other services. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q3. What is VPC CNI?
text: > It is the Kubernetes networking plugin used in EKS that integrates Pod networking with the AWS VPC networking model. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q4. Why can Pods run out of IPs?
text: > Pod IP allocation depends on available subnet address space and networking/instance limits. A cluster can therefore have enough CPU but still be unable to schedule additional Pods because it cannot allocate IP addresses. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q5. How does a Pod access S3 securely?
text: > Use workload identity such as EKS Pod Identity or IRSA to associate the workload with a least-privilege IAM role instead of embedding long-lived AWS credentials in the container. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q6. IAM vs RBAC?
text: > IAM controls access to AWS resources, while Kubernetes RBAC controls access to Kubernetes API resources. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q7. How does EKS expose an application?
text: A common approach: ```text Internet ↓ AWS Load Balancer ↓ Kubernetes Service ↓ Pods ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q8. HPA vs node autoscaling?
text: > HPA changes the number of application Pods, while node autoscaling changes the amount of compute capacity available to schedule those Pods. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q9. Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter?
text: > Cluster Autoscaler primarily adjusts existing node groups, while Karpenter can dynamically provision appropriate compute capacity based on pending workload requirements and constraints. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q10. EBS vs EFS?
text: ```text EBS → block storage → AZ-oriented EFS → shared filesystem → multi-AZ access ``` ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Q11. Why use private EKS nodes?
text: > To reduce direct Internet exposure of worker infrastructure while exposing only the required entry points such as load balancers. ---

title: Chapter 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Practical EKS setup the chapter describes but does not show
text: The chapter explains EKS concepts without setup commands. These are the concrete counterparts. Check current AWS documentation before using them in a real account (versions and flags change), and remember that a running EKS cluster, NAT gateways and load balancers all cost money. **1. Create a cluster (eksctl) and connect `kubectl`.** ```yaml # cluster.yaml apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5 kind: ClusterConfig metadata: name: devops-learning region: ap-south-1 managedNodeGroups: - name: general instanceType: t3.medium minSize: 2 desiredCapacity: 2 maxSize: 4 privateNetworking: true # nodes in private subnets (section 13) ``` ```bash eksctl create cluster -f cluster.yaml aws eks update-kubeconfig --region ap-south-1 --name devops-learning # writes ~/.kube/config kubectl get nodes eksctl delete cluster -f cluster.yaml # clean up to stop charges ``` **2. How an IAM identity gets Kubernetes permissions (authentication → authorization).** `kubectl` authenticates to the EKS API with an **IAM** identity (a token generated from your AWS credentials), then Kubernetes **RBAC** decides what that identity may do. The mapping from IAM principals to Kubernetes users/groups is configured with **EKS access entries** (current mechanism) or, in older clusters, the `aws-auth` ConfigMap. This is the practical meaning of "IAM vs RBAC" in section 58: IAM answers "may this principal reach the cluster?", RBAC answers "what may it do inside it?". **3. IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts).** The ServiceAccount is annotated with the role, and the role's trust policy trusts the cluster's OIDC provider for exactly that ServiceAccount: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: backend-sa namespace: production annotations: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/backend-s3-read ``` ```json { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:oidc-provider/oidc.eks.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/id/<OIDC_ID>" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "oidc.eks.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/id/<OIDC_ID>:sub": "system:serviceaccount:production:backend-sa" } } } ``` **4. EKS Pod Identity.** Install the *EKS Pod Identity Agent* add-on, give the IAM role a trust policy for the service principal `pods.eks.amazonaws.com` (actions `sts:AssumeRole` and `sts:TagSession`), then link ServiceAccount to role with an association — no OIDC annotation is needed: ```bash aws eks create-pod-identity-association \ --cluster-name devops-learning \ --namespace production \ --service-account backend-sa \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/backend-s3-read ``` **5. An Ingress handled by the AWS Load Balancer Controller** (creates an ALB; `target-type: ip` sends traffic straight to Pod IPs, section 41): ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: api annotations: alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTPS":443}]' alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:ap-south-1:<account-id>:certificate/<id> spec: ingressClassName: alb rules: - host: api.example.com http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: { name: api-service, port: { number: 80 } } ``` **6. Maximum Pods per node (the formula behind "Pod IP capacity").** With the default VPC CNI mode each Pod consumes a secondary IP address on one of the node's ENIs: ```text maxPods = ENIs × (IPv4 addresses per ENI − 1) + 2 ``` Example: an `m5.large` supports 3 ENIs with 10 IPv4 addresses each, so `3 × (10 − 1) + 2 = 29` Pods — regardless of how much CPU and memory are free. A bigger instance type therefore raises the Pod ceiling as well as capacity (sections 18–19). *Prefix delegation* (each ENI slot holds a /28 prefix) greatly increases the number of Pod IPs per node, and a *secondary CIDR* gives Pods a larger address range when the primary VPC CIDR is exhausted (section 20). **7. Other practical details.** - **Cluster endpoint access** can be public, private, or both; restrict public access by CIDR or make it private-only for stricter environments. - **Control-plane log types** you can enable: `api`, `audit`, `authenticator`, `controllerManager`, `scheduler`. - **Upgrades** move **one minor version at a time**: control plane first, then add-ons (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI), then nodes; check deprecated APIs before you start. Older versions eventually fall out of standard support, which can add cost or force an upgrade. - **Fargate** has constraints worth remembering: no DaemonSets, no EBS volumes (use EFS), and it needs a Fargate profile that selects which Pods run there. - **EKS Auto Mode** is a newer option where AWS also manages node capacity, load balancing and storage components — verify current features and pricing. - **Cost.** The EKS control plane has a fixed hourly charge in addition to EC2, EBS, load balancers, NAT gateways, data transfer and logging (verify current prices). --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 30: Service Mesh + Istio](ch30-service-mesh-istio.md) · [Chapter 32: Advanced Terraform](../06-iac-config/ch32-advanced-terraform.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch31-revision.md)

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Chapter 31 — Revision Sheet: Advanced Amazon EKS
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md). EKS sits at the intersection of **AWS + VPC + IAM + Kubernetes + Docker + ECR + load balancing + storage + autoscaling + security + observability.**

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: What EKS is
text: **EKS = Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service**, AWS-managed Kubernetes. AWS manages much of the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager, control-plane upgrades/availability); **you manage** applications (Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets), node infrastructure/configuration, networking configuration, IAM integration, observability. EKS doesn't replace Kubernetes concepts — you still use `kubectl` and manifests; EKS = AWS-managed Kubernetes + deep AWS integration. Use it when you have e.g. 20 microservices needing recovery, scaling, rolling deployments, private networking, load balancing, IAM, persistent storage, observability, HA. **Control plane:** API Server (auth → authorization → validation → store desired state → controllers reconcile), Scheduler, Controllers, **etcd** (cluster state: Deployments, Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, CRDs, config). You don't SSH into control-plane machines or manage etcd.

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Compute options
text: | Option | Notes | |---|---| | **Managed Node Groups** | EC2 instances managed as a Kubernetes node group; important for most backends | | **Self-managed nodes** | You manage more of the EC2 lifecycle; specialised needs, more operational work | | **Fargate** | Pods on serverless compute, no EC2 nodes to manage | | **Karpenter** | Dynamically provisions appropriate EC2 capacity from pending workload requirements | Multi-AZ nodes survive an AZ failure better (if the app and dependencies are also designed for it).

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Networking
text: - Nodes in **private subnets** (reduce exposure) behind a public load balancer: Internet → IGW → public LB → private EKS nodes → Pods → private RDS. Private nodes still need outbound access (images, OS packages, AWS APIs, external APIs): NAT Gateway → IGW, or **VPC endpoints** for AWS service traffic. - **CNI** (Container Network Interface) = standard interface for container networking; **Amazon VPC CNI** connects Pods to the VPC: ENIs/IP allocation → Pods can get VPC-routable IPs. Pod flow: scheduled → VPC CNI → allocate IP → configure networking → Pod gets identity. - **Pod IP capacity:** `kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=100` → Pods `Pending` because of insufficient IPs. Subnet IP capacity and node networking limits (ENIs, IPs per ENI, bandwidth differ per instance type) constrain scaling → **VPC CIDR planning matters**; "bigger node ≠ only more CPU/RAM". IP exhaustion is a real production failure mode (secondary CIDR/larger Pod address space). - **Security groups** (Internet → ALB SG :443 → EKS app → RDS :5432) and **Pod-level security groups** (e.g. Payment Pod with its own SG). **NetworkPolicy** (Pod A → Pod B allowed?) vs **AWS Security Group** (AWS network layer) — complementary.

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: IAM for Pods (very high-yield)
text: Never put `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET` in containers. Use workload identity: - **IRSA** (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) — older pattern, know well. **EKS Pod Identity** — newer EKS-native approach, know well. Flow: Pod → Kubernetes ServiceAccount → (IRSA / Pod Identity association) → IAM Role → temporary AWS credentials → AWS API. App just uses the AWS SDK. - ServiceAccount example: `kind: ServiceAccount, name: backend-sa, namespace: production`; Deployment `spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName: backend-sa`. - Least-privilege policy example: `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::my-company-assets/*`. - **Node IAM role vs Pod identity:** node role = broad permissions to everything on the EC2 node (dangerous if every Pod inherits them); Pod identity = per-workload (Pod A → S3 read, Pod B → SQS send, Pod C → Secrets Manager read). Example: User Service → DynamoDB; Image Service → S3; Payment Service → Secrets Manager — never `AdministratorAccess` for all three. - **IAM vs Kubernetes RBAC:** IAM controls AWS resources (S3, SQS, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager, ECR) — "Can this workload access AWS?"; RBAC controls Kubernetes API resources (Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps) — "Can this identity perform this Kubernetes API action?" (User → Role/ClusterRole → RoleBinding → API; workloads: ServiceAccount → RBAC permissions).

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: ECR, load balancing, storage
text: - **ECR + EKS:** Developer → Git → GitHub Actions → Docker build → ECR → EKS → Pod; image `<account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/backend:<tag>`; use immutable tags (`backend:a82f31c` = Git SHA, not `latest`). `ImagePullBackOff` → `kubectl describe pod` → wrong image/tag, ECR permissions, network, registry issue. - **AWS Load Balancer Controller:** Ingress → ALB; certain Services → NLB; reconciles AWS infrastructure from Kubernetes resources (desired state → controller → actual infrastructure — compare Ch.29). **ALB** = Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS, host, path, headers); **NLB** = Layer 4 (TCP/TLS, high performance). **Target type:** *instance* (ALB → Node → Service → Pod) vs *IP* (ALB → Pod IP; skips a hop; common in modern EKS). - **EBS CSI driver:** Pod → PVC → PV → EBS volume; EBS volumes are **AZ-bound** (Pod rescheduled to another AZ → attachment/scheduling constraints). **EFS:** managed network file system shared across AZs/Pods. Don't blindly put a database on EFS — prefer RDS. **StorageClass → CSI driver → AWS storage.** **CSI** = Container Storage Interface (EBS CSI, EFS CSI).

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Autoscaling
text: HPA = number of Pods; node autoscaling = compute capacity. Flow: traffic ↑ → CPU ↑ → HPA more replicas → Pods Pending → **Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler** provisions nodes → Pods schedule. **Cluster Autoscaler** primarily scales existing node groups (pending Pods → increase node group → new EC2); **Karpenter** dynamically provisions appropriate capacity (e.g. a Pod needing 8 CPU / 32 GB gets suitable capacity). **Resource requests** drive scheduling (node capacity + Pod requests); bad requests → overprovisioning, underprovisioning, Pending Pods, poor autoscaling.

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Security layers (defense in depth)
text: IAM (Pod identity → AWS permissions), Network (SG/NACL, NetworkPolicy), Kubernetes (RBAC, ServiceAccounts), secrets, encryption, image security, pod security, audit logs. Secrets: don't commit real secrets; AWS Secrets Manager → External Secrets/workload integration → Kubernetes Secret → Pod. Encryption: TLS (in transit) + encryption at rest (KMS-backed where supported). **Pod security:** `securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true`, read-only filesystem where possible, drop unnecessary capabilities, resource limits, seccomp. **Image security:** dependency scanning, image scanning, minimal images, non-root, signed/verified artifacts where appropriate, immutable tags, least privilege.

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Observability
text: Monitor cluster (node availability, API server health, capacity), node (CPU, memory, disk, network), Pod (restarts, CPU, memory, readiness, liveness), application (request rate, error rate, latency), AWS (ALB, RDS, EBS, NAT Gateway, S3). Structured logs with `requestId`/`service`; tracing example Order 50 ms, Payment 400 ms, DB 350 ms. **Control-plane logs** can go to CloudWatch Logs (API requests, authentication, authorization, audit, scheduler/controller); check current AWS docs for categories.

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Upgrades, add-ons, DNS
text: Upgrade process: check compatibility → check deprecated APIs → upgrade test environment → control plane → add-ons → nodes → validate workloads. Deprecated APIs (Ingress, CRDs, operators, admission controllers) can break deployments. **Add-ons:** VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI driver (some managed as EKS add-ons; compatibility matters). **CoreDNS** gives `payment.default.svc.cluster.local`; DNS failure makes services look unreachable even with healthy Pods.

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Troubleshooting a 503 (outside in)
text: Load balancer (healthy? listeners? target groups? SGs?) → Ingress (`kubectl get/describe ingress`: host, path, backend, events) → Service (ports, targetPort, selector) → Endpoints/EndpointSlices (none ⇒ selector mismatch) → Pods (`get pods -o wide`: Pending/CrashLoopBackOff/ImagePullBackOff/Running-not-Ready) → `describe pod` (Events) → `logs` (`--previous`, `-c <container>`) → Node (`describe node`: CPU/memory/disk pressure, taints, capacity, allocatable) → Networking (DNS, route, SG, NetworkPolicy, port 5432, RDS availability) → IAM (ServiceAccount → Pod identity/IRSA → IAM role → policy; don't modify the node role). | Classic failure | Checks | |---|---| | **Pods Pending** | CPU/memory, node selector, taints/tolerations, affinity, no available nodes, **IP exhaustion**, PVC problems | | **ImagePullBackOff** | image name, tag, ECR permissions, network, registry | | **CrashLoopBackOff** | logs/`--previous`; bad env var, app crash, wrong command, DB unavailable, missing Secret, bad config | | **App can't access S3** | ServiceAccount → Pod Identity → IAM role → S3 policy → bucket policy; VPC endpoint/NAT | | **Pods can't communicate** | Service, Endpoints, DNS, NetworkPolicy, SGs, CNI, ports | | **Pods can't get IPs** | VPC CNI → subnet IP capacity → ENI/IP limits |

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Architecture, flows, cost
text: - Production: Internet → Route 53 → CloudFront → WAF → AWS Load Balancer → AZ-a/AZ-b EKS nodes (Pods) → private RDS/Redis/S3/SQS. Terraform provisions AWS; GitHub Actions → Docker → ECR; ArgoCD → EKS; Helm packages apps. - **Request flow (`GET /orders/123`):** Route 53 → CloudFront/WAF → load balancer → AWS integration routes to EKS workload → Service → Pod → app → RDS/Redis/S3/SQS (private networking + IAM) → metrics/logs/traces emitted. - **Deployment flow:** `git push` → Actions (lint, typecheck, test, build, security checks) → Docker build → ECR push → GitOps repo image tag update → ArgoCD → EKS Deployment update → rolling update → new Pods. - **Terraform provisions:** VPC, subnets, IAM, EKS, node groups, SGs, RDS, S3, Redis, load-balancing infra; Kubernetes/Helm/ArgoCD manage workloads. EKS + Operators (PostgreSQL Operator → Postgres CR) and EKS + Istio (Envoy) work as in Ch.29/30. - **Cost:** EKS control-plane charges, EC2, EBS, load balancers, NAT Gateway, data transfer, CloudWatch, ECR, RDS, ElastiCache; bad designs (many NAT Gateways + cross-AZ traffic + oversized EC2 + unused load balancers + unbounded logging) get expensive. **Availability vs cost:** 1 node cheaper vs 3 AZs multi-node fault tolerance — explain trade-offs (cost, availability, performance, operational complexity), not "always use three AZs".

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Checklists
text: Security: private nodes where appropriate, least-privilege IAM, Pod identity, RBAC, NetworkPolicies, SGs, Secrets Manager, encryption, non-root containers, image scanning, resource limits, audit/control-plane logging, regular upgrades, restricted API access, minimal permissions. Production: Networking (multi-AZ, private subnets, CIDR planning, VPC CNI, IP capacity), Compute (managed node groups, autoscaling, requests, instance sizing), Security (IAM, Pod Identity, RBAC, Secrets, NetworkPolicy), Deployment (ECR, immutable tags, Helm, ArgoCD, rolling), Observability (logs, metrics, traces, alerts).

title: Revision 31 — Advanced Amazon EKS
heading: Interview answers (12)
text: EKS (AWS-managed Kubernetes integrated with AWS infrastructure/services) · why EKS (reduced control-plane burden + AWS networking/IAM/LB/storage integration) · VPC CNI · why Pods run out of IPs (subnet address space + networking/instance limits: enough CPU but cannot allocate IPs) · Pod → S3 securely (Pod Identity or IRSA, least-privilege role) · IAM vs RBAC · exposing an app (Internet → AWS LB → Service → Pods) · HPA vs node autoscaling · Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter · EBS vs EFS (block/AZ vs shared FS/multi-AZ) · private nodes (limit exposure; only LB entry points) · debug a 503. **Depth:** 🔥 EKS architecture, EKS + VPC, subnets, VPC CNI, Pod IP allocation, IAM, Pod Identity/IRSA, ECR, AWS LB Controller, Services, Ingress, HPA, node scaling, EBS/EFS, RBAC, NetworkPolicy, troubleshooting · 🟡 Managed Node Groups, Fargate, Karpenter, CSI, control-plane logging, upgrades, add-ons, Pod-level SGs · ⚪ control-plane internals, custom CNI, Karpenter internals, kernel networking, scheduler implementation, etcd internals.
