title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
text: > **Source:** Response 32 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-32.txt`, lines 1–3135) · **Part II — Advanced extension (Responses 25–36)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch32-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) · *includes an editorial supplement at the end* <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We're continuing exactly on the roadmap. You already learned Terraform fundamentals in **[Chapter 21](ch21-terraform.md)**: - HCL - providers - resources - variables - outputs - data sources - `init / plan / apply / destroy` - state - modules - remote state - drift - Terraform + GitHub Actions So I will **not repeat the basics**. This response goes into how Terraform is actually structured and operated in a production team. The goal is: > **Be able to design, explain, review, troubleshoot, and safely use Terraform for real AWS infrastructure.** ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 1. First: What Terraform Is Really Doing
text: At a high level: ```text Terraform Configuration ↓ Desired Infrastructure ↓ Terraform ↓ AWS APIs ↓ Actual Infrastructure ``` Terraform continuously tries to make: ```text Actual Infrastructure ≈ Desired Configuration ``` It does this using: ```text Configuration + State + Provider + Refresh/read operations + Dependency graph ``` The most important production concepts are therefore: ```text State Modules Dependencies Environments Remote state Locking Drift CI/CD Security ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 2. Terraform State — The Most Important Advanced Concept
text: You've already seen: ```text terraform.tfstate ``` But let's understand **why it exists**. Suppose your code says: ```hcl resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" { bucket = "my-company-assets" } ``` Terraform creates: ```text AWS S3 Bucket ``` Terraform needs to remember: > "This particular AWS object corresponds to this particular Terraform resource." That's what state helps track. Conceptually: ```text Terraform resource ↓ aws_s3_bucket.assets ↓ AWS object ID ↓ actual infrastructure ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 3. State Is Not Just a Cache
text: A common beginner mistake: > "Terraform state is just a copy of AWS." Not exactly. State contains Terraform's understanding of managed resources and relationships. It helps Terraform answer: ```text What do I manage? What infrastructure object corresponds to this resource? What attributes are known? What changed? ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 4. Why State Is Dangerous
text: Terraform state can contain sensitive information. For example: ```text resource attributes IDs connection information sensitive values ``` Therefore: **Never casually commit `terraform.tfstate` to Git.** Your `.gitignore` should generally include: ```gitignore *.tfstate *.tfstate.* .terraform/ .terraform.lock.hcl ``` Actually, one nuance:

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Don't ignore `.terraform.lock.hcl`
text: The lock file should normally be committed because it pins provider versions/checksums. So a better `.gitignore` is: ```gitignore .terraform/ *.tfstate *.tfstate.* *.tfplan ``` while keeping: ```text .terraform.lock.hcl ``` in Git. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 5. Local State vs Remote State
text: For a personal experiment: ```text Terraform ↓ local terraform.tfstate ``` For a team: ```text Developer A ↓ Remote State ↑ Developer B ``` You need centralized state. A common AWS architecture is: ```text Terraform ↓ S3 ↓ Remote state ``` with state locking supported through the configured backend capabilities. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 6. Why Remote State?
text: Imagine two developers: ```text Developer A terraform apply Developer B terraform apply ``` If both use independent local state: ```text A's state ≠ B's state ``` This can cause dangerous inconsistencies. Remote state provides a shared source of Terraform state. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 7. State Locking
text: Suppose: ```text Developer A ``` is applying infrastructure. At the same time: ```text Developer B ``` starts an apply. We don't want both operations modifying the same state simultaneously. Conceptually: ```text Terraform Apply ↓ Acquire lock ↓ Modify infrastructure/state ↓ Release lock ``` Modern Terraform/AWS S3 backend configurations can use **native S3 state locking**, while older tutorials commonly show DynamoDB-based locking. For current projects, follow the backend documentation for the Terraform/AWS versions you're actually using. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 8. Why Locking Matters
text: Without proper coordination: ```text A reads state B reads state A changes infrastructure B changes infrastructure A writes state B writes stale state ``` Now Terraform's state can become inconsistent with reality. Therefore: > **Remote state + locking is fundamental for team Terraform.** ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 9. State Backend
text: A backend determines where Terraform stores state and how state operations are handled. Conceptually: ```hcl terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "company-terraform-state" key = "production/network/terraform.tfstate" region = "..." } } ``` Now state isn't sitting on your laptop. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 10. State Bucket Security
text: Your Terraform state bucket is extremely sensitive. Use: ```text encryption versioning restricted IAM private access logging/monitoring ``` You should **not** make your Terraform state bucket public. Architecture: ```text Terraform CI │ │ IAM ↓ Private S3 state bucket ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 11. Bootstrap Problem
text: Interesting problem: > Who creates the S3 bucket that stores Terraform state? Terraform can't use the remote backend before the backend exists. So you often have a bootstrap step. Conceptually: ```text Bootstrap Terraform ↓ Creates state infrastructure ↓ S3 backend ↓ Main Terraform configuration ``` In larger organizations, the state bucket/backend is often provisioned separately and managed centrally. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 12. State File Versioning
text: Suppose someone accidentally destroys or corrupts state. S3 versioning can provide historical versions. Conceptually: ```text state-v1 state-v2 state-v3 ``` This gives you a recovery mechanism. But: > Don't treat versioning as a replacement for proper Terraform workflows. It's a safety mechanism. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 13. Terraform State Commands
text: You've seen these, but now understand when to use them. ```bash terraform state list ``` Shows managed resources. ```bash terraform state show aws_instance.web ``` Shows details. ```bash terraform state rm aws_instance.web ``` Removes the resource from Terraform state **without necessarily deleting the real AWS resource**. This is dangerous if misunderstood. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 14. State RM Example
text: Suppose AWS has: ```text EC2 instance ``` and Terraform state tracks it. You run: ```bash terraform state rm aws_instance.web ``` Now: ```text AWS: EC2 still exists Terraform: doesn't know it manages that EC2 anymore ``` If the resource remains in configuration and you run `plan`, Terraform may attempt to create another resource or otherwise show reconciliation changes. So: > `state rm` changes Terraform's tracking, not AWS itself. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 15. Terraform Import
text: Suppose someone manually created: ```text S3 bucket ``` in AWS. Now you want Terraform to manage it. That's where import comes in. Conceptually: ```text Existing AWS resource ↓ Terraform import ↓ Terraform state ↓ Terraform configuration ``` Modern Terraform supports import blocks as well as CLI workflows. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 16. Import Does Not Automatically Give You Perfect Code
text: This is important. Importing: ```text AWS resource ``` doesn't mean: ```text Beautiful Terraform configuration automatically created ``` You still need configuration that correctly represents the resource. Think: ```text Import → bring resource under Terraform management Configuration → describe how Terraform should manage it ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 17. Terraform Plan After Import
text: After importing, run: ```bash terraform plan ``` You may see changes. Why? Because: ```text Existing infrastructure ≠ your Terraform configuration ``` Your job is to reconcile them. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 18. Terraform Drift
text: Suppose Terraform says: ```text EC2 type = t3.medium ``` Then someone manually changes it in AWS: ```text t3.large ``` Now: ```text Terraform config ↓ t3.medium AWS actual ↓ t3.large ``` That's drift. Terraform can detect the difference during planning/refresh behavior. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 19. Why Drift Is Dangerous
text: Imagine: ```text Terraform ↓ production infrastructure ``` but engineers also make manual console changes. Eventually: ```text Terraform ≠ AWS ``` Now nobody knows what the actual intended configuration is. Therefore: > **Infrastructure should preferably be managed through the declared Terraform workflow rather than ad-hoc console changes.** This is one reason IaC improves operational consistency. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 20. Terraform Modules
text: Now the most important reusable architecture concept. Suppose you repeatedly create: ```text VPC Subnets Route tables NAT Security groups ``` Instead of copying hundreds of lines: ```text production-vpc.tf staging-vpc.tf dev-vpc.tf ``` create: ```text modules/ └── vpc/ ``` Then: ```text production ↓ VPC module staging ↓ VPC module development ↓ VPC module ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 21. Why Modules?
text: Modules provide: ```text reuse consistency abstraction standardization maintainability ``` Think of a Terraform module like a reusable function. In programming: ```typescript createDatabase(config) ``` Terraform: ```hcl module "database" { source = "./modules/database" } ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 22. Module Structure
text: Example: ```text modules/ └── network/ ├── main.tf ├── variables.tf ├── outputs.tf └── README.md ```

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: `main.tf`
text: Resources.

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: `variables.tf`
text: Inputs.

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: `outputs.tf`
text: Outputs. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 23. Example Module
text: `variables.tf`: ```hcl variable "vpc_cidr" { type = string } ``` `main.tf`: ```hcl resource "aws_vpc" "this" { cidr_block = var.vpc_cidr } ``` `outputs.tf`: ```hcl output "vpc_id" { value = aws_vpc.this.id } ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 24. Calling the Module
text: Root configuration: ```hcl module "network" { source = "./modules/network" vpc_cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" } ``` Then: ```hcl module.network.vpc_id ``` can be used elsewhere. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 25. Module Input/Output Flow
text: Think: ```text Root Module │ │ inputs ↓ Child Module │ │ creates infrastructure ↓ outputs │ ↓ Root Module ``` This is the same idea as function arguments and return values. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 26. Good Module Design
text: A good module should expose: ```text important configuration ``` but hide: ```text implementation details ``` For example: ```hcl module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc" cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" az_count = 3 } ``` The caller shouldn't need to know every route-table resource inside. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 27. Don't Over-Modularize
text: This is a common Terraform mistake. Bad: ```text module-vpc module-subnet module-route-table module-route module-security-group module-rule ``` for every tiny resource. That can make the code harder to understand. Prefer meaningful modules: ```text network eks database observability ``` when those boundaries make sense. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 28. Root Module vs Child Module
text: Your project might look like: ```text terraform/ │ ├── main.tf ├── variables.tf ├── outputs.tf │ └── modules/ ├── network/ ├── eks/ ├── rds/ └── monitoring/ ``` The root module composes the infrastructure. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 29. Environment Structure
text: Now the big question: > How do we manage dev, staging, and production? One pattern: ```text environments/ ├── dev/ ├── staging/ └── prod/ ``` Each environment calls shared modules. ```text dev ↓ modules staging ↓ modules prod ↓ modules ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 30. Why Separate Environment State?
text: You generally don't want: ```text development staging production ``` all sharing one state file. Instead: ```text dev state staging state prod state ``` Conceptually: ```text S3 ├── dev/terraform.tfstate ├── staging/terraform.tfstate └── prod/terraform.tfstate ``` This reduces blast radius. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 31. Blast Radius
text: Suppose one Terraform state manages: ```text dev + staging + prod ``` A mistake can potentially affect everything. Instead: ```text State A → dev State B → staging State C → prod ``` Now the blast radius is smaller. This is a very important production principle. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 32. Terraform Workspaces
text: Terraform also provides: ```bash terraform workspace ``` which can maintain separate state instances using the same configuration. For example: ```text dev prod ``` But workspaces aren't automatically the best environment architecture. For serious infrastructure, many teams prefer separate root configurations/state backends because they make environment boundaries explicit. Interview answer: > Workspaces provide separate state instances for the same configuration, but they should not automatically be treated as the solution to every environment-management problem. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 33. Environment Pattern I Recommend You Understand
text: For your projects: ```text infra/ ├── modules/ │ ├── vpc/ │ ├── eks/ │ ├── rds/ │ └── redis/ │ └── environments/ ├── dev/ ├── staging/ └── prod/ ``` This is easy to reason about. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 34. Variable Strategy
text: You don't want: ```hcl replicas = 3 ``` hardcoded everywhere. Use variables: ```hcl variable "environment" { type = string } variable "instance_type" { type = string } ``` Then environment-specific values can be provided through appropriate variable files/configuration. For example: ```text dev.tfvars prod.tfvars ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 35. Sensitive Variables
text: Example: ```hcl variable "db_password" { type = string sensitive = true } ``` But: > `sensitive = true` does not magically make the secret secure everywhere. It mainly affects how Terraform displays the value. You still need proper secret handling. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 36. Don't Store Production Secrets in `.tfvars`
text: Avoid: ```text prod.tfvars ``` containing: ```text DB_PASSWORD=actual-production-password ``` and committing it to Git. Better: ```text AWS Secrets Manager SSM Parameter Store CI/CD secret store appropriate external secret system ``` depending on the architecture. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 37. Data Sources
text: You learned data sources earlier. Now understand their production value. Suppose a VPC already exists. Instead of creating: ```hcl resource "aws_vpc" ... ``` you can look it up: ```hcl data "aws_vpc" "existing" { ... } ``` Then: ```hcl data.aws_vpc.existing.id ``` can be passed to other resources. So: ```text resource → Terraform creates/manages it data source → Terraform reads existing information ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 38. Dependency Graph
text: Terraform builds a dependency graph. Suppose: ```hcl resource "aws_subnet" "private" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id } ``` Terraform sees: ```text VPC ↓ Subnet ``` So it knows the subnet depends on the VPC. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 39. Implicit Dependencies
text: This is preferred. Example: ```hcl vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id ``` Terraform understands: ```text Subnet → VPC ``` automatically. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 40. Explicit Dependencies
text: Sometimes Terraform can't infer a dependency. Then: ```hcl depends_on = [ aws_iam_role_policy.example ] ``` can explicitly tell Terraform: > Don't proceed until this resource exists. But don't overuse `depends_on`. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 41. Why Overusing `depends_on` Is Bad
text: If you write: ```text everything depends on everything ``` you unnecessarily serialize operations. Terraform loses opportunities for parallelism. Prefer: ```text implicit dependency ``` whenever possible. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 42. Terraform Graph
text: You can inspect the dependency graph: ```bash terraform graph ``` Conceptually: ```text VPC ├── Subnet │ └── EC2 └── Route Table ``` This is useful for understanding complex infrastructure. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 43. Lifecycle Meta-Arguments
text: Terraform has lifecycle controls. One important one: ```hcl lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } ``` Useful for critical resources. For example: ```text production database ``` You may want additional protection against accidental destruction. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 44. `create_before_destroy`
text: Example: ```hcl lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } ``` Conceptually: ```text Old resource │ ├── keep │ Create new resource │ ↓ switch │ ↓ remove old ``` Useful where replacement can cause downtime, assuming the resource supports the behavior and constraints allow it. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 45. `ignore_changes`
text: You may encounter: ```hcl lifecycle { ignore_changes = [ tags ] } ``` This tells Terraform to ignore changes to specified attributes. But be careful. If you ignore too much: ```text Terraform ≠ actual infrastructure ``` and drift becomes harder to detect. Use it intentionally. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 46. Terraform Plan
text: `terraform plan` is one of your safest tools. It tells you approximately: ```text + create ~ modify - destroy ``` Example: ```text + aws_s3_bucket.assets ~ aws_instance.web - aws_instance.old ``` Before production apply: > **Read the plan.** Never blindly run: ```bash terraform apply -auto-approve ``` against production. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 47. Saved Plans
text: You can create: ```bash terraform plan -out=tfplan ``` Then: ```bash terraform apply tfplan ``` This lets you apply the plan that was reviewed/generated. This is useful in CI/CD. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 48. Terraform CI/CD
text: A production pipeline can look like: ```text Pull Request ↓ terraform fmt ↓ terraform validate ↓ security/static checks ↓ terraform plan ↓ review ↓ approval ↓ terraform apply ``` For production: ```text manual approval ``` is often valuable. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 49. GitHub Actions Example
text: Conceptually: ```yaml name: Terraform on: pull_request: jobs: plan: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3 - run: terraform init - run: terraform fmt -check - run: terraform validate - run: terraform plan ``` For actual production infrastructure, authentication should use short-lived credentials/workload identity such as OIDC rather than storing long-lived AWS access keys. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 50. Terraform Apply Pipeline
text: A more complete model: ```text PR ↓ fmt ↓ validate ↓ security scan ↓ plan ↓ human review ↓ merge ↓ apply ``` For production: ```text merge ↓ approval ↓ apply ``` This gives you controlled infrastructure changes. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 51. Terraform Security
text: A secure Terraform workflow should avoid: ```text AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY ``` hardcoded in: ```text GitHub secrets source code Terraform files ``` where possible. Instead: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ OIDC ↓ AWS IAM Role ↓ temporary credentials ↓ Terraform ``` You learned this architecture earlier. Now you're applying it to Terraform. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 52. Terraform Provider Lock File
text: When you run: ```bash terraform init ``` Terraform can create: ```text .terraform.lock.hcl ``` Commit it. Why? It records provider selections/checksums so different environments are less likely to unexpectedly use incompatible provider builds. Think: ```text Terraform code + provider lock = more reproducible infrastructure ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 53. Provider Version Constraints
text: Example: ```hcl terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "~> 6.0" } } } ``` Don't blindly use: ```text latest ``` without considering compatibility. Pin sensible version ranges and review upgrades. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 54. Terraform Upgrade
text: A provider or Terraform upgrade can change behavior. Safe process: ```text Read changelog ↓ Upgrade dev ↓ terraform init -upgrade ↓ plan ↓ test ↓ staging ↓ production ``` Don't upgrade infrastructure tooling directly in production without testing. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 55. Terraform Version Management
text: Teams should agree on Terraform versions. You can specify: ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.x, < 2.0" } ``` Use a range appropriate for your project's compatibility policy. The exact version should be chosen deliberately rather than copied blindly. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 56. Modules: Local vs Registry
text: Modules can come from: ```text local directory Git repository Terraform Registry ``` Example: ```hcl module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc" } ``` or: ```hcl module "vpc" { source = "..." } ``` For production teams, internal modules can standardize company infrastructure. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 57. Internal Terraform Modules
text: Imagine your company wants every service to use: ```text standard VPC standard logging standard IAM standard encryption ``` Create: ```text company-network-module company-eks-module company-service-module ``` Then teams consume them. This creates: ```text Platform Team ↓ Reusable Modules ↓ Engineering Teams ``` This is a major platform-engineering use case. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 58. Module Versioning
text: Don't blindly point production at a constantly changing module. Prefer versioning: ```text v1.0 v1.1 v2.0 ``` Then: ```text production → module v1.2 ``` while staging tests: ```text module v1.3 ``` This allows controlled promotion. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 59. Terraform + Kubernetes
text: This is important for your stack. Terraform can create: ```text VPC EKS RDS S3 IAM ``` Then Kubernetes manages: ```text Deployments Services Pods ConfigMaps ``` So: ```text Terraform → infrastructure Kubernetes → application orchestration ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 60. Terraform + Helm
text: Terraform can also manage Helm releases. Conceptually: ```text Terraform ↓ Helm provider ↓ Helm release ↓ Kubernetes ``` For example: ```hcl resource "helm_release" "app" { name = "backend" repository = "..." chart = "backend" } ``` But be careful with ownership boundaries. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 61. Terraform + ArgoCD
text: A common production split: ```text Terraform ↓ EKS infrastructure ``` and: ```text ArgoCD ↓ Application deployments ``` This is often cleaner than having Terraform continuously manage every application manifest. Think: ```text Terraform → platform/infrastructure ArgoCD → application delivery ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 62. Terraform + Helm + ArgoCD
text: Your complete architecture: ```text Terraform │ ├── VPC ├── EKS ├── IAM ├── RDS └── supporting infrastructure │ ▼ EKS │ ArgoCD │ Helm │ Workloads ``` This is an excellent production mental model. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 63. Terraform vs Ansible
text: You've already learned Ansible. Remember:

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Terraform
text: ```text Provision infrastructure ``` Example: ```text VPC EC2 RDS EKS S3 ```

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Ansible
text: ```text Configure/manage machines ``` Example: ```text install nginx configure server manage service ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Terraform
text: ```text AWS infrastructure ```

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Kubernetes
text: ```text container workloads ``` Example: ```text Terraform → create EKS Kubernetes → create Deployment ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Terraform
text: ```text Infrastructure provisioning ```

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Helm
text: ```text Kubernetes application packaging ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Terraform
text: ```text Infrastructure lifecycle ```

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: ArgoCD
text: ```text Kubernetes application GitOps ``` These tools can coexist. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 67. Terraform State Separation
text: One advanced design principle: Don't put everything into one giant state. Bad: ```text terraform.tfstate ├── VPC ├── EKS ├── RDS ├── S3 ├── 100 applications └── every environment ``` This creates a huge blast radius. Better: ```text network state EKS state database state environment state ``` depending on organizational needs. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 68. Why Smaller States?
text: Benefits: ```text smaller plans faster operations smaller blast radius better ownership less contention easier troubleshooting ``` But don't split so aggressively that dependencies become impossible to manage. It's a balance. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 69. Cross-State References
text: Suppose: ```text Network state ``` creates: ```text VPC ID ``` and: ```text EKS state ``` needs it. Terraform supports mechanisms such as remote-state data access. Conceptually: ```text Network state ↓ VPC ID ↓ EKS state ``` However, excessive cross-state coupling can become difficult to maintain. Prefer clear boundaries. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 70. Terraform Refresh / Reconciliation
text: Terraform needs to compare: ```text Configuration + State + Actual infrastructure ``` to determine changes. Conceptually: ```text config ───────┐ ├── Terraform ──→ plan state ────────┤ │ actual ───────┘ ``` This is why drift can be detected. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 71. `terraform refresh` — Important Nuance
text: Older tutorials often teach: ```bash terraform refresh ``` as a standalone command. Modern Terraform workflows generally incorporate refreshing state information into normal planning/apply behavior, and you should follow the version's current recommended workflow. The important concept is: > Terraform needs current information about real infrastructure before producing an accurate plan. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 72. Sensitive State
text: Even if: ```hcl sensitive = true ``` hides a value from CLI output, the value may still exist in state. Therefore: ```text Sensitive variable ≠ secret automatically secured ``` Protect the backend itself. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 73. State Access Control
text: Only authorized people/workloads should access: ```text Terraform state bucket ``` For example: ```text Developer ↓ limited IAM CI/CD ↓ Terraform role S3 state ↓ restricted access ``` Don't give every developer unrestricted production state access. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 74. Terraform Disaster Recovery
text: Suppose: ```text Terraform state deleted ``` Your infrastructure may still exist. But Terraform loses its mapping. Therefore: ```text state backup/versioning + controlled access ``` is important. If necessary, recovery/import workflows can reconstruct management. But recovery is much easier when state is properly backed up. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 75. Terraform Plan as a Safety Mechanism
text: Imagine someone changes: ```hcl instance_type = "t3.large" ``` to: ```hcl instance_type = "t3.nano" ``` and Terraform says: ```text ~ change ``` The plan lets you catch mistakes before apply. For destructive changes: ```text - destroy ``` you should stop and investigate. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 76. Production Guardrails
text: Useful guardrails include: ```text code review plan review protected branches CI checks policy-as-code approval gates least privilege separate production credentials ``` Some organizations also use policy tools such as: ```text OPA Sentinel ``` to prevent dangerous infrastructure changes. You only need awareness of these for your target. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 77. Terraform Policy Example
text: Imagine a policy: > "Production S3 buckets must not be publicly accessible." Then: ```text Terraform Plan ↓ Policy check ↓ ❌ reject ``` This prevents bad infrastructure before deployment. This is an example of: > **Policy as Code** ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 78. Terraform Security Scanning
text: You may encounter tools that inspect Terraform configuration for issues such as: ```text public S3 overly broad IAM unencrypted resources open security groups ``` The exact tool isn't the important part for your SWE interview. The concept is: ```text IaC ↓ static/security analysis ↓ prevent insecure infrastructure ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 79. Terraform Testing
text: Infrastructure code should also be tested. At basic level: ```bash terraform fmt terraform validate terraform plan ``` More advanced: ```text module tests integration tests policy tests ``` You don't need to become a Terraform testing specialist, but understand: > Infrastructure is code and should be reviewed/tested like code. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 80. Terraform Deployment Strategy
text: A production deployment might be: ```text Developer ↓ PR ↓ Terraform fmt ↓ Validate ↓ Security scan ↓ Plan ↓ Review ↓ Merge ↓ Production approval ↓ Apply ``` This is the mature workflow. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Situation
text: You have: ```text Production EKS RDS VPC S3 ``` Someone manually changes the RDS instance class. Terraform detects: ```text Configuration: db.t3.medium Actual: db.r6g.large ``` What do you do? Don't immediately apply. First ask: > Was the manual change intentional? If intentional: ```text Update Terraform configuration ``` Then: ```bash terraform plan ``` If accidental: ```text Determine whether Terraform should restore intended state ``` This is infrastructure change management. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Developer says:
text: > "Terraform wants to destroy our production database!" Your response should be: ```text STOP APPLY ``` Then: ```text terraform plan ``` inspect: ```text why replacement? ``` Potential causes: ```text immutable field changed resource address changed module refactor provider behavior configuration mismatch import/state issue ``` Never blindly approve a destructive plan. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 83. Resource Address Changes
text: Suppose you move: ```hcl resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" ``` into: ```hcl module "storage" { ... } ``` Terraform may think: ```text old resource removed new resource created ``` even though it's logically the same infrastructure. Modern Terraform supports mechanisms such as `moved` blocks to tell Terraform: > This resource changed its address; it isn't a new real-world resource. Conceptually: ```text old address ↓ moved ↓ new address ``` This is an important production refactoring technique. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 84. Example `moved`
text: Conceptually: ```hcl moved { from = aws_s3_bucket.assets to = module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.assets } ``` Now Terraform can preserve resource identity across the refactor. This can prevent unnecessary destroy/create operations. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 85. `for_each` vs `count`
text: Another useful Terraform concept.

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: `count`
text: Good for simple numeric repetition. ```hcl count = 3 ``` Resources get numeric indexes. ```text resource[0] resource[1] resource[2] ```

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: `for_each`
text: Better when resources have meaningful identities. ```hcl for_each = { api = "..." worker = "..." } ``` Then: ```text resource["api"] resource["worker"] ``` For infrastructure, `for_each` is often easier to manage when items have stable names. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 86. Why `for_each` Can Be Safer
text: Suppose: ```text count = 3 ``` and you remove the second item. Indexes can shift. With: ```text for_each ``` keys can remain stable: ```text api worker scheduler ``` Terraform can more accurately identify which logical resource changed. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 87. Locals
text: Locals let you avoid repeating expressions. Example: ```hcl locals { name_prefix = "${var.project}-${var.environment}" } ``` Then: ```hcl name = "${local.name_prefix}-api" ``` Useful for consistent naming. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 88. Naming Conventions
text: Production Terraform should use predictable names. For example: ```text project-environment-component ``` Such as: ```text payments-prod-eks payments-prod-rds payments-prod-assets ``` This helps: ```text operations billing debugging security ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 89. Tags
text: AWS resources should generally receive useful tags such as: ```text Project Environment Owner ManagedBy CostCenter ``` Example: ```hcl tags = { Project = "payments" Environment = "production" ManagedBy = "terraform" } ``` Tags help with: ```text cost allocation search operations governance ``` ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: 90. Terraform + EKS Best Practice Boundary
text: For your architecture:

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Q1. Why does Terraform need state?
text: > State maps Terraform resources to real infrastructure and stores information Terraform needs to calculate changes and manage resource lifecycle. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Q2. Why remote state?
text: > To provide a shared, centralized state representation for team collaboration and CI/CD. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Q3. Why state locking?
text: > To prevent concurrent Terraform operations from corrupting or conflicting over the same state. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Q4. What is drift?
text: > Drift occurs when actual infrastructure differs from the configuration Terraform expects, often because of manual or external changes. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Q5. What is a module?
text: > A reusable package of Terraform configuration that abstracts and standardizes infrastructure creation. ---

title: Chapter 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Complete Terraform snippets for the fragments in this chapter
text: The chapter describes several features using partial snippets (`source = "..."`, `for_each = { api = "..." }`, "remote-state data access"). Here are complete, working forms. Check the Terraform and provider documentation for the versions you use. **1. A complete S3 backend** (sections 9–10) with encryption and native locking (Terraform ≥ 1.10; older setups used a DynamoDB table): ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.10, < 2.0" # a real range; the chapter's ">= 1.x" is a placeholder backend "s3" { bucket = "company-terraform-state" key = "production/network/terraform.tfstate" # one key per state region = "ap-south-1" encrypt = true use_lockfile = true # S3-native state locking } } ``` **2. `count` vs `for_each`** (sections 85–86). With `count`, items are identified by position, so removing the middle item shifts the others and Terraform plans to destroy and recreate resources. With `for_each` each item has a stable key: ```hcl variable "services" { type = map(string) default = { api = "t3.small" worker = "t3.medium" scheduler = "t3.small" } } resource "aws_instance" "svc" { for_each = var.services ami = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id instance_type = each.value tags = { Name = "${local.name_prefix}-${each.key}" } # addresses: aws_instance.svc["api"], ["worker"], ... } # count form (positional): aws_instance.web[0], [1], [2] resource "aws_instance" "web" { count = 3 ami = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id instance_type = "t3.micro" } ``` **3. `lifecycle` in practice** (sections 43–45): ```hcl resource "aws_db_instance" "main" { # ... lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true # any plan that would destroy this errors out } } resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "app" { # ... lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true ignore_changes = [desired_capacity] # autoscaling changes this outside Terraform } } ``` Caveat: `prevent_destroy` only protects while the resource block (and its lifecycle setting) stays in the configuration — if you delete the whole block, Terraform no longer sees the protection and will plan the destroy. Review plans for removed resources. **4. `moved` blocks and imports** (sections 15–17, 83–84): ```hcl moved { from = aws_s3_bucket.assets to = module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.assets } import { # Terraform ≥ 1.5 to = aws_s3_bucket.legacy id = "my-existing-bucket" } ``` `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` can draft configuration for resources declared in `import` blocks, which softens (but doesn't remove) the chapter's point that you must still review and own the resulting code. Newer Terraform also has a `removed` block to stop managing a resource without destroying it, the declarative counterpart of `terraform state rm`. **5. Reading another state's outputs** (section 69): ```hcl # in the EKS configuration data "terraform_remote_state" "network" { backend = "s3" config = { bucket = "company-terraform-state" key = "production/network/terraform.tfstate" region = "ap-south-1" } } resource "aws_eks_cluster" "this" { # ... vpc_config { subnet_ids = data.terraform_remote_state.network.outputs.private_subnet_ids } } ``` The network configuration must expose `private_subnet_ids` as an `output`. Reading a remote state requires read access to that state file. **6. Useful commands the chapter implies.** | Command | Purpose | |---|---| | `terraform apply -refresh-only` | Update state to match real infrastructure without changing resources (the modern replacement for standalone `terraform refresh`, section 71) | | `terraform state mv <from> <to>` | Rename/move an address in state (CLI alternative to a `moved` block) | | `terraform apply -replace=<address>` | Force recreation of one resource (replaces the deprecated `taint`) | | `terraform force-unlock <id>` | Release a stuck lock — only when you are sure no run is active | | `terraform plan -lock-timeout=5m` | Wait for a lock instead of failing immediately | | `terraform plan -target=<address>` | Plan one resource — an escape hatch that can leave things inconsistent; not for routine use | | `terraform output -json`, `terraform console`, `terraform graph` | Inspect outputs, evaluate expressions, view the dependency graph | **7. Tooling for the "policy / scanning / testing" sections (76–79).** Static analysis and policy: `tflint`, Checkov, Trivy (the successor to tfsec), OPA/Conftest, Sentinel (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise). Native testing: `terraform test` (Terraform ≥ 1.6) with `.tftest.hcl` files; integration tests commonly use Terratest. --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 31: Advanced Amazon EKS](../05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md) · [Chapter 33: Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers](../04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch32-revision.md)

heading: Chapter 32 — Revision Sheet: Advanced Terraform
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/06-iac-config/ch32-advanced-terraform.md). Goal: **design, explain, review, troubleshoot and safely use Terraform for real AWS infrastructure.** Builds on [Chapter 21](../docs/06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md).

title: Revision 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: What Terraform is really doing
text: Configuration (desired) + **State** + **Provider** + refresh/read operations + **dependency graph** → plan → AWS APIs → actual infrastructure ≈ desired. Production concerns: state, modules, dependencies, environments, remote state, locking, drift, CI/CD, security. Plan inputs: config ∥ state ∥ actual infrastructure → plan (this is how drift is detected).

title: Revision 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: State (the most important advanced concept)
text: - State maps `aws_s3_bucket.assets` ↔ the real AWS object ID, and records what Terraform manages, attributes known and what changed. **State is not just a cache/copy of AWS.** - **Dangerous:** may contain sensitive data (resource attributes, IDs, connection info, sensitive values). `sensitive = true` only hides values in CLI output — they can still be in state. Protect the backend. - **`.gitignore`:** `.terraform/`, `*.tfstate`, `*.tfstate.*`, `*.tfplan` — but **commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`** (the chapter first lists it as ignored, then corrects: it pins provider versions/checksums → more reproducible infrastructure). - **Remote state + locking** are fundamental for teams: independent local state ⇒ A's state ≠ B's state; without locking: A and B read state, both change infrastructure, B writes stale state ⇒ inconsistent. Locking flow: acquire lock → modify infrastructure/state → release. Modern S3 backend supports **native S3 locking**; older tutorials use a DynamoDB table — follow the docs for your versions. ```hcl terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "company-terraform-state" key = "production/network/terraform.tfstate" region = "..." } } ``` - **State bucket security:** encryption, versioning, restricted IAM, private access, logging/monitoring; never public. CI uses IAM to reach the private bucket; limit developer access (CI role vs limited developer IAM). - **Bootstrap problem:** who creates the S3 bucket that stores state? A bootstrap Terraform creates the state infrastructure first (often managed centrally in larger organisations). **Versioning** (state-v1, v2, v3) is a recovery safety mechanism, not a replacement for proper workflows. **Disaster recovery:** if state is deleted, infrastructure still exists but Terraform loses its mapping → backups/versioning + controlled access; imports can reconstruct management. - **Commands:** `terraform state list`, `terraform state show aws_instance.web`, `terraform state rm aws_instance.web` — removes the resource from **state without deleting the real AWS resource** (EC2 still exists; if the block remains in config, `plan` may try to create another). - **Import:** existing AWS resource → `terraform import` → state → configuration. Import doesn't write perfect code; you still need configuration that represents the resource; run `terraform plan` after import and reconcile differences (modern Terraform also has `import` blocks). - **Drift:** config `t3.medium` but someone changes AWS to `t3.large` → detected during planning/refresh. Dangerous because nobody knows the intended configuration → manage infrastructure through the declared workflow, not ad-hoc console changes. - **Refresh:** old tutorials teach standalone `terraform refresh`; modern workflows incorporate refresh into plan/apply — Terraform needs current information before producing an accurate plan.

title: Revision 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Modules
text: - Reuse, consistency, abstraction, standardisation, maintainability — a module is like a reusable function (`createDatabase(config)`). Layout: `modules/network/{main.tf (resources), variables.tf (inputs), outputs.tf (outputs), README.md}`. ```hcl # variables.tf variable "vpc_cidr" { type = string } # main.tf resource "aws_vpc" "this" { cidr_block = var.vpc_cidr } # outputs.tf output "vpc_id" { value = aws_vpc.this.id } # root module "network" { source = "./modules/network" vpc_cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" } # use: module.network.vpc_id ``` Flow: root module →inputs→ child module → creates infrastructure → outputs → root (like arguments and return values). - **Good design:** expose important configuration (`cidr_block`, `az_count = 3`), hide implementation details (route tables). **Don't over-modularise** (module-vpc, module-subnet, module-route-table, module-route, module-security-group, module-rule…): prefer meaningful modules — `network`, `eks`, `database`, `observability`. - **Sources:** local directory, Git repository, Terraform Registry. **Internal modules** let a platform team standardise VPC, logging, IAM, encryption (Platform Team → reusable modules → engineering teams). **Module versioning** (v1.0, v1.1, v2.0): production pinned at v1.2 while staging tests v1.3 → controlled promotion. - **Root vs child:** `terraform/ {main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, modules/{network, eks, rds, monitoring}}`.

title: Revision 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Environments and blast radius
text: - Pattern to know: `infra/modules/{vpc,eks,rds,redis}` + `infra/environments/{dev,staging,prod}`, each environment calling shared modules, **each with separate state** (`S3: dev/terraform.tfstate, staging/…, prod/…`). One state for dev+staging+prod ⇒ a mistake can affect everything. **Blast radius** = how much a mistake can affect → smaller states reduce it. - **Workspaces** (`terraform workspace`): separate state instances for the same configuration; not automatically the best environment architecture — many teams use separate root configurations/state backends for explicit boundaries. *Interview:* "Workspaces provide separate state instances for the same configuration but shouldn't automatically be treated as the solution to every environment-management problem." - **State separation:** don't put VPC, EKS, RDS, S3, 100 applications and every environment into one giant state. Smaller states = smaller plans, faster operations, smaller blast radius, better ownership, less contention, easier troubleshooting — but don't split so much that dependencies become unmanageable. **Cross-state references** (remote-state data access, e.g. network state → VPC ID → EKS state); excessive coupling is hard to maintain; prefer clear boundaries.

title: Revision 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Variables, secrets, data sources, dependencies
text: - Variable strategy: `variable "environment" { type = string }`, `variable "instance_type"`; env-specific values via `dev.tfvars` / `prod.tfvars`. **Never** put production secrets in committed `.tfvars` (`DB_PASSWORD=…`) — use Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, CI/CD secret store. - **`data` vs `resource`:** `data "aws_vpc" "existing" {…}` → `data.aws_vpc.existing.id` (read existing information) vs resource (create/manage). - **Dependency graph:** `vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id` → implicit dependency (VPC → Subnet), preferred. `depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.example]` for non-inferable dependencies — overuse serialises operations and loses parallelism. `terraform graph` visualises it. - **Lifecycle:** `prevent_destroy = true` (critical resources like the production database), `create_before_destroy = true` (replace without downtime when the resource supports it), `ignore_changes = [tags]` (careful — hides drift). - **`moved` blocks:** moving `aws_s3_bucket.assets` into `module "storage"` makes Terraform think "old removed, new created"; `moved { from = aws_s3_bucket.assets to = module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.assets }` preserves identity and avoids destroy/create. - **`count` vs `for_each`:** `count = 3` → `resource[0..2]`; `for_each = { api = …, worker = … }` → `resource["api"]`. `for_each` is safer when items have stable names (with `count`, removing the second item shifts indexes). - **Locals/naming/tags:** `locals { name_prefix = "${var.project}-${var.environment}" }` → `name = "${local.name_prefix}-api"`; names like `payments-prod-eks`, `payments-prod-rds`, `payments-prod-assets`; tags `Project`, `Environment`, `Owner`, `ManagedBy`, `CostCenter` for cost allocation, search, operations, governance.

title: Revision 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Plan, apply, CI/CD
text: - `terraform plan` shows `+ create`, `~ modify`, `- destroy`; **read the plan**; never `terraform apply -auto-approve` against production. **Saved plans:** `terraform plan -out=tfplan` → `terraform apply tfplan` (applies exactly the reviewed plan; useful in CI/CD). - **Mature pipeline:** PR → fmt → validate → security/static checks → plan → review → approval → (merge) → apply; production adds manual approval. GitHub Actions: `actions/checkout@v4`, `hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3`, `terraform init/fmt -check/validate/plan`. Credentials: GitHub Actions → OIDC → IAM role → temporary credentials (no long-lived keys in GitHub secrets/source/Terraform files). - **Versioning:** commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`; pin provider ranges (`version = "~> 6.0"`) and don't blindly use `latest`; `required_version` for Terraform (choose a real range; the chapter's `">= 1.x, < 2.0"` is a placeholder). **Upgrade process:** read changelog → upgrade dev → `terraform init -upgrade` → plan → test → staging → production. - **Guardrails:** code review, plan review, protected branches, CI checks, policy-as-code, approval gates, least privilege, separate production credentials. **Policy as code** (OPA, Sentinel): e.g. "production S3 buckets must not be publicly accessible" → Plan → policy check → ❌ reject. **Security scanning** of IaC: public S3, overly broad IAM, unencrypted resources, open security groups. **Testing:** `fmt`, `validate`, `plan`; more advanced module/integration/policy tests — infrastructure is code.

title: Revision 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Tool boundaries and ownership
text: | Tool | Owns | |---|---| | **Terraform** | AWS networking, EKS, node groups, IAM, RDS, S3, load-balancer infrastructure, supporting infrastructure | | **ArgoCD** | Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Helm releases, application configuration | | **Kubernetes** | Runtime reconciliation (Pods, ReplicaSets, HPA, Jobs) | | Helm | Kubernetes packaging | | Ansible | Configure/manage machines (install nginx, configure server, manage service) | Terraform can also manage Helm releases (`resource "helm_release" "app"`) but watch ownership boundaries. **Two tools managing one resource** (Terraform and ArgoCD on the same Deployment) ⇒ conflicting desired states ⇒ **ownership conflict** → define clear boundaries. Terraform → EKS infrastructure → ArgoCD → Helm → workloads.

title: Revision 32 — Advanced Terraform
heading: Production scenarios
text: 1. **Someone manually changed the RDS class** (config `db.t3.medium`, actual `db.r6g.large`): don't immediately apply. Was it intentional? If yes, update the configuration and `terraform plan`; if accidental, decide whether Terraform should restore the intended state. 2. **"Terraform wants to destroy our production database!"** → **STOP APPLY**, inspect the plan: immutable field changed, resource address changed, module refactor, provider behaviour, configuration mismatch, import/state issue. Never blindly approve a destructive plan. 3. **Resource address changes** after refactors → `moved` block. 4. **Plan as safety mechanism:** `t3.large` → `t3.nano` shows `~ change`; `- destroy` ⇒ stop and investigate.

text: Why state; why remote state; why locking; drift; module; `resource` vs `data`; Terraform vs Ansible; Terraform vs Kubernetes; why Terraform and ArgoCD shouldn't manage the same resource; how to protect production Terraform (remote state, locking, IAM, PR review, plan review, approval, CI/CD, policy checks, separate environments, least privilege); what to do if Terraform wants to destroy production RDS; why `moved` blocks. **Depth:** 🔥 state, remote state, locking, modules, environments, drift, lifecycle, dependencies, CI/CD, security, Terraform/Kubernetes/ArgoCD boundaries · 🟡 workspaces, policy-as-code, testing, advanced module publishing, cross-state dependencies · ⚪ Terraform internals, provider development, specialised enterprise tooling.
