title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
text: > **Source:** Response 33 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-33.txt`, lines 1–3500) · **Part II — Advanced extension (Responses 25–36)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch33-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) · *includes an editorial supplement at the end* <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> We're now at **33/36**. You've already learned the AWS foundation: - IAM - EC2 - S3 - VPC - RDS - ALB - Lambda - SQS/SNS - Route 53 - CloudFront - WAF - CloudWatch - EKS - ECR - Terraform So this response is about something more important than memorizing more AWS services: > **How do you choose the right AWS service for a backend system?** This is what separates someone who has "learned AWS" from someone who can actually **design a production backend on AWS**. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 1. The AWS Backend Engineer Mental Model
text: A production backend might look like: ```text Users │ ▼ Route 53 │ ▼ CloudFront │ ▼ WAF │ ▼ API Gateway / ALB │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ECS EKS Lambda │ │ │ └────────────┼────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ RDS DynamoDB ElastiCache │ │ │ └──────────────┼──────────────┘ │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ S3 SQS EventBridge ``` You don't use all of these simultaneously. The skill is knowing: > **Which component should solve which problem?** ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 2. The Big Compute Decision
text: You now have four major compute choices: ```text EC2 ECS EKS Lambda ``` Let's understand them properly. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 3. EC2
text: EC2 gives you virtual machines. ```text Your application ↓ EC2 ↓ Operating System ↓ AWS hardware ``` You control much of the machine environment. You can install: ```text Node.js Docker Nginx system packages monitoring agents ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Advantages
text: - maximum control - flexible - predictable long-running workloads - supports unusual requirements

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Disadvantages
text: You manage more: ```text OS patching scaling capacity processes security ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 4. ECS
text: ECS = **Elastic Container Service**. ECS is AWS's container orchestration service. Instead of managing containers manually: ```text EC2 └── Docker └── Node.js ``` you define: ```text ECS └── Task └── Container ``` AWS handles much of the orchestration. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 5. ECS Task
text: Think of an ECS task as a running instance of your container configuration. For example: ```text Task ├── backend container └── sidecar container ``` You define: ```text image CPU memory ports environment IAM role logging ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 6. ECS Services
text: An ECS Service keeps the desired number of tasks running. Example: ```text Desired count = 3 ``` ECS tries to maintain: ```text Task 1 Task 2 Task 3 ``` If one crashes: ```text Task 2 ↓ dies ↓ ECS starts replacement ``` This is the same desired-state idea you've already learned from Kubernetes. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 7. ECS Launch Types
text: Two important choices: ```text ECS on EC2 ECS on Fargate ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: ECS + EC2
text: ```text ECS ↓ EC2 instances ↓ Containers ``` You manage the EC2 capacity.

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: ECS + Fargate
text: ```text ECS ↓ Fargate ↓ Containers ``` AWS manages the underlying compute capacity. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 8. ECS vs EKS
text: This is one of the most important interview questions.

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: ECS
text: AWS-native container orchestration. ```text ECS ↓ AWS ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: EKS
text: Managed Kubernetes. ```text EKS ↓ Kubernetes ↓ AWS ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 9. When Would You Choose ECS?
text: ECS is attractive when: ```text you want containers + AWS-native orchestration + less Kubernetes complexity ``` For example: ```text Node.js API Docker ALB ECS Fargate RDS Redis S3 ``` This can be a very clean architecture. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 10. When Would You Choose EKS?
text: EKS becomes more attractive when: ```text you specifically need Kubernetes + many services + Kubernetes ecosystem + operators + Helm + GitOps + service mesh + portability ``` For your roadmap: ```text ECS → know well EKS → know deeply ``` because EKS is already one of your major skills. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 11. ECS vs EKS: Important Tradeoff
text: Don't answer: > "EKS is better." That's not technically meaningful. Instead: ```text ECS → simpler AWS-native container orchestration EKS → Kubernetes ecosystem + flexibility + more complexity ``` Choice depends on requirements. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 12. Lambda
text: Lambda is different. Instead of managing servers/containers directly: ```text Event ↓ Lambda function ↓ Code ``` Example: ```text S3 upload ↓ Lambda ↓ resize image ``` or: ```text SQS message ↓ Lambda ↓ process job ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 13. Lambda Is Event-Driven
text: Lambda is especially useful for: ```text short-lived tasks event processing background jobs scheduled tasks webhooks lightweight APIs ``` You pay based largely on execution rather than maintaining a permanently running server. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Lambda
text: ```text event ↓ function ``` Good when execution is naturally event-based.

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: ECS
text: ```text container ↓ long-running service ``` Good for persistent backend services. For example: ```text REST API → ECS Image processing after S3 upload → Lambda ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 15. Lambda Cold Starts
text: A Lambda function may not always have an already-running execution environment. So: ```text request ↓ initialize environment ↓ run code ``` can introduce startup latency. This is a: > **Cold start** This matters more for latency-sensitive applications. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 16. Lambda Concurrency
text: Suppose: ```text 1 request ``` requires: ```text 1 Lambda execution ``` Then: ```text 1,000 requests ``` can potentially create many concurrent Lambda executions. That's powerful. But it can overload dependencies. Example: ```text 1,000 Lambda executions ↓ 1,000 DB connections ↓ RDS overwhelmed ``` So serverless scaling doesn't mean your dependencies can scale infinitely. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 17. Lambda + RDS
text: This is a classic architecture problem. Bad: ```text Lambda ├── execution 1 → DB connection ├── execution 2 → DB connection ├── execution 3 → DB connection ├── ... └── execution 1000 → DB connection ``` Better approaches can include: ```text connection pooling strategies RDS Proxy architectural throttling async queues appropriate concurrency controls ``` depending on the workload. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 18. API Gateway
text: API Gateway provides an API entry point. Conceptually: ```text Client ↓ API Gateway ↓ Lambda / ECS / other backend ``` It can handle things like: ```text routing authentication integration authorization throttling API lifecycle monitoring ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 19. API Gateway vs ALB
text: Another important interview question.

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: ALB
text: Best thought of as: ```text HTTP load balancing ``` Example: ```text Internet ↓ ALB ↓ ECS/EKS ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: API Gateway
text: Best thought of as: ```text API management + API entry layer ``` Example: ```text Client ↓ API Gateway ↓ Lambda ``` API Gateway can also integrate with other backends. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 20. When API Gateway Makes Sense
text: Good examples: ```text public API serverless APIs API throttling API keys/usage plans different API consumers managed API lifecycle ``` If you simply need: ```text HTTPS ↓ load balance ↓ ECS service ``` an ALB may be simpler. Again: > There is no universal "better." ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 21. DynamoDB
text: Now databases. You've already learned RDS. DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL database. Think: ```text DynamoDB = highly scalable key-value/document database ``` It is fundamentally different from PostgreSQL. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: RDS
text: Relational: ```text tables rows columns joins SQL transactions ``` Example: ```text Users Orders Products ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: DynamoDB
text: NoSQL: ```text partition key sort key items attributes ``` The data model is designed around access patterns rather than arbitrary relational joins. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 23. DynamoDB Example
text: Suppose you need: ```text user_id → user profile ``` You might use: ```text PK = USER#123 ``` and store: ```json { "PK": "USER#123", "name": "Rachit", "email": "..." } ``` The important concept is: > Design DynamoDB tables around the queries you need to perform. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 24. Partition Key
text: DynamoDB distributes data using partitioning. A good partition key should distribute traffic reasonably well. Bad example: ```text PK = "ALL_USERS" ``` could concentrate traffic. Better: ```text PK = userId ``` when your access pattern is user-centric. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 25. Sort Key
text: You can also use: ```text PK SK ``` Example: ```text PK = USER#123 SK = ORDER#1001 ``` Then: ```text PK = USER#123 ``` can represent multiple related items. This is one of the core DynamoDB modeling patterns. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 26. Single-Table Design
text: You may encounter DynamoDB single-table design. Instead of: ```text Users table Orders table Products table ``` you may model multiple entity types within one table. For example: ```text PK SK USER#123 PROFILE USER#123 ORDER#1001 USER#123 ORDER#1002 ``` This can make specific access patterns extremely efficient. But it requires careful design. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 27. DynamoDB vs PostgreSQL
text: Don't say: > DynamoDB is faster than PostgreSQL. That's too simplistic. Instead: ```text PostgreSQL → relational queries → joins → flexible SQL → relational integrity → transactions DynamoDB → predictable access patterns → massive horizontal scale → key-value/document model → low-latency access at scale ``` Choose based on workload. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 28. DynamoDB Transactions
text: DynamoDB supports transactional operations. But don't assume: ```text NoSQL = no transactions ``` That's incorrect. The capabilities and tradeoffs differ from relational databases. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 29. DynamoDB Secondary Indexes
text: You can use: ```text GSI LSI ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: GSI
text: Global Secondary Index. Allows additional query patterns using different key attributes.

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: LSI
text: Local Secondary Index. Uses the same partition key but a different sort key and has specific constraints. For interviews: ```text GSI → alternative access pattern LSI → alternate sort key under same partition key ``` is enough. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 30. DynamoDB Capacity
text: You may encounter: ```text On-demand Provisioned ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: On-demand
text: AWS automatically handles capacity based on traffic. Useful when: ```text unpredictable workload ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Provisioned
text: You specify expected capacity. Useful when: ```text predictable workload ``` and you want more explicit capacity management. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 31. DynamoDB Streams
text: DynamoDB Streams capture item-level changes. Conceptually: ```text DynamoDB ↓ Stream ↓ Lambda ``` Example: ```text Order created ↓ DynamoDB ↓ Stream ↓ Lambda ↓ send notification ``` This enables event-driven architectures. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 32. ElastiCache
text: Now caching. You've already learned Redis. AWS provides managed caching through services such as: ```text ElastiCache ``` Common engines include: ```text Redis/Valkey Memcached ``` depending on the service/version and AWS offering. For your backend architecture, think: ```text Node.js ↓ ElastiCache ↓ RDS ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 33. Why Cache?
text: Suppose: ```text GET /products ``` is requested: ```text 100,000 times ``` but the database data changes only occasionally. Without cache: ```text 100,000 requests ↓ RDS ``` With cache: ```text 100,000 requests ↓ Redis ↓ few DB queries ``` This reduces database load and latency. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 34. Cache-Aside Pattern
text: The most important Redis pattern: ```text Request ↓ Check cache ↓ Hit? ├── YES → return │ └── NO ↓ DB ↓ store cache ↓ return ``` Example: ```typescript const cached = await redis.get(key); if (cached) { return JSON.parse(cached); } const product = await db.product.findUnique({ where: { id } }); await redis.set( key, JSON.stringify(product), { EX: 300 } ); return product; ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 35. Cache Invalidation
text: Caching creates a new problem: > What happens when the underlying data changes? Suppose: ```text DB: price = ₹100 ``` Redis: ```text price = ₹100 ``` Then DB changes: ```text price = ₹120 ``` but Redis still contains: ```text ₹100 ``` That's stale data. Therefore cache invalidation is critical. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 36. TTL
text: A simple solution: ```text cache entry ↓ TTL = 5 minutes ↓ expires ``` This limits how long stale data can survive. But TTL isn't always enough. For important data, invalidate/update the cache when the source changes. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 37. Cache Stampede
text: Imagine: ```text cache expires ``` and: ```text 10,000 requests ``` arrive simultaneously. All see: ```text cache miss ``` and hit the DB. ```text 10,000 requests ↓ RDS ``` Potentially causing overload. This is a: > **Cache stampede** Solutions include: ```text locking request coalescing jittered TTL background refresh stale-while-revalidate ``` You don't need every technique memorized, but understand the problem. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 38. SQS
text: You've already learned SQS. Let's now place it in architecture. Suppose: ```text Order API ``` needs to generate invoices. Don't make the user wait: ```text Request ↓ create order ↓ generate invoice ↓ send email ↓ respond ``` Instead: ```text Request ↓ create order ↓ SQS ↓ respond quickly ``` Worker: ```text SQS ↓ Worker ↓ generate invoice ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 39. Why SQS?
text: SQS provides: ```text decoupling buffering asynchronous processing retry DLQ ``` Architecture: ```text Producer ↓ SQS ↓ Consumer ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 40. Queue as a Shock Absorber
text: Suppose traffic suddenly increases: ```text 1,000 requests/sec ``` but workers can process: ```text 500 jobs/sec ``` Without a queue: ```text workers overwhelmed ``` With SQS: ```text Producer ↓ SQS ↓↓↓↓↓ Workers ``` The queue absorbs the temporary spike. This is a powerful distributed-systems pattern. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 41. Visibility Timeout
text: Suppose a worker receives: ```text Job A ``` SQS temporarily hides it from other consumers. If the worker successfully processes it: ```text delete message ``` If the worker crashes: ```text visibility timeout expires ↓ message becomes available again ``` This enables retry. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 42. Dead-Letter Queue
text: Suppose: ```text Job ↓ fail ↓ retry ↓ fail ↓ retry ↓ fail ``` Eventually: ```text DLQ ``` This prevents a permanently broken message from repeatedly blocking normal processing. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 43. Idempotency
text: Queues can deliver messages more than once depending on the queue/delivery semantics. Therefore: ```text consumer ``` should often be idempotent. Example: ```text Process payment ``` You don't want: ```text same message ↓ payment ↓ payment again ``` Use an idempotency key / deduplication strategy appropriate to the workflow. This is a **backend engineering** concept, not merely an AWS concept. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 44. SNS
text: SNS is primarily a publish/subscribe messaging service. Think: ```text Publisher ↓ SNS Topic / | \ / | \ SQS SQS Lambda ``` One event can fan out to multiple consumers. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: SQS
text: ```text queue ``` Usually: ```text one message → processed by one consumer in a competing-consumer model ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: SNS
text: ```text pub/sub ``` One published event can be delivered to multiple subscribers. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 46. SNS + SQS
text: This is a very useful pattern. ```text Order Service ↓ SNS Topic / \ ↓ ↓ SQS SQS Email Analytics Queue Queue ``` Now each subsystem processes independently. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 47. EventBridge
text: Now another event system. EventBridge is useful for event-driven architectures where you want: ```text events + routing rules + multiple targets ``` Think: ```text Event Producer ↓ EventBridge ↓ Rules ┌────┼────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Lambda SQS Step Functions ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 48. SNS vs EventBridge
text: Simplified:

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: SNS
text: Strong fit for: ```text pub/sub notifications fanout simple event delivery ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: EventBridge
text: Strong fit for: ```text event buses event routing many event sources rule-based routing AWS/service events SaaS/application integration ``` Don't think of EventBridge as "SNS but newer." They solve overlapping but distinct messaging/eventing needs. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 49. EventBridge Example
text: Suppose: ```text OrderCreated ``` event occurs. EventBridge rule: ```text source = ecommerce detail-type = OrderCreated ``` Targets: ```text Lambda SQS Step Functions ``` So: ```text OrderCreated ↓ EventBridge ↓ Rule ┌────┼──────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Email Analytics Workflow ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 50. Event-Driven Architecture
text: Now you can design: ```text Order API ↓ RDS ↓ OrderCreated event ↓ EventBridge ├── Notification ├── Analytics └── Fulfillment ``` This reduces direct coupling. Instead of: ```text Order Service ↓ call Notification ↓ call Analytics ↓ call Fulfillment ``` you have: ```text Order Service ↓ publish event ``` and independent consumers. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 51. Eventual Consistency
text: Event-driven systems often introduce: > **Eventual consistency** For example: ```text Order created ↓ RDS updated ↓ event published ↓ analytics updated later ``` For a short period: ```text Order system = updated Analytics = not yet updated ``` Eventually they converge. This is a fundamental distributed-systems tradeoff. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 52. Step Functions
text: Now orchestration. Suppose you need: ```text Process payment ↓ reserve inventory ↓ generate invoice ↓ send notification ``` and each step may fail. You can use: ```text AWS Step Functions ``` to model the workflow. Conceptually: ```text Start ↓ Payment ↓ Inventory ↓ Invoice ↓ Notification ↓ End ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 53. Why Step Functions?
text: Instead of writing a giant application function: ```typescript async function processOrder() { ... } ``` containing: ```text retry logic timeouts state management failure handling branching ``` Step Functions can represent the workflow explicitly. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 54. State Machine
text: A Step Functions workflow is essentially a state machine. Example: ```text START ↓ Charge Payment ↓ Success? ├── No → Retry / Fail │ └── Yes ↓ Reserve Inventory ↓ Generate Invoice ↓ Send Email ↓ END ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 55. Step Functions vs SQS
text: They solve different problems.

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: SQS
text: ```text queue work ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Step Functions
text: ```text orchestrate multi-step workflow ``` You can even combine them. ```text Step Functions ↓ SQS ↓ Worker ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 56. Secrets Manager
text: You've already seen this in earlier responses. Now let's make the architectural role clear. Don't put: ```text DB_PASSWORD API_KEY JWT_SECRET ``` directly in: ```text Git Dockerfile source code ``` Instead: ```text AWS Secrets Manager ↓ application/workload ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 57. Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store
text: Both can store configuration/secrets. Simplified:

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Secrets Manager
text: Strong fit for: ```text secrets credential lifecycle secret rotation ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Parameter Store
text: Useful for: ```text configuration parameters some secret storage ``` Don't assume every configuration value belongs in Secrets Manager. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 58. KMS
text: KMS = **Key Management Service**. Think: ```text KMS = managed cryptographic key management ``` Used with services such as: ```text S3 RDS EBS Secrets Manager ``` to support encryption. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 59. Encryption Layers
text: You should distinguish:

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Encryption in transit
text: ```text Client ↓ TLS Server ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Encryption at rest
text: ```text Database/storage ↓ encrypted data ``` KMS often participates in the encryption-at-rest architecture. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 60. Envelope Encryption
text: You may hear this term. Conceptually: ```text Data ↓ Data Encryption Key ↓ encrypted data KMS key ↓ protects data key ``` You generally don't need to implement envelope encryption manually for normal AWS application development. Understand the concept. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 61. Backend Architecture Example
text: Let's design a real application. Suppose: > E-commerce platform. We have: ```text Users Products Orders Payments Notifications ``` Architecture: ```text Internet │ CloudFront │ WAF │ API Gateway │ ECS/EKS │ ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ User Order Product Service Service Service │ │ │ └───────────────┼───────────────┘ │ RDS │ Redis │ EventBridge / \ ↓ ↓ SQS Queue Lambda ↓ Worker ↓ S3/Email ``` Now let's reason about each choice. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 62. Why RDS?
text: Orders have relationships: ```text user ↓ orders ↓ order_items ↓ products ``` Relational queries and transactional integrity are valuable. Therefore: ```text PostgreSQL/RDS ``` is a natural fit. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 63. Why Redis?
text: Product catalog and sessions may be read frequently. Use: ```text ElastiCache ``` for: ```text cache sessions rate limiting temporary state ``` where appropriate. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 64. Why SQS?
text: Invoice generation doesn't need to happen inside the HTTP request. So: ```text Order created ↓ SQS ↓ Invoice worker ``` decouples the work. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 65. Why EventBridge?
text: Multiple systems may care about: ```text OrderCreated ``` Instead of hardcoding: ```text Order → Analytics Order → Notification Order → Fulfillment ``` publish an event: ```text OrderCreated ↓ EventBridge ``` and route it. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 66. Why Lambda?
text: A small event processor might not justify a permanently running service. Example: ```text S3 upload ↓ Lambda ↓ generate thumbnail ``` Lambda is a good fit. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 67. Why ECS/EKS?
text: For the core API: ```text long-running HTTP Node.js ``` a containerized service is a natural choice. Depending on the team's needs: ```text ECS Fargate ``` could be simpler, while: ```text EKS ``` could be appropriate if Kubernetes ecosystem requirements justify it. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 68. Why S3?
text: Use S3 for: ```text images documents exports backups static assets ``` Don't store large binary files directly inside PostgreSQL unless there's a specific reason. A common architecture: ```text DB → metadata S3 → actual file ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 69. API Gateway vs ALB in This Architecture
text: If using: ```text Lambda-first API ``` you might choose: ```text API Gateway ``` If using: ```text ECS/EKS HTTP services ``` you might use: ```text ALB ``` You can also combine API Gateway with containerized backends when API management requirements justify it. Again: > Architecture follows requirements. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 70. The AWS Decision Matrix
text: Here's the mental table you should memorize. | Problem | Common AWS choice | |---|---| | Virtual machine | EC2 | | Managed containers | ECS | | Kubernetes | EKS | | Serverless function | Lambda | | Object storage | S3 | | Relational database | RDS/Aurora | | Key-value/document DB | DynamoDB | | Cache | ElastiCache | | Queue | SQS | | Pub/sub fanout | SNS | | Event routing | EventBridge | | Workflow orchestration | Step Functions | | API management | API Gateway | | HTTP load balancing | ALB | | Network load balancing | NLB | | Secrets | Secrets Manager | | Configuration parameters | Parameter Store | | Encryption/key management | KMS | | Container registry | ECR | | DNS | Route 53 | | CDN | CloudFront | | Web firewall | WAF | | Monitoring | CloudWatch | ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 71. RDS vs DynamoDB Decision
text: Ask:

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Do I need relational modeling?
text: ```text yes → PostgreSQL/RDS ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Do I need flexible document/key-value access at massive scale with predictable access patterns?
text: ```text yes → DynamoDB ``` Don't select DynamoDB simply because: > "NoSQL is faster." That's not a valid architecture argument. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 72. SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge
text: Remember: ```text SQS → queue SNS → pub/sub fanout EventBridge → event bus + routing ``` Example: ```text One worker: → SQS Many subscribers: → SNS Many event sources + rule-based routing: → EventBridge ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 73. ECS vs EKS vs Lambda
text: Think: ```text EC2 → maximum machine control ECS → containers with AWS-native orchestration EKS → Kubernetes ecosystem Lambda → event-driven serverless execution ``` This one diagram is worth remembering. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 74. API Gateway vs ALB
text: ```text ALB → HTTP load balancing API Gateway → API management/entry layer ``` If the requirement is: > "Distribute HTTP requests across containers." ALB is a natural fit. If: > "Expose APIs with managed API policies, throttling and serverless integrations." API Gateway becomes attractive. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 75. RDS vs ElastiCache
text: They aren't competitors. ```text RDS → source of truth Redis → fast temporary/access-optimized data ``` Architecture: ```text Application ↓ Redis ↓ miss RDS ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 76. S3 vs EBS vs EFS
text: Another classic interview question. ```text S3 → object storage EBS → block storage EFS → shared filesystem ``` Example: ```text Images → S3 EC2 disk → EBS Shared files → EFS ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 77. Queue vs Database
text: Don't use SQS as your primary database. SQS answers: > "What work needs to happen?" Database answers: > "What is the persistent state of the system?" Example: ```text Order DB → order exists SQS → invoice generation needs to happen ``` Different responsibilities. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 78. Event vs Command
text: A useful distributed-systems distinction.

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Command
text: > "Do this." Example: ```text ProcessPayment ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Event
text: > "This happened." Example: ```text PaymentProcessed ``` SQS is often naturally used for work/commands. EventBridge/SNS are often used for event propagation. The exact semantics depend on architecture. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 79. Reliability Architecture
text: Suppose RDS becomes slow. Your backend should have: ```text timeouts connection pooling retry with limits circuit breaking caching queues backpressure ``` AWS services don't automatically make the application reliable. You still need good application architecture. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 80. AWS Doesn't Remove Distributed Systems Problems
text: This is extremely important. Using: ```text Lambda SQS DynamoDB EventBridge ``` doesn't magically solve: ```text duplicates ordering timeouts partial failures eventual consistency idempotency race conditions backpressure ``` You still need to understand distributed systems. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 81. Example Failure
text: Suppose: ```text Order API ↓ SQS ↓ Worker ↓ Payment ``` Worker successfully charges payment. Then crashes **before acknowledging the message**. The message may be delivered again. Now: ```text same order ↓ charge payment ↓ charge payment again ``` Therefore: ```text idempotency ``` is required. For example: ```text idempotency_key = order_id ``` and payment processing checks whether that operation has already been completed. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 82. Another Failure: Event Duplication
text: Suppose: ```text OrderCreated ``` is delivered twice. Consumer: ```text send email ``` Without idempotency: ```text 2 emails ``` With idempotency: ```text first → send second → ignore ``` This is fundamental backend engineering. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 83. Backpressure
text: Suppose: ```text Producer = 10,000 events/sec Consumer = 1,000 events/sec ``` Don't let the consumer collapse. Use: ```text queue buffer rate limiting consumer scaling ``` Architecture: ```text Producer ↓ SQS ↓ Consumers ``` This creates controlled backpressure. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 84. Dead-Letter Queues
text: Never allow permanently broken messages to endlessly retry. Use: ```text Main Queue ↓ retries ↓ DLQ ``` Then operators can inspect: ```text why did these messages fail? ``` This is operationally important. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 85. AWS Well-Architected Thinking
text: You should also know the major AWS architecture pillars: ```text Operational Excellence Security Reliability Performance Efficiency Cost Optimization Sustainability ``` For interviews, you don't need to memorize every subcategory. But when designing architecture, ask: ```text Is it secure? Is it reliable? Will it scale? What does it cost? How do we operate it? ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 86. Example: Bad Architecture
text: Imagine: ```text Internet ↓ EC2 ↓ PostgreSQL ``` and: ```text EC2 has public IP database public SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0 password in code single EC2 single DB no backups ``` It might work. But it's not a good production architecture. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 87. Improved Architecture
text: ```text Internet ↓ Route53 ↓ CloudFront/WAF ↓ ALB ↓ Private ECS/EKS ↓ Redis ↓ Private RDS ``` With: ```text IAM Secrets Manager CloudWatch autoscaling multi-AZ backups least privilege ``` Now you have a production-oriented design. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 88. But Don't Overengineer
text: This is equally important. For a tiny application: ```text CloudFront WAF API Gateway EKS Istio Kafka EventBridge Step Functions DynamoDB RDS Redis ``` could be ridiculous. A small application may only need: ```text ALB ECS Fargate RDS S3 ``` Architecture should match requirements. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 89. A Strong Backend Engineer's Decision Process
text: When designing AWS architecture, ask:

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 1. What kind of workload?
text: ```text HTTP? event? batch? stream? workflow? ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 2. What compute model?
text: ```text EC2? ECS? EKS? Lambda? ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 3. What data model?
text: ```text relational? key-value? document? object? cache? ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 4. What communication model?
text: ```text synchronous? queue? pub/sub? event bus? workflow? ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 5. What reliability requirements?
text: ```text RTO? RPO? multi-AZ? retries? DLQ? ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 6. What security requirements?
text: ```text IAM? encryption? private networking? Secrets Manager? ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 7. What scale?
text: ```text requests/sec? data size? concurrency? burst? ```

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 8. What does it cost?
text: Always ask this. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: "Design a scalable image-processing backend."
text: A reasonable architecture: ```text User ↓ API ↓ S3 upload ↓ S3 event ↓ SQS ↓ Lambda / ECS worker ↓ process image ↓ S3 output ↓ DB metadata ``` Why? ```text S3 → large files SQS → buffering/retry Lambda/ECS → processing DB → metadata ``` That's much better than: ```text POST /upload ↓ Node.js server ↓ process 100 MB image synchronously ↓ respond ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: "Design a notification system."
text: ```text Application ↓ EventBridge / SNS ↓ ┌──┴─────────┐ ↓ ↓ Email Queue SMS Queue ↓ ↓ Workers Workers ``` Use: ```text SQS → buffering/retry SNS/EventBridge → distribution Workers → actual delivery ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: "Design a high-traffic product catalog."
text: Possible architecture: ```text Client ↓ CloudFront ↓ ALB ↓ ECS/EKS ↓ Redis ↓ miss RDS/DynamoDB ``` Use: ```text CloudFront → edge caching Redis → application caching DB → source of truth ``` The exact database depends on access patterns. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: "Design a payment workflow."
text: You might use: ```text API ↓ Order DB ↓ Step Functions ↓ Payment ↓ Inventory ↓ Invoice ↓ Notification ``` with: ```text idempotency timeouts retries compensation audit trail ``` This is where Step Functions can be useful. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 94. Compensation
text: Suppose: ```text Payment successful ↓ Inventory reservation fails ``` You can't simply: ```text throw error ``` You may need: ```text refund payment ``` This is a **compensating action**. Workflow: ```text Charge payment ↓ Reserve inventory ↓ FAIL ↓ Refund payment ``` This is important distributed transaction thinking. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 95. Why Not Use One Giant Transaction?
text: Because: ```text Payment service Inventory service Notification service ``` may be independent systems. A single ACID transaction across all of them may be impractical. Instead, distributed workflows often use: ```text events sagas compensating actions idempotency ``` Step Functions can help orchestrate such workflows. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 96. AWS Services You Should Now Recognize
text: You've now covered the major backend-oriented AWS ecosystem: ```text Compute ├── EC2 ├── ECS ├── EKS └── Lambda Storage ├── S3 ├── EBS └── EFS Databases ├── RDS ├── Aurora ├── DynamoDB └── ElastiCache Messaging ├── SQS ├── SNS └── EventBridge Workflow └── Step Functions Networking ├── VPC ├── ALB ├── NLB ├── API Gateway ├── Route 53 ├── CloudFront └── WAF Security ├── IAM ├── Secrets Manager └── KMS Containers ├── ECR ├── ECS └── EKS Observability └── CloudWatch ``` You don't need to memorize hundreds of AWS services. These are the ones especially relevant to your backend/SWE direction. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 97. The Ultimate AWS Decision Tree
text: When someone asks you: > "Which AWS service would you use?" Think: ```text Workload │ ┌────────────┼─────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ HTTP API Event Batch │ │ │ ┌───┴───┐ │ ECS/Lambda ↓ ↓ │ ECS/EKS Lambda │ ↓ SQS/EventBridge │ Worker ``` Then data: ```text Data │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ relational key-value files │ │ │ RDS DynamoDB S3 │ cache ↓ ElastiCache ``` And workflow: ```text multi-step process ↓ Step Functions ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 98. The AWS Architecture You Should Be Able to Explain
text: For a serious backend: ```text Users │ Route 53 │ CloudFront │ WAF │ ALB / API GW │ ┌────────┴────────┐ │ │ ECS EKS │ │ └────────┬────────┘ │ ┌────────┼─────────┐ │ │ │ RDS Redis S3 │ Event system ┌─────┴─────┐ │ │ SQS EventBridge │ │ Workers Lambda │ │ └─────┬─────┘ │ Step Functions ``` With: ```text Terraform → infrastructure ArgoCD → Kubernetes delivery IAM → identity Secrets Manager → secrets KMS → encryption CloudWatch/OpenTelemetry → observability ``` ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: 101. The Biggest Lesson From Chapter 33
text: Don't learn AWS as: ```text Service 1 Service 2 Service 3 Service 4 ... ``` Learn AWS as: ```text Problem ↓ Requirement ↓ Architecture ↓ AWS service ↓ Tradeoff ``` For example: > "I need asynchronous processing." Think: ```text SQS ``` > "I need multiple systems to receive an event." Think: ```text SNS/EventBridge ``` > "I need a relational source of truth." Think: ```text RDS ``` > "I need massive key-value/document scale with predictable access patterns." Think: ```text DynamoDB ``` > "I need caching." Think: ```text ElastiCache ``` > "I need a multi-step workflow." Think: ```text Step Functions ``` > "I need Kubernetes." Think: ```text EKS ``` > "I need simpler AWS-native containers." Think: ```text ECS ``` > "I need event-driven functions." Think: ```text Lambda ``` That's how you should approach AWS interview questions. ---

title: Chapter 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Concrete examples for the services this chapter compares
text: The chapter is a decision guide, so it has few configuration examples. These show what each choice looks like in practice. Account IDs, ARNs and names are placeholders. **1. An ECS Fargate task definition** (sections 4–7). Note the two different roles — a frequent interview point: the **task execution role** is used by ECS itself (pull the image from ECR, write logs, fetch secrets); the **task role** is the identity your application code uses to call AWS services (S3, SQS, DynamoDB …). ```json { "family": "backend", "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"], "networkMode": "awsvpc", "cpu": "512", "memory": "1024", "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole", "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/backend-task-role", "containerDefinitions": [ { "name": "backend", "image": "<account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/backend:a82f31c", "portMappings": [{ "containerPort": 3000, "protocol": "tcp" }], "environment": [{ "name": "NODE_ENV", "value": "production" }], "secrets": [ { "name": "DATABASE_URL", "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-south-1:<account-id>:secret:prod/db-AbCdEf" } ], "logConfiguration": { "logDriver": "awslogs", "options": { "awslogs-group": "/ecs/backend", "awslogs-region": "ap-south-1", "awslogs-stream-prefix": "ecs" } } } ] } ``` Vocabulary: a **task definition** is the blueprint (image, CPU, memory, ports, roles, logging); a **task** is a running instance of it; an **ECS service** keeps the desired number of tasks running and registers them with an ALB target group; a **cluster** groups tasks/services. With `awsvpc` networking each task gets its own ENI (and security group); the ALB uses `target-type: ip`. ECS services scale with Application Auto Scaling (target tracking on CPU, memory or request count). **2. DynamoDB: key design and queries** (sections 23–26). Table `app` with partition key `PK` and sort key `SK` (single-table design). Fetch a user's orders with one `Query` — never a table `Scan`: ```typescript import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand, QueryCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; const ddb = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION })); await ddb.send(new PutCommand({ TableName: "app", Item: { PK: "USER#123", SK: "ORDER#1001", total: 499, status: "PAID" }, })); const result = await ddb.send(new QueryCommand({ TableName: "app", KeyConditionExpression: "PK = :pk AND begins_with(SK, :sk)", ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":pk": "USER#123", ":sk": "ORDER#" }, })); ``` Facts to remember: an item is limited to about 400 KB; reads can be *eventually consistent* (default) or *strongly consistent*; on-demand capacity bills per request while provisioned mode uses read/write capacity units; a **hot partition** (one key receiving most traffic) throttles even when total capacity is available; a **local secondary index must be defined when the table is created**, whereas a global secondary index can be added later; the TTL feature can expire items automatically. **3. The Redis syntax in section 34 is library-specific.** `redis.set(key, value, { EX: 300 })` is the **node-redis v4** form. With **ioredis** the equivalent is `redis.set(key, value, "EX", 300)`. The cache-aside logic is the same. **4. Step Functions state machine with retry and compensation** (sections 52–54, 93–95). The `Catch` on `ReserveInventory` sends a failure to a compensating `RefundPayment` step — the saga idea in code: ```json { "Comment": "Order workflow with compensation", "StartAt": "ChargePayment", "States": { "ChargePayment": { "Type": "Task", "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke", "Parameters": { "FunctionName": "charge-payment", "Payload.$": "$" }, "Retry": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "IntervalSeconds": 2, "MaxAttempts": 3, "BackoffRate": 2.0 }], "Next": "ReserveInventory" }, "ReserveInventory": { "Type": "Task", "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke", "Parameters": { "FunctionName": "reserve-inventory", "Payload.$": "$" }, "Catch": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "Next": "RefundPayment" }], "Next": "GenerateInvoice" }, "RefundPayment": { "Type": "Task", "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke", "Parameters": { "FunctionName": "refund-payment", "Payload.$": "$" }, "Next": "OrderFailed" }, "GenerateInvoice": { "Type": "Task", "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke", "Parameters": { "FunctionName": "generate-invoice", "Payload.$": "$" }, "End": true }, "OrderFailed": { "Type": "Fail", "Error": "InventoryUnavailable", "Cause": "Payment was refunded" } } } ``` **5. Two distributed-systems patterns the chapter alludes to.** - **Saga** (section 95): a long business transaction is split into local transactions, each with a *compensating action*. **Orchestration** has a central coordinator (Step Functions, as above); **choreography** has services react to each other's events (EventBridge/SNS) with no central coordinator. - **Transactional outbox** (section 50): "write to RDS, then publish `OrderCreated`" is a *dual write* — the database commit can succeed while the publish fails (or vice versa). The outbox pattern writes the event into an `outbox` table **in the same database transaction** as the order, and a separate relay publishes outbox rows to EventBridge/SNS/SQS, retrying until delivered. Consumers must still be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once. **6. Smaller clarifications.** - **Aurora** (listed as "RDS/Aurora" in the decision matrix) is an AWS-built, MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible relational engine with a distributed storage layer and faster failover/read scaling. - **SQS FIFO queues** add ordering and deduplication (see Chapter 15 notes); Standard queues are at-least-once with best-effort ordering. EventBridge adds event **archive/replay** and **schema discovery**; SNS adds **message filtering** per subscription. - **Streaming workloads** (the chapter lists "stream?" in the decision questions without a service): Kinesis Data Streams or Amazon MSK (managed Kafka). - **API Gateway** comes in REST, HTTP and WebSocket API flavours, and integration timeouts/payload sizes are limited — check the current quotas when choosing it over an ALB for slow or large requests. --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 32: Advanced Terraform](../06-iac-config/ch32-advanced-terraform.md) · [Chapter 34: Advanced SRE](../07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch33-revision.md)

heading: Chapter 33 — Revision Sheet: Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
text: > Supplements [the full chapter](../docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md). The skill: **choose the right AWS service for a backend system** — Problem → Requirement → Architecture → AWS service → Trade-off. Not memorising more services.

title: Revision 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Mental model
text: Users → Route 53 → CloudFront → WAF → API Gateway / ALB → {ECS, EKS, Lambda} → {RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache} → {S3, SQS, EventBridge}. You never use all at once: *which component should solve which problem?*

title: Revision 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Compute: EC2 vs ECS vs EKS vs Lambda
text: | | Characteristics | |---|---| | **EC2** | VMs, maximum control (install Node.js, Docker, Nginx, packages, agents); flexible, predictable long-running workloads, unusual requirements. You manage OS, patching, scaling, capacity, processes, security | | **ECS** (Elastic Container Service) | AWS-native container orchestration. **Task** (running instance of container configuration: image, CPU, memory, ports, environment, IAM role, logging; may include a sidecar), **Service** (keeps desired count running — Desired = 3; failed task → replacement; same desired-state idea as Kubernetes). Launch types: **ECS on EC2** (you manage EC2 capacity) vs **ECS on Fargate** (AWS manages compute) | | **EKS** | Managed Kubernetes: Kubernetes ecosystem + flexibility + more complexity. Choose when you specifically need Kubernetes, many services, operators, Helm, GitOps, service mesh, portability | | **Lambda** | Event → function; short-lived tasks, event processing, background jobs, scheduled tasks, webhooks, lightweight APIs; pay mainly for execution | - **ECS vs EKS:** "EKS is better" is not meaningful — ECS = simpler AWS-native orchestration; EKS = Kubernetes ecosystem. Simple clean architecture: Node.js API + Docker + ALB + **ECS Fargate** + RDS + Redis + S3. For this roadmap: know ECS well, EKS deeply. - **Lambda vs ECS:** REST API → ECS; image processing after S3 upload → Lambda. **Cold start** = initialising a new execution environment (latency-sensitive apps). **Concurrency:** 1,000 requests → many concurrent executions → 1,000 DB connections → RDS overwhelmed — serverless scaling doesn't mean dependencies scale infinitely. **Lambda + RDS** fixes: connection pooling strategies, **RDS Proxy**, architectural throttling, async queues, concurrency controls. - **API Gateway vs ALB:** ALB = HTTP load balancing (Internet → ALB → ECS/EKS); API Gateway = API management + API entry layer (routing, authentication integration, authorization, throttling, API lifecycle, monitoring) → Lambda/ECS/other. API Gateway fits public/serverless APIs, throttling, API keys/usage plans, different consumers, managed lifecycle; for "HTTPS → load balance → ECS service" an ALB may be simpler. Lambda-first API → API Gateway; ECS/EKS HTTP services → ALB; they can be combined.

title: Revision 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: DynamoDB vs RDS
text: DynamoDB = highly scalable managed NoSQL key-value/document store; the data model is designed around **access patterns**, not arbitrary joins (design tables around the queries you need). RDS = relational (tables, rows, columns, joins, SQL, transactions). - **Keys:** partition key (distributes data/traffic; `PK = userId` good, `PK = "ALL_USERS"` concentrates traffic), sort key `SK` (e.g. `PK = USER#123`, `SK = ORDER#1001`). - **Single-table design:** multiple entity types in one table (`USER#123 / PROFILE`, `USER#123 / ORDER#1001`, …) — efficient for specific access patterns but needs careful design. - **Transactions:** DynamoDB supports transactional operations (NoSQL ≠ no transactions). **Indexes:** GSI (alternative access pattern via different key attributes) vs LSI (same partition key, different sort key, specific constraints). **Capacity:** on-demand (unpredictable workloads) vs provisioned (predictable). **Streams:** item-level changes → Lambda (Order created → DynamoDB → Stream → Lambda → notification). - *Don't say "DynamoDB is faster."* PostgreSQL → relational queries, joins, flexible SQL, integrity, transactions; DynamoDB → predictable access patterns, massive horizontal scale, key-value/document, low latency at scale. Need relational modelling → RDS; flexible key-value/document at massive scale with predictable access patterns → DynamoDB. **Don't choose NoSQL "because it's faster".**

title: Revision 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Caching (ElastiCache)
text: ElastiCache engines: Redis/Valkey, Memcached. Why: 100,000 `GET /products` with rarely-changing data → Redis → few DB queries (less DB load, lower latency). **Cache-aside:** ```typescript const cached = await redis.get(key); if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached); const product = await db.product.findUnique({ where: { id } }); await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(product), { EX: 300 }); return product; ``` - **Invalidation:** DB price ₹100 → ₹120 but Redis still has ₹100 = stale data. **TTL** (e.g. 5 min) limits staleness but isn't always enough — invalidate/update on source change for important data. - **Cache stampede:** entry expires → 10,000 simultaneous requests all miss → hit RDS. Solutions: locking, request coalescing, jittered TTL, background refresh, stale-while-revalidate. - RDS vs Redis aren't competitors: RDS = source of truth; Redis = fast temporary/access-optimised data. Use Redis for cache, sessions, rate limiting, temporary state.

title: Revision 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Messaging and events
text: | | | |---|---| | **SQS** | Queue → decoupling, buffering, async processing, retry, DLQ; competing-consumer model (one message → one consumer). **Shock absorber**: 1,000 req/s vs 500 jobs/s workers — queue absorbs the spike. **Visibility timeout** (worker crashes → message reappears → retry). **DLQ** prevents a permanently broken message blocking normal processing. Don't use SQS as your database: SQS = "what work needs to happen", DB = "persistent state" | | **SNS** | Pub/sub fan-out; one event → many subscribers (SQS, SQS, Lambda). **SNS + SQS**: each subsystem (email, analytics queues) processes independently | | **EventBridge** | Event bus + rule-based routing, many event sources, AWS/service events, SaaS/application integration; rule `source = ecommerce`, `detail-type = OrderCreated` → targets Lambda, SQS, Step Functions. *Not "SNS but newer"* — overlapping but distinct | | **Step Functions** | Workflow orchestration as a **state machine** (Start → Payment → Inventory → Invoice → Notification → End) with retries, timeouts, state, branching, failure handling expressed explicitly instead of a giant function. Step Functions orchestrate multi-step workflows; SQS queues work — they can be combined | Rule of thumb: one worker → SQS; many subscribers → SNS; many event sources + rule-based routing → EventBridge. - **Event vs command:** command = "do this" (`ProcessPayment`, naturally SQS); event = "this happened" (`PaymentProcessed`, SNS/EventBridge). **Event-driven architecture** reduces coupling: Order API → RDS → `OrderCreated` → EventBridge → {Notification, Analytics, Fulfillment}. **Eventual consistency** is the trade-off (order system updated, analytics later). - **Failures AWS doesn't remove:** worker charges payment then crashes before acknowledging → message redelivered → double charge → **idempotency** (`idempotency_key = order_id`, check whether already done). Duplicate `OrderCreated` → two emails unless idempotent. Also ordering, timeouts, partial failures, race conditions, backpressure. **Backpressure:** producer 10,000 events/s vs consumer 1,000/s → queue, buffer, rate limiting, consumer scaling. - **Compensation / sagas:** payment succeeded → inventory reservation fails → refund payment (compensating action). One giant ACID transaction across independent services is impractical → events, sagas, compensating actions, idempotency; Step Functions can orchestrate.

title: Revision 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Secrets, keys, encryption
text: - Secrets Manager (secrets, credential lifecycle, rotation) vs Parameter Store (configuration, parameters, some secret storage) — not every config value belongs in Secrets Manager. Never DB_PASSWORD/API_KEY/JWT_SECRET in Git, Dockerfile or source code. - **KMS** = managed cryptographic key management used with S3, RDS, EBS, Secrets Manager. Encryption in transit (TLS) vs at rest (KMS participates). **Envelope encryption:** data → data encryption key → encrypted data; the KMS key protects the data key — understand, don't implement manually. **Secrets Manager vs KMS:** store/manage secrets vs manage encryption keys.

title: Revision 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Decision matrix (memorise)
text: | Problem | Service | |---|---| | Virtual machine | EC2 | | Managed containers | ECS | | Kubernetes | EKS | | Serverless function | Lambda | | Object storage | S3 | | Relational DB | RDS/Aurora | | Key-value/document DB | DynamoDB | | Cache | ElastiCache | | Queue / Pub-sub fan-out / Event routing | SQS / SNS / EventBridge | | Workflow orchestration | Step Functions | | API management / HTTP LB / network LB | API Gateway / ALB / NLB | | Secrets / config parameters / encryption keys | Secrets Manager / Parameter Store / KMS | | Container registry / DNS / CDN / web firewall / monitoring | ECR / Route 53 / CloudFront / WAF / CloudWatch | | Storage trio | S3 = objects, EBS = block (EC2 disk), EFS = shared filesystem | **Rapid fire:** EC2 vs ECS (VMs vs container orchestration) · ECS vs EKS (AWS-native vs managed Kubernetes) · Fargate vs Lambda (long-running/container vs event-driven function) · RDS vs DynamoDB · SQS vs SNS · SNS vs EventBridge (fan-out vs event bus + rules) · Redis vs RDS (cache vs source of truth) · S3 vs EBS · API Gateway vs ALB · Secrets Manager vs KMS.

title: Revision 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Architecture examples
text: - **E-commerce:** CloudFront → WAF → API Gateway → ECS/EKS (User/Order/Product services) → RDS + Redis → EventBridge → SQS queue + Lambda → Worker → S3/Email. *Why:* RDS (relationships user → orders → order_items → products, transactions), Redis (catalog/sessions/rate limiting), SQS (invoice generation outside the HTTP request), EventBridge (multiple systems care about `OrderCreated`), Lambda (small event processor like thumbnails), ECS Fargate (simpler) or EKS (if Kubernetes ecosystem justified) for the core API, S3 for files (DB = metadata, S3 = bytes). - **Bad vs improved:** bad = Internet → public EC2 → public PostgreSQL, SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0, password in code, single EC2/DB, no backups. Improved = Route 53 → CloudFront/WAF → ALB → private ECS/EKS → Redis → private RDS with IAM, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch, autoscaling, multi-AZ, backups, least privilege. **Don't over-engineer:** a small app may only need ALB + ECS Fargate + RDS + S3 (not CloudFront + WAF + API Gateway + EKS + Istio + Kafka + EventBridge + Step Functions + DynamoDB + RDS + Redis). - **Image-processing backend:** User → API → S3 upload → S3 event → SQS → Lambda/ECS worker → process → S3 output → DB metadata (not synchronous processing of a 100 MB image in the Node.js server). - **Notification system:** Application → EventBridge/SNS → Email queue / SMS queue → workers (SQS = buffering/retry, SNS/EventBridge = distribution, workers = delivery). - **High-traffic product catalog:** Client → CloudFront (edge cache) → ALB → ECS/EKS → Redis → miss → RDS/DynamoDB (source of truth; choice depends on access patterns). - **Payment workflow:** API → Order DB → Step Functions → Payment → Inventory → Invoice → Notification with idempotency, timeouts, retries, compensation, audit trail.

title: Revision 33 — Advanced AWS for Backend Engineers
heading: Design process (8 questions)
text: 1. Workload (HTTP? event? batch? stream? workflow?) 2. Compute (EC2/ECS/EKS/Lambda) 3. Data model (relational/key-value/document/object/cache) 4. Communication (sync/queue/pub-sub/event bus/workflow) 5. Reliability (RTO, RPO, multi-AZ, retries, DLQ) 6. Security (IAM, encryption, private networking, Secrets Manager) 7. Scale (requests/s, data size, concurrency, burst) 8. **Cost — always ask.** **Well-Architected pillars:** Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability. **Reliability architecture** when RDS is slow: timeouts, connection pooling, bounded retries, circuit breaking, caching, queues, backpressure. *AWS doesn't remove distributed-systems problems:* duplicates, ordering, timeouts, partial failures, eventual consistency, idempotency, race conditions, backpressure. **Depth:** 🔥 EC2/ECS/EKS/Lambda, RDS vs DynamoDB, SQS/SNS/EventBridge, ALB vs API Gateway, S3/EBS/EFS, Redis/ElastiCache, IAM, Secrets Manager, KMS, autoscaling, queues, idempotency, eventual consistency · 🟡 Step Functions, DynamoDB indexes/streams, ECS task/service concepts, Fargate, EventBridge rules, API Gateway details · ⚪ rare services, analytics services, AWS internals.
