title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
text: > **Source:** Response 35 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-35.txt`, lines 1–3246) · **Part II — Advanced extension (Responses 25–36)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch35-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) · *includes an editorial supplement at the end* <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> Now we move from **learning individual DevOps technologies → combining everything into one system**. This response is deliberately practical. The goal is not to build another CRUD application. The goal is to build something you can explain in an interview from: **code → database → containers → CI → AWS → Kubernetes → deployment → observability → failure recovery.** ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 1. What We Are Building
text: We will build a **production-grade asynchronous order-processing platform**. Think of it as the backend infrastructure behind an e-commerce/order system. The system will support: ```text Client ↓ API ↓ Order Service ├── PostgreSQL ├── Redis ├── SQS └── S3 ↓ Workers ↓ notifications / processing ``` And around it: ```text Route 53 │ CloudFront │ WAF │ ALB │ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ EKS │ │ │ API Pods Worker Pods │ │ ┌───────┼───────┐ │ │ │ │ │ Redis PostgreSQL SQS ─┘ │ │ │ ↓ │ Workers │ └────────── Cache S3 │ Object Storage ``` Infrastructure: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS Infrastructure GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Docker ↓ ECR ↓ GitOps Repository ↓ ArgoCD ↓ EKS ``` Observability: ```text Application ↓ Metrics + Logs + Traces ↓ CloudWatch / Prometheus / Grafana ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 2. Why This Project Is Better Than a Basic CRUD App
text: A normal CRUD project demonstrates: ```text GET POST PUT DELETE ``` That's not enough to demonstrate serious backend/DevOps knowledge. Our project demonstrates: ```text REST APIs PostgreSQL Redis queues asynchronous processing Docker Kubernetes AWS Terraform CI/CD GitOps autoscaling observability security failure recovery caching idempotency retries dead-letter queues load testing disaster recovery ``` That's much closer to the kind of system you can discuss for 30–60 minutes. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 3. Project Architecture
text: Let's first understand the complete system. ```text INTERNET │ ▼ Route 53 │ ▼ CloudFront │ ▼ WAF │ ▼ ALB │ ┌───────────┴───────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ API Service Static/S3 │ ┌───────┼────────┐ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ PostgreSQL Redis SQS │ │ │ │ │ ▼ │ │ Worker │ │ │ │ │ ├── S3 │ │ └── External services │ │ └───────┴────────── ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 4. The Application
text: We'll use: ```text TypeScript Node.js Express PostgreSQL Prisma Redis AWS SDK ``` Why TypeScript? Because it matches your target backend stack. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 5. Repository Structure
text: We'll use a monorepo-style structure: ```text devops-platform/ │ ├── apps/ │ ├── api/ │ │ ├── src/ │ │ │ ├── controllers/ │ │ │ ├── services/ │ │ │ ├── repositories/ │ │ │ ├── middleware/ │ │ │ ├── routes/ │ │ │ ├── config/ │ │ │ └── server.ts │ │ ├── Dockerfile │ │ └── package.json │ │ │ └── worker/ │ ├── src/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ └── package.json │ ├── packages/ │ └── shared/ │ ├── prisma/ │ └── schema.prisma │ ├── infra/ │ └── terraform/ │ ├── deploy/ │ ├── helm/ │ │ └── order-platform/ │ │ ├── Chart.yaml │ │ ├── values.yaml │ │ ├── values-dev.yaml │ │ ├── values-prod.yaml │ │ └── templates/ │ │ │ └── argocd/ │ ├── .github/ │ └── workflows/ │ ├── docker-compose.yml ├── package.json ├── pnpm-workspace.yaml ├── .gitignore └── README.md ``` Don't worry if this looks large. We'll build it incrementally. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 6. Major Components
text: We have two main application workloads.

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: API
text: Responsible for: ```text authentication orders products API requests database operations cache publishing jobs ```

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Worker
text: Responsible for: ```text reading SQS processing background jobs retrying failures handling DLQ ``` This separation is important. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 7. Why Separate API and Worker?
text: Suppose you receive: ```text 10,000 orders ``` If the API itself performs expensive processing: ```text request ↓ API ↓ process everything ↓ response ``` the API becomes slow. Instead: ```text request ↓ API ↓ save order ↓ send job to SQS ↓ return quickly ``` Then: ```text SQS ↓ Worker ↓ process job ``` This is asynchronous architecture. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Synchronous
text: ```text Client ↓ API ↓ DB ↓ response ``` Client waits.

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Asynchronous
text: ```text Client ↓ API ↓ Queue ↓ response Queue ↓ Worker ↓ processing ``` Client doesn't wait for background work. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 9. Database Design
text: We'll keep the initial schema simple but realistic. ```text User │ └── Order │ └── OrderItem │ └── Product ``` Conceptually: ```text User ---- id email createdAt Product ------- id name price stock createdAt Order ----- id userId status totalAmount idempotencyKey createdAt OrderItem --------- id orderId productId quantity price ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 10. Order States
text: Don't use arbitrary strings everywhere. Use: ```text PENDING PROCESSING COMPLETED FAILED CANCELLED ``` State transitions: ```text PENDING ↓ PROCESSING ↓ COMPLETED ``` Failure: ```text PROCESSING ↓ FAILED ``` Cancellation: ```text PENDING ↓ CANCELLED ``` This becomes important for reliability. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 11. Idempotency
text: Suppose: ```http POST /orders ``` The client sends: ```text Idempotency-Key: abc123 ``` The API stores: ```text abc123 → order 456 ``` If the request is repeated: ```text abc123 ``` we don't create another order. Instead: ```text return existing order ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 12. Why This Matters
text: Imagine: ```text Client ↓ POST /orders ↓ Order created ↓ network timeout ``` Client thinks: ```text "Maybe it failed." ``` It retries. Without idempotency: ```text Order #1 Order #2 ``` With idempotency: ```text Order #1 Order #1 returned again ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 13. Redis
text: Redis will be used for: ```text caching rate limiting temporary data distributed coordination where appropriate ``` Example: ```text GET /products/123 ``` First request: ```text API ↓ Redis miss ↓ PostgreSQL ↓ Redis SET ↓ response ``` Next request: ```text API ↓ Redis hit ↓ response ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 14. Cache-Aside
text: We'll use: ```text Application ↓ Redis ``` If missing: ```text Redis miss ↓ DB ↓ Redis ↓ response ``` This is called: > Cache-aside. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 15. Cache Failure
text: Critical design question: > What if Redis goes down? Because Redis is a cache, we can often do: ```text Redis unavailable ↓ skip cache ↓ PostgreSQL ``` The system becomes slower but remains functional. That's graceful degradation. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 16. SQS
text: We'll use Amazon SQS for asynchronous processing. Example: ```text POST /orders ↓ create order ↓ SQS ↓ worker ``` Message: ```json { "event": "ORDER_CREATED", "orderId": "123", "attempt": 1 } ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 17. Why SQS?
text: It provides a buffer. Suppose: ```text API = 5,000 jobs/sec worker = 1,000 jobs/sec ``` Instead of immediately crashing: ```text API ↓ SQS ↓ jobs accumulate ↓ workers process ``` This is: > Backpressure through a queue. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 18. Worker Scaling
text: Suppose queue depth becomes: ```text 100 1,000 10,000 100,000 ``` We can increase workers. Conceptually: ```text Queue depth ↓ HPA/KEDA-like scaling strategy ↓ more workers ``` For the capstone, understand the architecture even if some production autoscaling integrations are treated as advanced implementation. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 19. SQS Visibility Timeout
text: Important concept. Suppose worker receives: ```text Message A ``` SQS temporarily hides it. Worker processes it. If worker succeeds: ```text delete message ``` If worker crashes: ```text message becomes visible again ``` Therefore: ```text visibility timeout ``` must be long enough for normal processing. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 20. DLQ
text: What if a message repeatedly fails? Example: ```text attempt 1 ❌ attempt 2 ❌ attempt 3 ❌ attempt 4 ❌ ``` Don't retry forever. Send to: ```text Dead Letter Queue ``` Then engineers can investigate. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 21. Worker Idempotency
text: Messages can be delivered more than once. Therefore: ```text worker ↓ process job ``` must be designed to tolerate duplicates. For example: ```text eventId = xyz123 ``` Store processed event IDs. If: ```text xyz123 ``` appears again: ```text already processed → ignore ``` This is critical in distributed systems. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 22. Docker Architecture
text: We'll create separate images: ```text api-image worker-image ``` Each image contains only what that workload needs. Example: ```text Node ↓ build TypeScript ↓ production JS ↓ runtime image ``` Use multi-stage builds. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 23. Production Dockerfile
text: Conceptually: ```dockerfile FROM node:22-alpine AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build FROM node:22-alpine AS runtime WORKDIR /app ENV NODE_ENV=production COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist USER node CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] ``` Important ideas: ```text multi-stage small runtime production dependencies non-root immutable image ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 24. Don't Put Secrets in Docker
text: Never: ```dockerfile ENV DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret123 ``` Don't put: ```text AWS keys DB passwords JWT secrets API keys ``` inside the image. Instead: ```text Kubernetes Secret AWS Secrets Manager environment injection ``` depending on the architecture. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 25. Local Development
text: Before AWS, everything must work locally. We'll use: ```text Docker Compose ``` for: ```text API PostgreSQL Redis Local worker ``` Architecture: ```text docker-compose │ ├── api ├── worker ├── postgres └── redis ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 26. Local Environment
text: Example: ```env NODE_ENV=development PORT=3000 DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:postgres@postgres:5432/orders REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379 AWS_REGION=ap-south-1 SQS_QUEUE_URL=... ``` Never commit real secrets. Use: ```text .env ``` and: ```gitignore .env ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 27. Health Endpoint
text: API: ```http GET /health ``` Response: ```json { "status": "ok" } ``` But production health endpoints should be more thoughtful. We can have: ```text /health/live /health/ready ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 28. Liveness
text: ```http GET /health/live ``` Means: > Is the process alive? Simple response: ```json { "status": "alive" } ``` It shouldn't necessarily depend on every external dependency. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 29. Readiness
text: ```http GET /health/ready ``` Can verify critical dependencies. For example: ```text PostgreSQL reachable? ``` If not: ```text ready = false ``` Kubernetes then stops sending traffic to that pod. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 30. Graceful Shutdown
text: Our API must handle: ```text SIGTERM ``` Sequence: ```text SIGTERM ↓ stop accepting new traffic ↓ finish active requests ↓ close DB ↓ close Redis ↓ exit ``` This matters when Kubernetes performs rolling deployments. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 31. Kubernetes Architecture
text: Eventually: ```text EKS Cluster │ ├── namespace: orders │ ├── API Deployment │ ├── pod │ ├── pod │ └── pod │ ├── Worker Deployment │ ├── pod │ └── pod │ ├── API Service │ ├── ConfigMap │ ├── Secret │ └── HPA ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 32. API Deployment
text: Conceptually: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: api spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: api template: metadata: labels: app: api spec: containers: - name: api image: <ECR_IMAGE> ports: - containerPort: 3000 resources: requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" limits: cpu: "1" memory: "512Mi" ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 33. Service
text: Pods are ephemeral. Their IPs can change. So: ```text Client ↓ Service ↓ Pods ``` Example: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: api spec: selector: app: api ports: - port: 80 targetPort: 3000 ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 34. Readiness Probe
text: Example: ```yaml readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /health/ready port: 3000 initialDelaySeconds: 5 periodSeconds: 10 ``` If readiness fails: ```text Pod remains alive but traffic is removed ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 35. Liveness Probe
text: ```yaml livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /health/live port: 3000 periodSeconds: 20 ``` If the application becomes genuinely stuck: ```text Kubernetes ↓ restart pod ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 36. Resource Requests
text: Suppose: ```yaml requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" ``` This tells Kubernetes roughly: > "I need at least this much capacity to schedule me." This affects scheduling. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 37. Resource Limits
text: ```yaml limits: cpu: "1" memory: "512Mi" ``` This establishes a resource ceiling. Important distinction: ```text requests → scheduling expectation limits → maximum resource boundary ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 38. HPA
text: Suppose: ```text API pods = 3 ``` Traffic increases. HPA can increase: ```text 3 ↓ 5 ↓ 8 ↓ 10 ``` based on metrics such as CPU or memory, and potentially custom/external metrics with the appropriate setup. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 39. Important Scaling Problem
text: Suppose: ```text API scales: 3 → 20 pods ``` But PostgreSQL has: ```text max connections = 200 ``` Each pod: ```text 20 DB connections ``` Then: ```text 20 × 20 = 400 ``` You have now overloaded your database. Therefore: > **Autoscaling the application doesn't automatically make the entire system scalable.** This is a very important interview point. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 40. Database
text: For AWS production: ```text EKS ↓ private network ↓ RDS PostgreSQL ``` Don't run your production database inside the same Kubernetes cluster unless there is a specific reason. Use a managed database when appropriate. Benefits: ```text backups patching Multi-AZ options monitoring managed storage ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 41. Redis
text: Similarly: ```text EKS ↓ ElastiCache Redis ``` rather than treating a random Redis pod as production infrastructure. Local: ```text Docker Redis ``` Production: ```text Managed Redis ``` This is an important environment distinction. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 42. S3
text: We'll use S3 for object storage. Possible future use: ```text order documents reports exports logs/artifacts ``` Database stores metadata: ```text document_id s3_key content_type created_at ``` S3 stores the actual bytes. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 43. Terraform Architecture
text: Terraform will provision: ```text VPC ├── public subnets ├── private subnets ├── route tables ├── NAT └── security groups EKS ├── cluster ├── node groups └── IAM RDS Redis S3 SQS ECR CloudWatch IAM roles ``` Conceptually: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS APIs ↓ Infrastructure ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 44. Terraform Repository
text: Example: ```text infra/terraform/ │ ├── main.tf ├── variables.tf ├── outputs.tf ├── providers.tf ├── versions.tf │ ├── modules/ │ ├── vpc/ │ ├── eks/ │ ├── rds/ │ ├── redis/ │ ├── s3/ │ └── sqs/ │ └── environments/ ├── dev/ └── prod/ ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 45. Environment Separation
text: Don't put: ```text dev prod ``` in one giant configuration with random conditionals. Prefer clear environment separation. Example: ```text dev ↓ smaller resources lower cost prod ↓ HA larger resources stronger safeguards ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 46. Terraform State
text: State tracks: ```text what Terraform believes exists ``` Production should use remote state. Conceptually: ```text Developer/CI ↓ Terraform ↓ S3 remote state ``` Use appropriate state locking/versioning strategy. Never casually delete production state. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 47. IAM
text: The system should follow least privilege. Example: API should not have: ```text AdministratorAccess ``` Instead: ```text API role ↓ only required permissions ``` Worker: ```text Worker role ↓ SQS receive/delete ↓ limited S3 access ``` This reduces blast radius. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 48. CI Pipeline
text: Now we connect GitHub Actions. Developer: ```text git push ``` Pipeline: ```text Checkout ↓ Install ↓ Lint ↓ Typecheck ↓ Unit tests ↓ Integration tests ↓ Build ↓ Docker build ↓ Security scan ↓ Push image to ECR ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 49. Image Tagging
text: Never rely only on: ```text latest ``` Use immutable identifiers: ```text orders-api:git-sha ``` For example: ```text orders-api:a8f91c2 ``` Now you know exactly which source produced the image. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 50. Why Git SHA Tags Matter
text: Suppose production has: ```text orders-api:a8f91c2 ``` and something breaks. You can identify: ```text commit a8f91c2 ``` and reproduce the build. With: ```text latest ``` you don't have that clarity. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 51. ECR
text: ECR = Elastic Container Registry. Pipeline: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ docker build ↓ ECR ↓ image ``` EKS then pulls: ```text ECR image ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 52. OIDC
text: Don't put: ```text AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY ``` in GitHub secrets if you can avoid long-lived credentials. Use: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ OIDC ↓ AWS IAM role ↓ temporary credentials ``` This is a major production security improvement. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 53. GitOps
text: Now we separate:

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: CI
text: Builds: ```text code → image ```

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: CD
text: Deploys: ```text image → cluster ``` With GitOps: ```text GitHub Actions ↓ build/test/push ECR ↓ update deployment config ↓ GitOps repository ↓ ArgoCD ↓ EKS ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 54. Why ArgoCD?
text: ArgoCD continuously compares: ```text desired state in Git ``` against: ```text actual state in Kubernetes ``` If they differ: ```text OutOfSync ``` ArgoCD reconciles them depending on your sync policy. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 55. Helm
text: Helm packages the Kubernetes application. Instead of maintaining: ```text deployment-dev.yaml deployment-prod.yaml deployment-staging.yaml ``` we can have: ```text Chart + values ``` Example: ```text values-dev.yaml values-prod.yaml ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 56. Deployment Flow
text: Our complete flow: ```text Developer │ ▼ GitHub │ ▼ GitHub Actions │ ├── test ├── build ├── scan └── Docker │ ▼ ECR │ ▼ GitOps update │ ▼ ArgoCD │ ▼ EKS │ ▼ API / Worker ``` This is the core DevOps pipeline you should be able to draw in an interview. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 57. Deployment Strategy
text: We'll use rolling deployments. Suppose: ```text 3 old pods ``` Deployment: ```text old pod ↓ new pod ↓ health check ↓ traffic ``` Gradually: ```text 3 old 2 old + 1 new 1 old + 2 new 0 old + 3 new ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 58. What If New Pods Are Broken?
text: Readiness fails. Kubernetes should not send traffic to them. Deployment can stop progressing. Then: ```text ArgoCD + Git + rollback ``` can restore the previous version. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 59. Canary Deployment
text: For advanced deployment: ```text 100% old ``` Deploy: ```text 5% new ``` Observe: ```text error rate latency business metrics ``` Then: ```text 5% ↓ 25% ↓ 50% ↓ 100% ``` This reduces blast radius. You don't necessarily need to implement full progressive delivery in this capstone, but you should understand it. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 60. Observability
text: Our API should expose: ```text /metrics ``` Example metrics: ```text http_requests_total http_request_duration_seconds http_errors_total ``` Prometheus scrapes: ```text API ↓ /metrics ↓ Prometheus ``` Grafana visualizes: ```text Prometheus ↓ Grafana ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 61. RED Metrics
text: For the API:

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Rate
text: ```text requests/sec ```

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Errors
text: ```text 5xx rate ```

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Duration
text: ```text p50 p95 p99 ``` These should become your first backend dashboard. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 62. Example Dashboard

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 63. Logs
text: Don't log: ```text console.log("something happened") ``` randomly. Use structured logs: ```json { "level": "info", "requestId": "abc123", "method": "POST", "path": "/orders", "statusCode": 201, "durationMs": 82 } ``` Now logs are searchable. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 64. Never Log Secrets
text: Never log: ```text password JWT AWS credentials API keys database URL payment credentials ``` This is an extremely common production mistake. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 65. Tracing
text: A request: ```text POST /orders ``` may produce: ```text API span ↓ PostgreSQL span ↓ Redis span ↓ SQS span ``` If order creation takes: ```text 2 seconds ``` tracing can reveal: ```text DB = 1.7 seconds ``` instead of blindly investigating the API. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 66. Alerting
text: Example alerts: ```text 5xx rate > 2% p95 latency > 500ms queue age > 60s DB connections > 90% pod restart rate increasing disk/storage approaching limit ``` But remember: > Don't create alerts just because a metric exists. Each alert should be actionable. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 67. Failure Scenario #1 — API Pod Dies
text: ```text API pod ↓ crashes ``` Kubernetes: ```text Deployment ↓ detect missing replica ↓ create replacement ``` Service: ```text continues routing to healthy pods ``` This demonstrates: ```text self-healing ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 68. Failure Scenario #2 — Redis Dies
text: ```text Redis ↓ unavailable ``` Application: ```text cache failure ↓ fallback DB ``` Monitoring: ```text Redis error metric ↑ ``` Alert: ```text Redis unavailable ``` Core API remains functional if the architecture allows that degradation. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 69. Failure Scenario #3 — Worker Dies
text: ```text Worker ↓ crashes ``` SQS message isn't successfully completed. Eventually: ```text message becomes visible ``` Another worker can process it. If repeated failures: ```text DLQ ``` This demonstrates: ```text fault tolerance + at-least-once processing + idempotency ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 70. Failure Scenario #4 — Database Slow
text: Observe: ```text p95 latency ↑ DB latency ↑ ``` Investigate: ```text slow queries connections CPU IOPS locks ``` Potential mitigation: ```text cache reduce load rollback optimize query scale DB appropriately ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 71. Failure Scenario #5 — Bad Deployment
text: ```text Git push ↓ CI ↓ ECR ↓ ArgoCD ↓ new version ↓ 5xx increases ``` Observability detects: ```text error rate ↑ ``` Response: ```text stop rollout ↓ rollback ↓ verify recovery ``` Then investigate root cause. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 72. Failure Scenario #6 — Traffic Spike
text: Normal: ```text 500 req/sec ``` Sudden: ```text 10,000 req/sec ``` System protections: ```text CloudFront/cache ↓ WAF ↓ ALB ↓ EKS autoscaling ↓ Redis ↓ PostgreSQL ``` But if DB cannot scale fast enough: ```text rate limiting queue load shedding ``` protect the system. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 73. Security Architecture
text: We should have: ```text Internet ↓ WAF ↓ ALB ↓ EKS ↓ private resources ``` RDS: ```text private subnet ``` Redis: ```text private ``` No direct public access. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 74. Security Groups
text: Conceptually: ```text Internet ↓ ALB SG ↓ API SG ↓ RDS SG ``` RDS should allow traffic from: ```text API security group ``` not: ```text 0.0.0.0/0 ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 75. Secrets Architecture
text: Production: ```text AWS Secrets Manager ↓ workload identity ↓ application ``` rather than: ```text password inside Git ``` or: ```text password inside Docker image ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 76. Network Architecture
text: A sensible AWS architecture: ```text Internet │ Route53 │ CloudFront │ WAF │ ALB │ ┌────────────┴────────────┐ │ │ Public Subnets Public Subnets │ ▼ ALB │ ▼ Private Subnets │ ├── EKS nodes ├── RDS └── Redis ``` NAT allows appropriate outbound traffic from private workloads. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 77. High Availability
text: We should distribute workloads across multiple Availability Zones. Conceptually: ```text EKS ┌─────┼─────┐ │ │ │ AZ-A AZ-B AZ-C │ │ │ Pods Pods Pods ``` If one AZ has problems: ```text other AZs ↓ continue serving ``` assuming the rest of the architecture is also designed for it. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 78. Disaster Recovery
text: Our capstone should include: ```text RDS backups S3 versioning where appropriate infrastructure as code container images in ECR GitOps configuration in Git ``` Why? If infrastructure disappears: ```text Terraform ↓ recreate infrastructure ``` Application: ```text ECR ↓ deploy ``` Configuration: ```text Git ↓ ArgoCD ``` This is a major advantage of Infrastructure as Code + GitOps. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 79. The "Rebuild From Nothing" Test
text: A powerful DevOps exercise: > Imagine the entire environment disappears. Can you recreate it? Ideally: ```text Terraform ↓ AWS infrastructure ArgoCD ↓ Kubernetes applications ECR ↓ container images RDS backup ↓ database ``` The goal is to minimize manual configuration. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 80. Cost Awareness
text: Production architecture shouldn't mean: ```text maximum AWS services everywhere ``` For learning: ```text small EKS small RDS small Redis limited NAT ``` For real production: ```text size according to traffic ``` Always ask: ```text Do we need this? What does it cost? What reliability does it buy? ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 81. Capstone Development Order
text: Don't build the entire thing simultaneously. We'll build it in this order: ```text 1. Backend foundation 2. PostgreSQL 3. Redis 4. Async worker 5. SQS 6. Docker 7. Docker Compose 8. Tests 9. CI 10. AWS infrastructure 11. Terraform 12. ECR 13. EKS 14. Helm 15. ArgoCD 16. Production deployment 17. Observability 18. Security 19. Load testing 20. Failure testing 21. Reliability improvements ``` This prevents the project from becoming unmanageable. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 82. Phase 1 — Backend
text: First build: ```text POST /users POST /orders GET /orders/:id GET /products GET /products/:id ``` Then: ```text POST /orders ``` will: ```text validate ↓ check idempotency ↓ create order ↓ publish event ↓ return ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 83. Phase 2 — Async Processing
text: Worker: ```text SQS ↓ receive message ↓ validate ↓ process ↓ update order ↓ delete message ``` Failure: ```text process fails ↓ don't delete ↓ SQS retry ``` Repeated failure: ```text DLQ ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 84. Phase 3 — Docker
text: Build: ```text api image worker image ``` Run: ```text API Worker PostgreSQL Redis ``` using Compose. At this point: > The entire application works without AWS. This is important. Cloud should not hide broken application logic. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 85. Phase 4 — CI
text: Every push: ```text install ↓ lint ↓ typecheck ↓ test ↓ build ↓ Docker build ``` Then: ```text push image to ECR ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 86. Phase 5 — Terraform
text: Provision: ```text VPC EKS RDS Redis SQS S3 ECR IAM ``` Use: ```text modules variables outputs remote state ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 87. Phase 6 — Kubernetes
text: Deploy: ```text API Worker ConfigMap Secrets Services HPA ``` Add: ```text readiness liveness resources rolling deployment ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 88. Phase 7 — Helm
text: Convert raw YAML: ```text deployment.yaml service.yaml hpa.yaml ``` into: ```text Helm Chart ``` Then: ```text values-dev.yaml values-prod.yaml ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 89. Phase 8 — GitOps
text: ArgoCD: ```text GitOps repository ↓ ArgoCD ↓ EKS ``` Now deployment state is controlled through Git. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 90. Phase 9 — Observability
text: Add: ```text structured logs metrics traces dashboards alerts ``` Then test: ```text pod failure DB latency Redis failure queue backlog bad deployment ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 91. Phase 10 — Load Testing
text: Use realistic traffic: ```text GET /products POST /orders GET /orders/:id ``` Measure: ```text RPS p50 p95 p99 5xx CPU memory DB Redis queue ``` Find the bottleneck. Then optimize it. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 92. Phase 11 — Security
text: Perform: ```text secret scanning dependency scanning container scanning IAM review network review ``` Verify: ```text no public RDS no hardcoded secrets no privileged containers least privilege IAM HTTPS authentication rate limiting ``` ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 93. Phase 12 — Failure Engineering
text: Intentionally: ```text kill API pod kill worker make Redis unavailable make DB slow create queue backlog deploy broken version generate traffic spike ``` Then document: ```text what happened how it was detected how it recovered what you changed ``` This turns the project into something you can defend deeply in an interview. ---

title: Chapter 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: 94. What Goes on Your Resume?
text: Eventually, something like: > **Production-Grade Distributed Order Processing Platform** > Built a TypeScript/Node.js backend using PostgreSQL, Redis and asynchronous SQS workers; containerized services with Docker and deployed them to AWS EKS using Terraform, Helm and ArgoCD, with GitHub Actions CI/CD, autoscaling, structured observability, idempotent processing, retry/DLQ handling and production failure testing. The exact resume wording should wait until we've actually built it. Don't claim technologies you haven't implemented. ---

heading: From design to a runnable starter
text: This chapter is a **design walkthrough**: architecture diagrams, a repository layout, reliability reasoning, failure scenarios and a build order — but it contains no complete application, and the source conversation stopped here (the promised Response 36 was never produced). To make the chapter usable as practice, the repository includes an **editorial reference starter**: [`code-examples/capstone/`](../../code-examples/capstone/README.md). | Chapter section | Where it is implemented in the starter | |---|---| | §9–11 data model, order states, idempotency | `db/init.sql` (`UNIQUE(idempotency_key)`), `prisma/schema.prisma`, `POST /orders` in `src/api.ts` | | §14–15 cache-aside, cache failure | `GET /orders/:id` — Redis errors fall through to PostgreSQL | | §16–21 SQS, visibility timeout, DLQ, worker idempotency | `src/worker.ts` (conditional `UPDATE … WHERE status='PENDING'`; message deleted only after success) | | §22–26 Docker, local development | `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.env.example` | | §27–30 health endpoints, graceful shutdown | `/health/live`, `/health/ready`, SIGTERM handler | | §32–38 Kubernetes Deployment, probes, requests/limits, HPA | `deploy/api.yaml` | | §18, §39 worker scaling, connection math | `deploy/worker-keda.yaml`, `DB_POOL_MAX` in `src/config.ts` | | §48–52 CI, SHA tags, ECR, OIDC | `ci/ci.yml` | **What is deliberately missing** (and is the learning value): the transactional outbox for the DB-write + queue-send gap, authentication, metrics and tracing, tests, Terraform, the Helm chart and the ArgoCD `Application`. Chapter 33 (outbox/saga), 21/32 (Terraform), 25 (Helm), 26 (ArgoCD) and 22/34 (observability) show how to add each. **The connection-pool trap from §39, as numbers.** With 20 API Pods and a pool of 20 each, the API alone can open `20 × 20 = 400` connections; a PostgreSQL limit of 200 will reject the surplus. Fix by lowering `DB_POOL_MAX`, adding RDS Proxy/PgBouncer, or capping `maxReplicas` — and remember worker replicas (KEDA may scale to 20) also hold connections. **Honest status.** The starter's TypeScript passes `tsc --noEmit` and builds, and its YAML parses; it has not been run end to end, so expect to debug the first `docker compose up`. --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 34: Advanced SRE](../07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md) · [Chapter 36: Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive](../01-foundations/ch36-virtualization-internals.md) → · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch35-revision.md)
