A reference starter is provided in [code-examples/capstone/](../code-examples/capstone/README.md) (see the editorial supplement in the chapter).

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: What is being built
text: A **production-grade asynchronous order-processing platform** (backend of an e-commerce/order system): Client → API → Order Service → {PostgreSQL, Redis, SQS, S3} → Workers → notifications/processing. Edge: Route 53 → CloudFront → WAF → ALB → EKS (API Pods + Worker Pods). Infrastructure: Terraform → AWS. Delivery: GitHub → GitHub Actions → Docker → ECR → GitOps repo → ArgoCD → EKS. Observability: metrics + logs + traces → CloudWatch / Prometheus / Grafana. **Why better than basic CRUD:** demonstrates REST APIs, PostgreSQL, Redis, queues, asynchronous processing, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Terraform, CI/CD, GitOps, autoscaling, observability, security, failure recovery, caching, idempotency, retries, dead-letter queues, load testing, disaster recovery — a system you can discuss for 30–60 minutes.

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Stack and repository structure
text: TypeScript · Node.js · Express · PostgreSQL · Prisma · Redis · AWS SDK. ```text devops-platform/ ├── apps/ │ ├── api/ {src/{controllers,services,repositories,middleware,routes,config}, server.ts}, Dockerfile, package.json │ └── worker/ {src/}, Dockerfile, package.json ├── packages/shared/ ├── prisma/schema.prisma ├── infra/terraform/ ├── deploy/{helm/order-platform/{Chart.yaml,values.yaml,values-dev.yaml,values-prod.yaml,templates/}, argocd/} ├── .github/workflows/ ├── docker-compose.yml, package.json, pnpm-workspace.yaml, .gitignore, README.md ``` **Two workloads:** **API** (authentication, orders, products, API requests, database operations, cache, publishing jobs) and **Worker** (reading SQS, background jobs, retrying failures, handling DLQ). Separate so expensive processing doesn't make the API slow: request → API → save order → send job to SQS → return quickly; SQS → Worker → process. **Sync** (client waits) vs **async** (client doesn't wait for background work).

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Data model and order lifecycle
text: ```text User(id,email,createdAt) ─┬─ Order(id,userId,status,totalAmount,idempotencyKey,createdAt) ── OrderItem(id,orderId,productId,quantity,price) ── Product(id,name,price,stock,createdAt) ``` **Order states** (not arbitrary strings): `PENDING → PROCESSING → COMPLETED`; failure `PROCESSING → FAILED`; cancellation `PENDING → CANCELLED`.

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Reliability design decisions
text: - **Idempotency (API):** `Idempotency-Key: abc123` → stored `abc123 → order 456`; a repeated request returns the existing order (client times out after order creation and retries → Order #1 returned again, not Order #2). - **Redis:** caching, rate limiting, temporary data, distributed coordination where appropriate; **cache-aside** (`GET /products/123`: miss → PostgreSQL → Redis SET → response; hit → response). **If Redis goes down** (a cache): skip cache → PostgreSQL — slower but functional = graceful degradation. Local = Docker Redis; production = managed Redis (ElastiCache), not a random Redis Pod. - **SQS:** message `{"event":"ORDER_CREATED","orderId":"123","attempt":1}`; buffer (API 5,000 jobs/s vs worker 1,000 jobs/s → jobs accumulate and workers process = backpressure through a queue). **Worker scaling** by queue depth (100 → 1,000 → 10,000 → 100,000) → more workers (HPA/KEDA-like strategy). **Visibility timeout** must be long enough for normal processing (crash → message visible again). **DLQ** after repeated failures (attempt 1–4 ❌ → DLQ for investigation). **Worker idempotency:** store processed `eventId` (e.g. `xyz123`); a repeat is ignored. - **Scaling problem:** API 3 → 20 Pods × 20 DB connections each = 400 vs PostgreSQL `max connections = 200` → *autoscaling the application doesn't automatically make the entire system scalable.* - **Managed services in AWS:** RDS PostgreSQL (backups, patching, Multi-AZ, monitoring, managed storage; don't run the production DB inside the cluster without reason), ElastiCache Redis, S3 for documents/reports/exports/logs (DB stores `document_id, s3_key, content_type, created_at`).

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Containers and local development
text: - Separate `api-image` and `worker-image`; multi-stage Dockerfile (`node:22-alpine` builder → runtime with `npm ci --omit=dev`, `COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist`, `ENV NODE_ENV=production`, `USER node`, `CMD ["node","dist/server.js"]`): small runtime, production dependencies, non-root, immutable image. **Never** put `ENV DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret123`, AWS keys, DB passwords, JWT secrets or API keys in the image → Kubernetes Secret / AWS Secrets Manager / environment injection. - **Local first:** Docker Compose with `api`, `worker`, `postgres`, `redis` (everything works without AWS — "cloud should not hide broken application logic"). `.env` example: `NODE_ENV=development`, `PORT=3000`, `DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:postgres@postgres:5432/orders`, `REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379`, `AWS_REGION=ap-south-1`, `SQS_QUEUE_URL=...`; `.gitignore` `.env`. - **Health:** `/health/live` (`{"status":"alive"}`, shouldn't depend on every external dependency) and `/health/ready` (e.g. PostgreSQL reachable? else `ready=false` → Kubernetes stops sending traffic). **Graceful shutdown** on SIGTERM: stop accepting traffic → finish active requests → close DB → close Redis → exit (matters in rolling deployments).

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Kubernetes, Terraform, IAM
text: - Namespace `orders`; API Deployment (3 Pods), Worker Deployment (2 Pods), API Service, ConfigMap, Secret, HPA. API Deployment: `replicas: 3`, image `<ECR_IMAGE>`, port 3000, requests `250m/256Mi`, limits `1/512Mi`; Service `port 80 → targetPort 3000`; `readinessProbe` `/health/ready` (initialDelay 5, period 10); `livenessProbe` `/health/live` (period 20). HPA: 3 → 5 → 8 → 10 on CPU/memory (or custom/external metrics). - **Terraform provisions:** VPC (public/private subnets, route tables, NAT, security groups), EKS (cluster, node groups, IAM), RDS, Redis, S3, SQS, ECR, CloudWatch, IAM roles. Repo `infra/terraform/{main,variables,outputs,providers,versions}.tf + modules/{vpc,eks,rds,redis,s3,sqs} + environments/{dev,prod}`; clear **environment separation** (dev smaller/cheaper; prod HA, larger, stronger safeguards); remote S3 state with locking/versioning; never casually delete production state. - **IAM least privilege:** API role — only needed permissions (never `AdministratorAccess`); Worker role — SQS receive/delete + limited S3 access → reduced blast radius.

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: CI/CD and GitOps
text: - **CI:** checkout → install → lint → typecheck → unit tests → integration tests → build → Docker build → security scan → push image to ECR. **Tag images** with Git SHA (`orders-api:a8f91c2`), never rely on `latest` — identify the commit and reproduce the build. **OIDC** (GitHub Actions → OIDC → IAM role → temporary credentials) instead of long-lived keys. - **GitOps:** CI builds `code → image`; CD deploys `image → cluster`: GitHub Actions (build/test/push ECR) → update deployment config in GitOps repo → ArgoCD → EKS. ArgoCD compares desired (Git) vs actual (Kubernetes) → `OutOfSync` → reconciles per sync policy. Helm: chart + `values-dev.yaml` / `values-prod.yaml` instead of per-environment YAML. - **Rolling deployment** (3 old → 2 old + 1 new → 1 old + 2 new → 0 old + 3 new; new Pods that fail readiness get no traffic and the rollout stalls; ArgoCD + Git rollback restores the previous version). **Canary:** 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% while watching error rate, latency, business metrics (understand even if not implemented).

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Observability
text: `/metrics` (`http_requests_total`, `http_request_duration_seconds`, `http_errors_total`) → Prometheus → Grafana. **RED:** rate (req/s), errors (5xx), duration (p50/p95/p99). Example dashboard: 1,250 req/s · 0.08% errors · p95 180 ms · p99 420 ms · DB connections 74/100 · queue depth 1,243. Structured logs `{"level":"info","requestId":"abc123","method":"POST","path":"/orders","statusCode":201,"durationMs":82}`; **never log** password, JWT, AWS credentials, API keys, database URL, payment credentials. Tracing: `POST /orders` 2 s → API span → PostgreSQL span (1.7 s) → Redis span → SQS span. **Alerts:** 5xx > 2%, p95 > 500 ms, queue age > 60 s, DB connections > 90%, Pod restart rate increasing, storage approaching limit — each actionable.

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Failure scenarios (rehearse these)
text: | # | Failure | Expected behaviour | |---|---|---| | 1 | API Pod dies | Deployment creates replacement; Service routes to healthy Pods → self-healing | | 2 | Redis dies | cache failure → fall back to DB; Redis error metric ↑ → alert; API stays functional | | 3 | Worker dies | message not completed → becomes visible again → another worker processes; repeated failure → DLQ → fault tolerance + at-least-once + idempotency | | 4 | Database slow | p95 ↑, DB latency ↑ → investigate slow queries, connections, CPU, IOPS, locks; mitigate: cache, reduce load, rollback, optimise query, scale DB | | 5 | Bad deployment | Git push → CI → ECR → ArgoCD → new version → 5xx ↑ → stop rollout → rollback → verify → root cause | | 6 | Traffic spike 500 → 10,000 req/s | CloudFront/cache → WAF → ALB → EKS autoscaling → Redis → PostgreSQL; if DB can't scale fast: rate limiting, queue, load shedding |

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Security, HA, DR, cost
text: - **Security architecture:** Internet → WAF → ALB → EKS → private resources; RDS in private subnets; Redis private; no direct public access. SGs: Internet → ALB SG → API SG → RDS SG (RDS allows the API security group, not `0.0.0.0/0`). Secrets: AWS Secrets Manager → workload identity → application (never password in Git/Docker image). Network: Route 53 → CloudFront → WAF → ALB (public subnets) → EKS nodes, RDS, Redis in private subnets; NAT for outbound. - **High availability:** distribute across AZ-A/B/C so other AZs continue serving (if the rest of the architecture also supports it). - **DR:** RDS backups, S3 versioning where appropriate, infrastructure as code, container images in ECR, GitOps configuration in Git → Terraform recreates infrastructure → ECR deploys → Git/ArgoCD restores configuration. **"Rebuild from nothing" test:** Terraform → AWS infrastructure; ArgoCD → applications; ECR → images; RDS backup → database; minimise manual configuration. - **Cost:** small EKS/RDS/Redis, limited NAT for learning; size by traffic in production; always ask "Do we need this? What does it cost? What reliability does it buy?"

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Build order (21 steps) and phases
text: 1 Backend foundation · 2 PostgreSQL · 3 Redis · 4 Async worker · 5 SQS · 6 Docker · 7 Docker Compose · 8 Tests · 9 CI · 10 AWS infrastructure · 11 Terraform · 12 ECR · 13 EKS · 14 Helm · 15 ArgoCD · 16 Production deployment · 17 Observability · 18 Security · 19 Load testing · 20 Failure testing · 21 Reliability improvements. - **P1 Backend:** `POST /users`, `POST /orders`, `GET /orders/:id`, `GET /products`, `GET /products/:id`; `POST /orders` → validate → check idempotency → create order → publish event → return. **P2 Async:** SQS → receive → validate → process → update order → delete message (failure: don't delete → retry → DLQ). **P3 Docker** (api image, worker image; Compose runs API, Worker, PostgreSQL, Redis). **P4 CI** (install → lint → typecheck → test → build → Docker build → push ECR). **P5 Terraform** (VPC, EKS, RDS, Redis, SQS, S3, ECR, IAM; modules, variables, outputs, remote state). **P6 Kubernetes** (API, Worker, ConfigMap, Secrets, Services, HPA + readiness, liveness, resources, rolling deployment). **P7 Helm.** **P8 GitOps.** **P9 Observability** (then test pod failure, DB latency, Redis failure, queue backlog, bad deployment). **P10 Load testing** (`GET /products`, `POST /orders`, `GET /orders/:id`; RPS, p50/p95/p99, 5xx, CPU, memory, DB, Redis, queue → find and optimise the bottleneck). **P11 Security** (secret scanning, dependency scanning, container scanning, IAM review, network review; verify no public RDS, no hard-coded secrets, no privileged containers, least-privilege IAM, HTTPS, authentication, rate limiting). **P12 Failure engineering** (kill API pod, kill worker, Redis unavailable, DB slow, queue backlog, broken deployment, traffic spike; document what happened, how detected, how recovered, what changed).

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Resume and interview
text: Resume wording (only after building): *Production-Grade Distributed Order Processing Platform — TypeScript/Node.js backend with PostgreSQL, Redis and asynchronous SQS workers; containerised with Docker and deployed to AWS EKS using Terraform, Helm and ArgoCD, with GitHub Actions CI/CD, autoscaling, structured observability, idempotent processing, retry/DLQ handling and production failure testing.* **Don't claim technologies you haven't implemented.** **Interviewer questions this project supports:** why SQS; why PostgreSQL instead of DynamoDB; Redis down?; Kubernetes 3 → 20 Pods?; worker crash?; can the same SQS message be processed twice?; how does EKS access AWS services?; how does code reach production?; why ArgoCD; why Terraform; Deployment vs bare Pods; why is RDS private; how do you know a deployment caused an outage; traffic 10×?; all DB connections exhausted?; rollback?; AZ failure?

title: Revision 35 — DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform
heading: Added notes (not in source)
text: - The chapter's builder/runtime Dockerfile uses `node:22-alpine` (musl). **Prisma on Alpine** needs OpenSSL available and the right `binaryTargets`; the pnpm monorepo layout also doesn't match a plain `COPY package*.json` + `npm ci` — and the build must run `prisma generate`. Ch8 recommends Debian *slim* for native-dependency safety. - Queue-depth autoscaling for workers is typically done with **KEDA** (an SQS scaler adjusts the worker Deployment's replicas from queue length); plain HPA doesn't read SQS by default. - Implementing idempotency robustly: a **unique constraint** on `Order.idempotencyKey` (insert, catch the unique-violation, return the existing row) avoids check-then-insert races; for workers, an atomic conditional transition (`UPDATE … SET status='PROCESSING' WHERE id=$1 AND status='PENDING'`) or a processed-events table makes duplicates harmless. "Save order then publish to SQS" is a dual write — see the transactional outbox in Ch.33. - Response 36 ("Final DevOps Mastery"), promised at the end of this chapter, does not exist in the source files (source file 36 is a different, stand-alone response on virtualization internals — [Chapter 36](ch36-revision.md)); the final consolidation material is Chapter 24 plus the global revision sheets in this repository. <!-- NAV --> --- ← [Sheet 34](ch34-revision.md) · [Full chapter 35](../docs/08-production/ch35-devops-capstone.md) · [All revision material](README.md) · [Sheet 36](ch36-revision.md) →

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
text: > **Source:** Response 36 of the original conversation (`source-archive/src-36.txt`, lines 3–2006) · **Part II — Advanced extension (Responses 25–36)** > **Study aids:** [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch36-revision.md) · [Contents](../../CONTENTS.md) · [Glossary](../../GLOSSARY.md) · *includes an editorial supplement at the end* <!-- SOURCE-BEGIN --> The goal is that after this, if an interviewer asks: > **"What actually happens when a VM runs on a physical machine?"** you can explain the entire chain from **CPU → hypervisor → VM → virtual CPU → memory translation → virtual devices → I/O**. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 1. Start With the Physical Machine
text: A physical server has: ```text Physical Server │ ├── CPU ├── RAM ├── Storage ├── Network Card └── Other hardware ``` Normally: ```text Application ↓ Operating System ↓ Hardware ``` For example: ```text Chrome ↓ Linux ↓ CPU / RAM / Disk / Network ``` The OS directly manages hardware. With virtualization, we insert another layer: ```text VM 1 VM 2 VM 3 │ │ │ Guest OS Guest OS Guest OS │ │ │ └─────────────┼─────────────┘ ↓ Hypervisor ↓ Physical Hardware ``` The hypervisor is responsible for making each VM believe it has its own machine. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 2. What Is the Hypervisor Actually Doing?
text: Suppose the physical machine has: ```text 16 CPU cores 64 GB RAM 1 TB SSD ``` We might create: ```text VM1 → 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM VM2 → 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM VM3 → 2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM ``` The hypervisor manages these resources. It provides each VM with **virtual hardware**. The VM thinks: ```text I have: 4 CPUs 16 GB RAM a disk a network card ``` But those aren't necessarily dedicated physical devices. They're abstractions created by the virtualization layer. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 3. Type 1 Hypervisor
text: A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware. ```text Hardware ↓ Hypervisor ↓ VMs ``` Examples include: - VMware ESXi - Microsoft Hyper-V - Xen - KVM-based virtualization environments This is often called: > **Bare-metal virtualization** It's common in data centers. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 4. Type 2 Hypervisor
text: Type 2 runs as an application on a normal operating system. ```text Hardware ↓ Host OS ↓ Hypervisor Application ↓ VM ``` Examples include: - VirtualBox - VMware Workstation - Parallels This is convenient for desktop development. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 5. Why Is Virtualization Hard?
text: The fundamental problem is: > **The guest OS thinks it owns the hardware.** Suppose Linux inside a VM executes: ```text "Give me access to CPU." ``` But the guest cannot simply be allowed to control the physical CPU directly. Otherwise it could: ```text disable interrupts modify privileged registers access another VM's memory control hardware ``` That would destroy isolation. So the hypervisor must control privileged operations. This leads to one of the most important concepts in virtualization:

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 6. CPU Privilege Levels
text: Modern CPUs provide privilege mechanisms. Conceptually: ```text Ring 0 ↓ Most privileged ↓ Operating system kernel Ring 3 ↓ Less privileged ↓ Applications ``` Normally: ```text Application ↓ Ring 3 ↓ System Call ↓ Kernel ↓ Ring 0 ``` The kernel can execute privileged operations. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 7. But What About the Guest OS?
text: Inside a VM: ```text Guest Application ↓ Guest Kernel ↓ ??? ↓ Physical CPU ``` The guest kernel **believes** it is operating with high privilege. But we can't simply let it control the physical machine. Historically, virtualization therefore required sophisticated techniques to intercept or transform privileged operations. Modern CPUs make this much easier with hardware virtualization. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 8. Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
text: Modern CPUs provide virtualization extensions. Examples: ```text Intel VT-x AMD-V ``` These provide CPU support for virtualization. Conceptually: ```text Host / Hypervisor ↓ CPU virtualization hardware ↓ Guest VM ``` The CPU provides special execution modes allowing the hypervisor to maintain control while guest OS code executes efficiently. You don't need to memorize the processor implementation, but understand the principle: > Hardware-assisted virtualization lets guest operating systems execute efficiently while the hypervisor retains control over privileged operations. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 9. VM Exit
text: This is an important interview concept. Suppose the guest executes an operation that requires hypervisor intervention. The CPU can transition from: ```text Guest execution ``` to: ```text Hypervisor ``` This is called a: > **VM exit** Conceptually: ```text Guest VM │ │ privileged/special operation ▼ VM Exit │ ▼ Hypervisor │ ▼ Handle operation │ ▼ Return to VM ``` The opposite transition is essentially entering guest execution again. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 10. Why VM Exits Matter
text: VM exits have overhead. If a VM constantly causes exits: ```text Guest ↓ VM exit ↓ Hypervisor ↓ Guest ↓ VM exit ↓ Hypervisor ``` performance suffers. Therefore modern virtualization tries to minimize unnecessary exits and handle operations efficiently. This is one reason hardware virtualization support matters. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 11. CPU Virtualization
text: Suppose the physical server has: ```text 8 physical cores ``` You create: ```text VM1 = 2 vCPU VM2 = 4 vCPU VM3 = 2 vCPU ``` Those vCPUs aren't necessarily physical cores. They are virtual CPU execution contexts scheduled onto physical CPUs. Conceptually: ```text vCPU 1 ──┐ vCPU 2 ──┤ vCPU 3 ──┤ vCPU 4 ──┼──> Physical CPUs vCPU 5 ──┤ vCPU 6 ──┤ vCPU 7 ──┤ vCPU 8 ──┘ ``` The hypervisor schedules them. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 12. CPU Scheduling
text: Imagine: ```text Physical CPUs = 4 ``` but: ```text VM1 = 4 vCPU VM2 = 4 vCPU VM3 = 4 vCPU ``` Total: ```text 12 vCPUs ``` The hypervisor schedules execution. Very simplified: ```text time → VM1 VM1 VM2 VM3 VM1 VM2 VM3 ... ``` Each vCPU gets time on physical CPU resources. This is analogous to an OS scheduling processes onto CPUs. In fact: > Virtualization introduces another scheduling layer. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 13. CPU Overcommitment
text: You can sometimes assign more virtual CPUs than there are physical CPU cores. Example: ```text Physical = 8 cores VMs: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 vCPUs ``` This is: > CPU overcommitment / oversubscription. It's possible because VMs don't necessarily use their maximum CPU simultaneously. But if every VM becomes CPU-heavy: ```text VM1 ████████ VM2 ████████ VM3 ████████ VM4 ████████ ``` contention occurs. Performance becomes worse. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 14. CPU Pinning
text: Sometimes workloads need predictable CPU placement. The hypervisor can associate a VM's vCPU with particular physical CPUs. Conceptually: ```text vCPU0 → Physical Core 0 vCPU1 → Physical Core 1 ``` This is: > CPU pinning / CPU affinity. Useful for certain high-performance workloads. For normal cloud applications, you usually don't need to manage this directly. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 15. Now the Hard Part: Memory Virtualization
text: This is one of the most important virtualization internals. Imagine: ```text VM ↓ Guest OS ↓ Guest process ``` The process sees an address: ```text Virtual Address ``` The guest OS translates it to: ```text Guest Physical Address ``` But that isn't actual physical RAM yet. The hypervisor must translate: ```text Guest Physical Address ↓ Host Physical Address ``` Therefore: ```text Guest Virtual Address ↓ Guest Physical Address ↓ Machine/Host Physical Address ``` This is the key concept. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 16. Three Address Spaces
text: Remember:

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Guest Virtual Address
text: Used by applications inside the VM. ```text Application ↓ Virtual Address ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Guest Physical Address
text: What the guest OS believes is physical memory. ```text Guest OS ↓ Guest Physical Address ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Host Physical Address
text: Actual RAM location. ```text Physical RAM ``` So: ```text GVA ↓ GPA ↓ HPA ``` ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 17. Why Can't Guest Physical = Real Physical?
text: Suppose VM1 thinks: ```text GPA 0x1000 ``` means its first memory page. VM2 can also have: ```text GPA 0x1000 ``` That's completely fine. Because: ```text VM1 GPA 0x1000 ``` and: ```text VM2 GPA 0x1000 ``` must map to different physical memory regions. The hypervisor controls this mapping. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 18. Traditional Memory Virtualization
text: Historically, virtualization could involve techniques such as: ```text shadow page tables ``` The hypervisor maintains mappings corresponding to guest page tables. Conceptually: ```text Guest Page Table ↓ Hypervisor-managed mapping ↓ Physical memory ``` But maintaining these mappings could be expensive. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 19. Nested Paging
text: Modern CPUs support hardware-assisted memory virtualization. Examples: ```text Intel EPT AMD NPT ``` The basic idea is: ```text Guest page translation + Second-level translation ↓ Host physical memory ``` So: ```text GVA ↓ Guest page tables ↓ GPA ↓ EPT/NPT ↓ HPA ``` This significantly improves virtualization performance compared with purely software-based approaches. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 20. TLB
text: Now another important piece: > Translation Lookaside Buffer. Without a TLB, address translation would require repeatedly walking page tables. The CPU caches recent translations. Conceptually: ```text Virtual Address ↓ TLB │ ┌────┴────┐ │ │ Hit Miss │ │ ▼ ▼ Physical Page Table Address Walk ``` Virtualization makes translation more complicated because there may be another translation layer. Modern CPUs provide hardware support to make this practical. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 21. VM Memory Allocation
text: Suppose: ```text Physical RAM = 64 GB ``` We allocate: ```text VM1 = 16 GB VM2 = 16 GB VM3 = 8 GB ``` The hypervisor maintains ownership/mapping of memory. Conceptually: ```text Physical RAM ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ VM1 16GB │ ├──────────────────────────┤ │ VM2 16GB │ ├──────────────────────────┤ │ VM3 8GB │ ├──────────────────────────┤ │ Hypervisor/other │ └──────────────────────────┘ ``` The guest doesn't directly know the actual physical addresses. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 22. Memory Isolation
text: This is critical. VM1 must never be able to read: ```text VM2 memory ``` Otherwise: ```text VM1 ↓ read VM2 secrets ``` would be a catastrophic security failure. The hypervisor and hardware memory-translation mechanisms enforce isolation. Therefore virtualization provides: > **Resource isolation + security boundaries** although cloud security still requires correct configuration. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 23. Ballooning
text: An interesting virtualization technique is: > Memory ballooning. Suppose: ```text VM1 allocated 16 GB ``` but currently uses only: ```text 4 GB ``` The hypervisor may want to reclaim some memory. A balloon driver inside the guest can allocate memory and effectively allow the hypervisor to reclaim corresponding physical pages. Conceptually: ```text VM ↓ Balloon driver ↓ Guest releases/relinquishes memory ↓ Hypervisor reclaims memory ``` This allows more flexible memory management. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 24. Memory Overcommitment
text: Suppose: ```text Physical RAM = 64 GB ``` but configured VM memory totals: ```text VM1 32 GB VM2 32 GB VM3 32 GB = 96 GB ``` This is memory overcommitment. It can work if VMs don't actually use all their memory simultaneously. But if they all demand: ```text 32 + 32 + 32 ``` you have a problem. Possible techniques include: ```text ballooning page sharing swapping ``` but excessive memory pressure hurts performance. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 25. Storage Virtualization
text: Now suppose the VM sees: ```text /dev/sda ``` It might believe it has a physical disk. But underneath: ```text VM ↓ Virtual Disk ↓ Hypervisor ↓ Disk / Storage System ``` The virtual disk might be represented by: ```text VMDK VHDX QCOW2 raw image ``` depending on the virtualization platform. The exact format isn't the important part. The important concept is: > A VM's disk is usually an abstraction over underlying storage. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 26. Virtual Disk
text: Suppose VM executes: ```text write block 100 ``` The guest OS thinks: ```text Disk ↓ block 100 ``` The hypervisor translates that operation to underlying storage. Conceptually: ```text Guest ↓ Virtual Disk ↓ Hypervisor ↓ Storage Backend ``` The backend could be: ```text local SSD network storage cloud block storage distributed storage ``` ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 27. Copy-on-Write
text: Some virtual disk systems use copy-on-write techniques. Suppose base image: ```text Ubuntu Base Image ``` VM starts with: ```text Base Image ``` Instead of immediately copying everything, changes can be stored separately: ```text Base Image + Changed Blocks ↓ VM Disk ``` This makes cloning VMs much faster. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 28. Snapshots
text: Virtual machines can also have snapshots. Conceptually: ```text VM State ↓ Snapshot ``` You can later restore that state. But remember: > A snapshot is not automatically the same thing as a complete backup strategy. Production backup/DR requires careful consideration of: - application consistency - database consistency - retention - independent storage - restore testing ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 29. Virtual Network Card
text: A VM might see: ```text eth0 ``` just like a physical server. But: ```text VM ↓ Virtual NIC ↓ Hypervisor / virtual switch ↓ Physical NIC ↓ Network ``` The VM doesn't need to know it's virtualized. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 30. Virtual Switch
text: The hypervisor may provide a virtual switch. Imagine: ```text VM1 ──┐ VM2 ──┼── Virtual Switch ── Physical NIC VM3 ──┘ ``` VMs can communicate through the virtual network. The virtual switch can implement things like: ```text switching VLANs traffic filtering bridging ``` depending on the environment. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 31. Virtual NIC vs Physical NIC
text: A VM may have: ```text MAC address IP address virtual NIC ``` The guest OS interacts with the virtual NIC exactly like a network interface. The hypervisor translates/forwards traffic appropriately. Cloud networking takes this concept much further with virtual networks, virtual interfaces, security groups, routing, overlays, and software-defined networking. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 32. Device Virtualization
text: The same principle applies to: ```text CPU RAM Disk NIC USB GPU ``` The hypervisor presents virtual devices to the guest. Some devices can be: ```text fully emulated ``` while others can use: ```text paravirtualization ``` or: ```text hardware passthrough ``` ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 33. Full Device Emulation
text: The hypervisor can pretend to be a hardware device. For example: ```text Guest ↓ virtual disk controller ↓ hypervisor ↓ real storage ``` The guest believes it is talking to hardware. This is highly compatible but can have more overhead. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 34. Paravirtualization
text: Instead of pretending everything is exactly physical hardware, the guest can use virtualization-aware drivers. For example: ```text Guest ↓ VirtIO driver ↓ Hypervisor ↓ Hardware ``` This reduces overhead. A common example in Linux virtualization environments is: ```text VirtIO ``` for virtual network and block devices. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 35. Hardware Passthrough
text: For some workloads, a physical device can be assigned more directly to a VM. For example: ```text Physical GPU ↓ VM ``` This can provide much better performance. But it complicates: ```text sharing migration management isolation ``` GPU virtualization is particularly important for AI/ML infrastructure. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 36. I/O Virtualization
text: The VM generates I/O: ```text read disk send network packet ``` The hypervisor must mediate it. Historically, this could involve significant overhead: ```text Guest ↓ VM exit ↓ Hypervisor ↓ device emulation ↓ hardware ``` Modern virtualization uses techniques such as: ```text VirtIO SR-IOV hardware-assisted I/O ``` to reduce overhead. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 37. SR-IOV
text: This is a useful awareness/interview concept. SR-IOV allows a physical PCIe device to expose multiple virtual functions. Conceptually: ```text Physical NIC │ ┌────┼────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ VF1 VF2 VF3 │ │ │ VM1 VM2 VM3 ``` This allows VMs to access networking hardware more efficiently. You generally don't need to implement SR-IOV for SWE interviews, but knowing why it exists is valuable. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 38. VM Isolation
text: Virtualization needs to isolate: ```text CPU Memory Storage Network Devices ``` between VMs. Think: ```text VM1 │ ├── CPU isolation ├── memory isolation ├── disk isolation └── network isolation VM2 │ ├── CPU isolation ├── memory isolation ├── disk isolation └── network isolation ``` The hypervisor is a critical security boundary. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 39. What Happens When VM Boots?
text: Let's follow the entire process.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Step 1
text: Hypervisor allocates: ```text vCPU memory virtual disk virtual NIC ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Step 2
text: VM firmware starts. Conceptually: ```text BIOS/UEFI ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Step 3
text: Bootloader loads. ```text GRUB ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Step 4
text: Guest kernel loads. ```text Linux kernel ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Step 5
text: Kernel initializes: ```text CPU memory virtual devices network filesystem ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Step 6
text: Userspace starts. ```text systemd ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Step 7
text: Services start. Now the VM is operational. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 40. What Happens When a Program Runs?
text: Suppose: ```text Node.js ``` inside the VM executes code. ```text Node.js ↓ Guest Linux ↓ Guest virtual memory ↓ Guest CPU ↓ Virtualization layer ↓ Physical CPU ``` For normal CPU instructions, the guest can execute efficiently. For operations requiring hypervisor intervention: ```text VM exit ↓ Hypervisor ↓ operation handled ↓ VM resumes ``` ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 41. VM vs Container Internals
text: This is extremely important.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: VM
text: ```text Hardware ↓ Hypervisor ↓ VM ↓ Guest OS ↓ Application ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Container
text: ```text Hardware ↓ Host OS ↓ Container Runtime ↓ Container ↓ Application ``` A container normally **does not have its own kernel**. Containers share the host kernel. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 42. Why Containers Start Faster
text: VM: ```text boot virtual hardware ↓ boot guest kernel ↓ start userspace ↓ application ``` Container: ```text start process ↓ application ``` Therefore: ```text VM → heavier isolation, more overhead Container → lighter, faster startup ``` But this isn't simply "VM bad, container good." They solve somewhat different problems. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 43. How Linux Containers Actually Work
text: This is another important internal concept. Containers rely heavily on Linux kernel features. Two major concepts: ```text Namespaces cgroups ``` ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 44. Namespaces
text: Namespaces provide isolation. They can isolate things such as: ```text PID network mounts hostname users IPC ``` For example, a container may see: ```text PID 1 ``` while the host sees the corresponding process as another PID. So: ```text Container process ↓ PID namespace ↓ Host kernel ``` ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 45. cgroups
text: Control groups manage resources. They can limit: ```text CPU memory I/O processes ``` Conceptually: ```text Container ↓ cgroup ↓ CPU/memory limits ``` This is how containers can be constrained without creating a whole guest OS. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 46. This Gives Us the Full Picture
text: Now: ```text Virtualization ↓ Hypervisor ↓ Virtual Machines ↓ Virtual hardware ↓ Guest OS ``` while: ```text OS-level virtualization ↓ Namespaces + cgroups ↓ Containers ``` This distinction is extremely important. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 47. Why Cloud Providers Use Virtualization
text: Imagine a physical server: ```text 64 CPU 256 GB RAM ``` Instead of dedicating it to one customer: ```text Customer A → entire server ``` virtualization allows: ```text VM1 → Customer A VM2 → Customer B VM3 → Customer C VM4 → Customer D ``` This allows better resource utilization and isolation. Cloud providers can dynamically provision virtual machines. That's one of the foundations of IaaS. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 48. How AWS Fits In
text: When you launch an EC2 instance, conceptually: ```text Your EC2 ↓ Virtual machine ↓ AWS virtualization infrastructure ↓ Physical AWS hardware ``` You don't manage the physical server. AWS manages: ```text physical machines hypervisor/infrastructure data center power networking infrastructure ``` You manage the resources exposed to your instance and the guest OS/configuration depending on the service. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 49. Modern Cloud Virtualization
text: Modern cloud virtualization has evolved beyond the simplistic: ```text "VMware-style hypervisor" ``` Cloud providers use specialized virtualization infrastructure and hardware/software optimizations. For example, AWS developed **Nitro** architecture to offload virtualization/network/storage functions to dedicated hardware and firmware components. The important conceptual takeaway: ```text Traditional virtualization ↓ general-purpose hypervisor work Modern cloud virtualization ↓ hardware-assisted + specialized virtualization ↓ lower overhead better isolation higher performance ``` You don't need Nitro implementation details for a normal SWE OA. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 50. VM Migration
text: Another powerful virtualization capability is: > Live migration. Suppose: ```text Physical Server A ↓ VM ``` needs to move to: ```text Physical Server B ``` The system can transfer VM memory/state while the VM is still running, then briefly pause it to complete the final state transfer. Conceptually: ```text VM running on A ↓ copy memory ↓ copy changed memory ↓ copy again ↓ short pause ↓ transfer remaining state ↓ resume on B ``` This can enable maintenance with limited downtime. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 51. Why Live Migration Is Hard
text: The VM is changing while memory is being copied. Suppose: ```text Memory page X ``` is copied. Then VM changes it. Now the copied version is stale. Therefore migration repeatedly tracks changed pages until the remaining state becomes manageable. This is called, conceptually: > **pre-copy migration** There are other migration techniques too. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 52. VM Snapshot vs Live Migration
text: Don't confuse them.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Snapshot
text: Capture: ```text VM state/storage ``` for later restoration or cloning.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Live migration
text: Move: ```text running VM ``` from one physical host to another. Different goals. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 53. Security Risks
text: The hypervisor is a huge security boundary. A serious vulnerability could potentially allow: ```text Guest VM ↓ hypervisor vulnerability ↓ host ↓ other VMs ``` This is why virtualization security is extremely important in cloud environments. You may hear terms such as: ```text VM escape hypervisor vulnerability side-channel attack ``` For SWE interviews, know the concepts rather than researching exploit details. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 54. Side Channels
text: Even if VMs are logically isolated, shared hardware can sometimes leak information through observable behavior. Examples of resources that can create side-channel concerns include: ```text CPU caches timing memory behavior shared hardware resources ``` Again, this is primarily security-specialist territory. For your interviews: > Virtualization provides strong isolation, but shared hardware can introduce sophisticated side-channel risks. That's enough unless specifically interviewing for security/hypervisor engineering. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 55. The Entire Internal Pipeline
text: Memorize this diagram: ```text APPLICATION │ ▼ GUEST OS │ ┌────────┴────────┐ │ │ CPU ops Memory access │ │ ▼ ▼ vCPU / VM Guest Virtual Address │ │ ▼ ▼ Hypervisor Guest Page Tables │ │ ▼ ▼ Physical CPU GPA │ ▼ EPT / NPT │ ▼ HPA │ ▼ Physical RAM I/O: Application ↓ Guest OS ↓ Virtual Device ↓ Hypervisor / VirtIO / hardware assist ↓ Physical Device ``` If you understand this diagram, you understand the core of virtualization internals. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 56. The Most Important Interview Questions
text: You should now be able to answer these.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q1. What is virtualization?
text: Creating an abstraction of physical computing resources so multiple isolated virtual machines can share physical hardware.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q2. What is a hypervisor?
text: The virtualization layer that creates/manages VMs and controls access to physical resources.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q3. Type 1 vs Type 2?
text: ```text Type 1: Hardware → Hypervisor → VMs Type 2: Hardware → Host OS → Hypervisor → VMs ```

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q4. How does a VM get CPU?
text: Through virtual CPUs that the hypervisor schedules onto physical CPU resources.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q5. What is a VM exit?
text: A transition from guest execution to the hypervisor when an operation requires virtualization-layer handling.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q6. How does VM memory translation work?
text: ```text GVA → GPA → HPA ``` with hardware mechanisms such as EPT/NPT assisting the second-level translation.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q7. What is EPT?
text: Intel's hardware-assisted second-level address translation mechanism used in virtualization.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q8. What is ballooning?
text: A mechanism allowing the hypervisor to reclaim/rebalance memory through a guest balloon driver.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q9. What is paravirtualization?
text: The guest uses virtualization-aware interfaces/drivers instead of requiring complete hardware emulation.

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Q10. VM vs container?
text: VM virtualizes a machine and normally has a guest OS; containers isolate processes while sharing the host kernel. ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 57. The OA-Level Mental Model
text: If you only have 30 seconds in an OA/interview: ```text Physical Hardware ↓ Hypervisor ↓ Virtual Machines ↓ Guest OS ↓ Applications ``` Hypervisor provides: ```text CPU → vCPU scheduling Memory → GVA → GPA → HPA Disk → virtual disk Network → virtual NIC Devices → virtualized/paravirtualized hardware ``` Modern CPUs help with: ```text hardware-assisted virtualization VT-x / AMD-V EPT / NPT ``` Containers are different: ```text Host Kernel ↓ Namespaces + cgroups ↓ Containers ``` ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: 58. Where This Fits in Your Cloud Roadmap
text: You've now gone one level deeper than the normal SWE Cloud syllabus: ```text Cloud Computing ↓ Virtualization ↓ Hypervisors ↓ CPU Virtualization ↓ Memory Virtualization ↓ I/O Virtualization ↓ Virtual Networking ↓ VM Isolation ↓ Containers ↓ Namespaces + cgroups ↓ Docker ↓ Kubernetes ↓ Cloud Infrastructure ``` So yes — **you now have both the practical cloud knowledge and the internal virtualization knowledge needed for strong SWE OAs/interviews.** The only areas we deliberately aren't turning into a separate specialization are **hypervisor implementation/kernel development, CPU microarchitecture, and advanced virtualization security research**. Those are beyond what your general SWE placement target requires. <!-- SOURCE-END --> ---

title: Chapter 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: See it on a real Linux machine, and a few precise points
text: This chapter is entirely conceptual. The commands below make the ideas observable; they are standard Linux tooling but were **not run** during the audit (the authoring machine is Windows). Run them on any Linux VM or container host. **1. Am I inside a VM or container? Does this CPU support virtualization?** ```bash systemd-detect-virt # prints e.g. kvm, microsoft, oracle, none systemd-detect-virt --container # prints docker, lxc, ... or none lscpu | grep -i -E "hypervisor|virtualization" # inside a VM: "Hypervisor vendor", "Virtualization type: full" grep -E -c '(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo # >0 means VT-x (vmx) or AMD-V (svm) is exposed to this OS ls -l /dev/kvm # present when the KVM module is loaded and usable ``` Inside most cloud VMs the `vmx`/`svm` flags are absent (no nested virtualization) unless the instance type explicitly supports it. **2. Namespaces by hand** — the chapter's PID-namespace example (§44): ```bash sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash # new PID + mount namespace ps aux # this bash is PID 1; host processes are invisible exit sudo unshare --uts bash # new hostname namespace hostname demo-container && hostname # changed only inside exit ``` **3. cgroups by hand** (cgroup v2; paths vary by distribution and systemd version): ```bash cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.controllers # available controllers: cpu memory io pids ... docker run -d --name limited --memory 256m --cpus 0.5 nginx docker inspect limited --format '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' docker rm -f limited ``` **4. Precise points the chapter simplifies** - **Rings vs VMX modes.** Rings 0–3 are privilege levels *inside* an execution context. VT-x/AMD-V add a second, orthogonal dimension: **root mode** (hypervisor) and **non-root/guest mode**. The guest kernel really does run in guest-mode Ring 0; what changed is that sensitive operations now cause a **VM exit** to root mode instead of being executed on the hardware. - **Cost of two-level translation.** With nested paging a TLB miss walks guest page tables whose every step needs an EPT/NPT walk. With 4-level tables on both sides the worst case is commonly cited as `(4+1)×(4+1) − 1 = 24` memory references versus 4 natively — the reason TLBs, large pages and hardware page-walk caches matter in virtualized hosts. - **Overcommit ratios** (source examples): vCPU overcommit = `total vCPUs / physical cores` → `16 / 8 = 2:1`; memory overcommit = `configured VM memory / physical RAM` → `96 GB / 64 GB = 1.5×`. - **Type 1 vs Type 2 is a spectrum.** KVM turns the Linux kernel itself into the hypervisor; Hyper-V runs the host OS as a privileged VM. Use the labels for explaining *where the hypervisor sits*, not as rigid categories. - **What the cloud customer sees.** Public-cloud instances generally do not expose CPU/memory overcommit knobs; you choose an instance type and the provider handles placement. EC2 also offers **bare-metal instance types** (the `.metal` family) where no provider hypervisor sits between you and the hardware, and **Nitro** moves networking/storage virtualization into dedicated cards so more of the host's CPU goes to guests. AWS Lambda and Fargate isolate workloads with **Firecracker microVMs** — a lightweight KVM-based VM, a middle ground between full VMs and containers. *(Reference: AWS Nitro System and Firecracker documentation; not independently re-verified here.)* - **Why a container is not a security boundary like a VM.** All containers on a host share one kernel: a kernel vulnerability affects all of them, whereas a VM escape requires breaking the hypervisor. This is why multi-tenant platforms often run each tenant's containers inside separate VMs/microVMs. - **Snapshot consistency.** A VM or EBS snapshot is *crash-consistent* by default (like pulling the plug); for databases quiesce or use engine-native backups for *application-consistent* recovery. **5. Where this connects to the rest of the course** | This chapter | Connects to | |---|---| | vCPU, RAM, virtual disk, virtual NIC | EC2 instance types, EBS, ENIs ([Chapter 10](../04-aws/ch10-ec2-compute.md), [Chapter 12](../04-aws/ch12-vpc-networking.md)) | | Namespaces + cgroups | Docker and Kubernetes requests/limits ([Chapter 7](../02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md), [Chapter 8](../02-containers/ch08-docker-production.md), [Chapter 19](../05-kubernetes/ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md)) | | CPU contention / noisy neighbours | CPU throttling vs OOMKill, HPA ([Chapter 20](../05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md)) | | Snapshots vs backups | RDS backups, DR strategies ([Chapter 13](../04-aws/ch13-rds-databases.md), [Chapter 34](../07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md)) | | Live migration | maintenance with limited downtime; contrast with pod rescheduling in Kubernetes ([Chapter 18](../05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md)) | --- **Navigation:** ← [Chapter 35: DevOps Capstone: Build a Production-Grade Backend Platform](../08-production/ch35-devops-capstone.md) · [Revision sheet](../../revision/ch36-revision.md)

text: | | Type 1 (bare-metal) | Type 2 (hosted) | |---|---|---| | Stack | Hardware → Hypervisor → VMs | Hardware → Host OS → Hypervisor app → VMs | | Examples | VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, Xen, KVM-based | VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels | | Where | data centers | desktop development |

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Why it is hard, and the CPU story
text: - The guest OS **thinks it owns the hardware**; letting it run privileged operations (disable interrupts, edit privileged registers, read another VM's memory) would destroy isolation → the hypervisor must control **privileged instructions**. - Ring 0 (kernel) vs Ring 3 (apps). Old approach: intercept/transform privileged operations in software. Modern: **hardware-assisted virtualization (VT-x / AMD-V)**. - **VM exit** = guest → hypervisor transition for operations needing hypervisor handling; then return to the VM. Exits cost time → modern designs minimise them. - **vCPU** = execution context scheduled onto physical CPUs (another scheduling layer, like an OS scheduling processes). 12 vCPUs on 4 cores is time-sliced. - **CPU overcommitment**: more vCPUs than cores (e.g. 16 on 8) works while VMs aren't all busy; contention when they are. **CPU pinning/affinity**: fix vCPU→core for predictable performance (rarely needed for normal cloud apps).

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Memory story
text: ```text GVA --(guest page tables)--> GPA --(EPT/NPT)--> HPA ``` - Three address spaces: Guest Virtual (apps), Guest Physical (what the guest believes is RAM), Host Physical (real RAM). Two VMs can both have GPA `0x1000`; the hypervisor maps them to **different** host pages. - Old: **shadow page tables** (expensive). Modern: **nested paging** (Intel EPT / AMD NPT) — big performance gain. **TLB** caches translations (hit → physical address; miss → page-table walk); virtualization adds a translation layer. - Allocation: hypervisor tracks ownership of RAM per VM. **Memory isolation** is critical (VM1 must never read VM2). - **Ballooning**: guest balloon driver takes memory so the hypervisor can reclaim pages. **Memory overcommitment** (e.g. 96 GB configured on 64 GB): works if VMs don't use it all; tools: ballooning, page sharing, swapping; heavy pressure hurts.

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Storage and networking
text: - **Virtual disk** (VMDK, VHDX, QCOW2, raw) = abstraction over local SSD / network / cloud block / distributed storage. - **Copy-on-write**: base image + changed blocks → fast cloning. - **Snapshot ≠ backup** (needs app/DB consistency, retention, independent storage, restore tests). - **Virtual NIC** (MAC/IP) → **virtual switch** (switching, VLANs, filtering, bridging) → physical NIC. Cloud extends this into VPCs, security groups, overlays, SDN.

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Devices and I/O
text: | Technique | Idea | Trade-off | |---|---|---| | **Full emulation** | Hypervisor pretends to be real hardware | Compatible, more overhead | | **Paravirtualization (VirtIO)** | Guest uses virtualization-aware drivers | Lower overhead, needs guest drivers | | **Hardware passthrough** | Give a physical device (e.g. GPU) to a VM | Best performance; harder sharing, migration, management, isolation | | **SR-IOV** | One PCIe device exposes multiple virtual functions (VF1..n) to different VMs | Efficient NIC access | Historic I/O path: Guest → VM exit → hypervisor → device emulation → hardware (slow). Modern: VirtIO, SR-IOV, hardware assist.

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: VM boot and program execution
text: Boot: hypervisor allocates vCPU/RAM/disk/NIC → BIOS/UEFI → GRUB → guest kernel → initialises CPU/memory/devices/network/filesystem → `systemd` → services. Normal CPU instructions run efficiently on the physical CPU; operations needing intervention cause a VM exit and resume.

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: VM vs container internals
text: | | VM | Container | |---|---|---| | Stack | Hardware → Hypervisor → VM → Guest OS → App | Hardware → Host OS → Runtime → Container → App | | Kernel | Own guest kernel | **Shares host kernel** | | Start | Boot virtual hardware + kernel + userspace | Start a process | | Isolation | Stronger (hardware-assisted, smaller attack surface) | Lighter; kernel shared | "Not simply VM bad, container good — they solve different problems." Containers use **namespaces** (isolate PID, network, mounts, hostname, users, IPC — a container sees PID 1, the host sees another PID) and **cgroups** (limit CPU, memory, I/O, processes).

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Cloud context
text: Virtualization lets one 64-CPU/256 GB server host VMs for customers A–D (utilization + isolation, a foundation of IaaS). On AWS you manage the guest OS/config, AWS manages hardware, hypervisor/infrastructure, data center, power, networking. **Nitro** offloads virtualization/network/storage to dedicated hardware/firmware → lower overhead, better isolation, higher performance (implementation details not needed for a normal SWE OA).

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Live migration
text: Move a running VM from host A to B: copy memory while running → copy changed pages again → repeat → short pause → transfer remaining state → resume on B. Hard because the VM keeps dirtying pages; the technique is **pre-copy migration** (others exist). **Snapshot ≠ live migration** (state capture for restore/clone vs moving a running VM).

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Security
text: Hypervisor = huge security boundary. Threats: **VM escape**, hypervisor vulnerabilities, **side channels** (CPU caches, timing, memory behaviour). Interview line: *virtualization provides strong isolation, but shared hardware can introduce sophisticated side-channel risks.*

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Interview Q&A (the source's ten)
text: 1. **Virtualization?** Abstraction of physical resources so multiple isolated VMs share hardware. 2. **Hypervisor?** Layer that creates/manages VMs and controls access to physical resources. 3. **Type 1 vs 2?** Hardware→Hypervisor→VMs vs Hardware→Host OS→Hypervisor→VMs. 4. **How does a VM get CPU?** vCPUs scheduled by the hypervisor onto physical CPUs. 5. **VM exit?** Guest→hypervisor transition for operations needing virtualization-layer handling. 6. **VM memory translation?** GVA→GPA→HPA, with EPT/NPT assisting the second level. 7. **EPT?** Intel's hardware second-level address translation for virtualization. 8. **Ballooning?** Hypervisor reclaims/rebalances memory via a guest balloon driver. 9. **Paravirtualization?** Guest uses virtualization-aware drivers instead of full hardware emulation. 10. **VM vs container?** VM virtualizes a machine with a guest OS; containers isolate processes sharing the host kernel.

title: Revision 36 — Virtualization Internals — Deep Dive
heading: Traps
text: - "A vCPU is a physical core" — it is a schedulable context. - "Snapshot = backup" / "snapshot = live migration" — neither. - "Container = lightweight VM" — different isolation mechanism, shared kernel. - Overcommit is a bet on non-simultaneous peaks.

heading: D
text: - **DaemonSet** — Runs a Pod on each matching node. *([Ch 20](docs/05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md))* - **Database migration** — Controlled, versioned schema change (Prisma Migrate, Knex, etc.). *([Ch 13](docs/04-aws/ch13-rds-databases.md))* - **Data plane** — Components that handle actual traffic (Envoy proxies). *([Ch 30](docs/05-kubernetes/ch30-service-mesh-istio.md))* - **Data source (Terraform)** — Reads existing information from a provider without creating it. *([Ch 21](docs/06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md))* - **Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)** — Queue holding messages that repeatedly failed processing. *([Ch 15](docs/04-aws/ch15-lambda-serverless-messaging.md))* - **Declarative configuration** — Describing the desired end state rather than steps. *([Ch 26](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch26-gitops-argocd.md))* - **Declarative pipeline** — Structured Jenkinsfile syntax: pipeline/agent/stages/stage/steps. *([Ch 27](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch27-jenkins-advanced-cicd.md))* - **Default route** — 0.0.0.0/0: used when no more specific route matches. *([Ch 4](docs/01-foundations/ch04-networking.md))* - **Defense in depth** — Multiple layered security controls. *([Ch 17](docs/04-aws/ch17-monitoring-security.md))* - **Dependency failure matrix** — Table of each dependency's failure strategy (retry, fallback, queue, fail fast). *([Ch 34](docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md))* - **Dependency graph (Terraform)** — Graph of resource dependencies used to order and parallelize operations. *([Ch 32](docs/06-iac-config/ch32-advanced-terraform.md))* - **depends_on** - Compose start-order dependency; does not guarantee readiness. *([Ch 8](docs/02-containers/ch08-docker-production.md))* - Explicit dependency between resources. *([Ch 21](docs/06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md))* - **Deployment** — Controller maintaining a desired number of Pod replicas and managing rollouts. *([Ch 18](docs/05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md))* - **Deprecated API** — Kubernetes API version removed in later releases, breaking old manifests. *([Ch 31](docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md))* - **Depth tiers (Master/Strong/Awareness)** — Study-depth classification used to prioritize topics for SWE roles. *([Ch 24](docs/09-interview/ch24-interview-oa-mastery.md))* - **Desired state** — Declared target configuration Kubernetes tries to maintain. *([Ch 18](docs/05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md))* - **DestinationRule** — Istio resource defining destination subsets and policies. *([Ch 30](docs/05-kubernetes/ch30-service-mesh-istio.md))* - **Detached HEAD** — HEAD pointing directly to a commit rather than a branch. *([Ch 5](docs/01-foundations/ch05-git-github.md))* - **Detached mode (-d)** — Run container in background. *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **Detect-Diagnose-Mitigate-Recover-RCA** — The incident lifecycle used for production failures. *([Ch 23](docs/08-production/ch23-production-architecture-troubleshooting.md))* - **DevOps** — Practices for how development and operations build, test, deploy and operate software together efficiently and reliably. *([Ch 1](docs/01-foundations/ch01-cloud-devops-fundamentals.md))* - **DevSecOps** — Integrating security throughout the whole lifecycle rather than at the end. *([Ch 1](docs/01-foundations/ch01-cloud-devops-fundamentals.md))* - **Disaster Recovery (DR)** — Ability to recover from a large failure (e.g. a whole region) using infrastructure elsewhere. *([Ch 1](docs/01-foundations/ch01-cloud-devops-fundamentals.md))* - **Disaster recovery strategies** — Backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active. *([Ch 34](docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md))* - **Distributed tracing** — Following a request across multiple services. *([Ch 22](docs/07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md))* - **DNS** — Domain Name System; translates names to IPs/other records. *([Ch 4](docs/01-foundations/ch04-networking.md))* - **DNS propagation** — Delay before cached DNS results expire everywhere. *([Ch 16](docs/04-aws/ch16-route53-cloudfront-waf.md))* - **Docker** — Platform/tooling for building, distributing and running applications in containers. *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **Docker CLI** — Command-line client (docker build/run/ps...) talking to the daemon. *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **Docker Compose** — Declarative definition of multi-container applications (docker compose up). *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **Docker daemon** — Background service that manages images, containers, networks, volumes. *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **docker exec** — Run a command inside a running container. *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **Dockerfile** — File of instructions for building an image. *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **.dockerignore** — File listing paths excluded from the build context. *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **Docker network** — Virtual network for container-to-container communication. *([Ch 8](docs/02-containers/ch08-docker-production.md))* - **Drift (GitOps)** — Cluster state diverging from the Git-declared state. *([Ch 26](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch26-gitops-argocd.md))* - **Durability** — How unlikely stored data is to be lost. *([Ch 11](docs/04-aws/ch11-s3-storage.md))* - **Dynamic inventory** — Inventory generated from a cloud API instead of a static file. *([Ch 28](docs/06-iac-config/ch28-ansible.md))* - **Dynamic provisioning** — Automatic creation of PVs from a StorageClass when a PVC is created. *([Ch 19](docs/05-kubernetes/ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md))* - **DynamoDB** - AWS managed NoSQL key-value/document database. *([Ch 13](docs/04-aws/ch13-rds-databases.md))* - Managed NoSQL key-value/document database. *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **DynamoDB Streams** — Item-level change stream, e.g. to Lambda. *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))*

title: Glossary
heading: E
text: - **EBS** — Elastic Block Store: persistent block storage for EC2. *([Ch 10](docs/04-aws/ch10-ec2-compute.md))* - **EBS CSI driver** — Plugin letting Kubernetes use EBS volumes. *([Ch 31](docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md))* - **EC2** — Elastic Compute Cloud: virtual servers (instances) in AWS. *([Ch 10](docs/04-aws/ch10-ec2-compute.md))* - **EC2 instance** — A virtual machine created from an AMI with a chosen instance type. *([Ch 10](docs/04-aws/ch10-ec2-compute.md))* - **ECR** — Elastic Container Registry: AWS container image registry. *([Ch 18](docs/05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md))* - **ECS** — Elastic Container Service: AWS-native container orchestration. *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **ECS on EC2 vs Fargate** — You manage EC2 capacity vs AWS manages compute. *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **ECS service** — Keeps a desired number of tasks running and integrates with a load balancer. *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **ECS task** — Running instance of a task definition (one or more containers). *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **Edge location** — AWS point of presence closer to users, used by CloudFront for caching. *([Ch 9](docs/04-aws/ch09-aws-fundamentals-iam.md))* - **EFS** — Elastic File System: shared file storage across compute. *([Ch 11](docs/04-aws/ch11-s3-storage.md))* - **EFS CSI driver** — Plugin letting Kubernetes use EFS shared file systems. *([Ch 31](docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md))* - **EKS** — Elastic Kubernetes Service: managed Kubernetes control plane on AWS. *([Ch 18](docs/05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md))* - **EKS add-ons** — Managed cluster components such as VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI. *([Ch 31](docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md))* - **EKS control plane** — AWS-managed Kubernetes API server, scheduler, controllers and etcd. *([Ch 31](docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md))* - **EKS Pod Identity** — Newer EKS-native way to associate IAM roles with ServiceAccounts. *([Ch 31](docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md))* - **ElastiCache** — Managed caching (Redis/Valkey, Memcached). *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **Elastic IP** — Persistent public IPv4 address assignable to an instance. *([Ch 10](docs/04-aws/ch10-ec2-compute.md))* - **Elasticity** — Automatic adjustment of resources up and down according to demand. *([Ch 1](docs/01-foundations/ch01-cloud-devops-fundamentals.md))* - **Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)** — AWS managed load-balancing service family. *([Ch 14](docs/04-aws/ch14-load-balancing-scaling.md))* - **emptyDir** — Temporary Pod-scoped volume deleted with the Pod. *([Ch 19](docs/05-kubernetes/ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md))* - **EndpointSlice** — Kubernetes object listing the Pod endpoints behind a Service. *([Ch 20](docs/05-kubernetes/ch20-kubernetes-networking-scaling.md))* - **Endpoints = none** — A Service with no matching Pods (selector/label mismatch). *([Ch 23](docs/08-production/ch23-production-architecture-troubleshooting.md))* - **ENI** — Elastic Network Interface; attached to nodes and used for Pod IPs. *([Ch 31](docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md))* - **ENTRYPOINT** — Dockerfile instruction defining the always-run executable (see supplement). *([Ch 8](docs/02-containers/ch08-docker-production.md))* - **Envelope encryption** — Data key encrypts data; KMS key protects the data key. *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **envFrom** — Pod spec field injecting all keys of a ConfigMap/Secret as environment variables. *([Ch 19](docs/05-kubernetes/ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md))* - **Environment variable** — Named value in a process environment used for configuration (export PORT=3000). *([Ch 2](docs/01-foundations/ch02-linux.md))* - **Envoy** — High-performance proxy used as the Istio data-plane proxy. *([Ch 30](docs/05-kubernetes/ch30-service-mesh-istio.md))* - **Ephemeral build agent** — Short-lived Kubernetes Pod created for a build and removed afterwards. *([Ch 27](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch27-jenkins-advanced-cicd.md))* - **Error budget** — Allowed unreliability implied by the SLO (1 - SLO) over a period. *([Ch 22](docs/07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md))* - **Error budget (SRE)** — 1 - SLO: the amount of unreliability the SLO allows over a window. *([Ch 34](docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md))* - **etcd** — Distributed key-value store holding cluster state. *([Ch 18](docs/05-kubernetes/ch18-kubernetes-fundamentals.md))* - **EventBridge** - AWS event bus service for routing events (awareness). *([Ch 15](docs/04-aws/ch15-lambda-serverless-messaging.md))* - Event bus with rule-based routing to targets. *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **Event-driven architecture** — Services communicate through events rather than direct calls. *([Ch 15](docs/04-aws/ch15-lambda-serverless-messaging.md))* - **Eventual consistency** — System components converge to the same state after a delay. *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **Execution role (Lambda)** — IAM role granting the function permissions. *([Ch 15](docs/04-aws/ch15-lambda-serverless-messaging.md))* - **Exit status (exit code)** — Number returned by every command: 0 = success, non-zero = failure; read with `$?`. *([Ch 3](docs/01-foundations/ch03-bash-automation.md))* - **Expand-and-contract** — Migration strategy: add compatible structure, migrate, switch, remove old later. *([Ch 13](docs/04-aws/ch13-rds-databases.md))* - **Explicit deny** — A Deny statement that always overrides any Allow. *([Ch 9](docs/04-aws/ch09-aws-fundamentals-iam.md))* - **Exponential backoff** — Increasing delay between retries. *([Ch 22](docs/07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md))* - **EXPOSE** — Dockerfile instruction documenting the intended port; does not publish it. *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **Express** — Node.js web framework used by the API. *([Ch 35](docs/08-production/ch35-devops-capstone.md))* - **External Secrets** — Operator syncing secrets from external managers into Kubernetes Secrets. *([Ch 26](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch26-gitops-argocd.md))*

title: Glossary
heading: F
text: - **Facts (Ansible)** — Information gathered about managed hosts (OS, IP, memory). *([Ch 28](docs/06-iac-config/ch28-ansible.md))* - **Fail open / fail closed** — On failure allow access vs deny access. *([Ch 34](docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md))* - **Failure engineering** — Deliberately inducing failures and documenting detection and recovery. *([Ch 35](docs/08-production/ch35-devops-capstone.md))* - **Failure injection** — Deliberately causing a specific failure (e.g. latency) to test handling. *([Ch 34](docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md))* - **Fargate** — Serverless compute running Pods without managing EC2 nodes. *([Ch 31](docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md))* - **Fast-forward merge** — Merge done by just moving the branch pointer; no merge commit. *([Ch 5](docs/01-foundations/ch05-git-github.md))* - **Fault tolerance** — A system continuing to operate even when some components fail. *([Ch 1](docs/01-foundations/ch01-cloud-devops-fundamentals.md))* - **Fetch** — Download remote changes without integrating them. *([Ch 5](docs/01-foundations/ch05-git-github.md))* - **Finalizer** — Marker making Kubernetes wait for cleanup before completing deletion. *([Ch 29](docs/05-kubernetes/ch29-crds-operators.md))* - **Firewall** — Rule-based control of network traffic. *([Ch 4](docs/01-foundations/ch04-networking.md))* - **Fix forward (roll forward)** — Shipping a new fix instead of reverting; sometimes safer than rollback. *([Ch 23](docs/08-production/ch23-production-architecture-troubleshooting.md))* - **for_each** — Meta-argument creating instances keyed by map/set keys. *([Ch 32](docs/06-iac-config/ch32-advanced-terraform.md))* - **Fork** — Your own copy of another repository on the hosting platform. *([Ch 5](docs/01-foundations/ch05-git-github.md))* - **Forward proxy** — Proxy that acts on behalf of clients. *([Ch 4](docs/01-foundations/ch04-networking.md))* - **Four golden signals** — Latency, traffic, errors, saturation. *([Ch 34](docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md))* - **FROM** — Dockerfile instruction selecting the base image. *([Ch 7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md))* - **Full device emulation** — Hypervisor pretends to be a real hardware device; highly compatible but higher overhead. *([Ch 36](docs/01-foundations/ch36-virtualization-internals.md))*

title: Glossary
heading: G
text: - **Game day** — Planned exercise simulating an incident to practice response. *([Ch 34](docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md))* - **Gateway endpoint** — VPC endpoint type for S3 and DynamoDB. *([Ch 12](docs/04-aws/ch12-vpc-networking.md))* - **General purpose instances** — Balanced CPU/memory instance family. *([Ch 10](docs/04-aws/ch10-ec2-compute.md))* - **Git** — Distributed version-control system that runs locally. *([Ch 5](docs/01-foundations/ch05-git-github.md))* - **Git Flow** — Branching model with main, develop, feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*. *([Ch 5](docs/01-foundations/ch05-git-github.md))* - **GitHub** — Hosted platform for Git repositories and collaboration (PRs, reviews, Actions). *([Ch 5](docs/01-foundations/ch05-git-github.md))* - **GitHub Actions** — GitHub's CI/CD system; workflows triggered by events; files in .github/workflows/. *([Ch 6](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch06-cicd-github-actions.md))* - **GitHub Environments** — development/staging/production targets with own secrets, variables, protection rules and approvals. *([Ch 6](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch06-cicd-github-actions.md))* - **.gitignore** — File listing patterns of untracked files Git should ignore; doesn't untrack already tracked files. *([Ch 5](docs/01-foundations/ch05-git-github.md))* - **GitOps** — Operating model where Git holds declarative desired state and controllers continuously reconcile the environment to it. *([Ch 26](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch26-gitops-argocd.md))* - **GitOps repository** — Repository holding deployment configuration, separate from application source. *([Ch 26](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch26-gitops-argocd.md))* - **Graceful degradation** — Keeping core functionality when non-critical parts fail. *([Ch 34](docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md))* - **Graceful shutdown** — Handling SIGTERM to finish work and close resources before exit. *([Ch 22](docs/07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md))* - **Grafana** — Dashboard/visualization tool for metrics and other data sources. *([Ch 22](docs/07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md))* - **GSI** — Global Secondary Index: alternative access pattern with different keys. *([Ch 33](docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md))* - **GuardDuty** — Threat detection service (awareness). *([Ch 17](docs/04-aws/ch17-monitoring-security.md))* - **Guest OS** — The operating system running inside a VM, which believes it owns the hardware. *([Ch 36](docs/01-foundations/ch36-virtualization-internals.md))* - **Guest Physical Address (GPA)** — What the guest OS believes is physical memory. *([Ch 36](docs/01-foundations/ch36-virtualization-internals.md))* - **Guest Virtual Address (GVA)** — Address used by applications inside the VM. *([Ch 36](docs/01-foundations/ch36-virtualization-internals.md))*

title: Glossary
heading: H
text: - **Handler** — Task triggered by notify only when a change occurs. *([Ch 28](docs/06-iac-config/ch28-ansible.md))* - **Handler (Lambda)** — The exported function Lambda invokes, e.g. index.handler. *([Ch 15](docs/04-aws/ch15-lambda-serverless-messaging.md))* - **Hardware-assisted virtualization** — CPU extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) letting guest code run efficiently while the hypervisor retains control of privileged operations. *([Ch 36](docs/01-foundations/ch36-virtualization-internals.md))* - **Hardware passthrough** — Assigning a physical device (e.g. GPU) more directly to a VM for performance, at the cost of sharing, migration, management and isolation. *([Ch 36](docs/01-foundations/ch36-virtualization-internals.md))* - **HCL** — HashiCorp Configuration Language used for Terraform files. *([Ch 21](docs/06-iac-config/ch21-terraform.md))* - **HEAD** — Pointer to what is currently checked out (normally current branch -> current commit). *([Ch 5](docs/01-foundations/ch05-git-github.md))* - **HEALTHCHECK** — Dockerfile instruction defining how Docker tests application health. *([Ch 8](docs/02-containers/ch08-docker-production.md))* - **Health check (ALB)** — Periodic request (e.g. GET /health) deciding whether a target receives traffic. *([Ch 14](docs/04-aws/ch14-load-balancing-scaling.md))* - **Health live vs ready (capstone)** — /health/live process alive; /health/ready dependencies reachable. *([Ch 35](docs/08-production/ch35-devops-capstone.md))* - **Health status (ArgoCD)** — Healthy, Progressing, Degraded, Missing, Unknown (and Suspended). *([Ch 26](docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch26-gitops-argocd.md))* - **Helm** — Package manager, templating and release-management tool for Kubernetes applications. *([Ch 25](docs/05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md))* - **Helm dependency** — Another chart a chart declares as required. *([Ch 25](docs/05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md))* - **Helm dry run** — --dry-run: simulate an install/upgrade without applying. *([Ch 25](docs/05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md))* - **helm history** — Show revisions of a release. *([Ch 25](docs/05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md))* - **helm lint** — Check a chart for problems. *([Ch 25](docs/05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md))* - **helm rollback** — Revert a release to an earlier revision. *([Ch 25](docs/05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md))* - **helm template** — Render chart manifests locally without installing. *([Ch 25](docs/05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md))* - **helm upgrade --install** — Install a release if absent, otherwise upgrade it. *([Ch 25](docs/05-kubernetes/ch25-helm.md))* - **Hidden file** — File whose name begins with `.` (.env, .gitignore, .ssh);
