(Reference: AWS WAF Developer Guide) | | B7 | [4](docs/01-foundations/ch04-networking.md) (§37), [16](docs/04-aws/ch16-route53-cloudfront-waf.md) (§39) | Diagrams put EC2 in public subnets behind the ALB. | Simplified; recommended layout (Ch 12/14/23) is ALB public, app and DB private. | | B8 | [22](docs/07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md) (§14) | Mentions latency metric but sample defines only a Counter. | Percentiles need a histogram/summary. | | B9 | [19](docs/05-kubernetes/ch19-kubernetes-config-storage.md) | Lab Secret has key `API_KEY`; the Deployment references `DATABASE_URL`/`JWT_SECRET`. | Separate illustrations; create matching keys to run end to end. | | B10 | [7](docs/02-containers/ch07-docker-fundamentals.md) (§13) | Container lifecycle: Created/Running/Stopped/Removed. | Docker also has paused, restarting, exited, dead. |

title: README
heading: DevOps for SDEs — Knowledge Base
text: A complete, organised and searchable knowledge base for software engineers learning **Linux → Git → CI/CD → Docker → AWS → Kubernetes → Terraform → GitOps → observability/SRE → virtualization internals**, built from a long educational conversation (36 source responses). It is meant to be the primary study resource for online assessments (OAs), interviews, revision, hands-on practice and long-term reference. > **Honest status:** every source file with content is imported **line for line** (a source→output audit confirms it), and everything the editor added is clearly separated from the original text. Read [PROGRESS.md](PROGRESS.md) for what is verified, what is not, and what is still open before relying on any claim of completeness.

title: README
heading: How to study
text: 1. Start with the [study guide](docs/00-start-here/study-guide.md) (a 10-week plan and an interview-prep sequence). 2. Read each **chapter** once; use its **revision sheet** afterwards. 3. Do the [labs](exercises/labs.md); the source insists that reading without doing is not learning. 4. Before interviews: [master cheat sheet](revision/00-master-cheatsheet.md), [comparisons](revision/01-comparisons.md), [Q&A bank](revision/03-interview-qa.md), [troubleshooting playbooks](revision/04-troubleshooting-playbooks.md).

title: README
heading: Run the website locally
text: The site renders the repository's Markdown in your browser. It needs an HTTP server rooted at the **repository root** (browsers block `fetch` from `file://`): ```bash cd knowledge-base python -m http.server 8000 # open http://localhost:8000/website/ ``` No build step or `npm install` is needed: the two libraries it uses (`marked`, `highlight.js`) are vendored in `website/vendor/` with their licences. Features: sidebar navigation (by topic or by number), full-text search (`/` focuses the box), table of contents per page, previous/next, **Full notes ↔ Revision sheet** toggle, copy buttons on code blocks, light/dark theme, per-chapter completion tracking (stored in your browser only), responsive layout.

title: README
heading: Rebuild and verify
text: ```bash python -X utf8 tools/build.py # regenerate chapters, contents, glossary, indexes, extracted code python -X utf8 tools/audit.py # independent source→output audit → AUDIT_REPORT.md python -X utf8 tools/gen_coverage.py # SOURCE_COVERAGE.md python -X utf8 tools/gen_labs.py # exercises/labs.md python -m http.server 8765 & # then: python -X utf8 tools/test_website.py --crawl # headless-browser tests (needs selenium + Edge/Chrome) ``` Requires Python 3.10+ with `PyYAML` (audit only). Do **not** edit generated chapter files by hand: change `source-archive/`-derived content through `_work/trims.csv`, add editorial text in `supplements/` or `revision/`, then rebuild.

title: README
heading: Publish to GitHub (not done automatically)
text: Nothing has been committed or pushed. To publish yourself: ```bash cd knowledge-base git init # if not already a repository git add . git commit -m "Add DevOps for SDEs knowledge base" git branch -M main git remote add origin https://github.com/<you>/<repo>.git git push -u origin main ``` To host the website on **GitHub Pages**: repository *Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Deploy from a branch → `main` / `(root)`*. The site is then at `https://<you>.github.io/<repo>/website/` (it loads the Markdown through relative paths, so the repo root must be the Pages root). Add a `LICENSE` of your choice first — **no licence has been chosen**, and the source material's provenance/rights are yours to confirm before publishing.

title: Course design notes
heading: Course Design Notes
text: > Preserved verbatim from the conversational parts of the original source that were removed from the chapter files. > They explain how the course was scoped and why it is taught the way it is. Cross-references were renamed from > "Response N" to "Chapter N"; nothing else was changed.

title: Course design notes
heading: Opening reply before Chapter 2 (scope of 'fundamentals')
text: *Source: `source-archive/src-02.txt`, lines 1–6* Yes — **zero to hero for your goal**. The word "fundamentals" in the roadmap doesn't mean shallow coverage. It means the first response establishes the foundation. For example, in Linux, we won't stop at knowing `ls`, `cd`, and `chmod`. We'll progress from **basic Linux → processes → networking → services → SSH → logs → troubleshooting → automation → production usage**. Let's continue. ---

title: Course design notes
heading: Reply before Chapter 8 — where testing belongs in the roadmap
text: *Source: `source-archive/src-08.txt`, lines 1–118* Yes — **we are following the locked 24-response Cloud + DevOps roadmap**, and Chapter 8 is still Docker Deep Dive + Production. One important clarification about **testing** before we start: ##### Where does testing belong? Testing is primarily a **Software Engineering / Backend Engineering discipline**, not a DevOps-only topic. But DevOps heavily **automates and operationalizes testing** through CI/CD. Think of it like: ```text Software Engineering │ ├── Unit Testing ├── Integration Testing ├── API Testing ├── E2E Testing ├── Mocking ├── Test Design └── Test Strategy │ ↓ CI/CD │ ├── Run tests ├── Quality gates ├── Reports └── Block bad deployments ``` ##### Are all testing topics in this 24-response DevOps roadmap? **No — intentionally.** The 24-response roadmap is designed to make you **SWE + Cloud/DevOps interview-ready**, not to turn this particular roadmap into a complete QA/testing curriculum. We've already covered the **CI/CD side of testing** in Chapter 6: - Unit/integration/E2E distinction - Automated tests in CI - linting - TypeScript type checking - build validation - pipeline failures - quality gates - test → build → deploy flow But if your goal is: > **"I want to be able to handle essentially any testing question expected from an SWE/backend fresher."** then **yes, you need a dedicated Backend/SWE Testing section elsewhere in your overall preparation.** I'd want you to cover at least: ```text Testing Fundamentals ↓ Unit Testing ↓ Integration Testing ↓ API/Backend Testing ↓ Mocking & Stubbing ↓ Database Testing ↓ E2E Testing ↓ Test Doubles ↓ Assertions & Test Design ↓ Code Coverage ↓ Test Isolation ↓ Fixtures / Factories ↓ Testing Async Code ↓ Testing Authentication/Authorization ↓ Testing External APIs ↓ Performance / Load Testing ↓ CI Integration ↓ Debugging Failed Tests ``` For **your TypeScript backend path**, we'd use tools such as: ```text Vitest / Jest Supertest Node.js Express/NestJS PostgreSQL Redis Docker GitHub Actions ``` You don't need to become a dedicated QA engineer. The target is: > **"I can write, explain, debug, and integrate good tests for a production backend."** That's enough for the SWE/backend interviews you're targeting. So I recommend we **keep the 24-response Cloud + DevOps roadmap unchanged** rather than bloating it. Testing will be treated wherever it naturally belongs — especially CI/CD, production engineering, and your broader SWE/backend preparation. --- ---

title: Course design notes
heading: Reply before Chapter 11 — scope of the AWS block (Responses 9–17)
text: *Source: `source-archive/src-11.txt`, lines 1–51* Absolutely. **AWS is intentionally getting a large portion of this 24-response roadmap**, because for your SWE/backend target, AWS is one of the areas where breadth + practical understanding matters. We are **not trying to cover every AWS service**—there are far too many. We're covering the services and concepts that give you the strongest SWE/backend/cloud foundation. Our AWS coverage is: ```text Chapter 9 AWS Fundamentals + IAM ↓ Chapter 10 EC2 + Compute ↓ Chapter 11 S3 + Storage ← NOW ↓ Chapter 12 VPC + AWS Networking ↓ Chapter 13 RDS + Databases ↓ Chapter 14 Load Balancing + Scaling ↓ Chapter 15 Lambda + Serverless + Messaging ↓ Chapter 16 Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF ↓ Chapter 17 AWS Monitoring + Security ``` So **Chapters 9–17 are essentially our AWS block**. After that: ```text 18–20 → Kubernetes 21 → Terraform 22 → Observability + Reliability 23 → Production Architecture + Troubleshooting 24 → Complete Interview/OA Mastery ``` By the end, you'll have covered the AWS concepts most relevant to a backend SWE without wasting time learning obscure services. --- ---

title: Course design notes
heading: Reply before Chapter 15 — change of teaching style to hands-on
text: *Source: `source-archive/src-15.txt`, lines 1–8* Yes — that's a fair criticism. **So far we've been building the conceptual foundation, but from Chapter 15 onward we should shift much more heavily toward actually using the tools.** The roadmap is still correct, but the teaching style should now be: > **Concept → Why → Setup → Commands/code/config → Build it → Deploy it → Test it → Break it → Debug it → Interview questions** And we'll also go back and connect the AWS pieces you've already learned into an actual DevOps workflow rather than treating them as isolated services. ---

title: Course design notes
heading: Closing note of Chapter 15 — 'Build It / Set It Up' commitment for later chapters
text: *Source: `source-archive/src-15.txt`, lines 1809–1870*

title: Course design notes
heading: Roadmap Progress — 15/24
text: ```text 1. Cloud + DevOps Fundamentals ✅ 2. Linux ✅ 3. Bash + Automation ✅ 4. Networking ✅ 5. Git + GitHub ✅ 6. CI/CD + GitHub Actions ✅ 7. Docker Fundamentals ✅ 8. Docker Deep Dive + Production ✅ 9. AWS Fundamentals + IAM ✅ 10. EC2 + Compute ✅ 11. S3 + AWS Storage ✅ 12. VPC + AWS Networking ✅ 13. RDS + Databases on AWS ✅ 14. Load Balancing + Scaling ✅ 15. Lambda + Serverless + Messaging ✅ 16. Route 53 + CloudFront + CDN + WAF ⏭️ 17. AWS Monitoring + Security 18. Kubernetes Fundamentals 19. Kubernetes Configuration + Storage 20. Kubernetes Networking + Scaling 21. Terraform 22. Observability + Reliability 23. Production Architecture + Troubleshooting 24. Complete Cloud + DevOps Interview/OA Mastery ``` ##### One important adjustment going forward From **Chapter 16 onward**, I'll explicitly include a **"Build It / Set It Up" section** in every major technology response. We'll progressively build one realistic production system rather than learning each service independently: ```text GitHub ↓ GitHub Actions ↓ Docker ↓ AWS ↓ VPC ↓ ALB ↓ EC2 / Containers ↓ RDS ↓ S3 ↓ Lambda/SQS ↓ Monitoring ↓ Terraform ↓ Production deployment ``` So by Chapter 24, you won't just be able to **define DevOps technologies** — you'll be able to explain **how to set them up, connect them, deploy with them, and troubleshoot them**. ---

title: Course design notes
heading: Reply before Chapter 18 — scope of DevOps coverage and containers
text: *Source: `source-archive/src-18.txt`, lines 1–10* Yes. **For your goal — SWE/backend placements + OA + interviews + being able to actually use DevOps in projects — the 24-response roadmap is designed to cover the major DevOps areas you need.** And yes, **containers are absolutely covered**. We already did Docker deeply in Chapters 7–8, and Kubernetes now builds on top of that. One clarification: we're covering **SWE-level DevOps comprehensively**, not every niche topic needed to become a dedicated DevOps/SRE engineer. I don't want to waste your limited time on things like advanced Kubernetes internals or obscure Jenkins administration. With that clear, let's continue. --- ---

title: Roadmap
heading: The AWS block
text: The source states that Responses 9–17 form the AWS block (IAM → EC2 → S3 → VPC → RDS → load balancing → Lambda/SQS/SNS → Route 53/CloudFront/WAF → monitoring and security), after which Kubernetes (18–20), Terraform (21), observability (22), integration (23) and interview mastery (24) follow. Part II then deepens and broadens: Helm, GitOps/ArgoCD, Jenkins, Ansible, CRDs/Operators, service mesh, advanced EKS/Terraform/AWS/SRE, and a capstone specification.

title: Roadmap
heading: Depth tiers used throughout the source
text: Each chapter ends with what to know **deeply** (🔥), **reasonably/medium** (🟡) and at the **awareness** level (⚪/🟢). Chapter 24 gives the overall tiering; the per-chapter tiers are preserved at the end of each chapter and repeated in its revision sheet. The target the source repeatedly names is: *a backend/SWE engineer with strong Cloud + DevOps capability*, not a dedicated DevOps specialist.

title: Roadmap
heading: Teaching style (as stated in the source)
text: Concept → Why → Setup → Commands/code/config → Build it → Deploy it → Test it → Break it → Debug it → Interview questions. The change to this hands-on style was made at Chapter 15 — see [course design notes](course-design-notes.md).

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Labs and Exercises
text: Two parts: **(A)** the hands-on labs that exist *in the source chapters* (linked, not copied — the full text lives in the chapter), and **(B)** *editorial* labs added to give every chapter a practice task. Part B is not source material. > Labs touching AWS create billable resources. Use a sandbox account, set a budget alarm, and destroy resources afterwards (`terraform destroy`, delete clusters/NAT gateways/load balancers).

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 1 — [cloud devops fundamentals](../docs/01-foundations/ch01-cloud-devops-fundamentals.md)
text: - Draw the request path of a web app on a napkin: user → DNS → LB → app → DB. Mark which parts scale horizontally and which are stateful. - Compute allowed downtime per month for 99.9% and 99.99%; then compute the availability of two 99.9% services in series.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 3 — [bash automation](../docs/01-foundations/ch03-bash-automation.md)
text: - Write `backup.sh` with `set -euo pipefail`, a `trap` cleanup, argument validation and a log function; make it fail fast on an unset variable. - Write a cron entry that runs it daily at 02:00 and appends output to a log.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 4 — [networking](../docs/01-foundations/ch04-networking.md)
text: - With `dig`, `curl -v`, `ss -tulpn` and `traceroute`, trace a real HTTPS request and label DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP phases. - Compute the address count and range for 10.0.0.0/16 split into /24 subnets across 2 AZs.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 6 — [cicd github actions](../docs/03-cicd-gitops/ch06-cicd-github-actions.md)
text: - Create a GitHub Actions workflow: checkout → setup-node → `npm ci` → lint → test → build, with a matrix of two Node versions and dependency caching.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 15 — [lambda serverless messaging](../docs/04-aws/ch15-lambda-serverless-messaging.md)
text: - Create an SQS queue with a DLQ (maxReceiveCount 3) and a consumer that is idempotent; send a poison message and watch it land in the DLQ.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 17 — [monitoring security](../docs/04-aws/ch17-monitoring-security.md)
text: - Create a CloudWatch alarm on 5xx rate with an SNS notification; then find the corresponding API call in CloudTrail.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 22 — [observability reliability](../docs/07-observability-sre/ch22-observability-reliability.md)
text: - Instrument a small Node API with prom-client (RED metrics); scrape with Prometheus; chart p95 in Grafana; write an alert on error ratio.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 23 — [production architecture troubleshooting](../docs/08-production/ch23-production-architecture-troubleshooting.md)
text: - Take the production checklist and score your own project against it; list the five biggest gaps.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 24 — [interview oa mastery](../docs/09-interview/ch24-interview-oa-mastery.md)
text: - Time yourself answering the Chapter 24 scenario questions aloud in 2 minutes each, using the Prevent → Detect → Contain → Recover → Learn frame.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 28 — [ansible](../docs/06-iac-config/ch28-ansible.md)
text: - Write an inventory + playbook that installs nginx, templates a config and restarts via a handler; run it twice and confirm the second run reports `changed=0`.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 29 — [crds operators](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch29-crds-operators.md)
text: - Define a small CRD and create a custom resource; observe that nothing happens without a controller; then deploy a controller that sets `status`.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 30 — [service mesh istio](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch30-service-mesh-istio.md)
text: - Install Istio (demo profile), label a namespace, split 90/10 traffic with a VirtualService/DestinationRule, and enforce strict mTLS.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 31 — [advanced eks](../docs/05-kubernetes/ch31-advanced-eks.md)
text: - Create an EKS cluster with eksctl or Terraform, install the AWS Load Balancer Controller, and give a Pod S3 access with Pod Identity/IRSA.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 32 — [advanced terraform](../docs/06-iac-config/ch32-advanced-terraform.md)
text: - Create an S3 backend with locking, split a config into two modules, import one existing resource and use a `moved` block for a rename.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 33 — [advanced aws backend](../docs/04-aws/ch33-advanced-aws-backend.md)
text: - Build S3 → SQS → worker image-processing flow locally against LocalStack; add a DLQ and verify duplicate handling.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 34 — [advanced sre](../docs/07-observability-sre/ch34-advanced-sre.md)
text: - Define an SLO (99.9% availability, p95 < 300 ms), compute the error budget, and write the multi-window burn-rate alerts; then run a k6 test to find the knee of the latency curve.

title: Hands-on labs
heading: Chapter 35 — [devops capstone](../docs/08-production/ch35-devops-capstone.md)
text: - Follow `code-examples/capstone/` (editorial starter) and extend it with one failure-injection test.

title: Hands-on labs

title: Revision — 02-formulas-and-numbers
heading: Availability, SLOs and error budgets (Ch 1, 22, 34)
text: ```text Availability = Uptime / Total time = successful requests / total requests Allowed downtime = (1 − target) × period Error budget = 1 − SLO (budget in requests = (1 − SLO) × total requests) Burn rate = observed error rate / (1 − SLO) (added formula) ``` | Availability | Downtime / month (avg 730 h) | Downtime / 30 days (43,200 min) | |---|---:|---:| | 99% | 7 h 18 m | 7.2 h | | 99.9% | 43 m 49 s | 43.2 min | | 99.99% | 4 m 23 s | 4.32 min | | 99.999% | 26 s | 26 s | Worked: SLO 99.9%, 1,000,000 requests → budget 1,000 failures. Observing 1% errors against a 0.1% allowance = burn rate **10**. *(added)* Composite availability: serial `A₁ × A₂ × …` (0.999³ ≈ 99.7%); redundant `1 − (1 − A)ⁿ` (two 99% → 99.99%, if independent); `Availability ≈ MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)`. Latency example: 99 requests × 50 ms + 1 × 10 s → average 149.5 ms but p99 = 10 s.

title: Revision — 02-formulas-and-numbers
heading: Reliability mechanics
text: - **Exponential backoff:** 100 → 200 → 400 → 800 ms (+ jitter). *(added)* `delay = min(cap, base × 2^attempt) + random`. - **Circuit breaker states:** CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN → CLOSED/OPEN. - **Token bucket:** tokens refill at a fixed rate, requests consume tokens (bursts + sustained rate). - **RTO / RPO:** restore time / data-loss window (examples: RTO 1 h, RPO 5 min). - **MTTD / MTTR:** failure 10:00, alert 10:02 → MTTD 2 min; restored 10:15 → MTTR 15 min.

title: Revision — 02-formulas-and-numbers
heading: Kubernetes sizing units (Ch 19)
text: `250m` = 0.25 CPU core; `Mi` = mebibytes; requests drive scheduling and HPA percentages; exceeding CPU limit → throttled; exceeding memory limit → **OOMKilled** *(added)*.

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: Interview Q&A Bank
text: Consolidated from the interview sections of all 36 chapters, with concise answers. Many of the source's own question lists give pointers without answers; the answers here are taken from the chapter text, and any that go beyond it are marked *(added)*. Say them aloud. Chapter in brackets.

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: Fundamentals and Linux
text: 1. **Scalability vs elasticity?** Scalability = can handle growth by adding resources; elasticity = automatically adds *and removes* resources with demand. (1) 2. **HA vs fault tolerance?** HA = redundancy keeps the service accessible; fault tolerance = continues operating correctly despite component failure. (1) 3. **RTO vs RPO?** Time to restore service vs amount of data (in time) you can lose. (1, 34) 4. **Cloud vs DevOps?** Cloud = infrastructure and services; DevOps = how teams build, test, deploy and operate together. (1) 5. **What is Linux?** An OS kernel; distributions package it with utilities. (2) 6. **Process vs program?** Running instance vs file on disk. *(added)* (2) 7. **`chmod 755`?** Owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x. (2) 8. **App is "down", you SSH in — what first?** Don't restart; process → port → logs → `curl localhost` → config → CPU/mem/disk → firewall/SG → LB → DNS. (2) 9. **Disk full?** `df -h`, then `du -sh *` down the tree; check `/var/log`, Docker images, temp files. (2, 10) 10. **What does `set -euo pipefail` do?** Exit on error, error on unset vars, fail pipelines if any stage fails. (3, 24) 11. **Deployment script: command 3 of 6 fails but 4–6 run — fix?** `set -e` / explicit exit-code checks, fail fast, validate before destructive steps, rollback. (3) 12. **Pipe / `2>&1` / `$?`?** stdout→stdin of next command; send stderr to stdout's destination; last exit status. (3)

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: Networking
text: 13. **TCP vs UDP?** Reliable ordered connection-oriented vs connectionless low overhead; HTTP/3 runs on QUIC (UDP). (4) 14. **Trace `https://api.example.com/users`.** DNS → TCP handshake → TLS → HTTP request → CDN/WAF/LB → app → DB → response back. (4) 15. **Why would an app on `localhost:3000` be unreachable?** Bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0; port not published; firewall/SG. (4, 7) 16. **Public vs private subnet?** Route to an Internet Gateway vs none; private can still reach out via NAT. (4, 12) 17. **SG vs NACL?** Stateful/resource-level/allow vs stateless/subnet-level/allow+deny. (4, 12) 18. **A, AAAA, CNAME?** Name→IPv4, name→IPv6, name→name. (4, 16) 19. **What does a 502 mean?** Proxy/LB got an invalid response from upstream — check target health, port, SG, app logs. (4)

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: Git and CI/CD
text: 20. **Merge vs rebase? When avoid rebase?** Preserve history vs rewrite to linear; avoid on shared history. (5) 21. **Reset vs revert?** Rewrite/move history vs add undoing commit (safe for shared). (5) 22. **Committed a password and pushed?** Rotate/revoke first, remove from history, investigate use, add secret scanning, use secret management. (5) 23. **CI vs CD?** CI integrates and validates continuously; Delivery keeps release-ready with approval; Deployment auto-releases. (6) 24. **Why `npm ci`?** Reproducible install from the lockfile. (6) 25. **Rolling vs blue-green vs canary?** Gradual replace; two environments + switch; small % first. (6) 26. **Why immutable image tags?** Traceability and easy rollback; `latest` is mutable. (6, 8) 27. **CI passes, deploy succeeds, users get 500s?** Image/env/secrets/migrations/logs/health/dependencies/LB → rollback if needed. (6) 28. **Why Jenkins when Actions exists?** Mature extensible server with huge plugin ecosystem; existing infra; customised pipelines. (27) 29. **GitOps definition?** Git holds declarative desired state; a controller reconciles the cluster to it. (26) 30. **Dev manually changed a prod Deployment under GitOps?** Decide if intentional; change Git via review or revert the drift; with `selfHeal` ArgoCD reverts it. (26)

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: Docker
text: 31. **Image vs container? Container vs VM?** Immutable template vs running instance; shared kernel vs guest OS. (7) 32. **`RUN` vs `CMD` vs `ENTRYPOINT`; what does `EXPOSE` do?** Build time / default start command / always-run executable *(supplement)*; documents only. (7, 8) 33. **Why multi-stage builds? Why copy `package.json` first?** Smaller, safer runtime image; cache the dependency layer. (7, 8) 34. **Why not root, why not secrets in images?** Least privilege; secrets persist in layers/history. (8) 35. **Running vs healthy?** Process up vs able to serve (health checks). (8) 36. **Container exits immediately / can't reach the API?** `docker ps -a`, `logs`, port mapping, `0.0.0.0` binding, env vars, network. (7, 8)

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: AWS
text: 37. **Region vs AZ; why multi-AZ?** Geographic area vs isolated location; survive AZ failure. (9) 38. **User vs role; least privilege; how should a Node app access S3?** Role with temporary credentials, minimal permissions, never hard-coded keys. (9, 10) 39. **GitHub Actions → AWS securely?** OIDC federation to an IAM role, short-lived credentials. (9, 17) 40. **Debug `AccessDenied`.** `aws sts get-caller-identity`, then policies, explicit deny, resource ARN. (9) 41. **AMI vs instance; stop vs terminate; why not DB on EC2?** Template vs VM; restartable vs deleted; you'd own backups/HA/patching → RDS. (10) 42. **S3 vs EBS vs EFS?** Object / block / shared filesystem. (11) 43. **Upload a 1 GB file efficiently?** Presigned (multipart) URL straight to S3. (11) 44. **Design a VPC for a Node API + PostgreSQL.** ALB in public subnets, EC2/EKS in private, RDS in private DB subnets; IGW, NAT, SG chain, ≥2 AZs. (12) 45. **Multi-AZ vs read replica?** Failover vs read scaling. (13) 46. **Scaled 2→20 instances and PostgreSQL rejects connections?** Instances × pool size exceeded DB limit → tune pools, RDS Proxy, caching. (13) 47. **ALB vs ASG roles; what if an instance is unhealthy?** ALB routes; ASG sizes. Health check fails → ALB stops routing → ASG replaces → check passes → traffic. (14) 48. **Why stateless?** Any instance can serve any request → scaling/replacement easy. (14) 49. **Lambda vs EC2; SQS vs SNS?** Event functions vs servers; queue vs pub/sub. (15, 33) 50. **Visibility timeout, DLQ, idempotency?** Hides in-flight message; stores repeatedly failing messages; makes duplicate processing safe. (15) 51. **Route 53 vs CloudFront; WAF vs SG?** DNS vs CDN; HTTP-aware filtering vs network access. (16) 52. **CloudWatch vs CloudTrail?** Metrics/logs/alarms vs API audit. (17) 53. **Monitor an EC2 server?** CloudWatch + agent (memory/disk need the agent *(added)*) + logs + alarms. (17) 54. **Choose compute?** EC2 control, ECS simple AWS-native containers, EKS Kubernetes ecosystem, Lambda events. (33) 55. **RDS vs DynamoDB?** Relational/joins vs access-pattern key-value at scale; not "faster". (13, 33) 56. **SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge?** Queue / fan-out / bus + rules. (33) 57. **Design an image-processing backend.** Upload to S3 → S3 event → SQS → Lambda/ECS worker → S3 output → DB metadata. (33) 58. **Compensation / saga?** Undo completed steps (refund) when a later step fails. (33)

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: Kubernetes
text: 59. **Why Kubernetes; Docker vs Kubernetes?** Orchestration at scale (scheduling, scaling, self-healing, discovery, rollouts). (18) 60. **Pod vs container; why Services?** Pod wraps containers; Pod IPs are ephemeral. (18) 61. **Control-plane components?** API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd; kubelet on nodes. (18) 62. **What happens when a Pod dies?** Controller sees missing replica → creates one → scheduler places → readiness → Service routes. (19) 63. **Liveness vs readiness?** Restart vs traffic eligibility. (19, 20) 64. **Ingress vs Ingress Controller?** Rules vs implementation. (20) 65. **HPA vs node autoscaling; why does HPA need requests/Metrics Server?** Pods vs nodes; percentages are relative to requests, metrics must exist. (20) 66. **Pod Pending / CrashLoopBackOff / ImagePullBackOff / Service no endpoints?** Scheduling constraints / app crash logs / image or auth / selector mismatch. (20, 23) 67. **Secrets "encrypted"?** Only base64 by default; enable encryption at rest, restrict RBAC. (19) 68. **CRD vs operator; spec vs status; finalizer?** Type vs controller; desired vs observed; cleanup before deletion. (29) 69. **What is a service mesh; when not to use?** Sidecar-based service-to-service layer; avoid for small apps (overhead). (30) 70. **Why can EKS Pods run out of IPs?** VPC CNI uses subnet IPs/ENIs; maxPods = ENIs × (IPs per ENI − 1) + 2 *(added)*. (31) 71. **IRSA/Pod Identity; IAM vs RBAC?** Per-workload AWS credentials; AWS vs Kubernetes API authorization. (31) 72. **Helm chart vs release; Helm vs Operator?** Package vs installed instance; install vs continuous management. (25, 29)

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: IaC and configuration
text: 73. **Why Terraform; state; remote state; locking?** Reproducible infra as code; maps config↔reality; shared; prevents concurrent corruption. (21, 32) 74. **Drift?** Real infra differs from config — `plan` shows it. (21) 75. **Someone changed RDS manually?** Intentional? update code and plan; accidental? decide whether to restore. (32) 76. **Terraform wants to destroy prod RDS?** STOP, read the plan (address change, immutable field, refactor), use `moved`/fix. (32) 77. **Why not Terraform and ArgoCD on the same resource?** Ownership conflict. (32) 78. **Terraform vs Ansible; why Ansible is agentless; idempotency; why modules over `shell`?** Provision vs configure; SSH + modules; same end state on re-run; modules know desired state. (28)

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: Observability and SRE
text: 79. **Logs/metrics/traces; RED; percentiles?** What happened / how much / where time went; rate-errors-duration; averages hide tails. (22) 80. **SLI/SLO/SLA/error budget/burn rate?** Measurement / target / contract / allowed failure / consumption speed. (22, 34) 81. **Retries, backoff, jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead, rate limiting, idempotency?** Recover transients; avoid hammering; avoid sync retries; fail fast; isolate; protect; safe repeats. (22, 34) 82. **How would you make your backend reliable?** Prevent → Detect → Contain → Recover → Learn. (34) 83. **API returns 30% 500s?** Confirm impact, metrics, recent deploy, logs, traces, dependencies, DB, mitigate/rollback, verify, RCA, postmortem. (34) 84. **Traffic 10×?** Find the bottleneck; autoscale, CDN/cache, rate limit, queue, shed load, protect DB. (14, 34) 85. **Why load test / chaos test?** Find capacity and bottlenecks / verify failure handling. (34) 86. **Multi-AZ vs multi-region; DR strategies?** AZ vs region failure; backup-restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active. (34) 87. **Postmortem?** Blameless review: what, impact, cause, why safeguards missed it, fixes. (34)

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: Virtualization internals
text: 91. **What is a hypervisor; Type 1 vs Type 2?** Layer that creates/manages VMs and controls physical resources; bare-metal (Hardware→Hypervisor→VMs) vs hosted (Hardware→Host OS→Hypervisor→VMs). (36) 92. **What is a VM exit and why does it matter?** Guest→hypervisor transition for operations needing hypervisor handling; costs time, so modern designs minimise exits. (36) 93. **How does VM memory translation work?** GVA→GPA (guest page tables)→HPA (EPT/NPT); TLB caches translations. (36) 94. **Ballooning, overcommitment, paravirtualization, SR-IOV?** Reclaim memory via guest driver; allocate more than physical hoping peaks don't coincide; guest-aware drivers like VirtIO; one PCIe device exposing virtual functions to VMs. (36) 95. **VM vs container internals; why do containers start faster?** Guest kernel on virtual hardware vs shared host kernel isolated with namespaces + cgroups; starting a process vs booting a kernel. (7, 36) 96. **Snapshot vs live migration?** State capture for restore/clone vs moving a running VM between hosts (pre-copy). (36)

title: Revision — 03-interview-qa
heading: Whole-system
text: 88. **Deploy a production Node.js app.** Multi-stage Docker → ECR immutable tags → Kubernetes (EKS if justified) → stateless Pods behind Service + LB → Terraform → RDS/S3/Redis → private DB → CI/CD with scans → probes/limits/HPA → logs/metrics/traces + actionable alerts → outside-in troubleshooting. (23) 89. **`git push` to production — walk through it.** Git → GitHub → Actions (test/build/scan) → Docker → ECR → GitOps repo → ArgoCD → rolling update. (24, 26) 90. **Production 503 — debug layer by layer.** DNS/TLS → WAF/edge → LB → Ingress/Service → endpoints → Pod readiness → app → dependencies. (23, 31) --- [← Revision index](README.md)

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: Troubleshooting Playbooks
text: The source's consistent method: **don't restart blindly; go layer by layer, outside in, and use evidence** (metrics → logs → traces). Each playbook below consolidates the decision paths taught across chapters.

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: 0. Universal method
text: ```text Confirm impact → check metrics → recent changes/deployments → logs → traces → identify the failing layer/dependency → mitigate (rollback/scale/fail over) → verify recovery → root cause → postmortem ```

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: 1. "App on a server is unreachable" (Ch 2, 4, 10, 12)
text: 1. Is the process running? `ps aux | grep node` / `docker ps` 2. Listening on the right port and address? `ss -tulpn | grep 3000` — `127.0.0.1` vs `0.0.0.0` 3. Works locally? `curl http://localhost:3000/health` 4. Docker: port published (`-p`)? logs (`docker logs`)? 5. Linux firewall → Security Group → NACL → route table → IGW/NAT → public IP 6. Load balancer: target health, listener, SG chain 7. DNS: `dig`, TTL/propagation 8. WAF blocking? TLS certificate?

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: 2. HTTP error codes (Ch 4, 23, 31)
text: | Code | First suspects | |---|---| | 4xx | client/request, auth (401/403), 404 routing, 429 rate limit | | 500 | application error → logs/traces; recent deploy; dependency (DB/Redis) | | 502 | LB/proxy got invalid upstream response → target health, target port, SG, app logs | | 503 | no healthy targets / Pods not Ready / Service has no endpoints / overload / readiness failing | | 504 | upstream timeout → slow dependency (traces), timeouts mis-set |

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: 3. AWS connectivity (Ch 12)
text: - **EC2 → RDS fails:** endpoint, port 5432, route tables, RDS SG allows source SG, NACL, DB running, credentials, pool. - **Internet → EC2 fails:** running? listening on `0.0.0.0`? port? SG? route? IGW? public IP? NACL? - **Private EC2 cannot reach the Internet:** route to NAT? NAT in a public subnet with IGW route? SG/NACL/DNS? - **EC2 reaches Internet but Internet can't reach it:** public IP + route + IGW + SG + NACL + app listening (this is the intended behavior for private subnets). - **`AccessDenied`:** `aws sts get-caller-identity` (wrong account/role?) → policy action/resource ARN → explicit deny → bucket policy → KMS permissions *(added)*.

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: 4. Performance (Ch 10, 14, 34)
text: | Symptom | Check | |---|---| | CPU 100% | `top`; loop? traffic spike? inefficient code — diagnose before resizing | | Memory | `free -h`; leak, too many processes, undersized | | Disk full | `df -h`; logs, Docker images, temp files, data | | Slow API, low API CPU, high DB CPU | DB bottleneck — scaling API won't help; queries, indexes, locks, pool | | p95 up, CPU/mem normal | traces: slow dependency (Redis, DB, external API) | | DB "too many connections" | instances × pool; connection leak; slow queries; RDS Proxy | | Queue growing | producer vs consumer rate, queue age, failing consumers → scale consumers, DLQ poison messages |

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: 5. Kubernetes (Ch 18–20, 23, 31)
text: ```text kubectl get pods → describe pod (Events) → logs [--previous] → exec → env/config/network/resources ``` | Status | Causes | |---|---| | **Pending** | insufficient CPU/memory, node selector, taints/tolerations, affinity, no nodes, **IP exhaustion (EKS)**, PVC unbound | | **ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull** | wrong image/tag, registry auth/permissions, network | | **CrashLoopBackOff** | app crash, missing env var/Secret, bad config, DB unavailable, wrong command, OOM | | **Running but not Ready** | readiness probe path/port wrong, dependency down, slow startup | | **Service has no traffic** | `kubectl get endpointslices` empty → selector ≠ Pod labels; port/targetPort mismatch | | **HPA not scaling** | Metrics Server missing, no resource requests, wrong target, no load, `maxReplicas` reached | | **PVC Pending** | no provisioner, wrong StorageClass, capacity, access-mode mismatch | | **ConfigMap change ignored** | env vars don't update → `kubectl rollout restart` | | **Secret not found** | wrong namespace (namespace-scoped) | | **App can't call AWS** | ServiceAccount → Pod Identity/IRSA → role → policy; network/VPC endpoint | | **CRD resource does nothing** | operator not running / RBAC denied / CRD missing | | **Pod sidecar missing (Istio)** | namespace labelled after Pod creation → rollout restart |

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: 6. Bad deployment (Ch 6, 23, 34)
text: Stop rollout → `kubectl rollout status` → compare v1/v2 logs, config, secrets, migrations → `kubectl rollout undo` (or Helm rollback / Git revert for GitOps) → verify error rate/latency → investigate. **Rollback is not always safe** (applied DB migrations, security fixes) → roll forward; prefer expand-and-contract migrations.

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: 7. Pipelines and IaC (Ch 6, 21, 27, 32)
text: - **CI fails:** which stage? exit codes → lint/typecheck/test/build → credentials/registry. - **Jenkins:** agent offline (network, process, disk, credentials), disk full (workspace, Docker images, artifacts, logs), push failed (ECR reachable? credentials? repo? tag?). - **Terraform plan shows destroy:** stop; address change? immutable field? module refactor? → `moved` block / fix config. **Drift:** was the manual change intentional? **State lock stuck:** confirm nobody is applying, then `force-unlock` *(added)*. - **ArgoCD OutOfSync:** repo, branch, path, rendered Helm/manifests, values, permissions, cluster access, resource conflict. - **Ansible FAILED:** SSH (host/user/key/SG), `become`/sudo, wrong module/OS/package, `-vvv`; non-idempotent task if it keeps changing.

title: Revision — 04-troubleshooting-playbooks
heading: 8. Incidents (Ch 34)
text: Detect → acknowledge → triage (SEV) → mitigate → recover → communicate → postmortem. **Mitigation before root cause.** Dependency questions: can it fail? what happens? retry? fallback? cache? queue? fail fast? --- [← Revision index](README.md)

title: Revision — 05-traps-and-misconceptions
heading: Traps and Misconceptions
text: The "X ≠ Y" distinctions and common wrong answers flagged across the chapters (Chapter 24 lists the OA/MCQ set). *(added)* = editorial.

title: Revision — 05-traps-and-misconceptions
heading: High-value "not the same" list (Ch 24)
text: Image ≠ Container · Pod ≠ Container · Multi-AZ ≠ Read replica · Private subnet ≠ no Internet access · Authentication ≠ Authorization · S3 ≠ EBS · Horizontal ≠ Vertical scaling · Continuous Delivery ≠ Continuous Deployment · Logs ≠ Metrics ≠ Traces · Terraform state ≠ configuration · **Running ≠ Ready** · HPA ≠ node autoscaling · Base64 ≠ encryption (Ch 19) · Public IP ≠ permission to connect (Ch 10) · Managed service ≠ zero responsibility (Ch 13) · Availability ≠ Reliability (Ch 1).

title: Revision — 05-traps-and-misconceptions
heading: Wrong-but-tempting statements
text: | Wrong | Better | |---|---| | "A branch is a copy of the project." | A branch is a movable pointer to a commit (5) | | "Deleting the commit fixes the leaked password." | Rotate/revoke first; deleted history may have been copied (5) | | "`.gitignore` removes a file already committed." | It only affects untracked files (5) | | "TCP is faster than UDP." | Different trade-offs; oversimplification (24) | | "`EXPOSE` publishes the port." | Only documents; use `-p` (7) | | "Smaller image (Alpine) is always better." | musl libc can break native deps; slim is a safe default (8) | | "A container is a tiny VM." | Isolated process sharing the host kernel (7) | | "`depends_on` waits until the DB is ready." | Start order only; need health checks + retry logic (8) | | "Scaling the API scales the system." | The database/connection limit is often the bottleneck (13, 14, 22, 35) | | "Auto Scaling means infinite scaling." | Bounded by max capacity and other bottlenecks (14) | | "Make the S3 bucket public for simplicity." | Keep private; presigned URLs (11) | | "Queues deliver exactly once." | Assume duplicates → idempotency (15, 33) | | "NAT lets the Internet reach private EC2." | NAT is outbound-only (12) | | "Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted." | Base64 unless encryption at rest is enabled (19) | | "Kubernetes requires Docker Engine." | It needs a CRI runtime such as containerd (18) | | "Ingress routes traffic by itself." | An Ingress Controller implements it (20) | | "HPA creates machines." | HPA creates Pods; node autoscaling adds nodes (20) | | "Pod = container." | Pod is the unit that may contain several (18) | | "Namespaces isolate network traffic." | Not by default — NetworkPolicy *(added)* (18, 20) | | "A CRD makes Kubernetes do something." | Only a controller/operator implements behaviour (29) | | "Helm manages secrets." | It is not a secret-management solution (25) | | "GitOps replaces CI/CD." | It is an approach to CD; CI still builds (26) | | "`automated` sync reverts manual drift." | Only with `selfHeal: true` (verified) (26) | | "Service mesh is needed with Kubernetes." | Often unnecessary; overhead (30) | | "Retries make systems reliable." | Unbounded retries cause retry storms (22, 34) | | "NoSQL = no transactions / faster." | DynamoDB has transactions; choose by access pattern (33) | | "Terraform `sensitive` secures the value." | Hides it in output; still in state (21, 32) | | "`terraform state rm` deletes the resource." | Only stops tracking (32) | | "Average latency is enough." | Use percentiles; tail latency matters (22, 34) | | "100% reliability is the goal." | SLOs and error budgets balance reliability with change (34) | | "Untested backups are fine." | They are assumptions until a restore is tested (34) | | "Rollback is always right." | Applied migrations / security fixes may require roll-forward (23, 34) | | "Alert on every metric." | Alert on actionable, user-impacting conditions (22, 34) | | "`ps aux | grep node | wc -l` counts node processes." | Also counts the grep itself *(added)* (3) | | "`kubectl rollout undo` reverts the whole release." | Only the Deployment template; not DB/config/infra *(added)* (23) |

title: Revision — 05-traps-and-misconceptions
heading: Security reflexes
text: - Never commit or bake credentials (Git, Docker image, Dockerfile `ENV`, Terraform files, tfvars, Helm `values.yaml`, Jenkinsfile). - Never log secrets, tokens, DB URLs. - Roles + temporary credentials over long-lived keys; OIDC for CI. - Least privilege everywhere (IAM, SGs, RBAC, Pod identity, CI roles); private subnets for DB/app; only expose what must be exposed. - State files and CI servers are crown jewels — protect them. --- [← Revision index](README.md)
